### [1] [PanDent: Toward Comprehensive Tooth-Level Structure-Language Consistency in Dental Radiology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27378)
*Xiaohan Li,Xinyu Liu,Chang Liu,Sum Wing Au Yeung,Jun Liu,Yixuan Yuan,Hui Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PanDent is a large-scale, clinically grounded benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in dental panoramic radiography (OPG), comprising 9,524 expert-validated OPGs with fine-grained tooth-level annotations and clinically consistent radiology reports. Experiments show current MLLMs produce fluent but clinically inconsistent reports, while fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves visual localization, diagnostic accuracy, and structure-language consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate evaluation of MLLMs in dental panoramic radiography is limited by the lack of fine-grained, clinically reliable benchmarks that reflect expert interpretation. Existing benchmarks fail to assess whether MLLMs generate reports that are clinically consistent with expert-level tooth-level findings.

Method: The authors construct PanDent, a benchmark of 9,524 high-quality OPGs with expert-validated tooth-level structured annotations from experienced dentists and additional validation by an oral and maxillofacial radiologist. Clinically consistent radiology reports are generated from expert-validated findings via clinician-defined reporting logic, establishing explicit correspondence between structured clinical evidence and free-text descriptions. Diverse MLLMs are evaluated, including SOTA proprietary models, general-domain open-source models, and medical-specific models, followed by fine-tuning on PanDent.

Result: Current MLLMs can generate fluent radiology reports but fail to produce clinically consistent descriptions, with substantial errors in fine-grained localization and tooth-level diagnosis. Fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves structure-language consistency, visual localization accuracy, and diagnostic correctness, bringing model outputs closer to expert dental interpretation.

Conclusion: PanDent serves as a rigorous benchmark for evaluating tooth-level clinical reasoning in MLLMs and a valuable resource for clinically grounded dental AI, demonstrating that fine-grained expert-validated benchmarks are essential for advancing clinically reliable multimodal dental intelligence.

Abstract: Accurate evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in dental panoramic radiography (orthopantomogram, OPG) is limited by the lack of fine-grained, clinically reliable benchmarks that reflect expert interpretation. This work introduces PanDent, a large-scale, clinically grounded OPG benchmark built upon fine-grained, expert-validated tooth-level annotations. The dataset comprises 9,524 high-quality OPGs, each associated with comprehensive structured annotations produced by experienced dentists and further validated by an oral and maxillofacial radiologist, providing clinically reliable supervision for tooth-level diagnosis and reasoning. Clinically consistent radiology reports are constructed from expert-validated findings using clinician-defined reporting logic, establishing explicit correspondence between structured clinical evidence and free-text descriptions. This design enables evaluation of whether MLLMs generate reports that are not only linguistically coherent but also clinically consistent with expert-validated tooth-level findings. Experiments are conducted on diverse MLLMs, including state-of-the-art (SOTA) proprietary models, general-domain open-source models, and medical-specific models. Results show that current MLLMs can generate fluent reports, yet fail to produce clinically consistent descriptions, exhibiting substantial errors in fine-grained localization and tooth-level diagnosis. Fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves structure-language consistency, substantially enhancing visual localization accuracy and diagnostic correctness, and bringing model outputs closer to expert dental interpretation. These results establish PanDent as a rigorous benchmark for evaluating tooth-level clinical reasoning in MLLMs and a valuable resource for clinically grounded dental AI.

</details>


### [2] [Theia: Large-Scale Multimodal Captioning and Automated Validation of the Incidents1M Dataset for Data-Free Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28269)
*Simone Giano,Lorenzo Severini,Alessandro Galdelli,Adriano Mancini*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a methodology to construct and automatically validate a large-scale multimodal disaster-response dataset by generating text descriptions for 100,000 images from the vision-only Incidents1M dataset using Qwen3.5 models (4B dense and 35B MoE). A novel image-blind LLM-as-a-Judge validation pipeline using Qwen3.5-9B simulates the student model's modality gap in Data-Free Knowledge Distillation, achieving 78.65/100 semantic agreement and revealing conservative captioning behavior with high precision (77.6%) and low recall (46.0%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying VLMs in critical domains like disaster management requires high-quality multimodal datasets for Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (DFKD), yet existing datasets either lack descriptive text entirely (Incidents1M) or suffer from severe text-image semantic misalignment (CrisisMMD). There is a need for a scalable method to generate and validate large-scale multimodal data suitable for cross-modal knowledge transfer.

Method: The authors recover 100,000 images from the vision-only Incidents1M dataset and generate high-fidelity captions using two Qwen3.5 architectures (4B dense and 35B Mixture-of-Experts). They introduce an image-blind LLM-as-a-Judge validation pipeline using Qwen3.5-9B that intentionally obscures the original image from the evaluator to simulate the student model's modality gap during data-free distillation. The validation evaluates semantic agreement across 173,179 label pairs and measures precision/recall of the captioning.

Result: The evaluation shows high semantic agreement (78.65/100) between the two captioning architectures across 173,179 label pairs. The automated evaluation reveals conservative captioning behavior characterized by high Precision (77.6%) and low Recall (46.0%), which minimizes false positive noise while exposing underlying human annotation inconsistencies in the original ground truth.

Conclusion: The work provides a scalable, LLM-validated multimodal dataset and a reproducible framework to advance cross-modal knowledge distillation, addressing the gap in reliable multimodal datasets for disaster management applications.

Abstract: The deployment of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in critical domains like disaster management requires high-quality multimodal datasets, especially for transferring knowledge via Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (DFKD). However, existing datasets in this domain either entirely lack descriptive text, such as Incidents1M, or suffer from severe text-image semantic misalignment, such as CrisisMMD. In this work, we present a novel methodology to construct and automatically validate a large-scale multimodal dataset for disaster response. Starting from the vision-only Incidents1M, we successfully recovered 100,000 images and generated high-fidelity textual descriptions using two distinct Qwen3.5 architectures: a 4B dense model and a 35B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model. To ensure the generated captions provide reliable semantic anchoring for DFKD, we introduce an image-blind LLM-as-a-Judge validation pipeline leveraging Qwen3.5-9B. By intentionally obscuring the original image from the judge, this evaluator accurately simulates the modality gap of the student model during data-free distillation. Our evaluation across 173,179 label pairs demonstrates a high semantic agreement (78.65/100) between the two architectures. Furthermore, the automated evaluation reveals a conservative captioning behaviour, characterized by a high Precision (77.6%) and low Recall (46.0%). This minimizes the false positive noise, while simultaneously exposing underlying human annotation inconsistencies in the original ground truth. This work provides a scalable, LLM-validated multimodal dataset and a reproducible framework to advance cross-modal knowledge distillation.

</details>


### [3] [Theatre Chapbooks At Scale: A Statistical Comparative Analysis of Typography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27266)
*Diego Belzarena,Seginus Mowlavi,Paula Casariego Castiñeira,Alejandra Ulla Lorenzo,Gregory Randall,Jean-Michel Morel*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A statistical method quantifies typeface similarity between historical printed books using character prototypes derived from automatic image extraction and clustering, with an a contrario framework for significance testing. Applied to 17th-century Spanish theatre chapbooks, it enabled new printer attributions and revisions validated by human experts, demonstrating potential for large-scale digital bibliography.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Philological analysis of printed historical books traditionally relies on systematic visual inspection by human experts, which is infeasible at large scale. There is a need for an automated, quantitative tool to compare typefaces across books to accelerate and scale printer attribution and philological analysis.

Method: The method automatically extracts character images from books, clusters and aligns them to derive character prototypes, and defines a typeface distance between any two books. An a contrario statistical framework is developed to interpret the significance of the computed typeface distances. The method supports comparison of both Roman and Italic typefaces extracted from different books.

Result: Applied to 17th-century Spanish printed theatre chapbooks at a scale exceeding human visual inspection capacity. The method was validated by human experts and led to discovery of new printer attributions and revision of former attributions.

Conclusion: The success strongly suggests the method has potential to enable digital bibliography on a larger scale than previously possible, offering a scalable tool for philological analysis of printed historical documents.

Abstract: We propose a statistical methodology that quantifies the similarity of typefaces between printed historical books. This provides a tool that accelerates philological analysis. Using character prototypes derived from clustering and aligning automatically extracted character images, the method defines a typeface distance between any two books. To produce actionable outputs, we develop an a contrario statistical framework to interpret the significance of the computed typeface distances. We apply the method to the philological study of 17 th -century Spanish printed theatre chapbooks in a quantity that exceeds the capabilities of systematic visual inspection by human experts. Our method enables the automatic comparison of Roman and Italic types extracted from different books. After validation by human experts, our method has led to new printer attributions being discovered, and former printer attributions being revised. This success strongly suggests that our method has the potential to enable digital bibliography on a larger scale than was previously possible.

</details>


### [4] [OVEarth-Bench: Evaluating Category Breadth and Query Diversity for Open-Vocabulary Earth Observation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27278)
*Kaiyu Li,Zepeng Xin,Zixuan Jiang,Jing Fu,Lanxuan Xue,Lingyu Zhang,Xiangyong Cao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces OVEarth-Bench, a comprehensive open-vocabulary Earth observation benchmark extending existing evaluations through broader hierarchical category coverage (with positive/negative expressions) and diverse query types (vocabulary, referring, reasoning), supporting mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol. Evaluation of general and EO-specific methods reveals limited overall performance, with MLLM-based methods performing best and EO-specific methods underperforming general models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing open-vocabulary EO benchmarks suffer from narrow category vocabularies and limited query forms, failing to reflect the complexity of real-world geospatial language understanding tasks.

Method: OVEarth-Bench extends prior evaluation along two axes: (1) category breadth via broad hierarchical category coverage including positive and negative expressions, and (2) query diversity via vocabulary, referring, and reasoning queries. The benchmark supports both mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol, and evaluates a broad set of general and EO-specific methods.

Result: Three key findings: (1) current method performance remains limited, while broader category coverage produces more stable model rankings; (2) MLLM-based methods achieve the strongest overall performance; (3) EO-specific methods generally underperform general models and rarely match the strongest methods.

Conclusion: The findings offer guidance for future open-vocabulary EO method design and underscore the importance of developing more realistic, diverse, high-quality, and large-scale benchmarks for reliable evaluation.

Abstract: Open-vocabulary Earth observation (EO) aims to localize geospatial concepts specified in natural language rather than a fixed label set. Existing benchmarks, however, usually cover narrow category vocabularies or limited query forms. To fill this gap, we introduce OVEarth-Bench, which extends existing evaluation in two directions: category breadth, through broad hierarchical category coverage with positive and negative expressions, and query diversity, through vocabulary, referring, and reasoning queries. The benchmark supports mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol. We evaluate a broad set of general and EO-specific methods. The evaluation reveals that: (1) the performance of current methods remains limited, while broader category coverage yields more stable model rankings; (2) MLLM-based methods achieve the strongest overall performance; and (3) EO-specific methods generally underperform general models and rarely match the strongest methods. These findings provide guidance for future open-vocabulary EO method design and highlight the importance of developing more realistic, diverse, high-quality, and large-scale benchmarks for reliable evaluation. Our data and evaluation package are released at https://earth-insights.github.io/OVEarth-bench.

</details>


### [5] [MeshFM: 2D Features Are All You Need for 3D Shape Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27592)
*Jinfan Zhou,Richard Liu,Itai Lang,Rana Hanocka*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MeshFM is an efficient feedforward framework that distills 2D features from visual foundation models into 3D features. It uses a two-stage training strategy (optimizing a 3D feature field from 2D supervision, then regressing it with a feedforward network) requiring no 3D annotations. Learned features generalize to downstream tasks like part segmentation, dense correspondence, and mesh deformation, performing on par with 3D-supervised methods while being robust to extreme input rotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To obtain rich 3D features without expensive 3D annotations or per-instance optimization at inference time, by leveraging the powerful semantic information already present in 2D visual foundation models.

Method: Two-stage training: (1) optimize a 3D feature field using only 2D feature supervision from visual foundation models; (2) train a feedforward network to regress this feature field in a single forward pass. No 3D annotation is needed, and the model is trained to be robust to extreme rotations.

Result: Experiments show MeshFM, trained solely with 2D supervision, performs on par with methods explicitly trained with 3D supervision across downstream tasks including part segmentation, dense correspondence, and mesh deformation, even without task-specific fine-tuning, while also being robust to extreme input rotations.

Conclusion: MeshFM demonstrates that high-quality 3D features can be efficiently and effectively learned by distilling 2D foundation feature knowledge into a feedforward 3D network, achieving competitive performance with 3D-supervised methods without requiring 3D annotations or inference-time optimization.

Abstract: We present MeshFM, an efficient feedforward framework for extracting rich features from 3D inputs. Our method distills 2D features from visual foundation models into 3D. We train a feedforward network to directly predict 3D features without requiring optimization during inference. The approach utilizes a two-stage training strategy. First, we optimize a feature field in 3D using only 2D feature supervision. Second, we train a network to regress this feature field. The entire procedure requires no 3D annotation, instead relying on the powerful information in 2D foundation models. We demonstrate that our learned features can be immediately applied to downstream tasks, including part segmentation, dense correspondence, and mesh deformation. Extensive experiments show that MeshFM, trained solely with 2D supervision, performs on par with methods trained explicitly with 3D supervision, even without task-specific fine-tuning. Moreover, our model is trained to be robust to extreme rotations of the input objects. Project page: https://threedle.github.io/MeshFM/

</details>


### [6] [VETO: Towards Protecting Images From Frontier AI Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27292)
*Jonas Grebe,Hossein Shakibania,Tobias Braun,Marcus Rohrbach,Anna Rohrbach*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VETO is a subtle anti-edit cloak that disrupts the joint-attention mechanism through which modern image-editing models like FLUX.2 read reference images, along with VetoBench, a benchmark evaluating defenses on both localized edits and broader contextual recontextualizations. VETO outperforms existing defenses across two editing models and three benchmarks while offering a stronger protection-fidelity trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern image-editing models have expanded from localized modifications to full recontextualization of objects and identities, broadening the space of potential misuse. Existing anti-edit defenses target the semantic bottleneck of legacy diffusion pipelines, but newer editors distill reference information through joint-attention blocks, circumventing these protections.

Method: VETO introduces a subtle anti-edit cloak that disrupts the inner joint-attention mechanism through which modern editors read the source image. Additionally, VetoBench is introduced to evaluate defenses on both conventional localized edits and broader contextual shifts (recontextualizations).

Result: Across two contemporary editing models and three benchmarks, VETO consistently outperforms existing defenses while providing a stronger protection-fidelity trade-off.

Conclusion: Targeting the joint-attention mechanism (rather than the semantic bottleneck) is the effective strategy for defending against modern image-editing models, and broader benchmarks that include recontextualization scenarios are needed for fair evaluation of anti-edit defenses.

Abstract: The rise of powerful, accessible image-editing models such as FLUX.2 has brought high-fidelity editing within broad reach. Their capabilities now extend beyond localized modifications to extracting and recontextualizing objects and identities in entirely new scenes. By allowing prompt and generation tokens to attend directly to reference-image tokens, modern models blur the boundary between conventional editing and text-to-image synthesis. This expanded generative freedom also broadens the space of potential misuse, as harmful transformations are no longer confined to a predictable set of localized edits. Existing anti-edit defenses are designed to disrupt the semantic bottleneck of the reference-image encoding in legacy diffusion pipelines. However, newer editors distill reference information through joint-attention blocks, thereby often circumventing these protections. We therefore introduce VETO, a subtle anti-edit cloak that disrupts this inner mechanism through which modern models read the source image. Additionally, as existing editing benchmarks leave comprehensive recontextualizations largely untested, we introduce VetoBench, which evaluates defenses not only on conventional localized edits but also on broader contextual shifts. Across two contemporary editing models and three benchmarks, VETO consistently outperforms existing defenses while providing a stronger protection-fidelity trade-off.

</details>


### [7] [S-Avatar: Diffusion-Guided Gaussian Head Avatars from a Single Image](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28164)
*Hail Song,Seokhwan Yang,Jiwon Yang,Woojin Cho,Woontack Woo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: S-Avatar generates photorealistic 3D head avatars from a single image using a three-stage pipeline: diffusion-guided 3D Gaussian Splatting generation, FLAME parametric model alignment, and binding-template-based deformation for real-time animation. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in novel-view and expression generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-image head avatar reconstruction is crucial for lifelike VR applications, but existing approaches struggle to preserve 3D consistency under unseen viewpoints.

Method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) synthesize high-resolution 3DGS directly from a single image using a diffusion-based Gaussian splat generation module; (2) align the parametric head model FLAME with the generated 3DGS by optimizing its parameters and spatial transformations; (3) construct a binding template encoding spatial relationships between initial splats and FLAME to enable real-time dynamic avatar rendering via 3DGS deformation.

Result: Evaluations on public datasets demonstrate S-Avatar outperforms state-of-the-art methods in novel-view and expression generation, achieving superior realism and consistency.

Conclusion: The approach represents a significant advance in accessible avatar creation, applicable to a wide range of VR/AR applications.

Abstract: We propose S-Avatar, a novel method for generating photorealistic 3D head avatars from a single image using a diffusion-guided 3D model generation module and strategies for animating 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). While single-image head avatar reconstruction is crucial for lifelike Virtual Reality (VR) applications, existing approaches often struggle to preserve 3D consistency under unseen viewpoints. S-Avatar addresses this limitation through a three-stage pipeline. First, a high-resolution 3DGS is synthesized directly from a single image using a diffusion-based Gaussian splat generation module. Next, the parametric head model FLAME is aligned with the generated 3DGS by optimizing its parameters and spatial transformations. Finally, to adapt the 3DGS to FLAME variations, we construct a binding template that encodes the spatial relationship between the initial splats and FLAME. The dynamic 3D head avatar can then be rendered in real time by deforming the 3DGS with the binding template. By combining diffusion-guided canonical 3DGS generation with FLAME-based control, our method achieves efficient and accurate reconstruction with enhanced 3D consistency. Evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that S-Avatar outperforms state-of-the-art methods in novel-view and expression generation, achieving superior realism and consistency. Consequently, our approach represents a significant advance in accessible avatar creation, applicable to a wide range of VR/AR applications. The project page is available at https://github.com/hailsong/savatar.

</details>


### [8] [Bunraku: Turning a Single Illustration into an Editable Live2D Character](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27348)
*Junhao Chen,Jingjia Mao,Dayong Li,Chenghai Li,Saining Zhang,Zhihao Li,Hao Zhao,Yufei Wang,Ruqi Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents the first system that takes a single illustration and generates a complete, structured Live2D character model—including ordered RGBA layers, per-layer deformation meshes, and parameter-driven keypose vertex offsets—using a two-stage pipeline: layered diffusion for decomposed image generation, and joint self-attention across all mesh vertices for coherent keypose displacement prediction. It also introduces Live2D-Bench, a standardized benchmark, and an 8,884-model corpus.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Authoring a Live2D model currently requires weeks of manual work—layer separation, occlusion completion, mesh placement, and keyframing—and no prior generative method produces such a structured asset end-to-end, limiting the accessibility and scalability of this dominant 2D character-animation format.

Method: The pipeline has two stages. Stage 1 performs layered decomposition via a layered diffusion process under a Live2D-aware organ-level taxonomy, yielding an ordered RGBA stack with hidden-region completion. Stage 2 constructs a content-conforming triangle mesh per layer from its alpha channel alone, then predicts keypose displacement fields for all layers jointly by treating every vertex as a token in a self-attention mechanism spanning layer boundaries; each displacement is factorized into a bounded direction and log-magnitude.

Result: On 50 held-out characters under true generation (no teacher forcing), Stage 2 achieves a per-vertex direction cosine of 0.768 (median 0.828). Joint prediction is the largest gain, whereas scaling the network 112x yields no improvement. Re-texturing of clothing layers via natural language is supported since meshes derive from alpha channels.

Conclusion: Joint prediction across layers is essential for coherent character results, and the proposed two-stage system successfully generates all structured information a Live2D runtime consumes from a single illustration, complemented by a new benchmark and corpus for the task.

Abstract: Live2D is the dominant 2D character-animation format for anime characters and virtual avatars, representing each character as a stack of RGBA layers driven by per-layer mesh deformation. Despite its wide use in virtual streaming, mobile games, and interactive characters, authoring a Live2D model still demands weeks of manual layer separation, occlusion completion, mesh placement, and keyframing, and no prior generative method produces such a structured asset end-to-end. We present the first system that, from a single illustration, generates all the structured information a Live2D runtime consumes: ordered RGBA layers, a deformation mesh per layer, and the parameter-driven keypose vertex offsets that make the character move. Stage 1 casts layered decomposition as a layered diffusion process under a Live2D-aware organ-level taxonomy, producing an ordered RGBA stack with hidden-region completion. Stage 2 builds a content-conforming triangle mesh for each layer from its alpha channel alone, then predicts the keypose displacement field of all layers jointly: every vertex of every layer is one token, self-attention spans layer boundaries, and each displacement is factorised into a bounded direction and a log-magnitude. Joint rather than independent prediction is what makes the result a coherent character instead of separately plausible parts, and is our largest gain; scaling the network 112x yields none. On 50 held-out characters, under true generation with no teacher forcing, Stage 2 attains a per-vertex direction cosine of 0.768 (median 0.828). Because a layer's mesh derives from its alpha channel, a clothing layer can be re-textured from a natural-language instruction while the mesh and predicted animation are reused byte-for-byte. We further contribute Live2D-Bench, the first standardized benchmark for the task, and an 8,884-model Live2D corpus with layer and animation supervision.

</details>


### [9] [Shared Semantic Codebook Distillation for Unpaired Cross-Modal Medical Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27357)
*Dillan Imans,Phuoc-Nguyen Bui,Duc-Tai Le,Hyunseung Choo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SSCD proposes a shared discrete codebook distillation method for cross-modal knowledge transfer when medical image modalities are unpaired and geometrically incompatible, improving student performance by aligning distributional representations over a common vocabulary without requiring paired samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-modal knowledge distillation typically assumes paired data between modalities, but in medical imaging, modalities are often collected from different patient cohorts with incompatible feature spaces, making instance-level distillation and direct feature matching invalid or unreliable.

Method: SSCD builds a shared discrete codebook representing images as distributions over a common modality-agnostic vocabulary. Teacher and student representations are aligned by matching these distributions globally and class-conditionally. The codebook is updated online via exponential moving average, with entropy regularization and dead-code restart to maintain diversity. At inference, only the student encoder and classifier remain.

Result: On OCT-to-fundus retinal disease classification and CT-to-chest-X-ray pneumonia classification, SSCD improves the student from 64.5 to 70.2 macro-F1 and from 73.8 to 76.3 macro-F1, respectively, outperforming all evaluated distillation baselines on both settings.

Conclusion: The shared codebook approach effectively enables cross-modal knowledge distillation in unpaired medical imaging settings, producing substantial gains over baselines while keeping deployment lightweight by discarding teacher and codebook components at inference time.

Abstract: Cross-modal knowledge distillation can transfer diagnostic knowledge from a strong but costly teacher modality to a cheaper and more deployable student modality. In medical image analysis, however, the two modalities are often unpaired: they are collected from different patient cohorts and occupy geometrically incompatible feature spaces. This makes instance-level distillation invalid and direct feature matching unreliable. To address these challenges, we propose Shared Semantic Codebook Distillation (SSCD), which compares teacher and student representations through a shared discrete codebook. Each image is represented as a distribution over a common, modality-agnostic vocabulary, and knowledge is transferred by aligning these distributions across modalities, both globally and class-conditionally, without requiring paired samples or directly comparable raw features. The codebook is evolved online by exponential moving average and kept diverse through entropy regularization and dead-code restart. At inference, all teacher-side and codebook modules are discarded, leaving only the student encoder and classifier. On two heterogeneous unpaired settings, OCT-to-fundus retinal disease classification and CT-to-chest-X-ray pneumonia classification, SSCD improves the student from 64.5 to 70.2 macro-F1 and from 73.8 to 76.3 macro-F1, respectively, outperforming all evaluated distillation baselines on both settings. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/DillanImans/SSCD-unpaired-distillation

</details>


### [10] [VideoCoCo: Code-as-CoT for Physically-Consistent Video Generation via an Agentic Dual-Engine System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27380)
*Haodong Li,Tianfei Ren,Xiaoxiao Ma,Chunmei Qing,Zhen Fang,Sipeng He,Ziyu Guo,Haoyu Wu,Juanxi Tian,Yihang Zou,Ruichuan An,Dongzhi Jiang,Boxue Yang,Ji Xie,Xu Huang,Wenhao Yan,Jialv Zou,Zhengrong Yue,Yaxin Luo,Xiaotong Li,Yuzhu Wang,Junyan Ye,Jinjing Zhao,Zehui Chen,Lin Chen,Renye Yan,Feng Zhao,Pheng-Ann Heng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VideoCoCo is an agentic dual-engine framework that uses executable Blender code as a process-level chain of thought for text-to-video generation. A coding agent synthesizes Blender programs specifying scene dynamics, which are executed to produce deterministic spatiotemporal drafts, then transformed into photorealistic videos by a generative editor. It achieves state-of-the-art results on PhyGenBench (0.558) and VBench-2.0 (77.88).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-to-video models struggle to generate physically consistent dynamics because temporal evolution is inferred implicitly from compressed text prompts. Existing chain-of-thought approaches use intermediate plans or visual states that are non-executable or temporally sparse, limiting their ability to instantiate and control the complete spatiotemporal process.

Method: VideoCoCo employs a dual-engine architecture: (1) a coding agent that synthesizes executable Blender code explicitly defining the scene and its temporal evolution; (2) a simulation engine that runs the program to generate a deterministic spatiotemporal draft; and (3) a generative video engine that transforms the draft into photorealistic video via draft-conditioned editing. The framework also introduces VideoCoCo-3K, a curated dataset of draft-instruction-target triplets for adapting the video editor to simulated drafts.

Result: VideoCoCo improves OmniWeaving from 0.475 to 0.558 on PhyGenBench and from 52.18 to 77.88 on VBench-2.0, achieving the best average scores on both benchmarks.

Conclusion: Executable code serves as an effective, controllable, and inspectable intermediate representation for physically consistent video generation, separating process-level reasoning from high-fidelity visual realization.

Abstract: Text-to-video models have achieved remarkable visual quality, yet they still struggle to generate physically consistent dynamics because the temporal evolution of a scene must be inferred implicitly from a highly compressed text prompt. Existing chain-of-thought approaches introduce intermediate plans or visual states, but these representations are typically non-executable or temporally sparse, limiting their ability to instantiate and control the complete spatiotemporal process. To address this limitation, we introduce VideoCoCo, an agentic dual-engine framework in which executable Blender code serves as a process-level chain of thought. Given a text prompt, a coding agent synthesizes a Blender program that explicitly specifies the scene and its temporal evolution. The executable simulation engine runs the program to produce a deterministic spatiotemporal draft, which is subsequently transformed into a photorealistic video by a generative video engine through draft-conditioned editing. This decomposition separates process-level reasoning from high-fidelity visual realization. To adapt the video editor to simulated drafts, we construct VideoCoCo-3K, a curated dataset of draft-instruction-target triplets. VideoCoCo improves the OmniWeaving baseline from 0.475 to 0.558 on PhyGenBench and from 52.18 to 77.88 on VBench-2.0, achieving the best average score on both benchmarks. These results demonstrate that executable code provides an effective, controllable, and inspectable intermediate representation for physically consistent video generation.

</details>


### [11] [IGME: Efficient Chained Method Ensemble for Transferable Semantic Segmentation Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27465)
*Mengqi He,Jing Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces IGME, an efficient single-source attack method for generating transferable adversarial perturbations on semantic segmentation models. It composes attack components as a chained computation to share expensive gradient computations from a single source model, and uses integrated-gradient-style path-averaged directions to stabilize updates. IGME achieves competitive transferability versus single-source baselines while being much faster than model-ensemble attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generating transferable adversarial perturbations for semantic segmentation is computationally expensive, and existing approaches rely on multiple surrogate models (ensembles), which further escalates cost. The authors aim to find an efficient single-source alternative that maintains transferability while reducing computation.

Method: IGME formulates transferable attack composition as a chained computation over differentiable attack components, enabling gradient sharing from a single source model. To mitigate update instability from chained composition, it employs an integrated-gradient-style path-averaged direction as a stabilization heuristic.

Result: Experiments on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes show IGME achieves competitive transferability compared with single-source baselines and favorable runtime compared with model-ensemble attacks, while requiring access to only one source model across CNN- and transformer-based segmentation models.

Conclusion: Single-source transferable attacks on segmentation can be made efficient via chained gradient sharing and path-averaged stabilization, offering a practical trade-off between transferability and computational cost without needing multiple surrogate models.

Abstract: Semantic segmentation models are vulnerable to transferable adversarial perturbations, yet evaluating transfer attacks on dense prediction models can be computationally expensive. Existing ensemble attacks often rely on multiple surrogate models, increasing the computation cost, even harder for segmentation. This paper studies an efficient single-source alternative for transferable attacks on semantic segmentation. We formulate transferable attack composition as a chained computation over differentiable attack components, allowing the expensive source-model gradient computation to be shared. To reduce the update instability introduced by chained composition, we further use an integrated-gradient-style path-averaged direction as an empirical stabilization heuristic. Experiments on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes evaluate the resulting transferability efficiency trade-off across CNN- and transformer-based segmentation models. IGME achieves competitive transferability compared with single-source baselines and favorable runtime compared with model-ensemble attacks, while requiring access to only one source model.

</details>


### [12] [ProgFormer: Hierarchical Voxel Diffusion Transformer for Longitudinal Brain MRI Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27537)
*Dexuan Ding,Yuankai Qi,Luping Zhou,Jian Yang,Quan Z. Sheng,Ming-Hsuan Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ProgFormer is a hierarchical voxel-space Diffusion Transformer for longitudinal brain MRI prediction that uses a coarse pathway for global volumetric prediction and a fine pathway for voxel-level refinement, jointly estimating a velocity field via conditional flow matching directly in voxel space to generate future brain scans from Gaussian noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for longitudinal brain MRI prediction either suffer from information loss due to latent-space compression-reconstruction, or use unified prediction pathways in voxel space where subtle local disease-progression changes are overshadowed by dominant stable brain structure. A model is needed that preserves global consistency while remaining sensitive to fine-grained regional changes.

Method: ProgFormer is a hierarchical voxel-space Diffusion Transformer with two pathways: a coarse pathway performs primary volumetric prediction from 3D patch tokens modeling overall brain structure and longitudinal context, and a fine pathway uses coarse representations as spatio-temporal grounding for voxel-level refinement within individual patches. Both pathways jointly estimate a velocity field directly in voxel space through conditional flow matching, enabling end-to-end prediction without a separately learned image autoencoder. The predicted scan is generated from Gaussian noise by integrating the velocity field over Euler steps.

Result: Extensive experiments on ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS benchmarks under both pairwise and trajectory settings demonstrate favorable performance compared to several state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: The hierarchical coarse-to-fine voxel-space approach effectively addresses the trade-off between preserving global brain structural consistency and detecting subtle disease-related changes, achieving competitive performance on multiple standard longitudinal brain MRI benchmarks.

Abstract: Predicting future structural MRI of a brain is challenging because longitudinal changes are often subtle and confined to specific anatomical regions, while most subject-specific brain structure remains stable over time. An effective model should therefore preserve global brain structural consistency while remaining sensitive to fine-grained disease progression. Existing latent-space-based methods improve computational efficiency, but suffer from information loss during their compression-reconstruction procedure. In contrast, direct voxel-space methods avoid latent reconstruction but commonly use a unified prediction pathway to model brain structure and progression-related changes. Subtle local changes may therefore be overshadowed by the dominant stable brain structure. To address these challenges, we propose ProgFormer, a hierarchical voxel-space Diffusion Transformer for longitudinal brain MRI prediction. ProgFormer uses a coarse pathway to perform the primary volumetric prediction from 3D patch tokens. This pathway models overall brain structure and longitudinal context. The fine pathway then uses the coarse representations as spatio-temporal grounding for voxel-level refinement within individual patches. The two pathways jointly estimate a velocity field directly in voxel space through conditional flow matching, enabling end-to-end prediction without a separately learned image autoencoder. The predicted future scan is then generated from Gaussian noise by integrating the estimated velocity field over a sequence of Euler steps. Extensive experimental results on three widely used benchmarks, ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS, under both pairwise and trajectory settings demonstrate favourable performance compared against several state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [13] [Drawing-Recode: Annotation Grounding for Parametric CAD Code Generation from Raster 2D CAD Drawings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27558)
*Mingi Kim,Yongjun Kim,Hyungki Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Drawing-Recode is a framework that recovers Parametric CAD sequences (as CAD code) from raster 2D CAD drawings by extracting geometric features via an image encoder, recognizing dimensional annotations through a text recognition module, explicitly grounding annotations to geometry via cross-attention and an Annotation Grounding Loss, and feeding the fused features into an LLM to generate Structured Parametric CAD Code (SPCC). It outperforms baselines and is robust on scanned drawings resembling industrial conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for parametric CAD sequence recovery either handle only vector drawings or are limited to specific domains, and fail to explicitly connect dimensional annotations to geometric information, thereby underusing dimensional information for 3D parametric CAD sequence recovery from raster drawings.

Method: Drawing-Recode uses an image encoder to extract geometric features, a text recognition module to recognize annotations, and explicitly grounds annotations to geometric information via cross-attention and a proposed Annotation Grounding Loss (AGL). The fused features are input to an LLM that generates CAD code in the Structured Parametric CAD Code (SPCC) format.

Result: Drawing-Recode outperforms existing baselines and remains robust on scanned drawings resembling industrial conditions.

Conclusion: Drawing-Recode contributes to digitizing raster 2D CAD drawings in industrial settings, supporting part reproduction and manufacturing automation.

Abstract: Recovering Parametric CAD sequences from raster-format 2D Computer-Aided Design (CAD) drawings accumulated prior to digital transformation is important for part reproduction and manufacturing process automation. However, existing studies either process only vector drawings or are limited to specific domains, and fail to explicitly connect dimensional annotations to geometric information, limiting their use of dimensional information for 3D Parametric CAD sequences recovery. We propose Drawing-Recode, a framework that generates Parametric CAD sequences as CAD code from raster 2D CAD drawings. Drawing-Recode extracts geometric features via an image encoder and recognizes annotations through a separate text recognition module, then explicitly grounds annotations to geometric information using cross-attention and our proposed Annotation Grounding Loss (AGL). The resulting features are fed into a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate CAD code in the Structured Parametric CAD Code (SPCC) format. Experiments show that Drawing-Recode outperforms existing baselines and remains robust on scanned drawings resembling industrial conditions. We expect Drawing-Recode contributes to digitizing raster 2D CAD drawings in industrial settings and to part reproduction and manufacturing automation.

</details>


### [14] [Inference-Time Agentic Decision Rules Beat Longer Evolving Search for Multi-Image Medical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27564)
*Site Li,Jianyi Hao,Xiaofeng Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates Multi-image medical Visual Question Answering (VQA) as an agentic decision-making problem rather than a prompt-length issue. Through a controlled comparison of five inference-time agentic strategies on MedFrameQA, the "order-vote" policy—a simple robust aggregator—achieves the best final-test accuracy (57.89%), significantly outperforming both the fixed baseline (52.73%) and a more complex order-rerank variant (55.79%). Notably, doubling the evolutionary search budget (50→100 generations) provides no generalization benefit, with final-test accuracy actually dropping to 56.02%. The authors conclude that defining the correct agentic decision rule matters more than expanding optimization search budget for multi-image medical reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper challenges the prevailing assumption that multi-image medical VQA difficulties stem primarily from prompt-length constraints. Instead, it frames the problem as a fundamental agentic decision-making challenge, where medical vision-language agents must aggregate evidence across ordered images, remain robust to answer-order perturbations, and avoid overfitting to noisy search-time feedback—motivating a systematic comparison of agentic strategies.

Method: The study conducts a controlled comparison of five inference-time agentic strategies on the MedFrameQA dataset. All strategies are optimized using the same high-budget ShinkaEvolve configuration and evaluated on a reproducible internal frozen split (1,331 evolution, 665 holdout, 855 final test). Each strategy is run across five independent repeated runs, with statistical significance assessed via paired bootstrap analysis. The search budget is also varied (50 vs. 100 generations) to test the impact of optimization effort on generalization.

Result: The order-vote policy—the simplest robust aggregator—achieves 57.89±0.65% final-test accuracy, significantly outperforming the fixed baseline (52.73±0.42%) and the complex order-rerank variant (55.79±0.43%). Paired bootstrap analysis confirms significant gains. Extending evolutionary search from 50 to 100 generations yields no generalization benefit: holdout performance marginally increases but final-test accuracy drops from 57.89% to 56.02%.

Conclusion: For multi-image medical reasoning, selecting the correct agentic decision rule is substantially more impactful than expanding the optimization search budget. Simpler, robust aggregation strategies (order-vote) outperform more complex but brittle approaches, suggesting that agentic architecture design should be prioritized over optimization resource allocation.

Abstract: Multi-image medical VQA is not merely a prompt-length problem; it is a fundamental challenge of agentic decision-making. Medical vision-language agents must aggregate evidence across ordered images, remain robust to answer-order perturbations, and avoid overfitting to noisy search-time feedback. We study MedFrameQA through a controlled comparison of five inference-time agentic strategies, optimized using the same high-budget ShinkaEvolve configuration and evaluated on a reproducible internal frozen split (1,331 evolution, 665 holdout, 855 final test). Across five independent repeated runs, the strongest method emerges as the simplest robust aggregator: the \textbf{order-vote} policy achieves $57.89 \pm 0.65\%$ final-test accuracy, significantly outperforming the fixed baseline ($52.73 \pm 0.42\%$) and the more complex, albeit brittle, order-rerank variant ($55.79 \pm 0.43\%$). Paired bootstrap analysis confirms these significant gains. Extending the evolutionary search budget from 50 to 100 generations yields no generalization benefit: while holdout performance marginally increases, final-test accuracy drops from $57.89\%$ to $56.02\%$. Our findings suggest that for multi-image medical reasoning, defining the correct agentic decision rule is substantially more impactful than expanding the optimization search budget.

</details>


### [15] [Objective-Aligned Direct Answer SFT for Robust Multi-Frame Medical VQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27566)
*Site Li,Jianyi Hao,Xiaofeng Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: On MedFrameQA, direct decoder-only answer SFT on MedGemma-1.5-4B emerges as the strongest robust adaptation family compared to complex alternatives like controller-style inference, localization-aware reranking, and static hard-negative mixing, when evaluated with fixed splits, matched budgets, repeated seeds, and calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-frame medical VQA has seen increasing architectural complexity (controller-style inference, localization-aware reranking, static hard-negative mixing, staged continuation). The authors question whether such complexity is necessary, hypothesizing that methods tightly aligned with the benchmark's final answer objective constitute the strongest robust adaptation family once evaluation is properly controlled.

Method: The authors systematically compare controller-based methods, scaffold evolution, static mixed supervision, continuation-heavy variants, and direct answer-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on MedFrameQA using MedGemma-1.5-4B. Evaluation is controlled across fixed splits, matched budgets, repeated seeds, and calibration. Post-hoc calibration is applied to repair confidence estimation, and transferability is checked on Qwen2.5-VL-3B.

Result: Direct decoder-only answer SFT is the strongest robust family, yielding substantial gains in held-out report accuracy over frozen baselines with high stability across repeated seeds and matched controls. Post-hoc calibration repairs confidence without hurting accuracy, and the approach transfers to secondary backbones like Qwen2.5-VL-3B.

Conclusion: Objective-aligned direct answer SFT, not complex auxiliary mechanisms, is the strongest robust adaptation family for MedFrameQA. The work establishes a strong minimalist baseline and urges the community to redirect focus toward fundamentally robust optimization rather than architectural complexity.

Abstract: Multi-frame medical VQA appears to reward increasingly complex adaptation: controller-style inference, localization-aware reranking, static hard-negative mixing, and staged continuation all appear plausible from first principles. We test a simpler competing hypothesis on MedFrameQA: methods that remain tightly aligned with the benchmark's final answer objective should be the strongest \emph{robust} adaptation family once evaluation is controlled across fixed splits, matched budgets, repeated seeds, and calibration. We compare controller-based methods, scaffold evolution, static mixed supervision, continuation-heavy variants, and direct answer-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The strongest robust family is direct decoder-only answer SFT on MedGemma-1.5-4B. Empirically, this family yields substantial improvements in held-out report accuracy over frozen baselines while remaining remarkably stable across repeated seeds and matched controls, ensuring our claims reflect true family-level robustness rather than an isolated hyperparameter peak. Furthermore, post-hoc calibration effectively repairs confidence estimation without compromising accuracy, and the core approach transfers consistently to secondary backbones like Qwen2.5-VL-3B. The main result is therefore not that a complex auxiliary mechanism wins, but that objective-aligned direct answer SFT is the strongest robust adaptation family we found for MedFrameQA. By establishing this strong, minimalist baseline, we hope to redirect community focus toward fundamentally robust optimization rather than architectural complexity.

</details>


### [16] [ZMIS-SAM: Segment Anything Model Enhanced with Wavelet Transform for Zooplankton Microscopy Image Instance Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27585)
*Dekun Yuan,Zhongwei Li,Zheng Qiao,Jie Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes ZMIS-SAM, an instance segmentation model based on Segment Anything Model (SAM) combined with wavelet transform for zooplankton microscopic image segmentation. It introduces three core innovations—ZM-ViT adapters for zooplankton-specific feature modeling, a Neighboring Feature Aggregation Module (NFAM) for continuous segmentation of slender appendages, and a Wavelet-based Multi-scale Multi-directional Feature Enhancement (WM2FE) module for boundary refinement—achieving state-of-the-art performance on zooplankton datasets with strong cross-domain generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Zooplankton are crucial primary consumers in marine food chains, but the original SAM performs poorly on microscopic zooplankton image segmentation due to its lack of zooplankton-specific domain knowledge, leading to inaccurate classification, discontinuous segmentation of slender appendages, and incomplete boundary segmentation.

Method: The framework introduces three innovations: (1) ZM-ViT enhances SAM's morphological and intensity distribution modeling via two lightweight adapters; (2) the Neighboring Feature Aggregation Module (NFAM) integrates general-purpose and domain-specific features to improve continuous segmentation of semi-transparent slender appendages; (3) the Wavelet-based Multi-scale Multi-directional Feature Enhancement (WM2FE) module recovers high-frequency details to refine boundary segmentation completeness.

Result: Extensive experiments show ZMIS-SAM achieves state-of-the-art instance segmentation performance on the zooplankton dataset and demonstrates strong generalization capability across multiple public cross-domain datasets.

Conclusion: The proposed ZMIS-SAM effectively addresses the limitations of SAM on zooplankton microscopic image segmentation, achieving superior performance and strong cross-domain generalization.

Abstract: As primary consumers in the marine food chain, zooplankton play a crucial role in maintaining marine ecological balance. However, the Segment Anything Model (SAM) exhibits limited performance in microscopic image instance segmentation due to its lack of zooplankton-specific domain knowledge. To address these challenges, we propose a novel instance segmentation model based on SAM and wavelet transform (ZMIS-SAM), effectively tackling issues such as inaccurate classification, discontinuous segmentation of slender appendages, and incomplete boundary segmentation. Our framework incorporates three core innovations: ZM-ViT enhances SAM's capability to model zooplankton morphology and image intensity distributions through two lightweight adapters, the Neighboring Feature Aggregation Module (NFAM) improves continuous segmentation of semi-transparent slender appendages by integrating general-purpose and domain-specific features, and the Wavelet-based Multi-scale Multi-directional Feature Enhancement (WM2FE) module effectively recovers high-frequency details to refine boundary segmentation completeness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ZMIS-SAM achieves state-of-the-art instance segmentation performance on the zooplankton dataset and exhibits strong generalization capability across multiple public cross-domain datasets.

</details>


### [17] [MPIE-Bench: Benchmarking Anatomically Plausible Multi-Person Interaction Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27616)
*Jiajia Lin,Mingxuan Du,Tuowen Zhou,Benfeng Xu,Hongtao Xie*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MPIE-Bench is a 2,500-sample benchmark for multi-person contact image editing with 405 scenes, 14 interaction categories, and four contact densities. It introduces MPIE-Eval, a mesh-based evaluation with two axes—Anatomy and Interaction—that assess body completeness and contact geometry. Results show all ten editors fail on at least one axis (max 0.65 Anatomy, 0.72 Interaction), whereas VLM judges saturate above 0.95, revealing that existing checklist evaluations miss obvious anatomical errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current text-to-image and personalized editing models can generate high-quality single-subject images but fail to place multiple named people into shared contact actions (embrace, carry, grapple), producing fused limbs, invented extremities, and interpenetrating bodies. Existing evaluations overlook these anatomical and geometric issues, and VLM-as-a-judge checklists saturate on Interaction while errors remain obvious to humans—so a more accurate benchmark and evaluation metric are needed.

Method: MPIE-Bench is built from video-mined editing triplets: 2,500 samples across 405 scenes, 14 interaction categories, and four contact densities (C0-C3). MPIE-Eval uses a frozen public multi-person mesh reconstruction to score two axes: Anatomy (whether every human-like mass is explained by a complete set of reconstructed bodies) and Interaction (whether penetration and surface distance between reconstructed bodies match the requested contact). Ten editors were evaluated; validation included a five-rater human study comparing against a zero-shot VLM judge, plus ablation of weights and thresholds.

Result: Across ten editors, mesh Anatomy tops out at 0.65 and mesh Interaction at 0.72 on two different models—no single editor is strong on both axes. VLM checklists rate the same images above 0.95, confirming saturation and unreliability. A five-rater study confirms both MPIE-Eval axes track human judgement more closely than a zero-shot VLM judge, and rankings remain stable under ablation of every weight and threshold.

Conclusion: Existing VLM checklist evaluations grossly overestimate multi-person contact editing quality, while MPIE-Bench and MPIE-Eval reveal that current editors universally fail at anatomical completeness and contact geometry. No editor currently succeeds on both axes, establishing clear headroom for future multi-person contact editing research.

Abstract: Text-to-image and personalized editing models now synthesize high-fidelity single-subject images with ease. Yet placing multiple named people into shared contact actions such as embrace, carry, or grapple still exposes major failures: fused limbs, invented extremities, and interpenetrating bodies. Existing evaluations largely overlook these anatomical and geometric issues, and VLM-as-a-judge checklists often saturate on Interaction while the errors remain obvious to humans. We introduce MPIE-Bench, a 2,500-sample benchmark of video-mined editing triplets spanning 405 scenes, 14 interaction categories, and four contact densities (C0-C3). We also propose MPIE-Eval, whose two new axes score contact-time geometry from a frozen public multi-person mesh reconstruction. Anatomy asks whether every human-like mass is explained by a complete set of reconstructed bodies, and Interaction asks whether the penetration and surface distance between those bodies match the contact the instruction asked for. Across ten editors, mesh Anatomy tops out at 0.65 and mesh Interaction at 0.72 on two different models, so no single editor is strong on both, while VLM checklists rate the same images above 0.95. A five-rater study confirms that both axes track human judgement more closely than a zero-shot VLM judge, and the rankings hold under ablation of every weight and threshold.

</details>


### [18] [MedXplore: Towards Reliable and Unbiased Generalized Category Discovery in Medical Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27620)
*Jianwei He,Kailin Lyu,Junhao Dong,Long Xiao,Wenjie Hou,Jingze Lu,Di Wu,Lin Shu,Jie Hao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MedXplore is a unified framework for reliable and unbiased Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) in medical imaging, achieving an average 8.5% gain in All accuracy over strong baselines and reducing false-old errors from 14.50% to 0.80% on Kvasir.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most deep learning methods in medical image analysis depend on large-scale annotations and a closed-world assumption that is rarely valid in clinical practice. Although GCD has advanced on natural images, it remains largely unexplored in medical imaging, creating a gap for reliable and unbiased category discovery in this domain.

Method: MedXplore optimizes GCD from two levels. (1) Perceptual level: Frequency-SNR Adaptive Attention and Consistency (FAAC) performs learnable full-spectrum filtering and global-local energy contrast activation to highlight local abnormal signals relative to global context, while providing semantic anchors for patch consistency learning. (2) Decision level: Adaptive Cosine-Angular Margin (ACAM) adjusts angular margins using semantic difficulty and feature confidence to balance intra-class compactness and inter-class separability.

Result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show an average 8.5% gain in All accuracy over the strongest competing methods. On Kvasir, MedXplore reduces false-old errors from 14.50% to 0.80%, demonstrating strong robustness under severe old-new ambiguity.

Conclusion: The two complementary modules improve lesion-sensitive representation learning and mitigate old-class bias, making MedXplore a reliable and unbiased solution for medical GCD.

Abstract: Deep learning has shown strong potential in medical image analysis, but most existing methods rely on large-scale annotations and a closed-world assumption that rarely holds in clinical practice. Although Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) has advanced rapidly on natural images, it remains underexplored in medical imaging. To address this issue, we propose MedXplore, a unified framework for reliable and unbiased medical GCD, optimizing from both perceptual and decision levels. Specifically, at the perceptual level, taking a frequency domain perspective, Frequency-SNR Adaptive Attention and Consistency (FAAC) performs learnable full-spectrum filtering and global-local energy contrast activation to not only highlight local abnormal signals relative to the global context, but also provide reliable semantic anchors for patch consistency learning. At the decision level, Adaptive Cosine-Angular Margin (ACAM) adjusts angular margins using semantic difficulty and feature confidence to balance intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. Together, the two modules improve lesion-sensitive representation learning and mitigate old-class bias. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show an average \textbf{8.5\%} gain in \textit{All} accuracy over the strongest competing methods. On Kvasir, MedXplore reduces false-old errors from 14.50\% to 0.80\%, demonstrating strong robustness under severe old-new ambiguity.

</details>


### [19] [BlindPSNR: A No-Reference Fidelity Predictor for Low-Light Image Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27628)
*Mingzhe Lyu,Jinqiang Cui,Hong Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes BlindPSNR, a lightweight no-reference network that predicts PSNR for low-light image enhancement without a ground-truth reference, using windowed cross-attention between the enhanced and degraded images and heteroscedastic regression. It achieves 89.5% top-1 selection accuracy (vs. 54.4% for scalar regression baseline) with regret dropping to 0.026 dB, and generalizes to unseen datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-light image enhancement methods have tunable parameters that are typically fixed, causing performance degradation across different scenes. Manually selecting optimal parameters is time-consuming and impractical. PSNR is the natural fidelity criterion for automating parameter selection but requires ground-truth references that are typically unavailable in practice.

Method: BlindPSNR is a lightweight no-reference network that fuses the enhanced image with the degraded low-light input via windowed cross-attention and estimates PSNR through heteroscedastic regression. With paired training data, ground-truth PSNR is analytically computable, providing exact supervision without a separate teacher network.

Result: BlindPSNR achieves 89.5% top-1 selection accuracy (vs. 54.4% for a scalar-regression baseline), with regret dropping from 1.62 dB to 0.026 dB, and generalizes to unseen datasets with SRCC = 0.61-0.67. All seven NR-IQA baselines tested achieve 0% top-1 selection accuracy on their benchmark.

Conclusion: BlindPSNR demonstrates that no-reference PSNR prediction is feasible for low-light image enhancement, significantly outperforming NR-IQA surrogates and scalar regression baselines. The approach provides a practical solution for automating parameter selection in LLIE without requiring ground-truth references at inference time.

Abstract: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) methods involve tunable parameters that are typically fixed, often leading to performance degradation when applied across scenes. Manually selecting the best configuration, however, can be time-consuming and not always practical. Peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) is the natural fidelity criterion for automating parameter selection, yet it requires a ground-truth reference that is typically unavailable. To our knowledge, no learning-based method addresses no-reference PSNR prediction for low-light image enhancement; the natural surrogate, no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA), targets perceptual quality rather than signal fidelity, and all seven baselines we test achieve 0% top-1 selection accuracy on our benchmark. With paired training data, the ground-truth PSNR is analytically computable, providing exact supervision without a separate teacher network. Building on this, we propose BlindPSNR, a lightweight no-reference network that fuses the enhanced image with the degraded low-light input via windowed cross-attention and estimates PSNR through heteroscedastic regression. While a scalar-regression baseline achieves top-1 accuracy of 54.4%, BlindPSNR raises this to 89.5% with regret dropping from 1.62 dB to 0.026 dB, and generalizes to unseen datasets (SRCC = 0.61-0.67).

</details>


### [20] [4DHumanDiff: Direct Text-to-4DGS Generation for Consistent 360-Degree Dynamic Humans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27634)
*Renlong Wu,Haoran Chen,Yuxiang Wei,Xiaowei Jin,Wangmeng Zuo,Hui Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: 4DHumanDiff is a diffusion framework that directly generates 360-degree dynamic human assets represented by 4D Gaussian Splatting from text prompts, avoiding video pre-generation and per-scene reconstruction. It uses a 3D U-Net with temporal attention, a large-scale 60K text-to-4DGS dataset, 2D regularization, and training-free 4D interpolation, achieving consistent results in under one minute with 10x faster inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for text-to-dynamic-human generation typically synthesize monocular/multi-view videos first and then fit a 4D representation, which is expensive and suffers from incomplete geometry and view-inconsistent renderings.

Method: A diffusion framework that directly models the structured 4D Gaussian Splatting representation space end-to-end, using a 3D U-Net backbone with temporal attention for motion-aware generation, trained on a newly constructed 60K-pair text-to-4DGS dataset, with 2D regularization and training-free 4D interpolation for improved rendering quality and motion smoothness.

Result: Generates consistent 360-degree dynamic humans within one minute, achieves better temporal and multi-view consistency, and reduces inference time by more than 10x compared to previous approaches.

Conclusion: Direct end-to-end generation of 4D Gaussian Splatting representations is a viable and superior alternative to generate-from-video-then-fit pipelines for dynamic human asset creation, offering both quality and efficiency gains.

Abstract: Generating high-quality 360-degree dynamic human assets from text prompts is challenging. Existing methods usually synthesize monocular or multi-view videos first and then fit a 4D representation, which is expensive and often causes incomplete geometry or view-inconsistent renderings. We present 4DHumanDiff, a diffusion framework that directly generates dynamic humans represented by 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) from text prompts. By modeling the structured 4D representation space end-to-end, 4DHumanDiff avoids video pre-generation and per-scene reconstruction, making it better suited for view-consistent and temporally coherent asset generation. The model uses a 3D U-Net backbone with temporal attention for motion-aware generation. We further construct a large-scale text-to-4DGS dataset with 60,000 high-quality pairs, and introduce 2D regularization and training-free 4D interpolation to improve rendering quality and motion smoothness. Experiments show that 4DHumanDiff generates consistent 360-degree dynamic humans within one minute, achieves better temporal and multi-view consistency, and reduces inference time by more than 10x.

</details>


### [21] [MMOOC: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Out-of-Context Evaluation in Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27637)
*Wenjie Zhu,Yabin Zhang,Wenjun Zeng,Lei Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents MMOOC, a large-scale benchmark with over 41K image-question pairs to evaluate MLLMs' ability to refuse truly out-of-context questions while correctly answering shifted in-context questions. It covers eight shift types, three question formats, and six visual scenarios, using Accuracy and Refusal Rate metrics plus an LLM-as-a-Judge scoring method. Experiments reveal current MLLMs struggle to balance answerability and refusal under shifted contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs perform well on standard vision-language tasks but fail under imperfect or shifted contexts. Existing benchmarks overlook answerable Shifted IC cases and only cover limited OOC shift types, leaving a gap in evaluating whether models can properly distinguish between questions that should be refused (OOC) and those that should be answered (Shifted IC).

Method: The authors build MMOOC, a benchmark with over 41K image-question pairs including both answerable Shifted IC and unanswerable OOC cases. It spans three question formats, eight shift types, and six visual scenarios. Data quality is ensured via MLLM-based filtering and human verification. Evaluation uses Accuracy and Refusal Rate, plus an LLM-as-a-Judge metric for assessing reasoning correctness.

Result: Experiments on diverse MLLMs show current models still struggle to balance answerability and refusal under shifted contexts. The analysis identifies key failure patterns and demonstrates that post-training can improve model robustness.

Conclusion: MMOOC fills a critical gap in evaluating MLLM refusal and robust answering under shifted contexts. The benchmark highlights persistent limitations in current models and shows that post-training offers a pathway to improved robustness. The benchmark will be released publicly.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks, but often fail under imperfect or shifted contexts. A reliable MLLM should refuse truly out-of-context (OOC) questions with subject-level context shifts while still answering shifted in-context (Shifted IC) questions with non-subject context shifts. Existing benchmarks mainly target OOC or visually unanswerable questions, but overlook answerable Shifted IC cases and cover limited OOC shifts. To fill this gap, we present MMOOC, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating refusal and robust answering abilities of MLLMs. MMOOC contains over 41K image-question pairs, including answerable Shifted IC cases and unanswerable OOC cases, spanning three question formats, eight shift types and six visual scenarios, with data quality ensured through MLLM-based filtering and human verification. We evaluate model responses using Accuracy and Refusal Rate, and further introduce an LLM-as-a-Judge metric to assess the correctness of model reasoning. Experiments on diverse MLLMs show that current models still struggle to balance answer-ability and refusal under shifted contexts. We further analyze key failure patterns and show that post-training can improve robustness. MMOOC will be made publicly available.

</details>


### [22] [Learning Color Grading, No Photo Sharing: Federated Aesthetic Preference Learning for Personalized Image Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27659)
*Chuanzhi Xu,Ziyuan Tao,Jean Julien KNell,Yanrong Chen,Haolan Guo,Xuanhua Yin,Adnan Mahmood,Weidong Cai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FedPAIE is a federated framework for personalized image aesthetic enhancement that trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer, personalizes it on local support sets, and uses it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer—all without centralizing raw photos or ratings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalized image enhancement should reflect individual aesthetic taste, but learning such preferences typically requires private photos and ratings that cannot be centrally collected. There is a need to infer preferences from sparse, heterogeneous user feedback and translate them into natural-looking color transformations on resource-constrained devices.

Method: FedPAIE trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer, calibrates it into a personalized scorer on a small local support set, and freezes it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer from unpaired local photographs. Fidelity constraints and an excess-gap penalty regularize scorer-guided adaptation to avoid proxy-score over-optimization while preserving content and natural appearance.

Result: Scorer learning updates at most 0.787M parameters, enhancer adaptation updates 0.265M, and inference retains only a 0.293M-parameter personalized enhancer. Experiments on MIT-Adobe FiveK and Flickr-AES demonstrate effective open-world personalization and a favorable balance between user preference and image fidelity.

Conclusion: FedPAIE connects decentralized preference learning with efficient personalized image transformation without requiring paired user retouches, demonstrating that federated personalized aesthetic enhancement is both practical and effective on resource-constrained devices.

Abstract: Personalized image enhancement should reflect individual aesthetic taste, yet learning such preferences commonly depends on private photos and ratings that are unsuitable for centralized collection. The task must infer preference from sparse, heterogeneous feedback and translate it into natural-looking color transformations on resource-constrained user devices. We introduce FedPAIE, a federated personalized aesthetic image enhancement framework for user-adaptive color grading without centralizing raw photos or ratings. FedPAIE trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer, calibrates it into a personalized scorer on a small local support set, and freezes it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer from unpaired local photographs. Fidelity constraints and an excess-gap penalty regularize scorer-guided adaptation to limit proxy-score over-optimization while preserving content and natural appearance. Training remains lightweight throughout the pipeline: scorer learning updates at most 0.787M parameters, enhancer adaptation updates 0.265M, and inference retains only a 0.293M-parameter personalized enhancer. Experiments on MIT-Adobe FiveK and Flickr-AES demonstrate effective open-world personalization and a favorable balance between user preference and image fidelity. FedPAIE thus connects decentralized preference learning with efficient personalized image transformation without requiring paired user retouches.

</details>


### [23] [Witness Evidence Portfolios: Single-Prefill Risk Detection for Closed Multimodal Answers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27667)
*Fexiang Liu,Shiye Wang,Qiang Qiu,Zheng Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WEP is a training-free inference-time risk detection method for closed visual answers in multimodal large language models that estimates layer-by-layer visual evidence supporting or contradicting the predicted candidate via the white-box prefill path, summarizes it through interpretable route families, and fuses it with candidate confidence to decide whether an answer should be trusted, reviewed, or routed to a stronger system.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable deployment of MLLMs requires deciding whether a confident visual answer should be trusted, reviewed, or routed to a stronger system. Existing confidence scores capture candidate margins but not where the estimated signed visual readouts associated with those margins come from or how they are distributed, leaving a gap in understanding the provenance and concentration of visual evidence.

Method: WEP first estimates, layer by layer, which visual contributions support or contradict the predicted candidate. It summarizes these contributions through two interpretable route families: question-related evidence provenance and signed evidence concentration. Nested grouped validation selects the more reliable family and a sparse top-k route portfolio, which is fused with candidate confidence. The method requires no image perturbation, decoding change, backward pass, or external verifier.

Result: Across three MLLMs and four binary-answer benchmarks, WEP improves mean error AP by 0.134. All 12 model-dataset gains are positive, and image-cluster bootstrap intervals are strictly positive on 10 pairs.

Conclusion: WEP targets white-box closed-answer systems and uses a labeled calibration slice, providing an effective inference-time risk detection approach that leverages the same white-box prefill path used to produce the answer.

Abstract: Reliable deployment of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) requires deciding whether a confident visual answer should be trusted, reviewed, or routed to a stronger system.
