Confidence scores capture candidate margins, but not where the estimated signed visual readouts associated with those margins come from or how they are distributed. We study inference-time risk detection for closed visual answers using the same white-box prefill path that produces the answer. Witness Evidence Portfolios (WEP) first estimates, layer by layer, which visual contributions support or contradict the predicted candidate. It summarizes these contributions through two interpretable route families: question-related evidence provenance and signed evidence concentration. Nested grouped validation chooses the more reliable family and a sparse top-k route portfolio, which is fused with candidate confidence. WEP needs no image perturbation, decoding change, backward pass, or external verifier. Across three MLLMs and four binary-answer benchmarks, WEP improves mean error AP by 0.134. All 12 model--dataset gains are positive, and image-cluster bootstrap intervals are strictly positive on 10 pairs. WEP targets white-box closed-answer systems and uses a labeled calibration slice.

</details>


### [24] [JigShape: Evaluating Visual-Geometric Reasoning in VLMs through Jigsaw Puzzles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27670)
*Shawn Li,Wei Yang,Jike Zhong,Jiate Li,Jiawei Yang,You Qin,Ryan Rossi,Franck Dernoncourt,Roger Zimmermann,Yue Wang,Zhengzhong Tu,Vicente Ordonez,Mohit Bansal,Yue Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces \ours{}, a jigsaw puzzle benchmark with interlocking tab-and-blank pieces that eliminates ambiguity from rectangular cuts. Evaluating 95K instances across grid sizes from 4×4 to 16×16, it finds that frontier VLMs largely lack geometric reasoning, and all models including fine-tuned ones collapse on larger grids, revealing a "scaling cliff" in consistent constraint satisfaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing jigsaw puzzle benchmarks use rectangular cuts that produce ambiguous ground truth in texture-repeated regions, making it hard to properly evaluate visual-geometric reasoning in vision-language models.

Method: Introduces \ours{}, a benchmark with tab-and-blank interlocking jigsaw pieces where geometric constraints impose strong local compatibility requirements, combined with visual content to yield unambiguous ground truth. Evaluates 95K instances across four grid densities (4×4 to 16×16) on zero-shot VLMs and supervised fine-tuned models.

Result: Only one of five frontier VLMs (GPT-5.5) exceeds random baseline on 4×4 puzzles; others perform at chance. Fine-tuned models reach >97% on 4×4 but all models collapse on larger grids: GPT-5.5 drops from 70% to near-random on 8×8, and fine-tuned models fall below 5% on 12×12.

Conclusion: Current architectures cannot maintain consistent geometric constraint satisfaction as puzzle size increases, establishing scalable geometric reasoning as an open challenge for vision-language models.

Abstract: Jigsaw puzzle solving requires jointly reasoning about visual content and geometric constraints, yet existing benchmarks use rectangular cuts that create ambiguous ground truth in texture-repeated regions. We introduce \textit{\ours{}}, a benchmark with tab-and-blank interlocking pieces where geometric constraints provide strong local compatibility requirements that, combined with visual content, yield unambiguous ground truth. Across 95K instances at four grid densities (4$\times$4 to 16$\times$16), we find that \textbf{zero-shot VLMs largely lack geometric reasoning}: only one of five frontier models (GPT-5.5) exceeds random baseline on 4$\times$4 puzzles, while all others perform at chance level. While supervised fine-tuning achieves $>$97\% on 4$\times$4, \textbf{all models collapse on larger grids}: GPT-5.5 drops from 70\% to near-random on 8$\times$8, and even fine-tuned models fall below 5\% on 12$\times$12. This ``scaling cliff'' suggests current architectures cannot maintain consistent constraint satisfaction as the number of pieces increases. \ours{} establishes scalable geometric reasoning as an open challenge for vision-language models.

</details>


### [25] [RefineSVG: Visual Feedback-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Image-to-SVG Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27699)
*Shaobo Liu,Feiqiao Mao,Shuaishuai Zhou,Yan Zhan,Weiqi Tan,Zhiqiong Lu,Zhengping Liang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RefineSVG is a single-step closed-loop visual feedback framework that enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perform high-fidelity image-to-SVG generation through self-correction, using an external rendering engine to generate visual residual maps (Diff-Map) as ReAct-style correction signals, with an SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary that compresses token sequences by over 52%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLM-based image-to-SVG approaches rely on single-pass open-loop inference, where the model receives visual input only once and must generate thousands of SVG code tokens without intermediate verification. This leads to geometric drift, error accumulation, and visual hallucination on complex images.

Method: RefineSVG invokes an external rendering engine after an initial SVG generation pass to compare the rendered output against the target image. The comparison yields a multi-dimensional visual residual map (Diff-Map) fed back as a ReAct-style correction signal for targeted correction. The framework includes an SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary compressing token sequences by over 52%, and a progressive training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampling cold-start data construction, and end-to-end agentic reinforcement learning.

Result: Extensive experiments show RefineSVG consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity, structural accuracy, and code efficiency.

Conclusion: Closed-loop visual feedback with self-correction significantly improves image-to-SVG generation quality compared to single-pass open-loop methods, and the render-observe-correct paradigm is effective for MLLM-based code generation tasks.

Abstract: We propose RefineSVG, a single-step closed-loop visual feedback framework that enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perform high-fidelity image-to-SVG generation through self-correction. Existing MLLM-based approaches rely on single-pass open-loop inference, where the model receives visual input only once and must generate thousands of SVG code tokens without intermediate verification. This paradigm inevitably leads to geometric drift, error accumulation, and visual hallucination on complex images. RefineSVG overcomes this limitation by invoking an external rendering engine after an initial SVG generation pass to compare the rendered output against the target image. The comparison yields a multi-dimensional visual residual map (Diff-Map) that is fed back to the model as a ReAct-style correction signal, driving a targeted correction step. To support this render-observe-correct interaction, we further introduce an SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary that compresses token sequences by over 52%. A progressive training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampling cold-start data construction, and end-to-end agentic reinforcement learning aligns the model with closed-loop visual correction. Extensive experiments show that RefineSVG consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity, structural accuracy, and code efficiency.Code is available at https://github.com/liuxiaobo66/RefineSVG.

</details>


### [26] [Calibrate Before Reason: Robust Visual Token Reduction against Semantic Drift in VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27700)
*Jiasheng Li,Zhong Ji,Yan Zhang,Huihui Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CaRe is a training-free framework for visual token reduction in VLMs that calibrates compact visual representations before reasoning to preserve semantic fidelity, outperforming SOTA baselines while pruning 94.4% of visual tokens and retaining 96.4% of full-token performance with up to 2.30x faster inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual token reduction methods improve efficiency by pruning or compressing redundant tokens but fail to examine whether the resulting representation remains semantically consistent with the original, potentially causing severe semantic drift that deviates the VLM's understanding.

Method: CaRe introduces the principle of 'Calibrate Before Reason' and consists of two complementary modules: 1) Perturbation-Robust Calibration Anchoring, which identifies calibration anchors with stable model-side influence under multi-directional perturbations; 2) Confidence-Gated Token Calibration, which extracts reliable calibration signals from unselected tokens and injects them into anchors.

Result: Extensive evaluations across diverse VLM architectures and benchmarks show CaRe outperforms state-of-the-art token reduction baselines. While pruning 94.4% of visual tokens, it retains 96.4% of the original full-token performance and delivers up to 2.30 times faster end-to-end inference speed.

Conclusion: CaRe demonstrates that calibrating compact visual representations before reasoning is an effective training-free strategy to preserve semantic fidelity in VLMs during aggressive visual token reduction, achieving strong efficiency gains without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) suffer from prohibitive inference overhead due to long sequences of visual tokens. However, existing visual token reduction methods mainly improve efficiency by pruning or compressing redundant tokens without examining whether the resulting representation remains semantically consistent with the original representation. Mapping the original N-token visual sequence to K tokens may discard, dilute, or misassign critical visual cues, triggering severe semantic drift that deviates the VLM's understanding. In this paper, we first introduce the principle of 'Calibrate Before Reason' to visual token reduction and propose CaRe, a training-free robust framework that calibrates compact visual representations before reasoning to preserve semantic fidelity in VLMs. CaRe consists of two mutually complementary modules: 1) Perturbation-Robust Calibration Anchoring, which identifies calibration anchors with stable model-side influence under multi-directional perturbations; 2) Confidence-Gated Token Calibration, which extracts reliable calibration signals from unselected tokens and injects them into anchors. Extensive evaluations across diverse VLM architectures and benchmarks verify that CaRe outperforms state-of-the-art token reduction baselines. While pruning 94.4% of visual tokens, our method retains 96.4% of the original full-token performance, delivering up to 2.30 times faster end-to-end inference speed relative to unpruned vanilla models.

</details>


### [27] [PrintAnything: Learning an Intermediate Representation for 3D printing G-code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27729)
*Sangmin Hong,Daniel Sungho Jung,Heewon Kim,Kyoung Mu Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PrintAnything is a novel framework that generates executable 3D printing G-code directly from point clouds, bypassing the need for watertight mesh reconstruction. It introduces a slice-wise point projection strategy and a Geometric plan (G-plan) map—a compact 2D representation with occupancy, region, and flow maps—to bridge point clouds and toolpath synthesis in a fully mesh-free pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most 3D printing pipelines require watertight meshes as input, which prevents direct use of point clouds. Existing workaround approaches reconstruct meshes from point clouds, but the resulting meshes often contain geometric artifacts (incorrect faces, topological inconsistencies) that are difficult to repair and can lead to printing failures. The authors aim to eliminate this mesh dependency entirely.

Method: The framework learns to generate executable G-code directly from point clouds. It introduces a slice-wise point projection strategy that transforms unstructured 3D point clouds into slice-aligned 2D representations matching the layer-by-layer nature of fused deposition modeling. It also proposes the Geometric plan (G-plan) map, a compact 2D representation composed of occupancy, region, and flow maps that encode geometric and extrusion properties needed for toolpath synthesis.

Result: The proposed method accurately generates printable G-code directly from point clouds, achieving a practical and fully mesh-free pipeline for 3D printing. Code is publicly available on GitHub.

Conclusion: PrintAnything successfully overcomes the limitation of mesh dependency in 3D printing by enabling direct point-cloud-to-G-code generation, providing a mesh-free alternative pipeline that avoids the artifacts and failures associated with mesh reconstruction.

Abstract: Point clouds are one of the most fundamental and widely used 3D representations, serving as the most basic geometric representation of 3D shapes. Nevertheless, most existing 3D printing pipelines require a watertight mesh as input, preventing the direct use of point clouds for fabrication. A common workaround is to reconstruct meshes from point clouds; however, the resulting meshes often contain geometric artifacts, such as incorrect faces or topological inconsistencies, that are difficult to repair and may lead to printing failures. To overcome these limitations, we propose PrintAnything, a novel framework that learns to produce executable 3D printing G-code directly from 3D point clouds without requiring mesh reconstruction. To enable point clouds to serve as direct input for slice-wise toolpath generation, we introduce a slice-wise point projection strategy that transforms unstructured 3D point clouds into slice-aligned 2D representations consistent with layer-by-layer nature of fused deposition modeling in 3D printing. To eliminate mesh dependency and provide a unified representation that bridges point clouds and G-code, we propose Geometric plan (G-plan) map, a compact 2D representation composed of occupancy, region, and flow maps that encode the geometric and extrusion properties required for toolpath synthesis in 3D printing. As a result, our proposed method accurately generates printable G-code directly from point clouds, enabling a practical and fully mesh-free pipeline for 3D printing. The code is publicly available at \href{https://github.com/Sangminhong/PrintAnything}{https://github.com/Sangminhong/PrintAnything}.

</details>


### [28] [Articulated Object Reconstruction from Rest-State Observation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27749)
*Daeun Lee,Jaeah Lee,Woosung Kim,Haebeom Jung,Jaesik Park*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces a rest-state formulation for reconstructing articulated objects from a single closed configuration, using an explicit mesh intermediate representation for cross-model verification/fusion and a video diffusion model to synthesize and validate articulation hypotheses through geometric consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for articulated object reconstruction require observable motion from multiple articulation states, but the setting of reconstructing from a single closed configuration is inherently ill-posed and remains unsolved.

Method: The framework uses an explicit mesh as an intermediate representation to reconcile noisy outputs from vision-language and segmentation models into spatially consistent part structures. Joint parameters are estimated without observed motion by using a video diffusion model to synthesize articulation hypotheses, validated through geometric consistency.

Result: The approach achieves accurate part decomposition and physically plausible articulation, performing competitively with motion-observing reconstruction-based, generation-based, and modular pretrained-model baselines.

Conclusion: Reconstructing articulated objects from a single closed configuration is feasible by compensating for the absence of motion cues with geometry, semantics, and motion priors, achieving competitive performance without requiring observed motion.

Abstract: Building interactive digital twins requires recovering both 3D geometry and the kinematic structures that govern how objects articulate. Yet existing methods for articulated object reconstruction require explicitly observable motion from multiple articulation states. We introduce a rest-state formulation that reconstructs articulated objects from a single closed configuration, an inherently ill-posed setting where geometry, semantics, and motion priors compensate for the absence of motion cues. Our framework adopts an explicit mesh as an intermediate representation for cross-model verification and fusion, reconciling noisy outputs from vision-language and segmentation models into spatially consistent part structures. To estimate joint parameters without observed motion, we use a video diffusion model to synthesize articulation hypotheses and validate them through geometric consistency. Our approach achieves accurate part decomposition and physically plausible articulation, performing competitively with motion-observing reconstruction-based, generation-based, and modular pretrained-model baselines.

</details>


### [29] [EgoGVAE: Ego-body Mesh Reconstruction via Guided Variational Autoencoder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27755)
*Jaehun Jung,Wonjun Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes a novel method for recovering full-body mesh from head pose only, using a variational autoencoder-based guidance network whose latent distribution is aligned with a head-to-motion network. This enables one-step sampling that is over 50× faster than diffusion-based approaches while improving ego-body mesh reconstruction performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing head-conditioned generative models for full-body mesh recovery from head pose rely on diffusion-based iterative processes, which are computationally expensive and time-consuming. There is a need for a faster yet effective alternative.

Method: A two-network framework: (1) a guidance network, a variational autoencoder taking full-body poses as input to learn latent distributions, and (2) a head-to-motion network whose latent distribution is enforced to be similar to the guidance network's distribution. By decoding latent features sampled from the guided (aligned) distribution, natural full-body poses can be produced from only head poses via a one-step sampling mechanism.

Result: The proposed method achieves remarkably fast inference, more than 50 times faster than diffusion-based approaches, while efficiently improving ego-body mesh reconstruction performance on benchmark datasets.

Conclusion: Aligning the latent distribution of a lightweight head-to-motion network with a full-body pose-conditioned VAE guidance network enables one-step, fast, and accurate full-body mesh recovery from head pose only, offering a practical and efficient alternative to diffusion-based methods.

Abstract: We address the problem of recovering the full-body mesh from only the head pose. This task has become essential for various applications based on head-mounted devices or smart glasses. The challenge of this task lies in estimating the pose information of unobserved body parts based solely on a single joint (i.e., head) trajectory. Several studies have begun to adopt head-conditioned generative models, however, such previous methods are costly and time-consuming due to the diffusion-based iterative process. As an alternative, we propose a simple yet novel method that leverages the latent space of the guidance network, which is designed as a variational autoencoder taking full-body poses as inputs. By enforcing latent distributions of this guidance network and our head-to-motion network to be similar, latent features sampled from the 'guided' distribution, i.e., distribution learned in our head-to-motion network, can be reliably decoded for natural representations of full-body poses even only with the head pose. One important advantage of the proposed method is that one-step sampling scheme achieves remarkably fast inference (more than 50 times faster) compared to diffusion-based approaches. Experimental results on benchmark datasets show that the proposed method efficiently improves the performance of ego-body mesh reconstruction.

</details>


### [30] [DS@GT ARC at ImageCLEFmedical 2026: Architectural Diversity for Concept Detection and Foundation-Model Scaling for Caption Prediction in Medical Image Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27763)
*Bowen Wang,Youwen Zhang,Ritesh Mehta*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DS@GT submissions to ImageCLEFmedical Caption 2026: For Concept Detection (Task 1), a late-fusion ensemble of ConvNeXt-V2, BiomedCLIP ViT-B/16, and DenseNet-169 with Honest Threshold Tuning ranked first (F1=0.5790), while a training-free KNN retrieval over frozen BiomedCLIP embeddings nearly matched it (F1=0.5780). For Caption Prediction (Task 2), a fine-tuned Gemma-3 27B ranked third (0.3571), alongside a BLIP pipeline (0.3564) and zero-shot MedGemma-4B (0.3186).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To compete in and advance the ImageCLEFmedical Caption 2026 challenge, a long-running benchmark on ROCOv2, which includes Concept Detection (assigning UMLS CUIs) and Caption Prediction (generating natural-language captions). The team explores both high-accuracy fine-tuned ensembles and cost-efficient training-free baselines to characterize the performance-cost trade-off.

Method: Task 1: A three-way late-fusion ensemble of ConvNeXt-V2, BiomedCLIP ViT-B/16, and DenseNet-169 using a regularized 'Honest Threshold Tuning' procedure to avoid validation overfitting on rare concepts. In parallel, a training-free KNN retrieval pipeline over frozen BiomedCLIP embeddings. Task 2: A fine-tuned Gemma-3 27B, a fully fine-tuned BLIP pipeline with custom Vizwins merging, and a zero-shot MedGemma-4B run with a PubMed-style prompt.

Result: Task 1: ensemble ranked first with primary F1=0.5790 and secondary F1=0.9657; KNN retrieval achieved primary F1=0.5780 and secondary F1=0.9599, essentially matching the fine-tuned ensemble at much lower cost. Task 2: Gemma-3 27B scored 0.3571 (third), BLIP scored 0.3564, and zero-shot MedGemma-4B scored 0.3186.

Conclusion: An ensemble with careful threshold regularization achieves state-of-the-art performance in concept detection, while a training-free retrieval approach provides a competitive, cost-effective alternative. For caption generation, fine-tuned transformer and vision-language models of varying scales all perform well, with the largest model ranking third.

Abstract: We describe the DS@GT submissions to the ImageCLEFmedical Caption 2026 challenge, which continues a long-running benchmark on the ROCOv2 dataset with two tracks: Concept Detection (Task 1), assigning UMLS Concept Unique Identifiers (CUIs) to radiology images, and Caption Prediction (Task 2), generating natural-language captions. For Task 1, our primary submission was a three-way late-fusion ensemble of ConvNeXt-V2, BiomedCLIP ViT-B/16, and DenseNet-169 with a regularized ''Honest Threshold Tuning'' procedure designed to avoid validation overfitting on rare concepts; this submission ranked first on the official submission with a primary $F_1$ of $0.5790$ and a secondary $F_1$ of $0.9657$. In parallel, we submitted a training-free KNN retrieval pipeline over frozen BiomedCLIP embeddings, which reached a primary $F_1$ of $0.5780$ and a secondary $F_1$ of $0.9599$-essentially matching the fine-tuned ensemble on the primary track at a fraction of the cost. For Task 2, our submissions included a fine-tuned Gemma-3 27B model (overall $0.3571$, ranking third in the official submission), a fully fine-tuned BLIP pipeline with custom Vizwins merging ($0.3564$), and a zero-shot MedGemma-4B run with a PubMed-style prompt ($0.3186$), spanning a wide range of model scales and training costs. Code: https://github.com/dsgt-arc/imageclef-caption-2026.

</details>


### [31] [Private Face Recognition Training Dataset Publication via Identity-Decoupled and Geometry-Preserving Face Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27764)
*Shuhuan Chen,Xiangyu Zhu,Weisong Zhao,Siran Peng,Tianshuo Zhang,Haoyuan Zhang,Haichao Shi,Xiao-Yu Zhang,Zhen Lei*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Private Face Distillation, a framework for publishing private face recognition training datasets that decouples source-identity semantics from recognition-useful proxy identity geometry. It uses Orthogonal Geometry Preservation to construct decoupled proxy identities while maintaining hyperspherical geometry, and Relational Topology Alignment to preserve identity relations. Experiments show it outperforms publication baselines, improving TAR@FAR=1e-3 by 3.94% on IJB-C surveillance while reducing linkability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Publishing private FR training datasets is privacy-sensitive because faces expose identity information. Existing approaches face an identity paradox: identity cues that make released faces useful for recognition are also the cues that make them linkable to real individuals. The paper argues this paradox stems from conflating source-aligned identity semantics (which should be suppressed) with recognition-useful proxy identity geometry (which should be preserved).

Method: The proposed Private Face Distillation framework has two key components: (1) Orthogonal Geometry Preservation, which constructs decoupled proxy identities from private identity representations while maintaining hyperspherical geometry, and (2) Relational Topology Alignment, which preserves identity relations to support recognition learning on the published data.

Result: Experiments across multiple domain-shifted FR scenarios show Private Face Distillation achieves stronger utility than evaluated publication baselines. On IJB-C surveillance, it improves TAR@FAR=1e-3 by 3.94% over the baseline while simultaneously reducing source-identity linkability.

Conclusion: Private FR training dataset publication should decouple source-identity correspondence while preserving proxy identity geometry. This separation between source-aligned identity semantics and recognition-useful geometry resolves the identity paradox and enables both effective FR model training and reduced privacy linkage risk.

Abstract: Publishing private face recognition~(FR) training datasets is privacy-sensitive because faces expose identity information. Private FR training dataset publication mitigates this risk by releasing protected proxies as substitutes for private training faces. However, training FR models with such data introduces an identity paradox: \emph{the identity cues that make released faces useful for recognition supervision are also the cues that make them linkable to real individuals.} A protected face should be decoupled from the original identity, yet still behave as a reliable identity sample for training. Removing these cues too aggressively may destroy the class structure needed for recognition learning, whereas preserving them too faithfully may increase source-identity linkability. We argue that this paradox stems from conflating source-aligned identity semantics with recognition-useful proxy identity geometry. The former should be suppressed to reduce linkage to private individuals, while the latter should be preserved for FR learning. Based on this insight, we propose \textbf{Private Face Distillation}, an identity-decoupling and geometry-preserving framework. It uses Orthogonal Geometry Preservation to construct decoupled proxy identities from private identity representations while maintaining hyperspherical geometry, and Relational Topology Alignment to preserve identity relations for recognition learning. Experiments across multiple domain-shifted FR scenarios show that Private Face Distillation achieves stronger utility than the evaluated publication baselines. On IJB-C surveillance, it improves $\mathrm{TAR}@\mathrm{FAR}{=}1\text{e-}{3}$ by 3.94\% over the baseline while reducing source-identity linkability. These results suggest that private FR training dataset publication should decouple source-identity correspondence while preserving proxy identity geometry.

</details>


### [32] [CXR-Retrieve: Compositional Text-to-Image Retrieval in Chest Radiography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27779)
*Tomer Erez,Moshe Kimhi,Chaim Baskin,Ehud Rivlin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CXR-Retrieve is a benchmark for compositional chest X-ray text-to-image retrieval with 5,159 test images and 145 queries covering conjunctive and negative findings. The authors propose a label-aware contrastive fine-tuning objective that explicitly models pathology constraints (including confirmed absences), improving Precision@5 by 8.5 points on conjunctions and 22.0 points on negations over CXR-CLIP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large chest radiography archives are hard to search because studies are paired with free-text reports rather than structured annotations. Existing biomedical vision-language models are optimized for report-to-image matching, not short clinical queries, leading to an objective mismatch where models may retrieve images matching query words but fail the full clinical constraint (e.g., "atelectasis and no pneumonia").

Method: The authors introduce CXR-Retrieve, a structured benchmark built from the MIMIC-CXR-JPG test split containing 5,159 images and 145 textual queries spanning single/conjunction findings with positive and negative assertions. They also propose a label-aware contrastive fine-tuning objective that attracts image-text pairs with compatible asserted pathology constraints (including shared confirmed absences) while explicitly repelling contradictory pairs.

Result: Starting from the in-domain CXR-CLIP checkpoint, the proposed method improves Precision@5 over CXR-CLIP by 8.5 percentage points on two-pathology conjunctions and by 22.0 percentage points on negation queries.

Conclusion: Reliable chest X-ray retrieval requires training objectives that model not only which findings are mentioned, but also how they are clinically asserted—i.e., the assertion status of pathologies (positive or negative) must be explicitly captured in the contrastive objective.

Abstract: Large chest radiography archives are difficult to search because most studies are paired only with free-text reports rather than structured clinical annotations. Vision-language models offer a natural interface for text-to-image retrieval, but current biomedical models are primarily optimized for report-to-image matching rather than for satisfying short clinical search queries. This creates an objective mismatch: a model may retrieve images related to words in the query while failing to satisfy the full clinical constraint, especially for conjunctions and negations such as ``atelectasis and no pneumonia.''
  We introduce CXR-Retrieve, a structured benchmark for compositional chest X-ray text-to-image retrieval. The benchmark contains 5,159 test images from the official test-split of MIMIC-CXR-JPG and 145 textual queries spanning single and conjunction findings, both positive and negative. Relevance is defined by whether a retrieved image satisfies all asserted pathology constraints, rather than by whether it matches a paired report.
  We further propose a label-aware contrastive fine-tuning objective for clinical retrieval. Our method attracts image-text pairs with compatible asserted pathology constraints, including shared confirmed absences, while explicitly repelling contradictory pairs. Starting from the in-domain CXR-CLIP checkpoint, our method improves Precision@5 over CXR-CLIP by 8.5 percentage points on two-pathology conjunctions and by 22.0 percentage points on negation queries. These results show that reliable chest X-ray retrieval requires training objectives that model not only which findings are mentioned, but also how they are clinically asserted.

</details>


### [33] [FDDWAN: A Frequency-Decoupled Diffusion Network for Watermarking Attack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27800)
*Chunpeng Wang,Yuxin Li,Xiaoyu Wang,Jidong Yang,Suo Gao,Qi Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FDDWAN is a coarse-to-fine invisible watermark removal framework using wavelet-domain decomposition and residual diffusion refinement, achieving a better trade-off between watermark suppression and perceptual fidelity than existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing invisible watermark removal methods struggle to accurately capture watermark-bearing features, resulting in an unfavorable trade-off between watermark suppression and perceptual fidelity.

Method: FDDWAN consists of two stages: (1) the Wavelet-based Frequency-domain Preliminary Attack Module (WFPAM) decomposes watermarked images into low- and high-frequency subbands and applies frequency-specific attack strategies; (2) the Frequency-domain Residual Diffusion Attack Module (FRDAM) separately models residual distributions between preliminary attacked outputs and watermark-free references, selectively refining frequency-domain residuals to target remaining watermark discrepancies while minimizing content modification.

Result: Experiments on CelebA and ImageNet across four representative watermarking schemes show FDDWAN achieves a more favorable trade-off between watermark removal effectiveness and visual fidelity compared to conventional and learning-based attack methods.

Conclusion: Frequency-decoupled decomposition combined with residual-guided diffusion refinement provides an effective coarse-to-fine strategy for invisible watermark removal that balances attack strength with perceptual quality.

Abstract: Existing invisible watermark removal methods often struggle to accurately capture the watermark-bearing features, leading to an unfavorable trade-off between watermark suppression and perceptual fidelity. In this paper, we propose the Frequency-Decoupled Diffusion Watermark Attack Network (FDDWAN), a coarse-to-fine framework that performs watermark removal through wavelet-domain decomposition and residual diffusion refinement. In the initial stage, the Wavelet-based Frequency-domain Preliminary Attack Module (WFPAM) decomposes the watermarked image into low- and high-frequency subbands and applies frequency-specific attack strategies tailored to their respective contributions to watermark robustness and perceptual quality. In the next stage, the Frequency-domain Residual Diffusion Attack Module (FRDAM) separately models the residual distributions between the preliminarily attacked outputs and the corresponding watermark-free references during training. Rather than reconstructing the entire image, FRDAM selectively refines frequency-domain residuals, directing the diffusion process toward the remaining watermark related discrepancies while minimizing modifications to image content. Extensive experiments on CelebA and ImageNet across four representative watermarking schemes demonstrate that FDDWAN achieves a more favorable trade-off between watermark removal effectiveness and visual fidelity than conventional and learning-based attack methods.

</details>


### [34] [LoMeVQA: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Longitudinal Medical VQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27806)
*Zhilin Wu,Zhangkai Ni,Chengmei Yang,Longzhen Yang,Yihang Liu,Ying Wen,Lianghua He*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces LoMeVQA, a comprehensive benchmark with 206K longitudinal VQA pairs for temporal medical image analysis, and MedLong-8B, a model achieving state-of-the-art performance across five tasks in this benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Longitudinal medical visual reasoning remains largely underexplored despite rapid advancement of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Since patients often undergo multiple imaging examinations over successive visits, modeling temporal information is critical for reliable assessment of disease progression and treatment response, yet existing benchmarks and models fail to address this need.

Method: The authors build LoMeVQA via an automated pipeline that (1) organizes patient records chronologically, (2) extracts clinically meaningful entities using a medical knowledge graph, and (3) models temporal evolution to guide LLMs in generating high-quality longitudinal VQA pairs. The benchmark covers five tasks: progress classification, progress description, progress report generation, differential region grounding, and differential region description. They also introduce MedLong-8B to address the identified limitations.

Result: Extensive evaluations show both general-purpose and medical-domain MLLMs perform poorly on LoMeVQA, revealing substantial limitations in temporal reasoning. MedLong-8B achieves state-of-the-art performance across all five tasks. Detailed analyses uncover key failure modes in existing models.

Conclusion: Longitudinal medical visual reasoning is a significant gap for current MLLMs, and LoMeVQA provides a comprehensive benchmark to drive progress. MedLong-8B demonstrates the feasibility of improving temporal reasoning in medical imaging, and the failure mode analyses offer actionable insights for future improvements.

Abstract: In clinical practice, patients often undergo multiple imaging examinations over successive visits, yielding longitudinal data. Modeling such temporal information is crucial for reliable assessment of disease progression and treatment response. However, despite the rapid advancement of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), longitudinal medical visual reasoning remains largely underexplored. To fill this gap, we propose LoMeVQA, a comprehensive benchmark consisting of 206K longitudinal visual question answering (VQA) pairs for temporal medical image analysis. LoMeVQA covers five tasks: progress classification, progress description, progress report generation, differential region grounding, and differential region description. To construct the dataset, we develop an automated pipeline that (1) organizes patient records chronologically, (2) extracts clinically meaningful entities via a medical knowledge graph, and (3) models their temporal evolution to guide large language models in generating high-quality longitudinal VQA pairs. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that both general-purpose and medical-domain MLLMs perform poorly on LoMeVQA, revealing substantial limitations in temporal reasoning. To address these limitations, we introduce MedLong-8B, which achieves state-of-the-art performance across all tasks. Beyond benchmarking, we conduct detailed analyses that uncover key failure modes and shed light on how to improve longitudinal medical visual reasoning. Our data is available at: https://github.com/pepperbubble/LoMeVQA

</details>


### [35] [SPFM-Net: Semantic-Prior-Guided Frequency-Constrained Mamba for Invisible Watermark Attack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27811)
*Chunpeng Wang,Yanan Shi,Zhiqiu Xia,Jidong Yang,Suo Gao,Qi Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SPFM-Net is a semantic-prior-guided and frequency-constrained Mamba framework for invisible watermark attacks, using high-ratio masking, a partially fine-tuned Masked Autoencoder, multi-scale residual frequency feature interaction, and a Mamba-based global state-space feature modeling unit to achieve a favorable trade-off between watermark removal effectiveness and perceptual fidelity across diverse watermarking schemes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing watermark attacks rely on predefined signal-processing operations or locally constrained restoration networks, which fail to capture long-range dependencies of globally distributed watermark signals and suffer from an unfavorable trade-off between removal effectiveness and visual fidelity.

Method: SPFM-Net employs: (1) high-ratio masking to disrupt spatial coherence of watermark signals; (2) a partially fine-tuned pretrained Masked Autoencoder for semantically consistent reconstruction while suppressing watermark information; (3) a Multi-scale Residual Frequency Feature Interaction module to aggregate watermark-related residual features across receptive fields while suppressing irrelevant regions; (4) a lightweight Mamba-based Global State-space Feature Modeling (GSFM) unit to capture long-range dependencies and separate watermark features from image content; (5) a multi-level objective with spatial-, frequency-, and edge-domain constraints for optimization.

Result: Extensive experiments on spatial-domain, transform-domain, orthogonal moment-based, and deep learning-based watermarking schemes demonstrate that SPFM-Net achieves a favorable trade-off between watermark attack effectiveness and perceptual fidelity.

Conclusion: SPFM-Net effectively addresses the limitations of prior watermark attack methods by integrating semantic priors, frequency-domain modeling, and Mamba-based global state-space modeling, delivering superior watermark suppression while preserving perceptual quality across diverse watermarking paradigms.

Abstract: Existing watermark attacks typically rely on predefined signal-processing operations or locally constrained restoration networks, making it difficult to capture the long-range dependencies of globally distributed watermark signals and resulting in an unfavorable trade-off between removal effectiveness and visual fidelity. In this paper, we propose SPFM-Net, a semantic-prior-guided and frequency-constrained Mamba framework for invisible watermark attack. SPFM-Net first employs high-ratio masking to disrupt the spatial coherence of invisible watermark signals, and then utilizes a partially fine-tuned pretrained Masked Autoencoder to reconstruct semantically consistent image from sparse observations while suppressing watermark-related information. A Multi-scale Residual Frequency Feature Interaction module subsequently aggregates watermark-related residual features across multiple receptive fields, while adaptively suppressing responses from watermark-irrelevant regions. To further capture the long-range dependencies of globally distributed watermark signals, a lightweight Mamba-based Global State-space Feature Modeling (GSFM) unit is introduced to separate watermark-related features from natural image content and suppress the remaining watermark traces. In addition, SPFM-Net is optimized using a multi-level objective that jointly imposes spatial-, frequency-, and edge-domain constraints, enabling effective watermark suppression while preserving perceptual quality. Extensive experiments on representative spatial-domain, transform-domain, orthogonal moment-based, and deep learning-based watermarking schemes demonstrate that SPFM-Net achieves a favorable trade-off between watermark attack effectiveness and perceptual fidelity.

</details>


### [36] [Hallucinations Leave a Grounding Signature:Verifier-Guided Decoding for Selective Object Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27823)
*Lei Yang,Xinze Liu,Dayan Wu,Ding Wang,Hengjie Zhu,Zihao Zhang,Tianzhu Hu,Hanqi Wu,Peng Fu,Zheng Lin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Verifier-Guided Decoding (VGD), a decoding framework that leverages an Intrinsic Grounding Signature (IGS)—a distributed signed attention pattern encoding visual support for object mentions—to detect and roll back hallucinated object mentions during LVLM generation. VGD suppresses hallucinated objects and their synonyms while preserving grounded object coverage and visual understanding, achieving state-of-the-art hallucination reduction on CHAIR and AMBER-G benchmarks without shortening captions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LVLMs frequently hallucinate absent objects, and existing mitigation methods lack reliable object-level grounding diagnostics. They apply coarse-grained interventions that impair visual understanding, shorten responses, and reduce coverage of genuinely grounded objects. The key challenge is detecting whether each emerging object mention is visually supported during generation so hallucination can be mitigated selectively.

Method: The paper first identifies an Intrinsic Grounding Signature (IGS)—a distributed signed attention pattern in the model that remains informative even for confident hallucinations where output confidence reflects next-token plausibility rather than visual support. Based on IGS, VGD employs a lightweight verifier that examines each emerging object mention, rolls back the KV cache when a mention is flagged as high risk, suppresses the object and synonyms, and regenerates the affected continuation. Interventions are applied only to high-risk object mentions, preserving visual understanding and grounded coverage elsewhere.

Result: Experiments on CHAIR and AMBER-G show VGD achieves state-of-the-art hallucination reduction: at @rec90, it cuts AMBER-G CHAIR by 43.6% while retaining 99.6% of grounded-object coverage, and reduces CHAIR-MSCOCO CHAIR_i/CHAIR_s by 37.0%/30.4% without shortening captions.

Conclusion: VGD demonstrates that selectively intervening only on high-risk object mentions—guided by an intrinsic attention-based grounding signature—can substantially reduce object hallucination while preserving the model's original visual understanding and grounded object coverage, overcoming the limitations of coarse-grained mitigation approaches.

Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate objects that are absent from an image. Despite recent progress, existing mitigation methods still lack reliable object-level grounding diagnostics and therefore tend to apply coarse-grained interventions, which can impair visual understanding, shorten responses, and reduce coverage of genuinely grounded objects. The key challenge is thus to detect, during generation, whether each emerging object mention is supported by reliable visual evidence, so that hallucination can be mitigated selectively. Yet output confidence reflects next-token plausibility rather than visual support, allowing language priors to make absent objects appear certain. We show that the missing diagnostic evidence is encoded in an Intrinsic Grounding Signature (IGS), a distributed signed attention pattern that remains informative for such confident hallucinations. Based on IGS, we propose Verifier-Guided Decoding (VGD), a decoding framework in which a lightweight verifier examines each emerging object mention, rolls back the KV cache when the mention is identified as high risk, suppresses the object and its synonyms, and regenerates the affected continuation. Because VGD intervenes only on object mentions identified as high risk, it reduces object hallucination while preserving the model's original visual understanding and grounded object coverage. Experiments on CHAIR and AMBER-G show that VGD achieves state-of-the-art object hallucination reduction: at @rec90, it cuts AMBER-G CHAIR by 43.6\% while retaining 99.6\% of grounded-object coverage, and reduces CHAIR-MSCOCO CHAIR$_i$/CHAIR$_s$ by 37.0\%/30.4\% without shortening captions.

</details>


### [37] [Thinking Once Is Enough: Intermediate-Layer Evidence Routing for High-Resolution VQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27830)
*Zhongkuan Mao,Xianjie Liu,Tianyu Meng,Yidong Wang,Wenzhuo Zhao,Ronghao Xian,Yao Jiang,Fei Shen,Junfeng Fang,Yong Dai,Yi Zhang,Keren Fu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Thinking-Once is a training-free, single-visual-pass evidence-routing method for high-resolution visual question answering (HR-VQA) that re-routes question-conditioned attention at an intermediate-layer routing window, preserving core entity tokens and compact background context without extra visual encoding. It consistently improves or matches five base models across V*Bench, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K, achieving a cross-benchmark mean of 82.7 with ZwZ-8B and reducing inference time by 97.2% over DeepScan while improving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper challenges the prevailing assumption that HR-VQA failures stem from insufficient evidence acquisition (requiring cropping, re-encoding, or multi-round search). The authors demonstrate that fine-grained evidence often already survives visual encoding and becomes identifiable within an intermediate-layer routing window, but is later diluted before answer generation. This reframing motivates a method that routes existing evidence rather than acquiring new visual inputs.

Method: Thinking-Once is a training-free, single-visual-pass approach that reconstructs question-conditioned attention at an intermediate-layer routing window, preserves core entity tokens and compact background context, and routes this evidence to later layers. It avoids additional visual encoding by leveraging evidence already present in the model's intermediate representations.

Result: Across five base models, Thinking-Once improves or matches the base setting, increasing average scores on V*Bench, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K by +3.1, +3.0, and +2.7 points while reducing average peak memory by about 4GB. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it improves the three benchmarks by +9.9, +4.6, and +5.5 points (mean 72.5→79.1). With ZwZ-8B it reaches a mean of 82.7. Against 11 open-source HR-VQA baselines, it achieves the best or tied-best score on all three benchmark averages and the best overall mean, reducing V*Bench inference time by 97.2% versus DeepScan while improving the cross-benchmark mean from 77.8 to 79.1.

Conclusion: HR-VQA can be substantially improved by routing already-encoded evidence rather than repeatedly acquiring new visual inputs. This demonstrates that the problem is not solely about insufficient evidence acquisition but also about evidence dilution in later layers, and that single-pass evidence routing offers an effective, training-free, memory-efficient alternative to multi-pass approaches.

Abstract: High-resolution visual question answering (HR-VQA) is often treated as a problem of insufficient evidence acquisition, where failing multimodal large language models must inspect images again through cropping, re-encoding, or multi-round search. We show that this view is incomplete: in many cases, fine-grained evidence has already survived visual encoding and become identifiable and influential within an intermediate-layer routing window, but is later diluted before answer generation. We propose Thinking-Once, a \textbf{training-free, single-visual-pass} evidence-routing method that reconstructs question-conditioned attention at this window, preserves core entity tokens and compact background context, and routes this evidence to later layers without extra visual encoding. Across five base models, Thinking-Once consistently improves or matches the corresponding base setting, increasing the average scores on V$^*$Bench, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K by \textit{+3.1}, \textit{+3.0}, and \textit{+2.7} points while reducing the average peak memory by about 4,GB. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it improves the three benchmarks by \textit{+9.9}, \textit{+4.6}, and \textit{+5.5} points, raising the cross-benchmark mean from 72.5 to 79.1. With the ZwZ-8B base model, Thinking-Once reaches a mean score of 82.7. Against 11 open-source HR-VQA baselines, it obtains the best or tied-best score on all three benchmark averages and the best overall mean; for example, compared with DeepScan, it reduces V$^*$Bench inference time by \textbf{97.2\%} while improving the cross-benchmark mean from 77.8 to 79.1. These results show that HR-VQA can be improved by routing already encoded evidence rather than repeatedly acquiring new visual inputs. Code is available in the appendix.

</details>


### [38] [SAFViT: Spatial Attention Fusion Gating for Vision Transformer-Based Nucleus Segmentation and Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27835)
*Harshit Mittal,Arash Rabbani*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Spatial Attention Fusion (SAF) Gating module that replaces standard skip connections in a CellViT-based encoder-decoder model for cell segmentation and classification. The SAF gate fuses encoder and upsampled decoder features via pointwise convolutions and a channel-wise softmax to produce a per-pixel "heatmap of trust," improving detection of the minority "Dead" cell class. On PanNuke and MoNuSeg datasets, SAF Gating outperforms six gating alternatives, achieving the highest multi-class panoptic quality (mPQ) of 0.471, driven primarily by a 14.5-point improvement in Dead-class F1 score over the ungated baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard direct skip connections in encoder-decoder architectures treat every spatial location equally, causing redundant and potentially conflicting information to reach the decoder. Existing gating mechanisms primarily filter encoder information but neglect leveraging global contextual information from the decoder, leaving room for more effective feature fusion in cell segmentation and classification.

Method: The proposed SAF Gating module is integrated into a CellViT-based model, replacing conventional skip connections. Each SAF gate concatenates encoder skip features with upsampled decoder features, compresses them through two pointwise convolutions with an intermediate ReLU activation, and applies a channel-wise softmax to produce a per-pixel "heatmap of trust" that sums to unity at every spatial location, allowing the network to learn the trustworthiness of each feature source.

Result: SAF Gating achieves the highest mPQ of 0.471 on PanNuke among all compared methods, including no gating, attention gates, squeeze-and-excitation, CBAM, cross-attention, and attentional feature fusion. The performance gain is primarily driven by a 14.5-point improvement in Dead-class F1 score compared to the ungated CellViT baseline, with evaluations also conducted on the MoNuSeg dataset.

Conclusion: Incorporating decoder contextual information into the gating mechanism via SAF significantly improves cell segmentation and classification performance, particularly for minority classes like "Dead" cells, demonstrating that bidirectional feature fusion across encoder and decoder is more effective than encoder-only filtering approaches.

Abstract: Accurate cell segmentation and classification are foundational to digital pathology, enabling quantitative tissue analysis for diagnosis and treatment planning. Encoder-decoder architectures that fuse multi-scale features through skip connections have become the dominant paradigm for this task, yet standard direct skip connections treat every spatial location equally, which leads to redundant and potentially conflicting information reaching the decoder. To overcome this problem, various gating mechanisms have been introduced, but most of them operate solely on filtering encoder information, neglecting the benefit of global contextual information from the decoder. This study proposes replacing conventional skip connections in a CellViT-based model with a novel Spatial Attention Fusion (SAF) Gating module. Each SAF gate concatenates the encoder skip and upsampled decoder features, compresses them through two pointwise convolutions with an intermediate ReLU, and applies a channel-wise softmax to produce a per-pixel "heatmap of trust" that sums to unity at every spatial location, allowing the network to learn where each source is most trustworthy. The resulting fused features improve the model's ability to detect the minority "Dead" class, which in turn enhances the multi-class panoptic quality (mPQ) on the PanNuke dataset. SAF Gating is compared against six gating alternatives including no gating, attention gates, squeeze-and-excitation, CBAM, cross-attention, and attentional feature fusion on PanNuke and MoNuSeg datasets. SAF Gating achieves the highest mPQ (0.471), a gain driven primarily by a 14.5-point improvement in Dead-class F1 score compared to ungated CellViT baseline.

</details>


### [39] [FeatFix: Reuse What You Verify through Local Exact-Feature Correction for Faster Cached Diffusion Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27842)
*Hanshuai Cui,Zhiqing Tang,Zhi Yao,Qianli Ma,Fanshuai Meng,Weijia Jia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FeatFix is a training-free acceleration method for diffusion models that reuses exact block features computed during verification as corrections, replacing draft outputs at fixed sparse layer-timestep sites to reduce feature error and achieve up to 6.70x speedup over vanilla diffusion inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models are computationally intensive due to iterative denoising. Existing training-free accelerators reuse cached intermediate features or forecast future ones, but when an exact feature is computed for verification, it is typically discarded after measuring discrepancy. The authors observe this exact feature can be reused for correction, resetting local draft residual and reducing downstream error.

Method: FeatFix operates at a fixed sparse set of layer-timestep sites. At each selected site, it replaces the complete draft block output with the exact output computed from the same incoming state. This avoids token- or channel-level partial replacement and full-timestep recomputation. The previously computed verification feature is forwarded at the verification site to reset the local draft residual.

Result: Experiments across four image and video backbones show FeatFix consistently accelerates generation, achieving a speedup of up to 6.70x over Vanilla while maintaining competitive output quality.

Conclusion: Reusing verification-computed exact features for local correction is an effective strategy to control draft drift and accelerate diffusion inference without training, improving both speed and output quality compared to prior caching/forecasting methods.

Abstract: Diffusion models are widely used to generate high-quality images and videos, but their iterative denoising process remains computationally intensive. A growing class of training-free accelerators reduces this cost by reusing cached intermediate features or forecasting future ones. To control draft drift, these methods sometimes compute an exact block feature for verification. Yet the resulting exact feature is typically used only to measure discrepancy or guide a later decision and is then discarded. We find that this previously computed feature can instead be reused for correction. Forwarding it at the verification site resets the local draft residual and reduces downstream feature error. Based on this observation, we introduce FeatFix, a local exact-feature correction method for cached diffusion inference. FeatFix operates at a fixed sparse set of layer--timestep sites. At each selected site, it replaces the complete draft block output with the exact output computed from the same incoming state, avoiding token- or channel-level partial replacement and full-timestep recomputation. Experiments across four image and video backbones show that FeatFix consistently accelerates generation, achieving a speedup of up to $6.70\times$ over Vanilla while maintaining competitive output quality.

</details>


### [40] [VCP-DCN: Beyond Visual Concealed Property via Depth Collaborative Network for Camouflaged Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27843)
*Songsong Duan,Xi Yang,Nannan Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VCP-DCN is a depth collaborative network for Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) that mines distinguishable multi-modality features beyond visual concealed prototypes in the depth domain, progressively performing multi-modality alignment, interaction, and fusion via three novel modules (SPE, MDA, DAI), achieving effective results on three authoritative datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing COD methods using depth maps ignore modality-specific characteristics of concealed objects in the depth domain, relying on complementary RGB-D feature learning without mining distinguishable modality-specific features.

Method: VCP-DCN progressively performs multi-modality alignment, interaction, and fusion for COD. It includes three key modules: (1) Separable Prototype Embedding (SPE) for alignment, which learns modality-consistency and modality-specific RGB/depth prototype tokens via prototype contrastive learning; (2) Multi-modality Dual Attention (MDA) for interaction, which enhances cross-modal feature representation through local response maps between modality-consistency prototype tokens and visual tokens; (3) Depth Adaptive Injection (DAI) for fusion, which adaptively measures RGB/depth feature contributions via a decision-making mechanism based on similarity distances between modality-specific and modality-consistency prototype tokens.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of VCP-DCN on three authoritative datasets, showing improved COD performance over existing methods.

Conclusion: The proposed depth collaborative network effectively addresses the limitation of ignoring modality-specific characteristics in the depth domain by progressive alignment, interaction, and fusion of multi-modality features, yielding superior camouflaged object detection performance.

Abstract: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to identify and segment camouflaged objects in complex environments, which are often concealed because their color and texture are similar to the background. Several existing COD methods introduce depth maps to boost detection performance via learning complementary RGB-D features, ignoring modality-specific characteristics of concealed objects in the depth domain. To address this issue, we propose a depth collaborative network, called VCP-DCN, to mine distinguishable multi-modality features beyond visual concealed prototype in depth domain. Specifically, VCP-DCN progressively performs multi-modality alignment, interaction, and fusion for the COD task. In the \textbf{alignment} stage, we propose a Separable Prototype Embedding (SPE) module to learn modality-consistency and modality-specific RGB/depth prototype tokens through prototype contrastive learning. Furthermore, we develop a Multi-modality Dual Attention (MDA) module to enhance the cross-modal feature representation through local response maps between modality-consistency RGB/depth prototype tokens and visual tokens on the \textbf{interaction} stage. Finally, we design a Depth Adaptive Injection (DAI) module to adaptively measure contribution of RGB/depth features with a decision-making mechanism, which calculates similarity distance between RGB/depth modality-specific prototype tokens and modality-consistency ones on the \textbf{fusion} stage. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our VCP-DCN on three authoritative datasets.

</details>


### [41] [Benchmarking Foundation and Large Language Models for Few-Shot Medical Image Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27856)
*Jinghong Liu,Yuchuan Deng,Fanping Liu,Meng Huang,Xirong Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FAME is a unified benchmark for evaluating few-shot medical image segmentation (FS-MIS) methods, containing 14,958 test samples across 7 anatomical sites, 9 imaging modalities, and 14 ROI categories. It evaluates models under zero-shot and ten-shot settings with additional target-absence recognition and generalization assessments. Key findings include: direct visual adaptation outperforms prompt-based strategies, more support examples only help when models can effectively utilize them, and semantic transfer is harder than imaging-domain adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing FS-MIS solutions span diverse paradigms (specialists, SAM-based, CLIP-based, MLLM-based) but are evaluated under inconsistent settings, leaving their relative effectiveness unclear. A unified benchmark is needed to provide fair comparison and comprehensive understanding.

Method: FAME constructs a benchmark covering 4 paradigm categories of FS-MIS methods, with 14,958 test samples across 7 anatomical sites, 9 imaging modalities, and 14 ROI categories. Evaluation is performed under zero-shot and ten-shot settings, with additional assessment of target-absence recognition and generalization under covariate and semantic shifts.

Result: Three main findings: (1) direct visual adaptation of support examples generally outperforms prompt-based strategies; (2) increasing support examples improves performance only when models can effectively exploit them; (3) semantic transfer is substantially more challenging than imaging-domain adaptation, and strong localization ability does not guarantee reliable target-absence recognition.

Conclusion: FAME provides a comprehensive and standardized evaluation framework for FS-MIS methods, uncovering key insights about effective support utilization and generalization challenges, aiming to facilitate development of more effective and reliable few-shot medical segmentation methods.

Abstract: Few-shot medical image segmentation (FS-MIS) aims to segment novel regions of interest (ROIs) from a few annotated support examples. Despite rapid progress, existing FS-MIS solutions span diverse paradigms but are evaluated under inconsistent settings, leaving their relative effectiveness unclear. We introduce FAME, a unified benchmark for evaluating FS-MIS solutions, covering specialists, SAM-based methods, CLIP-based methods, and MLLM-based methods. FAME contains 14,958 test samples across 7 anatomical sites, 9 imaging modalities, and 14 ROI categories, and evaluates models under zero-shot and ten-shot settings with additional assessment of target-absence recognition and generalization under covariate and semantic shifts. Our evaluation reveals several findings. First, effective few-shot segmentation depends on how models exploit support examples: direct visual adaptation generally outperforms prompt-based strategies. Second, increasing support examples improves performance only when models can effectively utilize them. Third, semantic transfer remains substantially more challenging than imaging-domain adaptation, and strong localization ability does not necessarily imply reliable target-absence recognition. We hope FAME provides a comprehensive understanding of current FS-MIS solutions and facilitates the development of more effective and reliable few-shot medical segmentation methods.

</details>


### [42] [EEG-EditBench: Probing Visual Information in EEG-Image Retrieval Models with Controlled Image Edits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27857)
*Kaifan Zhang,Lihuo He,Yuqi Ji,Junjie Ke,Lukun Wu,Tianhao You,Xinbo Gao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces EEG-EditBench, a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating EEG-to-image retrieval models on fine-grained visual discrimination through controlled edits (object identity, attributes, background, object presence) to 200 THINGS-EEG2 test images. Results show strong standard retrieval performance does not transfer to edit-based evaluation, with fine-grained attribute changes being the hardest, revealing model behavior hidden by aggregate accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing EEG-to-image retrieval benchmarks only measure whether a model can identify a viewed image from semantically diverse candidates, which does not reveal what specific visual information supports the match. A model may succeed at coarse-level discrimination but fail to distinguish subtle visual details like replacing a cheetah with a dog in an otherwise identical scene. The authors aim to diagnose whether models truly preserve fine-grained visual information.

Method: The authors construct EEG-EditBench from the 200 THINGS-EEG2 test images, applying controlled edits across four dimensions: object identity, attributes, background, and object presence. The benchmark contains 2,137 quality-controlled edited image variants. Eight representative EEG visual decoding models are evaluated on this benchmark.

Result: Strong standard retrieval accuracy does not consistently transfer to edit-based evaluation. Fine-grained attribute changes pose the greatest challenge to existing models, and the benchmark reveals model behaviors that aggregate retrieval accuracy obscures.

Conclusion: EEG-EditBench provides a controlled diagnostic basis for understanding what visual information EEG-image models preserve, highlighting gaps between aggregate retrieval success and genuine fine-grained visual understanding in EEG-based visual decoding.

Abstract: Recent EEG-to-image retrieval models have achieved strong performance in identifying viewed images from semantically diverse candidates. Yet such success does not reveal what visual information supports the match. A model may readily identify a cheetah among tools, plants, and vehicles, but can it still distinguish the viewed cheetah from the same scene with the cheetah replaced by a dog? Motivated by this question, we introduce EEG-EditBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines this question through controlled edits of object identity, attributes, background, and object presence. Built from the 200 THINGS-EEG2 test images, EEG-EditBench contains 2,137 quality-controlled edits and evaluates eight representative EEG visual decoding models. Our results show that strong standard retrieval does not consistently transfer to edit-based evaluation, with fine-grained attribute changes presenting the greatest challenge. EEG-EditBench reveals model behavior hidden by aggregate retrieval accuracy and provides a controlled basis for studying what visual information EEG-image models preserve. The code and complete dataset are publicly available.

</details>


### [43] [Learning to Understand Body Language from Flight through Robust 3D Avatar Placing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27865)
*Dragos Costea,Alina Marcu,Cristina Lazar,Marius Leordeanu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Drones2BodyLanguage, a dataset that grounds human motion in real UAV footage by placing 3D avatars manifesting ten communicative intents into unmodified 4K drone scenes with metrically correct position, scale, and orientation across hundreds of frames of camera motion. The dataset generation is enabled by a lightweight geometric world model using semantically selected anchors lifted to 3D via streaming monocular depth, with rigid-invariant affine anchor weights and an SVD-fitted ground rotation for re-rendering. Training on this data lifts mean intent accuracy across twelve architectures for real, retargeted, and generated motion, with gains confirmed on in-the-wild scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Perceiving human motion and intent at long range is essential for socially intelligent aerial robots, but the data required to learn this capability barely exists. The paper addresses this data scarcity problem by creating a large-scale, geometrically accurate synthetic dataset grounded in real UAV footage.

Method: The method constructs a lightweight geometric world model of the local scene by semantically selecting anchors, lifting them to 3D through streaming monocular depth, and predicting a placement point as an affine anchor combination with provably rigid-invariant weights. Avatars with ten communicative intents are then re-rendered into unmodified 4K drone scenes under an SVD-fitted ground rotation, maintaining metrically correct position, scale, and orientation across hundreds of frames of camera motion.

Result: Across twelve architectures on scene- and motion-disjoint splits, training on placed data improves mean intent accuracy by a wide margin for real, retargeted, and generated motion alike. The gains are further confirmed on two in-the-wild drone scenes.

Conclusion: The proposed data synthesis approach effectively addresses the long-range human motion and intent perception data gap for aerial robots, yielding consistent and substantial accuracy improvements across diverse architectures and motion types, including in real-world settings.

Abstract: Perceiving human motion and intent at long range is a prerequisite for socially intelligent aerial robots, yet the data to learn it barely exists. We introduce Drones2BodyLanguage, a dataset grounding human motion in real UAV footage: avatars manifesting ten communicative intents are placed into unmodified 4K drone scenes with metrically correct position, scale and orientation, maintained over hundreds of frames of camera motion. Enabling it is a lightweight geometric world model of the local scene - semantically selected anchors lifted to 3D through streaming monocular depth - in which a placement point is predicted as an affine anchor combination with provably rigid-invariant weights, and re-rendered under an SVD-fitted ground rotation. Across twelve architectures on scene- and motion-disjoint splits, training on placed data lifts mean intent accuracy by a wide margin for real, retargeted and generated motion alike, with gains confirmed on two in-the-wild scenes.

</details>


### [44] [DECODE: Tackling Representation and Decision Degradation in Continual AI-Generated Image Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27882)
*Zihao Cai,Xinghan Li,Ruiyan Yang,Xue Song,Haijun Shan,Jingjing Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DECODE is a decoupled continual learning framework for AI-generated image detection that jointly mitigates representation- and decision-level forgetting, achieving 99.36% average accuracy across 19 generative domains with only 0.39% forgetting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing continual learning methods for AI image detectors exclusively treat catastrophic forgetting as a representation-level issue by stabilizing features. However, the authors show this perspective is incomplete: even when features remain discriminative, the decision boundary can drift as the classification head is continually optimized, jointly causing a compound failure mode called Dual Degradation.

Method: DECODE decouples representation-level and decision-level forgetting mitigation. It introduces Subspace Diversity Regularization (SDR) to preserve diverse forensic representations across generative domains, and Closed-Form Decision Alignment (CDA) to recalibrate the shared classification head after each adapter merge without requiring manual hyperparameter tuning.

Result: On 19 generative domains, DECODE achieves 99.36% average accuracy with only 0.39% forgetting, and generalizes to 11 unseen generators with 95.36% accuracy.

Conclusion: Both representation-level and decision-level forgetting must be jointly addressed in continual AI-generated image detection. The decoupled framework with subspace diversity regularization and closed-form decision alignment effectively overcomes the compound Dual Degradation failure mode and generalizes well to unseen generators.

Abstract: As generative models continue to evolve, AI-generated image detectors must incrementally adapt to emerging generative domains while preserving knowledge acquired from previous ones. This continual learning setting is particularly challenging because forensic traces are often subtle and generator-specific, making detectors highly vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. Existing methods primarily address this problem by stabilizing feature representations, implicitly treating forgetting as a representation-level issue. In this paper, we show that this perspective is incomplete. We demonstrate that even when feature representations remain discriminative, the decision boundary can progressively drift as the classification head is continually optimized on new domains. These two effects jointly give rise to a compound failure mode, termed Dual Degradation. To overcome this challenge, we propose DECODE, a decoupled continual detection framework that jointly mitigates representation- and decision-level forgetting. Specifically, we introduce Subspace Diversity Regularization (SDR) to preserve diverse forensic representations and Closed-Form Decision Alignment (CDA) to recalibrate the shared classification head after each adapter merge without manual hyperparameter tuning. Extensive experiments on 19 generative domains show that DECODE achieves an average accuracy of 99.36% with only 0.39% forgetting, while further generalizing to 11 unseen generators with 95.36% accuracy.

</details>


### [45] [Unifying Adversarially Robust Model Experts in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27897)
*Nguyen Duc Thai,Junhao Dong,Sua Qi Rong,Hua Yu,Yew-Soon Ong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CARE is a collaborative adversarial fine-tuning framework for vision-language models (VLMs) like CLIP that maintains multiple robustness-specialized experts, enables knowledge exchange through embedding-space alignment, and consolidates them into a single unified robust model that inherits complementary robustness properties from all experts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs such as CLIP are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, and while adversarial fine-tuning is a prominent defense, different fine-tuning strategies produce specialized models that each excel only in certain evaluation settings while failing in others, limiting overall defensive capability.

Method: CARE maintains multiple robust model experts during training, facilitates knowledge exchange between experts through embedding-space harmonization, and consolidates the collectively learned knowledge into a single unified robust model, allowing experts to benefit from one another while preserving their individual specializations.

Result: Extensive experiments on image classification and downstream vision-language tasks show CARE outperforms individually learned model experts, demonstrating that collaborative learning across model experts improves adversarial robustness.

Conclusion: Collaborative learning across robust model experts is a promising direction for improving adversarial robustness in VLMs, as the unified model can inherit complementary robustness properties from multiple specialized fine-tuned experts.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, posing a serious problem for real-life applications and deployment. Adversarial fine-tuning emerges as a prominent defense method; however, different fine-tuning strategies often produce specialized models with distinct robustness characteristics. Each fine-tuned model in turn thrives in some evaluation settings but falters on others, limiting their defensive capabilities. We refer to these specialized fine-tuned models as robust model experts and propose a collaborative adversarial fine-tuning framework: CARE - Collaborative Adversarial Robustness fine-tuning using Embedding alignment. CARE maintains multiple experts during training, enables knowledge exchange through embedding-space harmonization, and consolidates the learned knowledge into a single unified robust model. Experts benefit from one another while preserving their individual specializations, enabling the final model to inherit complementary robustness properties. In this paper, we demonstrate CARE on two different adversarial fine-tuning strategies with complementary robustness behaviors. Extensive experiments on classic image classification and downstream vision-language tasks display the effectiveness of our approach, with CARE being able to outperform individually learned model experts.
