The results suggest that collaborative learning across model experts is a promising direction for improving adversarial robustness.

</details>


### [46] [CoRE-UIR: Prior-guided common and residual experts for efficient all-in-one remote sensing image restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27898)
*Zaiyan Zhang,Qiangqiang Yuan,Jie Li,Ziyang Lihe,Yu Wan,Yuzeng Chen,Xin Su,Liangpei Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CoRE-UIR is a prior-guided global-local framework for universal image restoration that decomposes restoration capacity into common dense and low-rank residual experts, improving PSNR by 1.05 dB while running 11.83× faster and reducing memory by 85.3% over the strongest baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: UAV and satellite remote sensing images suffer from compound degradations (adverse weather, illumination variation, imaging artifacts) that jointly induce global distribution shifts and local structural corruption. Existing All-in-One restoration methods suffer from weak/implicit degradation cues and parameter redundancy from full-rank multi-expert designs with overlapping restoration behaviors.

Method: CoRE-UIR is built around the Common-and-Residual Expert Block (CoRE), which decomposes restoration capacity into a common dense expert for degradation-invariant restoration and low-rank residual experts for degradation-specific compensation. It also includes Degradation Prior Embedding (DPE) that adapts frozen CLIP features into explicit restoration-oriented priors, and Global Feature Modulation (GFM) that aligns global feature statistics before local residual compensation. Additionally, the paper constructs MDVD-108K, a large-scale UAV restoration dataset covering single and compound degradations, plus a real-world test set.

Result: Extensive experiments show CoRE-UIR improves average PSNR by 1.05 dB while running 11.83× faster and reducing peak memory by 85.3% relative to the strongest baseline (BaryIR). Downstream task evaluations and unseen degradation tests validate the generalizability of the method.

Conclusion: CoRE-UIR achieves a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off for universal image restoration in remote sensing, demonstrating that explicit decomposition into common and residual experts enables adaptive specialization without redundant expert replication. The code and dataset will be publicly released.

Abstract: Remote sensing images acquired by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and satellites are often degraded by adverse weather, illumination variation, and imaging artifacts, which may co-occur and jointly induce global distribution shifts and local structural corruption. Although All-in-One image restoration offers an appealing unified alternative to task-specific pipelines, existing methods still suffer from weak or implicit degradation cues and parameter redundancy caused by full-rank multi-expert designs with overlapping restoration behaviors. We propose CoRE-UIR (Common and Residual Experts for Universal Image Restoration), a prior-guided global-local framework centered on the Common-and-Residual Expert Block (CoRE). CoRE explicitly decomposes restoration capacity into a common dense expert for degradation-invariant restoration and low-rank residual experts for degradation-specific compensation, enabling adaptive specialization without redundant expert replication. Built on this design, Degradation Prior Embedding (DPE) adapts frozen CLIP features into an explicit restoration-oriented prior, while Global Feature Modulation (GFM) aligns global feature statistics before local residual compensation. We also construct MDVD-108K (Multi-Degradation VisDrone), a large-scale UAV restoration dataset covering both single and compound degradations, together with a real-world test set. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets show that CoRE-UIR improves the overall average PSNR by 1.05 dB while running 11.83$\times$ faster and reducing peak memory by 85.3% relative to the strongest baseline, BaryIR, thereby maintaining a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. Evaluations on downstream tasks and unseen degradation also validate the generalizability of CoRE-UIR. The code and dataset will be released at https://github.com/zzaiyan/CoRE-UIR.

</details>


### [47] [One Patch Is Enough: Reinforcement-Optimized Visual Token Grounding for MLLM-Based Scene Text Spotting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27902)
*Rui Tang,Wentao Yang,Peirong Zhang,Yongxin Shi,Shun Zhang,Huiguo He,Lianwen Jin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SPaTS is a vision-centric framework for scene text spotting that routes each text instance through a single anchor visual token (instead of multiple patches), uses reinforcement learning for anchor selection, and refines geometry via full-image cross-attention, outperforming frontier MLLMs and OCR MLLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous multi-patch visual-token grounding paradigms for scene text spotting in MLLMs introduce redundant noise and localization ambiguity, particularly for dense or small text instances, motivating a cleaner single-token routing approach.

Method: SPaTS proposes: (1) Single-Patch Text Spotting, routing each text instance through one anchor visual token with full-image refinement; (2) Single-Patch Selective Optimization (SPaSO), a reinforcement learning framework optimizing discrete visual-token selection via patch-level rewards without oracle labels; (3) Directional Embedding Alignment (DEA) to suppress norm bias by decoupling feature magnitude and direction; (4) Patch-Enhanced Decoding (PED) to fuse the routed anchor with language semantics and cross-attend over full-image features for geometry-aware boundary regression.

Result: Extensive experiments show SPaTS consistently and significantly outperforms both frontier closed-source MLLMs and specialized OCR MLLMs in scene text spotting.

Conclusion: Single-anchor visual token routing with reinforcement learning optimization and full-image geometric refinement is a more effective paradigm than multi-patch grounding for MLLM-based scene text spotting.

Abstract: Scene text spotting requires high-precision alignment between textual recognition and spatial localization. While visual-token grounding has emerged as a promising formulation for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), the previous multi-patch paradigm often introduces redundant noise and localization ambiguity, particularly for dense or small text instances. To address this, we propose Single-Patch Text Spotting (SPaTS), a vision-centric framework that routes each text instance through a single anchor visual token and then recovers geometry via full-image refinement. To accurately identify this anchor without oracle labels, we introduce Single-Patch Selective Optimization (SPaSO), a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes discrete visual-token selection using patch-level rewards. To further improve representation robustness and localization precision, we introduce Directional Embedding Alignment (DEA) to suppress unstable norm bias by decoupling feature magnitude and direction, and Patch-Enhanced Decoding (PED) to fuse the routed anchor with language semantics and cross-attend over the full-image feature map for geometry-aware boundary regression beyond coordinate-space surrogates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPaTS consistently and significantly outperforms both frontier closed-source MLLMs and OCR MLLMs. Code will be released soon.

</details>


### [48] [ARD-REFSM: Enhancing Reflection Symmetry Detection with Asymmetric Denoising and Rotation Equivariance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27927)
*Dongfu Yin,Rourou Su,Cong Zhao,Fei Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes an Asymmetric Region Denoising (ARD) module and a Rotation Equivariant Feature Similarity Matching (REFSM) module for reflection symmetry detection, along with a new benchmark dataset GMSYM. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on four standard datasets and the new benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reflection symmetry detection is challenged by asymmetric background clutter that disrupts symmetric pattern matching, and by conventional CNNs lacking rotation equivariance, which causes inconsistent feature representations under rotational transformations.

Method: The method comprises two key components: (1) an Asymmetric Region Denoising (ARD) module that suppresses asymmetric interference to refine symmetric patterns, and (2) a Rotation Equivariant Feature Similarity Matching (REFSM) module that enhances rotation equivariance via feature similarity matching between original and rotated images. The dual-input REFSM framework uses a rotation loss to maximize consistency between score maps of original and rotated images for precise rotation-equivariant symmetry axis prediction. Additionally, a new benchmark dataset GMSYM is introduced with diverse scenarios and various interferences.

Result: Extensive experiments on four standard datasets (DENDI, NYU, LDRS, SDRW) and the proposed GMSYM dataset demonstrate that the method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and robustness.

Conclusion: The proposed ARD and REFSM modules effectively address asymmetric interference and rotation equivariance issues in reflection symmetry detection, and the GMSYM benchmark provides a more comprehensive evaluation setting for future research.

Abstract: Reflection symmetry detection remains challenging due to interference from asymmetric regions and arbitrary orientations of symmetric patterns. Asymmetric regions introduce background clutter that disrupts symmetric pattern matching, whereas conventional convolutional neural networks lack rotation equivariance, leading to inconsistent feature representations under rotational transformations. To address these issues, we propose an Asymmetric Region Denoising (ARD) module and a Rotation Equivariant Feature Similarity Matching (REFSM) module. The ARD module suppresses asymmetric interference to refine symmetric patterns, while the REFSM module enhances rotation equivariance through feature similarity matching between original and rotated images. Specifically, our dual-input REFSM framework leverages rotation loss to maximize consistency between the score maps of original and rotated images, thereby enabling precise prediction of rotation-equivariant symmetry axes. Furthermore, we introduce GMSYM, a new benchmark dataset that categorizes images into diverse scenarios and incorporates various interferences to address the limitations of existing reflection symmetry detection benchmarks. Extensive experiments on four standard datasets (DENDI, NYU, LDRS, SDRW) and our proposed GMSYM dataset demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and robustness.

</details>


### [49] [LAST: The Last Query Token Guides Visual Token Pruning for Edge-Cloud Collaborative MLLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27952)
*Feng Yang,Xinrui Ju,Keyang Zhang,Xiandong Meng,Rongqun Lin,Howard Leung,Shiqi Wang,Haoliang Li,Chris Xing Tian*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LAST is a training-free framework for query-dependent visual token pruning in edge-cloud collaborative MLLM inference, using a compact edge-side VLM as a guidance proxy and an importance signal derived from the last query token's attention to visual tokens. It preserves 95.4% of full-token accuracy while retaining only 12.5% of visual tokens across 11 multimodal benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge-cloud visual intelligence is shifting to token-based interfaces where edge devices encode visual inputs for cloud MLLMs, but dense visual-token sequences increase cloud inference costs. Existing pruning methods either operate before cloud execution but are query-agnostic (vision-driven), or are query-aware but rely on the target MLLM's internal states (query-guided), making them unsuitable for edge-cloud settings. Compact guidance models exist but may require costly attention aggregation or auxiliary generation.

Method: LAST uses a compact edge-side VLM as a guidance proxy and derives a lightweight importance signal from the last query token's attention to visual tokens. Under causal attention, the last query token can attend to the full visual sequence and entire query context, enabling query-aware pruning without cloud-model access, autoregressive generation, or aggregated attention over multiple query positions. A diverse set of query-relevant visual tokens is retained under a fixed token budget.

Result: Evaluated on 11 multimodal benchmarks under multiple token budgets against pruning methods with different guidance strategies. LAST consistently achieves the strongest performance, preserving 95.4% of full-token accuracy while retaining only 12.5% of visual tokens, with low edge-side selection overhead and reduced cloud-side computation.

Conclusion: LAST demonstrates that a training-free, edge-side guidance proxy can enable effective query-dependent visual token pruning without requiring access to the cloud MLLM's internal states, achieving strong performance retention with significant computational savings.

Abstract: Multimodal foundation models are reshaping edge-cloud visual intelligence from task-specific feature pipelines into token-based interfaces, where edge devices encode visual inputs into tokens for a general-purpose cloud MLLM. However, dense visual-token sequences increase cloud-side inference costs. Existing pruning methods mainly target centralized inference: vision-driven methods can operate before cloud execution but are typically query-agnostic, whereas query-guided methods often rely on internal states of the target MLLM and cannot determine token relevance before transmission. Compact guidance models offer an alternative, but existing designs may require costly attention aggregation or auxiliary generation. We propose LAST, a training-free framework for query-dependent visual token pruning in edge-cloud collaborative MLLM inference. LAST uses a compact edge-side VLM as a guidance proxy and derives a lightweight importance signal from the last query token's attention to visual tokens. Under causal attention, the last query token can attend to the full visual sequence and the entire query context, enabling query-aware pruning without cloud-model access, autoregressive generation, or costly aggregation over multiple query positions. LAST then retains a diverse set of query-relevant visual tokens under a fixed token budget. We evaluate LAST on 11 multimodal benchmarks under multiple token budgets against pruning methods with different guidance strategies. Experiments show that LAST consistently achieves the strongest performance, preserving 95.4% of the full-token accuracy while retaining only 12.5% of the visual tokens, with low edge-side selection overhead and reduced cloud-side computation.

</details>


### [50] [FiRE: Enhancing MLLMs with Fine-Grained Context Learning for Complex Image Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27959)
*Bohan Hou,Haoqiang Lin,Xuemeng Song,Haokun Wen,Meng Liu,Yupeng Hu,Xiangyu Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes an automated pipeline for constructing fine-grained multimodal quintuple datasets and a two-stage fine-grained fine-tuning strategy to improve MLLMs as universal image retrievers, particularly for complex tasks like long-text-to-image retrieval, visual dialog retrieval, and composed image retrieval (CIR). The method separates fine-tuning into context reasoning-oriented and retrieval-oriented stages, achieving superior zero-shot retrieval performance over existing approaches even with a lighter backbone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLM-based image retrievers overlook the potential of fine-grained context modeling and disentangled fine-tuning objectives, which are crucial for complex retrieval tasks such as long-text-to-image retrieval, visual dialog retrieval, and composed image retrieval.

Method: The authors introduce (1) an automated fine-grained multimodal quintuple dataset construction pipeline that generates comprehensive CIR data with fine-grained captions and modification text, and (2) a two-stage fine-grained fine-tuning strategy—stage one focuses on fine-grained context reasoning, and stage two on fine-grained retrieval-oriented alignment—to sequentially improve context understanding and query-target matching.

Result: Extensive experiments across five datasets covering diverse and complex image retrieval tasks show notable superiority over existing approaches in zero-shot retrieval settings, even with a more lightweight MLLM backbone.

Conclusion: Disentangled two-stage fine-tuning combined with fine-grained context modeling significantly enhances MLLM-based image retrieval performance on complex tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results under zero-shot conditions.

Abstract: Due to their strong generalizable multimodal processing and reasoning capabilities, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated significant potential as universal image retrievers, effectively addressing diverse real-world image retrieval tasks. Nevertheless, pioneering studies, while promising, overlook the potential of fine-grained context modeling and disentangled fine-tuning objectives in enhancing MLLMs' retrieval performance, particularly for complex tasks such as long-text-to-image retrieval, visual dialog retrieval, and composed image retrieval (CIR). Therefore, in this work, we propose an automated fine-grained multimodal quintuple dataset construction pipeline and a novel two-stage fine-grained multimodal fine-tuning strategy. The dataset generation pipeline produces a comprehensive CIR dataset with fine-grained image captions and modification text, facilitating fine-grained context modeling. Beyond the previously entangled fine-tuning paradigm, our approach separates the fine-tuning process into two distinct stages: (1) fine-grained context reasoning-oriented fine-tuning and (2) fine-grained retrieval-oriented fine-tuning. These stages aim to sequentially enhance the model's context understanding and query-target alignment capabilities, thereby improving retrieval performance. Extensive experiments across five datasets encompassing diverse and complex image retrieval tasks demonstrate the remarkable superiority of our method over existing approaches in zero-shot retrieval settings, even with a more lightweight MLLM backbone compared to those methods.

</details>


### [51] [FootprintNet: State-Transition-Guided Dynamic Footprint Learning for Multi-temporal Remote Sensing Change Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27969)
*Haotian Zhang,Hao Chen,Han Guo,Zhengxia Zou,Zhenwei Shi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Urban Building Dynamics Detection (UBDD) and a novel network called FootprintNet to detect building-change dynamic footprints (temporal intervals of change) from multi-temporal remote sensing imagery. It models building-change processes as state-action interactions, introduces an independent multi-change class for recurrent changes, and proposes the Building Change Dynamics Score (BCDS) metric to better evaluate temporal proximity between predictions and labels. Extensive experiments on three datasets show FootprintNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-temporal change detection (MTCD) methods use a single change category associated with the final observation, which fails to characterize regions undergoing recurrent changes closely related to human activities. This implicit single-change assumption limits the capability of MTCD in dynamic urban environments.

Method: The authors propose (1) UBDD, a task that identifies building-change dynamic footprints (temporal intervals of change) with pixel-wise classification masks; (2) an independent multi-change class for unified representation of single- and multi-change processes; (3) FootprintNet, which abstracts building-change as interactions between latent states and actions with state-action transition constraints for causally coherent change trajectories, and exploits temporal change-boundary cues to enhance feature contrast; and (4) the Building Change Dynamics Score (BCDS) metric that evaluates predictions based on change semantics preservation and temporal offsets from labels.

Result: Extensive experiments on TSCD, MUDS, and WUSU datasets demonstrate that FootprintNet outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in detecting building-change dynamic footprints.

Conclusion: By moving beyond single-change assumptions and explicitly modeling recurrent changes as state-action interactions, FootprintNet improves the detection accuracy of building-change dynamic footprints, and BCDS provides a more faithful metric for temporal dynamics evaluation.

Abstract: Despite substantial progress in remote sensing multi-temporal change detection (MTCD), most existing MTCD methods still represent the dynamic process at each spatial location over the entire observation period using a single change category associated with the final observation. This implicit single-change assumption limits their ability to characterize regions of recurrent change closely related to human activities. To address this limitation, we introduce Urban Building Dynamics Detection (UBDD), which identifies building-change dynamic footprints, i.e., the temporal intervals in which changes occur, from multi-temporal imagery and produces pixel-wise classification masks. For regions undergoing two or more changes, UBDD introduces an independent multi-change class for unified representation, thereby enabling unified modeling of single- and multi-change processes. Furthermore, we propose FootprintNet, which abstracts building-change processes as interactions between latent states and actions, and imposes state-action transition constraints to guide the learning of causally coherent change trajectories. It further exploits temporal change-boundary cues to enhance feature contrast across boundary sides, thereby improving the discrimination among different dynamic footprints and enabling accurate detection of dynamic footprints. Moreover, we introduce the Building Change Dynamics Score (BCDS) to address the inability of conventional metrics to reflect the temporal proximity between predicted footprints and labels. It evaluates predictions according to their preservation of change semantics and temporal offsets from the corresponding labels. Extensive experiments on TSCD, MUDS, and WUSU demonstrate that FootprintNet outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/zmoka-zht/FootprintNet.

</details>


### [52] [Now You Have My Healthy Attention: A U-DiT for Brain-MRI Inpainting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27974)
*Danilo Danese,Angela Lombardi,Tommaso Di Noia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper presents a deterministic regression model for the ASNR-MICCAI BraTS Local Synthesis (Inpainting) task, using a U-DiT architecture with constrained self-attention and contralateral-symmetry priors to achieve strong distortion metrics (SSIM 0.864, PSNR 24.7 dB, MSE 4.6e-3) on the BraTS-2026 validation leaderboard.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The task requires anatomically plausible completion of healthy brain tissue in masked T1-weighted MRI regions to provide tumor-free anatomical references. Since scoring uses distortion metrics (SSIM, PSNR, MSE), the authors build a deterministic regression model with inductive biases tailored to inpainting rather than generative approaches.

Method: The network follows the U-DiT principle: a volumetric encoder-decoder with a downsampled global self-attention block using 3D rotary position embeddings for long-range context, while convolutions and skip connections preserve high-frequency detail. Two key ideas: (1) attention is constrained so void tokens attend only to known-healthy tokens of the same volume with a learned bias toward the contralateral homologue; (2) a contralateral-symmetry input supplies the mirrored healthy hemisphere as a patient-specific prior, leveraging approximate bilateral brain symmetry and typically unilateral lesions.

Result: On the official BraTS-2026 validation leaderboard, the submission achieves mean healthy-region SSIM of 0.864, PSNR of 24.7 dB, and MSE of 4.6e-3 over 219 cases.

Conclusion: The paper discusses the inherent residual smoothness of distortion-optimal regression and its implications for anatomical realism, acknowledging that distortion-optimal outputs may not be maximally anatomically realistic even when scoring well on distortion metrics.

Abstract: The ASNR-MICCAI BraTS Local Synthesis (Inpainting) task asks for the anatomically plausible completion of healthy brain tissue within a masked region of a T1-weighted MRI, providing a tumor-free anatomical reference for downstream analysis. As the task is scored by distortion metrics (SSIM, PSNR, MSE), we build a deterministic regression model and focus on giving it inductive biases tailored to inpainting. Our network follows the U-DiT principle of performing self-attention on a downsampled token grid: a volumetric encoder-decoder imports long-range context through a downsampled global self-attention block with three-dimensional rotary position embeddings, while convolutions and skip connections preserve high-frequency detail. Two ideas drive our results. First, we constrain the attention so that occluded ("void") tokens attend only to known-healthy tokens of the same volume, with a learned bias toward each query's contralateral homologue, forcing the completion to be inferred from observed anatomy rather than from other unknown regions. Second, we add a contralateral-symmetry input that supplies the mirrored healthy hemisphere as a patient-specific prior; since the brain is approximately bilaterally symmetric and lesions are typically unilateral, this prior improves the distortion metrics at matched structural similarity. On the official BraTS-2026 validation leaderboard our submission reaches a mean healthy-region SSIM of $0.864$, PSNR of $24.7$\,dB and MSE of $4.6{\times}10^{-3}$ over $219$ cases. We further analyse the residual smoothness inherent to distortion-optimal regression and discuss its implications for anatomical realism.

</details>


### [53] [ViP-Rig: Visual-Prompted Controllable Rigging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27982)
*Zihan Qin,Mingze Sun,Yifan Mao,Jialei Xu,Jingfeng Guo,Changrong Hu,Wenbo Zhao,Junjun Jiang,Xianming Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ViP-Rig is a visual-prompted rigging framework that injects features from user-drawn 2D skeletal and rigidity prompts into frozen pretrained backbones, supporting both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing for controllable skeleton generation and skinning prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rigging is task-dependent and artists typically need to iteratively edit initial rigs to meet specific animation requirements. Existing automatic methods only generate plausible rigs from geometry with limited explicit control over the resulting skeleton and deformation behavior.

Method: ViP-Rig has two stages: (1) Skeleton Generation, where skeletal sketches are processed via Dense-to-Compact Visual Prompt Encoding into compact conditioning tokens, injected into a frozen autoregressive generator through gated adapters; (2) Skinning Prediction, where rigidity maps are processed with the same visual encoding design and tokens are symmetrically injected into point and joint streams of a frozen skinning backbone to modulate point-joint compatibility and skinning weights.

Result: Experiments on Articulation-XL2.0 and zero-shot evaluation on ModelsResource show ViP-Rig recovers target skeletons and skinning weights more accurately than geometry-conditioned baselines under prompt-guided evaluation. Qualitative results demonstrate explicit, localized control in both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing.

Conclusion: Visual prompting enables explicit and localized control over rigging by injecting user-drawn skeletal and rigidity features into frozen pretrained backbones, outperforming geometry-only conditioning baselines while supporting both initial rigging and iterative editing workflows.

Abstract: Rigging is inherently task-dependent because the same mesh may require different skeletons and deformation behaviors across animation tasks. In practice, artists often inspect an initial rig and repeatedly edit its skeletal structure and deformation behavior to meet specific animation requirements. Existing automatic methods primarily generate a plausible rig from geometry, offering limited explicit control over the resulting skeleton and deformation behavior. In this work, we present ViP-Rig, a visual-prompted framework that supports both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing by injecting features extracted from user-drawn or edited 2D skeletal and rigidity prompts into frozen pretrained backbones. Specifically, ViP-Rig consists of two stages, Skeleton Generation and Skinning Prediction. In the first stage, the skeletal sketch is processed by the Dense-to-Compact Visual Prompt Encoding to produce compact, fixed-length conditioning tokens. The resulting tokens are injected into a frozen pretrained autoregressive generator through gated adapters to control joint placement and branching structure while preserving the generator's geometric prior. In the second stage, the rigidity map is processed using the same visual encoding design, while the pretrained skinning backbone remains frozen. The resulting tokens are symmetrically injected into the point and joint streams to modulate point-joint compatibility and the resulting skinning weights. Experiments on Articulation-XL2.0 and zero-shot evaluation on ModelsResource show that ViP-Rig more accurately recovers target skeletons and skinning weights than geometry-conditioned baselines under prompt-guided evaluation. Qualitative results further demonstrate explicit and localized control in both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing.

</details>


### [54] [Deep learning-based hierarchical insect classification using camera trap imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28005)
*Zaki Mahfoud,Juan A. Chiavassa,Simon Walther,Florian Haselbeck,Ehsan Yaghoubi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a deep learning-based hierarchical classification model for automated insect biodiversity monitoring using camera trap imagery, built on a manually curated dataset of ~1 million insect images annotated with a five-level, 34-class taxonomy, achieving 80-99% per-level accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Insect populations are declining, making reliable biodiversity monitoring urgent. However, current monitoring is hindered by a lack of standardized data and costly, time-consuming manual identification by expert entomologists. Deep learning on automated camera trap data could scale monitoring, but challenges include acquiring expert-annotated datasets, generalizing across taxonomic levels, handling highly imbalanced data, and designing models that default to coarser, higher-confidence predictions when uncertain about finer levels.

Method: The authors curate a long-tailed dataset of ~1 million insect images from 1,801 camera-trap videos, annotated with a five-level, 34-class hierarchy. They adapt a hierarchical classification model architecture to this five-level variable-depth hierarchy with class-balanced weighting, leveraging biological taxonomy to extract granularity-specific visual features and producing hierarchy-consistent predictions down to the deepest taxonomic level meeting a confidence threshold (T=0.6).

Result: The model achieved per-level accuracy of 80-99% on test data across the five levels of the hierarchy, and improved on non-hierarchical classifiers by leveraging biological taxonomy for granularity-specific feature extraction.

Conclusion: A hierarchical deep learning approach with confidence-based pruning enables more reliable and scalable insect biodiversity monitoring from camera trap imagery, outperforming flat classifiers by exploiting biological taxonomy structure.

Abstract: Declining insect populations make reliable biodiversity monitoring increasingly urgent, yet monitoring of insect biodiversity is hampered by a lack of standardised data and by costly and time-consuming manual identification by expert entomologists. Deep learning-based image classifiers, processing data from automated non-lethal camera traps, have the potential to transform and scale insect biodiversity monitoring. However, challenges remain in acquiring expert-annotated datasets, developing model architectures that generalise well across diverse taxonomic levels and training models on highly imbalanced data. Hierarchical data also benefits from designing models that default to higher-confidence, coarser-level predictions, when uncertain about finer taxonomic levels. In this paper we address these challenges with a deep learning-based hierarchical classification model. First, we present a manually curated, long-tailed dataset of around one million images of insects, extracted from 1,801 camera-trap video recordings and annotated with a five-level, 34-class hierarchy. Further, we adapt a hierarchical classification model architecture to a five-level variable-depth hierarchy, with class-balanced weighting. Our model improves on non-hierarchical classifiers by leveraging biological taxonomy to extract granularity-specific visual features and makes hierarchy-consistent predictions to the deepest taxonomic level that meets a confidence threshold (T = 0.6). Our model achieved a per-level accuracy of 80-99% on test data, across five levels of hierarchy. Furthermore ...

</details>


### [55] [Beyond Classification: Pathology Foundation Models as Detection Encoders for Mitotic Figures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28007)
*Sweta Banerjee,Alireza Teimoury,Nils Porsche,Alexandra K. Stoll,Viktoria Weiss,Niklas Hargarter,Jonas Ammeling,Thomas Conrad,Christoph Stroblberger,Christopher Kaltnecker,Robert Klopfleisch,Christof A. Bertram,Katharina Breininger,Marc Aubreville*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether current pathology foundation models (FMs) such as UNI, UNI2-h, Virchow, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, and H-optimus-1 provide latent space features sufficiently discriminant and spatially resolved to serve as backbones for dense object detection, specifically mitotic figure detection. The FMs are evaluated with three detector paradigms (RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, Deformable DETR) on MIDOG++ and TUPAC16 datasets against an end-to-end ResNet50 baseline. H-optimus-0 and Virchow achieve competitive performance, with FMs showing slight robustness advantages on out-of-domain data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While pathology foundation models are known to yield regularized latent spaces effective for downstream classification tasks (including mitotic figure vs. other cell classification), it remains unclear whether these latent spaces are also discriminatory and spatially well-resolved enough to serve as backbones for dense object detection paradigms. This work systematically investigates this open question.

Method: Six current pathology foundation models (UNI, UNI2-h, Virchow, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, H-optimus-1) are combined as backbones with three detector heads representing different paradigms: single-stage (RetinaNet), dual-stage (Faster R-CNN), and self-attention-based (Deformable DETR). Performance is evaluated on the multi-domain MIDOG++ dataset and the out-of-domain TUPAC16 dataset, compared against a fully end-to-end trained ResNet50 baseline.

Result: H-optimus-0 and Virchow foundation models yielded competitive performance for mitotic figure detection, comparable to or better than the end-to-end ResNet50 baseline. The latent spaces of current image-level self-supervised FMs are suitable for direct mitotic figure detection, with FMs demonstrating slightly more robustness on the out-of-domain TUPAC16 test case.

Conclusion: Current pathology foundation models, despite being trained on image-level self-supervision, provide latent space features that are sufficiently discriminant and spatially resolved to serve as effective backbones for dense object detection of mitotic figures. The approach shows competitive performance and slight out-of-domain robustness advantages. Code is made publicly available.

Abstract: Pathology foundation models (FMs) are models trained on vast amounts of typically unlabeled data and have been shown to yield regularized latent spaces that can be used effectively in downstream classification tasks. This is also true for the classification of mitotic figures vs. other cells. However, it is so far unclear if the latent space of current FMs provides features that are discriminant and spatially suitably resolved to also serve as a backbone for dense object detection paradigms. In this work, we investigate this question for common current pathology FMs (UNI, UNI2-h, Virchow, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, H-optimus-1) and compare their performance against a fully end-to-end trained baseline based on a ResNet50 architecture. We combine FM backbones with representatives of single stage, dual stage and self-attention-based detectors (RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, Deformable DETR respectively) on the multi-domain MIDOG++ dataset, and on the TUPAC16 dataset as an out-of-domain case. We show that the H-optimus-0 and Virchow models yielded competitive performance, indicating that the latent spaces of current FMs, all trained on image-level self-supervision, are suitable for direct mitotic figure detection and may be slightly more robust on our out-of-domain test case. All code is made available publicly at https://github.com/DeepMicroscopy/FM4MFdet.

</details>


### [56] [ENCORE: Event-Assisted Complementary Motion Refinement for Learned Video Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28020)
*Shuhan Ye,Hongbin Yu,Chenqi Kong,Pingchuan Ma,Chong Wang,Jun Wan,Qixin Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ENCORE is a learning-based video compression framework that uses event camera data as an auxiliary modality to refine motion estimation between frames. It decomposes aligned RGB-event features into complementary motion representations, calibrates event-specific responses, and routes corrections into the RGB flow, achieving significant BD-rate savings across multiple datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing learned video codecs estimate motion solely from discrete RGB frames, making them vulnerable to fast motion, blur, occlusion, weak texture, low illumination, and abrupt brightness changes. Event cameras capture fine-grained inter-frame intensity changes and can complement RGB-based motion estimation.

Method: ENCORE consists of three components: (1) Complementary Motion Representation (CMR) decomposes aligned RGB-event features into common and modality-specific motion representations; (2) Spatial Energy and Redundancy-Informed Calibration (SERIC) identifies active and novel event-specific responses while suppressing weak or redundant evidence to predict a candidate flow correction; (3) Energy-Aware Routing (EAR) determines where and how strongly the correction refines the RGB flow. Events serve only as auxiliary modality for motion modeling; RGB remains the sole coding and reconstruction target.

Result: Experiments on BS-ERGB, HQ-EVFI, and CED datasets show consistent BD-rate gains across different GOP lengths. On BS-ERGB, ENCORE achieves up to 20.80% PSNR-RGB and 22.14% MS-SSIM-RGB BD-rate savings.

Conclusion: Event-assisted complementary motion refinement significantly improves learned video compression by leveraging event data to correct RGB flow estimates, with consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks without requiring events during reconstruction.

Abstract: Learned video compression relies on accurate temporal modeling to remove redundancy between adjacent frames. However, most existing codecs infer motion solely from discretely sampled RGB frames, making their estimates vulnerable to fast motion, blur, occlusion, weak texture, low illumination, and abrupt brightness changes. Event cameras asynchronously capture fine-grained intensity changes between RGB timestamps and therefore provide complementary evidence about inter-frame dynamics. We propose ENCORE, an Event-Assisted Complementary Motion Refinement framework for learned video compression. ENCORE first employs Complementary Motion Representation (CMR) to decompose aligned RGB-event features into common and modality-specific motion representations. Spatial Energy and Redundancy-Informed Calibration (SERIC) then identifies event-specific responses that are active and novel relative to RGB, suppresses weak or redundant evidence, and predicts a candidate flow correction. Finally, Energy-Aware Routing (EAR) determines where and how strongly the correction should refine the RGB flow. Events serve solely as an auxiliary modality for motion modeling, while RGB remains the only coding and reconstruction target. Experiments on BS-ERGB, HQ-EVFI, and CED demonstrate consistent gains across datasets and GOP lengths. On BS-ERGB, ENCORE achieves up to 20.80% PSNR-RGB and 22.14% MS-SSIM-RGB BD-rate savings, while retaining clear improvements on the other two datasets.

</details>


### [57] [Split and Drive: Dual-Axis Disentanglement for Real-Time Gaussian Head Avatars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28032)
*MD Wahiduzzaman Khan,Mingshan Jia,Xiaolin Zhang,En Yu,Kaska Musial-Gabrys*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SpiD (Split and Drive) is a single-image Gaussian head avatar framework that disentangles along two axes: a compute axis internalizing per-frame driving to eliminate external tracking dependency, and a feature axis decomposing the avatar into three specialized Gaussian branches for geometrically distinct facial regions. It achieves state-of-the-art performance with the fastest end-to-end inference speed on a single GPU.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting head avatar methods depend on external tracking pipelines whose latency is excluded from inference measurements, and they use unified representations that entangle geometrically distinct facial regions, limiting expressiveness and rendering fidelity. Splitting the driving and the facial feature representation addresses both limitations.

Method: SpiD builds on two disentanglement axes: (1) a compute axis that internalizes per-frame driving within the model, removing external tracking at inference time, and (2) a feature axis that decomposes the avatar into three specialized Gaussian branches, each modeling a geometrically distinct facial domain.

Result: Extensive experiments show SpiD achieves consistently strong performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods while delivering the fastest inference speed among all compared methods on a single GPU, with the complete driving pipeline included in the measured latency.

Conclusion: SpiD demonstrates that disentangling both compute (driving) and feature (facial regions) within a Gaussian head avatar framework can simultaneously improve expressiveness and rendering fidelity while eliminating external tracking dependencies and achieving fast end-to-end inference.

Abstract: Creating photorealistic animatable head avatars from a single image remains a fundamental challenge in digital human synthesis. While recent 3D Gaussian Splatting methods have achieved promising results, they rely on external tracking pipelines whose latency is excluded from inference measurements. Furthermore, they adopt unified representations that entangle geometrically distinct facial regions, limiting both expressiveness and rendering fidelity. We propose SpiD (Split and Drive), a single-image Gaussian head avatar framework built on two disentanglement axes. The compute axis internalizes per-frame driving, eliminating external tracking dependency at inference. The feature axis decomposes the avatar into three specialized Gaussian branches, each modeling a geometrically distinct facial domain. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistently strong performance against state-of-the-art methods while achieving the fastest inference speed among all compared methods on a single GPU with the complete driving pipeline included.

</details>


### [58] [TongueReenact: Geometry-Anchored Tongue Synthesis for Face Reenactment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28039)
*MD Wahiduzzaman Khan,Mingshan Jia,Xiaolin Zhang,En Yu,Kaska Musial-Gabrys*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents the first framework for cross-identity tongue dynamics transfer in face reenactment, addressing the overlooked issue of tongue motion in existing reenactment systems. It introduces a foundation-model-assisted bootstrapping pipeline for tongue segmentation without curated annotations, and a spatially constrained latent masked diffusion model with adaptive mask dilation for realistic tongue synthesis. Results show over 2x improvement on all tongue-specific metrics, validated by a VLM-based evaluation protocol that replicates expert annotation at scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing face reenactment systems achieve impressive pose and expression transfer but largely ignore tongue dynamics, resulting in anatomically inconsistent mouth interiors during speech and expressive motions. No prior work addresses cross-identity tongue dynamics transfer in face reenactment.

Method: (1) A foundation-model-assisted bootstrapping pipeline that produces a dedicated tongue segmentation model for in-the-wild reenactment without requiring curated annotations. (2) A spatially constrained latent masked diffusion model for realistic tongue synthesis, incorporating adaptive mask dilation to achieve seamless mouth boundary transitions.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate improvements of more than two times over all baselines on every tongue-specific metric. A VLM-based evaluation protocol confirms perceptual superiority across all ablation variants, replicating expert annotation at scale.

Conclusion: The proposed framework is the first to achieve realistic cross-identity tongue dynamics transfer in face reenactment, significantly outperforming baselines on tongue-specific metrics and demonstrating perceptual superiority validated through an automated VLM-based evaluation protocol.

Abstract: Modern face reenactment systems achieve impressive pose and expression transfer using geometry-driven representations. However, they largely ignore tongue dynamics, leading to anatomically inconsistent mouth interiors during speech and expressive motions. We introduce the first framework for cross-identity tongue dynamics transfer in face reenactment. We propose a foundation-model-assisted bootstrapping pipeline that produces a dedicated tongue segmentation model for in-the-wild reenactment without curated annotations. We further introduce a spatially constrained latent masked diffusion model for realistic tongue synthesis, with adaptive mask dilation for seamless mouth boundary transitions. Extensive experiments demonstrate improvements of more than two times over all baselines on every tongue-specific metric. We additionally propose a VLM-based evaluation protocol that replicates expert annotation at scale, confirming perceptual superiority across all ablation variants.

</details>


### [59] [Temporal Concentration from Rollout Errors: Implicit Preference Optimization for Text-to-Video Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28058)
*Henglin Liu,Fangyuan Kong,Jing Wang,Yizhou Lin,Nisha Huang,Chang Liu,Xintao Wang,Pengfei Wan,Kun Gai,Xiu Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: cIPO (concentrated Implicit Preference Optimization) is a post-training framework for diffusion-based video generation that derives preference signals directly from the denoising process itself—treating original videos as preferred and their reconstructions as dispreferred—and concentrates optimization on high temporal reconstruction error segments, thereby addressing temporally sparse artifacts (motion collapse, flickering, oversaturation) without human annotations or external reward models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Temporally sparse artifacts such as motion collapse, object flickering, and color oversaturation severely degrade perceptual realism in video generation, yet existing preference alignment methods (e.g., DPO-based approaches) fail to address them due to two key limitations: (1) the preference attribution bottleneck—offline human annotations are costly and fail to capture learning dynamics, while online reward signals are unstable and biased; and (2) temporal credit misallocation—uniform supervision cannot effectively target the brief segments where artifacts actually occur.

Method: cIPO derives implicit preference signals directly from the denoising process: given a real video, the model adds forward noise and reconstructs it via iterative denoising, treating the original as the preferred sample and the reconstruction as the dispreferred one. This formulation captures inference-time errors without human annotations or external reward models. Additionally, frame-level discrepancies between original and reconstructed videos reveal when failures occur, and cIPO computes temporal reconstruction errors to concentrate optimization on high-error segments, enabling precise correction of failure-prone regions.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that cIPO consistently enhances video authenticity and temporal coherence across multiple datasets, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of implicit preference with temporally concentrated optimization.

Conclusion: cIPO effectively addresses temporally sparse artifacts in diffusion-based video generation by leveraging implicit preference signals from the denoising process and concentrating optimization on high-error temporal segments, achieving improved video authenticity and temporal coherence without costly human annotations or external reward models.

Abstract: Recent advances in preference alignment for diffusion-based video generation, particularly via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), have significantly improved visual quality. However, temporally sparse artifacts such as motion collapse, object flickering, and color oversaturation remain a major barrier to perceptual realism. Existing methods struggle with these issues due to two key limitations: (1) the preference attribution bottleneck, where offline human annotations are costly and fail to accurately capture learning dynamics, while online reward signals are rollout-aware but often unstable and biased; and (2) temporal credit misallocation, where uniformly applied supervision cannot effectively target the brief segments in which artifacts occur. To address these challenges, we propose concentrated Implicit Preference Optimization (cIPO), a post-training framework for video diffusion models. cIPO derives implicit preference signals directly from the denoising process: given a real video, the model adds forward noise and reconstructs it via iterative denoising, treating the original as the preferred sample and the reconstruction as the dispreferred one. This formulation captures inference-time errors without requiring human annotations or external reward models. Moreover, frame-level discrepancies between original and reconstructed videos reveal when failures occur. cIPO leverages this by computing temporal reconstruction errors and concentrating optimization on high-error segments, enabling more precise correction of failure-prone regions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that cIPO consistently enhances video authenticity and temporal coherence across multiple datasets, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of implicit preference with temporally concentrated optimization.

</details>


### [60] [Landmark shape spaces with induced metrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28064)
*Sarang Joshi,Peter W. Michor,Stefan Sommer*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper unifies Kendall's landmark shape spaces (where rigid motions are factored out and scale is fixed) with landmark configuration spaces equipped with Riemannian metrics derived from right-invariant Sobolev metrics on the diffeomorphism group. A novel "screened elasticity operator" whose null-space consists exactly of rigid motions enables a metric that prevents landmark collisions, is independent of landmark count, preserves local rigid transformations, removes global rigid motions, and fixes scale. Numerical methods for matching and geodesic computation are presented.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To combine the desirable properties of two separate landmark shape space frameworks: Kendall's shape spaces (which remove global rigid motions and fix scale) and diffeomorphism-based landmark configurations with Sobolev metrics (which provide geometric regularity and prevent collisions). The unification aims to leverage the strengths of both while overcoming their individual limitations.

Method: The paper defines a Sobolev-type operator called the screened elasticity operator, whose null-space is exactly the set of rigid motions. This operator descends to the landmark configuration space to yield a Riemannian metric that inherits desirable properties. The authors show how this construction removes global rigid motions and fixes scale while preserving local rigid transformations, and develop numerical approaches for solving matching problems and computing geodesics.

Result: The resulting landmark shape spaces achieve the defining properties of both Kendall's shape spaces and diffeomorphism-based landmark spaces: landmarks cannot collide (due to metric regularity), the metric is ambient and independent of the number of landmarks, local rigid transformations are preserved, global rigid motions are factored out, and scale is fixed.

Conclusion: The unified construction enables the use of landmark configuration spaces with sufficiently regular metrics in applications while retaining the shape invariances characteristic of Kendall's shape spaces, providing a bridge between the two classical approaches.

Abstract: We present a unification of Kendall's landmark shape spaces, where rigid motions are factored out and scale fixed on landmark configurations equipped with Euclidean geometry, with landmark configuration spaces carrying Riemannian metrics descending from right-invariant Sobolev metrics on the diffeomorphism group. The resulting new landmark shape spaces achieve the defining properties of both approaches: The regularity of the descending metric prevents landmarks from colliding, the metric is defined in the ambient space independent of the number of landmarks, local rigid transformations are preserved, global rigid motions are removed, and scale fixed. To achieve this, we define a particular Sobolev-type operator, the screened elasticity operator, whose null-space consists exactly of the rigid motions, we show how this operator descends to achieve the desired geometry, and we present approaches to solving matching problems and computing geodesics numerically. The resulting construction allows the use of landmark configuration spaces with sufficiently regular metrics in applications while retaining the shape invariances that are a hallmark of Kendall's shape spaces.

</details>


### [61] [BladeYOLO: Wind Turbine Blade Defect Detection with Limited Annotations and Weak-Saliency Awareness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28065)
*Yabin Xu,Fangtao Zhang,Fan Wang,Zhan Wang,Honghua Chen,Mingqiang Wei,Haoran Xie,Sam Kwong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: BladeYOLO is a wind turbine blade defect detection framework built on YOLOv12-L with a DINOv3-initialized Vision Transformer backbone, a Mamba-guided Weak-Defect Enhancement module, and a lightweight Style-Injector module. It achieves superior performance on the WTBlade-Defect dataset and outperforms the best competing method by 3.5% in mAP50 and 2.5% in mAP50-95 on the public Wind Surface Defect dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world wind turbine blade defect detection is highly challenging due to limited on-site data, small-scale and low-contrast defects, and visual similarity to complex backgrounds, which collectively limit the robustness of existing detectors.

Method: The framework integrates (1) a ViT backbone with DINOv3 self-supervised pre-trained weights into YOLOv12-L for transferring generic visual priors; (2) a Mamba-guided Weak-Defect Enhancement module with a Detail-Enhanced Multi-scale Branch for preserving high-frequency cues and a Cross-Mamba module for propagating semantic guidance to shallow features; (3) a lightweight Style-Injector that captures environment-related style via Fourier decomposition and injects it into ViT self-attention layers.

Result: BladeYOLO achieves superior performance on the WTBlade-Defect dataset, shows favorable performance under reduced training annotations in annotation-budget experiments, and demonstrates cross-dataset robustness by outperforming the best competing method by 3.5% in mAP50 and 2.5% in mAP50-95 on the public Wind Surface Defect dataset.

Conclusion: The proposed BladeYOLO effectively addresses the challenges of subtle and low-contrast blade defect detection under limited annotations and environment-induced appearance variations, demonstrating strong performance and cross-dataset generalization.

Abstract: Wind turbine blade defect detection remains highly challenging in real-world inspection scenarios due to limited on-site data and the subtle visual characteristics of defects. In practice, blade defects are often small-scale, low-contrast, and difficult to distinguish from complex backgrounds, which significantly limits the robustness of existing detectors. To address these challenges, we propose BladeYOLO, a defect detection framework for wind turbine blades. Specifically, we integrate a Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone initialized with DINOv3 self-supervised pre-trained weights into YOLOv12-L, enabling the transfer of large-scale generic visual priors to blade defect detection and improving feature representation under limited training annotations. To enhance the perception of subtle defects, we further develop a Mamba-guided Weak-Defect Enhancement module, which consists of a Detail-Enhanced Multi-scale Branch for preserving high-frequency structural cues and a Cross-Mamba module for progressively propagating high-level semantic guidance to shallow features. In addition, we introduce a lightweight Style-Injector module that captures environment-related style information via Fourier decomposition and injects it into selected ViT self-attention layers, thereby improving robustness against environment-induced appearance variations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BladeYOLO achieves superior performance on the WTBlade-Defect dataset, with additional annotation-budget experiments showing its favorable performance under reduced training annotations. Evaluation on the public Wind Surface Defect dataset further provides supportive evidence for the cross-dataset robustness of BladeYOLO. In particular, on this public dataset, BladeYOLO outperforms the best competing method by 3.5\% in mAP$_{50}$ and 2.5\% in mAP$_{50-95}$.

</details>


### [62] [mmRadarTwin: A Measurement-Calibrated Signal-Level Digital Twin Platform for Indoor mmWave Radar](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28108)
*Jianyi Zhou,Chenghao Zhang,Yanli Li,Dong Yuan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: mmRadarTwin is a signal-level, path-attributed digital-twin platform for indoor mmWave radar that links real FMCW measurements with Unreal Engine scene simulation through shared receive-channel and range-angle processing. Evaluated across 154 poses in an office, it recalls 70.8% of measurement-active geometry-supported response regions while exposing residuals from weak path support, shifted responses, and unsupported anchors, establishing a practical systems workflow for building, comparing, and diagnosing indoor radar digital twins.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Indoor mmWave radar perception is hard to reproduce because measured range-angle responses depend on scene geometry, material response, multipath, hardware conventions, and signal processing. Existing ray-tracing and digital-twin tools expose rendering, channel, or path-level quantities, but radar sensing requires complex signal products comparable in the same domain as real FMCW measurements.

Method: mmRadarTwin links a real radar measurement branch with an Unreal Engine scene-simulation branch through a shared receive-channel and range-angle processing interface. The simulator writes complex multi-channel receive grids and exports per-path contribution records identifying actor, material tag, propagation event, and output-bin support for each simulated return. Evaluation uses a commodity monostatic mmWave radar with mobile scene-capture hardware in an office deployment.

Result: Across 154 measured poses spanning 22 radar locations, the physics-only path-basis simulator recalls 70.8% of measurement-active geometry-supported response regions in the central usable field of view, while exposing residuals caused by weak or missing path support, shifted responses, unsupported anchors, and missing physical mechanisms.

Conclusion: mmRadarTwin does not claim complete radar-map reconstruction or cross-room generalization, but establishes a practical systems workflow for constructing, comparing, and diagnosing indoor radar digital twins, providing a shared domain for real measurements and simulations.

Abstract: Indoor mmWave radar perception is difficult to reproduce because measured range-angle responses depend on scene geometry, material response, multipath, hardware conventions, and signal processing. Existing ray-tracing and digital-twin tools often expose rendering, channel, or path-level quantities, while radar sensing requires complex signal products that can be processed and compared in the same domain as real FMCW measurements. We present mmRadarTwin, a signal-level and path-attributed digital-twin platform for indoor mmWave radar. mmRadarTwin links a real radar measurement branch with an Unreal Engine scene-simulation branch through a shared receive-channel and range-angle processing interface. The simulator writes complex multi-channel receive grids and exports per-path contribution records that identify the actor, material tag, propagation event, and output-bin support of each simulated return. We evaluate mmRadarTwin in an office deployment using a commodity monostatic mmWave radar and mobile scene-capture hardware. Across 154 measured poses spanning 22 radar locations, the current physics-only path-basis simulator recalls 70.8% of measurement-active geometry-supported response regions in the central usable field of view while exposing residuals caused by weak or missing path support, shifted responses, unsupported anchors, and missing physical mechanisms. Rather than claiming complete radar-map reconstruction or cross-room generalization, mmRadarTwin establishes a practical systems workflow for constructing, comparing, and diagnosing indoor radar digital twins.

</details>


### [63] [Towards Practical Algorithm Selection for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation in Medical Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28125)
*Yiheng Xiong,Luisa Gallée,Daniel Santak Wolf,Heiko Hillenhagen,Michael Götz*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes a label-free criterion for jointly selecting the best UDA algorithm and its hyperparameters without using target domain labels, by scoring candidate models against a two-level agreement reference constructed from multiple label-free selection signals aggregated across algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While many UDA algorithms exist, clinical practitioners cannot directly validate or compare them on the unlabeled deployment (target) domain, making it unclear which algorithm and hyperparameters to choose in practice.

Method: The approach builds a two-level agreement reference without target labels. First, multiple label-free selection signals each nominate a model within every algorithm. Second, nominated models are aggregated across algorithms to produce a reference prediction per target sample. Each candidate is scored by agreement with this reference, and the highest-scoring one is selected for deployment.

Result: On four brain MRI and four chest X-ray datasets across seven clinically relevant transfer scenarios, the method outperforms other selection approaches and remains effective across different algorithm pools.

Conclusion: The method advances practical, label-free algorithm and hyperparameter selection, facilitating reliable clinical deployment of UDA models.

Abstract: Numerous unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) algori-thms exist, but for clinical practice, selecting the best-suited one along with proper hyperparameters often remains unclear, as the unlabeled deployment (target) domain prevents direct evaluation. We propose a label-free criterion that jointly selects the algorithm and hyperparameters for UDA. Given a pool of candidate models from multiple algorithms trained with different hyperparameters, our approach scores each candidate against an agreement reference, and selects the one with the highest score. The agreement reference is constructed in two levels without using target labels. First, we leverage multiple label-free selection signals, using each to nominate a model within every algorithm. Second, the nominated models are aggregated across algorithms to form a reference prediction for each unlabeled target sample. The candidate whose predictions agree most with this reference is then selected for deployment. Experimental results on four brain MRI and four chest X-ray datasets across seven clinically relevant transfer scenarios show that our method achieves better selection performance than other methods and remains effective across different algorithm pools. Our approach takes a step towards practical, label-free algorithm selection for clinical deployment of UDA.

</details>


### [64] [Face and Voice Cross-modal Association with Learning Convex Feature Embedding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28129)
*Taewan Kim,Jiwoo Kang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes a cross-modal feature embedding method for face-voice association learning that addresses inter-modal heterogeneity by embedding features within a convex hull, combined with cross-modal attention to reduce false positives/negatives. The method achieves state-of-the-art results on the VoxCeleb dataset across verification, matching, and retrieval tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous cross-modal face-voice association works addressed cross-modal discrimination but underestimated inter-modal feature heterogeneity between audio and video, leading to numerous false positives and false negatives. Existing methods fail to properly handle the distributional and representational gaps between face and voice modalities.

Method: The proposed method learns cross-modal feature embeddings by introducing an additional feature between cross-modal features, causing voice and face features of the same person to be embedded within a convex hull. This is combined with cross-modal attention mechanisms and convex embedding techniques to minimize inter-class discrepancies and attenuate false positives/negatives.

Result: Extensive experiments on the large-scale VoxCeleb dataset for cross-modal verification, matching, and retrieval tasks demonstrate notable improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: The proposed convex embedding approach with cross-modal attention effectively addresses the heterogeneity problem in face-voice association, achieving superior performance and reducing false matching errors across all evaluated cross-modal tasks.

Abstract: Face-and-voice association learning is one of the most challenging tasks in deep learning. In this paper, we propose a simple but powerful cross-modal feature embedding method for the association of faces and voices. Previous work has studied cross-modal association tasks to establish the correlation between voice clips and facial images. These works have addressed cross-modal discrimination but underestimate the importance of handling heterogeneity in inter-modal features between audio and video, resulting in a lot of false positives and false negatives. To tackle the problem, the proposed method learns the embeddings of cross-modal features by making another feature exist between cross-modal features, facilitating the voice and face features of the same person to be embedded in a convex hull. Moreover, the incorporation of cross-modal attention mechanisms with convex embedding techniques represents a highly effective strategy for the attenuation of false positives and false negatives, accomplished via the minimization of inter-class discrepancies. We exhaustively evaluated our method for cross-modal verification, matching, and retrieval tasks on the large-scale VoxCeleb dataset. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves notable improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [65] [Collaborative Feature Aggregation for Face Super-Resolution and Robust Re-Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28130)
*Juheon Hwang,Taewan Kim,Jiwoo Kang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a transformer-based collaborative approach that jointly performs face super-resolution and person re-identification from multi-sequence or multi-view facial images. A transformer-based collaborative feature aggregation module unifies identity features across multiple correlated observations, and a cascade SR network progressively restores high-resolution face images. The unified identity representation enables accurate person re-identification under severe image degradation, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in both tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional face super-resolution methods suffer from blurring and distortion when recovering faces from low-quality images. Existing image- and video-based SR approaches using facial landmarks or segmentation also face similar challenges, motivating the need to leverage multiple correlated facial observations across time or viewpoints to improve reconstruction quality.

Method: The approach utilizes a transformer-based collaborative feature aggregation method to unify identity features from multi-sequence or multi-view facial data. This is combined with a cascade super-resolution network that progressively restores the target face's high-resolution image while gradually unifying facial features. The unified identity representation is also applied to person re-identification tasks.

Result: Extensive experimental results demonstrate the method consistently outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches in both face super-resolution and person re-identification, showing improvements even under severe image degradation conditions.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that joint identity reconstruction and progressive image restoration from multiple facial inputs effectively enhance downstream visual recognition tasks such as person re-identification.

Abstract: We propose a novel collaborative approach for face super-resolution (SR) and robust person re-identification from sequential or multi-view facial images. Traditional SR methods often suffer from blurring and distortion in faces recovered from poor-quality images due to low resolution. Image- and video-based facial SR methods using facial landmarks or segmentation also have similar challenges. To overcome these limitations, we leverage multiple correlated facial observations, across time or viewpoints, by introducing a transformer-based collaborative feature aggregation method that unifies identity features from multi-sequence or multi-view data. This allows faces in multiple sequences of an individual to contribute to accurately estimating common facial features. Furthermore, we propose a cascade SR network to progressively restore the high-resolution image of the target's face with gradual facial feature unification. The unified identity representation is further utilized in person re-identification scenarios, enabling accurate matching even under severe image degradation. The exhaustive experimental results and comparisons show that our method outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating consistent improvements in both face super-resolution and re-identification performance. Our work highlights the effectiveness of joint identity reconstruction and progressive image restoration from multiple facial inputs in enhancing downstream visual recognition tasks.

</details>


### [66] [Convolutional Neural Shading for High-Quality 3D Reconstruction from Multi-View Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28132)
*Juheon Hwang,Taewan Kim,Heeseok Oh,Jiwoo Kang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes Convolutional Neural Shading (CNS), a pipeline for high-quality 3D shape reconstruction from multi-view images that uses a convolutional neural shader to capture local geometric variations (unlike single-point neural radiance field methods) and a fine-detail displacement network to reduce surface irregularities at image boundaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural differentiable rendering methods (e.g., neural radiance fields) rely on single-point geometric information such as surface positions and normals, which leads to a lack of detailed local geometry, particularly in dark and textureless regions.

Method: The method introduces (1) a convolutional neural shader that leverages spatial/local information to capture variations even in dark and textureless regions, and (2) a fine-detail displacement network that uses spatial information of surface geometry to learn fine displacement details by correlating neighboring values in rendering coordinates, mitigating surface irregularities at image boundaries.

Result: Extensive experiments show significant quality improvements in reconstructed 3D shapes and rendered images over current state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: The convolutional neural shading approach overcomes the limitations of single-point geometry modeling in neural differentiable rendering, achieving more accurate geometry predictions and superior reconstruction quality.

Abstract: We propose a convolutional neural shading (CNS), a novel pipeline to reconstruct high-quality 3D shapes from multi-view images. Several recent studies have used neural radiance fields and other neural differentiable rendering methods to understand 3D geometry. However, these approaches rely on single-point geometric information, such as positions and normals of the surface, leading to a lack of detailed local geometry. Our approach addresses the inherent limitations of single-point information by leveraging a neural shader to capture variations even in dark and textureless regions with a convolutional neural shader, resulting in far more accurate geometry predictions. Additionally, our method mitigates surface irregularities at image boundaries by introducing a fine-detail displacement network, which utilizes spatial information of surface geometry and learns fine displacement details by correlating neighboring values in the rendering coordinates. Through extensive experiments, our proposed method has demonstrated significant quality improvements in the reconstructed shapes and rendered images over current state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [67] [What Makes Deep Learning Work for Traditional Chinese Medicine Tongue Diagnosis? A Comprehensive Ablation Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28148)
*Longxia Gao,Linan Wang,Yuhe Han,Junze Geng,Meng Zhang,Hanqing Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A systematic ablation study of deep learning models for automated tongue diagnosis in TCM, comparing 20+ model versions across backbones, loss functions, augmentations, and training strategies, yielding six key design principles and optimal weighted-F1 scores of 0.6625 (976 samples) and 0.7761 (11,101 samples).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although deep learning has shown promise for automated tongue diagnosis in traditional Chinese medicine, the design space of model configurations remains underexplored. This study aims to systematically identify optimal design choices for this task.

Method: A systematic ablation study was conducted over 20+ model versions with rigorous 5-fold cross-validation on TongueDx2 (5,109 images, 976 expert-annotated) and a merged dataset of 11,101 samples. Six backbone architectures, four loss functions, five augmentation strategies, and six training strategies were compared. The best configurations employed ConvNeXt-Tiny with restrained augmentation and weak-group ensemble.

Result: The best 976-sample model achieved weighted-F1 of 0.6625, and the best 11,101-sample model reached 0.7761. Key findings: BCE outperformed Asymmetric Loss by +2.7%; weak-group ensemble improved over probability averaging by +2.1%; data scaling yielded +20.6% improvement; expanding from 13 to 45 label dimensions caused catastrophic collapse (0.78 to 0.22); restrained color augmentation was critical; ConvNeXt-Tiny was optimally parameter-efficient.

Conclusion: Six generalizable design principles emerged for multi-label medical image classification with class imbalance, which extend beyond tongue diagnosis to broader medical imaging applications.

Abstract: Deep learning has shown promise for automated tongue diagnosis in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), yet the design space remains underexplored. We conducted a systematic ablation study spanning 20+ model versions under rigorous 5-fold cross-validation on TongueDx2 (5,109 images, 976 expert-annotated) and a merged dataset of 11,101 samples. We compared six backbone architectures, four loss functions, five augmentation strategies, and six training strategies. The best 976-sample model achieved weighted-F1 of 0.6625 using ConvNeXt-Tiny with restrained augmentation and weak-group ensemble, while the best 11,101-sample model reached weighted-F1 of 0.7761. Six key design principles emerged: (1) ConvNeXt-Tiny offers optimal parameter efficiency; (2) BCE substantially outperforms Asymmetric Loss (+2.7%); (3) restrained color augmentation is critical; (4) weak-group ensemble replacement (+2.1%) outperforms probability averaging; (5) data scaling yielded +20.6% improvement; (6) expanding from 13 to 45 label dimensions caused catastrophic collapse (0.78 to 0.22). These principles are generalizable to multi-label medical image classification with class imbalance.

</details>


### [68] [OPLD: On-Policy Latent Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28154)
*Shoutai Zhu,Tianyang Xu,Bin Sun,Mingyuan Xu,Yu Liu,Qinzhen Guo*

Main category: cs.CV
