For local queries, it adopts an event-aware frame selection strategy that performs event partitioning, segment-level frame allocation, and intra-event frame selection, jointly balancing relevance, coverage, and diversity with a limited number of input frames. Experiments show that VisualRouter consistently improves multiple LVLMs over uniform sampling, achieving gains of 5.2%, 7.7%, and 11.6% on Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and outperforming existing training-free visual sampling methods under the same setting.

</details>


### [90] [Can Vision-Language Models Reason about AI Edits in Images?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28464)
*Darsha Udayanga,Pin-Yu Chen,Payel Das,Qiang Ji*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a GRPO-based reinforcement learning framework to train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to reason about AI-generated image tampering without explicit reasoning supervision. The model produces structured reasoning traces and binary tampering predictions, which guide a lightweight segmentation model for pixel-level localization. The approach achieves competitive detection and localization performance versus state-of-the-art forgery detectors while requiring substantially weaker supervision, and introduces eff-IoU as a unified metric for joint evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional binary classifiers for detecting AI-tampered images lack interpretability and generalization. Existing VLM-based approaches rely on supervised finetuning with curated explanations rather than exploiting VLMs' inherent reasoning capabilities. The authors aim to investigate whether VLMs can learn to reason about AI-generated edits through reinforcement learning, eliminating the need for explicit reasoning supervision.

Method: The framework applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), an RL technique that incentivizes the model to generate thinking traces before producing answers. The VLM receives an input image, produces a structured reasoning trace, and predicts whether the image has been tampered with, using simple accuracy and format rewards. A lightweight segmentation model is then guided by the reasoning output to generate pixel-level localization masks. The paper also introduces effective intersection over union (eff-IoU), a unified metric for jointly evaluating detection and localization performance.

Result: Experiments across multiple image manipulation datasets show the approach achieves competitive detection and localization performance compared to state-of-the-art image forgery detectors, despite requiring substantially weaker supervision.

Conclusion: Reinforcement learning provides an effective and scalable mechanism for teaching VLMs to reason about AI-generated content, enabling competitive tamper detection and localization without explicit reasoning supervision.

Abstract: Detection and localization of AI-tampered images are critical for trustworthy AI, yet modern generative models have made such manipulations increasingly difficult to identify. While traditional binary classifiers can detect image tampering, they lack interpretability and generalization. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) offer a promising alternative due to their strong visual understanding and reasoning capabilities; however, existing approaches typically rely on supervised finetuning with curated explanations rather than exploiting their inherent reasoning capabilities. In this work, we investigate whether VLMs can be trained to reason about AI-generated image edits using reinforcement learning (RL) rather than explicit reasoning supervision. Motivated by the success in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), an RL technique that incentivizes the model to reason by generating thinking traces prior to giving the final answer, we propose a GRPO-based training framework that utilizes simple accuracy and format rewards. Given an input image, the model produces a structured reasoning trace and predicts whether the image has been tampered with. A lightweight segmentation model is then guided by the reasoning output to generate pixel-level localization masks. Experiments across multiple image manipulation datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive detection and localization performance compared to state-of-the-art image forgery detectors, despite requiring substantially weaker supervision. We introduce effective intersection over union (eff-IoU), a unified metric to jointly evaluate detection and localization. These results suggest that reinforcement learning provides an effective and scalable mechanism for teaching VLMs to reason about AI-generated content.

</details>


### [91] [Towards Real-Time PixOOD: Efficient Anomaly Segmentation for Autonomous Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28483)
*Luca de Martino,Federico Aromolo,Federico Nesti,Giorgio Buttazzo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents an efficient and accelerated anomaly segmentation pipeline for real-time autonomous driving and railway applications, built by reformulating the Neyman-Pearson scoring stage of the PixOOD out-of-distribution detection method and deploying the full pipeline via hardware-optimized TensorRT compilation. The system achieves up to 182 FPS on a desktop NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU and 75 FPS on the Jetson AGX Orin embedded platform, representing 20x and 18x speedups over the original baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-time anomaly segmentation is critical for autonomous system safety, but existing high-accuracy approaches suffer from excessive computational cost that limits deployment on embedded hardware. The goal is to bridge the gap between state-of-the-art detection accuracy and real-time onboard processing requirements.

Method: The proposed approach reformulates the Neyman-Pearson scoring stage of PixOOD, a state-of-the-art out-of-distribution detection method, and deploys the complete pipeline using hardware-optimized TensorRT compilation targeting both embedded (Jetson AGX Orin) and desktop (RTX 4060) platforms in the autonomous driving and railway domains.

Result: The optimized pipeline achieves up to 182 FPS on a desktop NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU and 75 FPS on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin embedded platform, respectively 20x and 18x faster than the original baseline.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate that advanced anomaly segmentation can be efficiently deployed for onboard processing in autonomous driving and railway applications, making real-time out-of-distribution detection feasible on resource-constrained embedded platforms.

Abstract: Real-time anomaly segmentation is essential for the safety of autonomous systems. Although recent approaches offer high accuracy, their computational cost limits their deployment on embedded hardware. This work presents an efficient and accelerated pipeline designed for both embedded and desktop platforms, targeting the autonomous driving and railway domains. The proposed approach reformulates the Neyman-Pearson scoring stage of PixOOD, a state-of-the-art out-of-distribution detection method, and deploys the full pipeline through hardware-optimized TensorRT compilation, reaching up to 182 FPS on a desktop NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU and 75 FPS on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin embedded platform, respectively 20x and 18x faster than the original baseline. The achieved results demonstrate that advanced anomaly segmentation can be efficiently deployed for onboard processing in autonomous driving and railway applications.

</details>


### [92] [AuricularWorld: Hierarchical Action-Guided World Modeling for Fine-Grained Auricular Structure Segmentation from CT Scans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28487)
*Jingwen Yang,Senmao Wang,Luoyao Kang,Runmeng Cui,Keying Zhang,Yunjia Bao,Haifan Gong,Lin Lin,Haiyue Jiang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A world-model-based segmentation framework using a deterministic recurrent state-space model in the latent space enables iterative anatomical reasoning for fine-grained auricular CT segmentation, improving accuracy and reducing HD95 by over 43% for small, irregular, and overlapping structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-grained auricular CT segmentation is challenging because the ear occupies a small region, cartilage boundaries are irregular, cartilage-soft tissue interfaces are ambiguous, and clinical annotations produce nested/overlapping labels (composite structures vs. cartilage-only). Conventional feed-forward prediction lacks iterative reasoning capability for such anatomically complex and ambiguous structures.

Method: The framework builds on an encoder-decoder architecture and introduces a deterministic recurrent state-space model in the intermediate latent space. Multi-scale encoder features and partially decoded representations are fused to form a structural observation that initializes latent dynamics. During inference, a three-step latent rollout (without ground-truth guidance) uses hierarchical anatomical actions to update the recurrent state and progressively refine the latent representation. The latent trajectory is projected back to the decoder and combined with high-resolution features for final segmentation. A balanced hierarchical action objective handles foreground sparsity, missing anatomical groups, and add/remove operation imbalance.

Result: Extensive experiments show consistent segmentation accuracy improvements, with HD95 reduced by more than 43% for small, irregular, and overlapping auricular structures in CT compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Latent world-model reasoning, which enables iterative anatomical refinement through recurrent state-space dynamics, proves effective for challenging medical image segmentation tasks involving small, irregular, and overlapping anatomical structures.

Abstract: Fine-grained segmentation of auricular structures in CT is challenging because the ear occupies a small image region, cartilage boundaries are highly irregular, and interfaces between cartilage and surrounding soft tissues are often ambiguous. Clinical annotations may also include both composite structures containing cartilage and adjacent skin and their corresponding cartilage-only regions, producing nested and overlapping labels. We propose a world-model-based segmentation framework that enables iterative anatomical reasoning beyond conventional feed-forward prediction. Built on an encoder-decoder architecture, the framework introduces a deterministic recurrent state-space model into the intermediate latent space. Multi-scale encoder features and partially decoded representations are fused to form a structural observation that initializes the latent dynamics. During inference, the model performs a three-step latent rollout without ground-truth guidance. Hierarchical anatomical actions update the recurrent state and progressively refine the latent representation. The resulting latent trajectory is projected back into the decoder and combined with high-resolution features to produce the final segmentation. To learn reliable latent transitions, we introduce a balanced hierarchical action objective that addresses foreground sparsity, missing anatomical groups, and imbalance between add and remove operations. Extensive experiments show that the proposed framework consistently improves segmentation accuracy and reduces HD95 by more than 43% for small, irregular, and overlapping auricular structures in CT. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of latent world-model reasoning for challenging medical image segmentation.

</details>


### [93] [RefCaptioner: Multi-Reference Image-Grounded Video Captioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28509)
*Tengfei Liu,Yang Shi,Yuran Wang,Xiaohan Zhang,Yuqing Wen,Yuqi Tang,Qixun Wang,Zhuoran Zhang,Xuanyu Zhu,Weihong Lin,Xinlei Yu,Yujie Wei,Xinwei Long,Fengxiang Wang,Xinlong Chen,Yue Ding,Jialu Chen,Haotian Wang,Yuanxing Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces multi-reference image-grounded video captioning, a new task requiring factual video descriptions with phrase-level grounding to multiple reference images. The authors propose RefCaptioner, a two-stage post-training framework combining mixed-data SFT and Hierarchical Coverage-Discounted GRPO, along with a new benchmark (MRVBench) and dataset (20,000 videos, 171,354 reference images). RefCaptioner achieves the best overall performance among open-source models while remaining competitive on standard video captioning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video captioning models generate natural video descriptions but cannot explicitly ground local visual elements to multiple reference images, limiting their ability to produce factual, verifiable captions where phrases are tied to specific reference sources.

Method: RefCaptioner uses a two-stage post-training framework: (1) mixed-data supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (2) Hierarchical Coverage-Discounted GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) to jointly optimize reference selection, phrase-level binding, distractor rejection, and cross-reference consistency. Training is supported by a constructed corpus of 20,000 videos and 171,354 reference images, and evaluation uses MRVBench on both real-world and AI-generated videos.

Result: RefCaptioner achieves the best overall performance among open-source models on the new task and remains competitive on standard video captioning benchmarks. Human evaluation shows annotators prefer its captions, and they enable more source-faithful video reconstruction with both open-source and proprietary video generators.

Conclusion: The work establishes multi-reference image-grounded video captioning as a distinct task and demonstrates that the proposed RefCaptioner framework effectively balances new grounding capabilities with preserved general video captioning ability, with human-verified improvements in caption preference and downstream source-faithful video reconstruction.

Abstract: Existing video captioning models generate natural descriptions of video content but cannot explicitly ground local visual elements to multiple reference images. We introduce multi-reference image-grounded video captioning, a new task requiring factual video descriptions with phrase-level reference grounding, and propose RefCaptioner, a two-stage post-training framework for this task. RefCaptioner combines mixed-data SFT with Hierarchical Coverage-Discounted GRPO to jointly improve reference selection, phrase-level binding, distractor rejection, and cross-reference consistency while preserving general video-captioning ability. To support training, we construct a corpus containing $20,000$ videos and 171,354 reference images. We further introduce MRVBench, a benchmark for evaluating caption factuality and multi-reference grounding on both real-world and AI-generated videos. Experiments show that RefCaptioner achieves the best overall performance among the open-source models while remaining competitive on standard video captioning benchmarks. Human evaluation further confirms that its captions are preferred by annotators and enable more source-faithful video reconstruction with both open-source and proprietary video generators.

</details>


### [94] [Beyond Frame Selection: Generative Latent Evidence Aggregation for Long-Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28516)
*Bowen Liu,Shuning Wang,Xinpeng Ding,Zhiheng Wu,Bodong Du,Xiaomeng Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GenEvA is a generative latent evidence aggregation framework that organizes query-relevant selected frames into cross-frame latent evidence before answer generation, improving long-video understanding in Video-MLLMs with minimal token overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing compact video understanding pipelines focus on retaining relevant visual content as explicit evidence but do not ensure that complementary cues across different moments are integrated for answer generation. Making evidence available is not sufficient; cross-frame integration is needed.

Method: GenEvA formulates a post-selection stage as a latent evidence interface. It uses a query-conditioned evidence distribution to focus aggregation on relevant frames, forming compact cross-frame latent evidence from frame-specific information. The same distribution also determines whether to insert this latent complement, enabling adaptive evidence invocation.

Result: Across four benchmarks and two Video-MLLM backbones, GenEvA consistently improves matched-frame baselines. At 8 frames, it raises the four-benchmark LLaVA-Video average by +5.2 points and Qwen2.5-VL accuracy on LVBench by +10.1 points, with only 0.11%-0.40% average video-token overhead.

Conclusion: Distribution-guided latent evidence aggregation provides task-aware allocation and benefits from adaptive evidence invocation, demonstrating that explicitly integrating cross-frame evidence before generation significantly improves long-video understanding.

Abstract: Long-video understanding commonly compresses videos into a small set of frames or visual tokens for answer generation. Existing compact pipelines focus on retaining relevant visual content as explicit evidence. Yet making evidence available does not ensure that complementary cues across moments are integrated for answering. Our key idea is to organize selected frames into query-relevant cross-frame evidence before generation. We formulate this post-selection stage as a latent evidence interface and instantiate it with GenEvA ($\textbf{Gen}erative$ $Latent$ $\textbf{Ev}idence$ $\textbf{A}ggregation$), a distribution-guided latent evidence aggregation framework. Specifically, GenEvA uses a query-conditioned evidence distribution to focus aggregation on relevant frames, forming compact cross-frame latent evidence from their frame-specific information. Since cross-frame integration is not always needed, the same distribution determines whether to insert this latent complement. Across four benchmarks and two Video-MLLM backbones, GenEvA consistently improves matched-frame baselines. At 8 frames, it raises the four-benchmark LLaVA-Video average by $+5.2$ points and Qwen2.5-VL accuracy on LVBench by $+10.1$ points. These gains require only $0.11\%$--$0.40\%$ average video-token overhead; analyses further show task-aware allocation and benefits from Adaptive Evidence Invocation.

</details>


### [95] [What to Remove, What to Preserve: Dual-Ambiguity Rectification for All-in-One Image Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28526)
*Cencen Liu,Wen Yin,Dongyang Zhang,Dongmin Li,Shan Zhao,Bing Su,Tao He,Jielei Wang,Guoming Lu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DAR-Net is a Dual-Ambiguity Rectification Network for all-in-one image restoration that addresses semantic and spatial ambiguities in a shared latent space via a Degradation Archetype Representation module with simplex-constrained archetype mixture modeling, plus Semantic and Spatial Ambiguity Rectification modules, achieving state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing all-in-one image restoration methods encode heterogeneous degradations in a shared latent space, where degradation-related cues and scene content remain entangled, leading to dual ambiguity: semantic ambiguity in channel-wise modulation and spatial ambiguity in restoration responses, which cause content corruption and residual artifacts.

Method: DAR-Net introduces three key components: (1) a Degradation Archetype Representation (DAR) module that constructs a structured degradation state via simplex-constrained archetype mixture modeling; (2) a Semantic Ambiguity Rectification (SeAR) module that generates degradation-aware prompts to improve channel-wise conditioning in the decoder; and (3) a Spatial Ambiguity Rectification (SpAR) module that regularizes degradation-aware and complementary features toward orthogonal response subspaces to reduce spatial interference between removal and preservation cues.

Result: DAR-Net achieves the best overall performance on standard all-in-one restoration benchmarks under both three-degradation and five-degradation settings, improving the average PSNR over the strongest competitor by 0.14 dB and 0.34 dB respectively, and shows superior performance on CDD-11 and WeatherBench.

Conclusion: By explicitly disentangling degradation-related cues from scene content and rectifying both semantic and spatial ambiguities, DAR-Net demonstrates that structured degradation state modeling and orthogonal feature regularization improve all-in-one image restoration performance across diverse degradation scenarios.

Abstract: All-in-one image restoration aims to handle diverse degradations within a unified framework. Existing methods commonly encode heterogeneous degradation conditions in a shared latent space, where degradation-related cues and scene content can remain entangled. We characterize the resulting challenge as dual ambiguity: semantic ambiguity in channel-wise modulation and spatial ambiguity in restoration responses, which can lead to content corruption and residual artifacts. To mitigate this issue, we propose DAR-Net, a Dual-Ambiguity Rectification Network for all-in-one image restoration. DAR-Net first introduces a Degradation Archetype Representation (DAR) module to construct a structured degradation state through simplex-constrained archetype mixture modeling. Based on this state, a Semantic Ambiguity Rectification (SeAR) module generates degradation-aware prompts to improve channel-wise conditioning in the decoder. A Spatial Ambiguity Rectification (SpAR) module further regularizes degradation-aware and complementary features toward orthogonal response subspaces, reducing spatial interference between removal and preservation cues. Extensive experiments on standard all-in-one restoration benchmarks show that DAR-Net achieves the best overall performance under both three-degradation and five-degradation settings, improving the average PSNR over the strongest competitor by 0.14 dB and 0.34 dB, respectively; it additionally shows superior performance on CDD-11 and WeatherBench.

</details>


### [96] [MarkushGlyph and OCSRGlyph: Improved Chemical Structure Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28532)
*Alex Andonian,Samuel G Rodriques,Andrew D White,Siddharth M Narayanan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces OCSRGlyph, a state-of-the-art optical chemical structure recognition (OCSR) model that improves performance by carefully handling stereochemistry, and MarkushGlyph, a vision-language model that reads entire Markush structures directly as images in a single-stage image-to-text translation approach. A new metric for evaluating Markush structure translation accuracy is also proposed to address failure modes in prior metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chemical structures in patents and literature appear as images and need to be converted to line notations for programmatic use. While single-molecule OCSR is mature, Markush structure parsing (representing families of molecules) remains challenging, and existing multi-stage systems process visual and text input separately rather than holistically.

Method: Both OCSR and Markush parsing are formulated as image-to-text translation problems. OCSRGlyph is trained with careful attention to stereochemistry to achieve state-of-the-art OCSR performance. MarkushGlyph is a vision-language model that reads the entire Markush structure as a single image, contrasting with prior multi-stage approaches. A new metric for Markush structure translation accuracy is introduced to handle failure modes in existing metrics.

Result: OCSRGlyph achieves state-of-the-art performance on OCSR tasks by improving stereochemical handling. MarkushGlyph provides an end-to-end vision-language approach for Markush structure parsing, and the proposed metric better captures translation accuracy by addressing failure modes present in prior metrics.

Conclusion: Treating both single-molecule and Markush structure recognition as image-to-text translation enables effective unified modeling. The proposed models advance state-of-the-art in OCSR and Markush parsing, and the new evaluation metric improves accuracy assessment for Markush translations.

Abstract: Chemical structures appear in patents and the scientific literature as images. For programmatic usage, such as indexing in databases or constructing machine learning model training sets, they must be transformed into line notations. The two common forms of this task are translating an image of a single molecule (optical chemical structure recognition - OCSR) and translating a Markush structure that represents a family of molecules. While prior work in the former case is quite mature, Markush structure parsing remains a challenging task. In this work, we treat both tasks as an image-to-text translation problem. We then propose OCSRGlyph, a state-of-the-art OCSR model, improving performance over prior methods by carefully considering stereochemistry. For the Markush task, we introduce MarkushGlyph, a vision-language model that reads the entire Markush structure as an image. This contrasts with prior systems, which often use multiple stages to separately process visual and text input content. Finally, we introduce a new metric for determining the accuracy of Markush structure translations, handling failure modes present in prior metrics.

</details>


### [97] [ScaFE: Data-Efficient Scar Classification with LLM-Generated Clinical Feature Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28538)
*Ruman Wang,Hangting Ye*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ScaFE (Scar Feature Engineering) transfers clinical knowledge from an LLM into deterministic, executable feature programs for classifying pathological scars, achieving 81.0% site-macro balanced accuracy on 600 photographs from three hospitals, exceeding BiomedCLIP by 10.0 percentage points while keeping raw images and patient-level outputs local for data governance and auditability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end image models are data-dependent and require large expert-labeled datasets, while hosted vision-language models present data-governance conflicts and produce decisions that are difficult to reproduce and audit. There is a need for a data-efficient, explainable, and privacy-preserving approach to classify keloids versus hypertrophic scars from clinical photographs across heterogeneous hospital acquisition settings.

Method: ScaFE uses a web-enabled LLM to retrieve clinical evidence and synthesize executable feature programs that measure visually assessable scar attributes. These programs run in a restricted local environment, returning only aggregate validation statistics and feature-level SHAP summaries for iterative repair and refinement (raw images and patient-level outputs stay local). A lightweight Random Forest classifier operates on the resulting structured representation. Evaluation uses leave-one-site-out on 600 photographs from three hospitals.

Result: ScaFE achieves 81.0% site-macro balanced accuracy, outperforming BiomedCLIP by 10.0 percentage points. With only 10% of development data, it retains 72.0% balanced accuracy with an 11.8-point lead. Iterative refinement raises the executable-program rate from 66.7% to 95.0%, with verified evidence for 91.7% of final features.

Conclusion: LLM knowledge can support data-efficient, cross-site medical image classification through local, auditable feature programs rather than direct VLM decisions, offering a practical alternative that balances accuracy, privacy, and explainability for pathological scar classification.

Abstract: Classifying pathological scars from clinical photographs requires distinguishing keloids from hypertrophic scars despite limited expert-labeled data and substantial acquisition variation across hospitals. End-to-end image models remain data-dependent, whereas sending photographs to a hosted vision-language model (VLM) may conflict with local data-governance requirements and yields decisions that are difficult to reproduce and audit. We introduce ScaFE (Scar Feature Engineering), which transfers clinical knowledge from a large language model (LLM) into deterministic, executable feature programs instead of asking the model to diagnose images. A web-enabled LLM retrieves clinical evidence and synthesizes programs that measure visually assessable scar attributes. Candidate programs execute in a restricted local environment, and only aggregate validation statistics and feature-level SHAP summaries are returned for iterative repair and refinement; raw images and patient-level outputs remain local. A lightweight Random Forest then operates on the resulting structured representation. On 600 photographs from three hospitals under leave-one-site-out evaluation, ScaFE achieves 81.0% site-macro balanced accuracy, exceeding the strongest baseline, BiomedCLIP, by 10.0 percentage points. With only 10% of the development data, ScaFE retains 72.0% balanced accuracy and an 11.8-point lead. Iterative refinement also raises the executable-program rate from 66.7% to 95.0%, with verified evidence for 91.7% of the final features. These results show that LLM knowledge can support data-efficient, cross-site medical image classification through local and auditable feature programs rather than direct VLM decisions.

</details>


### [98] [MIND: Multimodal Intent-Driven Network via Diffusion Transformers for Medical Image Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28565)
*Yunzhan Fu,Xiangyu Shen,Yifei Sun,Yuhan Chen,Jian Wu,Hongxia Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MIND is a multimodal intent-driven medical image fusion network built on Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). It uses BioMedGPT to generate diagnostic intent texts that guide fusion, a Multi-scale Latent Adapter to preserve 2D spatial continuity lost in 1D sequence flattening, and a medical semantic consistency loss to maintain alignment between fused images and diagnostic intents. Experiments on Harvard, BraTS, and GFP datasets show superior fusion quality, improved brain tumor segmentation, and flexible interactive fusion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical image fusion methods apply uniform fusion rules globally and fail to deeply understand diagnostic intents and pathological structures, limiting their clinical utility.

Method: MIND comprises three key components: (1) BioMedGPT-generated intent-driven fusion texts from source images to incorporate pathology-aware diagnostic intents; (2) a Multi-scale Latent Adapter that explicitly extracts source image features before serialization and injects them via strict dimensional alignment to counteract 2D spatial continuity loss from DiT 1D sequence flattening; and (3) a medical semantic consistency loss that locks deep semantic alignment between fused images and fusion texts while preserving physical manifold reconstruction stability.

Result: Comprehensive experiments on Harvard, BraTS, and GFP datasets demonstrate that MIND achieves superior fusion quality, significantly improves downstream brain tumor segmentation accuracy, and enables flexible interactive fusion.

Conclusion: MIND shows significant promise for intent-driven intelligent clinical decision support systems, offering a new paradigm for semantically guided medical image fusion.

Abstract: Medical image fusion aims to integrate complementary information from diverse imaging modalities to support clinical diagnosis. Existing methods typically apply uniform fusion rules globally, lacking a deep understanding of diagnostic intents and pathological structures. To address these limitations, we propose MIND, a Multimodal Intent-Driven Network via Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for medical image fusion. Specifically, we utilize BioMedGPT to generate intent-driven fusion texts from source images, guiding the fusion process with pathology-aware diagnostic intents. To combat the loss of 2D spatial continuity caused by 1D sequence flattening in DiTs, we design a Multi-scale Latent Adapter. This module explicitly extracts source image features before serialization, injecting them into the network via strict dimensional alignment to effectively supplement image features. To resolve the semantic shift caused by decoupling image outputs from diagnostic intents, we design a medical semantic consistency loss. This loss ensures deep semantic locking between fused images and fusion texts while maintaining the stability of the underlying physical manifold reconstruction. Comprehensive experiments on the Harvard, BraTS, and GFP datasets reveal that MIND delivers superior fusion quality, significantly improves downstream brain tumor segmentation accuracy, and enables flexible interactive fusion, holding significant promise for intent-driven intelligent clinical decision support systems.

</details>


### [99] [Finding Change in Satellite Archives from Text: How to Combine Before-and-After Images Efficiently](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28571)
*Simon Roy,Mark Bong,Giovanni Beltrame*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a controlled comparison of eight fusion module designs (from attention, state-space/Mamba, and learned-compression families) for bi-temporal satellite image change retrieval based on natural-language queries. Using a fixed frozen CLIP encoder and identical training recipe, it finds that a training-free two-stage search (cheap difference model + attention re-ranking) matches full-fusion recall while cutting query cost 10-15x; Mamba gives no practical speed benefit at typical vision-transformer patch counts (L=196); and temporal bottleneck fusion achieves 2.3x parameter and 1.6x latency reductions at a modest 0.007 BLEU-1 cost, though aggressive compression loses change-relevant detail.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Operational Earth observation demands efficient search over bi-temporal satellite image archives answering natural-language queries like "find image pairs where a new building appeared." Since the fusion module matching before/after pairs to text must run at query time over many candidates, its speed dominates search cost, motivating a principled controlled comparison of fusion designs.

Method: The authors fix one image encoder (frozen CLIP) and one training recipe across all variants, then evaluate eight fusion designs from three families: attention, state-space models (Mamba), and learned compression (Temporal Bottleneck Fusion, TBF). They test on two benchmarks (LEVIR-CC and Dubai-CC) with ten random seeds for statistical grounding, and propose a training-free two-stage search pipeline: a cheap difference model for shortlisting followed by attention fusion for re-ranking.

Result: Three key findings: (1) The two-stage training-free search matches or exceeds full-fusion recall on LEVIR-CC while reducing query cost 10-15x, with comparable R@1/R@5 on Dubai-CC; (2) Mamba's linear-time scan offers no practical speed benefit at L=196 patches due to memory-bandwidth limits, while attention scales well on parallel hardware; (3) TBF compresses fusion by 2.3x parameters and 1.6x latency with only 0.007 BLEU-1 degradation for change-only queries, but aggressive compression silently discards change-relevant detail hidden from aggregate metrics.

Conclusion: A training-free two-stage retrieval pipeline is the most cost-effective design for bi-temporal satellite change search; Mamba's theoretical complexity does not translate to real speed advantages; and while learned bottleneck compression offers efficiency gains, cautious tuning is required to avoid losing change-relevant information that aggregate metrics mask.

Abstract: Operational Earth observation increasingly calls for answering queries such as ``find the image pairs where a new building appeared.'' This means searching an archive of before-and-after (bi-temporal) satellite image pairs and ranking each pair by how well it matches a natural-language description of the change. The component that performs this match, the fusion module that combines the ``before'' and ``after'' views, must be run at query time across many candidate pairs, so its speed largely sets the cost of every search. We present a controlled comparison of how to build that module. Using one fixed image encoder (a frozen CLIP model) and one training recipe for all variants, we evaluate eight designs drawn from three families: attention, state-space models (Mamba), and learned compression (our Temporal Bottleneck Fusion, TBF). Each design is tested on two benchmarks (LEVIR-CC and Dubai-CC) with ten random seeds, so the reported differences are statistically grounded. We outline three findings: first, a training-free two-stage search (a cheap difference model that shortlists candidates, followed by attention fusion that re-ranks them) matches or exceeds full-fusion recall on LEVIR-CC while cutting query cost $10$-$15\times$, with comparable R@1/R@5 on Dubai-CC; second, the linear-time scan of Mamba, attractive on paper, gives no speed benefit at the patch counts typical of vision transformers ($L{=}196$): the scan is limited by memory bandwidth, whereas attention maps cleanly onto parallel hardware; and third, compressing the fused representation (TBF) reduces parameters by $2.3\times$ and latency by $1.6\times$ for a change-only BLEU-1 cost of $0.007$, although more aggressive compression quietly discards change-relevant detail that aggregate metrics fail to reveal.

</details>


### [100] [ROAD: Reciprocal-Objective Alignment of Discriminative Semantics for 3D Shape Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28581)
*Xiao Luo,Mingyang Du,Xin Zhou,Tianrui Feng,Xiwu Chen,Xiaofan Li,Jiangning Zhang,Dingkang Liang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ROAD is a framework that reduces the training cost of high-fidelity 3D generation by transferring rich priors from discriminative 3D foundation models into diffusion transformers. It introduces a reciprocal-objective alignment strategy (Holistic Semantic Condensing + Structural Optimal Alignment) to bridge semantic-structural heterogeneity between generative and discriminative latents. Using only 1.5% of the training data required by the industrial baseline Step1X-3D, it achieves highly competitive generation performance with significantly reduced computational overhead, and the foundation model is only used at training time, incurring no extra inference cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-fidelity 3D generation typically requires scaling model capacity and data, which is computationally prohibitive. The authors argue that discriminative 3D foundation models already encapsulate rich semantic and structural priors about the 3D world, and leveraging these priors can significantly reduce the cost of generative training instead of learning geometry from scratch.

Method: ROAD transfers discriminative priors into diffusion transformers via a reciprocal-objective alignment strategy that addresses the semantic-structural heterogeneity between generative and discriminative latent spaces. It combines Holistic Semantic Condensing for global semantic coherence and Structural Optimal Alignment, formulated as bipartite matching, to precisely align microscopic geometric details across the two latent spaces. The 3D foundation model provides training-time supervision only and is discarded at inference.

Result: Compared to the industrial baseline Step1X-3D, ROAD achieves highly competitive generation performance with only 1.5% of the training data, substantially reducing training costs and computational overhead for high-fidelity 3D generation. Code is publicly released.

Conclusion: Discriminative 3D foundation model priors can be effectively distilled into generative diffusion transformers to drastically cut the training cost of high-fidelity 3D generation without sacrificing generation quality and without adding any inference overhead.

Abstract: High-fidelity 3D generation predominantly relies on scaling model capacity and data, which incurs prohibitive computational costs. This paradigm typically requires learning geometry from scratch and overlooks the rich semantic and structural priors already encapsulated in discriminative 3D foundation models. We contend that leveraging the profound understanding of the 3D world possessed by these discriminative models can significantly reduce generative cost. To this end, we propose ROAD, a framework that reduces the training cost of 3D generation by transferring these rich discriminative priors into diffusion transformers. To address the inherent semantic-structural heterogeneity between generative and discriminative latents, we introduce a reciprocal-objective alignment strategy. This method synergizes Holistic Semantic Condensing to enforce global semantic coherence and Structural Optimal Alignment, which is formulated as a bipartite matching problem to rigorously align microscopic geometric details between disparate latent spaces. The 3D foundation model is only used for training-time supervision of alignment and is not used at inference, incurring no additional inference cost. Compared with the industrial baseline Step1X-3D, the proposed ROAD achieves highly competitive generation performance with only 1.5% of the training data and significantly reduces training costs, effectively reducing the computational overhead of high-fidelity 3D generation. Code is available at https://github.com/H-EmbodVis/ROAD.

</details>


### [101] [MixFrag: Fragility-Guided Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization for Vision Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28589)
*Md. Mehrab Hossain Opi,Robiul Islam Ryad,Md. Umar Faruk*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MixFrag is a fragility-guided mixed-precision post-training quantization framework for Vision Transformers that estimates component-level quantization fragility via KL divergence and formulates bit allocation as a Multiple-Choice Knapsack Problem, achieving state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet-1K and COCO tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PTQ methods for Vision Transformers use uniform bit-widths across all components, ignoring the heterogeneous sensitivity of different transformer components to quantization. This leads to inefficient precision allocation—wasting bits on components that are less sensitive to quantization while insufficiently protecting fragile ones.

Method: MixFrag first measures component-level quantization fragility by computing the KL divergence between full-precision and isolated quantized output distributions using a small calibration set. It then formulates the bit allocation problem as a Multiple-Choice Knapsack Problem (MCKP), enabling adaptive layer-wise precision assignment under a target bit budget.

Result: On ImageNet-1K, MixFrag achieves competitive classification performance under practical mixed-precision settings across multiple ViT architectures. On COCO object detection and instance segmentation, it achieves state-of-the-art performance among mixed-precision PTQ methods, improving the previous best by up to 9.6 AP under the challenging MP3/MP3 setting. Additional analyses validate the fragility metric and show its strong correlation with learned bit allocation.

Conclusion: MixFrag establishes itself as an effective and practical framework for mixed-precision post-training quantization of Vision Transformers, demonstrating that fragility-guided precision allocation outperforms uniform and prior mixed-precision approaches.

Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) has emerged as an effective solution for deploying Vision Transformers (ViTs) on resource-constrained devices. However, existing PTQ methods typically employ uniform bit-widths across transformer components, overlooking their heterogeneous sensitivity to quantization and leading to inefficient precision allocation. In this paper, we propose {MixFrag, a fragility-guided mixed-precision PTQ framework for Vision Transformers. MixFrag first estimates component-level quantization fragility by measuring the Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence between full-precision and isolated quantized output distributions using a small calibration set. It then formulates bit allocation as a Multiple-Choice Knapsack Problem (MCKP), enabling adaptive layer-wise precision assignment under a target bit budget. Extensive experiments on ImageNet-1K across multiple Vision Transformer architectures demonstrate that MixFrag achieves competitive classification performance under practical mixed-precision settings. Furthermore, evaluations on COCO object detection and instance segmentation show that MixFrag achieves state-of-the-art performance among existing mixed-precision PTQ methods, improving the previous best method by up to 9.6 AP under the challenging MP3/MP3 setting. Additional analyses validate the proposed fragility metric and demonstrate its strong correlation with the learned bit allocation. These results establish MixFrag as an effective framework for mixed-precision post-training quantization of Vision Transformers.

</details>


### [102] [VAD: Attributing Visual Evidence for Target Reconstruction in Multimodal On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28590)
*Kangning Zhang,Yixing Li,Shuai Shao,Qingyao Li,Zhengxi Lu,Zhiyuan Yao,Jianghao Lin,Wenxiang Jiao,Yuan Lu,Weiwen Liu,Weinan Zhang,Yong Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VAD is a counterfactual target-reconstruction algorithm for multimodal on-policy distillation that estimates the visually attributable part of teacher corrections by evaluating a fixed teacher with evidence present vs. removed, then reconstructing a student-anchored target from the counterfactual-aligned component, outperforming direct distillation and visual-advantage weighting on six fine-grained benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) transfers fine-grained visual knowledge via privileged-view teacher supervision, but its next-token corrections are source-mixed, combining visual signals with linguistic priors and teacher-specific effects. The key challenge is estimating which corrections are supported by visual evidence rather than merely where or how strongly to distill.

Method: VAD (Visual Attribution Distillation) is a counterfactual target-reconstruction algorithm. At each student-generated prefix, it evaluates the same fixed teacher with relevant evidence present and removed. The change in centered log-probabilities defines u_t, a signed proxy for the visual evidence direction estimating how revealing the evidence supports or refutes candidate tokens. The original correction is projected onto this proxy to split it into an intervention-aligned component and a proxy-unexplained residual, then a student-anchored target is reconstructed from the former. During training, the reconstructed target is the primary supervision signal while the privileged teacher serves as a weak regularizer.

Result: Across six fine-grained visual benchmarks at 4B and 9B scales, VAD outperforms direct privileged-view distillation and visual-advantage weighting. Token-level and controlled-target analyses show the proxy-aligned component is enriched in task-relevant visual corrections and yields stronger target shifts, especially when evidence refutes a mistaken answer.

Conclusion: Counterfactual target reconstruction is an effective alternative to source-mixed supervision for multimodal on-policy distillation, enabling more precise visual attribution in teacher corrections.

Abstract: Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) transfers fine-grained visual knowledge by supervising student-generated trajectories with a privileged-view teacher. Yet its next-token corrections are source-mixed, combining visual signals with linguistic priors and teacher-specific effects. The key challenge is to estimate which corrections are supported by visual evidence, not merely where or how strongly to distill. We introduce Visual Attribution Distillation (VAD), a counterfactual target-reconstruction algorithm that estimates the visually attributable part of a teacher correction. At each student-generated prefix, VAD evaluates the same fixed teacher with the relevant evidence present and removed. The corresponding change in centered log-probabilities defines ut, a signed proxy for the visual evidence direction that estimates how revealing the evidence supports or refutes candidate tokens. VAD projects the original correction onto this proxy to obtain an intervention-aligned component and a proxy-unexplained residual, then reconstructs a student-anchored target from the former. During training, this reconstructed target supplies the primary supervision signal, while the privileged teacher contributes a weak regularizer. Across six fine-grained visual benchmarks at 4B and 9B scales, VAD outperforms direct privileged-view distillation and visual-advantage weighting. Token- level and controlled-target analyses show that the proxy-aligned component is enriched in task-relevant visual corrections and yields stronger target shifts, especially when evidence refutes a mistaken answer. These results support counterfactual target reconstruction as an effective alternative to source-mixed supervision.

</details>


### [103] [Beacon: Knowing When and How to Perform Agentic Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28595)
*Qixun Wang,Yang Shi,Letian Cheng,Zhuoran Zhang,Yan He,Yuqi Tang,Qi Zhang,Xinlei Yu,Ruizhe Chen,Tianrun Xu,Yuanxing Zhang,Pengfei Wan,Haotian Wang,Xianghua Ying*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces Beacon, an agentic visual reasoning model that improves MLLM performance through two key dimensions of tool use: Mode Adaptiveness (knowing when tools are necessary) and Tool Effect (tools extending capabilities without harming solvable problems). Beacon uses Necessity-Aware Adaptive Reward and Hint-Guided Capability Expansion in reinforcement learning to achieve stronger overall performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agentic visual reasoning models exhibit limited Mode Adaptiveness and their tool-use gains on hard examples are offset by harm on easy examples—calling for a model that intelligently decides when to use tools and genuinely benefits from them.

Method: Beacon employs a Necessity-Aware Adaptive Reward to encourage adaptive tool invocation based on task necessity, and a Hint-Guided Capability Expansion mechanism to strengthen tool-use capability on the most challenging problems during reinforcement learning.

Result: Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate Beacon's strong overall performance with substantial improvements in both Mode Adaptiveness and Tool Effect.

Conclusion: Agentic visual reasoning should prioritize overall task success over merely sophisticated reasoning paradigms; adaptive tool use guided by necessity and targeted capability expansion yields genuine tool-induced performance gains.

Abstract: The fundamental goal of agentic visual reasoning is to improve the success rate of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on complex tasks, rather than merely equipping them with a sophisticated yet inefficient reasoning paradigm. In this work, we rethink agentic visual reasoning through two key dimensions of tool use: Mode Adaptiveness (MA) and Tool Effect (TE). Mode Adaptiveness characterizes whether an MLLM can recognize when tools are truly necessary and invoke them accordingly, thereby avoiding unnecessary computational overhead while improving performance on challenging problems that require tool assistance. Tool Effect characterizes the actual impact of tool use: tools should extend the model's capabilities on problems unsolvable through text-only reasoning, while avoiding additional errors on problems that the model can already solve without tools. We conduct a comprehensive analysis to quantify these two properties and empirically reveal that existing agentic visual reasoning models exhibit limited Mode Adaptiveness, while the gains produced by tool use on hard examples are largely offset by the harm introduced on easy examples that the models can already solve. Motivated by these observations, we propose Beacon, a novel agentic visual reasoning model that achieves stronger overall performance, improved Mode Adaptiveness, and genuine tool-induced performance gains. At the core of Beacon are the Necessity-Aware Adaptive Reward and the Hint-Guided Capability Expansion mechanism in the reinforcement learning stage, which respectively encourage adaptive tool invocation based on task necessity and strengthen the model's tool-use capability on the most challenging problems. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate the strong overall performance of Beacon and its substantial improvements in both Mode Adaptiveness and Tool Effect.

</details>


### [104] [Chimera: Designing and Chinchilla-Scaling Hybrid Visual Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28611)
*Chongjian Ge,Hanwen Jiang,Tianyu Wang,Jiuxiang Gu,Yiran Xu,Ziwen Chen,Shaoteng Liu,Jing Shi,Yicong Hong,Zefan Cai,Hailin Jin,Hao Tan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Chimera is a hybrid visual diffusion backbone combining Kimi Delta Attention (linear complexity), interleaved Multi-head Latent Attention, modality-aware convolutions, and sparse MoE layers. A HeteroP module-wise hyperparameter transfer scheme enables scaling, and Chinchilla-style compute-optimal laws are fitted to guide training. The resulting 11B-parameter (2B activated) model is up to 7.3x more compute-efficient than a full-attention Wan-2.1 2B baseline, extrapolates zero-shot from 5s to 30s video generation, and reveals distinct compute-optimal data-ratio behaviors for image vs. video pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full attention incurs quadratic cost in visual generation as resolution, video length, and multimodal context grow, making it prohibitive for long-context high-fidelity generation. The authors aim to design an efficient hybrid diffusion backbone and a principled scaling recipe.

Method: Chimera processes text, image, and video tokens in a single raster-ordered stream (no positional embeddings), using: (1) Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) for O(N) long-context state tracking, (2) interleaved Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) for direct global interaction, (3) modality-aware short convolutions for local spatiotemporal context, and (4) sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers to expand capacity while controlling activated compute. Scaling uses HeteroP, a module-wise scheme transferring hyperparameters across width and depth based on each tensor's functional fan-in and model depth, enabling a consistently tuned family to fit Chinchilla-style laws for activated size, token count, and image-video data ratio.

Result: (1) The dense backbone is 1.7x more compute-efficient than a matched full-attention Wan-2.1 2B baseline by pretraining diffusion loss, while the complete system reaches 7.3x. (2) Chimera extrapolates zero-shot from 5-second training clips to 30-second videos without length-specific fine-tuning, with only 6.5% FID degradation in the last five seconds. (3) Fitted laws show compute-optimal image pretraining splits compute nearly evenly between activated model size and training tokens, whereas video pretraining modestly favors model size at higher budgets.

Conclusion: The work establishes a foundation for designing and scaling efficient long-context diffusion architectures, demonstrating that hybrid attention/convolution/MoE backbones with principled scaling laws can substantially outperform full-attention baselines in compute efficiency while generalizing to longer video durations.

Abstract: Visual generation increasingly requires high-resolution images, long videos, and multimodal context, making the quadratic cost of full attention prohibitive. We introduce Chimera, a hybrid visual diffusion backbone with a principled scaling recipe. Chimera processes text, image, and video tokens in one raster-ordered stream without positional embeddings. It combines Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) for long-context state tracking with O(N) complexity, interleaved Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) for direct global interaction, and modality-aware short convolutions for local spatiotemporal context. Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers expand capacity while controlling activated compute. To scale this heterogeneous architecture, we introduce HeteroP, a module-wise scheme that transfers hyperparameters across width and depth according to each tensor's functional fan-in and model depth. HeteroP yields a consistently tuned family used to fit Chinchilla-style compute-optimal laws for activated model size, training-token count, and image-video data ratio. Guided by these laws, we train an 11B-parameter Chimera with 2B activated parameters. Experiments show three results. First, measured by pretraining diffusion loss, the dense backbone is 1.7x as compute-efficient as a matched full-attention Wan-2.1 2B baseline, while the complete system reaches 7.3x. Second, without length-specific fine-tuning, Chimera extrapolates zero-shot from 5-second training clips to 30-second videos, with only 6.5% FID degradation in the last five seconds. Third, the fitted laws show that compute-optimal image pretraining divides compute nearly evenly between activated model size and training-token count, whereas video pretraining modestly favors model size at higher budgets. These results establish a foundation for designing and scaling efficient long-context diffusion architectures.

</details>


### [105] [PhiZero: A World Model Built Around Physical Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28624)
*Shuyao Shang,Yuqi Wang,Ruopeng Gao,Xu Chen,Tieniu Tan,Lue Fan,Zhaoxiang Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PhiZero is a physical world model that uses "physical language," a compact discrete representation of world-state transitions, to explicitly reason about physical world evolution via a reason-then-render paradigm before generating videos. It learns this language from in-the-wild videos through self-supervision and demonstrates strong performance on generation and understanding benchmarks, plus capabilities in interactive world modeling, action-conditioned simulation, and zero-shot motion transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing physical world models predict future videos directly in pixel space, leaving world dynamics implicit within high-dimensional visual predictors. The authors are motivated by humans' ability to abstract predictive structure from visual experience and organize it in natural language for explicit reasoning about physical world evolution.

Method: PhiZero learns a compact discrete representation called physical language from in-the-wild videos via self-supervision. It adopts a reason-then-render paradigm: first infers future world evolution as a physical-language sequence, then renders the inferred transitions into videos.

Result: Extensive experiments across generation and understanding benchmarks validate PhiZero's ability to model physically coherent world evolution. It also demonstrates potential for realistic and interactive world modeling, fine-grained action-conditioned simulation, and zero-shot motion transfer.

Conclusion: Explicitly reasoning in a compact physical-language representation before rendering videos enables more physically coherent world modeling than direct pixel-space prediction, opening possibilities for interactive simulation and motion transfer.

Abstract: We introduce PhiZero, a physical world model built around physical language, a compact discrete representation of world-state transitions. Existing physical world models typically predict future videos directly in pixel space, leaving the underlying world dynamics implicit within high-dimensional visual predictors. Motivated by humans' ability to abstract predictive structure from visual experience and organize it in natural language for explicit reasoning, we learn physical language from in-the-wild videos through self-supervision and use it to explicitly reason about how the physical world evolves. Accordingly, PhiZero adopts a reason-then-render paradigm: it first infers future world evolution as a physical-language sequence and then renders the inferred transitions into videos. Extensive experiments across generation and understanding benchmarks validate the ability of PhiZero to model physically coherent world evolution. We further show its potential for realistic and interactive world modeling, fine-grained action-conditioned simulation, and zero-shot motion transfer.

</details>


### [106] [ACE-Data-0: Human-Centric Ambient Capture as Embodied Data Engine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28625)
*Yukang Cao,Haozhe Xie,Beichen Wen,Runmao Yao,Yinghao Liu,Yue Huang,Zhichao Liao,Yunxiang Wang,Haiheng Liu,Xingshun Tian,Dawei Su,Long Zhuo,Dacheng Tao,Xiaogang Wang,Liang Pan,Ziwei Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ACE is a human-centric data engine that transforms real home environments into spatially calibrated, temporally synchronized recording studios, producing ACE-Data-0: 150 hours, 17M video frames, and 75,000 interaction episodes across 200 task categories. The dataset provides unified multisensory streams (egocentric/exocentric video, full-body and hand motion, object geometry and trajectories, audio, tactile) at both table-scale and room-scale, enabling embodied AI learning across perception, kinematics, and contact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embodied intelligence faces a fundamental data bottleneck: existing datasets fragment real-world experience across viewpoints, modalities, and spatial scales, leaving the full perception-action loop only partially observed. A unified dataset that captures how perception, motion, manipulation, object state, sound, and touch evolve together is needed.

Method: ACE operates at two complementary scales: a table-scale configuration for hand-object manipulation and a room-scale configuration for whole-body motion and interactions. It records egocentric and multi-view exocentric video, full-body and articulated hand motion, object geometry and 6-DoF trajectories, audio, and tactile signals as a unified stream. Data is collected via goal-level instructions (not step-by-step) to preserve natural behavioral variation.

Result: ACE-Data-0 contains 150 hours, 17M video frames, 200 task categories, 50 participants, 2 environments, and 75,000 interaction episodes. A hierarchical benchmark progressing from signals to scene components to interactions reveals substantial gaps in state-of-the-art methods under contact, occlusion, egomotion, and long temporal horizons.

Conclusion: ACE-Data-0 provides synchronized human demonstrations with aligned perceptual, kinematic, and contact supervision, offering a scalable foundation for imitation learning, world models, vision-language-action systems, and embodied AI, while exposing limitations of current methods for contact-rich and long-horizon tasks.

Abstract: Embodied intelligence faces a fundamental data bottleneck. Models must capture how first-person perception, whole-body motion, dexterous manipulation, object state, sound, and touch evolve together as humans pursue goals over time. Existing datasets fragment this experience across viewpoints, modalities, or spatial scales, leaving the full perception-action loop only partially observed. We introduce the Ambient Capture Engine (ACE), a human-centric data engine that transforms real home environments into spatially calibrated, temporally synchronized recording studios. ACE operates at two complementary scales: a table-scale configuration resolves hand-object manipulation, while a room-scale configuration captures whole-body motion, locomotion, and interactions across a furnished home. ACE records egocentric and multi-view exocentric video, full-body and articulated hand motion, object geometry and 6-DoF trajectories, audio, and tactile signals as a unified multisensory stream. Using ACE, we build ACE-Data-0, comprising 150 hours and 17M video frames across 200 task categories, performed by 50 participants in 2 environments, for a total of 75,000 interaction episodes. The dataset spans atomic manipulation, long-horizon chains of household activities, and human-scene interaction, while preserving natural behavioral variation through goal-level rather than step-by-step instructions. We further introduce a hierarchical benchmark that progresses from signals to scene components and then to interactions. Evaluations of state-of-the-art methods expose substantial gaps under contact, occlusion, egomotion, and long temporal horizons. ACE-Data-0 provides synchronized human demonstrations with aligned perceptual, kinematic, and contact supervision, offering a scalable foundation for imitation learning, world models, vision-language-action systems, and embodied AI.

</details>


### [107] [ReToken: One Token to Improve Vision-Language Models for Visual Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28627)
*Yao Xiao,Reuben Tan,Zhen Zhu,Yuqun Wu,Jianfeng Gao,Derek Hoiem*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ReToken is a single learnable embedding trained as an explicit retrieval target that selects a sparse set of query-relevant visual tokens from a pre-filled visual KV cache, improving vision-language model performance on long-context image and video benchmarks while staying computationally lightweight enough to fit training and inference on a single H100.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long visual context degrades vision-language model performance as distractors increase, and processing all tokens at once is computationally infeasible under GPU memory constraints.

Method: ReToken introduces a single learnable embedding trained as an explicit retrieval target that selects a sparse set of query-relevant visual tokens from a pre-filled visual KV cache.

Result: Trained on a small image-QA dataset, ReToken improves Qwen3VL-8B by 13.4 points and InternVL3.5 by 12.4 points on Visual Haystacks (>20% relative), and transfers zero-shot to long video for an 8.0-point gain on LVBench with Qwen3VL-8B. Both training and long-video inference fit on a single H100.

Conclusion: A lightweight, learnable retrieval-based token selection mechanism effectively addresses long-context vision-language degradation and is efficient enough to run on a single GPU.

Abstract: Long visual context poses a challenge for vision-language models: performance degrades as the number of distractors grows, and processing all tokens at once is computationally infeasible under GPU memory constraints. We present ReToken, a single learnable embedding trained as an explicit retrieval target that selects a sparse set of query-relevant visual tokens from a pre-filled visual KV cache. Trained on only a small image-QA dataset, ReToken yields consistent gains across image and video benchmarks: on Visual Haystacks it improves Qwen3VL-8B by 13.4 points and InternVL3.5 by 12.4 points (>20% relative), and on LVBench it transfers zero-shot to long video for an 8.0-point gain with Qwen3VL-8B. Thanks to its lightweight design, both training and long-video inference fit on a single H100. Code is available at: https://github.com/avaxiao/ReToken

</details>

### [108] [Compact Representation of Mipmapped SVBRDFs via Shared Gaussians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27943)
*Fengdi Zhang,Haocheng Ren,Qing Luo,Yaqing Li,Jibing Lou,Hongwei Li*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: GTC is a compact 2D Gaussian-based representation for mipmapped SVBRDF texture stacks that achieves high-quality compression with flexible rate-distortion trade-offs by exploiting redundancy across mip levels and material maps, outperforming ASTC in quality and memory usage while supporting random-access, non-neural decoding for real-time rendering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SVBRDF textures impose substantial storage burdens, and existing compression methods face a fundamental trade-off between random access/hardware-friendly decoding (block-based), strong rate-distortion performance (image codecs), and high compression ratios (neural methods with runtime overhead). The authors aim to overcome this trade-off with a representation that is both compact and directly decodeable in real-time rendering pipelines.

Method: GTC represents mipmapped SVBRDF texture stacks using compact 2D Gaussians. The key insight is that redundancy exists across mip levels and material maps, and both share a common underlying structure: the same spatial support is reused with level- or map-specific information. Since 2D Gaussians explicitly separate spatial footprint from carried values, footprints can be shared while values vary per level and map. Gaussians are shared along both redundancy dimensions and trained via a progressive optimization pipeline.

Result: Experiments show GTC achieves higher reconstruction quality and lower memory usage than ASTC (the industry-standard GPU texture compression format), while supporting random-access and non-neural decoding suitable for real-time rendering.

Conclusion: GTC provides a practical compression method for SVBRDF textures that addresses the limitations of existing approaches, delivering state-of-the-art quality and compactness with hardware-friendly, real-time-compatible decoding.

Abstract: Spatially-varying BRDFs (SVBRDFs) are central to material representation in computer graphics, but their high-resolution, multi-channel, mipmapped textures impose a substantial storage burden. Existing compression methods face a fundamental trade-off: block-based compression provides random access and hardware-friendly decoding but exploits redundancy only within local blocks; image codecs offer strong rate-distortion performance but are not designed for direct real-time texture access; and neural texture compression achieves high compression ratios but requires neural inference during decoding, which introduces additional runtime overhead, especially on mobile platforms. We present Gaussian Texture Compression (GTC), a compact 2D Gaussian-based representation for mipmapped SVBRDF texture stacks that delivers high-quality compression with flexible rate-distortion trade-offs. Our method is based on a key observation that there are two dominant sources of redundancy in such data: across mip levels and across material maps. Both share a common underlying structure: the same spatial support is reused, with only level- or map-specific information attached. This property naturally suits 2D Gaussians, since each Gaussian explicitly separates its spatial footprint from the values it carries, allowing the footprint to be shared while the values vary per level and per map. Building on this property, GTC shares Gaussians along both redundancy dimensions and is trained via a progressive optimization pipeline. Experiments show that GTC achieves higher reconstruction quality and lower memory usage than ASTC, the industry-standard GPU texture compression format, while supporting random-access, non-neural decoding suitable for real-time rendering.

</details>


### [109] [A Query-Efficient Stochastic Volume Rendering Framework for Time-Varying Implicit Neural Volumes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28047)
*Alper Sahistan,Haichao Miao,Zhimin Li,Peer-Timo Bremer,Joshua A Levine,Valerio Pascucci*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: A query-efficient stochastic volume rendering framework based on delta tracking for time-varying implicit neural representations, achieving ~30-40 FPS at 1024x1024 resolution on an RTX 4090 GPU with ~1-2 ms timestep updates, using a four-stage pipeline with heterogeneous parallelism across ray tracing cores and tensor cores, plus ray budgeting and query pruning strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interactive volume rendering of implicit neural representations (INRs) is challenging because expensive neural inferences replace cheap memory lookups, making conventional ray marching with dense sampling impractical. Existing mitigations like resampling, caching, and retraining compromise convenience and accuracy, and become especially impractical for time-varying data. Direct rendering from the original INR representation is needed.

Method: A query-efficient stochastic volume rendering framework based on delta tracking, employing a four-stage pipeline that exploits heterogeneous parallelism—using ray tracing cores for traversal and tensor cores for batched neural evaluation. The system reduces INR queries via ray budgeting and query pruning to increase per-frame performance.

Result: The renderer achieves ~30-40 FPS at 1024x1024 resolution on an RTX 4090 GPU, converges to high-fidelity images, and enables interactive temporal exploration with timestep updates taking approximately 1-2 ms. Many time-varying INRs can be rendered directly from their original representation.

Conclusion: The proposed system successfully enables practical interactive volume rendering of time-varying INRs directly from their original representations, overcoming the performance bottlenecks of neural inference through delta tracking, heterogeneous parallelism, and query-reduction strategies.

Abstract: Time-varying implicit neural representations (INRs) provide a compact representation of scientific volumes and, for modalities such as dynamic X-ray computed tomography (CT), are often the only practical way to represent the data. However, interactive volume rendering of INRs is challenging, as cheap memory lookups are replaced by expensive neural inferences, hindering the performance. Therefore, conventional volume rendering methods such as ray marching with dense sampling are often impractical. While resampling, caching, and retraining can mitigate this cost, they compromise convenience and accuracy and become impractical for time-varying data. We tackle these challenges using a query-efficient stochastic volume rendering framework based on delta tracking. Our system employs a four-stage pipeline that exploits heterogeneous parallelism, using ray tracing cores for traversal and tensor cores for batched neural evaluation. Furthermore, we present strategies to reduce INR queries via ray budgeting and query pruning, thereby increasing per-frame performance. Using our renderer, many time-varying INRs can be rendered directly from their original representation. The system achieves ~30-40 FPS at 1024x1024 resolution on an RTX 4090 GPU and converges to high-fidelity images. Moreover, the system enables interactive temporal exploration of the continuous domain, with timestep updates taking approximately 1-2 ms.

</details>

### [110] [Multi-Head Attention Residuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27230)
*Cheng Luo,Zefan Cai,Junjie Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Multi-Head Attention Residuals (MHAR), which reshapes the single routing query in attention residuals into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over depth history. MHAR adds zero parameters, negligible compute, and achieves improved validation loss over standard Transformers at 100M, 350M, and 1B scales (-0.061, -0.149, -0.140), with H=4 or H=8 as the optimal head count. Fused Triton kernels improve throughput to 0.55-0.88x of baseline, and an identity-preserving conversion supports 8B mid-training with gains of +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Transformers propagate information through a single additive residual stream where each sublayer reads only the most recent state. Attention residuals allow attending through a learned softmax, but use a single shared query across the entire width, forcing all feature subspaces to read depth history through one distribution. As model width grows, subspaces increasingly disagree about which layers to read, making this forced compromise costly. The paper motivates MHAR as a way to give each feature subspace its own routing distribution without adding parameters.

Method: MHAR reshapes the routing query into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history. The read becomes block-diagonal, the reshape adds zero parameters and negligible compute, and H=1 recovers attention residuals exactly. Training is performed from scratch on a deduplicated Nemotron-based anneal corpus that is quality-filtered and STEM/code-heavy. Fused Triton routing kernels are used to improve attention-residual training throughput, and an identity-preserving conversion using delta attention residuals supports 8B mid-training.

Result: MHAR improves validation loss over a standard Transformer at 100M, 350M, and 1B scales (-0.061, -0.149, -0.140), achieving the best result among four methods in every setting with gains increasing at larger scales. Validation loss is U-shaped with respect to H, with a flat optimum at H=4 or H=8. Adopting H=8 for large-scale models, over-splitting (H=16) gives back part of the gain. The learned subspace disagreement is confirmed as the underlying driver. Fused Triton kernels improve throughput from 0.2-0.5x to 0.55-0.88x of baseline. The 8B mid-training achieves +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.

Conclusion: MHAR demonstrates that per-subspace routing in attention residuals is both parameter-free and compute-efficient, with consistent gains across scales. The head count H is a genuine design axis (U-shaped validation loss) rather than a free knob, with H=4 or H=8 optimal. The method scales effectively to 8B parameters via identity-preserving conversion, and direct probing confirms that learned subspace disagreement drives the improvement.

Abstract: Transformers propagate information across depth through a single additive residual stream: every sublayer reads only the most recent state. Attention residuals relax this by letting each sublayer attend, through a learned softmax. However, that read uses a single query shared across the entire width, so every feature subspace must read the depth history through one distribution. The cost of this forced compromise grows with how much the subspaces disagree about which layers to read, and disagreement grows with model width. We introduce Multi-Head Attention Residuals (MHAR): the routing query is reshaped into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history. The read becomes block-diagonal, the reshape adds zero parameters and negligible compute, and H = 1 recovers attention residuals exactly. Trained from scratch on a deduplicated Nemotron-based anneal corpus that is quality-filtered and STEM- and code-heavy, MHAR improves validation loss over a standard Transformer at 100M, 350M, and 1B (-0.061, -0.149, and -0.140). It achieves the best result among four methods in every setting, with the gain increasing from 100M to the larger scales. The head count is a real design axis rather than a free knob: validation loss is U-shaped with respect to H, with a flat optimum at H = 4 or H = 8 across scales. We adopt H = 8 for large-scale models; over-splitting beyond this point (H = 16) consistently gives back part of the gain. A direct probe of the trained queries confirms that learned subspace disagreement is the underlying driver. Fused Triton routing kernels increase attention-residual training throughput from 0.2-0.5x to 0.55-0.88x of the baseline while maintaining near-baseline peak memory.
