An identity-preserving conversion using delta attention residuals supports 8B mid-training, yielding improvements of +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.

</details>


### [111] [HyperClaim: Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Hypergraph Reasoning for Video Misinformation Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28375)
*Xiangbo Wang,Jiasheng Zhang,Xingtong Yu,Luoqiang Lei,Delvin Ce Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyperClaim is a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for video misinformation detection that captures higher-order cross-modal dependencies among query text, evidence tokens, and video frames. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (83.7%, 82.0%, 87.3%) on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV datasets under the FactGuard temporal protocol without relying on generated rationales or external tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video misinformation detection methods rely on global multimodal fusion or free-form reasoning, both of which under-represent localized authenticity cues arising from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. These interactions are inherently higher-order, and pairwise graph formulations cannot capture multi-way cross-modal dependencies.

Method: HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames. It applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units, performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration, and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout for sample-level authenticity classification.

Result: Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, HyperClaim achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV respectively, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights reveal interpretable token- and frame-level structure.

Conclusion: Hypergraph-based modeling is well-suited for capturing higher-order multi-way cross-modal and temporal dependencies in video misinformation detection. HyperClaim preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion tends to flatten, while avoiding dependence on generated rationales or external tool calls, achieving superior performance with interpretable evidence patterns.

Abstract: Video misinformation detection is often approached through global multimodal fusion or free-form multimodal reasoning. Both paradigms can under-represent localized authenticity cues that arise from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. Because such interactions are inherently higher-order, pairwise graph formulations are insufficient to capture multi-way cross-modal dependencies, whereas hypergraphs offer a suitable representation for these relations. We propose HyperClaim, a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for sample-level authenticity classification. Using the title or benchmark-provided paired text as a claim-like query, HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout. Without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, HyperClaim preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion tends to flatten. Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, it achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV, respectively, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights further reveal token- and frame-level structure.

</details>


### [112] [KernelGenBench: A Multi-Source and Multi-Chip Benchmark for LLM-based Kernel Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27231)
*Peiyu Zang,Jian Tao,Jialing Zhang,Yichen Yuan,Wentao Zhang,Guang Liu,Yonghua Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KernelGenBench is a unified benchmark for evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and six heterogeneous hardware platforms, revealing that agent-based methods outperform pure LLM sampling, significant cross-platform performance degradation occurs, and autonomous kernel generation remains extremely cost-intensive.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The increasing demand for efficient accelerator kernels driven by LLMs highlights the labor-intensive nature of kernel development. While LLM and agentic frameworks promise automatic kernel generation, there is no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms.

Method: The paper introduces KernelGenBench with two sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source) covering 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip) measuring performance portability on 110 operators across six heterogeneous hardware platforms. A large-scale evaluation consuming over 15 billion tokens was conducted comparing agent-based methods versus pure LLM sampling approaches.

Result: (1) Agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling, with cuBLAS operators being the most challenging; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation is highly cost-intensive, with specialized agents averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all at 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling.

Conclusion: Automatic kernel generation remains an open and challenging research problem. While agent-based approaches show promise, cross-platform portability and computational cost remain significant barriers; efficient kernel generation work must be evaluated on richer operator sources and heterogeneous hardware to be practical.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly increased the demand for efficient accelerator kernels, but kernel development remains a highly specialized and labor-intensive task. The recent rise of LLMs and agentic frameworks offers a promising pathway toward automatic kernel generation. However, despite rapid progress, there is still no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms. We present KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. It comprises two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source), evaluating 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip), measuring performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. Our large-scale evaluation, consuming over 15 billion tokens, shows: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling methods, while cuBLAS operators are the most challenging across all methods; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with even recent kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation remains highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaches 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling approaches.

</details>


### [113] [RadHarmony: Radiological Data Handling in the Era of Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27235)
*Frank Li,Bardia Khosravi,Mohammadreza Chavoshi,Theo Dapamede,YoungSeok Jeon,Janice Newsome,Hari Trivedi,Judy Gichoya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RadHarmony is an open-source Python library that provides a unified API for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting radiological datasets (focusing on chest X-rays, with early support for CT and MRI). It standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets, wraps MONAI datasets with caching, supports multiple annotation types, and includes an AI-agent skill for integrating new datasets. A reference vision transformer baseline (RadHarmony-ViT) demonstrates its utility by combining three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets without dataset-specific code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training deep learning models on radiological images requires integrating heterogeneous datasets that differ across sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types, creating significant friction in data preparation.

Method: RadHarmony provides: (1) standardized metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, (2) wrappers around MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching, (3) a single interface supporting classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and radiology report text, (4) an interactive visualization tool, and (5) an AI-agent skill that automates the dataset integration workflow from raw data inspection through code generation and testing.

Result: The paper demonstrates the library's utility by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a reference vision transformer baseline that combines three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code. Code and pretrained weights are publicly available.

Conclusion: RadHarmony lowers the barrier for integrating diverse radiological datasets and enables reproducible, dataset-agnostic model training pipelines for medical imaging.

Abstract: Training deep learning models on radiological images requires integrating heterogeneous datasets across different sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types. We present RadHarmony, an open-source Python library that provides a unified API for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting radiological datasets, with a primary focus on chest radiographs and early support for computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). RadHarmony standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, wraps MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching, and supports classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and radiology report text through a single interface, with an interactive visualization tool for dataset exploration and verification. To lower the barrier for integrating new datasets, RadHarmony introduces an AI-agent skill that guides the full integration workflow from raw data inspection through code generation and testing. We demonstrate the library's utility by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a reference vision transformer baseline that combines three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code. The code and pretrained model weights are available at https://github.com/f10409/RadHarmony.

</details>


### [114] [Asymmetric Collapse in Model Merging: When Refusal Over- writes Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27240)
*Aarnav Choudhary,Matheus Fonseca Rocha,Jiwon Seo,Vasu Sharma,Maheep Chaudhary*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Standard model merging of two safety-relevant fine-tunes (CARES harm classification and WildJailbreak refusal) leads to asymmetric transfer: jailbreak refusal rates remain high (81-85%) while classification accuracy collapses to ≤12.9%, regardless of merging method. This asymmetry is due to differing task-vector magnitudes rather than opposing directions, since the task vectors are nearly orthogonal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model merging is widely used to combine capabilities from fine-tuned models without retraining, but it is unclear whether standard merging methods can preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously. This paper investigates this question through a controlled case study.

Method: The authors use two Gemma-3-1B-IT fine-tunes targeting complementary safety objectives (CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal). They merge these using four standard methods (Linear, SLERP, TIES, DARE-TIES) and evaluate merged models on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. They also perform weight-space analysis of task vectors.

Result: Across all four merging methods, attack resistance transferred significantly better than classification accuracy: merged models retained 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates while CARES accuracy fell to at most 12.9%. The asymmetry is not due to opposing task-vector directions (cosine similarity is 0.011, nearly orthogonal) but rather due to the refusal fine-tune having consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, which favors refusal updates in magnitude-sensitive merging methods.

Conclusion: Standard model merging can collapse safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale, highlighting a critical limitation in merging safety-tuned models.

Abstract: Model merging is often used to combine capabilities from separately fine-tuned models without additional training, but it is unclear whether standard merging methods preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously. We study this question through a controlled case study using two Gemma-3-1B-IT finetunes on two complementary safety objectives: CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal. We merge the two fine-tunes using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES, and evaluate the merged models on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. Across all four methods, attack resistance transfers significantly more than classification accuracy: merged models retain 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates while CARES accuracy falls to at most 12.9%. Weight-space measurements suggest that this asymmetry is not caused by strongly opposing task-vector directions: the two task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011). Instead, the refusal fine-tune induces consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive methods to favor refusal updates. These results show that standard model merging can collapse safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale.

</details>


### [115] [Divergence Decoding: Training-Free Capability Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27248)
*Yimi Wang,Hao Li,Shuo Yang,He Cao,Dechen Zhang,Ziang Wu,Zhiyuan Yan,Fanyang Mo,Li Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Divergence Decoding is a training-free framework that fuses a general-purpose LLM with a domain-specialist model by using Jensen-Shannon divergence to detect token-level distributional disagreements. When the specialist shows significant divergence, control routes to the generalist, dynamically injecting general reasoning while preserving domain expertise. It outperforms both specialist and generalist baselines on scientific benchmarks across Qwen and Llama model families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models face a fundamental dilemma: generalists excel at reasoning but lack specialized knowledge, while domain specialists have expertise but suffer from side effects like diminished logic and reduced robustness due to specialization. This trade-off motivates the need for a mechanism to combine the strengths of both model types without expensive training.

Method: The method reconstructs the draft-and-verify skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. It uses Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor the distributional disagreement between the specialist and generalist at each token. When the specialist exhibits significant divergence from the generalist, it is flagged as a potential reasoning risk, and control is instantly routed to the generalist, enabling dynamic injection of general reasoning while preserving domain expertise. This achieves inference-time policy composition without any training.

Result: Evaluated on challenging scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench) across diverse model families (Qwen and Llama series), Divergence Decoding outperforms both the domain-specialized and general-purpose models individually, surpassing most single-model baselines.

Conclusion: Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration, effectively solving the generalist-specialist dilemma.

Abstract: While large language models excel in reasoning, these generalists often lack knowledge for specialized scientific domains. Conversely, domain models~(specialists), while knowledgeable, suffer from specialization side-effects including diminished logic and reduced robustness.To address this dilemma, we introduce Divergence Decoding, a training-free framework for capability fusion. It reconstructs the "draft-and-verify" skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. The core is using Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor the distributional disagreement between the two models at each token. When the specialist exhibits significant divergence, our method identifies it as a potential reasoning risk and instantaneously routes control to the generalist. This allows the dynamic injection of general reasoning while preserving domain expertise, achieving inference-time policy composition of the generalist and the specialist.We evaluate Divergence Decoding across diverse model families (Qwen and Llama series) on challenging scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench). Experimental results demonstrate that Divergence Decoding outperforms both the domain-specialized and general-purpose models, effectively surpassing the performance of most single-model baseline. This suggests that Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration.

</details>


### [116] [PIE-APT: A Unified Framework for Temporal Planning and Contradiction Hunting via Incremental Direct-Derivation Abduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27287)
*Amir Hossein Sharafi,Alireza Shahbazi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a unified framework for reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs, consisting of two modules (PIE-Abducer for incremental abduction and PIE-APT for temporal KG planning) that operate natively on Description Logic. It replaces Minimal Hitting Set enumeration with direct-derivation abduction that injects goal negations into consistent branches, and uses a recursive Generate-and-Test architecture with bounded backward-chaining A* search and forward-chaining validation. Evaluation on four OWL benchmarks demonstrates qualitative and quantitative superiority over classical planners and an MHS-faithful baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs face significant challenges in open-world environments with incomplete information. Existing action formalisms suffer from decidability issues, the Ramification Problem, and expansive combinatorial search caused by structural abduction for managing incomplete knowledge.

Method: The framework comprises PIE-Abducer (incremental direct-derivation abduction) and PIE-APT (Abductive Planning for Temporal KGs), both operating natively on Description Logic. State transitions are modeled as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories along a linear timeline. The incremental reasoner is treated as a black-box with actions represented natively in OWL, preserving logical decidability. PIE-Abducer circumvents MHS enumeration by injecting the logical negation of a target goal into a consistent branch and extracting missing premises via direct refutation consequences. PIE-APT employs recursive Generate-and-Test, interleaving backward-chaining A* search with PIE-Abducer up to a bounded causal depth, followed by forward-chaining Temporal Projection for validation.

Result: Evaluation on four OWL benchmarks—covering parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting—demonstrates qualitative superiority over classical planners. The direct-derivation approach also quantitatively outperforms an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.

Conclusion: The unified framework successfully addresses decidability, the Ramification Problem, and combinatorial explosion in DKG planning by leveraging native DL reasoning and direct-derivation abduction, proving both qualitatively and quantitatively superior to classical planning and MHS-based baselines.

Abstract: Reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs (DKGs) present significant challenges, especially in open-world environments with incomplete information. Existing action formalisms often face decidability issues and the Ramification Problem, while managing incomplete knowledge via structural abduction requires expansive combinatorial search. This paper introduces a unified framework with two integrated modules---\textbf{PIE-Abducer} (incremental direct-derivation abduction) and \textbf{PIE-APT} (Abductive Planning for Temporal KGs)---operating natively on the highly expressive Description Logic. We model state transitions along a linear timeline as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories. Treating the incremental reasoner as a black-box and representing actions natively in OWL without external modal operators preserves logical decidability. To address incomplete knowledge, \textbf{PIE-Abducer} circumvents traditional Minimal Hitting Set (MHS) enumeration. Instead of combinatorial syntactic search, it injects the logical negation of a target goal into a consistent branch and extracts missing premises via direct refutation consequences. \textbf{PIE-APT} then employs a recursive \textit{Generate-and-Test} architecture, interleaving backward-chaining A* search with \textbf{PIE-Abducer} up to a bounded causal depth, followed by strict validation via forward-chaining Temporal Projection. We evaluate four OWL benchmarks stressing semantic abilities absent in classical planning: parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting. Results demonstrate qualitative superiority over classical planners and prove our direct-derivation approach quantitatively outperforms an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.

</details>


### [117] [PAUSE: A User-Centric Benchmark for Personal AI Assistants in Unified Service Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27354)
*Haoyu Chen,Xirui Shi,Yuyao Wang,Jerry Chen,Di Niu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PAUSE is a user-centric benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments. It requires agents to coordinate across heterogeneous user-owned resources while maintaining consistency with environment state and authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions, and finds that even SOTA proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic service settings. Realistic assistants must reason over persistent user state, respect user-specific configurations/permissions, and sustain long-horizon, constraint-aware interactions across multiple services, but current evaluation infrastructure does not capture these challenges.

Method: PAUSE introduces a benchmark with stateful, service-integrated environments requiring agents to coordinate actions across heterogeneous user-owned resources under environment-state and authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions. It incorporates explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation, adopts a multi-regime evaluation framework (semantic and trajectory-level behavioral metrics for open-ended tasks; deterministic state-based verification for constraint-intensive tasks), and presents a user-centric synthesis pipeline for scalable generation of coherent service environments and reliably annotated tasks.

Result: State-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness, revealing consistent and interpretable failure patterns.

Conclusion: PAUSE demonstrates that current AI assistants are insufficient for real-world stateful, user-centric service management, and provides a scalable synthesis pipeline to support benchmark extensibility and future research.

Abstract: Personal AI assistants are increasingly deployed as task-oriented, tool-augmented agents that operate within unified service environments to support everyday user activities. In realistic settings, such assistants must reason over persistent user state, respect user-specific configurations and permissions, and sustain long-horizon, constraint-aware interactions across multiple services. Existing benchmarks, however, often fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic service settings. We introduce PAUSE, a user-centric benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments. PAUSE captures core challenges of real-world assistant deployment by requiring agents to coordinate actions across heterogeneous user-owned resources while maintaining consistency with environment state, authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions. The benchmark incorporates explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation, enabling evaluation beyond static tool execution. To support principled and reproducible evaluation, PAUSE adopts a multi-regime evaluation framework aligned with task characteristics. Open-ended service management tasks are assessed using semantic and trajectory-level behavioral metrics, while constraint-intensive tasks admit deterministic, state-based verification. Benchmark results show that even state-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness, revealing consistent and interpretable failure patterns. Finally, we present a user-centric synthesis pipeline that enables scalable generation of coherent service environments, user configurations, and reliably annotated tasks, supporting benchmark extensibility and future research.

</details>


### [118] [SkillMentor: LLM Agent Self-Evolution via Learning Blind-Spot Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27360)
*Xiaoyi Bao,Yuanzhen Xie,Yunzhi Tan,Jinghang Gu,Zhongqing Wang,Chu-Ren Huang,Bo Hu,Zang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillMentor trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to diagnose agent blind spots—generating diagnostic tasks, identifying recurrent failures, and curating corrective skills—improving executor performance by 44.2% on average across AppWorld and BFCLv3 without updating executor weights or using human supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent self-evolution has focused on learning how to act but has overlooked learning to discover what an agent does not know. Existing approaches assume failure discovery is given and focus only on repairing identified failures, leaving blind-spot diagnosis itself unexplored as a learnable capability.

Method: SkillMentor trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to perform three diagnostic functions: generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurrent failure modes, and curate failures into reusable corrective skills. The study isolates diagnosis from execution by excluding executor adaptation and human supervision, ensuring all improvement originates from the learned diagnostic capability.

Result: Across AppWorld and BFCLv3 benchmarks, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%.

Conclusion: Blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability that enables self-evolution without updating executor weights or relying on human-curated data, opening a new pathway for agent self-improvement.

Abstract: Agent self-evolution has primarily focused on learning how to act, while overlooking an equally important capability: learning to discover what an agent does not know. Existing approaches typically assume that failure discovery is given, focusing on how to repair failures once they are identified. We ask whether blind-spot diagnosis itself can be learned. We thus study diagnosis as an agent capability separate from execution, and exclude two alternative sources of progress: executor adaptation and human supervision. Under these constraints, performance cannot improve through executor updates or annotated examples, forcing all improvements to originate from the learned diagnostic capability. We propose SkillMentor, which trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurrent failure modes, and curate them into reusable corrective skills. Across AppWorld and BFCLv3, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%. These results suggest that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability, enabling self-evolution without updating executor weights or relying on human-curated data.

</details>


### [119] [Beyond the Bidirectional Promise: Re-evaluating the Robustness of Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27386)
*Saurabh Yadav,Badri Narayana Patro,Vijay Srinivas Agneeswaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates the robustness and calibration of Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) against autoregressive (AR) baselines using parameter-matched model pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. The authors find that while DLMs naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes due to stochastic loss landscapes, they offer no guaranteed defense against natural noise; DLMs exhibit systematic overconfidence; and mechanistic probing reveals that all models perfectly encode input corruption, with fragility stemming from decoder routing failure. Surface-level prompt patching fails, indicating robustness must be integrated into the iterative decoding loop rather than patched externally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion Language Models present a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation, yet their reliability under natural noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored, motivating a systematic evaluation of their robustness and calibration.

Method: The authors use parameter-matched model pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) to isolate architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors, testing across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses.

Result: DLMs show nuanced robustness: stochastic loss landscapes naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes but provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise; DLMs exhibit systematic overconfidence; mechanistic probing shows all models perfectly encode input corruption, isolating fragility to decoder routing failure; prompt patching fails to improve over noisy baselines.

Conclusion: DLM robustness cannot be patched on externally; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop.

Abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive (AR) generation by enabling bidirectional context and iterative refinement. However, their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored. To address this, we systematically evaluate DLM robustness and calibration against AR baselines, using two parameter-matched pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. This paired design effectively isolates architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors. We find a nuanced robustness profile: while highly stochastic DLM loss landscapes naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes, they provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise, proving that everyday robustness is weight-dependent rather than inherently architectural. Furthermore, DLMs exhibit systematic overconfidence, presenting a practical deployment hazard. Most crucially, mechanistic probing reveals that all models perfectly encode input corruption, isolating behavioral fragility entirely to a decoder routing failure. Consistent with this diagnosis, we show that surface-level prompt patching fails to improve over noisy baselines. Ultimately, DLM robustness cannot be patched on; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop.

</details>


### [120] [Bridging Inference-Time Scaling and Episodic Memory with Action-Centric Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27415)
*Xu Zheng,Chaohao Lin,Zhuomin Chen,Weijieying Ren,Haifeng Chen,Wei Cheng,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GAMER is a framework that bridges inference-time scaling and episodic memory for LLM agents by modeling historical reasoning as a dynamic Action-Centric Graph, decoupling memory from LLMs, and using dual-stream Temporal Difference learning to estimate positive (suggestion) and negative (avoidance) values of action nodes for bi-directional decision optimization during inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inference-time scaling methods for LLM agents suffer from critical inefficiency due to stateless operation and redundant search processes. Existing memory mechanisms rely heavily on LLM reasoning, leading to prohibitive computational costs.

Method: GAMER models historical reasoning as a dynamic Action-Centric Graph. It decouples the memory mechanism from LLMs to save token/money usage. A dual-stream Temporal Difference learning mechanism estimates positive (suggestion) and negative (avoidance) values of action nodes based on past successes and failures. During inference, the learned value function optimizes decision-making bi-directionally (positive values suggest actions, negative values flag high-risk actions) via efficient graph searches.

Result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show GAMER achieves superior performance with 20.81% improvement in success rate and 6.17% improvement in progress rate compared to vanilla baselines.

Conclusion: GAMER effectively bridges the gap between inference scaling and episodic memory, significantly improving the efficiency of inference-time scaling for LLM agents while maintaining superior task performance.

Abstract: Recent advancements in inference-time scaling have significantly unlocked the complex reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models~(LLMs). However, for agents, these approaches suffer from a critical inefficiency, operating in a stateless manner and engaging in redundant search processes. Existing memory mechanisms largely rely on the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, leading to prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, \textit{GAMER}~(Graph-based Action-centric Memory with Episodic Reasoning), that bridges the gap between inference scaling and episodic memory. Our approach models historical reasoning as a dynamic \textit{Action-Centric Graph}. By decoupling the memory mechanism from LLMs, our method can save token/money usage by providing less memory context than memory mechanism baselines. To extract knowledge from the graph effectively, we use a dual-stream Temporal Difference learning mechanism to estimate the positive~(suggestion) and negative~(avoidance) value of action nodes based on past successes and failures. During the inference phase, this learned value function optimizes decision-making bi-directionally, so that positive values provide action suggestions, while negative values indicate high-risk actions. By performing efficient searches on the graph, our method significantly improves the efficiency of inference scaling. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that \textit{GAMER} achieves superior performance by \textbf{20.81\%/6.17\%} for success/progress rate compared to vanilla baselines.

</details>


### [121] [Dimensionality and Measurement Precision in HLE's Multiple-Choice Subset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27420)
*Mayank Sharma,Savira Nadela,Tyler Matteson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HLE, despite its eight subject-domain categories, measures a single general reasoning factor (McDonald's ω_h = 0.998) rather than distinct latent abilities, and its measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels, dropping sharply in the range where frontier models sit, limiting its ability to discriminate among the strongest models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: HLE is widely used to evaluate frontier LLMs, and its domain subscores are often interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities. No prior study has assessed whether these categorical labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs or whether the benchmark effectively differentiates models of similar ability.

Method: The authors evaluate 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE (J = 428 items) and apply psychometric methods: fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model to assess dimensionality (McDonald's ω_h, variance explained by domain labels, within/between-domain residual correlations, domain-ability vs. total score correlations) and analyzing the test information function for measurement precision across ability levels.

Result: Convergent evidence indicates HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: ω_h = 0.998, domain labels explain only 3.5% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's d = 0.016), and domain-specific ability estimates correlate ≥ 0.81 with the total score. Test information analysis shows measurement precision peaks at moderate ability and drops sharply above θ = 0, where frontier models reside.

Conclusion: HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations, and the benchmark's ability to discriminate among the strongest models is limited.

Abstract: Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) is widely used to evaluate frontier language models. HLE organizes its questions into eight subject-domain categories, whose subscores are often interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities. However, no study has assessed whether these labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs, nor whether the benchmark effectively differentiates between models of similar ability. We evaluate 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE ($J = 428$ items) and apply psychometric methods to assess both the dimensionality of the benchmark and the distribution of its measurement precision. Fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model, we find convergent evidence that HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: McDonald's $ω_h = 0.998$, domain labels explain only 3.5\% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's $d = 0.016$), and domain-specific ability estimates are near-redundant with the total score ($r \geq 0.81$). A separate analysis of the test information function reveals that measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above $θ= 0$, where frontier models sit. These findings suggest that HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations and that the benchmark's ability to discriminate among the strongest models is limited.

</details>


### [122] [Leveraging Trajectory Graphs for Pre-Execution Error Diagnosis in Agentic LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27443)
*Xu Zheng,Zhuomin Chen,Chaohao Lin,Hua Wei,Haifeng Chen,Wei Cheng,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Trajectory Graph Copilot is a framework that diagnoses potential action errors in LLM-based agents before execution by modeling historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and using a Graph Neural Network to identify failure-prone action patterns, achieving a 14.69% average pass ratio improvement without costly fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks (e.g., embodied AI) due to compounding errors where a single suboptimal action derails the entire trajectory, exhausting the limited step budget on inefficient paths. Fine-tuning is costly, so a lightweight, pre-action diagnostic approach is needed.

Method: The Trajectory Graph Copilot framework includes a Graph Debugger that models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and employs a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure. It acts as a proactive diagnostic sandbox providing early warnings on potentially flawed actions, prompting the agent to self-correct before execution.

Result: Extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a 14.69% pass ratio improvement on average.

Conclusion: Pre-action error diagnosis significantly enhances the agent's ability to complete long-horizon tasks and prevents costly mistakes without requiring expensive fine-tuning.

Abstract: Large Language Model~(LLM)-based agents have demonstrated exceptional performance across a wide range of complex interactive tasks. However, they often struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks common in domains, such as embodied AI. The complexity and vast action spaces in these settings lead to compounding errors, where a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory, causing the agent to exhaust its limited step budget on inefficient or unrecoverable paths. To overcome this without costly fine-tuning, we draw inspiration from software debugging, where execution logs are analyzed to preemptively catch errors. We propose \textit{Trajectory Graph Copilot}, a novel framework that acts as a ``copilot'' for LLM agents by diagnosing potential action errors before they are executed. At its core,\textit{Graph Debugger} models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure. Functioning as a proactive diagnostic sandbox, our method provides early warnings on potentially flawed actions, prompting the agent to self-correct. This pre-action error diagnosis prevents costly mistakes, significantly enhancing the agent's ability to complete long-horizon tasks successfully. The extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a $14.69\%$ pass ratio improvement on average.

</details>


### [123] [VAmoS Bench: Voice Agent Simulation Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27453)
*Joshua Meyer,Sahar Shayegan,Ritiz Tambi,Ali Khan,Sun Kim,Victor Shih,Mehdi Jamei,Andi Partovi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VAmoS Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating complete voice-agent systems end-to-end in a stateful customer-support task. It simulates 100 phone-call scenarios in which a credit-card support agent (Riley) must resolve caller issues using real SQL tools against a seeded PostgreSQL backend, with binary assertions graded against full interaction traces to measure task containment, not just component quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing voice-agent benchmarks measure component quality (word error rate, latency, naturalness, turn-taking) and conversational properties, but few evaluate whether the agent actually handled a phone call correctly end-to-end. Contact centers use "containment" as the key metric: the share of calls resolved without human handoff. This gap motivates a benchmark that measures complete system performance in a realistic, stateful task.

Method: The benchmark defines 100 scenarios, each providing a simulated caller with a private goal and a seeded PostgreSQL backend. Each scenario populates an isolated simulation where the caller reaches a credit-card support agent (Riley) over audio; about one-third apply adversarial pressure. The agent can use five tools that execute real SQL against the backend. Each scenario defines binary assertions, which a grader evaluates against the complete trace (what caller and agent said, tool invocations, arguments, and returned rows) to catch both false claims (e.g., claiming a change without updating the database) and harmful actions (e.g., correct database change while leaking protected information).

Result: The paper introduces the benchmark framework and evaluation protocol. The first version focuses on financial services and supports an evolving leaderboard: additional voice agents can be evaluated on the same version, while later versions can expand tasks and scenarios. Specific benchmark performance numbers are not reported in this abstract.

Conclusion: VAmoS Bench fills the gap in voice-agent evaluation by measuring complete end-to-end task containment rather than only component-level quality, using stateful simulations with binary assertions against full interaction traces to catch both inaction and harmful actions.

Abstract: Production voice agents span cascaded, speech-to-speech, and hybrid architectures. Voice-agent benchmarks typically measure component quality and conversational properties such as word error rate, latency, naturalness, and turn-taking. Fewer measure whether the agent handled a phone call correctly on its own. Contact centers refer to this as ``containment'': the share of phone calls the automated system resolves without handing off to a human. On some phone calls the right outcome is refusal or a redirect. To address this gap, we introduce VAmoS Bench, the Voice Agent Simulation Bench. It measures complete voice-agent systems end to end in a stateful customer-support task. The agent is Riley, a credit-card support representative for a fictional bank who can freeze, cancel, replace, or activate a card. Each of 100 scenarios supplies a simulated caller with a private goal and a seeded PostgreSQL backend. The platform uses each scenario to populate and activate an isolated simulation in which the caller reaches Riley over audio; roughly one-third apply adversarial pressure. The agent can use five tools that execute real SQL against the backend. Each scenario also defines binary assertions. A grader evaluates them against the complete trace of what the caller and agent said and what the agent did, including tool invocations, arguments, and returned rows. This catches an agent that claims to have changed a card without updating the database, as well as one that makes the right database change while disclosing protected information. This first benchmark version focuses on financial services. Its evaluation protocol supports an evolving leaderboard: additional voice agents can be evaluated on the same version, while later versions can expand the tasks and scenarios.

</details>


### [124] [Skill Use or Skill Theater? Evaluating the Reasoning Backroom in Skill-Augmented Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27484)
*Jinwei Hu,Yi Qi,Xinmiao Huang,Youcheng Sun,Yi Dong,Xiaowei Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework that measures whether skill-augmented language agents actually rely on skills by comparing skill-conditioned answers against matched no-skill counterfactuals with interventions on skill content, wording, identity, and assignment. Through BACKROOMBench (a testbed spanning logic, competition math, single/multi-agent settings, and multiple model families), the authors discover a widespread "Reasoning Backroom"—a systematic gap between agents' stated skill use and intervention-measured influence—where observational signals (self-reports, text mentions, trace similarity, LLM judges) fail to identify genuine causal skill dependence, and where skill influence can persist even after its source is lost in multi-agent systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of skill use in language agents rely on observable signals like reasoning traces or self-attribution, which reveal what the agent appears to use rather than whether the skill actually changed its decision. The authors want to uncover whether there is a systematic gap between stated and actual skill influence—a "Reasoning Backroom"—requiring intervention-based measurement rather than observational inference.

Method: The authors propose BACKTRACE: an evaluation framework that (1) pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual, (2) intervenes on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and (3) elicits attribution only after the answer is committed. They instantiate this as BACKROOMBench, a verified testbed covering controlled logic and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single-agent and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families.

Result: The evaluation reveals a pervasive provenance failure: across models and domains, stated skill use remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing both silent uptake and performative use. Behavioral effects follow procedural content more reliably than displayed skill identity, while stated attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. Observational detectors (direct claims, text mentions, trace similarity, LLM judges) fail to identify which decisions actually depend on the skill. In multi-agent systems, skill influence can survive communication after its source is lost, and no-skill teams still name skills and sources never supplied.

Conclusion: The "Reasoning Backroom" is a general AI provenance problem: observational signals cannot reliably audit skill influence in language agents, and proper audit requires intervention-based measurement. This has broad implications for evaluating and trusting skill-augmented agent systems.

Abstract: Reusable skills are becoming a standard interface for extending language agents with task procedures. Yet evaluators usually infer skill use from visible reasoning or the agent's own attribution. These signals show what the agent appears to use, not whether the skill changed its decision. We ask whether skill-augmented agents exhibit a \textbf{Reasoning Backroom}, a systematic gap between stated skill use and intervention-measured influence. We introduce BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework that pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual, intervenes on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and elicits attribution only after the answer is committed. We instantiate the framework as BACKROOMBench, a verified testbed spanning controlled logic and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single-agent and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive provenance failure. Across models and domains, stated skill use often remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing both silent uptake and performative use. Behavioral effects follow procedural content more reliably than displayed skill identity, whereas stated attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. Observational detectors based on direct skill-use claims, text mentions, trace similarity, and an LLM judge do not identify which decisions actually depend on the skill. In multi-agent systems, skill influence can survive communication even after its source is lost, while no-skill teams still name skills and sources that were never supplied. These findings establish the Reasoning Backroom as a general AI provenance problem whose audit requires intervention.

</details>


### [125] [INCLAIR: Inception-Based Longitudinal Clinical Anomaly Detection with Informed Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27487)
*Maxx Richard Rahman,Wolfgang Maass*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: INCLAIR is a framework for detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles that scores observations against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision. It uses order-l U-statistics for variance decomposition and incomplete-subset approximation to control combinatorial cost, with validation-selected top-k pooling to mitigate attenuation of localized anomalies. It outperforms baselines on three clinical datasets and is validated against domain experts in a steroid profile case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles is clinically important but difficult due to sparse abnormal evidence, unequal patient history lengths, and costly expert explanations.

Method: INCLAIR scores each observation against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates grounded explanations. Under within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the mean subsequence score takes an order-l U-statistic form, enabling variance decomposition and incomplete-subset approximation that controls combinatorial cost independently of profile length. Validation-selected top-k pooling addresses mean aggregation's attenuation of localized anomalies.

Result: INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across three clinical datasets. A case study on longitudinal steroid profiles with domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis confirms practical relevance and clinical actionability.

Conclusion: INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision.

Abstract: Detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles is clinically important but difficult: abnormal evidence is often sparse, patient histories have unequal length, and expert explanations are costly. We propose INCLAIR, a framework that scores each observation against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision. Under stated within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the complete mean subsequence score takes an order-$l$ U-statistic form, yielding a variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation that controls combinatorial inference cost independently of profile length. The same analysis shows that mean aggregation attenuates localized anomalies by a factor set by the anomaly support and profile length, motivating validation-selected top-$k$ pooling. Across three clinical datasets, INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We further validate practical relevance through a case study on longitudinal steroid profiles, comparing INCLAIR's predictions and explanations against domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis. The results show that INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision.

</details>


### [126] [MedLLM: An Open Medical Language Model at the Sub-Billion Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27490)
*Maxx Richard Rahman,Asim Ahmed,Mihan Mohagheghzadeh,Wolfgang Maass*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MedLLM is an open 0.1B-parameter medical language model trained via a fully open three-phase pipeline (curriculum pretraining, domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb, and preference-aligned SFT+DPO). At sub-billion scale, medical competence does not degrade uniformly under compression: context-grounded QA performance nearly matches a medically adapted 7B model, while knowledge-recall QA splits—remaining at task floor on MedQA but significantly exceeding all baselines on MedMCQA—revealing that recall failures stem from model capacity, not adaptation, a dissociation masked at 7B scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open medical language models have all converged on a single scale of 7B parameters or larger, leaving the sub-billion parameter regime completely uncharacterized. The authors aim to explore whether smaller models can exhibit useful medical competence and to understand how compression affects medical capabilities.

Method: A three-phase fully open training pipeline: (1) general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, (2) domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb, a newly released reference-guided medical corpus selected from general web data via embedding similarity to medical QA data, and (3) preference-aligned fine-tuning combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with direct preference optimization (DPO).

Result: On context-grounded QA, MedLLM comes within 2.9 percentage points of a medically adapted 7B model and surpasses instruction-tuned and general-purpose 7B baselines. On knowledge-recall QA, it stays near task floor on MedQA but significantly exceeds every 7B and sub-7B baseline on MedMCQA, revealing that medical competence splits by task type under compression rather than degrading uniformly.

Conclusion: At sub-billion scale, medical capabilities dissociate by task type: context-grounded QA remains competitive while knowledge-recall QA becomes capacity-bound. This dissociation is invisible at 7B parameters where both capabilities coexist, and only surfaces when model capacity is scarce.

Abstract: Open medical language models have converged on a single scale: every widely used system runs at 7B parameters or more, leaving the sub-billion regime uncharacterized. We present MedLLM, an open 0.1B-parameter medical language model trained through a fully open three-phase pipeline: general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb, a reference-guided medical corpus we release that is selected from general web data by embedding similarity to medical question-answering (QA) data, and preference-aligned fine-tuning combining SFT with direct preference optimization (DPO). Across medical benchmarks, MedLLM shows a pattern visible only at sub-billion scale: medical competence does not degrade uniformly under compression but splits by task type. On context-grounded QA it comes within $2.9$pp of a medically adapted 7B model and surpasses the instruction-tuned and general-purpose 7B baselines; on knowledge-recall QA it stays near the task floor on clinical-vignette MedQA yet significantly exceeds every 7B and sub-7B baseline on MedMCQA, indicating that where recall fails the constraint is model capacity rather than adaptation. This dissociation is masked at 7B, where both capabilities are present, and surfaces only when capacity is scarce.

</details>


### [127] [A dataset of rated conceptual arguments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27499)
*Emery Cooper,Caspar Oesterheld,Linh Chi Nguyen,Alexander Kastner,Ethan Perez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a framework for evaluating LLM reasoning on conceptual questions—questions without verifiable ground truth—by scoring individual arguments rather than conclusions. The authors present a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts across topics like AI safety, decision theory, ethics, and politics, rated by six expert raters on dimensions such as centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. They propose two scoring functions and benchmark various models, finding performance tracks general capability rankings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs excel on tasks with verifiable answers (math, programming), little is known about their ability to reason on conceptual questions where no ground truth or accepted resolution methodology exists. The authors argue that although bottom-line conclusions are hard to evaluate, individual contextualized arguments can be evaluated far more reliably—motivating an argument-level evaluation framework.

Method: The authors construct a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts spanning AI safety, decision theory, ethics, and politics, with 1,458 ratings from six expert raters along dimensions including centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. They propose two scoring functions for aggregating argument-level judgments and benchmark a range of language models on these tasks.

Result: Model performance on the conceptual reasoning tasks tracks general capability rankings, suggesting that existing model capabilities transfer to evaluating arguments on conceptual questions, with stronger models performing better.

Conclusion: Evaluating individual arguments rather than final conclusions offers a tractable and reliable approach to assessing LLM reasoning on conceptual questions, and current models show capability that correlates with overall model strength.

Abstract: Large language models have improved rapidly on tasks with verifiable answers, such as mathematics and programming. Much less is known about their ability to reason about what we call conceptual questions: questions for which no ground truth is realistically accessible and no widely accepted resolution methodology exists, but on which progress can still be made by debating arguments. Most philosophical questions are of this kind, as are central components of questions in AI safety, decision theory, and social choice. Our approach is based on the view that while bottom-line conclusions on such questions are hard to evaluate, individual contextualized arguments can be evaluated far more reliably. We therefore introduce a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts, spanning topics from AI safety and decision theory to ethics and politics, with 1,458 ratings by six expert raters along dimensions including centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. We propose two scoring functions and benchmark a range of models. Performance tracks general capability rankings.

</details>


### [128] [Automated Transcript Analysis for Detecting Flaws in Agentic Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27518)
*Jeff Mohl,Nelson Gardner-Challis,Magda Dubois,Harry Coppock,Benjamin Allan-Rahill,Kaelan Yim,Damian Sójka,James Mann,Justin Olive*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes automated AI scanners to detect four types of validity issues (ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, answer format ambiguity) in agentic benchmark transcripts. Evaluated against human labels on Inspect Evals benchmarks, the scanners identified verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, though performance varied across benchmarks, criteria, and models, highlighting open challenges in scaling benchmark quality assurance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier model capabilities are assessed using agentic benchmarks, but manual audits (e.g., of SWE-Bench-Verified) have revealed validity flaws. Manual review does not scale, and it remains unclear whether automated methods can reliably surface benchmark validity issues.

Method: The authors developed AI scanners targeting four validity issue types: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. They created grading rubrics for human labeling and evaluated scanner performance against human labels on a held-out test set from Inspect Evals benchmarks.

Result: The scanners identified several verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. However, not all cases were identified, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria, and models.

Conclusion: Automated transcript analysis serves as a proof of concept for broader benchmark quality auditing. However, several open challenges remain, including standardization gaps in the evaluation field that degrade scanner performance, which must be addressed for stronger quality assurance claims.

Abstract: Capabilities of frontier models are often assessed using agentic benchmarks. To trust these results, benchmarks must accurately measure what they claim to and be free from invalidating flaws. Previous manual audits of benchmarks such as SWE-Bench-Verified have uncovered several validity issues in transcripts. However, manual review is difficult to scale, and it is unclear whether automated methods can reliably surface flaws that compromise benchmark validity. In this paper, we developed AI scanners to detect four types of validity issues: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. We produced grading rubrics for each to instruct human labeling, and evaluated the scanners against human labels on a held-out test set of Inspect Evals benchmarks. Our scanners identified several verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. Not all cases were identified, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria and models. We highlight several open challenges to be addressed to improve scanners for stronger quality assurance claims, including broader standardization gaps in the evaluation field that degrade scanner performance. Together, these results serve as a proof of concept for using automated transcript analysis to audit benchmark quality more broadly.

</details>


### [129] [AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27547)
*Brady D. Lund,Zoë Abbie Teel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper critiques existing AI literacy frameworks for being dominated by technical competency and responsible-use principles that enforce a consumer orientation toward AI. Drawing on Foucault's power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and digital literacy scholarship, the authors reconceptualize AI literacy as a critical practice that enables individuals to evaluate, resist, and govern AI systems. They propose a three-part framework—contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance—framed around cultivating epistemic agents rather than competent consumers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As generative AI becomes a major mode of knowledge production in society, questions of who can access and shape that production grow increasingly important. The authors argue that existing AI literacy frameworks are insufficient because they enforce a consumer orientation rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency, and they fail to address structural inequities in access that recapitulate epistemic injustices.

Method: The paper engages in theoretical reconceptualization, drawing on three intellectual traditions: Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and digital literacy scholarship. These are synthesized to develop a three-part framework of AI literacy comprising contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance.

Result: The paper proposes a reconceptualized, three-part framework of AI literacy based on contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance, which reframes literacy as the cultivation of epistemic agency rather than the training of competent consumers of AI-generated information.

Conclusion: AI literacy should be understood as a critical practice that equips individuals not only to use AI systems but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance. This framework must account for structural inequities in access and is oriented toward empowerment and epistemic agency.

Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes one of the most significant systems of knowledge production in our society today, questions relating to who can access and shape that production grow increasingly important in our discourse. This paper argues that the existing frameworks for AI literacy, which are dominated by technical competency and responsible-use principles, are insufficient because they enforce a "consumer" orientation toward AI rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. Based upon Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of AI literacy as a critical practice that equips individuals not just to use AI systems, but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance. The paper further argues that unequal access to AI tools in society recapitulates longstanding epistemic injustices, and that a literacy framework oriented toward empowerment must account for these structural inequities. A three-part framework of AI literacy based on the notions of contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance frames this literacy as a cultivation of epistemic "agents" rather than the training of competent consumers of AI-generated information.

</details>


### [130] [Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27553)
*Lennart Meincke,Karan Girotra,Gideon Nave,Christian Terwiesch,Karl T. Ulrich*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper compares AI-generated (GPT-4) product ideas with human-generated ideas for new products targeting college students. AI ideas outperform human ideas in average purchase intent and are seven times more likely to rank in the top 10% of ideas, but they are perceived as less novel and more homogeneous, particularly under few-shot prompting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To empirically evaluate whether large language models can effectively generate high-quality new product ideas, given the increasing availability and use of LLMs in creative and product development tasks.

Method: Three pools of product ideas (priced at $50 or less, for college students) were compared: (1) human-generated ideas from a university product design course, (2) GPT-4 zero-shot prompted ideas, and (3) GPT-4 few-shot prompted ideas. Idea quality was measured via average purchase intent probability using standard market research techniques. Text mining was used to assess idea similarity, and human raters evaluated novelty.

Result: AI-generated ideas outperformed human ideas in average purchase intent, with few-shot prompting slightly outperforming zero-shot. However, AI ideas were perceived as less novel and showed higher pairwise similarity (especially with few-shot prompting). AI-generated ideas were seven times more likely to rank in the top 10% of ideas, with this advantage considered a conservative estimate since it excludes AI's greater productivity.

Conclusion: Despite drawbacks such as reduced novelty and diversity, AI-generated ideas offer a substantial advantage in producing high-quality ideas for new product development, with the seven-to-one advantage in top-tier ideas underscoring the potential benefit of AI creativity.

Abstract: This research evaluates the efficacy of large language models (LLMs) in generating new product ideas. To do so, we compare three pools of ideas for new products targeted toward college students and priced at 50 dollars or less. The first pool of ideas was created by university students in a product design course before the availability of LLMs. The second and third pools of ideas were generated by GPT-4 from OpenAI using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, respectively. We evaluated idea quality using standard market research techniques to predict average purchase intent probability. We used text mining to assess idea similarity and human raters to evaluate idea novelty. We find that AI-generated ideas outperform human-generated ideas in terms of average purchase intent, with few-shot prompting yielding slightly higher intent than zero-shot prompting. However, AI-generated ideas are perceived as less novel and exhibit higher pairwise similarity, particularly with few-shot prompting, indicating a less diverse solution landscape. When focusing on the quality of the best ideas rather than the average ideas, we find that AI-generated ideas are seven times more likely to rank among the top 10 percent of ideas, demonstrating a significant advantage over human-generated ideas. We propose that this seven-to-one advantage is a conservative estimate because it does not account for the greater productivity of AI. Our findings suggest that despite some drawbacks, AI creativity presents a substantial benefit in generating high-quality ideas for new product development.

</details>


### [131] [Evaluating Agentic Bioinformatics through Function, Evidence, and Validation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27556)
*Phuc Pham,Truong-Son Hy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces the Function–Evidence–Validation (FEV) framework for assessing the scientific credibility of large language model (LLM) agents in bioinformatics. Rather than relying solely on final outputs or benchmark scores, FEV treats the inspectable workflow trajectory as the primary unit of analysis, separating demonstrated operations, traceable evidence for actions/claims, and use-case validation. The authors map 109 agentic systems and 28 benchmarks across 128 publications spanning genomics, single-cell omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics, finding that planning and tool-mediated execution have outpaced replayability, provenance, robust assessment, external validation, and prospective testing. The paper argues for workflow correctness over final-answer correctness as the standard for assessing agentic bioinformatics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fluent responses, successful tool calls, and benchmark performance do not establish scientific credibility for LLM agents in biology. Existing reviews organize agents by application, architecture, or capability, but fail to jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. This paper addresses that gap by making the inspectable workflow trajectory, rather than the final output or architecture, the central unit of analysis.

Method: The authors introduce the Function–Evidence–Validation (FEV) framework, which decomposes agent-generated workflows into three dimensions: (1) Function—demonstrated workflow operations; (2) Evidence—traceable support for actions and claims; and (3) Validation—use-case-specific assessment. Using FEV, they conduct a structured mapping of 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark or evaluation resources drawn from 128 unique publications across multiple bioinformatics domains.

Result: Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. This asymmetry indicates a maturity gap: the "doing" component of agents is far ahead of the "accountability" component.

Conclusion: Agentic bioinformatics should be assessed through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. The FEV framework provides a practical basis for comparing systems and for designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly plan, execute, and interpret biological analyses, yet fluent responses, successful tool calls, and benchmark performance alone do not establish scientific credibility. Existing reviews primarily organize biological agents by application, architecture, and agentic capability, but do not jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. We address this gap by treating the inspectable workflow trajectory, rather than architecture or final output alone, as the primary unit of analysis. We introduce the Function--Evidence--Validation (FEV) framework, which separates demonstrated workflow operations, traceable support for actions and claims, and use-case-specific validation. Using FEV, we map 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark or evaluation resources, representing 128 unique publications across genomics, single-cell and spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation. Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. We therefore argue that agentic bioinformatics should be assessed through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. FEV provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

</details>


### [132] [DeepResearch Agent System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27562)
*Yong Huang,Yulu Huang,for the team Collaboration*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The DeepResearch Agent System is a sparse-activated LLM-based agentic research system (30B total params, 3B activated per token) that achieves state-of-the-art performance on agent search benchmarks with 3.2x faster inference than dense counterparts, featuring a 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention, dual-mode reasoning (ReAct and IterResearch with up to 20 reasoning steps), multi-tool coordination achieving 92.1% tool-use accuracy, and GRPO-based reinforcement learning optimization. It reports 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA, and is fully open-sourced.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To build an efficient and capable large language model system specifically engineered for deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks, addressing challenges of long-context understanding, iterative reasoning, and multi-tool orchestration in agentic settings.

Method: The system employs a sparse activation architecture (30B total / 3B activated per token) for efficiency, a 128K-token context with hierarchical attention for long-range understanding, a dual-mode reasoning engine (ReAct and IterResearch modes supporting up to 20 reasoning steps), multi-tool coordination across retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing, GRPO-based reinforcement learning for token-level policy optimization, and an automated data synthesis pipeline with seed-based expansion.

Result: Achieves 3.2x faster inference than dense models of equivalent scale; 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements over standard long-context approaches; 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines with the dual-mode reasoning engine; 92.1% tool-use accuracy; 35% improvement in training stability and 42% faster convergence from GRPO; 92.5% data usability rate; benchmark scores of 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA.
