Conclusion: The DeepResearch Agent System delivers state-of-the-art agentic research capabilities with significant efficiency gains through sparse activation, effective long-context handling, versatile multi-step reasoning, robust tool coordination, and stable RL training. Its fully open-sourced nature supports broad applications in academic research, business analysis, R&D, and education.

Abstract: The DeepResearch Agent System is a large language model system engineered for deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks. Built upon a sparse activation architecture with 30 billion total parameters of which only 3 billion are activated per token, the system achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple agent search benchmarks while delivering 3.2 times faster inference compared to dense counterparts of equivalent scale. The system supports a 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention mechanisms that yield 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements over standard long-context approaches. A dual-mode reasoning engine provides both a ReAct paradigm for basic multi-step problem solving and an IterResearch mode for high-performance iterative research with up to 20 reasoning steps, collectively delivering a 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines. Multi-tool coordination integrates retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing modules to achieve 92.1% tool-use accuracy. A reinforcement learning optimization framework based on the GRPO algorithm provides token-level policy gradients that improve training stability by 35% and accelerate convergence by 42%. An automated data synthesis pipeline with seed-based expansion achieves a 92.5% usability rate. Benchmark results include 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA. The system is fully open-sourced, including data synthesis, training, and inference code, and supports applications in academic research, business analysis, R&D support, and education.

</details>


### [133] [What makes prompts a graph: necessary and sufficient conditions for prompt graph engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27578)
*Sandeco Macedo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the vocabulary gap in prompt engineering by proposing a constitutive definition of "prompt graph engineering" — treating prompts as nodes within explicit, executable, and improvable graphs. It reconstructs the genealogy of this idea, states four conditions (explicit structure, separation of structure from content, executable semantics, and graph as first-class artifact), operationalizes them as an inclusion/exclusion test against six real systems, and closes with a research agenda organized along four design tension axes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While industry frameworks (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow) and research systems have converged on graphs as the core structure connecting model calls, retrieval, routers, and aggregators, the vocabulary has not kept pace. Prompts are still discussed as isolated strings, and graph-related terminology is used inconsistently to describe reasoning topologies, multi-agent conversations, or orchestration artifacts. A reference definition treating prompts as nodes of an explicit, executable, improvable graph is missing.

Method: The authors conduct conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers complemented by primary grey literature. They reconstruct the genealogy from dataflow graphs and build systems, through prompt chaining and thought topologies (chain, tree, graph), to compiled and optimized graph artifacts. They then propose a constitutive definition with four conditions and operationalize them as an inclusion/exclusion test applied to six real systems.

Result: The four conditions of prompt graph engineering are: explicit structure, separation between structure and prompt content, executable semantics, and the graph as a first-class engineering artifact. The inclusion/exclusion test applied to LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, and Claude Code subagents yields consistent results. The paper also draws boundaries against six neighboring concepts.

Conclusion: The contribution is an operational definition and a shared vocabulary for a practice that industry already exercises daily without naming precisely. The paper closes with a research agenda organized along four design tension axes.

Abstract: Prompts stopped being isolated strings some time ago. In real systems, one model call feeds another, retrieval interleaves with generation, routers branch, and aggregators merge parallel results. Practice converged on a single structure to hold this together: the graph. Frameworks such as LangGraph, DSPy, and Prompt Flow expose it openly, and research systems already optimize it automatically. The vocabulary, however, lags behind. Graph names, variously, a reasoning topology inside one sampling strategy, a multi-agent conversation, or an orchestration artifact, while prompt engineering still evokes writing one good string. What is missing is a reference definition treating prompts as nodes of an explicit, executable, improvable graph. We build that definition through conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers, complemented by primary grey literature. We reconstruct the genealogy of the idea, from dataflow graphs and build systems, through prompt chaining and the thought topologies (chain, tree, graph), to graphs compiled and optimized as artifacts. We then propose a constitutive definition of prompt graph engineering, state its four conditions (explicit structure, separation between structure and prompt content, executable semantics, and the graph as a first-class engineering artifact), and operationalize them as an inclusion and exclusion test. We draw the boundary against six neighboring concepts and apply the test to six real systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, and Claude Code subagents); it includes and excludes consistently. We close with a research agenda organized along four design tension axes. The contribution is an operational definition and a shared vocabulary for a practice that industry already exercises daily without naming precisely.

</details>


### [134] [From Minds to Models: The Intersection of Psychology and LLM Behaviours](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27579)
*Oliver Guidetti,Reza Ryan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study adapted psychological methods (prompt-based Implicit Association Test) to test whether ChatGPT shows racial sentiment differences in open-ended text. Using 126 prompts crossed with eight racial categories, the study found only weak and analysis-dependent evidence of racial sentiment differences across GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, and GPT-4T.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are often compared to the human mind due to their complex, non-linear, and difficult-to-interpret decision-making. Psychological methods developed to investigate unobservable mental processes may help examine LLM behavior, particularly in high-stakes domains like government and healthcare, where bias detection is critical.

Method: The study built on prompt-based adaptations of the Implicit Association Test. Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, producing 126 prompts. Each prompt was submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, and GPT-4T, yielding 378 responses. Sentiment scores were derived from categorical labels and source scores (positive labels retained source score, negative labels assigned its negative, neutral coded zero). A two-way ANOVA was conducted along with a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis and Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons.

Result: A two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition (F(8,351)=2.04, p=.042, partial-eta squared=.044), but no effect of model and no interaction. The racial effect was not retained in a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis (F(8,351)=1.53, p=.145), and Tukey-corrected comparisons found no significant pairwise differences. An uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant but was post hoc and only hypothesis-generating. Evidence for sentiment differences was therefore weak and analysis-dependent.

Conclusion: The evidence for racial sentiment differences in ChatGPT was weak and inconsistent across analyses. Sentiment scoring cannot distinguish evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by prompts. The authors outline design changes to address these limitations and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioral measures of model bias.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often compared with the human mind because their decision-making is complex, non-linear and difficult to interpret. Psychological methods developed to investigate unobservable mental processes may therefore help examine LLM behaviour, particularly in government and healthcare. Building on prompt-based adaptations of the Implicit Association Test, this study tested whether ChatGPT produced sentiment differences across racial conditions in open-ended text. Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, producing 126 prompts. Each was submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4 and GPT-4T, yielding 378 responses. Sentiment scores were derived from categorical labels and source scores: positive labels retained the source score, negative labels were assigned its negative, and neutral responses were coded zero. A two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition, F(8, 351) = 2.04, p = .042, partial-eta squared = .044, but no effect of model, F(2, 351) = 0.07, p = .933, and no interaction, F(16, 351) = 0.23, p = .999. However, the effect was not retained in a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis, F(8, 351) = 1.53, p = .145, and Tukey-corrected comparisons found no significant pairwise differences. An uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant, but was selected post hoc and is reported only as hypothesis-generating. Evidence for sentiment differences was therefore weak and analysis-dependent. Sentiment scoring also cannot distinguish evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by a prompt. We outline design changes needed to address these limitations and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.
  Keywords: Implicit Bias, Psychological Research Methods, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Large Language Models, Sentiment Analysis

</details>


### [135] [Wiring diagram extraction and gluing: a case study in classifying figure skating jumps using 3D dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27598)
*Jason Lo,Mohammadnima Jafari*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a theory of gluing wiring diagrams to enable iterative Hasse clustering, addressing the combinatorial explosion that makes the algorithm infeasible with large cluster counts. The approach is validated on classifying figure skating jump videos.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hasse clustering extracts common patterns in sequential data but suffers from combinatorial complexity as the number of expected clusters grows, making it infeasible for large-scale problems. A method to decompose the computation is needed.

Method: The authors develop a theory of gluing wiring diagrams that allows Hasse clustering to be applied iteratively, producing results equivalent to a single application while avoiding the combinatorial blowup.

Result: The iterative approach achieves the same clustering results as a monolithic application, tested on classifying videos of figure skating jumps.

Conclusion: The gluing wiring diagram theory provides a scalable way to apply Hasse clustering to problems with large cluster counts, demonstrating practical utility in video classification tasks.

Abstract: Hasse clustering is an algorithm that extracts common patterns in sequential data and represents them in graphical forms. As the number of expected clusters grows, however, the algorithm can become infeasible to run due to combinatorial complexity. In this article, we describe a theory of gluing wiring diagrams, allowing iterative applications of Hasse clustering to achieve the same result as a single application. We test our theory in the context of classifying videos of figure skating jumps.

</details>


### [136] [HALO: Heterogeneous Admission through Localized Obligations for Safe Agentic Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27636)
*Taewoo Park,Kyeonghyun Yoo,Kiseok Kim,Seunghyun Yoo,Hwangnam Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HALO is a runtime admission-control protocol for agentic AI systems that selectively preserves supported response components whose prerequisites remain valid, rechecks actions before dispatch, and permits only fresh replacements for blocked actions—validated across unit tests, replay, and simulated drone cold-start scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI responses contain heterogeneous components (notices, requests, handoffs, actions) that may become unsupported as conditions change before external use. Rejecting the whole response wastes useful components, while checking components independently risks accepting dependents whose prerequisites are no longer valid.

Method: HALO implements a runtime protocol that: (1) preserves only supported components with still-supported declared prerequisites, (2) rechecks each exact action immediately before dispatch, and (3) restricts blocked action replacements to fresh candidates only.

Result: HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay it retained 248/248 supported components (128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes) versus 0/248 for a whole-response policy. In ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.

Conclusion: HALO provides a principled middle ground between whole-response rejection and fully independent component checking, preserving maximal utility while guaranteeing semantic consistency and safety through prerequisite-aware admission and per-action revalidation.

Abstract: Recent agentic AI systems may return a heterogeneous response containing notices, requests, handoffs, and actions. Conditions can change before external use, so components from the same response need not remain supported together. Rejecting the whole response discards useful components, whereas checking components independently can leave a dependent without its prerequisite. We present Heterogeneous Admission with Localized Obligations (HALO), a runtime protocol that preserves supported components whose declared prerequisites also remain supported, rechecks each exact action before dispatch, and allows blocked actions to be replaced only by fresh candidates. HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 supported components, including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes, while a whole-response policy retained 0/248. Across ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.

</details>


### [137] [World Action Planner: Generalizable Decision-Making with Action-Conditioned World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27599)
*Xiangcheng Zhang,Yilun Du*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: World Action Planner is a robot planning system combining Vision-Language Models for reasoning with a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model for physical grounding, enabling agents to propose and iteratively refine action plans through optimization and search over imagined world model rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Imitation learning-based policies succeed in specific training environments but fail to generalize to novel scenes and tasks. There is a need for agents that can generalize across diverse applications.

Method: The system leverages VLM reasoning capabilities combined with a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model. The agent proposes initial action plans and iteratively refines them via optimization and search, reasoning over imagined world model rollouts.

Result: The approach achieves superior performance across compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art end-to-end policies such as VLAs and WAMs.

Conclusion: Combining VLM reasoning with world model physical grounding enables strong generalization in robot planning, surpassing pure end-to-end policy models.

Abstract: Building generalizable agents for diverse applications remains a fundamental challenge. While imitation learning-based policies succeed in specific training environments, they often fail to generalize to novel scenes and tasks. In this work, we propose World Action Planner, a robot planning system that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and the physical grounding of a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model. Our system enables an agent to propose initial action plans and iteratively refine them via optimization and search, reasoning over imagined world model rollouts. We demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance across compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models such as VLAs and WAMs. Project website at worldactionplanner.github.io

</details>


### [138] [Old Tricks, New Models: How Simple Image Transformations Break Modern AI-based Content Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28187)
*Marco Alecci,Francesco Marchiori,Iyiola Emmanuel Olatunji,Tegawendé F. Bissyandé,Jacques Klein*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper conducts a large-scale black-box robustness evaluation of three commercial multimodal image-moderation APIs, finding that all can be bypassed by simple, gradient-free image transformations such as color inversion and grayscale conversion. Robustness varies across providers, datasets, and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm being particularly vulnerable, leading to the conclusion that foundation-model-based moderation APIs are not a reliable standalone security boundary and must be deployed within a layered moderation pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional task-specific moderation classifiers offer limited policy coverage and contextual understanding, while new commercial multimodal moderation APIs built on large foundation models promise broader and more capable safety filters. However, it is unclear whether this shift to foundation-model-based systems actually yields more robust image moderation.

Method: The authors conduct a large-scale black-box evaluation of three established commercial image-moderation services. They apply seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations and test them across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities to assess robustness and bypassability.

Result: (1) All three commercial services can be bypassed using inexpensive image transformations requiring no gradients, surrogate models, or knowledge of the target system. (2) Even fixed transformations like color inversion and grayscale conversion cause unsafe-to-safe decision changes while preserving human-recognizable content. (3) Robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm showing pronounced vulnerabilities.

Conclusion: Replacing conventional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not by itself provide a reliable security boundary. Such systems must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline rather than as standalone safety filters.

Abstract: While automated content-moderation systems have become essential for screening harmful content at scale, conventional task-specific classifiers often provide limited policy cov- erage and contextual understanding. Recently, commercial multimodal moderation APIs built on large foundation models have been introduced with the promise of providing broader and more capable safety filters. In this work, we analyze whether this shift also yields more robust image moderation. We conduct a large-scale black-box evaluation on three established commercial image-moderation services and compare their robustness. By evaluating seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities, we find that: (1) all three commercial services can be bypassed using inexpensive image transformations that require no gradients, surrogate models, or knowledge of the target system; (2) even fixed transformations such as color inversion and grayscale conversion induce unsafe-to-safe decision changes while preserving content that remains recognizable to humans; (3) their robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm exhibiting pronounced vulnerabilities. This yields the conclusion that replacing conventional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not, by itself, provide a reliable security boundary. Such systems must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline rather than as standalone safety filters.

</details>


### [139] [CORE: In-Context Reconstruction for Unified Tabular Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27615)
*Yunfeng Zhao,Qingfeng Chen,Yue Tan,Shiyuan Li,Yili Wang,Yixin Liu,Shirui Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes CORE, an in-context reconstruction approach for unified tabular anomaly detection that aligns heterogeneous features via a decorrelated feature alignment module and reconstructs samples using contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, eliminating the need for labeled or synthesized anomalies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing unified TAD methods rely on distance-based feature construction that obscures original feature semantics, and formulate anomaly detection as binary classification which overlooks diverse anomaly patterns and can be misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies. Aligning heterogeneous data across different datasets remains challenging.

Method: CORE consists of two key components: (1) a decorrelated feature alignment module that directly aligns heterogeneous features into a unified representation space while preserving semantic information, and (2) an in-context reconstruction module that reconstructs each sample by leveraging contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, where reconstruction errors reflect deviation from normality for unified TAD on arbitrary unseen datasets.

Result: The approach eliminates the need for labeled or synthesized anomalies by formulating unified TAD as an in-context reconstruction problem, where reconstruction errors serve as the anomaly score based on deviation from dataset-specific normal distributions.

Conclusion: The proposed CORE approach addresses the limitations of existing unified TAD methods by preserving feature semantics through decorrelated feature alignment and enabling anomaly detection without labeled or synthesized anomalies via in-context reconstruction on arbitrary unseen datasets.

Abstract: Tabular anomaly detection (TAD), which focuses on identifying abnormal samples that deviate from the majority in tabular data, has received growing attention. Recently, there has been an emerging trend towards unified TAD, which seeks to detect anomalies across different datasets using a single generalizable model. In unified TAD, aligning heterogeneous data remains challenging. While existing methods often rely on distance-based unified feature construction, they may obscure the semantics of the original features. Moreover, existing approaches typically formulate anomaly detection as a binary classification task, which may overlook diverse anomaly patterns from various datasets and be misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies. To address these challenges, we propose an in-COntext REconstruction approach for unified TAD (CORE for short). It introduces a decorrelated feature alignment module to directly align heterogeneous features into a unified representation space, which retains their semantic information. Meanwhile, CORE formulates unified TAD as an in-context reconstruction problem, eliminating the need for labeled or synthesized anomalies. Specifically, the in-context reconstruction module reconstructs each sample by leveraging contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, such that reconstruction errors reflect its deviation from normality, facilitating unified TAD on arbitrary unseen datasets.

</details>


### [140] [Hidden APIs in Language Models: Discovering Reusable Causal Interfaces from Forked Futures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27617)
*SiYuan Ma,Yiqin Luo,Zhangji,Canran Xiao,Albert Gao,Wei-Hsing Huang,Wei Wang,Qiwei Wu,Xinran Li,Jinfeng Wei,Qixin Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces "forked futures," a method for testing whether language-model hidden states support reusable causal interfaces by sampling future operations after a prefix state forms and comparing resultant response distributions. Among Shared, Local, Mixture, and Distributed interface hypotheses, Shared achieves the lowest held-out description length (gains of 0.216 nats on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B), strongest transplantation profile, and recovers 14/16 architectures in a blind test, supporting an economical reusable causal interface conditional on the tested operations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Identical language-model answers can arise from hidden states supporting different future computations, so current-answer probes cannot establish whether there exists a reusable internal interface. A new empirical method is needed to causally compare hidden states without relying on researcher-specified latent labels.

Method: The paper defines "forked futures": future operations are sampled only after a prefix state forms, and states are compared via the response distributions induced by those operations, yielding an empirical causal quotient over hidden states. Four interface hypotheses (Shared, Local, Mixture, Distributed) compete under prequential causal description length, constrained by future-signature fidelity and matched capacity. Evaluations include two detailed model tests, a five-backbone sweep, a figure-aligned transplantation analysis, mediation analysis with API-aligned versus null paths, and a blind four-class model-organism classification test.

Result: Shared interface has the lowest held-out description length, with gains of 0.216 nats on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B, while maintaining tightly clustered mean future-signature distortion. The five-backbone sweep preserves a positive direction of Sharedness Gain. Transplantation analysis gives Shared the strongest joint profile across target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite metrics. API-aligned paths mediate 0.749 of the target effect versus 0.150 for null paths. In the blind four-class test, 14/16 architectures are recovered, with one non-Shared to Shared error among 12 non-Shared organisms.

Conclusion: The results support an economical reusable causal interface within the tested operation banks. However, the claim is explicitly conditional on the candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures considered in the study.

Abstract: Identical language-model answers can arise from hidden states that support different future computations, so current-answer probes do not establish a reusable internal interface. We introduce forked futures: future operations are sampled only after a prefix state has formed, and states are compared through the response distributions induced by those operations. This yields an empirical causal quotient over hidden states without requiring researcher-specified latent labels. Shared, Local, Mixture, and Distributed interfaces then compete under prequential causal description length subject to future-signature fidelity and matched capacity constraints. In the two detailed model evaluations, Shared has the lowest held-out description length, with gains of 0.216 nats on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B, while maintaining tightly clustered mean future-signature distortion; a five-backbone sweep preserves the positive direction of Sharedness Gain. The figure-aligned transplantation analysis gives Shared the strongest joint target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite profile, and API-aligned paths mediate 0.749 of the target effect versus 0.150 for matched null paths. In the blind four-class model-organism test, 14/16 architectures are recovered, with one observed non-Shared to Shared error among 12 non-Shared organisms. These results support an economical reusable causal interface within the tested operation banks, while keeping the claim explicitly conditional on the candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures.

</details>


### [141] [SCOPE: Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27630)
*Nguyen Viet Tuan Kiet,Nguyen Huu Duc,Le Cong Bang,Tran Cong Dao,Huynh Thi Thanh Binh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCOPE is a general framework for black-box combinatorial optimization that learns synthetic conditional objectives from search history to evolve diverse search policies, with an outer loop adaptively selecting objectives and an inner loop returning a portfolio of top policies, consistently improving search performance under limited evaluation budgets across benchmark problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Black-box combinatorial optimization suffers from limited guidance from the unknown objective function when deciding where to explore next under a constrained evaluation budget.

Method: SCOPE learns synthetic objectives conditioned on accumulated search history, each exposing a distinct preference over candidates; these objectives evolve search policies generating diverse candidates, with an outer loop adaptively updating/selecting objectives and an inner loop returning a portfolio of top-performing policies to mitigate reliance on a single surrogate preference.

Result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems show SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.

Conclusion: Reframing objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration enables the search to exploit observed evidence while maintaining structured diversity across discrete solution spaces, yielding robust improvements in black-box combinatorial optimization.

Abstract: Black-box combinatorial optimization requires systematically identifying high-quality solutions under a limited evaluation budget, yet the unknown objective function provides little guidance for deciding where the search should explore next. We introduce SCOPE, a general framework for Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization. Rather than directly optimizing the inaccessible objective, SCOPE learns a set of synthetic objectives conditioned on the accumulated search history, where each objective is designed to expose a distinct and potentially useful preference over candidate solutions. These objectives are then used to evolve search policies that generate diverse candidates, whose true quality is subsequently assessed through black-box evaluations. The outer loop adaptively updates and selects synthetic objectives according to how effectively their induced policies discover promising regions. In contrast, the inner loop returns a portfolio of top-performing policies to reduce the risk of relying on a single surrogate preference. This formulation reframes objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration, enabling the search process to exploit observed evidence while maintaining structured diversity across discrete solution spaces. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems demonstrate that SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.

</details>


### [142] [ReDiPPO: Reference-Guided Value Calibration and Discrepancy-Aware Token Reweighting for Mathematical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27631)
*Zhenrong Zhang,Fei Wu,Jun Du,Jianshu Zhang,Si Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReDiPPO is a Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO framework that improves mathematical reasoning in LLMs by using reference answers as privileged training signals for more accurate token-level value estimation, and reweighting advantages based on reference-standard discrepancy to identify difficult reasoning states, outperforming PPO, DAPO, and GSPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PPO's learned critic can provide token-level credit assignment but struggles to accurately evaluate intermediate reasoning states in long-horizon mathematical reasoning tasks with sparse outcome rewards, leading to noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates.

Method: ReDiPPO introduces a reference-guided critic that leverages reference answers as training-time privileged signals for more accurate value estimation, while retaining a standard critic. The token-level discrepancy between the two critics serves as an indicator of difficult reasoning states, which is used to reweight token-level advantages during PPO optimization.

Result: Experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks show ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong baselines including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO in final reasoning performance.

Conclusion: ReDiPPO effectively addresses the challenge of reliable token-level credit assignment in PPO for mathematical reasoning by using reference-guided signals and discrepancy-aware advantage reweighting, achieving superior policy optimization performance.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for enhancing the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Among existing policy optimization methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains particularly appealing because its learned critic can, in principle, provide token-level credit assignment. However, in mathematical reasoning tasks characterized by long reasoning horizons and sparse outcome rewards, reliable token-level credit assignment remains challenging. The standard critic often fails to accurately evaluate intermediate reasoning states, resulting in noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates. In this paper, we propose ReDiPPO, a Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO framework for mathematical reasoning. ReDiPPO introduces a reference-guided critic that uses reference answers as training-time privileged signals to provide more accurate value estimation. Meanwhile, it retains a standard critic and quantifies the token-level reference-standard discrepancy between the standard value estimate and the reference-guided value estimate. This discrepancy serves as an indicator of difficult reasoning states and is used to reweight the corresponding token-level advantages during PPO optimization. Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong policy optimization baselines, including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO, in final reasoning performance. Our code is available on https://github.com/cii030/ReDiPPO.

</details>


### [143] [HealthCAT: An Interpretable Encoder-only Transformer Framework for Health Indicator Prediction and Temporal Interpretation of Wearable Sensor Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27635)
*Xiaotong Yu,Joshua Y. Kim,HaeJin Lee,Kalina Yacef*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HealthCAT is a flexible framework integrating an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token to provide class-specific, time-step-level interpretations of wearable sensor data, outperforming deep learning baselines by up to 17% in F1-score and 12% in accuracy on two real-world datasets (306 participants), with validated predictive informativeness of identified time steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep learning methods for wearable sensor data prioritize predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their application in health research where understanding when and how behavioural patterns occur is critical.

Method: HealthCAT integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations. These interpretations are mapped back onto behavioural cycles (e.g., time-of-day) for individual-level analysis. The model was evaluated on two real-world wearable sensor datasets with 306 participants total, using masking experiments to validate predictive informativeness.

Result: HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17% in F1-score and 12% in accuracy on both datasets (p<0.05). Masking experiments showed identified time steps carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all masking conditions (p<0.05).

Conclusion: HealthCAT advances wearable sensor analysis beyond aggregated metrics by coupling predictive performance with validated time-step-level interpretability, enabling accurate health indicator prediction while providing insights into when and how physical activity patterns occur, supporting health monitoring, behavioural pattern analysis, and intervention design.

Abstract: Wearable sensors continuously capture fine-grained multivariate time-series data, providing opportunities to model behavioural patterns associated with health outcomes. However, existing deep learning methods prioritise predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their application in health research. In this study, we present HealthCAT, a flexible framework that integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations. These interpretations can be mapped back onto behavioural cycles that are relevant to the domain (e.g., time-of-day), supporting individual-level analysis of wearable sensor data. We evaluated HealthCAT using two real-world wearable sensor datasets (306 participants in total). HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17\% in F1-score and 12\% in accuracy on both datasets ($p<0.05$). In masking experiments, the time steps identified by HealthCAT carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all masking conditions ($p<0.05$), indicating that the identified time steps are predictively informative. By coupling predictive performance with validated time-step-level interpretability, HealthCAT moves wearable sensor analysis beyond aggregated metrics towards temporal patterns that support health monitoring, behavioural pattern analysis, and intervention design in health research. The significance of this work is that it enables accurate prediction of health indicators from wearable sensor data while providing insights into when and how physical activity patterns occur, rather than relying solely on aggregated summary measures.

</details>


### [144] [Evaluating and Pricing Advertisements in AI-Generated Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27686)
*John L. Turner-Smith,Zimeng Huang,Yuhan Fu,Yihang Zhang,Tonghan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses the challenge of evaluating LLM-generated embedded advertisements by constructing a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework to generate supervision signals for click-through intent and ad quality. These signals are distilled into a parameter-efficient evaluator that produces smooth, differentiable estimates, which are then used to build a principled pricing mechanism and serve as a training objective for ad generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As search shifts toward LLM-driven answer engines, advertising becomes embedded in generated responses, requiring evaluation for both user utility and commercial value. However, click-through intent measurement is fundamentally challenged: behavioral logs are unavailable, human annotation resists calibration, and frontier LLM judges conflate intent with linguistic fluency. These gaps are compounding—principled pricing requires a continuous intent signal, but generating such a signal requires supervision that is currently unavailable.

Method: The authors construct missing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework, then distill it into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent and three companion dimensions of ad quality as smooth, differentiable estimates. Validation uses sign-certain behavioral perturbations. They build the pricing layer directly on these estimates, deriving the unique payment rule under which truthful bidding is optimal, demonstrating on best-of-k allocation, and extending to non-monotone allocations.

Result: The evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% versus 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalizes without error to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preference in 86% of pairwise judgements across five annotators, with agreement rising in the evaluator's confidence.

Conclusion: The differentiable intent signal enables both principled pricing—through a unique truthful-payment mechanism—and serves as a ready training objective for ad generation, closing the loop between evaluation, pricing, and generation for LLM-embedded advertising.

Abstract: As search increasingly shifts toward LLM-driven answer engines, advertising is becoming embedded within the generated response itself and should therefore be evaluated for both user utility and commercial value. The key challenge is click-through intent: behavioural logs are unavailable, human annotation resists calibration, and frontier LLM judges conflate intent with linguistic fluency. These gaps compound, as principled pricing presupposes a continuous intent signal, while generating such a signal presupposes supervision that is currently unavailable. We construct the missing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework, and distil it into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent, together with the three companion dimensions of ad quality, as smooth, differentiable estimates. Validated through sign-certain behavioural perturbations, the evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% versus 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalises without error to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preference in 86% of pairwise judgements across five annotators, with agreement rising in the evaluator's confidence. Upon its estimates we build the pricing layer directly, deriving the unique payment rule under which truthful bidding is optimal, demonstrating it on a best-of-k allocation, and extending the mechanism to non-monotone allocations. The same differentiable signal stands ready as a training objective for ad generation.

</details>


### [145] [Rehearse: Stepping Back from the Confidence Cliff in Self-Improving Autoresearch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27687)
*Jiazhen Ji,Shouhong Ding*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies the reliability of pre-execution judgment (whether a proposed code modification will work) in automated machine-learning (autoresearch) loops. The authors identify a "confidence cliff": an LLM judge's accuracy at predicting whether a modification is helpful drops substantially late in the autoreearch trajectory (from 82.8% to 56.9%) even as the judge remains willing to make decisions. They introduce "Rehearse," a lightweight skill that proposes multiple ideas, compares them before execution, runs the most promising, and judges using a focused memory of similar past attempts. Rehearse restores late selective accuracy to 83.5% and improves endpoint metrics across 4,000 budgeted training runs on three benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The efficiency of autoresearch loops (which propose, run, and keep helpful ML code changes) depends critically on the agent's ability to predict—before spending a training run—whether a proposed modification is likely to work. The authors observe that this pre-execution judgment capability degrades significantly as the loop progresses, wasting compute on unhelpful modifications and limiting the scaling of automated research.

Method: Using public AutoSOTA logs, the authors first document that the fraction of helpful modifications drops from 70% in the first two iterations to 43% by iteration 6+. They build a benchmark of 296 same-baseline modification pairs (each with one improving and one non-improving modification, outcomes hidden) from 39 paper-derived tasks, plus a 366-pair full benchmark. An LLM judge with candidate rationales but no prior-attempt history is tested for selective accuracy. The authors then propose "Rehearse": propose multiple ideas, compare them before execution, run the most promising one, and judge using a focused memory of similar past attempts and their outcomes.

Result: The LLM judge reaches 79.5% accuracy on pairs where strict consensus returns a verdict, but selective accuracy falls from 82.8% to 56.9% late in the loop—the "confidence cliff." Rehearse's focused outcome memory raises late selective accuracy to 83.5%. Across 4,000 budgeted training runs over three loops, Rehearse improves the endpoint metric under the same training-run budget on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting tasks.

Conclusion: Pre-execution judgment reliability in autoresearch degrades as successful modifications accumulate—a "confidence cliff" that wastes training compute. A lightweight loop skill (Rehearse) that adds pre-execution comparison and a focused memory of past attempts effectively mitigates this degradation, significantly improving end-to-end autoresearch performance under fixed compute budgets.

Abstract: Autoresearch improves machine-learning code by proposing changes, running full training jobs, and keeping changes that improve the metric. The efficiency of this loop depends not only on generating ideas, but also on the agent's ability to decide, before spending a training run, whether a proposed modification is likely to work. We study how the reliability of this pre-execution judgment changes over the course of an autoresearch trajectory. In public AutoSOTA logs (Li et al., 2026; Tsinghua FIB Lab, 2026), the fraction of helpful modifications falls from 70% in the first two iterations to 43% by iteration 6+. On 296 same-baseline modification pairs from 39 paper-derived AutoSOTA tasks, each containing one modification that improved the metric and one that did not, with measured outcomes hidden, an LLM judge given candidate rationales but no prior-attempt history reaches 79.5% accuracy on the pairs where strict consensus returns a verdict. On the full 366-pair benchmark, however, this ability weakens substantially late in the loop. As successful changes accumulate, selective accuracy - accuracy conditioned on a strict-consensus verdict - falls from 82.8% to 56.9%, while the judge remains willing to decide. We call this operational pattern the confidence cliff. Rehearse implements the loop change as a lightweight skill for autoresearch loops: propose several ideas, compare them before execution, run the most promising, and judge with a focused memory of similar past attempts and outcomes. This focused outcome memory raises late selective accuracy to 83.5%. Across 4,000 budgeted training runs over three loops, Rehearse improves the endpoint under the same training-run budget on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting.

</details>


### [146] [Guiding Large Language Models with Genetic Programming-Evolved Heuristic Knowledge for Dynamic Multi-Mode Project Scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27698)
*Yuan Tian,Yi Mei,Mengjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates using knowledge extracted from genetic programming (GP)-evolved heuristic rules to guide an online LLM decision maker in dynamic multi-mode project scheduling. Several knowledge-injection mechanisms (Feature Selection, Feature Hint, Rule Reference, Rule Follow) are evaluated for scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and rationale feature focus, finding that simplifying the decision context or providing explicit decision logic is more effective than mere feature highlighting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs offer a flexible interface for scheduling decisions but zero-shot LLM decisions may lack domain knowledge, consume excessive tokens, and exhibit variability across queries. GP-evolved priority rules encode high-quality scheduling knowledge but require domain expertise to design. The authors seek to reverse the typical LLM-GP integration direction, transferring knowledge from GP rules to guide LLMs rather than using LLMs to support heuristic evolution.

Method: The authors extract knowledge from high-quality GP-evolved rules and inject it into an online LLM decision maker via four mechanisms: Feature Selection (simplifying decision context), Feature Hint (highlighting important features), Rule Reference (referencing GP rules as context), and Rule Follow (supplying explicit decision logic to follow). These are evaluated across scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and the feature focus in generated rationales.

Result: GP-derived guidance generally improves upon the unguided LLM, but the representation of the guidance matters. Simplifying the decision context or supplying explicit decision logic is more effective than merely highlighting important features. Feature Selection provides the best token efficiency, Rule Follow achieves strong performance at greater token cost, and all guidance improves decision stability and alters the features expressed in generated rationales.

Conclusion: Knowledge transfer from GP-evolved rules to LLMs is a viable approach for improving LLM-based scheduling decisions. The representation of injected knowledge significantly impacts effectiveness, with context simplification and explicit logic being superior. The choice of injection mechanism involves a trade-off between performance, token efficiency, and decision stability.

Abstract: In dynamic multi-mode project scheduling, activities have alternative execution modes and uncertain durations, while precedence relations and limited resources constrain their execution. Heuristic priority rules support fast online decisions, but their design requires substantial domain expertise. Genetic programming (GP) hyper-heuristics can automatically evolve such rules. Large language models (LLMs), meanwhile, provide a flexible interface for interpreting scheduling information and explaining decisions. However, zero-shot LLM decisions may lack domain knowledge, consume many tokens, and vary across repeated queries. GP-evolved rules therefore provide a potential source of scheduling knowledge for guiding LLM decisions. Unlike existing LLM--GP hybrids that use LLMs to support heuristic evolution, we transfer knowledge in the reverse direction, using knowledge extracted from high-quality GP rules to guide an online LLM decision maker. We extract knowledge from high-quality GP rules and inject it through Feature Selection, Feature Hint, Rule Reference, and Rule Follow. These mechanisms are evaluated in terms of scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and the feature focus expressed in generated rationales. GP-derived guidance generally improves the unguided LLM, but its representation matters. Simplifying the decision context or supplying explicit decision logic is more effective than highlighting important features. Feature Selection offers the best token efficiency, whereas Rule Follow achieves strong performance at greater token cost. Guidance also improves decision stability and changes the features expressed in generated rationales.

</details>


### [147] [SpatialCLI: Learning to Reason With Spatial Tools, Then Without Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27703)
*Yang Zhou,Zixuan Huang,Sunzhu Li,Zhuo Yang,Chen Zhang,Shunian Chen,Caijun Yan,Jianyao Xu,Shunyu Liu,Weijie Fu,Peiliang Li,Xiaozhi Chen,Yuxiang Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SpatialCLI is a three-stage framework that teaches vision-language models (VLMs) to use spatial tools (specialist vision models) and progressively internalize their perceptual capabilities, raising Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% on the MindCube benchmark with tools and 73.8% without tools after internalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a fundamental capability mismatch in embodied agents: general VLMs can reason about overall tasks but miss crucial visual details, while specialist vision models capture details but cannot translate them into task-level decisions. This gap limits VLM effectiveness in embodied spatial reasoning tasks.

Method: SpatialCLI proceeds in three stages: (1) Call - exposes specialist vision models as spatial tools to augment VLM perception; (2) Learn - uses Cold-Start Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) to improve tool use; (3) Internalize - verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to internalize specialist perceptual capabilities. The authors also introduce SpatialCLI-Bench, a 516-example benchmark covering localization, segmentation, depth, and pose.

Result: On MindCube, SpatialCLI raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools, surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%), while retaining 73.8% without tools after internalization.

Conclusion: SpatialCLI effectively bridges VLMs and specialist vision models by enabling VLMs to leverage spatial tools and subsequently internalize those perceptual capabilities, achieving strong performance both with and without external tools.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in embodied agents to interpret visual inputs, reason about spatial relationships, and make task-level decisions based on that reasoning. However, a fundamental capability mismatch remains: general VLMs can reason about the overall task but often miss the visual details that determine success, while specialist vision models can capture those details but cannot translate them into task-level decisions. In this work, we propose SpatialCLI, a framework that teaches VLMs to reason with spatial tools and progressively internalize the specialist perceptual capabilities they provide. SpatialCLI proceeds in three stages: (1) Call exposes specialist vision models as spatial tools to augment the VLM's perception; (2) Learn uses Cold-Start SFT and agentic RL to improve tool use; and (3) Internalize verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to internalize specialist perceptual capabilities. We further introduce SpatialCLI-Bench, a 516-example benchmark for compositional perception across localization, segmentation, depth, and pose. On MindCube, SpatialCLI raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools, surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%), while retaining 73.8% without tools after internalization.

</details>


### [148] [Albilich: Steerable Proof-State Orchestration for LLM-Based Mathematical Research with CAS Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27705)
*Ting Gong,Michael Ruofan Zeng,Yong Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Albilich is an open-source agentic harness for mathematical autoresearch that integrates long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems, literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management. It solves 10/10 RealMath problems with CAS (9/10 without), produces a counterexample to Kourovka Problem 21.142 and a proof strengthening Problem 20.2, and demonstrates token/cost reductions and improved verifier outcomes when CAS and an advisor agent are enabled.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can contribute useful ideas to mathematics, but long-horizon proof attempts remain difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. This motivates the need for an open, structured environment that supports scalable AI-assisted mathematical research.

Method: Albilich combines long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems, literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management in an agentic harness. It is evaluated on the RealMath benchmark and on open problems from the Kourovka Notebook, with ablations analyzing the effects of CAS and an advisor agent.

Result: Albilich solved 10/10 RealMath problems with CAS and 9/10 without. On Kourovka problems, it produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem 20.2. An ablation on Problem 17.91 showed 32.0% token reduction with CAS enabled. An ablation on Problem 21.142 showed a higher verifier-rejection rate and failure to synthesize proof routes without the advisor agent.

Conclusion: Albilich serves as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research, demonstrating that structured tooling and agentic orchestration improve both performance and efficiency in long-horizon theorem proving.

Abstract: Large language models can contribute useful ideas to mathematical research, yet long-horizon proof attempts remain difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. We present Albilich, an open-source agentic harness for autoresearch in mathematics that combines long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management.
  We evaluate Albilich on the RealMath benchmark (Zhang et al. 2025) and on open problems in group theory from the Kourovka Notebook (Khukhro and Mazurov 2026). It solved 10/10 problems on RealMath with CAS and 9/10 with no CAS. On the Kourovka problems, Albilich produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem20.2. Anablation on Problem 17.91 demonstrates 32.0% token reduction when CAS is enabled. An ablation on Problem 21.142 demonstrates higher verifier-rejection rate and failure to synthesize proof routes in the absence of the advisor agent. These results support Albilich as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research.

</details>


### [149] [MECA: A Mechanism-Centered Agent for Constructing Well-Specified and Valuable Mathematical Conjectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27709)
*Wentao Long,Yunfei Zhang,Chenyi Li,Zaiwen Wen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MECA is a multi-agent framework that automatically constructs mathematical conjectures by jointly developing candidate statements and their supporting mechanisms, refining broad research directions into precise, well-specified conjectures with an identifiable unresolved core. It is evaluated against a generate-and-revise baseline for reconstructing target-paper conclusions and on 100 semi-open problems tested by automated provers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automatically constructing well-specified and valuable mathematical conjectures is a central challenge in AI-assisted mathematical discovery. Many existing open problems are too broad, underspecified, or difficult to connect to plausible proof or refutation strategies.

Method: MECA uses a multi-agent framework where Explorer agents propose mechanisms, test how they apply, and revise candidate conjectures, while critic agents assess mathematical validity and research value. The mechanism-centered approach connects assumptions to conclusions via structures like inequalities, invariants, decompositions, or reductions to intermediate claims.

Result: MECA outperforms a generate-and-revise baseline in reconstructing target-paper conclusions from target-conditioned but article-blind materials. It also produces 100 semi-open problems from literature-derived seeds and existing open problems, which remain challenging for current automated provers in independent proof/refutation attempts.

Conclusion: Mechanism-centered refinement produces well-specified, research-worthy conjectures that remain challenging for current automated provers, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly developing statements and supporting mechanisms.

Abstract: Automatically constructing well-specified and valuable mathematical conjectures remains a central challenge in AI-assisted mathematical discovery. Many existing open problems and conjectures are often too broad, underspecified, or difficult to connect to plausible proof or refutation strategies. We view a mathematical mechanism as a structure or reasoning principle that connects the assumptions of a candidate problem to its target conclusion, such as an inequality, invariant, decomposition, or reduction to an intermediate claim. We present MECA (MEchanism-centered Conjecture Agent), a multi-agent framework that constructs conjectures by jointly developing candidate statements and their supporting mechanisms. Explorer agents propose mechanisms, test how they apply, and revise the candidate conjecture accordingly, while critic agents assess their mathematical validity and research value. Their feedback guides changes to the assumptions, scope, and conclusion. Through this process, MECA transforms broad research directions into precise conjectures with substantive mathematical support while retaining a clearly identified unresolved core. We evaluate MECA in two complementary settings. First, we compare it with a generate-and-revise baseline on reconstructing preselected target-paper conclusions from target-conditioned but article-blind source materials. Second, we construct 100 semi-open problems from literature-derived seeds and existing open problems and evaluate them through independent proof and refutation attempts by automated provers. Our results indicate that mechanism-centered refinement produces well-specified and research-worthy conjectures that remain challenging for current automated provers.

</details>


### [150] [New Synchronous Computation Dynamics for Hopfield Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27720)
*Francisco Requena-Domínguez,Rafaela Benítez-Rochel,Ezequiel López-Rubio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new synchronous dynamics for Hopfield networks, called SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based on Discrete Differential Filter), which updates multiple neurons simultaneously per time step to maximize energy decrease and guarantee convergence, thereby reducing processing time compared to the original asynchronous Hopfield dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The original Hopfield network uses asynchronous (sequential) dynamics, updating only one neuron per time step, which leads to slow processing. The authors aim to reduce processing time by enabling simultaneous updates of multiple neurons while maintaining convergence guarantees.

Method: The authors introduce the Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) as a new tool to solve the combinatorial optimization problem of finding the next network state with maximum energy decrease under synchronous dynamics. Based on DDF, they develop a new synchronous dynamics called SD-DDF that updates one or more neurons simultaneously per step while ensuring guaranteed convergence and maximal energy decrease.

Result: The paper provides a theoretical justification for the SD-DDF dynamics and validates its performance through four computational experiments that empirically assess the speed-up in processing time compared to the original asynchronous Hopfield network dynamics.

Conclusion: The SD-DDF synchronous dynamics offers a faster alternative to the asynchronous Hopfield network by enabling simultaneous multi-neuron updates with guaranteed convergence and maximum energy decrease per step, leading to reduced total processing time.

Abstract: The dynamics of the original Hopfield network is asynchronous (sequential) (updates the state of only one neuron per time step). In this paper, we propose a new tool and a new dynamics to reduce the processing time by updating one or more neurons simultaneously per instant while ensuring process convergence and aiming for the maximum energy decrease at each step, thus guaranteeing the shortest total processing time. From the point of view of synchronous dynamics, calculating the next network state at which energy decreases the most from the current state while ensuring convergence is itself a combinatorial optimization problem. We develop and use a new tool to solve it. We call this new tool Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) and, based upon it, we develop a new synchronous dynamics which we call SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based upon Discrete Differential Filter). In this paper, we review the original asynchronous dynamics for Hopfield networks and present a new tool and a new synchronous dynamics with its theoretical justification and four computational experiments to assess the speed up in processing time empirically.

</details>


### [151] [Baikal: Structured Search for Deep Research over Data Lakes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27726)
*Dhruv Agarwal,Rishitha Guttapalle Mohan,Aarti Kumari,Ashi Sinha,Athulya Anil,Kavitha Srinivas,Horst Samulowitz,Andrew McCallum*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Baikal is a framework for deep research over data lakes that casts the problem as budgeted search. It clusters heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions and searches adaptively using policies (random, LLM-guided, Bayesian ε-greedy, UCB), improving research quality scores by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA over strong baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based deep research methods over data lakes use iterative retrieval and generation where accumulated context determines what to investigate next, leading to over-exploitation of locally promising evidence and poor coverage of distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget.

Method: Baikal casts deep research as a budgeted search problem. It clusters heterogeneous evidence (tables and passages) into semantic regions, then adaptively searches over these regions to balance exploration and exploitation. Within each selected region, it generates and investigates region-grounded subquestions, using finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates and guide search under policies including random, LLM-guided selection, Bayesian ε-greedy, and UCB.

Result: Evaluated on 15 queries each over HybridQA (10,993 tables) and TAT-QA (2,757 tables) data lakes with 227K Wikipedia and 13K financial passages. Assessed via a new rubric (groundedness, relevance, diversity, utility) scored by GPT-5-mini. Baikal's best configuration outperforms strongest baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA, with gains attributed to organized exploration of semantic regions improving groundedness, diversity, and usefulness under the same subquestion budget.

Conclusion: Structured semantic exploration over heterogeneous data lakes demonstrates significant value for systematic research and discovery, showing that organizing evidence into semantic regions and adaptively balancing exploration with exploitation markedly improves the quality of LLM-agent-driven deep research.

Abstract: Deep research over data lakes requires an LLM agent to investigate evidence across thousands of heterogeneous tables and passages to synthesize a report. Existing methods perform iterative retrieval and generation, letting accumulated context determine what to investigate next, which can overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget. To address this, we cast deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem and present Baikal - a framework that clusters heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions, then searches over them adaptively to balance exploration and exploitation. Within each selected region, Baikal generates and investigates region-grounded subquestions, using finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates and guide search under policies ranging from random and LLM-guided selection to Bayesian $ε$-greedy and UCB. We evaluate Baikal on 15 queries each over HybridQA and TAT-QA data lakes containing 10,993 and 2,757 tables, respectively, together with 227K Wikipedia passages and 13K financial report passages. We assess research quality with a new rubric covering groundedness, relevance, diversity, and utility, and use GPT-5-mini to score Baikal and strong baselines, including DeepSearcher and an OpenCode research agent with retrieval and clustering variants. Across both data lakes, Baikal performs strongly under several region-selection policies; its best configuration improves report scores over the strongest baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Our analyses attribute these gains to organizing and exploring semantic evidence regions, which improves groundedness and diversity and yields more useful findings under the same subquestion budget. These results demonstrate the value of structured semantic exploration for systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes.

</details>


### [152] [VeriSkill: A Self-Evolution Framework for Program Verification Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27733)
*Changguo Jia,Tianqi Zhao,Zhiyou Xiao,Weiming Zhang,Minghui Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriSkill is a self-evolution framework for program verification using LLM agents that translates verification failures into skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines skills while ensuring verification improvement and semantic preservation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-agent-based program verification depends on reusable skills for generating specifications, annotations, lemmas, and tool invocations. Existing skill self-evolution methods fail for verification because they cannot reliably attribute failures to specific skills or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback.

Method: VeriSkill attributes verification failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, iteratively refines candidate skills, and only admits revisions that both improve verification performance and preserve program semantics.

Result: VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.

Conclusion: A self-evolution framework tailored for program verification can overcome the limitations of generic skill evolution by providing reliable failure attribution and actionable feedback extraction from verifier outputs, yielding robust performance gains across diverse tooling and model configurations.

Abstract: Automating program verification with LLM agents requires generating specifications, annotations, auxiliary lemmas, and tool invocations, all of which depend on reusable skills. A natural remedy is skill self-evolution: distilling skills from trajectories and refining them through feedback. However, existing evolution methods struggle with program verification tasks because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback. In this paper, we propose VeriSkill, a self-evolution framework built for program verification. It attributes verification failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills, admitting only revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics. Experiments show that VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.

</details>


### [153] [SpecCal: Ambiguity-Aware Candidate Calibration for Infrared Spectrum-Based Molecular Structure Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27788)
*Yixuan Chen,Bo Liu,Yusen Tan,Guokun Yang,Wenjie Du,Jun Xia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SpecCal is a training-free, model-agnostic candidate calibration framework that improves IR-spectrum-to-molecule reconstruction by re-ranking base model candidates and introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IR-to-molecule prediction is fundamentally ambiguous because different molecules can produce highly similar spectra. Existing models generate ranked candidate sets that reflect the model's learned generation preference but may miss structures that best satisfy the observed spectral constraints, leaving reconstruction suboptimal.

Method: SpecCal operates as a plug-and-play, post-processing framework on the candidate outputs of existing base models. It improves the prediction set by (1) re-ranking current candidates and (2) introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives, both guided by spectral consistency, without requiring any parameter updates.

Result: Experiments across multiple benchmarks show SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models. Further analyses confirm that calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity is a practical way to improve molecular reconstruction from IR spectra.

Conclusion: Candidate calibration under spectral ambiguity provides a practical, training-free, and model-agnostic means of improving molecular reconstruction from IR spectra, with code made publicly available.

Abstract: Inferring molecular structures from infrared (IR) spectra is a fundamental yet challenging problem. A key difficulty is that an IR spectrum provides limited structural information: different molecules may share similar functional groups and local vibrational patterns, leading to highly similar spectral responses. Thus, even when an observed spectrum has a unique underlying structure, reconstructing it from the spectrum remains ambiguous. Existing IR-to-molecule models usually generate a ranked set of candidate molecules, but this set is largely determined by the model's learned generation preference and may not fully capture the structures that best satisfy the observed spectral constraints. To address this limitation, we propose SpecCal, a training-free candidate calibration framework for IR-to-molecule prediction. SpecCal operates on the candidate outputs of existing base models and improves the prediction set by re-ranking current candidates while introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency. The framework is plug-and-play and model-agnostic, requiring no parameter updates for integration with diverse base models. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models. Further analyses demonstrate that calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity provides a practical way to improve molecular reconstruction from IR spectra. The code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SpecCal-B18A.

</details>


### [154] [Annotating Topical Legal Insights from Case Proceedings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27792)
*Subinay Adhikary,Dwaipayan Roy,Debasis Ganguly,Shouvik Kumar Guha,Kripabandhu Ghosh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents LeDA, a web-based legal data annotation system for identifying and annotating concepts/topics in legal case proceedings. Its novel feature is dynamic tag creation, allowing annotators to discover and create new concept tags on-the-fly when no pre-defined ontology exists. The system was used by 3 assessors to annotate legal concepts from Indian Supreme Court cases, producing bag-of-concepts semantic representations for downstream tasks like prior case retrieval and judgment prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Structured representation of legal documents (as opposed to flat bag-of-words text) can significantly enhance processing capabilities. The authors aim to find concepts/topics from legal case proceedings to build such structured representations, but require an annotation system capable of handling domains where no pre-defined ontology exists.

Method: LeDA is a web-based annotation system that supports annotating and adjudicating entities/concepts within legal documents. Its key novel feature is dynamic creation of new semantic tags during annotation, enabling annotators to discover concepts organically rather than relying on a fixed pre-defined ontology. The system was deployed for 3 assessors to annotate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.

Result: The system is in active use for annotating concepts from legal documents, producing bags-of-concepts semantic representations. The annotation by 3 assessors of Indian Supreme Court case proceedings is described, demonstrating the system's practical utility in domains without pre-existing concept ontologies.

Conclusion: LeDA provides a generic and flexible annotation platform for legal documents, with dynamic tag creation being especially valuable for emerging or under-specified domains. The resulting bag-of-concepts representations can support downstream legal NLP tasks such as prior case retrieval and judgment prediction.

Abstract: In this paper, we mainly concentrate on finding concepts or topics from the legal case proceedings, since adopting a structured representation for legal documents, as opposed to a mere bag-of-words flat text representation, can significantly enhance processing capabilities. To achieve this objective, we put forward a set of diverse concepts for legal case proceedings. With this motivation, we propose LeDA, a system for Legal Data Annotation. The system offers the generic functionality of annotating and adjudicating entities or concepts within documents via a web-based interface. A novel feature of our system is that it allows to dynamic create new tags for annotation, which is a particularly useful provision for situations where there exists no pre-defined ontology for the entities (concepts) that need to be annotated - these being rather discovered by annotators as they continue examining more documents.
