The system that we demonstrate is currently in use to annotate a set of concepts from legal documents to construct semantic representations of documents as bags of concepts that can then be used for several downstream tasks, such as prior case retrieval, judgment prediction, and so on. Along with the system features in general, we also describe how LeDA was used by 3 assessors to annotate and adjudicate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.

</details>


### [155] [MemeBench: What LVLMs Miss When Interpreting Culture-Dependent Memes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27798)
*Weihang Wang,Kainan Tu,Jielei Zhang,Run Yang,Boheng Sheng,Yuchen He,Yu Xie,Pengyu Chen,Peiyi Li,Huyang Sun,Longwen Gao,Zhouhui Lian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemeBench is a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes with VIKR annotations (Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, Reasoning mechanisms) that decomposes meme interpretation errors. Across 26 LVLMs, all models handle visible content better than background knowledge (22.6% gap even for the best model). The proposed KAR (entity-guided retrieval baseline on CultureBase) improves VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% across four controlled models, though all retrieval methods reduce Visual coverage while improving Identity and Knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large vision-language models can describe visual content accurately but fail to interpret memes because meaning depends on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions beyond pixels. Existing meme benchmarks reduce interpretation to labels or holistic scores, obscuring where explanation breaks down, making it impossible to diagnose specific failure modes.

Method: Introduces MemeBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes (centered on anime, comics, games, and adjacent subcultures) with human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations. VIKR decomposes explanations into four components: Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, and Reasoning mechanisms. Also introduces KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase knowledge base.

Result: Across 26 LVLMs, all models cover visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed to interpret memes; even the strongest model retains a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. KAR raises VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% across four controlled models, repairing more answers and breaking fewer compared with generic retrieval. However, both retrieval conditions improve Identity and Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage in every comparison.

Conclusion: MemeBench reveals whether an interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills the diagnosed gap, providing a diagnostic tool rather than a mere performance score.

Abstract: Large vision-language models have improved at describing visual content, but accurate descriptions do not ensure interpretation when meaning depends on knowledge beyond the pixels. Memes expose this gap because they rely on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions. Most meme benchmarks reduce interpretation to labels or holistic scores, obscuring where an explanation breaks down. We introduce MemeBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes with human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations, centered on anime, comics, games, and adjacent online subcultures. Its VIKR schema decomposes explanations into Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, and Reasoning mechanisms. Across 26 LVLMs, every model covers visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed to interpret it, and even the strongest retains a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. To test whether this diagnosis can guide improvement, we introduce KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase. Across four controlled models, KAR raises VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% and, compared with generic retrieval, repairs more answers and breaks fewer. Yet both retrieval conditions improve Identity and Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage in every comparison. MemeBench reveals whether an interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills the diagnosed gap.

</details>


### [156] [STEREODISCO: Discovering Stereotypicality in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27824)
*Farane Jalali Farahani,Corina Dima,Mojtaba Nayyeri,Raphael H. Heiberger,Steffen Staab*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: STEREODISCO is a framework that adapts the semantic differential method to systematically discover stereotypical semantic axes in LLM internal representations. It constructs ~2,000 candidate axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers them as geometric axes in activation space, and identifies stereotypical axes via statistical testing. Applied to LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT, it finds LLMs agree more with each other than with humans on social group ratings, and discovers novel stereotypical axes (e.g., humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, cowardly vs. brave) confirmed by human annotators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior computational research on stereotypes in LLMs focuses on a small set of semantic axes from social psychology and operates on word embeddings, leaving unknown which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations and how LLMs internally represent these axes.

Method: STEREODISCO adapts the semantic differential method to LLM internal representations. It builds ~2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via linear probing, and identifies stereotypical axes through a statistical test on concept projections.

Result: The two LLMs (LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT) agree more with each other than with humans on social group stereotype ratings. The framework discovers novel stereotypical axes—humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave—not previously studied, which human annotators independently confirmed.

Conclusion: LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from human-documented stereotype content in social psychology, and the semantic differential approach can systematically uncover previously unexplored stereotypical axes in LLM internal representations.

Abstract: LLMs encode, convey, and perpetuate stereotypes. Prior computational research focuses on a small set of semantic axes investigated in social psychology, and operates on word embeddings produced by language models, leaving open which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs and how LLMs internally represent such axes. We introduce STEREODISCO, a framework that adapts the semantic differential method (Osgood et al., 1957) to the systematic study of stereotypes in LLM internal representations. STEREODISCO constructs approx. 2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via probing, and identifies stereotypical axes via a statistical test over concept projections. As a case study, we apply STEREODISCO to social group stereotypes with LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT. We find that the two LLMs agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans, suggesting that LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from that documented in social psychology. We also discover stereotypical axes not investigated in prior work -- including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which human annotators independently confirm.

</details>


### [157] [Sign Language Question Answering: A New Task, Benchmark, and Baseline for Sign Language Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27826)
*Shiwei Gan,Lichen Wang,Xiao Liu,Yafeng Yin,Kuizhuang Liu,Sanglu Lu,Lei Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA), a new task for evaluating sign language understanding by requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. The authors construct two SignQA benchmarks based on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily with five question categories, and propose a baseline model with Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling and in-domain knowledge transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SL understanding tasks (continuous SL recognition and SL translation) have predefined objectives and only assess a fixed mapping from sign videos to glosses or sentences, providing limited evaluation of whether models truly understand the semantic content of SL videos.

Method: (1) Propose SLQA, a new task requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. (2) Construct two SignQA benchmarks from PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily using template-based automatic question-answer generation, covering five categories: position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, and translation understanding. (3) Propose a baseline with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy.

Result: The proposed baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all question categories, establishing a strong benchmark for SLQA.

Conclusion: SLQA provides a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework for sign language understanding, assessing multiple reasoning capabilities beyond recognition and translation, and the released datasets enable future research on this task.

Abstract: Recent advances in sign language (SL) understanding (SLU) have led to remarkable progress in tasks such as continuous SL recognition and SL translation. However, these tasks are designed with predefined objectives, requiring models to learn a fixed mapping from sign videos to glosses or spoken-language sentences. As a result, they provide only a limited assessment of whether a model truly understands the semantic content of SL videos. To address this limitation, \textbf{we first propose a new task, Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA)}, which evaluates SL understanding by requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. Unlike previous SLU tasks, SLQA provides a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses multiple reasoning capabilities beyond recognition and translation. To facilitate this task, \textbf{we further construct two SignQA benchmarks} based on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily by automatically generating question-answer pairs from existing gloss and sentence annotations using carefully designed templates. The resulting datasets cover five complementary question categories, including position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, and translation understanding. \textbf{Finally, we propose a simple yet effective baseline model} equipped with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy, enabling effective knowledge transfer from existing SLU tasks while enhancing question-aware temporal feature modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all question categories, establishing a strong benchmark for future research on SLQA. Datasets are available at:{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hulala/SignQA-2026}.

</details>


### [158] [MemTxn: A Transaction Boundary for Source-Supported Updates and Complete-State Recovery in Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27834)
*Hanshuai Cui,Zhiqing Tang,Zhi Yao,Fanshuai Meng,Qianli Ma,Weijia Jia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemTxn is a governance layer for persistent memory in LLM agents that provides transaction boundaries for memory updates, enabling reliable verification of writes, conflict resolution, and fault recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent memory allows long-running LLM agents to reuse information, but errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems improve storage and retrieval but lack a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery.

Method: MemTxn operates as a governance layer outside the answer model. It verifies whether a memory update is supported by its source, selects the visible version when facts conflict using a Temporal Resolver, and restores application-visible state after a fault via a durable snapshot journal. It uses Ordered PatchTest to validate writes.

Result: On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo states, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, it achieves the highest average F1 across all twelve answer-model configurations, outperforming Dense by 17.06-24.07 points in five representative settings.

Conclusion: MemTxn demonstrates that a transaction-based governance layer for persistent memory can provide reliable, auditable, and recoverable memory updates for LLM agents, significantly outperforming existing approaches.

Abstract: Persistent memory lets long-running large language model agents reuse information across sessions and tasks. Yet errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems improve storage and retrieval, but they do not provide a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery. We therefore propose MemTxn, a governance layer outside the answer model. MemTxn verifies whether an update is supported by its source. It also selects the visible version when facts conflict and restores the application-visible state after a fault. The system uses Ordered PatchTest to validate writes, a Temporal Resolver to select versions, and a durable snapshot journal to recover state. On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo states, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the actual physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, MemTxn achieves the highest average F1 across all twelve answer-model configurations. It outperforms Dense by 17.06--24.07 points in five representative settings.

</details>


### [159] [Crossing the Margin Cliff: Toward Relearn-Robust LLM Unlearning via Margin Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27836)
*Xiangyu Yin,Jiaxu Liu,Zhen Chen,Chih-Hong Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Large language model (LLM) unlearning is shown to be fragile against relearn attacks—fine-tuning on just twenty forget examples restores forget-set ROUGE across all evaluated methods. The authors trace this to a "margin cliff": per-token answer margins of post-hoc unlearning methods converge into a narrow band above the retain reference in 41 of 42 method-size cells. They prove this cliff follows from a retain-coupling condition induced by token-saturating losses, and propose Margin Calibration (MC), a plug-in polish that adds a non-saturating margin hinge plus a KL probe, restoring forget-side pressure. MC wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and relearn cells across multiple benchmarks, lowering post-attack ROUGE-L from 0.41 to 0.18, with reduced retain-side utility as the main cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM unlearning methods are consistently vulnerable to relearn attacks, where fine-tuning on a small number of forget examples recovers leaked information. This fragility is a critical security concern, and the authors aim to understand its root cause and design a remedy that robustly withstands such attacks.

Method: The authors first diagnose the fragility through optimization geometry, showing that per-token answer margins of fourteen post-hoc unlearning methods converge into a narrow band above the retain reference (the margin cliff). They provide a theoretical proof that this cliff follows whenever the retain coupling holds the diagnostic log-odds of forget content above a floor, which token-saturating losses induce at stationarity. They then propose Margin Calibration (MC), a plug-in polish that adds a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference's per-token margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus. Under a gradient-dominance condition (verified via on-trajectory gradient signatures), MC's stationary set lies on the cliff-crossing side, yielding an attack-budget upper bound on the relearn margin lift.

Result: Across TOFU (three Llama-3 sizes, three forget tiers), MUSE-News on Llama-2-7B-hf, and a Phi-3.5 panel, a single frozen MC configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells. Panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L drops from 0.41 to 0.18, and raw membership AUC is lowered on 13/14 settings. The main cost is reduced retain-side utility. A deployment variant achieves the same gains without requiring a retain-trained reference.

Conclusion: The margin cliff is a systematic regularity underlying the fragility of LLM unlearning under relearn attacks, induced by token-saturating losses under retain coupling. Margin Calibration provides a principled, configurable, and broadly effective remedy that consistently outperforms existing methods across benchmarks and model sizes, at the cost of some retain-side utility, with a deployment-friendly variant available.

Abstract: Large language model unlearning is consistently fragile under relearn attacks. On TOFU, fine-tuning on twenty forget examples substantially recovers held-out forget-set ROUGE for every method we evaluate, and we trace this fragility to optimization geometry. The per-token answer margin of fourteen post-hoc methods spanning gradient, preference, and distillation families converges into a narrow band above the retain reference in 41 of 42 method--size cells, a regularity we call the margin cliff. We prove that this cliff follows whenever the retain coupling holds the diagnostic log-odds of forget content above a floor, a condition that token-saturating losses induce at stationarity and that we verify directly on 34 of 42 cells. Margin Calibration (\textsc{MC}) is a plug-in polish adding a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference's per-token margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus, restoring forget-side pressure where the native loss saturates. Under a stated gradient-dominance condition, whose on-trajectory gradient signature we measure by instrumenting the polish, its stationary set lies on the cliff-crossing side, yielding an attack-budget upper bound on the relearn margin lift. Across TOFU (three Llama-3 sizes, three forget tiers), MUSE-News on Llama-2-7B-hf, and a Phi-3.5 panel, a single frozen configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells (panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L $0.41$ to $0.18$) and lowers raw membership AUC on 13/14, with reduced retain-side utility as the main cost. A deployment variant matches these gains without a retain-trained reference.

</details>


### [160] [Virtual Process Dossier: A Process-Aware Data Catalogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27840)
*Lukas Kubelka,Alexander Bott,Frank Döhner,Saksham Kiroriwal,Georg Zeeb,Julia Butte,Julius Pfrommer,Jürgen Beyerer,Tobias Käfer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that captures both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance for multi-stage manufacturing, enabling FAIR dataset management and AI-based downstream optimization through an ontology, a provenance framework, and a user interface.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Downstream AI-based optimization tasks in multi-stage manufacturing require the ability to distinguish between datasets generated during individual workflow steps, necessitating a data catalogue that explicitly captures workflow provenance in a FAIR manner.

Method: VPD comprises three contributions: (1) a VPD ontology serving as the semantic core of the catalogue; (2) a provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation into the production environment; and (3) a user interface for human-centered interaction with the VPD Knowledge Graph.

Result: VPD provides a FAIR data catalogue for multi-stage manufacturing that makes both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance explicit, with ontology and code publicly available on GitHub.

Conclusion: The VPD demonstrates a Knowledge Graph-based approach to workflow provenance-aware data cataloguing in manufacturing, supporting AI-based optimization tasks while ensuring FAIR data principles.

Abstract: We propose the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that also captures workflow provenance. We developed VPD for multi-stage manufacturing use-cases where downstream AI-based optimization tasks require to distinct between datasets generated during individual workflow steps. VPD provides these datasets in a FAIR manner and makes both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance explicit. Our contributions are: (1) the VPD ontology that serves as the catalogue's semantic core; (2) the VPD provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation into the production environment; and (3) the VPD user interface that provides human-centered interaction with the VPD Knowledge Graph. The ontology and code are available at https://github.com/kubeluk/VirtualProcessDossier .

</details>


### [161] [Simplifying Neural Networks During Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27854)
*Lorenzo Sciandra,Samuele Fonio,Roberto Esposito*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a training framework inspired by Neural Collapse (NC) to simplify overparameterized deep networks during training. It monitors representation dynamics via the Inverse Fisher Criterion to identify the optimal split point between feature extraction and classification, then replaces trailing layers with a lightweight head to reduce parameters while maintaining accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overparameterized deep neural networks remain poorly understood in terms of training dynamics. Recent findings on Neural Collapse show structured geometry in class representations and classifiers, while the Tunnel Effect suggests only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction. The authors aim to combine these insights to simplify deep networks during training, reducing parameters without significant accuracy loss.

Method: The proposed framework uses the Inverse Fisher Criterion, a stable and efficient proxy for variability collapse behavior, to monitor representation dynamics during training. This identifies (1) the split point between feature extraction and classification layers and (2) the training stage at which simplification becomes viable. The trailing layers are then replaced with a lightweight classification head, and training continues on the reduced model.

Result: Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures demonstrate substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to the full model.

Conclusion: The NC-inspired training framework effectively simplifies deep networks during training by leveraging Neural Collapse dynamics, achieving significant parameter reduction with minimal accuracy degradation across multiple architectures.

Abstract: Understanding and exploiting the training dynamics of overparameterized deep neural networks remains a central challenge in modern machine learning. Recent evidence on Neural Collapse (NC) shows that class representations and classifiers exhibit highly structured geometry, while the Tunnel Effect suggests that only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction. We combine these two perspectives and propose an NC-inspired training framework for simplifying deep networks during training. Our method monitors representation dynamics through the Inverse Fisher Criterion, a stable and efficient proxy for the variability collapse behavior, to identify both the split point between feature extraction and classification and the training stage at which simplification becomes viable. We then replace the trailing layers with a lightweight classification head and continue training the reduced model. Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures show that the proposed method achieves substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to that of the full model. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at: https://github.com/LorenzoSciandra/NNS.

</details>


### [162] [Back to All-Entity Ranking: Sampler-Dependent Evaluation in Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27861)
*Minwoo Yu,Young-guk Ha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Next-destination prediction in CTDGs is evaluated by ranking an observed interaction against sampled negative destinations. The authors show that both the negative sampling distribution and candidate-set size distort Bayes-optimal rankings, model rankings, and measured module effects. They recommend all-entity ranking (evaluating every destination in a fixed catalog) as the primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with enumerable, fixed destination catalogs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sampled-negative evaluation introduces a hidden dependency on the negative distribution and candidate-set size that researchers choose arbitrarily, which can change model-superiority conclusions and ablation results. The authors aim to expose this mechanism and propose a sampling-free alternative to make benchmark conclusions robust and reproducible.

Method: The authors analyze how time-varying source-destination history membership transmits sampler influence to evaluation scores. They conduct a factorial evaluation of repeated vs. new positives against seen vs. unseen negatives, use a minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership, and perform controlled representation interventions. Experiments span six models across LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, and Wikipedia, comparing Uniform-20 vs. full-catalog rankings and varying candidate-set size and training objective.

Result: At least one model pair changes relative order between the expected Uniform-20 metric and the full catalog on three of four datasets. The measured effect of the same module changes in magnitude and direction depending on candidate-set size and training objective. Non-uniform negative distributions alter Bayes-optimal ranking, and even uniformly drawn finite candidate sets destabilize model rankings and measured module effects.

Conclusion: Model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the stated candidate configuration and cannot be treated as intrinsic model properties. All-entity ranking eliminates negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining the original scorer, and is recommended as the primary evaluation protocol for CTDG benchmarks with an enumerable, fixed destination catalog.

Abstract: Next-destination prediction in continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs) commonly ranks an observed interaction against sampled negative destinations. The resulting score is conditional on both the negative distribution and the number of candidates chosen by the researcher. We show that a non-uniform negative distribution changes the Bayes-optimal ranking, while even a finite candidate set drawn uniformly can destabilize model rankings and measured module effects.
  Time-varying source-destination history membership and model operations that use this information directly transmit the sampler's influence to the evaluation score. We examine this mechanism using a factorial evaluation of repeated and new positives against seen and unseen negatives, a minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership, and controlled representation interventions. Across six models on LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, and Wikipedia, at least one model pair changes relative order between the expected Uniform-20 metric and the full catalog on three of the four datasets. The measured effect of the same module also changes in magnitude and direction with the candidate-set size and training objective.
  These results establish that model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the stated candidate configuration. All-entity ranking evaluates every destination in a fixed catalog, eliminating negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining the original CTDG scorer. We therefore recommend all-entity ranking as the primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with an enumerable, fixed destination catalog.

</details>


### [163] [Orca: Neural Operators for Causal Reasoning in Continuous Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27867)
*Gerrit Großmann,David A. Selby,Sebastian J. Vollmer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Orca, a framework that extends structural causal models to continuous-time settings using neural operator learning. Each causal graph node is a time-varying function, and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces, enabling counterfactual reasoning for systems with irregular observations and feedback loops.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard structural causal models describe static variables and forbid cyclic dependencies, but many real-world systems (patients, climates, economies) evolve continuously, are observed irregularly, and contain feedback loops. Existing causal frameworks cannot naturally handle these settings.

Method: Orca extends neural operator architectures to express causal mechanisms. Each node in the causal graph is a function of time, and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces that takes multiple parent functions as input, respects the arrow of time (causality), and treats latent exogenous noise as a reusable function for counterfactual inference.

Result: The framework is formalized and counterfactual reasoning is demonstrated on synthetic continuous-time examples.

Conclusion: Neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in continuous-time, irregularly-observed, feedback-loop-containing systems, and Orca extends this to support counterfactual reasoning.

Abstract: Structural causal models are the standard language for reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, but they describe static variables, typically measured once, and usually forbid cyclic dependencies. Many systems we care about, such as patients, climates, and economies, instead evolve continuously in time, are observed at irregular time points, and contain feedback loops. We argue that neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in this setting, and propose Orca, a framework in which each node of the causal graph is a function of time and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces. We extend existing neural operator architectures to express causal mechanisms: a mechanism computes the function value of a node from its parent nodes by taking several parent functions as input, respects the arrow of time, and treats latent exogenous noise as a function that can be inferred and reused for counterfactuals. We formalize the model class and demonstrate counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples. Code is available at https://github.com/gerritgr/orca

</details>


### [164] [Search as Computation Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27871)
*Alexander Tuisov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper formalizes "terminal computation-allocation problems," where algorithms spend computational resources (e.g., bandit pulls, tree simulations, node expansions) to gather observations that update beliefs about a latent environment, but are evaluated solely by the quality of their terminal decision. The authors derive Bellman equations characterizing optimal allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification; relate value of computation (VOC) to information theory (showing mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, and is a knowledge-gradient quantity under simple regret); and demonstrate that maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many practical algorithms (search, bandits, tree search) allocate internal computation before producing a final decision, yet existing theory often evaluates them only by terminal output quality without a unifying framework. The paper aims to provide a formal, decision-theoretic treatment of how computational resources should be optimally allocated when only the final decision matters, and to connect computation value to established information-theoretic notions.

Method: The authors formalize terminal computation-allocation problems through a belief-state MDP/Bellman framework, deriving optimal allocation policies under three regimes: fixed computation budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. They establish analytical relationships between value of computation (VOC) and information measures—proving mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss and that VOC under simple regret is a knowledge-gradient quantity. They unify bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions as instances of the same model with different computation topologies, and derive an approximate VOC maximization procedure that reduces to weighted A* (with A* and greedy best-first search as limits) under a frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model.

Result: The paper proves that mutual information is exactly the myopic VOC under log loss, and that information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly relative to VOC (though it provides a one-sided upper bound). Under simple regret, VOC takes the form of a knowledge-gradient quantity. The framework subsumes bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions within a single model. Maximizing approximate VOC under a frontier-resolution/heuristic-error model recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases.

Conclusion: The theory identifies a shared underlying decision problem across diverse computation-allocation settings (search, bandits, simulations) without claiming any single acquisition rule is universally optimal. This provides a principled framework for comparing and justifying computation-allocation strategies, and clarifies the precise (and sometimes surprising) relationship between information gain and value of computation.

Abstract: Many algorithms spend an internal resource before returning a decision and are evaluated only by the quality of that terminal output. We formalize such procedures as terminal computation-allocation problems: costly computations produce observations, update beliefs about a latent environment, and matter only through terminal decision loss. Bellman equations characterize optimal allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. We then relate value of computation (VOC) to information. Mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, whereas under simple regret VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity; moreover, information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly, although it gives a one-sided upper bound on VOC. Bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions illustrate the same model under different computation topologies. Finally, under an explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model, maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases. The theory identifies a shared decision problem without asserting that one acquisition rule is universally optimal.

</details>


### [165] [An Empirical Study of Coordination Mode as the First-Class Citizen in From-Scratch Multi-Agent Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27877)
*Yanyu Ren,Yunfeng Bai,Xizheng Wang,Li Chen,Dan Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MSEval is a new benchmark for evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world, full-stack projects, addressing gaps in prior synthetic benchmarks. It includes an execution engine (LegoGent) testing 10 collaboration topologies with native CI/CD deployment and an automated grader (TAgent) measuring functional success, latency, and token cost. Key finding: organizational topology impacts performance nearly as much as model capability, shifting scores by over 30 points and doubling wall-clock time across 100 runs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-agent coding benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore real time/monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward superficial completion rather than genuine software delivery.

Method: MSEval evaluates multi-agent coding on 10 authentic full-stack projects across 10 domains, using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics for scoring. The LegoGent execution engine tests 10 collaboration topologies with periodic sync intervals and native CI/CD pipelines, while the TAgent grader dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost.

Result: Across 100 runs, organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed-cost-quality trade-off. Varying topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time for identical tasks and models. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, while heavy managerial oversight degrades performance.

Conclusion: MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software, and the benchmark is publicly released.

Abstract: Multi-agent vibe coding promises to accelerate software development, yet existing benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion. We introduce multi-agent from-scratch evaluation benchmark, MSEval, evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world tasks. Grounded in 10 authentic, full-stack projects across 10 domains, MSEval scores performance using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics.
  Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate via periodic sync intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. Concurrently, the automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Across 100 runs, MSEval reveals that organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed--cost--quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying the topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, whereas heavy managerial oversight degrades performance. Ultimately, MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software. The benchmark is released at https://github.com/robinren03/MSEval.

</details>


### [166] [Not All Tokens Deserve Equal Credit: Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation for Long-CoT Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27888)
*Qiangqiang He,Zhongheng Wu,ZiJian Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the reliability of privileged self-teacher signals in on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) for long-CoT reasoning, finding that likelihood shifts from self-teaching are largely driven by counterfactual sensitivity on substitutable surface-form tokens rather than answer-aligned directionality. The authors propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a GRPO extension that downweights highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages, achieving consistent gains on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Critic-free RLVR methods like GRPO broadcast response-level rewards uniformly across tokens, ignoring unequal token contributions. OPSD attempts to provide denser supervision via privileged self-teacher distillation, but implicitly assumes the resulting likelihood shifts are answer-aligned. The paper tests this premise and finds it unreliable, motivating a better credit assignment mechanism.

Method: The authors test OPSD's premise by fixing trajectories and re-scoring them under two opposing outcome conditions (correct vs. incorrect), analyzing overlap in induced optimization signals. They then propose CSCR, which estimates token-level counterfactual sensitivity, reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens, and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction.

Result: Findings show most affected tokens shift in the same direction under both correctness conditions, with few sign reversals and substantial signal overlap. Large shifts concentrate on substitutable surface-form tokens rather than problem-specific reasoning content. CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO on long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks with the same number of policy updates.

Conclusion: Privilege-induced likelihood shifts in OPSD do not provide reliable answer-aligned directions, and their magnitudes reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. Moderate downweighting of sensitive tokens (via CSCR) is most effective, while stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is central to improving long-CoT reasoning in large language models. Critic-free methods such as GRPO convert response-level rewards into advantages and uniformly broadcast them across tokens, overlooking their unequal contributions to the final outcome. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) instead provides dense distributional supervision by minimizing the forward KL divergence between an unprivileged policy and a privileged self-teacher, implicitly assuming that the resulting likelihood shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information. We test this premise by fixing each sampled trajectory and re-scoring it under two opposing outcome conditions, one asserting correctness and the other incorrectness. Most affected tokens shift in the same direction under both conditions, with few sign reversals and substantial overlap in the induced optimization signals. Large shifts also concentrate on highly substitutable surface-form tokens, whereas tokens carrying problem-specific reasoning content are less sensitive. These findings show that privileged shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions, while their magnitudes primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. Based on these observations, we propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a simple extension of GRPO that reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve both the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction. On long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO baseline with the same number of policy updates. Targeted ablations further corroborate our diagnosis: privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

</details>


### [167] [Dynamic Spectral Filtering for Temporal Graph Learning: Learning Evolving Propagation Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27891)
*Yan Kong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), a temporal graph learning method that makes the graph propagation mechanism itself evolve over time by representing it as a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients treated as recurrent states. DSF achieves competitive accuracy on MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks while using substantially fewer parameters, less GPU memory, and less training time than baselines, particularly DEFT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing temporal graph learning approaches typically evolve node states or encode interaction histories, but the authors identify an underexplored question: whether the graph propagation mechanism itself should evolve over time. This operator-centric perspective addresses a gap in the literature and is motivated by the desire for computational efficiency alongside competitive accuracy.

Method: DSF represents the propagation mechanism at each time step as a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. These compact multi-order coefficients serve as recurrent temporal states, where a recurrent branch proposes updates and multiplicative global plus order-specific gates regulate their magnitude. Importantly, the temporal state size is independent of the number of nodes, keeping complexity controllable.

Result: On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF runs achieve AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860 respectively, with 93K-133K parameters, 68-182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6-2.1 seconds per training epoch. Compared to DEFT, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and slightly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3-8.6x fewer parameters, 25-33x less GPU memory, and 5-19x less time per epoch. It uses 3.3-38.6x less GPU memory than all measured alternatives.

Conclusion: The results support direct spectral-response evolution as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement, demonstrating that evolving the propagation operator itself can be a competitive and highly resource-efficient strategy for temporal graph learning.

Abstract: Temporal graph learning is commonly organized around the evolution of node states or the encoding of interaction histories. We study an underexplored, operator-centric question: should the graph propagation mechanism itself evolve over time? We introduce Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), which represents propagation at snapshot t by a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. DSF explicitly treats these compact multi-order coefficients as recurrent temporal states. A recurrent branch proposes updates, while multiplicative global and order-specific gates regulate their magnitude. The temporal state is independent of the number of nodes. On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF runs attain AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860, respectively, with 93K to 133K trainable parameters, 68 to 182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6 to 2.1 seconds of training per epoch. Against the closely related DEFT baseline, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3 to 8.6 times fewer parameters, 25 to 33 times less GPU memory, and 5 to 19 times less time per epoch. Relative to all measured alternatives, it uses 3.3 to 38.6 times less GPU memory. These results support direct spectral-response evolution as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement.

</details>


### [168] [MMHBench: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark for Mental Health Understanding in Long-Form Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27895)
*Jinpeng Hu,Erqiang Wang,Shan Wang,Zhuo Li,Peipei Song,Xun Yang,Meng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces MMHBench, a multimodal benchmark with 268 long-form videos and 2,184 questions for multi-perspective mental health understanding, covering third-person assessment and first-person perspective-taking. A Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework synthesizes and refines questions. Evaluation of 22 MLLMs shows long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks reduce mental health understanding in long-form videos to coarse-grained classification, failing to assess whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations. A more nuanced, multi-perspective benchmark is needed.

Method: MMHBench comprises 268 long-form videos and 2,184 curated questions organized into two settings: third-person assessment (605 questions on observable behaviors and multimodal evidence) and first-person perspective-taking (1,579 questions requiring perspective-conditioned reasoning). A Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions, refined via multi-role feedback and iterative optimization, followed by expert-guided verification.

Result: Extensive evaluation of 22 representative multimodal large language models (MLLMs), including both open-source and leading closed-source models, demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging.

Conclusion: MMHBench reveals significant limitations in current MLLMs for nuanced mental health understanding in long-form video, highlighting the need for further advancements in this domain and providing a comprehensive evaluation resource moving forward.

Abstract: Mental health understanding in long-form videos requires nuanced reasoning over observable behavior, interpersonal context, and latent psychological states. Existing benchmarks largely reduce this task to coarse-grained classification, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations. To address this limitation, we introduce MMHBench, a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for multi-perspective mental health understanding, comprising 268 long-form videos and 2,184 carefully curated questions. MMHBench organizes the evaluation into two complementary settings: (1) third-person assessment, consisting of 605 questions that focus on the interpretation of observable behaviors and multimodal evidence, and (2) first-person perspective-taking, comprising 1,579 questions that require perspective-conditioned reasoning to identify the interpretation of the mental state supported by the available multimodal evidence. We propose a Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework that simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple perspectives. The generated questions are refined through multi-role feedback and iterative optimization, followed by expert-guided verification to ensure quality and validity. Extensive evaluation of 22 representative multimodal large language models (MLLMs), spanning both open-source and leading closed-source models, demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging.

</details>


### [169] [A Cross-Architecture Audit of Direction-Based Inference-Time Defences in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27910)
*Xiangyu Yin,Tora Bodin,Rohan Menon,Chih-Hong Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper compares five inference-time defence directions for VLM jailbreaks across 15 model-layer cells and four architectural families under a magnitude-controlled protocol. No single candidate dominates; the image conditioning shift is best on LLaVA 1.5/Pixtral 12B with minimal utility loss, the prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL, and the attack-specific residual on Qwen2 VL 2B. The CMRM refusal direction shows positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift across all cells, revealing partially overlapping refusal geometry, and direction-based defences must be calibrated per language decoder family.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inference-time defences against VLM jailbreaks typically subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream, but it is unclear which candidate direction performs best across different model architectures, and whether these directions share common refusal geometry. A systematic, magnitude-controlled comparison is needed.

Method: The authors compare five defence candidates (mean image conditioning shift, CMRM-style refusal direction, ShiftDC-style attack-specific residual, prompt instruction to ignore the image, and a random control) across 15 model-layer cells from four architectural families. They use a magnitude-controlled protocol matching intervention size per prompt and pair each direction with a random control of equal norm. Analyses include refusal recovery, utility preservation, direction specificity/transferability, and cosine alignment between CMRM and image conditioning directions with a sign test.

Result: No single candidate dominates on both refusal recovery and utility preservation. Image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate with utility loss at the measurement noise floor in every family. Prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL; attack-specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction-specific in 13/15 cells but architecture-specific and nontransferable across the only compatible pair (LLaVA 1.5 13B / Pixtral 12B). CMRM direction has positive cosine alignment with image conditioning shift in all 15 cells (mean 0.35, range 0.17–0.65, 15–25× random null, sign test p≈3e-5).

Conclusion: The two defence recipes (CMRM and image conditioning shift) recover partially overlapping refusal geometry. However, direction-based defences are architecture-specific and must be calibrated separately for each language decoder family, as no universal best candidate exists across VLMs.

Abstract: Inference time defences against vision language model jailbreaks often subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream at a chosen decoder layer. We compare five defence candidates across 15 model and layer cells from four architectural families under a magnitude controlled protocol that matches the intervention size for each prompt and pairs every direction with a random control of the same norm. The candidates are the mean image conditioning shift, a CMRM style refusal direction, a ShiftDC style attack specific residual, a prompt instruction to ignore the image, and a random control. No single candidate dominates on both refusal recovery and utility preservation. The image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate whose utility loss remains at the measurement noise floor in every family. The prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL, while the attack specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction specific in 13 of 15 cells, but strongly architecture specific and nontransferable across the only dimension compatible pair, LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. We also connect text only and multimodal refusal geometry. The CMRM direction has positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells, with mean 0.35, range 0.17 to 0.65, 15 to 25 times the random vector null, and a sign test p value of about 3e-5. These results show that the two recipes recover partially overlapping geometry and that direction based defences should be calibrated separately for each language decoder family.

</details>


### [170] [IFHierBench: Hierarchical Instruction Following for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27912)
*Yuetian Mao,Chunyang Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IFHierBench is a new hierarchical instruction-following benchmark with 600 prompts covering four constraint-tree depths and 35 constraint types, each with deterministic checkers per scope. Evaluation of seven leading LLMs shows best models barely exceed 50% prompt-level accuracy, with performance degrading sharply with constraint depth, revealing that reliable nested constraint following remains a major gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat constraints as a flat list applied uniformly to the response, failing to capture real-world deployments where a single LLM call must satisfy layered constraints scoped to specific sections and nested fields of the output.

Method: The authors introduce IFHierBench, a benchmark of 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints, each paired with a deterministic checker that verifies constraint satisfaction at every scope (overall artifact, structural sections, and nested fields).

Result: Evaluating seven leading proprietary and open-weight models, even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy, and accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth increases.

Conclusion: Reliably following nested or hierarchical constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, motivating future training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to improve instruction-following ability.

Abstract: Instruction-following ability is critical for deploying large language models in real-world applications, where downstream components depend on the output satisfying specific constraints. Modern deployments increasingly handle the full task in a single LLM call, with one prompt specifying a layered output whose overall artifact, structural sections, and nested fields must each satisfy concrete constraints. Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat the constraint set as a flat list applied uniformly to the response, so they cannot scope a check to a particular section of the output. We introduce IFHierBench, a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark of 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints, each prompt paired with a deterministic checker that verifies satisfaction at every scope. Evaluating seven leading proprietary and open-weight models, we find that even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy and that accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth grows. Reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, motivating future training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to achieve better instruction-following ability.

</details>


### [171] [One Anchor for All: Unified Multilingual and Multimodal Safety Alignment for LVLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27917)
*Enyi Shi,Fei Shen,Chuancheng Shi,Linxia Zhu,Shuyi Miao,Jinhui Tang,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes MLS-Neurons, a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework for large vision-language models (LVLMs) that identifies and updates a minimal subset of modality- and language-shared safety neurons (~0.03% of parameters) to defend against compound multilingual and multimodal attacks, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods while preserving general utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety defense methods for LVLMs isolate language and modality defenses, which is insufficient against compound attacks combining multilingual instructions with visual information. Additionally, safety data scarcity and high fine-tuning costs make it difficult for models to defend against these sophisticated attacks, motivating a more efficient and comprehensive alignment approach.

Method: The framework first identifies monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful and benign samples and quantifying functional saliency through activation strength and downstream impact. It then intersects these neurons within each language to extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons), and uses English as a semantic anchor to intersect MS-Neurons across languages, yielding modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). Only this minimal subset (~0.03% of parameters) is updated to transfer English-only safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.

Conclusion: By identifying and fine-tuning a minimal, shared set of safety-critical neurons, the approach achieves efficient cross-dimensional safety alignment in LVLMs, offering a scalable solution to compound multilingual-multimodal safety threats without compromising model performance.

Abstract: As large vision-language models (LVLMs) are deployed globally, the combination of multilingual instructions and visual information makes malicious attacks more covert and sophisticated than ever before. However, existing methods isolate language and modality defenses, which, coupled with the scarcity of safety data and high fine-tuning costs, makes it difficult for models to defend against compound attacks. To address this severe challenge, we propose a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework driven by modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). First, we identify monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful and benign samples, quantifying functional saliency through activation strength and downstream impact. Then, by intersecting these unimodal neurons within each language, we extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) responsive to both visual and textual risks, bridging the safety representation gap between modalities. Furthermore, using English as a semantic anchor, we intersect MS-Neurons across languages to identify modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons), serving as key defenses against compound attacks. Finally, we update only this minimal subset of shared neurons (~0.03% of parameters), transferring English-only safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.

</details>


### [172] [Meta-Task: Turning Terminal Task Synthesis into a Terminal Task for Scalable Agent Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27929)
*Zhihong Pan,Jiyuan He,Kai Zhang,Yupeng Han,Ze Liu,Yuze Zhao,Yongcong Ye,Zhaohua Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Meta-Task is a framework that redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself, where an agent operates within a real container to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks. This ensures internal consistency and executability during generation, decouples task requirements across multiple dimensions with a multi-phase mechanism, and uses LLM-as-Judge filtering. Fine-tuning on only 3,221 synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively on Terminal-Bench 2.0, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories, but acquiring such data is challenging. Existing synthesis methods suffer from weak reliability (disconnect between task generation and real execution) and limited diversity/scalability (dependence on existing repositories).

Method: Meta-Task redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task: an agent operates within a real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, ensuring synthesized components are checked for internal consistency and executability within the generation loop itself. The framework decouples target task requirements along multiple dimensions, uses a multi-phase mechanism to dynamically design novel task specifications before producing actual tasks, incorporates optional external material support for diversity and realism, and applies LLM-as-Judge filtering for final training data quality.

Result: On Terminal-Bench 2.0, fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.

Conclusion: Meta-Task demonstrates that treating task synthesis itself as an executable terminal task enables reliable, diverse, and scalable training data generation, achieving strong performance improvements with substantially less data compared to existing methods.

Abstract: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories, yet acquiring such data remains a significant challenge. Existing synthesis methods face two key limitations: (1) weak reliability caused by the disconnect between task generation and real execution, and (2) limited diversity and scalability due to dependence on existing repositories. We propose Meta-Task, a framework that redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself: an agent operates within a real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, so that synthesized components are checked for internal consistency and executability within the generation loop itself. Building upon this, we decouple the target task requirements along multiple dimensions, introduce a multi-phase mechanism that dynamically designs novel task specifications before producing the actual tasks, and incorporate optional external material support to enhance diversity and realism. We additionally apply LLM-as-Judge filtering to ensure the quality of the final training data. Experiments on Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.

</details>


### [173] [The Geometric Nature and a Free Proxy for Flow-Matching Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27933)
*Ziyang Rao,Yiren Zhao,Weiyu Guo,Ben Fei,Yandong Guo,Hui Xiong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes denoising acceleration (accel), a geometric uncertainty proxy for flow matching (FM)-based action heads in embodied models. It derives uncertainty from the deviation of the velocity field from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field, enabling cost-free uncertainty estimation and online failure detection with a single forward pass.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flow matching action heads are widely used but do not expose inherent uncertainty, producing faulty action chunks on misinterpreted scenes or OOD inputs. Existing uncertainty estimation methods require extra training, high compute, or lack generalization. A low-cost, generalizable uncertainty signal is needed for safe deployment.

Method: Provides a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing uncertainty corresponds to deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Introduces denoising acceleration (accel), a single-forward-pass uncertainty proxy measuring the bending of the denoising trajectory without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. Supported by theoretical analysis and empirical validation.

Result: accel is theoretically and empirically shown to be a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty. In online failure detection, it identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines under realistic deployment budgets.

Conclusion: Denoising acceleration is a highly generalizable, cost-free uncertainty proxy for flow matching action heads, enabling reliable online failure detection for safe deployment of embodied models.

Abstract: Flow matching (FM) has become a popular action head paradigm for modern embodied models. However, as a conditional generative model, it does not explicitly expose its inherent uncertainty, producing faulty action chunks even when it misinterprets the scene or encounters out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. Therefore, determining when an FM-generated action can be trusted is essential for safe deployment, yet existing uncertainty estimation methods on real-time control suffer from several issues: extra training budget, high computational overhead, and low generalization ability. In this work, we provide a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing that uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Building on this observation, we introduce denoising acceleration ($\mathrm{accel}$), a highly-generalizable and cost-free uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that $\mathrm{accel}$ is a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty and further test its utility in online failure detection. Results show that $\mathrm{accel}$ identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or even outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines across settings under realistic deployment budget. Code and demos available at: https://github.com/rrrrrrzy/fm-geometry.

</details>


### [174] [Shapes from Examples: Foundations of Shape Learning in Recursive SHACL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27934)
*Bente Gortworst,Cem Okulmus,Magdalena Ortiz,Anni-Yasmin Turhan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies the problem of automatically learning SHACL shape expressions from positive and negative example nodes in knowledge graphs. The authors focus on a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the Description Logic ELI, and investigate fitting existence and most specific fitting computation under well-founded, stable, and supported semantics, establishing tight exponential-time upper bounds and polynomial bounds for special cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SHACL shapes are used for data graph validation, and automatically learning these shapes is essential for knowledge graph applications. The paper addresses the fundamental fitting problem: given positive and negative example nodes, compute a shape expression (possibly recursive) that validates all positive examples and rejects all negative ones.

Method: The authors formalize the shape learning task for a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to Description Logic ELI, supporting recursive shape catalogs. They consider three semantics—well-founded, stable, and supported—and investigate two computational problems: fitting existence (does a fitting shape expression exist?) and most specific fitting computation (compute the most specific shape that fits). They provide complexity analyses with exponential-time upper bounds and identify polynomial-time special cases.

Result: The paper establishes tight exponential-time upper bounds for both the fitting existence problem and the most specific fitting computation problem in the general case, and obtains polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.

Conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive complexity analysis of the SHACL shape fitting problem for the ELI fragment, offering algorithmic guarantees for general cases (exponential) and efficient polynomial solutions for special cases, with implications for practical shape learning in knowledge graphs.

Abstract: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, making automatic shape learning essential for knowledge graph applications. We investigate the well-known fitting approach to this task: given sets P and N of positive and negative example nodes from an input graph, compute a shape expression C, possibly using shape names defined in a recursive shape catalogue, that validates at every node in P and none in N. We focus on the case where C is written in a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the Description Logic ELI. For the catalogue, we consider the well-founded, stable, and supported semantics. We address fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems, and obtain polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.

</details>


### [175] [From Scoring to Acting: Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27937)
*Xu Xia,Jinghua Piao,Min Yang,Xiaochong Lan,Jiaju Chen,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OVCSD is a new self-distillation method for LLM agents that uses outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop with under 3% privileged interaction overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing OPSD methods have two limitations: teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes, and action-level scores underuse rich information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship. The authors advocate outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning to overcome these issues.

Method: OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, retains only outcome-verified successful continuations, applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence, and distills the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior.

Result: On ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales, OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.

Conclusion: Outcome-verified comparative self-distillation is an effective approach for internalizing agent capabilities, outperforming prior self-distillation and RL baselines with minimal additional privileged interaction cost.

Abstract: Recent work on LLM agents is shifting from external capability elicitation to capability internalization, enabling agents to retain useful skills without retrieval at inference time. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising direction, but many existing methods typically supervise students by scoring actions along student-generated trajectories. Such supervision has two limitations: teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes, and action-level scores underuse information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship. We therefore advocate outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories. Based on this view, we propose Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD). OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, and retains only outcome-verified successful continuations. It then applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence and distills the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales show that OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.

</details>


### [176] [MARS-RA: Rank Aggregation for Credit Assignment via Multimodal Comparisons in Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27967)
*Dawei Wang,Di Zhao,Xinyuan Liu,Marci Chi Ma,Xiaoyang Liu,Chengming Zhou,Gary Ushaw,Richard Davison*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MARS-RA reformulates credit assignment in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning as a rank aggregation problem, using large multimodal model-based pairwise comparisons among agents to produce robust contribution scores for reward shaping in embodied AI settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Credit assignment is a fundamental challenge in cooperative multi-agent RL, especially in embodied AI where feedback is limited, delayed, and the number of active agents changes dynamically. Existing absolute estimation approaches are sensitive to noise and dynamic agent participation.

Method: MARS-RA converts credit assignment into a rank aggregation problem via contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents produced by large multimodal models. It shifts from absolute to relative estimation, transforms comparison results into contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping, and provides theoretical convergence/robustness justification with Shapley values as an interpretive reference.

Result: Experimental results on challenging tasks of various types demonstrate that MARS-RA effectively guides agents toward cooperative behavior.

Conclusion: MARS-RA offers a robust and theoretically grounded framework for credit assignment in dynamic multi-agent embodied AI settings, leveraging relative comparisons to overcome the limitations of absolute estimation.

Abstract: Credit assignment is a fundamental challenge in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly in embodied AI settings characterized by limited and delayed feedback as well as dynamically changing numbers of active agents. We propose MARS-RA, a framework that reformulates credit assignment as a rank aggregation problem using contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents generated by large multimodal models. This shift from absolute to relative estimation ensures robustness against noise and dynamic agent participation, converting comparison results into contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping. We provide theoretical justification for the convergence and robustness of the proposed framework, and show that Shapley values can be used as an interpretive reference. Experimental results on challenging tasks of different types indicate that MARS-RA can guide agents toward effective cooperation.

</details>


### [177] [Share the Judge, Learn the Deferral: Where Specialization Helps LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27984)
*Weining Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether domain specialization in agentic evaluation systems should be embedded in an evaluator's weights or in the rules governing when its judgment can be trusted. Using 99,952 rubric-conditioned examples and RewardBench 2, the authors find that learned domain-specific judges trained from scratch perform poorly, but sharing a base judge and adapting via family adapters (initialized from a shared trained judge) recovers accuracy. Crucially, placing specialization in a learned deferral/release boundary (a cascade routing mechanism) rather than in judgment itself yields superior results: a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade achieves 89.40% accuracy versus 84.75% for 8B alone at 0.415 normalized compute. The authors propose a qualified design rule: share judgment learning until sufficient data justifies a split, and locate domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
