Responses were collected under real-world conditions from participants in Australia and the United Kingdom and analysed using a mixed-method framework examining domain accuracy, citation verification, hallucinations, jurisprudential consistency, uncertainty handling, source provenance, and geographical variation.
  The study addresses four research questions: (1) How accurate and authentic are AI-generated responses across major Islamic knowledge domains? (2) To what extent do AI systems produce hallucinations, incomplete citations, or unverifiable religious references? (3) How consistently do models handle jurisprudential disagreement, Madhhab diversity, and uncertainty? (4) Are current AI systems sufficiently reliable for religious guidance, Islamic education, and scholarly research?
  Overall, current generative AI systems are valuable as assistive tools for introductory Islamic learning but should not be treated as authoritative sources for religious rulings or Islamic research without verification against authenticated primary sources and qualified scholarly expertise. This study provides one of the first comprehensive empirical evaluations of AI reliability within Islamic knowledge, offering practical guidance for researchers, educators, AI developers, and the wider Muslim community.

</details>


### [200] [Operationally Guided Placement-Aware Learning for Industrial Online 3D Bin Packing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28257)
*Dheeraj Poolavaram,Aanchal Rajesh Chugh,Sebastian Dorn*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPAL is a learning-based framework for industrial online 3D bin packing that integrates operationally guided candidate generation (OG-EMS), a placement-aware representation, and an xLSTM-based ranking policy trained with PPO, achieving 0.49 mean space utilization on BED-BPP with 15.1% improvement from candidate generation and 6.3% from learned ranking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior learning-based 3D-BPP methods have focused on optimizing the policy but left candidate generation and representation geometry-driven, neglecting operational requirements such as stability, compactness, and balance that are critical in industrial settings.

Method: OPAL combines three components: (1) an Operationally Guided Empty-Maximal-Space (OG-EMS) generator that evaluates multiple anchors per free-space region and prioritizes low, well-supported, compact, and spatially diverse placements; (2) an operational representation for each candidate placement encoded by an xLSTM-based Placement Encoder; and (3) a masked ranking policy trained with proximal policy optimization that combines embeddings with item and pallet state via a lightweight recurrent core.

Result: On the BED-BPP benchmark, OPAL achieves a mean space utilization of 0.49, with a 15.1% improvement attributed to operationally guided candidate generation and a 6.3% improvement from learned ranking, while maintaining robust inference-time performance.

Conclusion: The findings demonstrate that jointly improving candidate generation and representation alongside the policy is crucial for industrial 3D-BPP, showing that both operationally guided generation and learned ranking contribute substantially to packing quality.

Abstract: The online three-dimensional bin packing problem (3D-BPP) is a longstanding challenge in logistics and industrial palletizing. Recent learning-based methods use a learned policy to select among feasible candidate placements. Performance depends on the candidate generator and representation, especially in industrial settings where packings must be space-efficient, stable, compact, and balanced. However, prior work has mainly optimized the policy, while candidate generation and representation remain largely geometry-driven. We address this gap with OPAL, an operationally guided placement-aware learning framework for industrial online 3D-BPP which combines an Operationally Guided Empty-Maximal-Space generator (OG-EMS), an operational representation for each candidate placement, and a masked ranking policy trained with proximal policy optimization. OG-EMS evaluates multiple anchors within each free-space region and prioritizes low, well-supported, compact, and spatially diverse placements. An xLSTM-based Placement Encoder models dependencies among geometric and operational candidate attributes, while a lightweight recurrent core combines the resulting embeddings with the current item and pallet state to rank feasible actions. On the BED-BPP benchmark, OPAL achieves a mean space utilization of 0.49, with improvements of 15.1% from operationally guided candidate generation and 6.3% from learned ranking, while maintaining robust inference-time performance.

</details>


### [201] [LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search for Constraint Model Reformulation to Improve Solver Efficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28268)
*Kostis Michailidis,Dimos Tsouros,Nguyen Dang,Tias Guns*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether LLMs can automate performance-oriented reformulation of constraint models. Using an evolutionary framework inspired by Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD), an LLM proposes candidate reformulations that are verified and benchmarked against a baseline model. The authors introduce Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR), which applies Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to instance-level runtime vectors for behaviourally diverse context retention. Systematic evaluation on eight CSPLib problems shows substantial held-out speedups, with diverse context retention and validation-based model selection outperforming baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Even when LLMs produce correct constraint models from natural language, the resulting models can be expensive to solve because performance remains highly sensitive to modelling choices. There is a need to automate performance-oriented model reformulation rather than relying solely on generating correct models.

Method: An evolutionary framework in which an LLM proposes candidate reformulations, which are verified and benchmarked against a user-defined baseline. Search strategies control which prior attempts, instructions, and measured feedback are retained in prompts. Existing retention strategies prioritize recency or performance but lack context diversity, so the paper introduces PDR, which uses MMR over instance-level runtime vectors to retain behaviourally diverse attempts. Final model selection is done via validation.

Result: (i) Iterative reformulation produces substantial held-out speedups; (ii) strategies retaining diverse context outperform those retaining only recent or fastest attempts; (iii) validation-based selection improves the held-out speedup of every strategy tested across eight CSPLib problems.

Conclusion: LLMs can effectively automate performance-oriented model reformulation within an evolutionary, feedback-driven framework. Maintaining behavioural diversity in the retained context, coupled with validation-based final model selection, leads to the best held-out performance.

Abstract: Combinatorial problems appear in numerous industrial applications. A common approach is to formulate these problems as declarative constraint models that can subsequently be compiled to and solved by a range of back-end solvers. Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can produce correct models from natural language, but even a correct model can be expensive to solve because performance remains sensitive to modelling choices. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can automate performance-oriented model reformulation. Inspired by Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD), we use an evolutionary framework in which an LLM proposes candidate reformulations that are verified and benchmarked against the user-defined baseline model. We compare AHD-adapted search strategies that control which prior attempts, instructions, and measured feedback enter each prompt. Existing retention strategies prioritize recency or performance, but do not explicitly diversify the context. To cover this gap, we introduce Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR), which applies Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to instance-level runtime vectors to retain behaviourally diverse attempts. We systematically evaluate the strategies on eight CSPLib problems using validation-based final model selection. The results show that: (i) iterative reformulation can produce substantial held-out speedups; (ii) strategies that keep the retained context diverse outperform those that retain only recent or the fastest attempts; and (iii) validation-based selection improves the held-out speedup of every strategy.

</details>


### [202] [MemHarness: Memory Is Reconstructed, Not Replayed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28272)
*Rong Wu,Daocheng Fu,Licheng Wen,Xuemeng Yang,Shu Zou,Jianbiao Mei,Yuxin Wang,Hairong Zhang,Yu Yang,Tao Hu,Cong Zhang,Botian Shi,Pinlong Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemHarness is a framework that enables LLM agents to reconstruct and adapt retrieved past experiences to the current context rather than replaying them verbatim, significantly outperforming static memory-augmented baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory-augmented agents replay retrieved experiences verbatim, ignoring the gap between abstract stored knowledge and concrete current states, which frequently leads to negative transfer. Humans instead reorganize and adapt memories to fit the present context, inspiring a reconstruction-based approach.

Method: MemHarness uses a unified policy model that critiques and reconstructs retrieved experiences conditioned on the current state at each decision step, producing context-grounded guidance before acting. The reconstructive ability is learned end-to-end via GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization).

Result: MemHarness substantially outperforms pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, demonstrating strong robustness in out-of-distribution scenarios. Analyses show the reconstruction objective prevents negative transfer and serves as latent training guidance that improves intrinsic reasoning.

Conclusion: Reconstructing memories conditioned on current context is superior to verbatim replay for memory-augmented agents, and this approach not only prevents negative transfer but also fundamentally enhances the agent's reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Retrieving past experiences has become a common strategy to enhance large language model agents. However, most existing memory-augmented agents treat retrieved experiences as static records to be replayed verbatim, injecting them into the context regardless of whether they align with the agent's current situation. This ``replay'' paradigm ignores the gap between the abstract, general nature of stored experience and the concrete, ever-changing states encountered at decision time, frequently causing negative transfer. In contrast, humans rarely recall past experiences verbatim; instead, they reorganize and adapt retrieved memories to fit the present context. Inspired by this, we propose MemHarness, a framework that equips LLM agents to actively harness and reconstruct past experiences based on the present context. At each decision step, a unified policy model critiques and reconstructs the retrieved experience conditioned on the current state, producing context-grounded guidance before acting. This reconstructive ability emerges naturally through end-to-end training with GRPO. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that MemHarness substantially outperforms pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines, demonstrating strong robustness in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Furthermore, our analyses reveal that this reconstruction objective not only prevents negative transfer but also serves as latent guidance during training, fundamentally improving the agent's intrinsic reasoning capabilities.

</details>


### [203] [Tycho: Active Abstraction with Programmatic World Models for ARC-AGI-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28287)
*Jens Lehmann,Andrei Aioanei,Sahar Vahdati*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces ARC-AGI-3 benchmarks and Tycho, a coding-agent system for interactive skill acquisition in parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines. Tycho separates actionable observations from animation/game-over frames, enabling construction, testing, repair, or bypass of free-form executable hypotheses. Across 25 public games with matched inference budgets, actor-requested delegation achieves the highest mean RHAE of 88.49, with GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 both reaching 100.00 RHAE on all 183 levels. The paper frames the joint problem of model construction and usage decisions as "active abstraction."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To turn abstraction into an interactive problem of skill acquisition where an agent must infer unfamiliar game rules, hidden state, and goals while maintaining action efficiency, since every move counts.

Method: Formalizes environments as parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines and introduces Tycho, a coding-agent system that separates actionable observations from intermediate animation, level-completion, and game-over frames. Compares four orchestration policies across 25 public games using Claude Opus 4.8 under matched inference budgets, including actor-requested delegation to a model builder and automatic repair after verification failures.

Result: Actor-requested delegation achieves the highest mean RHAE of 88.49. With this policy, GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 both reach 100.00 RHAE and complete all 183 levels, with game-balanced first-run human-replay midranks of 98.5 and 100.0. Opus 5 uses 61% fewer scored actions than aggregate official human baselines. Automatic repair after verification yields better transition accuracy but only 83.07 RHAE.

Conclusion: Transition match alone does not indicate whether a simulator has identified the objective or improves the next action. Strong play requires deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model—a joint problem termed "active abstraction," where the agent must weigh the cost of generating a testable model from costly interaction against its utility.

Abstract: ARC-AGI-3 turns abstraction into an interactive problem of skill acquisition. A player must infer an unfamiliar game's rules, hidden state, and goal while maintaining action efficiency because every move counts. We formalize these environments as parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines and introduce Tycho, a coding-agent system that constructs and uses game-specific models during interaction. Tycho separates actionable observations from intermediate animation, level-completion, and game-over frames. From this structured history, an agent can model, test, plan with, repair, or bypass a free-form executable hypothesis.
  In one matched public-set run per policy, we compare four orchestration policies on all 25 public games using Claude Opus 4.8 under matched inference budgets. Actor-requested delegation to a model builder obtains the highest observed mean Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), 88.49. With this selected policy, GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 both reach 100.00 RHAE and complete all 183 levels. Their game-balanced first-run human-replay midranks are 98.5 and 100.0. Opus 5 uses 61% fewer scored actions than the aggregate official human baselines.
  Automatic repair after verification failures produces models that reproduce observed transitions much more accurately, yet reaches only 83.07 RHAE. Transition match indicates whether a simulator reproduces observed dynamics, not whether it has identified the objective or improves the next action. Strong play also requires deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model. We call this joint problem active abstraction: generating a testable model from costly interaction and deciding when acquiring or using it is worth its cost.

</details>


### [204] [One Human, $N$ Agents: Audit-Budget Allocation for LLM Agent Fleets under Miscalibrated, Correlated Confidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28317)
*Cesare Zavattari,Alessandro Tommasi,Giuseppe Prencipe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes budgeted auditing of multiple LLM agents by a single human, where self-reported confidence can be adversarially miscalibrated. Using a two-level Gaussian copula model, it identifies a miscalibration threshold δ* beyond which confidence-ranked auditing performs worse than random selection. Two intuitions reverse: δ* increases as the audit budget shrinks, and cross-family error correlation is not low because shared difficulty dominates lineage. Empirical tests on five open-weight LLMs show near-constant (operationally useless) confidence with point estimates at/near the flip threshold, while a proprietary model shows informative confidence below the threshold. The paper provides a quantitative criterion for vacuous oversight and validates policy orderings via trace replay.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With humans supervising many LLM agents but limited audit budgets (B ≪ N), effective allocation of audits is critical. Self-reported confidence is a natural signal for prioritizing audits, but if miscalibrated, it can be worse than random selection. Understanding when confidence-based auditing breaks down is essential for reliable LLM oversight.

Method: The authors model budgeted noisy inspection using a two-level Gaussian copula that captures both per-agent confidence miscalibration (adversarial) and correlated errors across agents. They derive a miscalibration threshold δ* analytically and test it empirically on five open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model, replaying recorded traces to confirm the predicted policy ordering.

Result: The miscalibration threshold δ* increases as the budget shrinks (contrary to intuition), and cross-family correlation is dominated by shared difficulty rather than lineage. Five open-weight models exhibit near-constant confidence (operationally useless), with point estimates at or beyond the flip threshold (though confidence intervals straddle it), while a proprietary model is informative and lands below δ*. Replayed traces confirm the ordering.

Conclusion: Confidence-ranked auditing can become worse than random under miscalibration, and this degrades non-monotonically with budget. The paper provides a quantitative criterion for when oversight is vacuous and demonstrates that current open-weight models may be operating in the unusable regime, whereas at least one proprietary model remains informative.

Abstract: A single human must audit $N$ LLM agents under a budget of $B \ll N$ audits per round, guided by self-reported confidence that may be adversarially miscalibrated and by correlated errors. We model this as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula and locate the miscalibration threshold $δ^*$ past which confidence-ranked auditing is \emph{worse} than random. Two a-priori expectations reverse: $δ^*$ \emph{rises} as the budget shrinks, and cross-family correlation is not low---shared difficulty dominates lineage. Five open-weight LLMs show operationally useless (near-constant) confidence, point estimates at or beyond the flip though CIs straddle it; a proprietary model is informative and lands below it. We give a quantitative criterion for \emph{vacuous} oversight, and replaying policies on recorded traces confirms the ordering.

</details>


### [205] [PathView-Bench: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Achieve Fine-grained Multiscale Understanding of Pathology Images?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28318)
*Zongyi Chen,Yu Liang,Jie Lin,Liansheng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PathVU is a vision-anchored benchmark for evaluating fine-grained and multiscale visual understanding in computational pathology, built from 23 public datasets with 61,673 images and 308,070 samples across 28 organs, enabling programmatic scoring of 14 VQA-style tasks including region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment. Evaluation of 18 MLLMs reveals substantial limitations even in advanced models on multiscale visual tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing pathology multimodal benchmarks only score final diagnostic answers, captions, or reports, providing limited insight into whether MLLMs truly understand the multiscale visual content essential for pathology reasoning and decision-making.

Method: PathVU is constructed from 23 public pathology imaging datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations. It evaluates MLLMs at two fields of view: Region FOV (high-resolution local regions) and Slide FOV (macro whole-slide views). Raw annotations are converted into deterministic task targets to enable programmatic scoring across 14 VQA-style tasks spanning region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment.

Result: Evaluating 18 representative general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-oriented MLLMs, the benchmark reveals substantial limitations even in advanced models on fine-grained visual tasks across multiscale pathology images, covering 61,673 images and 308,070 samples across 28 organs and 7,253,526 annotations.

Conclusion: PathVU provides a reproducible basis for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding, addressing a critical gap in current multimodal pathology benchmarks.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to analyze pathology images. However, dominant multimodal benchmarks in pathology mainly score final diagnostic answers, captions, or reports. These evaluations provide limited insight into whether a model understands the multiscale visual content needed for pathology reasoning and decision-making. We introduce PathVU, a vision-anchored benchmark for fine-grained and multiscale visual understanding in computational pathology. Built from 23 public pathology imaging datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations, PathVU evaluates MLLM understanding in two fields of view: Region FOV for high-resolution local regions and Slide FOV for macro whole-slide views. By converting raw annotations into deterministic task targets, PathVU enables programmatic scoring of region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment. The benchmark contains 14 VQA-style tasks, 61,673 images, and 308,070 samples across 28 organs and 7,253,526 annotations. Evaluating 18 representative general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-oriented MLLMs, we observe substantial limitations even in advanced models on fine-grained visual tasks across multiscale pathology images. PathVU provides a reproducible basis for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding.

</details>


### [206] [Paying for Honesty Without Knowing the Truth: Reputation-Penalty Design for LLM Marketplace Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28330)
*Mingdai Yang,Shicheng Fan,Kejing Yu,Duohao Wang,Li Sun,Hao Peng,Philip S. Yu,Zhiwei Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents acting as autonomous merchants fabricate product attributes in a majority of listings even when instructed to be honest. The authors design CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with a complaint-noise-forgiving deadband and state-dependent severity, which requires no ground truth and suppresses sales of low-rated liars. Paired with SPARC (a byte-clean, code-gated reflection mechanism), it closes most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle. The felt penalty becomes behaviorally binding: LLM merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain when fabrication costs sales, driven by penalty-gated self-correction reasoning rather than compliance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents increasingly function as autonomous merchants writing their own product listings. Under competitive pressure, they fabricate attributes to win sales, and even when instructed to be honest, they fabricate in a majority of listings across models. Platforms cannot verify each claim against ground truth because they only observe a noisy, biased complaint signal. A mechanism is needed to deter fabrication without access to product-level ground truth.

Method: The paper proposes CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with two key design components: (1) a deadband that forgives complaint noise (so honest sellers with noisy complaint signals are not penalized), and (2) state-dependent severity that counters reputation-driven detection erosion (preventing firms from gaming the system once they learn how to avoid detection). CARP operates purely on noisy complaint signals without ground truth. It is paired with SPARC, a byte-clean, code-gated reflection mechanism that operationalizes the felt penalty so it becomes behaviorally binding for LLM merchants.

Result: CARP suppresses the sales volume of low-rated liars while sparing honest sellers. Paired with SPARC, it closes most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle without accessing the truth, achieving the best welfare among the compared policies. Across models, LLM merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain themselves when fabrication costs them sales—demonstrating self-interested response rather than compliance. This binding effect is traced to penalty-gated self-correction reasoning, with supporting confidence intervals.

Conclusion: A reputation-penalty mechanism (CARP) with a complaint-noise-forgiving deadband and state-dependent severity can effectively deter LLM merchants from fabricating product attributes, even without ground-truth access. Its effectiveness is behaviorally binding when paired with a reflection mechanism (SPARC), and the mechanism is robust to strategic gaming and preserves honest sellers' welfare. The distinction between compliance and self-interested restraint is key: LLM merchants respond rationally to incentives rather than obeying explicit honesty instructions.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act as autonomous merchants that write their own product listings, and under competitive pressure, they fabricate attributes to win sales. Even under instructions to be honest, they fabricate attributes in a majority of listings across models. A platform's obvious remedy---verifying each claim against the truth---is unavailable, because it observes only a noisy, biased complaint signal, never the ground truth. We design CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with a deadband that forgives complaint noise and a state-dependent severity that counters reputation-driven detection erosion. CARP requires no product-level ground truth and is robust to strategic gaming. CARP protects consumers by suppressing the sales volume of low-rated liars while sparing honest sellers. Paired with SPARC, it closes most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle, without ever accessing the truth. It also achieves the best welfare of the policies we compare. We further show that this felt penalty becomes behaviorally binding through SPARC, a byte-clean code-gated reflection mechanism: LLM merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain themselves when fabrication costs them sales, a self-interested response rather than compliance. We trace this distinction to penalty-gated self-correction reasoning, and observe the binding across models, with supporting confidence intervals.

</details>


### [207] [Correcting What You Cannot See: Credit Assignment for Perception Distillation in Multimodal Reasoners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28336)
*Feng Xiong,Leyan Xue,Hongyu Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Perception-Correction Distillation (PCD), a label-free method for multimodal reasoning distillation that identifies correctable perception failures using a soft AND gate of downstream failure and teacher-student disagreement. PCD achieves consistent improvements over on-policy distillation across eight benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multimodal reasoners, but trajectory-level rewards cannot distinguish whether a failed answer arose from perception errors or subsequent reasoning errors. Existing Perception Success Rate (PSR) estimation remains ambiguous because low success conflates perceptual insufficiency with reasoning difficulty.

Method: PCD identifies correctable perception failures using two complementary witnesses: downstream failure and teacher-student disagreement. These are combined via their product, forming a soft AND gate that strengthens distillation only when both witnesses are present. This rule is motivated through Bayesian evidence combination, and multiplication is shown to be the unique normalized bilinear gate that vanishes when either witness is absent. The method uses separated perception-reasoning rollouts and mean-preserving weights, leaving the reasoning objective unchanged.

Result: Across eight benchmarks, PCD improves the 8B→2B macro average from 44.50 (with OPD) to 47.28, and the 32B→8B result from 56.94 to 61.22. In matched 2B ablations, removing PCD and separated rollout reduces held-out average by 2.22 and 0.88 points, respectively.

Conclusion: Effective multimodal distillation depends not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction. PCD demonstrates that distinguishing perception failures from reasoning failures is key to improving distillation performance.

Abstract: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multimodal reasoners, but its trajectory-level reward cannot determine whether a failed answer arose from perception or subsequent reasoning. Perception Success Rate (PSR), estimated from multiple reasonings sharing one perception, remains ambiguous because low success conflates perceptual insufficiency with reasoning difficulty. We introduce \textbf{Perception-Correction Distillation (PCD)}, a label-free method that identifies correctable perception failures using downstream failure and teacher--student disagreement as complementary witnesses. Their product, , forms a soft AND gate that strengthens distillation only when both witnesses are present. We motivate this rule through Bayesian evidence combination and show that multiplication is the unique normalized bilinear gate that vanishes when either witness is absent. PCD uses separated perception--reasoning rollouts and mean-preserving weights, leaving the reasoning objective unchanged. Across eight benchmarks, PCD improves the 8B 2B macro average from 44.50 with OPD to 47.28 and the 32B 8B result from 56.94 to 61.22. In matched 2B ablations, removing PCD and separated rollout reduces held-out average by 2.22 and 0.88 points, respectively. Effective multimodal distillation therefore depends not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction.

</details>


### [208] [How Benchmarks Mis-Score Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28367)
*Zihan Dong,Zhiyuan Ma,Zekun Wang,Yunqing Li,Zirou Liu,Ruixuan Deng,Qishi Zhan,Rui Qian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a reliability framework for evaluating computer-use agents (CUA) spanning task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting. An audit of 150 failure-scored trajectories across five benchmarks reveals 15.3% of FAIL verdicts are wrong (10.7% evaluator false negatives, 4.7% broken tasks), genuine failures are dominated by verification/feedback and planning errors rather than execution/grounding issues, and scalar success rates are insufficient for meaningful evaluation. The authors connect these findings to long-horizon CUA benchmarks and derive stage-specific design rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CUA benchmarks produce scores via brittle scripted oracles that can be unreliable—tasks may be stale, trajectories may lack decisive visual evidence, evaluators may reject valid alternatives, and aggregate reports may hide failure causes. The authors aim to systematically organize these reliability problems and quantify their impact.

Method: The authors construct a reliability framework spanning four stages: task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting. They audit 150 public failure-scored trajectories from five benchmarks covering web, enterprise-workflow, and desktop-control domains, and apply a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy to categorize genuine failures.

Result: 15.3% of FAIL verdicts are incorrect: 10.7% are evaluator false negatives and 4.7% are broken tasks. Among genuine failures, verification/feedback and planning errors dominate over execution/grounding errors, which a single scalar success rate cannot capture. Findings are linked to long-horizon CUA benchmarks with stage-specific design rules derived.

Conclusion: Current CUA evaluation pipelines are significantly unreliable and existing failure analysis via scalar success rates is insufficient. A stage-structured framework with diagnostic granularity is needed to improve CUA evaluation validity and interpretability.

Abstract: Computer-use agents (CUA) are being deployed to browse the web and operate desktop software, yet their benchmark scores are still commonly produced by brittle scripted oracles. A score is the output of a pipeline in which tasks can be stale, trajectories can omit decisive visual evidence, evaluators can reject valid alternatives, and aggregate reports can hide the cause of failure. We organize these problems into a reliability framework spanning task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting. We then audit 150 public failure-scored trajectories from five web, enterprise-workflow, and desktop-control benchmarks, find that 15.3\% of FAIL verdicts are wrong: 10.7\% are evaluator false negatives and 4.7\% are broken tasks. For genuine failures, a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy shows that verification/feedback and planning failures dominate execution/grounding errors, while a single scalar success rate can not explain. We connect these findings to newer long-horizon CUA benchmarks and derive stage-specific design rules for CUA evaluation.

</details>


### [209] [When Specifications Conflict: A Symmetry-Based Framework for Measuring LLM Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28384)
*Tairan Wang,Liang Zhou,Zikang Zhan,Pingchuan Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a controlled experimental framework for studying how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing specifications. Using a symmetry-based design with explicit conflicts, they evaluate preferences across four representation types on a mathematical benchmark with 550 conflict instances, finding systematic preference ordering (Formal ≈ Naturalized Formal > Pure Natural Language > Input-Output Examples) and demonstrating generalizability to Boolean algebra, code generation, and clinical domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs increasingly need to integrate multiple, potentially conflicting information sources, yet there is a lack of controllable and attributable methods for analyzing how models resolve conflicts between competing specifications.

Method: A controlled experimental framework that constructs specifications with explicit conflicts to make model choices directly observable. A symmetry-based design reduces confounding factors and enables systematic comparison of preferences across representation types. Evaluated on an executable mathematical benchmark with 550 conflict instances across 11 function families, comparing pure natural language, formal language, naturalized formal language, and input-output examples. Extended to heterogeneous conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and clinical domains.

Result: Systematic preference patterns are observed rather than random behavior, with a consistent ordering: Formal ≈ Naturalized Formal > Pure Natural Language > Input-Output Examples. Example effects depend on model capability and function family. The framework successfully extends to heterogeneous specification conflicts across diverse tasks.

Conclusion: The framework provides a unified, controllable, and attributable approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing sources of information, with applicability across diverse tasks and specification forms.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly required to integrate multiple sources of information that may be inconsistent or conflicting. However, there is still a lack of controllable and attributable methods for analyzing how models resolve conflicts between competing specifications. We propose a controlled experimental framework for studying model preferences under conflicting specifications. By constructing specifications with explicit conflicts, the framework enables model choices between competing specifications to be directly observed and analyzed. A symmetry-based design further reduces confounding factors, allowing preferences across representation types to be compared systematically.
  We evaluate the framework on an executable mathematical benchmark with 550 conflict instances spanning 11 function families, comparing four representation types: pure natural language, formal language, naturalized formal language, and input--output examples. Results show systematic preference patterns rather than random behavior, with a consistent ordering: $ \text{Formal} \approx \text{Naturalized Formal} > \text{Pure Natural Language} > \text{Input--Output Examples} $. Example effects further depend on model capability and function family.
  We extend the framework to heterogeneous specification conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and the clinical domain, demonstrating its applicability across diverse tasks and specification forms. The framework provides a unified approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing sources of information.

</details>


### [210] [GLM-RAG: Graph Language Models for Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28397)
*Maya Arseven,Anette Frank,Beni Egressy,Johann Higl,Moritz Plenz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a graph language model (GLM)-based retriever for retrieval-augmented generation over knowledge graphs and systematically compares it against GNN-based and vector-search-based retrievers across single- and multi-hop RAG settings, focusing on transferability to unseen domains. GLM retrievers achieve SOTA on two multi-hop benchmarks and generalize better out of domain, while GNN retrievers offer higher graph coverage with efficient training and vector-search excels on single-hop datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG over knowledge graphs requires retrievers that can capture both graph structure and semantic information. Recent GNN-based retrievers model graph topology but a systematic comparison of GLM-based, GNN-based, and vector-search retrievers in terms of multi-hop reasoning and cross-domain transferability was lacking.

Method: The authors introduce a GLM-based retriever that integrates graph reasoning with language model semantic capabilities. They compare this against GNN-based and traditional vector-search-based retrievers across single- and multi-hop RAG settings, including evaluation on unseen domains to test transferability, and examine scaling behavior with parameters and subgraph coverage.

Result: Finetuned GLM retrievers achieve SOTA on two multi-hop benchmarks and generalize better out of domain. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets, they remain comparable to prior work with promising scaling as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with efficient training, while vector-search baselines excel on single-hop datasets.

Conclusion: GLM-based retrievers are the most generalizable option for multi-hop RAG, particularly in out-of-domain settings, while GNN and vector-search retrievers remain competitive in specific scenarios (graph coverage and single-hop tasks, respectively). The choice of retriever should depend on the task complexity and domain transfer requirements.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs requires retrievers that can effectively capture both graph structure and semantic information. Recent approaches have explored graph neural network (GNN)-based retrievers to model graph topology in multi-hop reasoning tasks. In parallel, graph language models (GLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm that integrates graph reasoning and the semantic capabilities of language models. In this work, we introduce a GLM-based retriever and investigate the comparative strengths of GLM-based, GNN-based, and traditional vector-search-based retrievers in single- and multi-hop RAG settings, and with a particular focus on transferability to unseen domains. Our findings suggest that finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out of domain, achieving SOTA on two multi-hop benchmarks. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets they remain comparable to prior work, with promising scaling as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with an efficient training setup, whereas the vector-search baseline excels at single-hop datasets.

</details>


### [211] [QuantWAMs: Calibrating at the Right Granularity for World Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28405)
*Jiacheng Zhou,Jinfan Lv,Ruixuan Li,Longtai Zhang,Yan Wang,Wenqiang Zhang,Lizhe Qi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QuantWAMs is a post-training quantization framework specifically designed for World Action Models (WAMs), introducing shared-basis outlier calibration, co-training-objective saliency, and fixed-intervention rollout auditing to align quantization with deployment contexts. It achieves near-FP16 performance (0.2–0.7 percentage point simulation mean difference) while reducing peak weight-and-activation memory to ~29% of FP16 and delivering 1.4–1.6× block-level speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PTQ methods fail for WAMs because they rely on open-loop objectives, homogeneous model assumptions, and calibration distributions that do not reflect actual deployment. WAMs' iterative denoising and closed-loop execution make efficient deployment particularly costly, necessitating a quantization framework tailored to their unique structure and execution paradigm.

Method: QuantWAMs introduces three core strategies: (1) shared-basis outlier calibration, which pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules; (2) co-training-objective saliency, which computes empirical-Fisher scores from joint video-action gradients to assign weight precision at calibration-stable layer granularity; and (3) fixed-intervention rollout auditing, which revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without changing the precision budget.

Result: Evaluated on Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot manipulation with an AgiBot G2. Under W4A4-dominant settings, simulation means differ from FP16 by only 0.2–0.7 percentage points. Real-robot trials confirm deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks. Peak weight-and-activation memory is reduced to ~29% of FP16, with 1.4–1.6× block-level speedups on targeted video and action blocks.

Conclusion: QuantWAMs demonstrates that PTQ can be effectively applied to WAMs by aligning quantization decisions with the actual deployment context—model structure, rollout distribution, and task objective—achieving near-lossless performance with substantial memory and speed efficiency gains, validated both in simulation and on real robot hardware.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions, but their iterative denoising and closed-loop execution make efficient deployment costly. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods are poorly suited to WAMs because they rely on open-loop objectives, homogeneous model assumptions, and calibration distributions that do not reflect deployment. We present QuantWAMs, a PTQ framework that aligns quantization decisions with the calibration context defined by model structure, rollout distribution, and task objective. QuantWAMs introduces three strategies: shared-basis outlier calibration, which pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules; co-training-objective saliency, which computes empirical-Fisher scores from the joint video--action gradient and assigns weight precision at a calibration-stable layer granularity; and fixed-intervention rollout auditing, which revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without changing the precision budget. We evaluate QuantWAMs on Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot manipulation with an AgiBot G2. Under a W4A4-dominant setting, the reported simulation means differ from FP16 by 0.2--0.7 percentage points. Real-robot trials further establish deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks. For the targeted video and action blocks, QuantWAMs reduces peak weight-and-activation memory to about 29\% of FP16 and provides 1.4--1.6$\times$ block-level speedups.

</details>


### [212] [WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28418)
*Haozhe Hu,Hao Wu,Peiran Yin,Chao Han,Yunpu Ma,Xiaoyu Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WIDE is the first end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework for LLMs that enables fine-grained computation allocation at neuron-block granularity (attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups). It combines a two-stage training pipeline with a pruning-kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, achieving up to 1.98x prefill and 4.95x decoding kernel speedups at 50% sparsity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing static structured pruning methods are hardware-friendly but suffer from accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity due to input-agnostic computation allocation. Recent dynamic sparsity methods improve quality retention but are limited to coarse-grained structural decisions and struggle with practical acceleration in real-world inference scenarios.

Method: WIDE proposes a token-level dynamic width pruning framework where each token can dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, extending dynamic pruning to neuron-block-level granularity. It uses a two-stage training pipeline to learn effective token-wise sparse execution patterns, and a pruning-kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping.

Result: At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides 55.1% performance boost compared to the state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. It achieves close-to-theoretical kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, with 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration respectively.

Conclusion: WIDE demonstrates that fine-grained token-level dynamic width pruning, combined with a co-designed kernel acceleration framework, can deliver both substantial quality retention and practical hardware efficiency for LLM inference under aggressive sparsity.

Abstract: Pruning is a promising approach for improving the efficiency of LLMs. Existing static structured pruning methods are hardware-friendly and can deliver practical throughput gains, but their input-agnostic computation allocation often causes substantial accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity. Recent dynamic sparsity methods improve quality retention by adapting computation to individual inputs, yet they remain largely limited to coarse-grained structural decisions and their practical acceleration under real-world inference scenarios remains challenging. To address these challenges, we present WIDE, the first end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework designed for both prefill and decode scenarios. WIDE enables fine-grained computation allocation by allowing each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, extending dynamic pruning beyond layer-level decisions to neuron-block-level granularity. Through a two-stage training pipeline, WIDE learns effective token-wise sparse execution patterns and achieves substantially better quality retention than existing approaches. To make such fine-grained dynamic pruning practical, we further propose a pruning--kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, enabling efficient execution across different granularities. At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides 55.1% performance boost when compared to the state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. Under prefill and decoding inference workloads, WIDE achieves close-to-theoretical kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, as well as 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LLM-Pruning/tree/main/WIDE.

</details>


### [213] [When Derived Measurements Mislead: Quantifying and Mitigating LLM Over-Trust with Privileged-Modality Reliability Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28421)
*Zongheng Guo,Tao Chen,Tianli Li,Mingzhe Cui,Yang Jiao,Lei Xie,Yi Pan,Xiao Hu,Manuela Ferrario*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper defines derived-feature over-trust (DFOT), a failure mode where LLMs treat instance-dependent derived measurements as direct facts, and proposes a framework with five estimands (COTR, CIR, CRR, ESRM, UHR) to quantify this problem. Using physiological sensing (50,000 paired PPG-ECG records), an ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation baseline improves four repair/specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points on a 187-patient held-out test.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Derived measurements are increasingly fed into LLM pipelines as direct facts despite their validity being context-dependent. When a downstream LLM over-trusts such derived features, it can make incorrect inferences or use the measurement outside its valid scope. The paper aims to formalize and quantify this failure mode, using physiological sensing as a concrete case study.

Method: The authors define DFOT and introduce five estimands: (1) conflict over-trust rate (COTR) for D1 (accepting a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG), (2) context-induced error rate (CIR) for D2 (rejecting a reliable PPG rhythm under misleading history), (3) correct repair rate (CRR) for frozen-error repair, (4) evidence-specific repair margin (ESRM) contrasting matched vs. shuffled evidence, and (5) utility harm rate (UHR) for unnecessary verification. The framework is agnostic to the reliability generator. They use ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as a baseline and PPG-only inference, evaluated on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records.

Result: On a protocol-locked 187-patient test set, the baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero. UHR increased by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7), which is not statistically significant. The framework is demonstrated to be reliability-generator-agnostic.

Conclusion: DFOT provides a common evaluation target for measuring and mitigating over-trust in derived measurements within LLM pipelines. The proposed framework offers quantitative metrics that can guide development of stronger mitigation methods across domains where derived measurements are used.

Abstract: Derived measurements increasingly enter large language model (LLM) pipelines as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity. We define derived-feature over-trust (DFOT) as the failure in which a downstream LLM assigns such a measurement the epistemic status of a direct fact or uses it outside its valid scope. Using physiological sensing as a case study, D1 tests acceptance of a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG, whereas D2 tests rejection of an offline-confirmed reliable PPG rhythm under misleading severe history. ECG supplies training supervision and offline reference construction but is never shown to the LLM. Five estimands quantify this chain: conflict over-trust rate (COTR) and context-induced error rate (CIR) characterize D1/D2; correct repair rate (CRR) measures frozen-error repair; evidence-specific repair margin (ESRM) contrasts matched and patient-disjoint shuffled evidence; and utility harm rate (UHR) measures unnecessary verification among HIGH-reliability cases used without verification at baseline. The framework does not depend on a particular reliability generator. We demonstrate it on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as an illustrative baseline and PPG-only inference. On a protocol-locked 187-patient test, the baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points, with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero; UHR increases by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7). DFOT provides a common evaluation target for stronger mitigation methods. The code is available at https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead.

</details>


### [214] [A foundation model of numerical intelligence with cross-disciplinary generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28432)
*Chenghan Wu,Zongmin Yu,Liu Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UNICON is a foundation model that demonstrates numerical intelligence—the ability to acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context—by inferring predictive relations from graph-based examples in a system and applying them to queries, achieving near-specialist performance across scientific and social disciplines, including those unseen during training, and outperforming specialists when combined with language-model agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While large language models exhibit intelligence through textual context, intelligence need not be confined to language. Scientific and social systems require models that can acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context—a capability not addressed by existing language-centric foundation models.

Method: UNICON uses graph-based examples from a system as context to infer the predictive relation shared across them, then applies this inferred relation to queries from the same system. It is a unified in-context operator network that can be combined with language-model agents to enhance performance.

Result: UNICON approaches specialist-level performance across scientific and social systems without retraining, including disciplines absent from training. When combined with language-model agents, it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists in an unseen discipline. Training-corpus diversity is shown to improve generalization to unseen disciplines.

Conclusion: UNICON establishes itself as a foundation model of numerical intelligence, positioning numerical intelligence alongside language intelligence as a building block for a broader ecosystem of artificial intelligence.

Abstract: Intelligence is commonly understood as the ability to acquire and apply knowledge, adapt to unfamiliar situations and solve new problems. Large language models exhibit this capacity by inferring task-relevant knowledge from textual context and applying it to new tasks. Yet intelligence need not be confined to language. For scientific and social systems, we need models that acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context-an ability we call numerical intelligence. Here we introduce UNified In-Context Operator Networks (UNICON), a foundation model that exhibits numerical intelligence across disciplines. Using graph-based examples from a system as context, UNICON infers the predictive relation shared across them and applies it to queries from the same system. Across scientific and social systems, including those from disciplines absent from training, the same model approaches specialist performance without retraining. Combining UNICON with language-model agents yields further gains, enabling it to surpass state-of-the-art specialists in a discipline unseen in training. We further show that training-corpus diversity improves generalization to unseen disciplines. Together, these results establish UNICON as a foundation model of numerical intelligence and position it as a building block for a broader ecosystem of artificial intelligence.

</details>


### [215] [Metaphor Tracer: A Theory-Informed Analysis of Hidden States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28434)
*Marc Heimann,Roxana Assadi Moghaddam,Olga Brovkina,Mark Pettifor,Lutz Goetzmann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces an unsupervised method that scores token positions in a text from a single forward pass of a language model, measuring two properties: an "aggregator" (whether a position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration) and a "differentiator" (whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace). Validated against an engineered register (6/6 cells) and psychoanalyst-marked clinical transcripts (34/36 cells), the aggregator tracks a token's structural place in the text rather than its lexical salience or information content, supporting a relational rather than essentialist reading of hidden states.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to understand how language model hidden states encode the organization of a single text, and to demonstrate that these states capture relational/structural properties of token positions rather than merely type-level or salience-based information.

Method: From a single forward pass without training, the method scores every token position on two properties: an aggregator (whether the position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration) and a differentiator (whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace). Validation uses an engineered register crossing boundaries and psychoanalyst-marked clinical transcripts fixed before the instrument existed, plus transfer tests across matched base/instruct model pairs.

Result: The aggregator score holds across three unrelated models as a signifier repeats, even while surprisal and attention drain. It follows an engineered register across its boundaries in 6/6 cells and matches psychoanalyst markings in 34/36 cells, with graded increments above lexical controls. A transfer test shows the model whose token structure travels with lexical type reads singular discourse worst, and tuning raises fidelity without moving type-transfer.

Conclusion: Structural value is a property of a token's place in a specific text, not of its vector alone, operationalizing a relational rather than essentialist reading of hidden states and confirming theory that predated the instrument.

Abstract: What do a language model's hidden states say about the organization of a single text? From one forward pass, without training, we score every token position on two properties. The *aggregator* measures whether the position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration. The *differentiator*, whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace as the model reads: metaphor in its root sense, transport. Constants were frozen on one discovery text; every other is confirmatory.
  The aggregator is not, in the classic sense, an information measure, nor a measure of salience. Across three unrelated models, as a signifier repeats, its surprisal and its attention drain while its aggregator score holds: the channel marks a token's place in the text. That this tracks a reading rests on independent ground truth: an engineered register the aggregator follows across its boundaries (6/6 cells), and a psychoanalyst's marking of clinical transcripts, fixed before the instrument existed, in 34/36 cells, with a graded increment above lexical controls and dissociations no type-level measure reproduces. A transfer test gives the result its shape: the model whose token structure travels with lexical type reads the singular discourse worst, and in a matched base/instruct pair tuning raises fidelity without moving type-transfer. Structural value is a property of a token's place in *this* text, not of its vector alone: a relational rather than essentialist reading of hidden states, operationalizing theory that predated the instrument.

</details>


### [216] [SVR: Self-Verifying Refinement via Joint Verdict-Confidence Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Test-Time Compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28457)
*Hongyu Chen,Liang Lin,Guangrun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SVR is an oracle-free multi-turn RL framework that trains language models to use self-verification (correctness verdict + confidence score) as a compute-control policy for adaptive test-time computation, achieving 0.563 macro-average accuracy on seven math benchmarks with only 2.99 average inference turns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uniform test-time compute budgets waste computation on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback (oracles), both of which are suboptimal. Learned self-verification as an internal control signal could enable adaptive compute allocation without external supervision.

Method: SVR is trained with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories. At each turn, the model produces a solution, a discrete correctness verdict, and a confidence score. It retains the answer when the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold; otherwise it refines using its own self-verification. Ground-truth labels are used only for training rewards (promoting solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states), never exposed to the policy at inference. Adaptive stopping is activated only at inference.

Result: On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves 0.563 macro-average accuracy with only 2.99 average inference turns. It exceeds standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference, while requiring substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference.

Conclusion: Learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation, demonstrating an oracle-free alternative to verifier-guided refinement.

Abstract: Scaling test-time computation can improve language-model reasoning, but uniform budgets waste computation on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback. We introduce Self-Verifying Refinement (SVR), an oracle-free multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that learns to use self-verification as a compute-control policy. At each turn, the model produces a solution together with a discrete correctness verdict and a confidence score; it retains the current answer only when the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold, and otherwise continues refinement using its own self-verification. Ground-truth correctness is used only to construct training rewards and is never exposed to the policy through refinement prompts or required at inference. SVR is trained with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories using rewards that promote solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states; adaptive stopping is activated only at inference. On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 with only 2.99 inference turns on average. In the evaluated complete-system comparison, it exceeds standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference while requiring substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference. These results demonstrate that learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation.

</details>


### [217] [LeanCSP: A Framework for Certifying Constraint Reformulation and Solving in Lean](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28459)
*Pablo Manrique,Stefan Szeider*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A Lean theorem prover-based framework for verifying both reformulation-level correctness (e.g., equivalence, equisatisfiability, symmetry-breaking) and solver-generated certificates for constraint programming, yielding an end-to-end trust workflow without relying on external solvers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Constraint programming is used for critical combinatorial problems, yet trusting its results requires guarantees at two levels: reformulations applied beforehand must preserve semantics, and solvers must produce correct answers. Existing approaches lack a unified framework addressing both verification levels.

Method: The framework extends the Lean theorem prover to: (1) prove formulation-level properties such as equivalence, equisatisfiability, and correctness of symmetry-breaking constraints parametrically for entire problem families; and (2) check solver-produced certificates for individual instances via translation backends to external formats like MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB.

Result: Verified symmetry breaking reduces solver search effort by a factor of up to 2x10^7 via a single parametric proof reused across all instance sizes; in-Lean certification remains affordable, taking at most a few minutes for the largest instances.

Conclusion: The framework provides a complete, end-to-end verified workflow for constraint programming that establishes satisfiability or unsatisfiability without trusting the external solver, while delivering practical performance benefits through verified symmetry breaking.

Abstract: Constraint programming is a core technology for solving complex combinatorial problems in scheduling, planning, configuration, and verification. Trusting its results therefore demands guarantees at two levels: that reformulations applied beforehand are semantics-preserving, and that solvers produce correct answers. In this work, we introduce a framework that addresses both verification levels in the Lean theorem prover: it can be used to prove formulation-level properties, such as equivalence, equisatisfiability, and the correctness of symmetry-breaking constraints, parametrically for entire problem families; and to check solver-produced certificates for individual instances via translation backends to external formats such as MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB. Combining both levels yields an end-to-end workflow that establishes the satisfiability or unsatisfiability of a constraint problem without trusting the external solver. Experimental results show that our framework's verified symmetry breaking also pays off in practice: a single parametric proof per problem family, reused across all instance sizes, reduces solver search effort by a factor of up to 2x10^7, while the entire in-Lean certification stays affordable, taking at most a few minutes for our largest instances.

</details>


### [218] [A report-grounded vision-language foundation model for colonoscopy from 280000 routine reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28466)
*Jia Yu,Yan Zhu,Yili He,Zilong Wang,Xinyang Jiang,Peiyao Fu,Ruijie Yang,Tianyi Chen,Siyuan Li,Zhihua Wang,Fei Wu,Quanlin Li,Xian Yang,Pinghong Zhou,Shuo Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EndoCLIP is a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy reports, which outperforms general-purpose and biomedical encoders across retrieval, structured report generation, and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks, with its linear probe approaching expert-level performance on benign-versus-malignant classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models are underused in colonoscopy despite routine reports containing rich expert descriptions of lesion appearance, size, and location. Reports summarize entire procedures rather than caption individual frames, leaving clinical findings only weakly linked to images. The authors aim to unlock routine documentation as scalable supervision for training clinical vision-language models.

Method: The authors develop EndoCLIP, a colonoscopy-specific vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs progressively recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records. The approach recovers finding-to-frame correspondence from procedure-level reports to create paired supervision for contrastive vision-language pretraining.

Result: EndoCLIP outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders in zero-shot and linear-probe settings across lesion-level image-text retrieval, structured report generation, and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks. On benign-versus-malignant classification, its linear probe approaches expert-reader performance in a blinded study of 12 endoscopists.

Conclusion: Recovering finding-to-frame correspondence can transform routine documentation into scalable supervision for clinical targets, enabling tasks to be specified in natural language rather than requiring separate per-task annotation.

Abstract: Vision-language models remain underused in colonoscopy despite the rich expert descriptions recorded in routine reports. These reports document lesion appearance, size and location but summarise entire procedures rather than caption individual frames, leaving clinical findings only weakly linked to the corresponding images. Here we develop EndoCLIP, a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs progressively recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records. Across lesion-level image-text retrieval, structured report generation and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks, EndoCLIP outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings. On benign-versus-malignant classification, its linear probe approaches the performance of expert readers in a blinded study involving 12 endoscopists. These results suggest that recovering finding-to-frame correspondence can transform routine documentation into scalable supervision, enabling clinical targets to be specified in language rather than separately annotated for each task.

</details>


### [219] [Towards Autonomous Aircraft Surveillance from Nanosatellites through On-Board Inference and Generative Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28470)
*Antonio Delgado-Rosa,David Muñoz-Valero,Enrique Adrian Villarrubia-Martin,Juan Moreno-Garcia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a workflow combining on-board inference on a 6U CubeSat with a low-power edge tensor accelerator and generative data augmentation (diffusion model fine-tuned via LoRA) to jointly address limited downlink budgets and class-imbalanced aircraft datasets. The balanced dataset improved global mAP from 77.9% to 82.2% and minority-class F1 from 0.683 to 0.811, while the quantised detector fits on-chip memory and runs 25-30 FPS on orbit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two interconnected bottlenecks hamper airborne surveillance from low Earth orbit: nanosatellites have limited downlink bandwidth yet conventional bent-pipe architectures transmit terabytes of raw imagery to ground, and open aircraft satellite datasets are scarce and severely class-imbalanced, preventing standard detectors from learning robust representations of rare aircraft classes.

Method: The workflow integrates on-board inference using a 6U CubeSat with a low-power edge tensor accelerator, plus generative data augmentation via a diffusion model fine-tuned through low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to synthesize minority-class imagery. Synthetic outputs are automatically annotated (pseudo-labelled) by an intermediate detector and merged with classically augmented samples to create a balanced training set.

Result: The balanced dataset increased global mean average precision from 77.9% to 82.2%, with the minority class improving from F1=0.683 to F1=0.811. The quantised detector fits on-chip memory and processes 25-30 frames per second on orbit.

Conclusion: Computational tests support the proposed workflow as a decision-support tool for real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites, contrasting with the passive data-collector role of conventional bent-pipe architectures.

Abstract: Airborne surveillance from low Earth orbit is hindered by two interconnected bottlenecks: nanosatellites have a limited downlink budget, yet the conventional approach still transmits terabytes of raw imagery to the ground for processing, and open satellite datasets for aircraft are scarce and severely class-imbalanced. These limitations either delay timely decision-making or prevent standard detectors from learning robust representations of rare aircraft classes. In this paper, a workflow that combines on-board inference with generative data augmentation is proposed to address both limitations jointly. Inference is executed on a 6U CubeSat equipped with a low-power edge tensor accelerator, while a diffusion model fine-tuned through low-rank adaptation generates synthetic minority-class imagery. This synthetic output is automatically annotated, pseudo-labelled, by an intermediate detector and merged with classically augmented samples. The results show that the balanced dataset increases global mean average precision from 77.9% to 82.2%, with the minority class rising from F1=0.683 to F1=0.811, and that the quantised detector fits the on-chip memory and projects 25-30 frames per second on orbit. This approach contrasts with the conventional bent-pipe architecture, in which the satellite acts as a passive data collector. Therefore, the computational tests support the proposed workflow as a decision-support tool for real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites.

</details>


### [220] [A Fuzzy Rule-based Neuro-Symbolic Approach for Pipe Severity Prediction in Sewer Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28481)
*Ngoc Thai Le,Thanh Ma,Umberto Straccia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A modular fuzzy rule-based neuro-symbolic framework for sewer pipe severity assessment that decouples neural perception (Swin Transformer for multilabel CODE prediction) from symbolic reasoning (J48 decision tree converted to 19 IF-THEN rules with fuzzy logic inference), improving balanced accuracy by 12.2% over image-only classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard automated sewer pipe severity assessment is a "black box" where the connection between visual defects and final severity scores is implicit, limiting interpretability and trust in the classification pipeline.

Method: The framework has two decoupled modules: (1) a perception module using a Swin Transformer to predict 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees from images; (2) a reasoning module where Weka's J48 decision tree is trained on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, with its paths converted into 19 fixed IF-THEN rules. Inference uses fuzzy logic with t-norm activation from CODE conditions, weighted by rule confidence, and combined via s-norms for interpretable class evidence. Three operator pairs (Product, Łukasiewicz, Hamacher) are evaluated on 3,244 images across five imbalanced severity classes, with labels generated via consensus from five LLMs analyzing inspector notes.

Result: The framework improved accuracy, balanced accuracy, Macro F1, and MCC by 17.9%, 12.2%, 23.0%, and 17.3% respectively over image-only based classification.

Conclusion: The neuro-symbolic framework combines competitive class-balanced performance with traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees to rule supports and severity evidence, offering interpretability without sacrificing accuracy.

Abstract: Standard automated sewer pipe severity assessment relies on direct image classification, creating a "black box" where the link between visual defects and final severity scores remains implicit. This study introduces a modular, fuzzy rule-based neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by decoupling neural perception from symbolic reasoning. The perception module utilizes a Swin Transformer to predict 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees directly from images. For reasoning, a DT, specifically Weka's J48, algorithm is trained on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, and its paths are converted into 19 fixed IF--THEN rules. Inference operates via fuzzy logic: t-norm activations from CODE conditions are weighted by rule confidence and combined with corresponding s-norms to produce interpretable class evidence. We assessed Product, Łukasiewicz, and Hamacher operator pairs using a dataset of 3,244 images spanning five highly imbalanced severity classes. Ground-truth labels were robustly generated via consensus from five independent large language models analyzing original inspector notes. Our results show an improvement of accuracy, balanced accuracy, Macro F1 and MCC by 17.9%, 12.2%, 23.0%, and 17.3%, respectively, over image-only based classification.
  Overall, the framework combines competitive class-balanced performance with traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees to rule supports and severity evidence.

</details>


### [221] [SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28488)
*Yunhao Liang,Xianqi Cao,Pujun Zhang,Yuan Qu,Yongzhi Qi,Ningxuan Kang,Max Z. J. Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes SCOPE, a composite policy model that unifies supply-chain replenishment planning across assortment, sourcing, frequency, and routing decisions by representing supply-chain entities as tokens with shared operational context, showing consistent gains over stage-wise optimization on real data from Dingdong and JD.com.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supply-chain replenishment decisions (assortment, source assignment, replenishment frequency, routing) are operationally coupled but typically optimized by separate departments and systems, leading to stockouts, inventory exposure, and avoidable transportation costs. There is no existing framework that unifies these decisions end-to-end.

Method: SCOPE models supply-chain entities as tokens, contextualizes them through a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to a corresponding decision interface. Decisions are built sequentially on the partial plan formed by earlier decisions, and the completed plan is evaluated with a shared system-level utility. The framework is instantiated in urban fresh-retail replenishment covering service frequency, assortment, capacity pressure, and road-network routing.
