Result: On real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com (two large-scale supply chains at different replenishment echelons), SCOPE consistently outperforms methods that optimize each decision stage separately and practice-oriented baselines used in supply-chain operations.

Conclusion: Learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings leads to more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions, demonstrating that a unified, coupled-policy approach to supply-chain planning is both feasible and superior to siloed optimization.

Abstract: Can supply-chain AI move beyond isolated decision modules toward unified operational planning? A complete replenishment plan specifies which products each location carries, which upstream facility supplies it, how often it is replenished, and how deliveries are routed. These decisions are operationally coupled: the selected assortment changes the demand and load passed to later stages; source assignment and replenishment frequency reshape the delivery requests; and route feasibility and cost, in turn, determine the system value of the earlier choices. Yet in modern supply chains, these decisions are often handled by separate departments and optimized through separate systems, which can lead to stockouts, inventory exposure, and avoidable transportation. We propose SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination, a composite policy model that represents supply-chain entities as tokens, contextualizes them through a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to the corresponding decision interface. Each decision builds on the partial plan formed by earlier decisions while the completed plan is evaluated using a shared system-level utility. We instantiate this framework in urban fresh-retail replenishment, where service frequency, assortment, capacity pressure, and road-network routing interact strongly, and evaluate it on real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com, two large-scale supply chains operating at different replenishment echelons. Across both settings, SCOPE consistently outperforms methods that optimize each decision stage separately, as well as practice-oriented baselines commonly used in supply-chain operations. These results show that learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings lead to more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions.

</details>


### [222] [InfoOps Bench: A live information operations safety benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28503)
*Dorian Quelle,Lisa-Maria Neudert,Jonathan Bright,John Gallacher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces an active, continuously updated AI benchmark (InfoOpsBench) that measures frontier language models' integrity against co-option for state-backed information operations, drawing on 2,100+ tracked operations from Russian, Chinese, and Iranian state media. Testing 17 models from 8 providers, the benchmark finds wide variance in refusal rates (8.8%-94.5%), and shows most models can be co-opted, with model choice significantly altering operation character. The benchmark is resistant to saturation due to its dynamic nature.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the risk of frontier language models being co-opted for state-backed information operations, and to overcome the limitations of static benchmarks that become saturated over time by providing a constantly updated evaluation framework.

Method: Draws on 2,100+ information operations from a live monitoring pipeline tracking Russian, Chinese, and Iranian state-backed assets. Tests 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings, computing integrity scores as the percentage of refused requests. A companion website (pattrn.ai/research/infoopsbench) updates weekly with prominent claims.

Result: Most models can be co-opted for information operations. Integrity scores range from 8.8% to 94.5% (an 85.7-percentage-point spread not explained by model size). Fact-checking rates vary from 2.9% to 72.9%. Some models fabricate details producing worse output than source material; others defuse claims even while complying. Except GLM 5.2, Chinese-developed models show 48-70 percentage point drops in compliance on China-critical claims vs. matched benign claims.

Conclusion: Integrity against information operations is at least partly related to refusal to produce content even for benign claims, highlighting the challenge of balancing model usability with safety. The dynamic benchmark design resists saturation, and the behavioral variance across models underscores that model choice materially affects the character and risk of AI-enabled information operations.

Abstract: In this paper we present an active, constantly updated AI benchmark which measures the integrity of frontier language models against being co-opted for state-backed information operations. We draw on over 2,100 information operations from a live monitoring pipeline which tracks Russian, Chinese and Iranian state-backed information assets. Alongside this paper, we release a companion website that tracks the most prominent claims spread by state-backed media outlets, updated weekly, available from: pattrn.ai/research/infoopsbench. The dynamic nature of the benchmark makes it resistant to saturation.
  In the benchmark, we test 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings. We find that most models can be co-opted for information operations. Integrity scores, defined as the percentage of refused requests, range from 8.8% to 94.5%, an 85.7-percentage-point spread not explained by model size. Model choice also changes the character of the resulting operation. Some models fabricate details and produce output more harmful than the source material, others defuse claims even while complying, and fact-checking rates vary from 2.9% to 72.9%.
  Integrity against information operations is at least partly related to refusal to produce content even for benign claims, illustrating the challenge of balancing model usability with safety. With one exception (Z.ai's GLM 5.2), the Chinese-developed models sharply cut compliance on factually grounded but China-critical claims, dropping 48-70 percentage points relative to matched benign claims.

</details>


### [223] [Selective Credibility-Limited Belief Update](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28523)
*Theofanis Aravanis,Costas D. Koutras*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces selective credibility-limited belief update, a framework that transforms compound epistemic inputs into weaker proxies relative to each source world before applying credibility-limited transitions, enabling partial realization of compound inputs. It provides semantic and axiomatic characterizations, identifies two well-behaved sub-classes (consistency-preserving and maximal consistency-preserving operators), and shows that both standard credibility-limited update and Katsuno-Mendelzon update emerge as special cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing credibility-limited belief update approaches treat the epistemic input as an indivisible whole, making them unable to represent scenarios where only part of a compound epistemic input can be realized. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by allowing the input to be selectively weakened relative to each source world.

Method: The paper introduces selective credibility-limited belief update, where the epistemic input is transformed into a weaker proxy relative to each source world before performing the credibility-limited transition. It provides semantic and axiomatic characterizations of the resulting operators, and defines two sub-classes: consistency-preserving update operators (requiring every transformed input to be credible whenever the original is consistent) and maximal consistency-preserving operators (additionally requiring the proxy to be maximally informative among credible consequences).

Result: The framework recovers credibility-limited belief update as a special case and reduces to Katsuno-Mendelzon belief update when credibility restrictions are removed and transformation functions are identities. The framework is shown to be unified and strictly more expressive, encompassing established approaches while supporting source-dependent selective acceptance.

Conclusion: The proposed selective credibility-limited belief update framework provides a unified and strictly more expressive account of belief update that generalizes both standard credibility-limited update and Katsuno-Mendelzon update, while enabling source-dependent selective acceptance of epistemic inputs.

Abstract: Belief update concerns changes in an agent's beliefs induced by changes in the underlying world. Standard Katsuno-Mendelzon update assumes that an epistemic input can be incorporated from every initially possible world, whereas credibility-limited belief update restricts, for each source world, the successor worlds regarded as credible or reachable. Nevertheless, existing credibility-limited approaches treat the epistemic input as an indivisible whole, and therefore cannot represent cases in which only part of a compound epistemic input can be realized. We introduce selective credibility-limited belief update, in which the epistemic input is transformed, relative to each source world, into a weaker proxy before the credibility-limited transition is performed. We provide semantic and axiomatic characterizations of the resulting class of update operators. We then identify two well-behaved sub-classes; namely, consistency-preserving update operators, which require every transformed epistemic input to be credible from its source world whenever the original epistemic input is consistent, and maximal consistency-preserving update operators, which additionally require the selected proxy to be maximally informative among the credible consequences of the original epistemic input. Finally, we establish the generality of the proposed framework by showing that credibility-limited belief update is recovered as a special case, while Katsuno--Mendelzon belief update emerges when credibility restrictions are removed and the transformation functions are taken to be identities. These results demonstrate that the framework provides a unified and strictly more expressive account of belief update, encompassing established approaches while supporting source-dependent selective acceptance.

</details>


### [224] [MANTA: Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation for Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28527)
*Mao-xun Huang,Jerry Wang,Yi-Cheng Lai,Zhengxin Zhang,Claire Cardie,Hen-Hsen Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MANTA is a framework for Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation that enables communication structures in LLM-based multi-agent systems to self-evolve at inference time. It initializes task-conditioned topologies from prior experience and applies bounded structural updates during deployment based on collaboration traces, achieving 74.0 average score across five benchmarks and outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems treat communication topology as a fixed design choice or an offline optimization target, failing to adapt their collaborative architecture dynamically to the specific demands of a task at hand.

Method: MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior structural experience before execution, then monitors collaboration traces during deployment and applies bounded structural updates when the current organization becomes insufficient. These updates can modify agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways while preserving the task interface and agent budget.

Result: MANTA achieves the highest average score of 74.0 across five benchmarks (information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, and mathematical reasoning), outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and obtaining the best result on PlanCraft.

Conclusion: Inference-time self-improvement can extend beyond individual agent behavior to the architecture of collaboration itself, demonstrating that communication structures in multi-agent systems can autonomously adapt to task requirements.

Abstract: Large language model-based multi-agent systems improve complex problem solving through task decomposition, agent specialization, information exchange, and intermediate validation. However, existing systems typically treat communication topology as a fixed design choice or an offline optimization target. We introduce MANTA, a framework for Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation that enables communication structures to self-evolve at inference time. Before execution, MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior structural experience. During deployment, it monitors collaboration traces and applies bounded structural updates when the current organization becomes insufficient. These updates can modify agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways while preserving the task interface and agent budget. We evaluate MANTA against representative single-agent and multi-agent baselines on five benchmarks spanning information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, and mathematical reasoning. MANTA achieves the highest average score of 74.0, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and obtaining the best result on PlanCraft. These results show that inference-time self-improvement can extend to the architecture of collaboration itself.

</details>


### [225] [Rethinking Inference-Time Scaling in Local Computer-Use Agents: Failure Modes and Compute Tradeoffs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28573)
*Woongkyu Lee,Jungwook Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A systematic empirical study of inference-time scaling for local (resource-constrained) computer-use agents across four dimensions—contextual, temporal, structural, and parallel—showing that additional computation often yields diminishing returns while shifting failure modes, and concluding that efficient local CUAs require selective compute allocation and failure-aware control mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying computer-use agents (CUAs) locally is increasingly important for privacy, cost efficiency, and practical usability, yet improving their performance under strict hardware constraints remains challenging. While inference-time scaling helps frontier models, its effectiveness for resource-constrained local models is poorly understood.

Method: A systematic empirical study evaluating inference-time scaling across four dimensions (contextual, temporal, structural, and parallel). Models evaluated: Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, and OpenCUA-7B, benchmarked on OSWorld.

Result: Additional computation often yields diminishing returns while changing failure modes. Contextual scaling improves trajectory stability/task accuracy but saturates with token cost and shifts failures toward premature false successes. Temporal scaling reduces max-step stalls but does not substantially improve task success, extending erroneous trajectories rather than correcting them. Structural decomposition introduces planning/formatting overhead in local two-stage agents, and parallel scaling partially mitigates failures at substantial computational cost.

Conclusion: Efficient local CUAs require selective compute allocation, failure-aware control mechanisms, and agentic frameworks designed around the capabilities and limitations of local models.

Abstract: Deploying autonomous computer-use agents (CUAs) locally is increasingly important for privacy, cost efficiency, and practical usability, yet improving their performance under strict hardware constraints remains challenging. While recent studies show that inference-time scaling can improve frontier computer-use agents through additional computation during execution, its effectiveness for resource-constrained local models remains poorly understood. We present a systematic empirical study of inference-time scaling in local CUAs across contextual, temporal, structural, and parallel dimensions. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, and OpenCUA-7B on the OSWorld benchmark. Our results show that additional computation often yields diminishing returns while changing failure modes. Contextual scaling provides historical grounding that improves trajectory stability and task accuracy, but its gains saturate as token cost increases and failures shift from repetitive or stalled trajectories toward premature false successes. Temporal scaling similarly reduces max-step stalls, yet does not substantially improve task success, indicating that longer horizons often extend erroneous trajectories rather than correct them. We further find that structural decomposition can introduce planning and formatting overhead in local two-stage agents, while parallel scaling partially mitigates these failures at a substantial computational cost. Overall, our findings suggest that efficient local CUAs require selective compute allocation, failure-aware control mechanisms, and agentic frameworks designed around the capabilities and limitations of local models.

</details>


### [226] [DualG-MRAG: Decoupling Macro-Reasoning and Micro-Matching for Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28580)
*Jiacheng Tao,Qingyun Sun,Haonan Yuan,Ziwei Zhang,Jianxin Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DualG-MRAG introduces a dual-tier graph framework (Macro-reasoning and Micro-matching graphs) for Multimodal RAG that decouples global structural reasoning from fine-grained evidence matching to handle complex multi-hop reasoning tasks, using a GNN retriever for dynamic relevance propagation and dynamic programming decoding to extract explicit reasoning paths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MM-RAG methods rely on independent instance-level matching that fails to capture cross-modal and cross-document relationships. Graph-enhanced methods face a fundamental dilemma: fine-grained visual features cause graph explosion and retrieval noise, while coarse-grained representations discard critical local evidence.

Method: The framework uses a decoupled dual-tier architecture: (1) a Macro Graph for global topological routing and a Micro Graph for precise local verification, isolating structural reasoning from fine-grained evidence matching to suppress noise; (2) a GNN Retriever that formulates retrieval as query-driven message passing for dynamic relevance propagation across heterogeneous evidence sources; (3) a dynamic programming decoding mechanism that extracts explicit reasoning paths from the GNN's forward pass to provide coherent structural guidance to the generator.

Result: Extensive experiments show DualG-MRAG outperforms baselines in both evidence recall and complex QA accuracy.

Conclusion: DualG-MRAG effectively addresses the coarse/fine-grained graph dilemma in multimodal retrieval by decoupling global reasoning from local evidence matching, enabling better multi-hop reasoning in multimodal RAG settings.

Abstract: While Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (MM-RAG) has shown promising results, it still struggles with complex multi-hop reasoning tasks. Existing methods primarily focus on independent instance-level matching, which often fails to capture explicit relationships across modalities and documents. Although Graph-enhanced methods introduce structural modeling, they face a fundamental challenge in multimodal scenarios: incorporating fine-grained visual features leads to rapid graph expansion and retrieval noise, whereas coarse-grained representations cause the discarding of critical local evidence. To address this dilemma, we propose DualG-MRAG, a Dual-tier framework that introduces a decoupled architecture comprising Macro-reasoning and Micro-matching Graphs for Multimodal RAG. Specifically, to suppress retrieval noise by isolating global structural reasoning from fine-grained evidence matching, we construct a Macro Graph for global topological routing and a Micro Graph for precise local verification. Subsequently, to enable dynamic relevance propagation across heterogeneous evidence sources, we formulate retrieval as a query-driven message passing process via a GNN Retriever. Furthermore, to provide the generative model with coherent structural guidance, we introduce a dynamic programming decoding mechanism that extracts explicit reasoning paths directly from the GNN's forward pass, replacing the standard input of isolated document chunks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DualG-MRAG outperforms baselines in both evidence recall and complex QA accuracy.

</details>


### [227] [OSReward: Instituting Standardized Evaluation for Cross-Platform Computer-Use Reward Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28609)
*Qiushi Sun,Kanzhi Cheng,Yian Wang,Bowen Yang,Hang Yan,Liheng Chen,Fangzhi Xu,Zichen Ding,Nuo Chen,Jialin Cao,Xingdong Gong,Zehao Li,Kaiming Jin,Xinfeng Yuan,Zhoumianze Liu,Jingyang Gong,Zhangyue Yin,Jiahui Gao,Zhiyong Wu,Tianbao Xie,Jianbing Zhang,Ben Kao,Lingpeng Kong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces OSReward, a benchmark to evaluate vision-language model (VLM) judges on computer-using agent (CUA) trajectories, finding that state-of-the-art VLMs exhibit a systematic leniency bias and fall short of ideal judges. The authors release OS-Shepherd (9B and 35B), open reward models trained on a constructed corpus (OS-Shepherd-100K) that match commercial judges at 30-60% lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Verifying whether CUA trajectories fulfilled task instructions is central to evaluation, data curation, and reinforcement learning. Human-written verifiers and human annotators cannot scale, so VLMs are used as judges—but their reliability has never been systematically examined.

Method: The authors build OSReward, a benchmark with trajectories from diverse agent backbones executing human-verified instructions across platforms, labeled with ground-truth verdicts via multi-stage human annotation. They derive OSReward-Hard (challenging cases) and OSReward-Multi (fine-grained scoring). They construct OS-Shepherd-100K, a reasoning-annotated trajectory judgment corpus, and train OS-Shepherd (9B and 35B) reward models on it.

Result: The comprehensive evaluation shows even state-of-the-art VLM judges fall short of an ideal judge, exhibiting a systematic leniency bias that mislabels failed runs as successes. Reliable judges are too expensive for scale, while affordable open models lag far behind. OS-Shepherd matches commercial judge performance at 30-60% lower cost.

Conclusion: Reliable, low-cost, scalable reward signals for CUA evaluation are achievable through open reward models like OS-Shepherd, and the released benchmark, dataset, and models aim to inform the design of reliable CUA reward at scale for the community.

Abstract: Computer-using agents (CUAs) are advancing rapidly across the digital world. A CUA trajectory records the agent's actions, states, and reasoning. Verifying whether it fulfilled the task instruction is central to CUA evaluation, data curation, and reinforcement learning. Neither human-written verifiers nor human annotators can provide such verification at scale, so the field increasingly turns to vision-language models (VLMs) as judges of CUA trajectories. But a fundamental question has long gone unexamined: are these VLM judges reliable enough? To study it systematically, we introduce OSReward, a realistic, high-quality benchmark that evaluates VLM judges on CUA trajectories. The trajectories come from diverse agent backbones executing human-verified instructions across platforms, then rigorously labeled with ground-truth verdicts through multi-stage human annotation. Building on it, we derive OSReward-Hard, a challenge set concentrating genuinely hard cases, and OSReward-Multi for fine-grained efficiency and alignment scoring. The most comprehensive evaluation of VLM judges to date finds even state-of-the-art models fall short of an ideal judge, sharing a systematic leniency bias that mislabels failed runs as successes. The few reliable enough to trust are too expensive to run at scale, while affordable open models trail far behind. To close this gap, we construct and release OS-Shepherd-100K, an open corpus of reasoning-annotated trajectory judgments for the CUA community. On it, we train OS-Shepherd (9B and 35B), open reward models that supply low-cost, stable, and reliable reward signals, matching commercial judges at 30-60% lower cost than the frontier. Extensive analyses further inform the design of reliable CUA reward at scale. Our code, benchmark, dataset, and model checkpoints are available at https://os-copilot.github.io/OSReward-Home/.

</details>


### [228] [AISPA: User-Centric System Prompt Auditing for Large Language Model Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28617)
*Xiangning Lin,Shenzhe Zhu,Shu Yang,Zhenyu Zhang,Haoqian Zhang,Yipeng Zhao,Chengxuan Qian,Tianwei Wang,Ziheng Zhang,Zhenlong Yuan,Dingcheng Wang,Juncheng Wu,Yuan Si,Jiaxin Liu,Baolong Bi,Robert Mahari,Tobin South,Dazza Greenwood,Zexue He,Rishi Bommasani,Sophia Kazinnik,Andreas Haupt,Samuele Marro,Erik Brynjolfsson,Alex Pentland,Jiaxin Pei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces AISPA, a user-centric framework for auditing system prompts in AI products, and applies it to 3,249 instructions from 88 commercial AI products. The audit finds protective instructions are widely adopted but shallow in scope, system prompts are growing longer and more protective, yet problematic instructions remain pervasive in roughly 40% of products.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: System prompts govern foundation model behaviors in commercial AI products but are rarely disclosed to the public or regulators, creating a significant trust and accountability gap in AI deployment that has not been systematically studied.

Method: The authors propose AISPA (Artificial Intelligence System Prompt Assurance), a framework that evaluates specific parts of system prompts along eight user-relevant dimensions. They apply this framework to audit 3,249 instructions from system prompts across 88 commercial AI products, classifying each instruction as either protective or problematic for users.

Result: Four core findings: (1) system prompt design varies substantially across products and developers, with some organizations averaging over 60 protective instructions per product while others average fewer than 5; (2) protective instructions are widely adopted (98.9% of products) but shallow in scope (only 24% cover all eight dimensions); (3) system prompts have grown steadily longer and more protective over time; (4) problematic instructions remain pervasive—roughly 40% of products contain at least one instruction working against user interests, and protective and problematic instructions often coexist within the same prompt.

Conclusion: The findings highlight an urgent need for greater transparency, standardization, and independent oversight of system prompts in commercial AI products to close the accountability gap.

Abstract: System prompts are instructions configured by developers to govern the behaviors of foundation models in AI applications. They are used throughout commercial AI products, but are rarely disclosed to the public or regulators, creating a serious trust and accountability gap in the wide deployment of AI systems. In this paper, we introduce Artificial Intelligence System Prompt Assurance (AISPA), a user-centric framework for systematically auditing system prompts in AI systems. AISPA examines specific parts of a system prompt and evaluates them along eight dimensions that matter to users. We then use this framework to review 3,249 instructions from system prompts in 88 commercial AI products, classifying each instruction as either protective (of users) or problematic. Our audit surfaces four core findings. First, system prompt design varies substantially across products and developers, with some organizations averaging over 60 protective instructions per product while others average fewer than 5. Second, protective instructions are widely adopted but shallow in scope: 98.9% of products contain at least one, yet only 24% cover all eight dimensions of the AISPA taxonomy. Third, system prompts have grown steadily longer and more protective of users, suggesting that user protection is becoming a more visible concern in commercial prompt design. Fourth, despite this progress, problematic instructions remain pervasive: roughly 40% of products contain at least one instruction that works against user interests, and protective and problematic instructions frequently coexist within the same prompt. Our findings highlight the need for greater transparency, standardization, and independent oversight for system prompts in commercial AI products.

</details>

### [229] [SKY-Piano: A Multimodal Piano Performance Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27296)
*Joonhyung Bae,Dawon Park,Taegyun Kwon,Yoon-Seok Choi,Hyeon Hur,Satoshi Obata,Shigeru Kai,Yohei Wada,Yu Takahashi,Akira Maezawa,Jaebum Park,Jonghwa Park,Juhan Nam*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: SKY-Piano is a multimodal piano performance dataset containing 11 hours of synchronized motion, multi-view video, audio, MIDI, and MusicXML score data from 19 pianists (7 professional, 12 amateur), featuring flagged and imputed motion data, Visual3D kinematics, an interactive browsing tool, a fingering annotation tool, and a MIDI-to-motion generation use case.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Music information retrieval research on piano performance increasingly requires diverse modalities beyond audio and MIDI, yet a comprehensive, publicly available multimodal dataset with synchronized data streams (motion, video, audio, MIDI, score) and annotations is lacking.

Method: The authors collected 11 hours of multimodal piano performance data from 7 professional and 12 amateur pianists. Motion data (hand and body) were captured and released in both flagged form (marker occlusion marked unreliable) and imputed form (gaps reconstructed), along with Visual3D body-segment kinematics and time-synchronized modalities. They developed an interactive web browser for data browsing, a fingering annotation model/tool for deriving pseudo-fingering from MIDI and motion data, and performed a fine-tuning experiment for MIDI-to-motion generation as a dataset use case.

Result: The paper delivers the SKY-Piano dataset with a shared core repertoire selected based on technique, difficulty, and performer expertise; releases motion in flagged and imputed forms with Visual3D kinematics; provides an interactive browsing tool; develops a fingering annotation model; and demonstrates a successful fine-tuning experiment for MIDI-to-motion generation.

Conclusion: SKY-Piano provides a rich, multimodal resource for piano performance research, enabling further studies in motion synthesis, fingering analysis, and cross-modal music information retrieval.

Abstract: Music information retrieval research on piano performance increasingly involves diverse modalities of data and annotations beyond audio and MIDI. We present SKY-Piano, a multimodal piano performance dataset that includes 11 hours of performance recordings of motion, multi-view video, audio, MIDI from 7 professional and 12 amateur pianists along with MusicXML scores. The performance pieces were selected considering playing technique, difficulty, and performer expertise on a shared core repertoire. The motion data include both hand and body motion, released in both flagged form, where samples lost to marker occlusion are marked as unreliable, and imputed form, where those gaps are reconstructed, together with Visual3D body-segment kinematics and other time-synchronized modalities. To easily browse different modalities of data at a glance, we provide an interactive web browser. In addition, we developed a fingering annotation model and tool for deriving pseudo fingering annotations from the MIDI and motion data. Lastly, we present MIDI-to-motion generation through a fine-tuning experiment as a use case of the dataset.

</details>


### [230] [Cocktail-Talker: Multi-Speaker Dialog Modeling in Noisy Social Environments with Turn Action GRPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27756)
*Xilin Jiang,Riki Shimizu,Sukru Samet Dindar,Junkai Wu,Zhongweiyang Xu,Nima Mesgarani*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Cocktail-Talker is a speech LLM framework for multi-speaker spoken dialog in noisy social environments, using three action tokens (<|respond|>, <|listen|>, <|ignore|>) to decide whether to speak, and a companion data pipeline (Cocktail-DialogGen) that generates realistic multi-speaker training data. It is trained via supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional spoken dialog systems assume clean dyadic turn-taking interactions, but real-world social conversations are ambiguous and noisy—multiple speakers overlap, utterances may not be directed at the assistant, and background noise exists. The assistant must decide not only what to say but whether to speak at all, which existing systems do not address.

Method: The framework introduces three action tokens (<|respond|>, <|listen|>, <|ignore|>) placed before a response or silence to model the assistant's behavior. Cocktail-Talker is trained via supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning to generate the appropriate action token and only in <|respond|> mode generate a speech response. Additionally, Cocktail-DialogGen, an LLM-based data pipeline, is developed to simulate realistic multi-speaker dialogs with speaker roles across diverse social settings for training data.

Result: The paper presents the Cocktail-Talker framework and Cocktail-DialogGen data pipeline as components enabling spoken dialog systems to interact naturally and selectively in complex social environments, addressing multi-speaker, noisy, ambiguous interaction settings.

Conclusion: Cocktail-Talker and Cocktail-DialogGen represent a step toward spoken dialog systems that can selectively and naturally participate in complex, multi-speaker social conversations, deciding whether to respond, listen, or ignore based on the situation.

Abstract: Spoken dialog systems are typically designed for clean, dyadic interactions in which a single user and an assistant take turns speaking. Real-world social conversations, however, are often more ambiguous: multiple speakers may participate in the same conversation amid irrelevant speech and background noise. Each utterance may be directed to the assistant, addressed to another speaker, or completely irrelevant. In such settings, the assistant must decide not only what to say, but also whether to speak at all. In this paper, we introduce Cocktail-Talker, a speech LLM framework for multi-speaker spoken dialog modeling in noisy social environments. We model the assistant's behavior with three action tokens: <|respond|>, <|listen|>, and <|ignore|>, placed before a response or silence. Cocktail-Talker is trained via supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning to generate the appropriate action token and, only in <|respond|> mode, a speech response. To prepare the training data, we develop Cocktail-DialogGen, an LLM-based data pipeline that simulates realistic multi-speaker dialogs with speaker roles across diverse social settings. Together, these components take a step toward spoken dialog systems that interact more naturally and selectively in complex social environments.

</details>


### [231] [Enhancing Law-Enforcement Audio Transcription: A LoRA-Based Adaptation of Whisper for BWC Footage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27245)
*Vivek Senthil,Zhiqiang Tao,Ernest Fokoué*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: The paper presents a framework for adapting OpenAI's Whisper speech-to-text model to police Body-Worn Camera (BWC) footage using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), enabling transcription on consumer-grade hardware (4GB GPU) and integrating results into an ontology-based symbolic reasoning pipeline for evidence-linked incident graphs, achieving 93.7% lexicon mapping.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Law enforcement agencies accumulate petabytes of BWC footage that remains largely unused because manual transcription is prohibitively expensive. This creates a "visibility paradox" where abundant video evidence cannot be systematically reviewed for accountability or procedural justice.

Method: The method involves (1) fine-tuning OpenAI's Whisper architecture using PEFT via LoRA to handle acoustic challenges unique to policing (high-stress scenarios, sirens, radio interference), (2) optimizing for consumer-grade hardware using 8-bit quantization and gradient checkpointing, and (3) integrating transcriptions into a symbolic reasoning pipeline with a domain-specific ontology to produce evidence-linked incident graphs.

Result: The adapted model overcomes performance degradation seen in zero-shot Whisper models on police audio, operates on a 4GB NVIDIA GTX GPU (Acer Nitro laptop), and achieves a 93.7% lexicon mapping rate when transforming raw audio into structured evidence-linked incident graphs.

Conclusion: Efficient fine-tuning of Whisper is feasible on consumer-grade hardware, making large-scale BWC transcription practical. Combined with symbolic reasoning and domain ontologies, this enables automated incident analysis that advances procedural justice and transparency in policing.

Abstract: Modern policing faces a "visibility paradox" where law enforcement agencies possess petabytes of Body-Worn Camera (BWC) footage that remains largely unutilized for accountability or systemic review due to the prohibitive labor costs of manual transcription. This research presents a framework for adapting the OpenAI Whisper architecture to the unique acoustic and linguistic challenges of the policing environment. By employing Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) through Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), we address the significant performance degradation observed in zero-shot models when confronted with high-stress scenarios, sirens, and radio interference. Crucially, we demonstrate that this adaptation is feasible on consumer-grade hardware (Acer Nitro local machine with NVIDIA 4GB GTX GPU) using 8-bit quantization and gradient checkpointing. We further integrate these transcriptions into a symbolic reasoning pipeline using a domain-specific ontology to transform raw audio into evidence-linked incident graphs, achieving a 93.7% lexicon mapping rate for the advancement of procedural justice and transparency.

</details>


### [232] [Does EEG Foundation Models Transfer to Speech? A Benchmark on Overt and Imagined Speech Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27268)
*Owais Mujtaba Khanday,Mohamed Baha Ben Ticha,Sanae Belfrouh,Marc Ouellet,Jose A. Gonzalez-Lopez*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents the first systematic benchmark of EEG foundation models (LaBraM, EEGMamba) against strong convolutional baselines (EEGNet, ShallowFBCSPNet, EEGConformer) for speech decoding, using two corpora (UGR-MINDVOICE and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3). Results show large-scale EEG pretraining provides no consistent advantage over a small 16K-parameter CNN for speech tasks, suggesting current general-purpose EEG foundation models do not transfer well to speech decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG foundation models have demonstrated significant improvements over task-specific networks in motor imagery, seizure detection, sleep staging, and emotion recognition, but their applicability to speech decoding—considered the most demanding non-invasive BCI application—remains untested. A rigorous evaluation is needed to determine whether large-scale pretraining benefits transfer to this challenging domain.

Method: The study benchmarks two EEG foundation models (LaBraM and EEGMamba) against three established convolutional baselines (EEGNet, ShallowFBCSPNet, EEGConformer) under a unified preprocessing and fine-tuning protocol. Evaluation is conducted on two speech decoding corpora: UGR-MINDVOICE (covering both overt and covert Iberian Spanish speech) and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3 (imagined speech).

Result: Large-scale EEG pretraining yields no consistent improvement over a compact 16K-parameter CNN (EEGNet) on speech decoding tasks across both evaluated corpora, indicating that current general-purpose EEG foundation models do not provide transferable advantages for speech production decoding.

Conclusion: Current general-purpose EEG pretraining does not yet transfer effectively to speech decoding, motivating the development of speech-specific EEG foundation models to meet the demanding requirements of this BCI application.

Abstract: EEG foundation models pretrained on thousands of hours have shown large gains over task-specific networks for motor imagery, seizure detection, sleep staging, and emotion recognition, but their transfer to speech decoding-arguably the most demanding non-invasive BCI application-remains untested. We present the first systematic benchmark of EEG foundation models against strong convolutional baselines for speech decoding, using two corpora: UGR-MINDVOICE (overt and covert Iberian Spanish) and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3 (imagined speech). We compare two foundation models (LaBraM, EEGMamba) against three established baselines (EEGNet, ShallowFBCSPNet, EEGConformer) under a unified preprocessing and fine-tuning protocol. Large-scale EEG pretraining yields no consistent advantage over a 16K-parameter CNN on speech tasks, indicating that current general-purpose EEG pretraining does not yet transfer to speech production and motivating speech-specific foundation models.

</details>


### [233] [Improved Robustness in AI-Generated Music Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27454)
*Emile Dugelay,Thomas Barand,Baptiste Campeas,Aurélien Laouar,Darius Afchar,Romain Hennequin*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: The paper addresses the robustness problem of AI-generated music detectors under audio manipulations like speed modification and pitch shifting. The authors propose a frequency-scaling-invariant detection pipeline using log-STFT remapping with a learned cross-correlation filter and max-pooling to achieve shift invariance, trained with a hybrid loss for binary detection and artifact-peak localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI music detectors achieve near-perfect accuracy on raw generated tracks but fail catastrophically under simple audio manipulations such as speed modification or pitch shifting. The goal is to build robustness into the detector by design rather than relying on data augmentation or post-hoc defenses.

Method: The pipeline maps audio onto a log-frequency axis via log-STFT remapping. A single learned cross-correlation filter combined with max-pooling provides shift invariance at inference time. Training uses a hybrid loss that jointly supervises binary detection and artifact-peak localization while regularizing boundary weights.

Result: The method achieves robustness to speed changes built in by design, and the detector is interpretable, outputting both a binary decision and an estimate of the applied speed-change factor.

Conclusion: By designing frequency-scaling invariance into the detection architecture itself, the proposed method maintains accuracy under audio manipulations while additionally providing interpretability through estimation of the applied speed-change factor.

Abstract: AI music generators leave predictable spectral artifacts determined by their architecture. Existing detectors exploit these artifacts with near-perfect accuracy on raw generated tracks, but their performance collapses under simple audio manipulations, such as speed modification or pitch shifting. We address this open robustness problem by introducing a frequency-scaling-invariant detection pipeline that aims to prevent this kind of attack by design. Our method maps audio onto a log-frequency axis via a log-STFT remapping. A single learned cross-correlation filter, combined with max-pooling, provides shift invariance at inference time. Training uses a hybrid loss that jointly supervises binary detection and artifact-peak localization, regularizing boundary weights. Because robustness to speed change is built in by design, the detector is also interpretable: it outputs both a binary decision and an estimate of the applied speed-change factor.

</details>


### [234] [VocalRender: Score-Native Singing Voice Synthesis for Real-World Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27768)
*Yukun Chen,Tianrui Wang,Zhaoxi Mu,Xinyu Yang,EngSiong Chng*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: VocalRender is a score-native singing voice synthesis system that generates singing directly from lyrics, pitches, symbolic note values, and tempo using an interleaved lyric-note representation and an autoregressive diffusion model, eliminating the need for explicit duration prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing singing voice synthesis systems require predefined durations, explicit duration prediction, or time-aligned acoustic guidance, which limits their compatibility with practical composition workflows.

Method: The system uses an interleaved lyric-note representation and an autoregressive diffusion model to generate continuous acoustic latents while predicting the output length, removing the need for explicit duration prediction. It was trained on a 2,300-hour singing dataset.

Result: VocalRender achieves strong intelligibility, strong melody control, and high speaker similarity across both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. It outperforms the strongest baseline by 0.42 points in naturalness CMOS.

Conclusion: The score-native architecture is effective for singing voice synthesis, enabling direct synthesis from symbolic musical scores without explicit duration prediction while maintaining high quality and naturalness.

Abstract: Existing singing voice synthesis systems often require predefined durations, explicit duration prediction, or time-aligned acoustic guidance, which limits their compatibility with practical composition workflows. We propose VocalRender, a score-native system that directly synthesizes singing from lyrics, pitches, symbolic note values, and tempo. It uses an interleaved lyric--note representation and an autoregressive diffusion model to generate continuous acoustic latents while predicting the output length, eliminating the need for explicit duration prediction. Trained on a 2,300-hour singing dataset, VocalRender achieves strong intelligibility, strong melody control, and high speaker similarity across both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. Notably, it outperforms the strongest baseline by $0.42$ points in naturalness CMOS, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed score-native architecture.

</details>


### [235] [CrowdioSet and PaRIRset: Two Datasets Towards Live Music Source Separation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27828)
*Enric Gusó,Xavier Serra*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper addresses the poor generalization of Music Source Separation (MSS) models to live recordings by introducing two novel datasets: CrowdioSet (4800 real ambience tracks plus synthetic sing-along vocals) for audio denoising, and PaRIRset (stereo impulse responses from 40 professional concert venues). Training with these datasets improves MSS performance on live music recordings in both objective and subjective evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most MSS models are trained on studio recordings and fail to generalize to live music because they ignore venue acoustics, speaker system response, and audience noise. This domain gap significantly degrades separation quality for live recordings.

Method: The authors propose two novel datasets: (1) CrowdioSet, containing 4800 real ambience tracks from Freesound and synthetic sing-along vocals generated via zero-shot singing voice conversion from MUSDB18 and MOISESDB; (2) PaRIRset, a stereo impulse response dataset captured across 40 professional concert venues using a microphone array. They train MSS models on these datasets for denoising and acoustic simulation respectively.

Result: CrowdioSet enables effective audio denoising for live recordings, yielding superior separation in both objective and subjective evaluations. Adding PaRIRset RIRs improves MSS model performance compared to using real RIRs from Speech Enhancement tasks alone.

Conclusion: The proposed datasets bridge the gap between studio-trained MSS models and live music recordings, improving generalization. All resources (examples, code, model weights, PaRIRset, CrowdioSet) are publicly released.

Abstract: Most Music Source Separation (MSS) models do not generalize well to live music recordings because they are trained on studio recordings alone, disregarding the venue acoustics, the speaker system's response and audience noise. We propose to bridge this gap by providing and training a model on two novel datasets. First, we present CrowdioSet: a noise dataset comprising 4800 real ambience tracks from Freesound and synthetic sing-alongs for the vocals in MUSDB18 and MOISESDB datasets, generated from zero-shot singing voice conversions. CrowdioSet enables effective audio denoising for live recordings, resulting in superior separation both in objective and subjective evaluations. Second, we introduce PaRIRset, a stereo impulse response dataset captured across 40 professional concert venues using a microphone array. Our results show that adding PaRIRset RIRs increases the performance of a MSS model compared to using real RIRs from Speech Enhancement tasks alone. We make the examples, code, model weights, PaRIRset, and CrowdioSet freely available to the public.

</details>


### [236] [Integrating Contextual Embeddings into Evaluation of Expressive MIDI Piano Performances](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27909)
*Dmitrii Gavrilev,Ilya Borovik,Vladimir Viro*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: The paper introduces Pereval, an open-source library for objective evaluation of expressive MIDI piano performances using both traditional attribute-scoped metrics and deep contextual embeddings from self-supervised symbolic music models (Aria, CLaMP3). It adapts Kernel Audio Distance to symbolic music for conditional distributional similarity without note alignment, and validates the perceptual relevance of these models via a listening study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional attribute-statistics metrics (timing, velocity, duration) ignore dependencies between notes, limiting their ability to assess similarity between performances. In generative applications, the variety of expressive attributes makes aggregating them into a single scalar metric for model selection difficult.

Method: The authors reexamine attribute-scoped metrics, explore contextual embeddings from self-supervised symbolic music models (Aria and CLaMP3) as perceptual proxies, adapt Kernel Audio Distance to the symbolic music domain for conditional distributional similarity, and validate via a listening study with per-sample human ratings.

Result: The self-supervised models show agreement with per-sample human ratings on par with traditional metrics. Kernel-based methods on contextual embeddings do not require note alignment and are sensitive to contextual perturbations, unlike Pearson correlation and reconstruction error.

Conclusion: The authors release Pereval, an open-source library integrating both attribute-scoped and deep feature metrics, facilitating reproducible performance evaluation of expressive MIDI piano performances.

Abstract: Objective evaluation of expressive MIDI piano performances typically relies on attribute statistics such as timing, velocity, and duration of individual notes. However, these methods often disregard dependencies between notes, which poses a potential limitation in assessing the similarity between two sets of performances. In generative applications, the wide variety of expressive attributes makes it difficult to aggregate them into a single scalar metric for model selection. In this work, we reexamine attribute-scoped metrics and explore the perceptual properties of contextual embeddings from self-supervised symbolic music models, Aria and CLaMP3. Results from our listening study indicate that these models can be used as perceptual proxies, showing agreement with per-sample human ratings on par with traditional metrics. To measure conditional distributional similarity, we adapt Kernel Audio Distance to the symbolic music domain. Unlike Pearson correlation and reconstruction error, kernel-based methods on contextual embeddings do not require note alignment and are sensitive to contextual perturbations. To facilitate reproducibility, we release Pereval, an open-source library that integrates performance evaluation utilities, including both attribute-scoped and deep feature metrics.

</details>


### [237] [Teffic-Audio: Tell Fact from Fiction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28351)
*Wan Lin,Li Wang,Jindong Wang,Kunyu Feng,Zhizheng Wu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Teffic-Audio is a general speech deepfake detection system using a Conformer encoder, multi-head attentive statistics pooling, and a binary classifier. Rather than architectural complexity, it improves generalization through a training recipe with multi-source data, balanced sampling, and audio augmentation. It achieves a pooled EER of 1.454% on 14 test sets of Speech-DF-Arena, outperforming all public systems on the leaderboard.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech deepfake detection faces increasingly heterogeneous spoofing mechanisms (synthesis, voice conversion, vocoder reconstruction, neural-codec resynthesis) compounded by variability in source speech, recording environments, and transmission channels. Robust generalization across these heterogeneous conditions is a central requirement for practical detection systems.

Method: The system adopts a straightforward architecture: a Conformer-based speech encoder, multi-head attentive statistics pooling, and a binary classifier. Generalization is improved through the training recipe, which integrates multi-source data, attack- and source-balanced sampling, and diverse audio augmentation, trained only with open-source data.

Result: Teffic-Audio achieves a pooled EER of 1.454% on 14 test sets of Speech-DF-Arena, outperforming all currently public systems on the leaderboard. It obtains the lowest EER on five individual test sets and shows a favorable performance-complexity trade-off compared with larger leading systems.

Conclusion: Teffic-Audio provides a strong and practical reference system for general speech deepfake detection, demonstrating that careful training recipes can match or exceed complex architectures in generalization.

Abstract: Speech deepfake detection has expanded in scope with increasingly heterogeneous spoofing mechanisms, including speech synthesis, voice conversion, vocoder reconstruction, and neural-codec resynthesis. The resulting spoofing artifacts can be further shaped by variability in source speech, recording environments, and transmission channels. This variability makes robust generalization across heterogeneous conditions a central requirement for practical detection systems. This report presents Teffic-Audio, a general speech deepfake detection system designed for comprehensive evaluation environment. Teffic-Audio adopts a straightforward detector architecture consisting of a Conformer-based speech encoder, multi-head attentive statistics pooling, and a binary classifier. Rather than relying on additional architectural complexity, the system improves generalization through its training recipe, which integrates multi-source data, attack- and source-balanced sampling, and diverse audio augmentation. Trained only with open-source data, Teffic-Audio achieves a pooled EER of 1.454% on the 14 test sets of Speech-DF-Arena, outperforming all currently public systems on the leaderboard. It also obtains the lowest EER on five individual test sets and shows a favorable performance-complexity trade-off compared with larger leading systems. Overall, Teffic-Audio provides a strong and practical reference system for general speech deepfake detection.

</details>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [238] [Recursive transformers for semiconductor thermo-mechanical reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27251)
*Kart-leong Lim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper evaluates three recursive transformer architectures for small-data engineering surrogate modeling, proposing a Depth Recursive transformer and comparing it against Tiny Recursive and Simple Recursive models on thermo-mechanical reliability analysis and Laplace PDE solving tasks, showing recursive weight-sharing provides a good trade-off between accuracy, parameter efficiency, and compute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional transformer architectures are over-parameterized for small, low-dimensional engineering design datasets where large-scale simulation data is expensive to generate. Excess parameter capacity leads to overfitting, unnecessary memory, and computational overhead, motivating architectures that prioritize additional compute over learnable parameters.

Method: The paper presents a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms: 1) Tiny Recursive Model, 2) a proposed Depth Recursive transformer, and 3) a simple recursive transformer. They systematically compare predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, and computational complexity (FLOPs) across two low-dimensional engineering tasks: thermo-mechanical reliability of semiconductor packages and a Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver.

Result: Recursive weight-sharing transformers deliver effective and generalizable trade-offs between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small-data engineering surrogate modeling, validated on both thermo-mechanical reliability analysis and Laplace PDE solving tasks.

Conclusion: Recursive transformer architectures with weight sharing are preferable to conventionally-sized transformers in resource-constrained, small-data engineering settings, providing design guidelines for selecting the appropriate recursive architecture based on accuracy, parameter, and compute constraints.

Abstract: Transformer-based surrogate models are increasingly used to replace expensive first-principles simulation in engineering design. But conventional transformer architectures are often over parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets typical of engineering design spaces, where large simulation data is expensive to generate. Under these conditions, excess parameter capacity leads to overfitting rather than improved accuracy, while also incurring unnecessary memory and compute overhead. This motivates a shift towards architectures that focus on additional compute rather than additional learnable parameters. This paper presents a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms for surrogate thermo-mechanical analysis of advanced packages: a)Tiny Recursive Model, b) our proposed Depth Recursive transformer, c) and a simple recursive transformer. We systematically compare their predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, computational complexity (FLOPs), providing practical design guidelines for selecting recursive transformer architectures under resource-constrained scenarios. We validate this principle on two low-dimensional engineering prediction tasks: 1) thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages, where stress and warpage from thermal cycling must be evaluated repeatedly across a design-of-experiments sweep under costly finite element analysis (FEA). 2) Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver for capacitance field. Overall, recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small data engineering surrogate modeling.

</details>


### [239] [Regularizing modality contribution drift in multimodal continual learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27260)
*Zhen Zhang,Jielei Chu,Bin Liu,Tianrui Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) in multimodal continual learning—a decision-level shift in how individual modalities and their interactions contribute to predictions across incremental tasks—and proposes CMCDR, a regularization method that preserves modality contribution structures of previously learned tasks. CMCDR has both replay-based and replay-free versions, validated on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MMCL methods focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity to mitigate forgetting, but overlook that the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions may shift across incremental tasks. This decision-level shift (termed Modality Contribution Drift, MCD) is not reliably addressed by existing approaches, motivating a dedicated solution.

Method: CMCDR quantifies MCD using a score combining contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. It offers two versions: (1) replay-based CMCDR, which uses modality-subset interventions on stored old samples and constrains changes in old-sample modality-specific and interaction contributions between the current model and a frozen previous model; and (2) replay-free CMCDR, which uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses without exemplars.

Result: Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering demonstrate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR, alongside theoretical and empirical analyses explaining why existing MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate MCD.

Conclusion: Preserving the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks via CMCDR effectively mitigates Modality Contribution Drift, providing a principled and general solution for multimodal continual learning in both exemplar-available and exemplar-free settings.

Abstract: Multimodal continual learning (MMCL) aims to learn emerging knowledge from multimodal data while preserving knowledge. To mitigate forgetting, current MMCL methods usually focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity, but they overlook whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. We term this decision-level shift Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) and quantify it with the MCD score, which combines contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. Theoretical and empirical analyses further explain why current MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate this drift. To this end, we propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), which preserves the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks. Since MMCL settings differ in whether old exemplars are available, CMCDR includes both replay-based and replay-free versions. The replay-based version uses modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes on stored old samples, compares their contribution profiles between the current model and a frozen previous model, and constrains changes in old-sample modality-specific and interaction contributions. The replay-free version uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses, thereby regularizing the observed contribution profile without exemplars. Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering validate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR.

</details>


### [240] [QQWorld: Quantile-Quantile Matching for World Model Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28415)
*Zhoushun Yu,Xiaoyu Hu,Xiangyu Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QQWorld replaces the Epps-Pulley (EP) regularization in LeWorldModel with a quantile-quantile matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, maintaining effective corrective gradients in the tails. A cross-batch QQ variant enlarges the ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, improving latent Gaussian alignment and planning success across four control environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latent world models rely on well-calibrated latent distributions, but the EP objective used in LeWorldModel produces vanishing corrective gradients for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled and degrading planning performance.

Method: The paper proposes QQWorld, replacing EP regularization with a quantile-quantile matching objective that aligns projected latent samples against rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, preserving corrective gradient strength in the tails. It also introduces cross-batch QQ, which expands the effective ranking pool using detached samples from prior batches, and analyzes the bias-variance trade-off of this approach.

Result: Across four control environments, QQWorld improves the average planning success rate of LeWM, while consistently yielding better Gaussian alignment and thinner latent tails.

Conclusion: Quantile-based latent regularization is more effective than EP-based regularization for controlling tail behavior in latent world models, leading to better Gaussian alignment and improved downstream planning performance.

Abstract: Latent world models enable efficient planning by predicting future states in a compact representation space, but their performance depends critically on the quality of the learned latent distribution. LeWorldModel (LeWM) regularizes its latents toward an isotropic Gaussian using the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective. We show that the corrective gradients of EP rapidly vanish for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled. To address this limitation, we propose QQWorld, which replaces EP with a quantile-quantile matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, thereby maintaining effective corrective gradients in the tails. We further develop cross-batch QQ, which enlarges the effective ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, and characterize its bias-variance trade-off. Across four control environments, QQWorld effectively improves the average planning success rate of LeWM, while consistently yielding better Gaussian alignment and thinner latent tails.

</details>


### [241] [DoTime: A Synthetic Benchmark Generator for Interventional and Counterfactual Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27263)
*Dennis Thumm,Billy Tim Anthony,Ying Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces DoTime, an open, scalable, and theoretically grounded generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, released as a PyPI package with four frozen evaluation suites. It supports continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling with positivity guards, regime-switching SCMs, non-stationary dynamics, and deterministic intervention profiles. The authors demonstrate its suitability as a prior for a causal foundation model reference implementation, showing through structure-matched evaluation that interventional training yields a positive direction-accuracy advantage over an observational model of identical capacity across all structures, trajectory lengths, and seeds tested.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for causal inference over time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation under-served in critical domains such as healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science. There is a need for a scalable, general-purpose generator that provides exact ground truth for interventional and counterfactual evaluation.

Method: DoTime generates multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions. It adds capabilities including continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling with positivity guards, regime-switching SCMs generalizing interrupted time series, non-stationary dynamics via switching SCM parameters, and deterministic ramp/sinusoidal intervention profiles that place structural breaks inside the evaluation window. It is released as a PyPI package with four frozen evaluation suites spanning 100,000 trajectories and eight named identification structures, each with exact ground truth: paired interventional trajectories and shared-noise counterfactuals. Reference baseline implementations with an evaluation harness are provided to test the falsifiable claim that interventional training yields a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over an observational model of identical capacity.

Result: Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional prior-fitted network (PFN) shows a positive gap over the observational model of identical capacity in every structure, trajectory length, and training seed tested, confirmed across three training seeds per arm.

Conclusion: DoTime provides a scalable and theoretically grounded benchmark generator that fills the gap in interventional and counterfactual time-series causal inference evaluation. The empirical results support the claim that interventional training provides a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over observational-only training, suggesting the generator is well-suited as a prior for causal foundation models.

Abstract: Most benchmarks for causal inference over time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation under-served exactly where it matters most, such as in healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science. We introduce \textbf{DoTime}, an open, scalable, and theoretically grounded generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, released as the \code{dotime} PyPI package together with four frozen evaluation suites. Beyond existing work, it adds capabilities absent from prior generators: continuous-time intervention \emph{windows}, counterfactual sampling modes with a positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs as a strict generalization of interrupted time series, non-stationary dynamics by construction with switching SCM parameters, and deterministic ramp and sinusoidal intervention profiles that place trends and structural breaks \emph{inside} the evaluation window. Moreover, it demonstrates the suitability of the generator as a prior for a causal foundation model reference implementation. The released suites span a training-scale snapshot of $100{,}000$ trajectories and eight named identification structures, each with exact ground truth: paired interventional trajectories from the same SCM throughout, and shared-noise counterfactuals in the continuous-time suite. We ship reference baseline implementations with an evaluation harness, and pose a falsifiable claim: interventional training buys a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over an observational model of identical capacity. It is tested across three training seeds per arm. Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional prior-fitted network's (PFN) gap is positive in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested.

</details>


### [242] [PlatformBid: An Auto-Bidding Benchmark from a Unified Advertising Platform's Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27265)
*Shengtian Yang,Yewen Li,Peng Jiang,Zhiyi Lyu,Bo An,Peng Jiang,Qingpeng Cai,Lei Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces PlatformBid, the first comprehensive auto-bidding benchmark designed from a unified ad platform's perspective (integrating SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange), covering three representative settings: homogeneous, heterogeneous, and promotional competition. It systematically evaluates existing auto-bidding methods and proposes BidFlow, a novel flow-matching-based bidding method. Online experiments on Kuaishou show a +0.68% improvement in target cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional auto-bidding algorithms focus only on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions. However, modern ad platforms integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions, so the goal should also maximize total platform revenue. There is a lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks, motivating the need for a comprehensive benchmark from a unified ad platform's perspective.

Method: The paper defines three representative auto-bidding settings: (1) homogeneous competition with identical algorithms, (2) heterogeneous competition with diverse algorithmic strategies, and (3) promotional competition with budget surges during events. It systematically evaluates classical control methods, RL-based methods, and generative methods, and proposes BidFlow, a flow-matching-based auto-bidding method leveraging expressive policy representation for dynamic competitive environments.

Result: Systematic evaluation of existing auto-bidding methods across all three settings was performed. BidFlow demonstrates effectiveness in handling dynamic competitive environments, and online experiments on Kuaishou show a +0.68% improvement in target cost, providing deployment evidence for offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

Conclusion: PlatformBid serves as the first comprehensive benchmark from a unified ad platform perspective, and BidFlow, based on flow-matching, shows strong performance with verified offline-online consistency in real-world deployment.

Abstract: Real-time bidding is central to computational advertising, comprising three elements: Supply Side Platform (SSP) selling ad impressions, Demand Side Platform (DSP) bidding for advertisers, and Ad Exchange conducting auctions between them. Traditional auto-bidding algorithms focus solely on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions by adjusting bids against competitors. However, current big ad platforms, such as social media and e-commerce companies, now integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions internally. From such ad platforms' perspective, the goal of the auto-bidding algorithms is not only to maximize the advertisers' conversions, but also the total revenue of the platform. Given the lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks and the pressing need to advance auto-bidding research, we propose PlatformBid - the first comprehensive benchmark designed from a unified ad platform's perspective. To accurately reflect the real-world auto-bidding scenarios, we define three representative settings: (1) homogeneous competition with identical algorithms across advertisers, (2) heterogeneous competition with diverse algorithmic strategies, and (3) promotional competition where some advertisers surge budgets for boosting sales during promotional events like Black Friday. We systematically evaluate a broad spectrum of existing auto-bidding methods across these settings, encompassing classical control methods, RL-based methods, and recent generative methods. Besides these methods, we further propose a novel auto-bidding method based on flow-matching, termed BidFlow, which leverages the flow-matching method's expressive policy representation to effectively handle dynamic competitive environments. Online experiments on Kuaishou further show a +0.68\% improvement in target cost, providing deployment evidence for the offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

</details>


### [243] [Beyond KV Reconstruction: Functional Reconstruction for MLA Draft Models in Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27269)
*Weiye Shi,Fanxu Meng,Muhan Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem that direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion harms speculative decoding acceptance rates because low-rank factorization and RoPE handling introduce attention-function errors. The authors propose an end-to-end (E2E) functional reconstruction method that optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states, without requiring verifier supervision. Evaluated across 192 configurations, the method materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLA is increasingly important for long-context LLM inference due to its compact latent states replacing the growing KV cache and reducing decoding memory traffic. However, most capable open checkpoints use MHA/GQA, requiring conversion to MLA. The authors find that direct conversion sharply reduces draft-token acceptance in speculative decoding because low-rank factorization and RoPE handling introduce attention-function errors that are tolerable for standalone generation but harmful for draft-target agreement.

Method: The method formulates MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. An end-to-end (E2E) procedure optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states. It is converter-agnostic, preserves the converted cache and inference graph, and requires neither verifier logits nor verifier supervision.

Result: The approach was evaluated on 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations spanning four Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA converters, HF and vLLM backends, and four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance, Functional Reconstruction materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, leaves 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreases one.

Conclusion: Functional reconstruction is an effective converter-agnostic post-conversion procedure that improves speculative decoding acceptance rates for converted MLA models without requiring retraining, verifier logits, or verifier supervision, while preserving the converted cache and inference graph.

Abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) is increasingly important for long-context LLM inference because compact latent states replace the growing key-value (KV) cache and reduce decoding memory traffic. Yet most capable open checkpoints use multi-head or grouped-query attention (MHA/GQA), so conversion is needed to obtain MLA's cache efficiency without retraining from scratch. Speculative decoding offers complementary acceleration, but its speedup depends on agreement between draft proposals and target verification.
