We find that direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion can sharply reduce this agreement: low-rank factorization and RoPE handling introduce attention-function errors that may be tolerable for standalone generation but substantially lower draft-token acceptance. We therefore formulate MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. Our end-to-end (E2E) method optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states. This converter-agnostic post-conversion procedure preserves the converted cache and inference graph and requires neither verifier logits nor verifier supervision. We evaluate 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations spanning four Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA, HF and vLLM, and four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance, Functional Reconstruction materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, leaves 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreases one. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/swyhahaha/FunctionalMLA.

</details>


### [244] [RLPF: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27271)
*Huihao Jing,Haozhe Cui,Wenbin Hu,Shaojin Chen,Haochen Shi,Changxuan Fan,Yuxuan Liu,Hanyu Yang,Sirui Zhang,Ziyi Chen,Haoran Li,Yangqiu Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RLPF (Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback) trains code agents to prefer faster correct implementations by turning execution outcomes into a staged reward: failed programs are ordered by execution progress, while correct programs are ranked by relative improvement from baseline toward an expert reference. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench improves correct-and-runnable solutions from 11.1% to 54.6% and relative efficiency from 8.1% to 38.6%, with transfer to EffiBench-X and competitive performance against stronger open-weight systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most code model training with execution feedback stops at correctness, ignoring runtime performance. Two programs can pass the same tests yet differ greatly in efficiency, which is especially important for systems code. Additionally, runtime is a fragile reward—it is only meaningful after a program is correct, varies across tasks, and provides little signal when most sampled programs fail to compile or run. This motivates designing a training approach that optimizes not just correctness but also performance.

Method: RLPF converts execution outcomes into a staged reward. Failed programs are ordered by their execution progress (giving useful signal before correctness is achieved), while correct programs are ranked by their relative improvement from a baseline toward an expert reference (providing performance-sensitive feedback after correctness). This composite reward is used to fine-tune a Qwen3-32B model via reinforcement learning.

Result: On PerfCodeBench, correct-and-runnable solutions improved from 11.1% to 54.6%, and relative efficiency improved from 8.1% to 38.6%. The model became competitive with stronger open-weight systems and showed modest transfer to EffiBench-X. Model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision than expert references, and the full composite reward outperforms correctness-only or runtime-only baselines.

Conclusion: Code agents can be trained not only to pass tests but also to optimize the programs they write. Staged, performance-aware reward signals effectively guide models toward both correctness and efficiency, suggesting that execution feedback beyond correctness is a valuable training signal for code generation.

Abstract: Code models are increasingly trained with execution feedback, but most training signals still stop at correctness. This leaves an important gap for systems code: two programs can pass the same tests while differing greatly in runtime. We study how to train code agents to prefer faster correct implementations, rather than treating efficiency only as an evaluation metric. The key difficulty is that runtime is a fragile reward. It is meaningful only after a program is correct, varies across tasks, and gives little guidance when most sampled programs fail to compile or run. We propose \textbf{RLPF}, reinforcement learning from performance feedback, which turns execution outcomes into a staged reward. Failed programs are ordered by execution progress, while correct programs are ranked by their relative improvement from the baseline toward the expert reference. This gives useful feedback before correctness and performance-sensitive feedback after correctness. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench raises correct-and-runnable solutions from $11.1\%$ to $54.6\%$ and improves relative efficiency from $8.1\%$ to $38.6\%$. The trained model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems, and its optimization behavior transfers modestly to EffiBench-X. Additional studies show that model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision, and that the full composite reward is more reliable than correctness-only or runtime-only baselines. These results suggest that code agents can be trained not only to pass tests, but also to optimize the programs they write.

</details>


### [245] [SDO: Structure-Aware Data Organization for Efficient LLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27273)
*Jinliang Gao,Ning Yang,Hai Wang,Baili Xiao,Pin Lyu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SDO is a plug-and-play data organization framework that uses exposure-driven feedback to dynamically manage mini-batch composition and sample exposure during LLM post-training, improving convergence and accuracy without permanent sample exclusion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing efficiency improvements for post-training focus on sample selection or training schedules, but data organization is treated as a static preprocessing step. Fixed partitions cannot adapt to evolving sample exposure during optimization, causing redundant updates for some samples while under-optimizing others.

Method: SDO operates epoch by epoch on frozen external embeddings. Within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal. Across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling records per-sample participation and reduces sampling probability of over-exposed samples to preserve long-term coverage.

Result: Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence with the largest gains in the early-to-mid phase, producing more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.

Conclusion: SDO demonstrates that adaptive, exposure-driven data organization can improve post-training efficiency and outcome balance without discarding samples, offering a general plug-and-play solution across different post-training paradigms.

Abstract: Post-training of large language models is expensive, and existing efficiency improvements mainly focus on selecting informative samples or designing training schedules. However, data organization itself is usually treated as a static preprocessing step: embedding-based grouping methods construct fixed partitions before training and cannot adapt to the evolving sample exposure during optimization. As a result, all samples receive similar exposure despite their different optimization needs, leading to redundant updates for some samples while leaving others under-optimized. To address this problem, we propose SDO (Structure-Aware Data Organization), a plug-and-play data organization framework with an exposure-driven feedback mechanism that organizes mini-batch composition and sample exposure according to representation-space structure. SDO operates epoch by epoch on frozen external embeddings, avoiding model warm-up training overhead: within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal; across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling records per-sample participation and reduces the sampling probability of over-exposed samples to preserve long-term coverage. Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence, with the largest gains observed in the early-to-mid phase, producing more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.

</details>


### [246] [Rethinking EEG-Based Disease Diagnosis: Decoupling Instance Representation Learning from Subject-Level Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27274)
*Zhiyuan Ma,Zeyuan Li,Zhiyi Lu,Jiacheng Hao,Youlang Du,Zhen Jiang,Xinche Zhang,Yuhao Sun,Sen Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BridgeMIL is a two-stage framework for EEG-based disease diagnosis that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains an encoder using contrastive-style alignment of temporally nearby windows and within-subject sub-bags with variance/covariance regularization (no negative pairs), and Stage 2 transfers it to an attention-based MIL aggregator with supervision only at the subject level. It achieves the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings and an overall 76.57% mean accuracy, 4.28 points above the strongest baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard EEG-based disease diagnosis pipelines segment recordings into instances that all inherit the subject label, implicitly assuming every instance provides equally reliable diagnostic evidence. While multiple instance learning (MIL) avoids this inherited-label problem by treating subjects as bags, EEG datasets have far fewer subjects than instances, limiting representation quality in end-to-end MIL. The paper motivates a framework that learns from abundant instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances while aligning supervision with the true subject-level prediction objective.

Method: BridgeMIL is a two-stage framework. Stage 1 pretrains an encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags; variance and covariance regularization prevent representation collapse and reduce redundancy without requiring negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the pretrained encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject-level predictions, and limits representation drift via feature retention.

Result: Across three EEG disease datasets and five representative backbones, BridgeMIL achieves the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings with an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 4.28 percentage points. Analyses show substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater sensitivity to subject scarcity than instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved class separation.

Conclusion: Aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances without inherited labels is crucial. The variation in inherited-label reliability and the greater sensitivity to subject scarcity highlight the need for subject-aware supervision. The resulting structured representation space with distinct subject clusters underscores the framework's effectiveness for EEG-based disease diagnosis.

Abstract: EEG-based disease diagnosis requires one prediction per subject, yet common pipelines segment recordings into short instances, inherit the subject label for every instance, and train instance-level classifiers. This assumes that all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence. Multiple instance learning (MIL) avoids inherited labels by treating each subject as a bag. However, EEG datasets contain far fewer subjects than instances, which can limit the quality of the representations learned by end-to-end MIL. We propose BridgeMIL, a two-stage framework that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags. Variance and covariance regularization prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject predictions, and limits representation drift through feature retention. Across three EEG disease datasets and five representative backbones, BridgeMIL attains the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings and an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater performance sensitivity to subject scarcity than to instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved separation between diagnostic classes. Together, these findings underscore the importance of aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances.

</details>


### [247] [Flat Score, Amplified Failures: How the Error Budget Masks Damage in Quantized LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27275)
*Jiwon Jang,Kisu Yang,Heuiseok Lim,Hyunwoo Park*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Post-training 4-bit weight quantization appears lossless on standard benchmarks for multi-turn tool-calling agents, but this masks real damage: quantization amplifies pre-existing failure patterns (e.g., tool-name hallucinations) by up to 2.5x in volume, while a large error budget hides the score gap. Shrinking the budget or applying a targeted repair prompt reveals and removes the exact damage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantization to 4-bit weights is widely claimed to be nearly lossless, but this claim is based on standard metrics that may mask underlying process-level degradation. The authors test this claim in the increasingly important setting of multi-turn, tool-calling agents where measurement fidelity matters most.

Method: The study evaluates two open-weight model families (dense and MoE variants) across two domains on τ²-bench at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weight quantization (eight cells, 456 episodes each). They compare standard task reward with process-level diagnostics: per-channel error rates, failure-set overlap (rank correlation), shrinking error budgets (10 to 2 errors), and equivalence testing to bound score changes. They also apply a targeted error-repair prompt across precisions.

Result: No score change survives multiple-comparison correction; the largest-damage cell has change bounded within ±7.5 points. However, quantization amplifies pre-existing failures (tool-name hallucination in telecom; same trend in retail) by up to 2.5x in volume (+17.6 points per task) while creating essentially no new failures (rank correlation ≥ 0.94, 0.18% novel events). The 10-error budget masks the gap; shrinking to 2 errors exposes a 17-point gap only in the cell with added error volume. A targeted repair prompt removes damage exactly where it exists.

Conclusion: Standard task reward can mask quantization damage in tool-calling agents. Two cheap diagnostics—per-channel error rate and success under a shrinking error budget—should be reported alongside task reward, since both derive from logs benchmarks already collect.

Abstract: Post-training quantization to 4-bit weights is widely reported to be nearly lossless. We test this claim for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, where it now matters most. On $τ^2$-bench, across two open-weight model families in dense and MoE variants and two domains (eight cells, 456 episodes each, at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weights), quantization indeed looks free on the standard metric. No cell shows a score change that survives multiple-comparison correction, and in the cell that carries the largest process damage, equivalence testing bounds the change within $\pm$7.5 points. The process tells a different story. Quantization amplifies the failure the model already exhibits at full precision (tool-name hallucination in telecom, with the same directional trend in retail entity errors) by up to 2.5$\times$ in volume (+17.6 points per task), while creating essentially no new failures. The failure set is the same at every precision (rank correlation $\geq$ 0.94, 0.18% novel events). The score stays flat because the benchmark's ten-error budget absorbs the extra failures. Shrinking the budget to two errors re-exposes a score gap of 17 points, and it does so only in the one cell where quantization added error volume, exactly as the masking account predicts. A targeted error-repair prompt, run for five telecom models at every precision, removes the damage exactly and only where it lives. Both diagnostics, the per-channel error rate and success under a shrinking budget, come from logs benchmarks already collect; we suggest reporting them alongside task reward.

</details>


### [248] [RIPPLE: Generating Multi-Channel Phase, Not Recovering It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27775)
*Jaehyuk Lee,Yeajin Lee,Dayeon Shin,Donghun Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues that phase should be generated rather than recovered in multi-channel generative models for spatial audio and seismograms, since inter-channel phase relationships carry physical content that channel-independent recovery cannot preserve. It presents RIPPLE, which reinterprets Griffin-Lim as a phase prior and uses a rectified flow with explicit inter-channel phase loss. Experiments on ambisonics and seismic tasks show RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines, reducing S-wave polarization error from 57.3° (random) to 33.8°.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing generative models synthesize high-fidelity magnitude spectra but delegate phase recovery to channel-independent modules (Griffin-Lim, vocoders, latent decoders). This fails for multi-channel waveforms where physical information (spatial audio, three-component seismograms) lives in inter-channel phase relationships. The failure is invisible because magnitude-based metrics don't capture inter-channel phase coherence collapse, so pipelines can discard physical information while scoring well.

Method: RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning) reinterprets Griffin-Lim as a phase prior rather than a final estimator. It initializes from the source phase to carry inter-channel structure, then uses a rectified flow to refine toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss.

Result: Tested on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation, RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on coherence metrics. In the seismic case, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the 57.3° random expectation, while learned phase reduces it to 33.8° across architecturally distinct generators.

Conclusion: Phase should be generated, not recovered, for multi-channel audio and seismic data. RIPPLE demonstrates that learned phase generation with inter-channel coherence preservation significantly outperforms channel-independent phase recovery, validated across two physically unrelated domains.

Abstract: Generative models synthesize magnitude spectra with high fidelity, while phase is delegated to a recovery module---Griffin--Lim, a vocoder, or a latent decoder---applied independently to each channel. For multi-channel waveforms this delegation is costly: the physical content of spatial audio and three-component seismograms lives in the phase relationships between channels, precisely what channel-independent recovery cannot produce. The cost is also invisible, since the magnitude-based metrics common to both fields barely move when inter-channel phase coherence collapses---so a pipeline can discard the physical information in its output while still scoring well. We argue that phase should be generated, not recovered, and present RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning), which reinterprets Griffin--Lim as a phase **prior** rather than a final estimator: initialized from the source phase, this prior carries the inter-channel structure to be preserved, and a rectified flow refines it toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss. Tested on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation---two physically unrelated domains---RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on the coherence metrics that downstream analyses consume. The seismic case is decisive: across architecturally distinct generators, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the $57.3^\circ$ random expectation, whereas learned phase reduces it to $33.8^\circ$.

</details>


### [249] [The Kinetics of Training: A Driven-Nucleation Rate Law for Emergence, Plasticity Loss, and Circuit Control in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27281)
*Lei Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Capability formation in language models is gated by a no-partial-credit joint alignment of circuit parts—a single rare event whose barrier scales with the number of missing parts. This yields a rate equation (sites × attempts × drive × exp(−βK) − destruction) that predicts forward ignition, backward catastrophic delays, and a targeted cure (re-initializing query-key slices).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding why capabilities appear suddenly in language models, and specifically identifying the rate-limiting step: the joint alignment of all circuit parts failing is worth nothing, so task performance is zero until every part aligns in one stochastic attempt.

Method: The authors derive a no-partial-credit joint alignment model leading to a rate equation: sites × attempts × drive × exp(−βK) − destruction. They test it three ways with preregistered frozen constants: (1) forward ignition prediction once a concentration floor is crossed; (2) backward analysis of learnability delays and critical steps beyond which capabilities never ignite; (3) ablation experiments across Pythia (7 capabilities, 3 scales) and a controlled gated-attention transformer, plus installing an annealed noise schedule to satisfy and manipulate circuit dynamics.

Result: Ablating one part leaves a median 17% of capability in 32/32 discriminating cells (partial credit predicts 50–83%, p=2e-10); random non-part heads leave 100%. The rate equation forward-predicts ignition (10/10 above concentration floor vs 0/12 below) and dates arrival within 5% median error on six held-out models. Backward, delays grow until a critical step where capabilities never ignite, though validation loss falls smoothly (standard monitors are blind). The cure—re-initializing only query-key slices—restores learnability 6/6, while value slices do nothing (0/6).

Conclusion: Capability formation is dominated by a single rare joint-alignment event whose barrier grows with missing parts. This yields an accurate rate equation in three preregistered regimes, a diagnostic of damage localized to query-key heads committing to base data, and a targeted cure. Applied up to 1.4B transformers, with annealed noise installed to control circuit melting and pinning on schedule.

Abstract: A capability appears in a language model when the last parts of its circuit align in one stochastic attempt, and getting all but one right is worth nothing. We show this no-partial-credit joint alignment is the rate-limiting step of capability formation. Two fingerprints: in a shortcut-free apparatus a five-part circuit missing three waits as long as a three-part circuit missing three (1.19-1.37), so the wait counts missing parts, not size; and on Pythia across seven capabilities and three scales, ablating one part leaves a median 17% of the capability in 32 of 32 discriminating cells, where partial credit predicts 50-83% (p = 2e-10), while a random non-part head leaves 100%.
  One rare event whose barrier grows with missing parts yields a rate equation -- sites x attempts x drive x exp(-beta*K), minus destruction -- read three ways, each preregistered with frozen constants. Forward: a capability flat at baseline ignites at a step of our choosing once the mix passes a concentration floor (10/10 above, 0/12 below), and while still flat its arrival is datable from its precursor to 5% median error on six held-out models. Backward: the delay to learn a withheld capability grows with waiting until, past a critical step, it never ignites -- yet validation loss falls smoothly throughout, so standard monitors are blind to it. We locate the damage (heads commit to the base data) and isolate the cure: re-initializing only the query-key slices restores learnability (6/6) while the value slices do nothing (0/6). We prove the mechanism in a controlled gated-attention model: occupation forces a deadline whose consequences need no mixing assumption. Completed: SGD's noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test, so we install one and anneal, melt and pin circuits on schedule. Scope: conjunction circuits in transformers to 1.4B.

</details>


### [250] [Benchmarking the Residual: What Long-Horizon Evaluations Add Beyond Matched Short-Task Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27283)
*Chao Peng,Zhiheng Lyu,Peijie Dong,Hande Dong,Qiang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This position paper argues that long-horizon benchmark failures must be rigorously diagnosed by comparing full-task success against a baseline prediction derived from short, individual stages, introducing the "horizon residual" metric to quantify the gap between predicted and actual performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current long-horizon benchmarks only show that agents fail more on longer tasks but don't explain why. Failures could stem from error compounding across stages, harder individual decisions, or trajectory-induced degradation (context rot, accumulated environment changes). The paper aims to clarify how to properly claim and diagnose "long-horizon failure."

Method: The paper proposes that benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction computed from short, individual stages using the same agent configuration. The log-ratio between prediction and actual success (horizon residual) quantifies how much the full rollout deviates from the stage-wise baseline. Stage selection, checkpoints, information, and budgets must be specified in advance.

Result: The horizon residual reveals whether full-task performance differs from the short-stage baseline; however, the residual alone does not explain the cause—targeted follow-up experiments are still required to identify whether the gap is due to error compounding, trajectory-induced degradation (e.g., context rot), or other factors.

Conclusion: To legitimately claim a "long-horizon failure," benchmarks must use a principled comparison between full-task and stage-wise performance with a pre-specified protocol. The horizon residual provides a rigorous diagnostic but should be paired with targeted experiments to explain the underlying mechanisms of degradation.

Abstract: Long-horizon benchmarks often show that agents fail more as tasks become longer. This observation is useful for deployment, but it does not by itself explain why failure occurs. More stages create more opportunities for ordinary errors to compound; longer tasks may also contain harder individual decisions or become harder as conversation history, tool outputs, and environment changes accumulate. We use trajectory-induced degradation to mean this last possibility: earlier execution makes later work harder. When the harmful accumulation is specifically the text visible to the model, it is often called context rot. In this position paper, we argue that to claim a "long-horizon failure", benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages. We call the log-ratio between this prediction and actual success the horizon residual. The comparison must use the same agent configuration and specify in advance how stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets will be chosen. The residual shows that the full rollout differs from the chosen baseline; targeted experiments are still needed to explain why.

</details>


### [251] [TIER-MoE: Trust-Informed Expert Routing via Conditional Modality Risk for Multimodal Fusion in Biomedical Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27289)
*Yu Chang,Anzhe Cheng,Chenwei Wu,Zhuoran Wang,Jiahao Chen,Tamoghna Chattopadhyay,Sophia I. Thomopoulos,Paul M. Thompson,Liyue Shen,Paul Bogdan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TIER-MoE is a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model for multimodal fusion that defines sample-specific modality reliability as the expected prediction loss of unimodal predictors, learned from out-of-fold predictions. It combines this risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing while an always-active shared path preserves multimodal complementarity. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods on four public multimodal biomedical datasets across Alzheimer's disease, skin-lesion malignancy, and retinal classification tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: More evidence in multimodal fusion does not always yield better predictions. Existing fusion models advance cross-modal interaction and sample-adaptive fusion, but the influence assigned to a modality during fusion does not reveal whether that source is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to a specialized expert—a critical limitation for reliable fusion.

Method: TIER-MoE defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss its unimodal predictor is expected to incur. This risk is estimated from out-of-fold predictions generated by models not trained on the corresponding sample. The model combines the estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while an always-active shared path preserves multimodal complementarity.

Result: Evaluated on four public multimodal biomedical datasets (Alzheimer's disease status, skin-lesion malignancy, retinal classification), TIER-MoE demonstrates superiority over state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score, and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

Conclusion: Risk-guided modality reliability, learned from out-of-fold predictions, enables principled sparse modality-expert routing in mixture-of-experts models, yielding better predictive performance, calibration, and generalization in multimodal biomedical classification.

Abstract: The promise of multimodal fusion lies in combining complementary sources of evidence, yet more evidence does not always yield a better prediction. Recent multimodal models have advanced fusion through richer cross-modal interaction and sample-adaptive fusion. However, the influence assigned to a modality during fusion does not reveal whether that source is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to a specialized expert. To address this limitation, we introduce TIER-MoE, a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model that defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss its unimodal predictor is expected to incur. This risk is learned from out-of-fold predictions generated by models that were not trained on the corresponding sample. TIER-MoE combines the estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while an always-active shared path preserves multimodal complementarity. We evaluate TIER-MoE on four public multimodal biomedical datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease status, skin-lesion malignancy, and retinal classification. Results demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

</details>


### [252] [EvoCause: LLM-Guided Evolution of Causal Graphs for Root Cause Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27290)
*Lei Zan,Keli Zhang,Shifeng Xie,Jiale Zheng,Zehao Xiao,Zhiwei Dong,Ke Zhang,Ruichu Cai,Malik Tiomoko,Lujia Pan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EvoCause is a framework that closes the loop between root cause analysis (RCA) and expert feedback by using LLMs to propose semantically plausible graph edits guided by expert labels, with deterministic validation ensuring correctness. It outperforms baselines on synthetic data and introduces TeleRCA, an expert-annotated benchmark from a production telecom network with 485,681 alarm events, 194 alarm types, and 5,621 resources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing causal-graph-based RCA methods learn a fixed graph from observational logs and predict zero-in-degree alarms as root causes. However, these learned graphs cannot be improved using expert diagnoses of historical incidents, leaving a gap between automated discovery and human knowledge that could refine causal structures.

Method: EvoCause leverages expert labels to constrain which alarms should be source nodes in the causal graph. Since labels do not specify exact edge edits, an LLM proposes semantically plausible graph modifications, while deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity. The best graph is retained on a labeled alignment set, producing a refined graph that yields transparent predictions at test time without requiring additional LLM calls.

Result: On synthetic data, EvoCause initialized with PC causal discovery improves over the unrefined PC baseline by 11.59 (Node F1), 9.40 (Case EM), and 4.59 (Graph F1) percentage points, while reducing normalized Structural Hamming Distance (nSHD) by 0.2379. On the TeleRCA benchmark, replacing human-readable alarm titles with anonymous identifiers degrades Node F1 by 6.12 and Case EM by 8.04 percentage points, showing the value of semantic alarm-name information.

Conclusion: EvoCause effectively integrates expert knowledge into causal graph refinement for RCA using LLM-guided edits with deterministic validation, achieving significant performance gains. The release of TeleRCA provides a valuable expert-annotated benchmark for future research, and the results highlight that semantic information in alarm names plays a critical role in graph refinement quality.

Abstract: Modern telecommunication, cloud, and microservice systems emit correlated alarm cascades when components fail. Root cause analysis (RCA) aims to identify the small set of alarms that initiate each cascade. A common approach learns a causal graph from observational logs and predicts all zero-in-degree alarms in each incident-induced subgraph. However, the learned graph remains fixed and cannot benefit from expert diagnoses of historical incidents. We close this loop with EvoCause. Expert labels constrain which alarms should be source nodes but do not specify the edge edits needed to satisfy those constraints. EvoCause uses a large language model (LLM) to propose semantically plausible graph edits, while deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity and retains the best graph on a labeled alignment set. At test time, the refined graph alone produces transparent predictions without an LLM call. We also release TeleRCA, an expert-annotated benchmark from a production telecommunication network containing $485{,}681$ alarm events spanning $194$ alarm types over $5{,}621$ resources. On synthetic data, EvoCause initialized with the PC causal discovery algorithm outperforms the unrefined PC baseline, raising Node F1, Case EM, and Graph F1 by $11.59$, $9.40$, and $4.59$ percentage points, respectively, while reducing nSHD by $0.2379$. On TeleRCA, replacing human-readable alarm titles with anonymous identifiers lowers Node F1 and Case EM by $6.12$ and $8.04$ percentage points, respectively, indicating that alarm-name information contributes to graph refinement.

</details>


### [253] [THGFM: Dual-Branch Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Fusion Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27303)
*Yixin Peng,Diego Collarana,Er Jin,Stefan Decker*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: THGFM is a web-scale temporal heterogeneous graph fusion model with a dual-path architecture combining shared-space and relational type-partitioned temporal attention branches, fused via Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion, plus Rotary Temporal Attention that injects relative time directly into the attention kernel. It achieves a +3.25% mean gain over six tasks across academic benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing temporal heterogeneous graph methods struggle to balance parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and typically encode time only as additive features outside the attention kernel rather than directly within it.

Method: THGFM proposes a unified dual-path architecture: (1) Shared-Space Temporal Attention branch for parameter-efficient cross-type transfer, (2) Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention branch for relation-aware specialization. These are integrated via Dual-Path Relational–Shared Fusion implemented with Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion, assigning independent type-conditioned feature-wise gates to each branch to avoid zero-sum competition. Additionally, Rotary Temporal Attention rotates queries and keys by half-phases of relative time before matching to incorporate temporal information directly into attention scores.

Result: THGFM outperforms baseline graph transformers on academic graph benchmarks with a +3.25% six-task mean improvement, including peak gains of +12.37% on OAG-CS PV, +4.87% on PF-L2, +1.18% on PF-L1, and +4.24%, +3.73%, +4.61% on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP respectively.

Conclusion: The dual-path architecture with type-conditioned non-competitive gated fusion and rotary temporal attention effectively reconciles cross-type transfer, relation-aware specialization, and direct temporal encoding, delivering consistent improvements over baseline methods on heterogeneous graph benchmarks.

Abstract: Temporal heterogeneous graphs offer a natural abstraction for dynamic relational systems in which diverse node and relation types co-exist and evolve over time. Learning on such graphs requires jointly modeling cross-type structural heterogeneity and the temporal dynamics of interactions, yet existing methods still struggle to reconcile parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and typically inject time only as additive features outside the attention kernel. We propose \textbf{THGFM}, a web-scale temporal heterogeneous graph fusion model that addresses both limitations within a unified dual-path architecture. THGFM couples a \textit{Shared-Space Temporal Attention} branch for parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with a \textit{Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention} branch for relation-aware specialization, and integrates them through \textit{Dual-Path Relational--Shared Fusion}, instantiated with \textit{Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion}: a adaptive mechanism that assigns independent, type-conditioned feature-wise gates to the shared and specialized branches, allowing both to be amplified or suppressed without zero-sum competition. To directly incorporate relative time into the attention score, THGFM further introduces \textit{Rotary Temporal Attention}, which rotates queries and keys by half-phases of relative time before matching. THGFM consistently outperforms baseline graph transformer models on academic graphs benchmarks, delivering a $+3.25\%$ six-task mean gain, with peak relative gains of $+12.37\%$ on OAG-CS PV, $+4.87\%$ on PF-$L_2$, and $+1.18\%$ on PF-$L_1$, and $+4.24\%$, $+3.73\%$, and $+4.61\%$ on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP, respectively.

</details>


### [254] [Position, Not Provenance: Separating Reasoning Mediation from Sycophancy in Medical Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27304)
*Supratik Bhowal,Subhrajyoti Basu,Aritra Gir Mahanta,Anik Pal Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoT-Mediate is a behavioral framework that perturbs clinically meaningful attributes within a medical VLM's own generated chain-of-thought reasoning to measure whether predictions causally follow the edited reasoning. Using a dual-arm protocol (re-prompting vs. prefix-forced continuation) and provenance-controlled interventions on LLaVA-Med and MedGemma across 1,000 VQA-RAD samples, the study finds that prefix-forced continuation yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting, and that contextual position—not stated provenance—is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical VLMs generate CoT reasoning before answering clinical questions, but it remains unclear whether this reasoning causally influences predictions or is merely post-hoc rationalization. Understanding the causal role of generated reasoning is critical for trustworthy clinical decision support.

Method: The framework (CoT-Mediate) combines (1) a dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence with prefix-forced continuation for injecting edited reasoning, and (2) a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to disentangle reasoning mediation from sycophancy. Evaluated on LLaVA-Med and MedGemma using 1,000 VQA-RAD samples.

Result: Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting. Provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Across both models, removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning, while laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute.

Conclusion: The mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness. Contextual position, rather than stated provenance, is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning for prediction.

Abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) generate chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning before answering clinical questions, but whether this reasoning causally influences predictions remains unclear. We present CoT-Mediate, a behavioral framework that perturbs a single clinically meaningful attribute within a model's own generated reasoning and measures whether the resulting prediction follows the edited reasoning. Our framework combines a dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence with prefix-forced continuation, together with a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to disentangle reasoning mediation from sycophancy. We evaluate LLaVA-Med and MedGemma on 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each. Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting, while the provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Across both models, removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning, whereas laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute. These results show that the mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness and that contextual position, rather than stated provenance, is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning.

</details>


### [255] [ZUNA1.1: A more flexible EEG foundation model for Denoising and Super-resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27308)
*Christopher Warner,Jonas Mago,JR Huml,Beren Millidge*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ZUNA1.1 is an open-source 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction, supporting variable-length sequences up to 30s, arbitrary channel configurations/locations, and partial temporal interval reconstruction, achieving performance at least on par with its predecessor ZUNA1 while substantially outperforming standard methods like spherical spline interpolation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a more flexible EEG signal reconstruction model that can handle arbitrary channel configurations, scalp locations, temporal intervals, and variable sequence lengths, overcoming the limitations of prior models and standard reconstruction methods.

Method: ZUNA1.1 is built as a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder that learns to reconstruct EEG signals with flexible input/output configurations—supporting variable-length sequences up to 30 seconds, an arbitrary number of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and reconstruction of arbitrary temporal intervals within channels as well as entire channels.

Result: ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with the earlier ZUNA1 model while being far more flexible across a wider range of reconstruction tasks. It continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods such as spherical spline interpolation used in the MNE package.

Conclusion: ZUNA1.1 represents an advancement in flexible EEG reconstruction, balancing performance parity with its predecessor while greatly expanding its applicability. The model is released open source under the Apache 2.0 license, making it accessible for broad research and clinical use.

Abstract: We introduce ZUNA1.1, a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction. ZUNA1.1 is capable of reconstructing variable length sequences of up to 30s, with an arbitrary number of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels in addition to reconstructing entire channels. We demonstrate that ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with our earlier ZUNA1 model, while being far more flexible and capable of handling a wide range of reconstruction tasks. ZUNA1.1 continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods such as spherical spline interpolation, which is ubiquitously deployed in the MNE package. The ZUNA1.1 model is released open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license.

</details>


### [256] [Modeling Decisions in Blockchain Analytics: A Leakage-Aware Evaluation of Tree-Based vs. Sequential Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27350)
*Michał Bartnicki,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates Sybil bot detection on Ethereum using leakage-aware evaluation. It introduces a Blind-Spot protocol to eliminate label leakage from high-signal smart contracts and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. Results show that under leakage-aware conditions, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while offering lower latency and energy consumption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sybil bots on Ethereum imitate legitimate users to extract airdrop rewards or influence governance. Existing deep learning-based detection methods are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, and their reported performance may be inflated by label leakage from high-signal smart contracts. The authors seek to determine whether sequence models truly outperform tree-based tabular models once leakage is controlled, and whether practical low-latency deployment is feasible.

Method: The approach consists of two key components: (1) a Blind-Spot protocol that eliminates shortcuts associated with high-signal contracts to prevent label leakage, and (2) a Transaction Grammar representation that models wallet behavior using rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. The authors evaluate this on Ethereum actor classification by comparing Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines.

Result: Under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models on Ethereum actor classification while providing lower latency and estimated energy use. The paper also contributes a framework for leakage-aware Ethereum actor classification and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior.

Conclusion: Tree-based tabular models with leakage-aware features are more practical and competitive than complex sequence models for Sybil bot detection, suggesting that reported performance gains of sequence models may be partly attributable to label leakage. The Transaction Grammar representation combined with simpler models offers a more deployable solution for real-time monitoring.

Abstract: Sybil bots are Ethereum actors that imitate legitimate users to extract airdrop rewards or influence governance. Recent Sybil detection methods increasingly use deep learning and treat blockchain activity as a quasi-linguistic sequence. However, complex sequence models are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, and their reported performance may be inflated by label leakage from high-signal smart contracts. We ask whether and how organic users, Sybil bots, and MEV bots differ in the structural complexity of their transaction histories; whether sequential models outperform tree-based tabular models once leakage is reduced; whether transaction order or timing provides the stronger behavioral signal; and whether the resulting models are practical for low-latency deployment. Our approach to leakage-aware Sybil bot detection consists of a Blind-Spot protocol and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. The former eliminates shortcuts associated with high-signal contracts, whereas the latter models wallets using rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. We evaluate this approach on Ethereum actor classification by comparing Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines. We contribute a framework for leakage-aware Ethereum actor classification and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. Our results demonstrate that, under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while providing lower latency and estimated energy use.

</details>


### [257] [Compression-Based Behavioral Similarity for Open-World Sybil Discovery on Ethereum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27370)
*Michał Bartnicki,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a training-free, compression-based behavioral framework for detecting Sybil attackers in EVM blockchains. It uses a symbolic Transaction Grammar synthesized from EVM traces to capture transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent; filters high-signal contracts via a "Blind-Spot Protocol"; and constructs behavioral graphs using Gzip-based Normalized Compression Distance (NCD). The method is validated against supervised ML baselines, temporal splits, and adversarial camouflage stress tests, positioning itself as a leakage-aware, training-free local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Sybil detection methods rely on graph construction requiring direct token transfers and supervised ML closed-set classification, both of which are vulnerable to evolving attack strategies, evasion tactics, and lack of generalization to open-world settings. The authors aim to determine whether compression-based similarity can differentiate Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bots without explicit financial links, and how to make behavioral graphs robust under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations.

Method: The method synthesizes a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM traces, capturing three behavioral dimensions: transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. High-signal contracts are filtered via the proposed Blind-Spot Protocol. Gzip-based Normalized Compression Distance (NCD) is then used to construct behavioral graphs for Sybil discovery. The framework is validated against supervised machine learning baselines, temporal splits, and synthetic camouflage stress tests.

Result: The framework demonstrates that compression-based similarity can differentiate Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bot wallets without direct financial links. The NCD-based core primitive requires no supervised training and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links. Validation includes comparisons against supervised ML baselines, robustness checks under temporal drift, and adversarial stress tests with synthetic camouflage.

Conclusion: The paper contributes a leakage-aware behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery that operates as a training-free local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits. It is explicitly positioned not as a formal open-set recognition system but as a practical, expandable tool for identifying suspicious wallets in dynamic Sybil detection scenarios.

Abstract: Sybil attackers are Blockchain actors that adopt the characteristics of regular users to exploit airdrops or influence governance. Current methods of Sybil actor detection include constructing graphs, which requires token transfers between examined wallets. Machine learning algorithms have been employed as well, but they treat the task as a closed-set classification problem, making them vulnerable to frequent changes in attack strategies or evasion tactics. We address the following questions: can compression-based similarity differentiate Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bot wallets without direct financial links? What is the effect of high-signal contracts on the discovery of Sybils, and how robust are behavioral graphs under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations? Our approach synthesizes a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) traces, capturing separately transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. The high-signal contracts are filtered with our own protocol, called the Blind-Spot Protocol. Gzip-based NCD is used to construct a behavioral graph for Sybil discovery. We validate this framework against supervised machine learning baselines, a temporal split, and synthetic camouflage stress tests. Ultimately, we contribute a leakage-aware behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery. Its core NCD primitive requires no supervised training and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links. We position the method as a training-free local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits, rather than as a formal open-set recognition system.

</details>


### [258] [Explorative Modeling: Unlocking a Third Pretraining Axis and End-to-End Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27372)
*Alexi Gladstone,Heng Ji,Yilun Du*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Explorative Modeling (XM), a new generative modeling paradigm that factors the training loop by exploring K candidate matches between model generations and data, and training on the best match. This novel approach lets predictions commit to modes rather than blurring them. XMs provide two benefits: (1) increasing exploration acts as a third pretraining axis (beyond parameters and data) that monotonically improves performance across images, video, and language, with efficiency gains of 4.1x in FLOPs, 6.2x in samples, and 47% in parameters, achieving 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance; and (2) enabling end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling that matches diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the success of end-to-end training in deep learning, generative modeling remains an exception because existing scalable approaches factor the generation procedure to handle multi-modal distributions, which prevents true end-to-end generation. The authors aim to address this fundamental limitation.

Method: Explorative Modeling factors the training loop instead of the generation procedure: it explores K candidate matches between generated outputs and training data, selects the best match, and trains the model on that choice. This allows predictions to commit to distinct modes rather than averaging (blurring) across them.

Result: Exploration scaling monotonically improves performance across continuous and discrete domains (images, video, language). Gains increase with scale (7% to 36% as data scales; 13% to 23% as models grow). Efficiency improves by 4.1x in FLOPs, 6.2x in samples, and 47% in parameters. Achieves 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance, and matches diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps.

Conclusion: Explorative Models establish a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and serve as a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm, offering both improved scaling properties and dramatically more efficient inference for reconstructive generative tasks.

Abstract: The deep learning revolution, kicked off by AlexNet, taught us that end-to-end training beats decomposing a problem into hand-designed stages. Generative modeling, however, has remained the exception-despite generative models being remarkably capable, they are still not trained end-to-end. This is because, at its core, generative modeling is about handling distributions with many modes, and existing scalable approaches handle this the same way, by factoring the generation procedure, which prevents end-to-end generation. In this work, we introduce Explorative Modeling, a new paradigm that instead factors the training loop, exploring K candidate matches between model generations and data, and training on the best, so predictions commit to modes rather than blurring them. We find Explorative Models (XMs) useful in two settings. First, increasing exploration adds a third pretraining axis beyond parameters and data for existing generative models-where scaling exploration monotonically improves performance across both continuous and discrete domains (images, video, and language). Notably, gains from exploration increase with scale, climbing from 7% to 36% as data scales and from 13% to 23% as models grow, with efficiency gains more than doubling at 3x the compute. Concretely, exploration improves FLOP efficiency by 4.1x, sample efficiency by 6.2x, parameter efficiency by 47%, lifts the strongest of image-generation recipes to a near-state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance, enables scaling how end-to-end existing models are, and unlocks scaling generalization. Second, XMs enable end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling, matching diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps. Together, these results establish XMs as both a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm.

</details>


### [259] [The Convergence Behavior of Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27383)
*Yijiang Pang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides the first convergence guarantees for plain vector-form Adam under heavy-tailed stochastic noise (bounded p-th central moment for p∈(1,2]). It generalizes the online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise, showing Adam converges to (ρ,ε)-stationary points but with suboptimal iteration complexity and p-dependent convergence. When the domain radius is known, the rate matches optimal complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While Adam variants achieve optimal complexity in bounded-variance nonconvex optimization, little is known about their behavior under heavy-tailed noise with only bounded p-th central moments—a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning. This paper addresses this gap.

Method: The authors generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise. They develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam without restrictive parameter coupling.

Result: Adam converges to (ρ,ε)-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise but exhibits suboptimal iteration complexity with p-dependent convergence. This suboptimality persists even when p=2 (bounded variance). When the domain radius is known, the convergence rate improves to match optimal complexity.

Conclusion: The findings provide new theoretical insight into the robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes, identifying both its convergence guarantees and the conditions under which optimal rates can be achieved.

Abstract: We establish the first convergence guarantees for the plain vector-form \emph{Adam} optimizer under heavy-tailed stochastic noise. While several Adam variants are known to achieve optimal iteration complexity in bounded-variance nonconvex optimization, little is understood about their behavior when stochastic gradients admit only a bounded $p$-th central moment for some $p \in (1,2]$, a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning. To address this gap, we generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise. Building on this generalized framework, we develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam, without restrictive parameter coupling. Our results show that Adam converges to $(ρ,ε)$-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise. However, it exhibits a suboptimal iteration complexity and $p$-dependent convergence, a suboptimality that persists even in the bounded-variance case ($p=2$). When the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, a standard setup in related literature, the convergence rate improves to match the optimal complexity. These findings provide new theoretical insight into the robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes.

</details>


### [260] [FunL2O: LLM-Guided Feature Function Design for Learning to Optimize](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27389)
*Bingheng Li,Junyang Cai,Yupeng Zhang,Bistra Dilkina,Jayant Kalagnanam,Dzung T. Phan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FunL2O is the first unified framework that automates feature design for Learning-to-Optimize (L2O) by using an LLM-driven FunSearch-style evolutionary loop to propose executable feature functions, which consistently outperform hand-crafted features across continuous and discrete optimization tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing L2O methods rely on hand-crafted feature functions to map problem instances to ML model inputs, making representation design manual and largely fixed across domains. This is a critical yet overlooked component of L2O pipelines that limits their generalizability and effectiveness.

Method: FunL2O operates in a FunSearch-style loop where an LLM proposes executable feature functions, and a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model while measuring downstream optimization performance to guide further evolution. It is evaluated on linear and quadratic programming (solution prediction and warm-starting), plus mixed-integer optimization via GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search.

Result: Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks and four different LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations, establishing LLM-driven feature evolution as a general and effective approach for automating representation design in L2O.

Conclusion: LLM-driven feature evolution is a general and effective approach to automating representation design in L2O, as demonstrated by consistent improvements over hand-crafted feature representations across diverse optimization problem types and LLMs.

Abstract: Learning-to-optimize (L2O) methods accelerate repeated optimization by training models to predict solutions, warm starts, branching decisions, or other forms of solver guidance. A critical yet largely overlooked component of these pipelines is the feature function that maps problem instances to inputs for machine learning models. Existing L2O methods typically rely on hand-crafted features, making representation design manual and largely fixed across domains. We introduce FunL2O, the first unified framework for automating feature design through LLM-driven program evolution for L2O. In a FunSearch-style loop, an LLM proposes executable feature functions, while a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model and measures downstream optimization performance. We evaluate FunL2O on linear and quadratic programming tasks involving solution prediction and warm-starting, as well as on mixed-integer optimization tasks using GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search. Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks and four LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations. These results establish LLM-driven feature evolution as a general and effective approach to automating representation design in L2O.

</details>


### [261] [ECG-InterpBench: Benchmarking the Interpretability of ECG Foundation Models with Matched-Scale Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27404)
*Yixuan Duan,Wei Qiu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ECG-InterpBench is a benchmark for systematically evaluating the interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations using sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments, spanning 450 cells across six models, five encoder depths, five dictionary widths, and three seeds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ECG foundation-model benchmarks only measure downstream predictive performance, offering no insight into whether internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses.

Method: The benchmark uses sparse autoencoders with matched capacity as measurement instruments. It evaluates six frozen ECG foundation models across five encoder depths, five dictionary widths, and three random seeds, producing a 450-cell interpretability atlas with 75 matched six-model comparison blocks. It assesses sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility/coverage of 49 clinical ECG measurements, and cross-seed feature reproducibility, plus patient-sampling uncertainty and parameterization sensitivity.

Result: ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles, and a matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms that reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models.

Conclusion: ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled and reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability, accompanied by executable evaluation code, manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits.

Abstract: Existing benchmarks for electrocardiogram foundation models primarily evaluate downstream predictive performance, providing limited insight into whether their internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses. We introduce ECG-InterpBench, a benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations. ECG-InterpBench uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments and matches their capacity across models to enable controlled comparisons. We evaluate six frozen ECG foundation models across five standardized encoder depths, five matched dictionary widths, and three random seeds, producing a 450-cell interpretability atlas comprising 75 exactly matched six-model comparison blocks. The benchmark evaluates complementary dimensions of representation interpretability, including sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility and coverage of 49 clinically meaningful ECG measurements, and cross-seed feature reproducibility. The evaluation further quantifies patient-sampling uncertainty, depth- and seed-dependent variation, and sensitivity to the sparsity parameterization. The benchmark reveals that ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles. A matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms that reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. The benchmark is accompanied by executable evaluation code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits. ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled and reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability.

</details>


### [262] [Context-Informed Ship Trajectory Prediction via Conditional Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27418)
*Yuan Guan,Chandler Squires,Timothy Hu,Pradeep Ravikumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The Conditional Informer is an encoder-decoder architecture for long-term ship trajectory prediction that formulates the task as conditional generation. It uses a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where vessel kinematic states query environmental contexts (weather) via cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates—but is not generated by—vessel dynamics. A Modality Masking training strategy prevents catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback. Experiments on AIS and ERA5 data show a 15.4% improvement in prediction accuracy over baselines, and Modality Masking reduces fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Transformer-based trajectory prediction models rely predominantly on historical kinematic states, treating vessel motion as an isolated system. They fail to properly encode the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions—either ignoring extrinsic factors like weather entirely or treating them as peer features in a joint distribution, which fails to capture the causal asymmetry between vessel dynamics and environmental context.

Method: The paper proposes the Conditional Informer, an encoder-decoder architecture that treats trajectory prediction as a conditional generation task. It introduces a Conditional Attention mechanism where vessel states explicitly query environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the causal prior that weather modulates vessel dynamics rather than being generated by them. Additionally, a Modality Masking training strategy is introduced to handle intermittency in real-world data and prevent catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback.

Result: Extensive experiments on AIS and ERA5 data demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Modality Masking effectively prevents shortcut learning, reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

Conclusion: Encoding directional physical dependence between vessel dynamics and environmental context via conditional attention improves long-term trajectory prediction accuracy, while robust training under modality masking ensures reliable performance even when environmental sensors are unavailable.

Abstract: Long-term ship trajectory prediction is a fundamental capability for maritime safety and autonomous navigation. While recent Transformer-based architectures have improved forecasting horizons, they predominantly rely on historical kinematic states, treating vessel motion as an isolated system. In reality, maritime navigation is profoundly modulated by extrinsic factors like weather and constrained by static vessel characteristics. Existing multimodal approaches fundamentally model the joint distribution over states and contexts, treating environmental variables as peer features rather than encoding the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions.
  In this work, we propose the Conditional Informer, a novel encoder-decoder architecture that formulates trajectory prediction as a conditional generation task. We employ a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where the vessel state explicitly queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates - but is not generated by - vessel dynamics. Furthermore, to address the intermittency of real-world data, we introduce a Modality Masking training strategy to prevent catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback. Extensive experiments on AIS and ERA5 data demonstrate that our approach outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Crucially, Modality Masking prevents shortcut learning, reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

</details>


### [263] [Good Rankers, Bad Objectives: Bilinear Contrastive Critics under Expressive Policy Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27422)
*Ayushman Singh,Siddharth Aphale*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Contrastive critics, despite good action rankings, are unsafe to maximize as value-like objectives. Unbounded bilinear scores suffer from norm drift inflating off-support values, and cosine bounding or hybrid critics do not fix the problem—all select off-support actions with comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated/inverted in top score deciles across OGBench navigation tasks and fail to order fixed-query actions by value, whereas Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds. Realized selection costs depend on the task (PointMaze and toy Q* show costs; AntMaze/HumanoidMaze show nulls due to controller self-correction). A training/readout decomposition traces lost ordering to the cosine training objective, and raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contrastive critics are increasingly used as value-like objectives for best-of-K selection, planning, and critic-guided generation, but it is unclear whether good action rankings imply that maximizing such critics is safe. The paper seeks to understand and decompose why unbounded bilinear and cosine-bounded contrastive critics fail as selection objectives.

Method: The authors perform a controlled support decomposition to attribute raw bilinear regret to norm drift, then compare cosine, hybrid, and contrastive critics across four OGBench navigation tasks. They conduct a training/readout decomposition separating the cosine training objective from inference-time normalization, and use simulator rollouts (PointMaze, AntMaze, HumanoidMaze, and a toy Q* setting) to measure realized selection costs. Bellman-trained TD-Q is used as a parameter-matched function-class control.

Result: Norm drift explains most raw bilinear regret; cosine and hybrid critics still select off-support actions with comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile on all four OGBench tasks and fail to order fixed-query actions by value. TD-Q succeeds in the same setting. Realized costs appear on PointMaze and the exact-Q* toy but are null on AntMaze and HumanoidMaze due to controller self-correction. Raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization, implicating the cosine training objective.

Conclusion: Candidate maximization of contrastive critics exploits false positives from norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics remain useful compatibility rankers on navigation and manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar objective.

Abstract: Good action rankings do not make a contrastive critic safe to maximize. These critics increasingly act as value-like objectives for best-of-$K$ selection, planning, and critic-guided generation. Unbounded bilinear scores can let large embedding norms inflate off-support values, but cosine bounding does not remove the failure. A controlled support decomposition attributes most raw bilinear regret to norm drift. Cosine and hybrid critics nevertheless select off-support actions from most pools and incur comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile across four OGBench navigation tasks, and they fail to order fixed-query actions by value. Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds, including in a parameter-matched function-class control. Realized costs depend on the task: simulator rollouts reveal single-step selection costs on PointMaze and the exact-$Q^*$ toy but well-powered nulls on AntMaze and HumanoidMaze, where the controller can self-correct. A training/readout decomposition traces the lost ordering to the cosine training objective; raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization. Candidate maximization can therefore exploit false positives caused by norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics remain useful compatibility rankers on navigation and manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar.

</details>


### [264] [SE(3)-MeanFlow: Few-Step Protein Backbone Generation on Lie Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27431)
*Yikun Bai,Binghang Lu,Yikai Liu,Elaheh Akbari,Soheil Kolouri,Linxuan Wang,Ping He,Shuchan Wang,Ruqi Zhang,Guang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SE(3)-MeanFlow is a few-step generative framework for protein backbone design that extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to the SE(3) Lie group geometry of protein frames, using closed-form average-velocity identities in the Lie algebra so(3) and R^3 for simulation-free training. It introduces an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective for warm-up and uses rectification-based post-training, achieving results that match or exceed flow-matching baselines using several times more sampling steps, with particular advantage in the few-step regime.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion and flow-matching models for protein backbone generation require numerically integrating an ODE over hundreds of network evaluations, each involving a Lie group exponential map, creating a computational bottleneck for high-throughput design campaigns.

Method: The method extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to SE(3) geometry of protein frames, working natively in the Lie algebra so(3) and R^3. It derives closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations, enabling simulation-free training targets. It also introduces an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that removes the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch, serving as a warm-up stage before switching to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss for pretraining and rectification-based post-training.

Result: SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps in protein backbone generation. Its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification allows it to lead at every matched sampling budget, though at a modest cost in diversity.
