Conclusion: SE(3)-MeanFlow provides an efficient few-step generative framework for protein backbone design on SE(3)^N that overcomes the computational bottleneck of ODE integration in existing flow-matching approaches while maintaining or improving generation quality, offering a practical solution for high-throughput protein design.

Abstract: Generative modeling of protein backbones promises the de novo design of proteins with prescribed structural and functional properties. Existing diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality backbones on SE(3)^N, but inference requires numerically integrating an ODE over hundreds of network evaluations, each involving a Lie group exponential map - a bottleneck for high-throughput design campaigns. We introduce SE(3)-MeanFlow, a few-step generative framework that extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to the Lie group geometry of protein frames. Working natively in the Lie algebra so(3) and in R^3, we derive closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations, giving simulation-free training targets. We further introduce an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that removes the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch and serves as a warm-up stage, after which training switches to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss that is used for the remainder of pretraining and for rectification-based post-training. In protein backbone generation, SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps, and its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification lets it lead at every matched budget - at a modest cost in diversity.

</details>


### [265] [Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN for Channel Modeling in Low-SNR Regimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27450)
*Chaofan Deng,Linyu Sun,Jaeho Lee,Arijit Raychowdhury*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NN-CLEAN embeds a multi-head residual network into the iterative CLEAN loop, replacing exhaustive grid search with rapid forward passes while keeping exact mathematical residual subtraction, achieving 96% accuracy at 5 dB SNR matching Grid-Search CLEAN with drastically lower computational cost and near-flat runtime/memory scaling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional ML-based estimators like CLEAN achieve high resolution but suffer from prohibitive computational complexity due to exhaustive grid search, while purely data-driven deep learning approaches lack physical grounding and generalize poorly across variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters.

Method: NN-CLEAN is a hybrid framework that embeds a multi-head residual network into the iterative CLEAN parameter extraction loop. It replaces the exhaustive grid search with rapid parallelizable neural network forward passes while delegating residual subtraction to exact mathematical models to prevent accumulation of non-physical errors.

Result: Monte Carlo simulations show NN-CLEAN achieves estimation accuracy exceeding 96% at 5 dB SNR, matching the Grid-Search CLEAN baseline, while providing massive computational complexity reduction and outperforming subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks. It exhibits near-flat runtime and memory scaling as batch sizes increase.

Conclusion: NN-CLEAN establishes itself as a robust, real-time solution for channel estimation in MIMO systems, leveraging highly efficient parallelization to overcome the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff inherent in existing multipath parameter estimation approaches.

Abstract: Accurate multipath parameter estimation is critical for modern wireless communication systems, particularly in challenging low-SNR environments. Traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation algorithms, such as CLEAN, provide high-resolution parameter extraction but suffer from prohibitive computational complexity due to exhaustive grid search. Conversely, purely data-driven deep learning approaches lack physical grounding and struggle to generalize across variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN (NN-CLEAN), a hybrid framework that embeds a multi-head residual network directly into the iterative CLEAN extraction loop. By replacing the exhaustive grid search with rapid, parallelizable forward passes while delegating residual subtraction to exact mathematical models, NN-CLEAN isolates physical multipath parameters without accumulating non- physical errors. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that NN-CLEAN achieves estimation accuracy exceeding 96% at 5 dB SNR, matching the traditional Grid-Search CLEAN (GS- CLEAN) baseline, while providing a massive reduction in computational complexity and substantially outperforming subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks. Crucially, NN-CLEAN exhibits a near-flat scaling in execution runtime and memory consumption as batch sizes increase. This highly efficient parallelization establishes NN-CLEAN as a robust, real- time solution for channel estimation in MIMO systems.

</details>


### [266] [FADEx: Feature Attribution and Distortion-based Explanation of Dimensionality Reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27463)
*Lucas Greff Meneses,Evandro S. Ortigossa,Claudio Silva,Luis Gustavo Nonato*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FADEx is a novel local per-instance feature attribution method for explaining dimensionality reduction (DR) outputs. It uses first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition via weighted least squares to provide local linear approximations, making it agnostic to the DR method and eliminating the need for out-of-sample mapping. It provides local feature attributions and distortion analysis, outperforming existing DR explanation approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Non-linear DR techniques act as opaque transformations, making it difficult to understand how individual features influence instance positioning in the reduced space. Existing DR explanation methods suffer from limitations such as multiple attributions per feature and restricted applicability to specific DR methods, hindering their practical use.

Method: FADEx computes local per-instance feature attributions by leveraging local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition. Local linear models are computed using weighted least squares, which eliminates the need for out-of-sample data mapping, making the approach agnostic to any DR method. It simultaneously provides local feature attributions and distortion analysis.

Result: Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, FADEx demonstrates effectiveness and versatility in explaining DR methods. Results show it yields robust and reliable explanations, outperforming existing approaches in several aspects.

Conclusion: FADEx provides a generalizable and reliable solution for explaining dimensionality reduction results, enabling better interpretation of structural patterns and reasoning about high-dimensional data organization in projected layouts.

Abstract: Dimensionality Reduction (DR) is a fundamental tool for high-dimensional data exploration, reducing the complexity of latent spaces of machine learning models, and assisting in the explanation of complex opaque models. However, non-linear DR techniques often function as opaque transformations themselves, making it challenging to understand how individual features influence instance positioning in the reduced space. This lack of transparency complicates the analysis and interpretation of structural patterns, hindering the ability to reason about the organization of high-dimensional data based on the projected layout. In order to address this challenge, dimensionality reduction explanation methods have shown promise in improving the understanding of the observed groups and cluster structures. Unfortunately, existing DR explanation approaches tend to suffer from limitations such as multiple attributions per feature and restricted applicability to specific dimensionality reduction methods, which hinder their use. In this work, we propose FADEx, a novel local per-instance feature attribution method that leverages local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition to provide explanations. FADEx computes the local linear models via weighted least squares, eliminating the need for out-of-sample data mapping, making it agnostic to the DR method, while simultaneously providing local feature attributions and distortion analysis. Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, we demonstrate FADEx's effectiveness and versatility in providing explanations and analytical resources for analyzing the behavior of DR methods. The results indicate FADEx yields robust and reliable explanations, outperforming existing approaches in several aspects.

</details>


### [267] [Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27479)
*Aryan Mishra,Randy Martinez,Lizhen Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring (SCGR), a group-theoretic method that augments graphs with a Schreier-Coset graph from a special linear group to mitigate over-squashing in GNNs. It provides theoretical guarantees of spectral gap and bounded effective resistance, reducing effective resistance by 5-40% while maintaining competitive accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-rewiring methods for alleviating over-squashing in GNNs introduce prohibitive structural and computational bottlenecks, fail to preserve critical graph properties, and massively increase edge counts.

Method: SCGR uses group theory to construct a Schreier-Coset graph from a special linear group and augments the input graph with it, creating a low-resistance bypass for long-range communication while providing theoretical guarantees on spectral gap and bounded effective resistance.

Result: Empirical evaluations show SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Conclusion: SCGR offers a theoretically grounded, group-theoretic rewiring approach that effectively mitigates over-squashing in GNNs with bounded structural overhead and preserved accuracy.

Abstract: The information flow in the graph neural networks (GNNs) is fundamentally constrained by over-squashing, where structural bottlenecks impede long range information propagation. Graph-rewiring methods, which modify graph topology, have been extensively used to alleviate this. However, existing approaches often introduce prohibitive structural and computational bottlenecks, fail to preserve the critical properties of original graphs, and increase the edge counts massively. We introduce a novel method Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring , a group-theoretic rewiring method that augments the input graph with a Schreier-Coset graph derived from a special linear group. Our method provides theoretical guarantees, a graph that exhibits spectral gap and a bounded effective resistance, creating a low-resistance bypass for long-range communication. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

</details>


### [268] [Latent States in Neural Networks: Recovering the Temporal Structure of Drifting Data from Model Weights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27482)
*Kevin Guan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether latent regimes in a temporally drifting data stream can be recovered by fitting a hidden Markov model (HMM) to the trajectory of model weights trained on consecutive temporal windows. Tested on Fakeddit (multimodal misinformation) and Yelp (sentiment analysis), the recovered states partition timelines into coherent phases, and classifiers generalize better within states than across state boundaries—an advantage that exceeds naive equal-size contiguous partitions and persists after controlling for temporal proximity and data distribution shifts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data streams commonly drift over time and may transition between discrete regimes rather than change smoothly. The authors ask whether these hidden regimes can be recovered purely from the weights of trained models, with the practical aim of improving transfer/generalization across temporally related data.

Method: Train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows, align their weights, fit an HMM to the chronologically ordered trajectory of weights to recover latent states, and evaluate within-state vs. cross-state transfer. Includes controls for temporal proximity, comparisons to naive equal-size contiguous partitions, correlation analyses with class distribution shifts and weight-space geometry, and permutation null tests after residualizing out class divergence and lag.

Result: On both Fakeddit and Yelp, classifiers generalize better to windows sharing their training window's state than to windows across state boundaries. The within-state advantage survives temporal-proximity control, modestly exceeds the naive contiguous partition baseline, and remains significant against permutation nulls after residualizing class divergence and lag. Effects replicate on both tasks but are attenuated on Yelp, whose label distribution is more temporally stable.

Conclusion: Latent regimes of a drifting data stream are recoverable from model-weight trajectories via HMM fitting. These states capture transfer-relevant structure beyond mere data distribution and temporal proximity, suggesting value in state-aware model selection and adaptation for non-stationary streams.

Abstract: A temporally drifting data stream may pass through discrete regimes rather than changing continuously. We ask whether such regimes are recoverable from the weights of models trained on the stream, using a hidden Markov model (HMM) fit to the chronologically ordered trajectory of those weights. We study this question in two domains known to drift over time: multimodal misinformation detection, using the Fakeddit dataset; and sentiment analysis, using the Yelp dataset. We train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows and fit an HMM to the trajectory of their aligned weights, recovering latent states that partition each timeline into coherent phases. On both datasets, classifiers generalize better to data from windows sharing the state of their training window than to windows across state boundaries. This within-state transfer advantage survives a control for temporal proximity and modestly exceeds the advantage recovered by a naive partition into contiguous states of equal size. Although the states are estimated solely from model weights, they correlate more strongly with shifts in the data's class distribution than with the weight-space geometry used to estimate them. After class divergence and lag are residualized out, the within-state advantage exceeds its permutation null on both tasks, indicating that the states recover structure relevant to transfer beyond the data distribution. Every effect replicates on both tasks but is attenuated on Yelp, whose label distribution is more temporally stable.

</details>


### [269] [A Lightweight Foundation Model for Collider Physics with Multi-Domain Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27501)
*Liangyu Wu,Qibin Liu,Alexander Yue,Julia Gonski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NEXUS is a lightweight foundation model (~3M parameters) using a fully connected autoencoder pre-trained on unlabeled LHC particle collision data. It fine-tunes effectively on downstream collider tasks (kinematic regression, event classification) with small labeled datasets, shows transfer benefits to out-of-domain scientific datasets (gravitational waves, flood forecasting, neural activity), and is computationally simpler than transformers, enabling power-efficient and edge deployments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To demonstrate that foundation modeling for scientific data can go beyond large-scale transformer architectures, achieving strong pre-training and transfer benefits with a lightweight, computationally efficient autoencoder suitable for real-time and edge applications.

Method: A fully connected autoencoder with ~3 million parameters is pre-trained without supervision on charged particle track features from large-scale LHC collision data. Downstream tasks (kinematic regression and event classification) are built on the pre-trained weights, and latent space representations are interpreted and evaluated for transfer to other scientific domains.

Result: Pre-trained NEXUS achieves improved accuracy on downstream collider tasks with small labeled datasets compared to scratch-trained equivalents. Latent space analysis validates representation quality, and transfer to gravitational wave, flood forecasting, and neural activity datasets demonstrates cross-domain applicability. The approach also shows computational advantages over transformer models at comparable scale.

Conclusion: A compact, fully connected autoencoder can serve as an effective foundation model for scientific data, offering competitive transfer learning performance with minimal computational footprint, making foundation models feasible for power-constrained and real-time scientific inference settings.

Abstract: We present a lightweight approach to foundation modeling (\textbf{NEXUS}) that leverages pre-trained learning from collider physics data towards out-of-domain tasks in other scientific datasets, using a fully connected autoencoder model with approximately 3 million parameters. The model pre-trains with no supervision over a large-scale collision dataset from the Large Hadron Collider modeled by charged particle track features. Downstream tasks for collider analyses, such as kinematic regression and event classification, are developed on pre-trained model weights and achieve improved accuracy with only small labeled datasets when compared to equivalent architectures trained from scratch. The benefits of pre-training are additionally investigated through latent space interpretation and application to other domains, including gravitational waves, flood forecasting, and neural activity. Furthermore, the relative computational simplicity of NEXUS is demonstrated compared to transformer approaches at comparable scale, opening the door to power-efficient inference and real-time or edge applications of foundation models in scientific experiments.

</details>


### [270] [Sparsity Induced Identifiability in Matrix Tri-Factorisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27507)
*Tingting Mu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents the first rigorous theoretical study of sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation, enabled by a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Matrix tri-factorisation offers greater modelling flexibility than two-factor models and sparsity improves interpretability and recovery, yet no rigorous theoretical guarantees exist for general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation despite extensive studies on two-factor cases.

Method: A novel decomposition strategy transforms the original tri-factorisation problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems while preserving structural information needed for recovering the original factor matrices.

Result: The derived recovery guarantees characterise how coefficient sparsity influences sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Monte Carlo experiments validate the theory with close agreement to empirical observations.

Conclusion: The work closes a theoretical gap in matrix tri-factorisation by establishing sparsity-induced identifiability guarantees, with validated agreement between theory and experiments.

Abstract: Matrix factorisation is a fundamental tool for exploiting low-dimensional structure in high-dimensional data, with applications such as data compression, denoising, structure discovery, interpretable representation learning, and dimensionality reduction. Compared to conventional two-factor models, matrix tri-factorisation provides greater modelling flexibility, while sparsity constraints often improve both interpretability and recovery performance. Although the role of sparsity has been extensively studied for two-factor matrix factorisation, rigorous theoretical guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation remain largely unexplored. To address this gap, we establish, to the best of our knowledge, the first rigorous theoretical study for sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation. Our analysis is enabled by a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the original problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems, while preserving the structural information necessary to the recovery of the original factor matrices from the observations. Building upon this decomposition, we derive recovery guarantees and structural consistency results that characterise how coefficient sparsity influences the sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments validate the proposed theory and demonstrate close agreement between the theoretical results and empirical observations.

</details>


### [271] [Expanding Data-Agnostic Pivotal Instances Selection Models with Proximity Trees and Ensemble Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27522)
*Alessio Cascione,Mattia Setzu,Cristiano Landi,Paolo Maria Mancarella,Riccardo Guidotti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model for constructing interpretable predictive models. Inspired by decision trees, the method selects representative pivots based on similarity to input instances, functioning as both a pivot selection technique and a standalone predictive model. It extends to pivot pairs (as used in proximity and oblique trees) and ensembles, is data modality-agnostic via pre-trained networks, and demonstrates competitive performance across tabular data, text, images, and time series datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing machine learning decision-making methods are often difficult to interpret. Since humans naturally make decisions by comparing new cases with representative examples, the authors aim to design an interpretable approach that selects pivots to build transparent predictive models.

Method: The method is a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model that selects pivots based on similarity between pivots and input instances, inspired by decision trees. It extends beyond single pivots to include pairs of pivots (as in proximity and oblique trees) and ensembles. The approach is data modality-agnostic, leveraging pre-trained networks for data transformation to handle diverse data types.

Result: Experiments on tabular data, text, images, and time series show the approach outperforms alternative instance selection strategies and achieves competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while maintaining a minimal number of pivots.

Conclusion: The proposed pivot selection model provides an interpretable predictive framework that is effective across multiple data modalities, competitive with state-of-the-art interpretable models, and achieves this with a minimal set of pivots, aligning with natural human decision-making processes.

Abstract: As decision-making processes grow more complex, machine learning tools have become essential for tackling business and societal challenges. However, many existing methods rely on decision-making procedures that are difficult to interpret. Since humans naturally make decisions by comparing new cases with a few representative examples, we aim to design an approach that selects such pivots to construct an interpretable predictive model. Inspired by decision trees, we propose a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model based on the similarity between pivots and input instances. Our method functions both as a pivot selection technique and a standalone predictive model. Extending beyond single pivots, we incorporate pairs of pivots that are used by proximity and oblique trees, as well as ensembles, which enhance the versatility and effectiveness of our proposal. Additionally, our approach is data modality-agnostic, leveraging pre-trained networks for data transformation. Experiments across diverse datasets, including tabular data, text, images, and time series, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming alternative instance selection strategies and achieving competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while maintaining a minimal number of pivots.

</details>


### [272] [Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps for Few-Step Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27529)
*Mansoor Ahmed,Yue-Tsz Fan,Hemanth Venkateswara,Murray Patterson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a from-scratch flow-map kernel for discrete text generation that expresses correlated denoising steps natively. LKF is a mixture of M factorized components tied by a single shared latent, allowing a single step to place mass on correlated completions with the same sampling time complexity as factorized models. The Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM) is shown to be a special case at M=1. Experiments on LM1B and WikiText-103 show 2.1x-3.3x generative perplexity improvements over likelihood baselines, with gains growing with M, surpassing distilled and rectified few-step samplers at M=8.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models factorize transitions across positions and decide every token independently to keep each step cheap, making few-step text generation challenging due to position couplings (e.g., subject-verb agreement). Existing few-step methods distill or rectify a slow teacher, inheriting the teacher's quality ceiling. The authors instead ask whether a model can express correlated steps natively without distillation.

Method: LKF introduces a flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M factorized components tied by a single shared latent. Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap and factorized, and the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M. One latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory, maintaining the same sampling time complexity as factorized models. MDLM is a special case at M=1.

Result: On LM1B and WikiText-103 benchmarks for unconditional text generation, LKF learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over likelihood baselines without losing diversity. The improvement grows with M, and at M=8, LKF surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers.

Conclusion: LKF demonstrates that correlated denoising steps can be expressed natively in flow-map kernels via a mixture-of-components architecture tied by a shared latent, bypassing the quality ceiling of distilled/rectified teachers while maintaining computational efficiency. The gains scale with the number of components M, offering a promising direction for few-step discrete text generation.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models denoise a sequence over many steps, but to keep each step cheap, they factorize the transition across positions and decide every token independently. This makes few-step generation challenging for text when the target couples two positions, such as a subject and a verb that must agree. An independent update commits to them separately, and many function evaluations are spent repairing the mismatch. Existing few-step methods buy back the lost correlation by distilling or rectifying a slow teacher, and so inherit the teacher's quality ceiling. We ask instead whether a model can express correlated steps natively, and answer with Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a from-scratch flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M factorized components tied by a single shared latent. Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap, and the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M. We show that a single step places mass on correlated completions with the same sampling time complexity as a factorized model, since one latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory. We also show that the Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM) is a special case of our LKF model at M=1. The experiments for unconditional text generation on the One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks show that our LKF model learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over the likelihood baselines without losing diversity. The gain grows with M, and at M=8, it surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mansoor181/lkf.git

</details>


### [273] [When Does Explicit View Routing Work? A Controlled Study of Multi-View Graph-Text Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27530)
*Xiao Yue,Guangzhi Qu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether multi-view graph-text retrieval models perform true semantic routing (content-based) or merely architectural channelization (head-based) when handling multiple semantic aspects of graphs. Using controlled MV-GTA experiments with deterministic text segments on BBBP and BACE datasets, they find evidence for explicit, externally grounded label and property routing, but not for free-form routing or consistent multi-view specialization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph-text retrieval models typically embed entire graphs and texts into a single space even when queries concern only one semantic aspect (e.g., class label vs. molecular property). Multiple heads can separate these aspects, but changing the query head may alter retrieval even when the wrong text is sent—indicating architectural channelization rather than semantic routing. The authors seek to resolve whether multi-head behavior reflects genuine content-based routing or merely architectural artifact.

Method: The authors construct a controlled version of MV-GTA using: (1) deterministic, verifiable text segments, (2) isolated text encoders, (3) view-specific graph heads, and (4) relevance derived from external labels or RDKit descriptors. They use correct routing versus per-sample derangements as a causal test of content-dependent retrieval on BBBP and BACE datasets. They compare joint models against separately trained Single specialists in a matched three-seed comparison, and evaluate property paraphrase augmentation against a matched-exposure canonical control. Hard-template and consistency extensions are also examined.

Result: Correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305 to 0.685 over deranged training. The expected graph head outperforms the best wrong head by 0.303 to 0.453. Topology does not specialize consistently across the two datasets. In a matched three-seed comparison, one joint model achieves mean topology/label/property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877 versus three Single specialists at 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140 and 0.147 over a matched-exposure canonical control. However, consistency and hard-template extensions can reduce canonical retrieval in some settings.

Conclusion: The evidence supports explicit, externally grounded label and property routing and observed multi-interface consolidation, but it does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to separately trained specialists, or superior downstream prediction performance. The distinction between architectural channelization and true semantic routing is therefore only partially resolvable.

Abstract: Graph-text retrieval typically maps a graph and its description to a single embedding, even when a query concerns only one semantic aspect, such as a class label or molecular property. Multiple heads can separate these aspects, but a change in the query head may alter retrieval even when the wrong text is sent to that head. Such behavior demonstrates architectural channelization, not necessarily semantic routing. We examine the conditions under which this distinction can be resolved. Our controlled version of MV-GTA uses deterministic, verifiable text segments; isolated text encoders; view-specific graph heads; and relevance derived from external labels or RDKit descriptors. Correct routing and per-sample derangements form a causal test of whether retrieval depends on content. On BBBP and BACE, correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305 to 0.685 over deranged training. The expected graph head exceeds the best wrong head by 0.303 to 0.453. Topology does not specialize consistently across the two datasets. In a matched three-seed comparison, one joint model obtains mean topology, label, and property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877; three separately trained Single specialists obtain 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation also improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140 and 0.147 over a matched-exposure canonical control. Consistency and hard-template extensions, however, reduce canonical retrieval in some settings. The evidence is therefore limited to explicit, externally grounded label and property routing and observed multi-interface consolidation. It does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or superior downstream prediction.

</details>


### [274] [Subtract or Replay? Exact Deletion from Language-Model Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27539)
*Vishwajith Ramesh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Exact deletion from pretrained language-model memory depends on memory representation: addressable/stationary influence can be removed algebraically (decrement), while influence entangled in shared recurrent state requires rewind-and-replay from before the offending write. Demonstrated in Gemma 3 with support-vector memory (decrement matches retained-key refit to median KL 5.4e-15 at 1B; indistinguishable from never-ingested floor under multiple attack vectors) and Kimi Linear hybrid at 48B (fixed decrement for additive writes, corrected decrement for diagonal decay, rewind-and-replay for delta-rule entanglement), achieving bit-for-bit exact deletion in deterministic MLX up to 18,842-token contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish that exact (not approximate) deletion from persistent language-model memory is possible in principle, and to characterize precisely which deletion strategy is required depending on how a record is represented in memory — enabling verifiable data removal with guarantees rather than heuristics.

Method: Compare two memory architectures: (1) Gemma 3 whose global-attention layers are replaced with support-vector memory, using algebraic decrement and low-rank recovery at scales 1B/4B/12B; validate against retained-key refit, masked-refit proxies, and attacks (elicitation, relearning, sampling, LiRA). (2) A 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, where additive writes use fixed decrement, diagonal decay uses a corrected decrement, and the delta rule requires checkpointed rewind-and-replay; validated with real clinical records up to 18,842 tokens in deterministic MLX, checking logits and all recurrent states bit for bit against never-ingested references; amendment via replayed correction.

Result: At 1B, decrement and retained-key refit agree at next-token output to median KL 5.4e-15 over 31 deletions, with +2.0% perplexity relative to matched fine-tune; masked-refit is indistinguishable from the never-ingested floor under all attack probes. Cost rises to 11.2% (4B) and 44.3% (12B) while certificate ordering persists. For Kimi Linear, additive and diagonal-decay writes admit closed-form decrements, but the delta rule makes 12–49% of record contribution suffix-dependent, requiring rewind-and-replay, which matches never-ingested states bit for bit at 18,842-token contexts.

Conclusion: Exact deletion is a property of how memory represents a record, not a generic capability: subtract addressable (stationary) records directly, and replay entangled (stateful) writes from a checkpoint before the write. This yields two complementary, exact deletion mechanisms and also supports exact amendment via replayed corrections.

Abstract: Exact deletion from persistent language-model memory depends on how that memory represents a record. Addressable influence can be removed by algebraic decrement; influence transformed by later writes inside shared recurrent state requires rebuilding from before the write. We test this distinction in two pretrained models against explicit record-omitted references. First, we replace Gemma 3's global-attention layers with support-vector memory. After low-rank recovery at 1B, decrement and retained-key refit agree at the next-token output to median KL $5.4\times10^{-15}$ over 31 support-token deletions, with $+2.0\%$ perplexity relative to a matched fine-tune. A masked-refit proxy is indistinguishable from the never-ingested floor under elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA attacks. At 4B and 12B, certificate ordering persists but utility cost rises to $11.2\%$ and $44.3\%$. Second, in a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, additive writes admit a fixed decrement and diagonal decay a corrected one, whereas the delta rule makes $12$--$49\%$ of a record's contribution suffix-dependent. Checkpointed rewind-and-replay deletes real clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens, matching never-ingested logits and all recurrent states bit for bit within a deterministic MLX implementation; replaying a correction provides exact amendment. Exact deletion is therefore a property of memory representation: subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes.

</details>


### [275] [Memory Efficient Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27546)
*Shuting Luo,Monika Mikhail Kanaan,Cameron Gordon,Anna Leontjeva,Simon Lucey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the memory requirements of Tabular Foundation Models (e.g., TabPFN) and demonstrates that model compression techniques can achieve up to 7.6x memory reduction (nearly 87%) while maintaining similar performance levels, providing practical guidance for efficient deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While Tabular Foundation Models like TabPFN have shown strong performance on in-context tabular machine learning tasks, often surpassing classical baselines, their practical deployment considerations—particularly memory requirements—have received far less attention. This gap motivates the need to study and address memory efficiency for real-world deployment.

Method: The authors investigate the memory footprint of Tabular Foundation Models and apply model compression approaches to reduce memory consumption while aiming to preserve model performance.

Result: Model compression approaches enable memory reductions of up to 7.6x (approximately 87% reduction in deployment memory requirements) with similar levels of performance compared to the uncompressed models.

Conclusion: The findings provide practitioners with actionable insight into efficient deployment of Tabular Foundation Models in practical settings, demonstrating that substantial memory savings are achievable without significant performance degradation.

Abstract: Tabular Foundation Models, such as TabPFN, have received a large amount of recent attention due to their performance on in-context tabular machine learning tasks, which often exceeds classical baselines. However, practical deployment considerations of these models has received less attention. In this paper we investigate the memory requirements for these models. We demonstrate that employing model compression approaches can enable memory reductions of up to 7.6 with similar levels of performance, reducing deployment requirements by nearly 87%. Our work provides insight to practitioners seeking efficient deployment of these models in practical settings.

</details>


### [276] [Strategies for Milestone-driven Start-ups in Multi-activity Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27563)
*Zhengli Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies optimal strategies for start-up firms in a milestone-oriented setting, where firm state evolves as a diffusion process and the entrepreneur chooses among multiple activities affecting drift and variance. The authors completely solve the stochastic control problem with 3+ controls by characterizing the optimal policy through an efficient frontier curve that orders controls by riskiness (drift-to-volatility) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost). Depending on model parameters, the frontier can take different types, leading to qualitatively different optimal policy structures—a first in stochastic control literature.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: New venture start-ups must survive through multiple milestone stages, yet existing stochastic control models with multiple (≥3) controls are extremely challenging to solve. The authors seek to provide a complete, explicit characterization of the optimal activity-selection policy for entrepreneurial firms, giving practitioners intuitive measures to evaluate activities and understand how strategies change across different scenarios.

Method: The paper develops a continuous-time stochastic control model where the start-up's state is modeled as a diffusion process. The entrepreneur selects among multiple controls (activities), each with different costs and effects on the drift and variance of the process. Success or failure depends on whether the process hits an upper or lower boundary. The authors introduce an efficient frontier curve that ranks controls by riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio), and fully solve for the optimal policy structure.

Result: The optimal policy is completely characterized and shows that only controls on the efficient frontier are used. A key novel finding is that the efficient frontier can be of different types depending on model parameters, producing qualitatively different optimal policy structures. This is the first stochastic control model admitting efficient frontiers of different types.

Conclusion: The work provides start-up firms with intuitive metrics (riskiness and cost-effectiveness) to evaluate activities and offers deep insights into how optimal milestone-oriented strategies shift qualitatively across scenarios. The results establish a foundational framework for entrepreneurial decision-making under uncertainty.

Abstract: New venture start-ups need to ``survive'' through multiple stages of reaching milestone targets. We investigate the strategies for start-ups in a milestone-oriented setting. We examine a model of an entrepreneurial start-up firm, where its state is captured by a diffusion process. The entrepreneur can choose between multiple activities (or controls), which incur different cost and determine the drift and the variance of the process. Depending on whether the process reaches a fixed upper boundary or a lower one, the start-up firm succeeds or fails. Continuous-time stochastic models with multiple ($\ge 3$) controls are typically very challenging to deal with. In this work, we are able to completely solve for the optimal policy and provide an explicit characterization of its structure. In particular, the optimal policy only uses controls from a set characterized by a so-called efficient frontier curve that orders the controls by two intuitive measures: riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio). A unique feature of our model is that depending on the model parameters, the efficient frontier curves can be of different types, resulting in qualitatively different structures of the optimal policy. As far as we know, this is the first study that analyzes a stochastic control model which admits efficient frontier curves of different types. Our work provides start-up firms with intuitive measures to evaluate their activities and offers valuable insights on how the optimal strategies in a milestone-oriented setting change qualitatively contingent upon the specific scenario. We believe the results provide a foundational block in the study of entrepreneurial decision-making.

</details>


### [277] [A Montage-Agnostic Encoder for Calibration-Light Cross-User Gesture Recognition from Surface Electromyography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27565)
*Jethro Odeyemi,W. J. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A montage-agnostic encoder that reads EMG electrodes with shared weights keyed by physical coordinates enables cross-user myoelectric pattern recognition, beating per-user baselines on two databases and falling short on a third, with performance tied to baseline signal fidelity rather than training pool size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Myoelectric pattern-recognition prostheses promise multi-gesture control but remain in the laboratory because recognizers trained on one user rarely transfer to another, typically requiring fresh labeled calibration for each end user.

Method: Introduces a montage-agnostic encoder that processes each electrode with shared weights and locates electrodes by physical coordinate rather than channel index, allowing a single architecture to ingest any channel count without montage-specific parameters. Trained across users and evaluated via ablation studies and a subject-count sweep.

Result: Exceeds per-user Hudgins and linear-discriminant classifier by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 across all held-out subjects and by 0.108 on DB2, but falls below it on ten-subject DB5. Each of the encoder's three key components accounts for over half of its 3-shot macro-F1 in an otherwise budget-matched ablation. The margin is flat from nine to thirty-nine training subjects. Self-supervised pretraining gave no benefit once a supervised model was adequately trained.

Conclusion: Cross-user training pool size acts only as a stability floor below which training fails to converge; the direction of comparison across databases is driven by the strength of the per-user baseline, determined by signal fidelity. Comparison outcomes depend on training budget and baseline quality.

Abstract: Pattern-recognition control promises a myoelectric prosthesis that responds to many intended gestures rather than one or two, but the promise has stayed in the laboratory. A recogniser trained on one person rarely transfers to the next, and useful performance usually demands a fresh round of labelled calibration from the end user. A montage-agnostic encoder is introduced that reads each electrode with shared weights and locates it by its physical coordinate rather than its index, so one architecture ingests any channel count without montage-specific parameters. Trained across users, it exceeds a per-user Hudgins and linear-discriminant classifier by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 for every held-out subject and by 0.108 on DB2, and falls below it on the ten-subject DB5. Each of the encoder's three key components individually accounts for more than half of its 3-shot macro F1 in an otherwise budget-matched ablation study. A controlled subject-count sweep shows the margin is close to flat from nine training subjects to thirty-nine, so the training pool binds only as a stability floor below which cross-user training fails to converge; what tracks the direction of the comparison across the three databases is instead the strength of the per-user baseline, which signal fidelity sets. Comparing against an LDA baseline depends on budget spent training models and on how good that baseline is, and self-supervised pretraining had no benefits once a supervised model was adequately trained.

</details>


### [278] [Recognition and Label-Free Adaptation Across Recording Sessions in Surface-EMG Gesture Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27568)
*Jethro Odeyemi,W. J. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A montage-agnostic encoder trained for cross-user, cross-montage transfer in myoelectric control retains 0.688 macro-F1 across recording sessions without recalibration, outperforming a per-user LDA pipeline (0.540) and published source-only baselines. Feature-statistic alignment is the only effective label-free test-time adaptation, recovering performance comparable to a single labelled calibration repetition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pattern-recognition myoelectric control systems suffer from day-to-day variability due to electrode movement, skin condition changes, and arm position differences when electrodes are removed and re-applied. Recalibrating for 20 minutes at every doff/don event is unrealistic, so a robust cross-session transfer solution is needed.

Method: A montage-agnostic encoder is trained for cross-user, cross-montage transfer using data from one recording session and applied unchanged to data from a later session. Trained on ten intact subjects of NinaPro DB6, its performance is compared to a per-user LDA classification pipeline and two published source-only baselines. Five label-free test-time adaptation strategies are also evaluated, including feature-statistic alignment and batch-normalisation re-estimation.

Result: Carried unchanged across recording sessions, the encoder retains 0.688 macro-F1 versus 0.540 for the per-user pipeline, and sits above both published source-only baselines on the per-window metric. Of five label-free test-time adaptations, only feature-statistic alignment improves every subject; batch-normalisation re-estimation collapses the architecture. Feature-statistic alignment recovers about what a single labelled calibration repetition would provide.

Conclusion: Cross-session transfer in myoelectric control can be achieved without user-specific recalibration via a montage-agnostic encoder, with feature-statistic alignment as the sole effective label-free test-time adaptation that broadly improves performance.

Abstract: Recognition accuracy obtained during a recording session does not persist when a user puts on the electrodes again after the electrodes had previously been removed. The electrodes may have moved slightly, the skin may be drier or wetter, or the elbow may be positioned differently; these factors all contribute to day-to-day variability and therefore represent a major obstacle to implementing successful pattern-recognition based myoelectric control systems in daily practice. However, simply recalibrating a user's hand for 20 min at every doff/don event is a clearly unrealistic expectation. A montage-agnostic encoder built for cross-user, cross-montage transfer is trained here using data collected during a particular recording session, and then applied to data collected later in a different recording session without adjusting anything, on the ten intact subjects of NinaPro DB6. The performance of this approach is compared to that of a per-user LDA classification pipeline, and to that of two published approaches that only rely on source data collected from the same recording session. Carried unchanged across recording sessions, the encoder retains 0.688 macro-F1 against 0.540 for the per-user pipeline, and, on the per-window metric the published baselines use, sits above both published source-only results, a band of two points that locates the encoder rather than ranking it. Of five label-free test-time adaptations, only feature-statistic alignment improves every subject; batch-normalisation re-estimation, a standard method in the domain-adaptation literature, collapses this architecture entirely. Aligning the encoder's feature statistics to the new session recovers about what a single labelled calibration repetition would.

</details>


### [279] [Policy Gradient Steering: Interventions from Behavioral Objectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27574)
*Yoann Poupart,Aurélie Beynier,Nicolas Maudet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Policy Gradient Steering (PGS), a method that formulates activation steering in LLMs as a reinforcement learning problem, constructing removable task vectors from policy gradients to enable temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across gridworld, chess, and football domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing activation steering methods fail to steer even a simple policy in a two-route gridworld environment, highlighting a fundamental limitation in current approaches for dynamically changing model behavior at inference time.

Method: PGS accumulates gradients of a temporary behavioral objective over a small set of rollouts or demonstrations to construct a removable task vector, treating steering as a reinforcement learning problem.

Result: PGS demonstrates calibration and reversibility in a two-route gridworld, shows that compatible tactical objectives accumulate constructively in chess puzzles when vectors are fitted independently and combined, and successfully alters specific team behaviors in competitive football with effects transferring across opponents.

Conclusion: Policy gradients provide a natural interface for constructing temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across diverse decision-making domains.

Abstract: Activation steering has emerged in large language models as a lightweight alternative for dynamically changing a model's behavior at inference time. However, we show that existing steering methods fail to steer even a simple policy in a two-route gridworld environment. To address this limitation, we propose Policy Gradient Steering (PGS), which formulates steering as a reinforcement learning problem. PGS accumulates gradients of a temporary behavioral objective over a small set of rollouts or demonstrations to construct a removable task vector. We first demonstrate the calibration and reversibility of PGS in a two-route gridworld environment. Using chess puzzles, we then evaluate independently fitted PGS vectors both in isolation and in combination, finding that compatible tactical objectives accumulate constructively. Finally, in competitive football, we show that PGS can alter specific team behaviors and that its effects transfer across opponents. Together, these results show that policy gradients provide a natural interface for constructing temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across diverse decision-making domains.

</details>


### [280] [MUGEN: A Unified Framework for Efficient Motion Understanding and Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27581)
*Zhankai Ye,Yukai Jin,Bingyang Wei,Bofan Li,Yusen Wu,Fangyi Li,Shangqian Gao,Xin Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MUGEN is a unified motion-language framework that eliminates quantization and multi-step decoding costs by using a single adaptive-length continuous latent autoencoder. It generates motion via one language-model draw and reads the same latent representation for understanding, achieving state-of-the-art results on HumanML3D and SnapMoGen while requiring only K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unified motion-language systems face a fundamental tension: discrete motion codebooks enable coupling but limit generation quality, while higher-quality generators pay growing costs through stacked residual codebooks, masked decoding stages, long autoregressive rollouts, or iterative diffusion chains—none of which benefit the understanding direction. The paper seeks a framework that avoids both the quality loss of quantization and the computational overhead of iterative decoding.

Method: MUGEN uses a single adaptive-length autoencoder that compresses arbitrary-length motion into a few continuous latent slots, which serve as the sole motion representation. A language model generates these slots for text-to-motion and reads them back for understanding. Depth-routed hidden states allow each slot to read from customized transformer depths, and a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, enabling a single draw to capture text-conditional cross-slot variation.

Result: MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D, raises retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen—all at a decoding cost of K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass.

Conclusion: MUGEN demonstrates that a unified motion-language system can achieve state-of-the-art generation and understanding quality without codebooks or iterative decoding, using a single continuous-latent representation with a single generative draw. This suggests that the shared-machinery approach need not compromise on either quality or efficiency.

Abstract: Grounding human motion in language, and language in motion, is a central step toward physical AI systems that can understand, generate, and communicate human behavior. Unified motion--language systems first coupled the two directions through a shared discrete motion codebook, but quantization limits generation quality. The strongest generators buy quality back at growing cost: stacked residual codebooks enlarge the representation; masked decoding stages, long autoregressive rollouts, and denoising chains of tens to hundreds of steps stretch inference; even the continuous-latent designs among them reach their latent only through an iterative diffusion head; and none of this decoding machinery serves understanding. We therefore propose MUGEN, a unified motion--language framework that pays neither cost: no codebook, one draw. A single adaptive-length autoencoder compresses any-length motion into a few continuous latent slots, the system's only motion representation: the language model generates them for text-to-motion and reads them back for motion understanding. Depth-routed hidden states let each slot read from the transformer depth it needs, and a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, so a single draw carries the text-conditional, cross-slot variation a description permits. At a decoding cost of K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass, MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D while raising retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen.

</details>


### [281] [Prox: Training-Free FFN Activation Sparsity via Approximate Intermediate-Channel Salience in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27591)
*Jinyi Liu,Wei Chen,Pengyu Chen,Xinyi Yuan,Minghe Bai,Guoquan Wu,Jun Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Prox is a two-stage training-free framework for activation sparsification of SwiGLU FFNs in LLMs, leveraging input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct channel masks from magnitude rankings rather than exact intermediate-state values, enabling efficient sparse execution of all three projections.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Feed-forward networks dominate memory traffic and computation in LLM inference, but existing training-free activation sparsification methods suffer substantial model-quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in channel-selection strategies. The SwiGLU intermediate state provides a highly effective selection signal, but obtaining it requires costly dense computation.

Method: Prox is a two-stage training-free framework. Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared channel mask derived from the magnitude ranking of intermediate-state entries. Stage 2 computes the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections in SwiGLU FFNs.

Result: Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieves up to 1.99x end-to-end decoding speedup at 70% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.

Conclusion: Prox demonstrates that constructing channel masks from magnitude rankings—rather than exact intermediate-state values—is sufficient for effective sparse SwiGLU FFN execution, delivering superior quality and speed without training.

Abstract: Feed-forward networks (FFNs) dominate memory traffic and computation in large language model (LLM) inference, making them a primary target for activation sparsification. However, existing training-free methods suffer substantial model-quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in their channel-selection strategies. We observe that the SwiGLU intermediate state provides a highly effective channel-selection signal, but obtaining it requires costly dense computation. To address this, we present \emph{Prox}, a two-stage training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs. Prox hinges on the key insight: sparse execution requires only the channel mask induced by the intermediate state, which can be constructed from the magnitude ranking of its entries rather than their exact values. Specifically, Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared mask; Stage 2 computes the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections. Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieves up to a $1.99\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup at 70\% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.

</details>


### [282] [Compliance2LoRA: On-Demand Safety Alignment on Arbitrary Policy Subsets via Hypernetwork-Generated LoRA Adapters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27594)
*Pankayaraj Pathmanathan,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes an adaptive hypernetwork-based framework (called \ours) for multi-policy compliance in large reasoning models (LRMs). Safety policies serve as inputs to a LoRA adapter generator that produces policy-compliant LoRA weights for a single LRM, enabling on-demand policy adjustments without retraining separate models or long-context generation overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LRMs become personalized for different downstream users with distinct safety policy subsets, training a separate model per policy subset incurs severe combinatorial overhead, while in-context learning methods introduce computational challenges from long-context generation. A unified approach that avoids both issues is needed.

Method: The framework uses an adaptive hypernetwork where safety policies are treated as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator. The generator learns to produce policy-compliant LoRA weights that are added to a single downstream LRM, enabling responses compliant with specified policy subsets on demand.

Result: Training the hypernetwork enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance, demonstrated across reasoning models of different sizes and various evaluation datasets.

Conclusion: Adaptive hypernetwork-based alignment is an effective and practical solution for multi-policy compliance in LRMs, addressing combinatorial training overhead and long-context computational challenges while maintaining task performance.

Abstract: Post-training alignment in large reasoning models (LRMs) has significantly improved their adaptability to diverse safety compliance settings. However, as LRMs personalization for downstream users takes center stage, the demand for varying levels of policy compliance grows as different user-specific LRMs must adhere to distinct subsets of safety policies. Training a separate LRM for each policy subset introduces severe combinatorial overhead. While in context learning methods overcome this combinatorial overhead, they introduce additional computational challenges associated with long context generation. To address this challenge, we propose \ours, a unified adaptive hypernetwork-based framework for multi-policy compliance. In our framework, safety policies serve as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator, which learns to produce policy compliant LoRA weights for downstream LRM. When added to the LRM these weights enable the generation of responses compliant with the specified policy subsets. In this work, we demonstrate that training such a hypernetwork enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance across reasoning models of different sized and different evaluation datasets. This highlights the effectiveness and practicality of adaptive hypernetwork based alignment in LRMs.

</details>


### [283] [Back from the Future: Key-Value Cache Management by Counter-Causal Surprise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27600)
*Stephen Gould,Anton van den Hengel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a KV cache eviction scheme for LLMs that removes tokens whose keys/values can be well-predicted from more recent tokens, using a counter-causal attention pass over existing cached representations to score eviction candidates. A fast single-layer approximation is also offered.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV caches grow linearly with context length and exhaust GPU memory for long prompts or outputs. Existing cache compression/eviction methods are needed to reduce memory footprint while preserving generation accuracy, but current approaches lack a principled, in-distribution scoring mechanism tied directly to actual cache contents.

Method: The method runs the model on tokens in their original order, reusing existing KV cache representations, and applies a counter-causal attention mask so each position attends only to its future context. Tokens that are well-predicted by more recent tokens are deemed redundant and evicted. A fast approximation restricts the counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer only, trading a small accuracy loss for significant speedup per refresh cycle.

Result: The strategy achieves competitive or improved performance over other state-of-the-art KV eviction methods across various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets, with the single-layer approximation providing a significant speedup at marginal accuracy cost.

Conclusion: Counter-causal scoring for KV eviction is a simple, effective, training-free approach that reduces memory footprint and speeds up inference while maintaining or improving generation quality.

Abstract: Key-value (KV) cache management through compression and eviction strategies has emerged as an important research direction in recent years. Computational demands of large language models (LLMs) and their multi-modal variants during output generation can be partially alleviated by caching previous key and value calculations needed by subsequent scaled dot-product attention operations. However, this leads to another problem: the size of the resulting KV cache grows linearly with context length and quickly consumes all available GPU memory when either the prompt or the generated output are long. KV cache management periodically prunes entries from the cache thereby reducing its memory footprint while attempting to retain sufficient information for accurate generation. A by-product is faster inference speed. We propose a simple yet effective KV eviction scheme motivated by the insight that past tokens which can be well-predicted from more recent tokens are redundant and their associated keys and values can be removed from the cache. To score entries for eviction we run the model on the tokens in their original order, reusing the key and value representations already stored in the KV cache, and applying a counter-causal attention mask so that each position attends only to its future context. This is in-distribution, tied directly to the actual cache contents, and requires no additional training. To further reduce cost, we additionally propose a fast single-layer approximation that restricts the counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer, achieving a significant speedup per refresh cycle at marginal accuracy cost. We evaluate our strategy on various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets showing competitive or improved performance over other state-of-the-art methods. Reference code is available at https://github.com/metacognitionai/counter_causal.

</details>


### [284] [Kalman Meets Curriculum: Efficient Dynamic Prompt Selection for Adaptive RL Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27610)
*Haodong Zhu,Yangyang Ren,Yanjing Li,Sheng Xu,Haiguang Liu,Linlin Yang,Baochang Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KGPS reformulates online prompt selection for RL finetuning of LLMs as a dynamic state estimation problem using a Kalman filter over latent prompt success rates, adaptively tracking policy drift in difficulty and selecting intermediate-difficulty prompts without extra rollouts, achieving SOTA accuracy and rollout efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL finetuning of LLMs requires selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty, but prompt difficulty evolves non-stationarily during training. Existing evaluation-based methods are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based methods are efficient but assume stationary difficulty, making both ill-suited to RL's dynamic training regime.

Method: KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space via a linear-Gaussian state-space model, couples process noise to the magnitude of policy updates, and uses a Kalman filter to maintain a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty. Prompts are selected by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility favoring intermediate-difficulty prompts while revisiting uncertain ones, requiring no additional rollouts.

Result: Across mathematics, planning, and geometry benchmarks with multiple RL algorithms, KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, it uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while improving average performance by 0.12 point across six math reasoning benchmarks.

Conclusion: KGPS establishes state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods by making the selection procedure adaptive to policy drift while remaining rollout-efficient, demonstrating that framing prompt selection as dynamic state estimation is a productive alternative to static difficulty prediction.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet its effectiveness critically depends on selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty for the current policy. This is challenging because prompt difficulty evolves throughout training. Existing online methods therefore face a trade-off: evaluation-based approaches are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based approaches are efficient but typically assume stationary difficulty, making them ill-suited to RL's non-stationary training dynamics. To address these issues, we propose a Kalman-Guided Prompt Selection method (KGPS), which reformulates prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem rather than static difficulty prediction. KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model, with process noise coupled to the magnitude of policy updates so that uncertainty increases when the policy changes more substantially. A Kalman filter then maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty, and prompts are selected by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while naturally revisiting uncertain ones. The resulting procedure is adaptive to policy drift and requires no additional rollouts beyond standard policy training. Extensive experiments across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks, as well as multiple RL algorithms, show that KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines, establishing state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods. For example, on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while even improving the average performance by 0.12 point across six math reasoning benchmarks.

</details>


### [285] [Real-Time Hard Peak Age-of-Information Safety with No-Regret Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27626)
*Wentao Zhang,Wentao Mo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces OCO-PAoI-Hard, an online convex optimization framework for safety-critical IoT systems that guarantees zero per-slot violations of peak Age of Information (PAoI) hard deadlines under adversarial channel conditions, achieving O(√T) regret with theoretical lower bounds and strong empirical results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety-critical IoT systems (industrial closed-loop control, V2X, teleoperation) require hard per-slot PAoI deadlines, not just average bounds. Existing approaches—Whittle-index AoI, deep RL, and long-term constrained OCO—only work under restrictive assumptions and fail to guarantee zero per-slot violations under adversarial conditions.

Method: The key insight is that the fractional peak-AoI deadline maps exactly to an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, reformulating hard real-time scheduling as time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility via one Euclidean projection per slot, a gradient step maintains no-regret behavior, and the virtual queue becomes an a-posteriori certificate.

Result: The method attains zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds on a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, while four baselines miss between 1.65% and 64.0% of slots. Closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds, a matching Ω(√T) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant against execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio are established.

Conclusion: OCO-PAoI-Hard provides the first principled framework guaranteeing zero per-slot PAoI deadline compliance under adversarial settings with provable no-regret guarantees, closing the gap between hard real-time scheduling requirements and online optimization theory.

Abstract: Safety-critical IoT systems such as industrial closed-loop control, V2X coordination, and remote teleoperation require every sensor's peak Age of Information (peak AoI, also abbreviated PAoI) to stay below a hard per-slot deadline, not merely an average bound. Existing approaches meet this requirement only under restrictive assumptions: stochastic channels for Whittle-index AoI, simulator rollouts for deep reinforcement learning, or sublinear cumulative violation for long-term constrained online convex optimization. Under adversarial coefficients, OCO-PAoI-Hard guarantees zero per-slot violation of the modeled AoI state under one-step viability and O(sqrt(T)) regret against any static safe comparator; packet-level safety requires stronger service assumptions. Our key observation is that the fractional peak-AoI deadline collapses exactly to an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, turning hard real-time scheduling into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility through one Euclidean projection per slot, the gradient step preserves no-regret behavior, and the classical virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate. We establish closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds, a matching Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant against execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio. On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAoI-Hard attains zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds, while four representative baselines miss between 1.65 percent and 64.0 percent of slots, and the empirical normalized regret stays below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.

</details>


### [286] [First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization Over Distributed Networks for Robust Coreset Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27632)
*Yang Jiao,Kaixuan Jiao,Kai Yang,Nadjib Aitsaadi,Ilhem Fajjari,Renwei,Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the underexplored problem of distributed robust coreset selection by formulating it as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints, and proposes F²CTO (Federated First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization), a distributed method that combines hierarchical composite value-function reformulation with a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm. F²CTO achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(ε^{-3/2}) and demonstrates effectiveness on continual learning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With the rapid growth of IoT, massive data is generated across distributed edge networks, making full-data training computationally expensive and storage-intensive, thus necessitating coreset selection. Given the privacy-sensitive nature of local data and the need for model robustness, a distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection is vital but remains largely unexplored.

Method: The paper (1) characterizes hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning, formulating distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints; (2) proposes F²CTO, which integrates a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation with a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm to solve the trilevel problem in a distributed manner.

Result: F²CTO is the first method for distributed robust coreset selection and the first distributed optimization approach for trilevel optimization with level-wise constraints. It achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(ε^{-3/2}) for finding an ε-stationary point, and extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning confirm its effectiveness and efficiency.

Conclusion: The proposed F²CTO effectively addresses distributed robust coreset selection through a novel trilevel optimization formulation and distributed algorithm, with provable convergence guarantees and demonstrated empirical performance.

Abstract: With the rapid advancement of the Internet of Things (IoT), massive amounts of data are generated across distributed edge networks. Training models on full data incurs significant computational overhead and storage bottlenecks, rendering coreset selection a critical paradigm.
