Furthermore, given the privacy-sensitive nature of local data and the escalating demand for model robustness in real-world deployments, developing an effective distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection is vital, yet remains largely unexplored. To this end, this work first characterizes the hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning, and formulates the distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints. Furthermore, to effectively solve the trilevel problem in a distributed manner, the \underline{F}ederated \underline{F}irst-order \underline{C}onstrained \underline{T}rilevel \underline{O}ptimization (F$^2$CTO) is proposed, which synergistically integrates a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation and a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, F$^2$CTO is the first method developed for distributed robust coreset selection, as well as the first distributed optimization approach for trilevel optimization problems with level-wise constraints. Additionally, we prove that the proposed method achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-3/2})$ for finding an $ε$-stationary point. Extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed F$^2$CTO.

</details>


### [287] [Certifying when decision-time information justifies adaptive experimentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27651)
*Jia Bi,Samuel Pinilla,Chenyang Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OPAL is a framework for deciding whether adaptive experimentation should be enabled at all, using a precommitted contract requiring non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk, and positive executed value after cost, with proven impossibility boundaries and empirical validation on Cell Painting data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most adaptive laboratory methods begin after adaptation is permitted, but no principled framework decides whether adaptation should be enabled at all in the first place. The paper addresses this gap by introducing opportunity-aware policy authorization.

Method: OPAL uses a precommitted contract that requires non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk, and positive executed value after cost. It establishes an impossibility boundary showing source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and derives a target-calibrated recovery.

Result: On an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities, achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion, and maintained a 5.18% false-activation upper bound below the 7.5% limit. Among six methods, only OPAL combined non-zero activation with risk control. Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability.

Conclusion: Authorization constitutes a distinct and necessary layer for safe adaptive science, separable from policy misalignment and non-certifiability, enabling safe adaptive experimentation through precommitted risk and value contracts.

Abstract: Adaptive laboratories choose measurements during experiments, yet most methods begin after adaptation is permitted. We introduce Opportunity-aware Policy Authorization for Laboratories (\OPAL{}), a framework that decides whether adaptation should be enabled at all. \OPAL{} uses a precommitted contract to require non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk and positive executed value after cost. We establish an impossibility boundary: source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and derive a target-calibrated recovery. Applied to an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities and achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion; its 5.18\% false-activation upper bound remained below a 7.5\% limit. Among six methods, only \OPAL{} combined non-zero activation with this risk control. Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability, establishing authorization as a distinct layer for safe adaptive science.

</details>


### [288] [Evaluation Protocols and Cross-Subject Generalization in EEG Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27655)
*Hanting Suo,Yuwen Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EEG emotion recognition reported accuracy depends on the full evaluation pipeline (target quantity, development procedure, reporting rule), not just the classifier. Using a DGCNN pathway on SEED and SEED-IV, the study shows dramatically different accuracy estimates depending on subject-dependent vs. subject-disjoint vs. cross-session evaluation, with held-out participant accuracy much lower than training-participant accuracy. The authors argue these evaluation settings answer different questions and should be reported separately.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reported accuracies in EEG emotion recognition are not comparable because they depend on the complete evaluation procedure—not merely the classifier. The paper aims to systematically separate the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule to reveal how evaluation choices distort reported performance and comparability across studies.

Method: The authors decompose the evaluation pipeline into target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule, then apply one archived DGCNN pathway to SEED and SEED-IV. They perform protocol-matched subject-dependent checks, 30 matched SEED subject-session trajectories with checkpoint selection via repeated test-set evaluation, five-fold subject-disjoint training with validation-selected checkpoints, and fully held-out participant evaluation with BCa confidence intervals. Supporting analyses examine participant rankings across representations/time scales and a deviation-selected tail-risk ensemble.

Result: SEED subject-dependent result within 1.47 percentage points of public reference; SEED-IV 3.40-point gap unresolved. Checkpoint selection via test-set evaluation raised mean window accuracy from 0.7855 (epoch 80) to 0.8892. Validation-selected checkpoints gave training-participant trial accuracies of 0.9990 (SEED) and 0.9920 (SEED-IV), but held-out participant accuracies were only 0.5348 (SEED) and 0.3954 (SEED-IV). Participant rankings depended on representation and time scale, and a tail-risk ensemble showed no positive gain in final evaluation.

Conclusion: Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results answer distinct scientific questions and must not be conflated. The large train-to-held-out-subject gaps challenge simple underfitting interpretations but do not isolate subject identity from other implementation factors. Evaluation settings should be reported explicitly and separately to enable meaningful comparison.

Abstract: Reported accuracy in electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition depends on the complete evaluation procedure, not only the classifier. We separate the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule, then use one archived dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) pathway on SEED and SEED-IV as an illustrative case. In a protocol-matched subject-dependent check, the SEED result was within 1.47 percentage points of the public reference value; the 3.40-point SEED-IV difference remained unresolved. Across 30 matched SEED subject-session trajectories, checkpoint selection based on repeated test-set evaluation increased mean window accuracy from 0.7855 at epoch 80 to 0.8892. Under five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation, validation-selected checkpoints achieved training-participant trial accuracies of 0.9990 on SEED and 0.9920 on SEED-IV. Accuracy for entirely held-out participants was 0.5348 (95% conditional subject-level bias-corrected and accelerated [BCa] interval [0.4667, 0.5985]) on SEED. The SEED-IV estimate was 0.3954 ([0.3343, 0.4648]) and is reported only as secondary sensitivity evidence because its protocol-matched compatibility check remained unresolved. The observed train-to-held-out-subject gaps are inconsistent with simple optimization underfitting, but they do not isolate subject identity from implementation, preprocessing, representation, or distributional factors. Supporting analyses further showed that participant rankings depended on representation and time scale, while a development-selected tail-risk ensemble did not establish a positive gain in a separate final evaluation. Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results should therefore be reported as answers to different questions.

</details>


### [289] [Looped Transformers with Source-Centered State Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27656)
*Bum Jun Kim,Kohei Hayashi,Shunsuke Kamiya,Masanori Koyama,Yusuke Iwasawa,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE), a method for looped Transformers that reconciles input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence. SCSE retains input dependence through a learned anchor and initial deviation, guarantees exact anchor invariance via a zero-deviation mask, and improves the recurrent quality frontier across multiple benchmarks including WikiText-2, WikiText-103, and LAMBADA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Looped Transformers reuse the same Transformer block over recurrent depth, but the shared block must govern an entire trajectory of hidden states at both trained and extrapolated depths. Additionally, additive-injection looped Transformers reintroduce an input-conditioned signal at every recurrent step, meaning the shared transition can still move the hidden state even at an input-conditioned reference. This motivates designing a recurrence that reconciles input conditioning with reference-preserving shared computation.

Method: SCSE retains input dependence through a learned anchor and initial deviation. It allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance through a zero-deviation mask, making the anchor a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias (the next deviation produced from the anchor itself) is set to zero, keeping nonzero deviations active for state-dependent recurrent computation.

Result: Across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier. Ablations show the learned anchor and anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence are the primary contributors to the gain, and a case study on a trained model grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

Conclusion: The zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom whose task effect can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial; SCSE resolves this choice in favor of exact anchor invariance by setting the bias to zero. This design yields consistent quality gains across multiple language modeling benchmarks.

Abstract: Looped Transformers create a useful train- and test-time compute axis by reusing the same Transformer block over recurrent depth, increasing effective depth at a fixed parameter count. However, that shared block must then govern an entire trajectory of varying hidden states over trained and extrapolated depths. Furthermore, in additive-injection looped Transformers, an input-conditioned signal is reintroduced at every recurrent step, so applying the shared transition at an input-conditioned reference can still move the hidden state. In this paper, we propose Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE), which is designed to reconcile input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence. Specifically, SCSE retains input dependence through its learned anchor and initial deviation, allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance through its zero-deviation mask. The designated anchor is thereby a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias is the next deviation produced from the anchor itself and vanishes in SCSE, while nonzero deviations remain active and support state-dependent recurrent computation. Our theory shows that the zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom whose task effect can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial; SCSE resolves this choice in favor of exact anchor invariance by setting the bias to zero. Across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier. Ablation studies identify the learned anchor and the anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as the primary contributors to the gain, and a trained-model case study grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

</details>


### [290] [Understanding Submodular Information Measure Based Objectives for Representation Learning: A Variance and Separation Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27660)
*Rishabh Iyer,Truong Pham,Anay Majee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides the first unified theoretical framework connecting Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) to classical concepts in representation learning, showing that Total Information objectives characterize intra-class structure (variance, covariance, imbalance-aware separation) while Mutual Information objectives capture inter-class structure (centroid separation, Mahalanobis-based discrimination, mode overlap), validated with controlled synthetic experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While SIMs have shown empirical success in representation learning through frameworks like SCORE, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood. This lack of theoretical grounding hinders principled selection and design of SIM-based objectives.

Method: The authors develop a unified theoretical framework that bridges SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition. They analyze three specific submodular functions (Graph Cut, LogDet, Facility Location) under two information measure types: Total Information (TI) and Mutual Information (MI), deriving theoretical characterizations for each combination and validating them with controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap.

Result: The theoretical analysis reveals that: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation emphasizing rare and confusable classes; Graph Cut MI relates to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation via Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap. Empirical results from controlled synthetic experiments closely match the theoretical predictions across all settings.

Conclusion: This work delivers the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures, offering principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning based on their formal mathematical properties.

Abstract: Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for representation learning and multimodal learning. In particular, the SCORE framework~\cite{majee2024score} demonstrated that SIMs can serve as effective objectives for supervised contrastive learning. Despite their empirical success, however, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood.
  In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition. We show that Total Information (TI) objectives characterize intra-class structure: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, and Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation that emphasizes rare and confusable classes. We further show that Mutual Information (MI) objectives capture complementary notions of inter-class structure: Graph Cut MI is closely related to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation through Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap.
  We validate these theoretical characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap. Across all settings, the empirical behavior closely matches the proposed theory. Our results provide the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures and offer principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

</details>


### [291] [FedOGL: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Federated Open-World Multimodal Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27665)
*Zekai Chen,Haodong Lu,Shihao Li,Weiwei Ji,Xunkai Li,Xun Wu,Yinlin Zhu,Rong-Hua Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedOGL is a semantic-structural memory preservation framework for federated graph learning that addresses catastrophic forgetting when clients learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while retaining historical knowledge and rejecting out-of-distribution samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In federated multimodal graph learning with evolving class spaces, catastrophic forgetting is not merely a classifier-level failure—old knowledge can be erased through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. No existing method adequately addresses all these forgetting mechanisms simultaneously while preserving privacy.

Method: FedOGL operates on both client and server sides. On the client side, it preserves historical decision behavior via replay and task-start distillation, and protects graph-propagation memory by projecting onto a globally shared structure basis. On the server side, it maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to enable cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data.

Result: Extensive experiments show that FedOGL reduces catastrophic-forgetting-induced performance degradation by 42.67% compared with the best-performing baselines, while maintaining or improving downstream task performance.

Conclusion: The proposed FedOGL framework effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting in federated multimodal graph learning via a dual-sided semantic and structural memory preservation strategy, without compromising data privacy.

Abstract: Federated graph learning enables collaborative training over decentralized graph data without sharing raw graph information. As such risks evolve, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams, retain historical categories, and reject samples outside the known class space. In this setting, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting samples outside the current known class space. The core challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which in federated multimodal graphs is not merely a classifier-level failure: old knowledge can be erased through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedOGL}, a semantic-structural memory preservation framework. On the client side, FedOGL preserves historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation, while protecting graph-propagation memory via projection onto a globally shared structure basis. On the server side, FedOGL maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to facilitate cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with the best-performing baselines, FedOGL reduces performance degradation caused by catastrophic forgetting by \textbf{42.67\%}, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.

</details>


### [292] [Tight Sample Complexity for Low-Rank Adaptation: Matching Bounds and Rank Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27680)
*Arunan J*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides a complete statistical characterization of LoRA fine-tuning by establishing a matching minimax lower bound of Ω(rd/n) for the excess risk of rank-r LoRA estimators, complementing an existing O(rd/n) upper bound. This yields a rank-selection dichotomy: for constrained empirical risk minimization (ERM), the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank and over-ranking hurts, while for adaptive nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators, over-ranking is harmless. The predictions are verified on synthetic and real fine-tuning tasks across DistilBERT and RoBERTa.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LoRA is a standard fine-tuning mechanism, yet its statistical properties are only partially understood: existing generalization bounds lack a matching lower bound, and there is no formal guidance on rank selection. This work aims to close both gaps.

Method: The authors use a local Rademacher argument to establish an O(rd/n) upper bound on excess risk for the rank-r constrained ERM. They then prove a matching minimax lower bound of Ω(rd/n) via a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of R^{d×d}. Combining these bounds yields a rank-selection dichotomy between constrained ERM and nuclear-norm-then-truncate adaptive estimators.

Result: The matching upper and lower bounds of Θ(rd/n) fully characterize the statistical complexity of rank-r LoRA in the locally quadratic regime. Rank-selection analysis shows the constrained ERM achieves optimal risk only at the intrinsic rank with over-ranking penalizing performance, whereas nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators are robust to over-ranking. Experiments on SST-2 and MRPC with DistilBERT and RoBERTa confirm the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks in two configurations.

Conclusion: The paper provides a complete statistical theory for LoRA fine-tuning, showing that the observed over-parameterization penalty is a property of unregularized ERM rather than an inherent limitation of the LoRA class. The results also offer formal guidance for rank selection in LoRA.

Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard mechanism for fine-tuning large pretrained models, yet its statistical properties remain only partially understood. Existing generalization results provide upper bounds of the form O~(sqrt(rd/n)) or O~(rd/n), but a matching lower bound is missing, and the question of how to choose the LoRA rank r has no formal answer. Both gaps are closed here. A local Rademacher argument establishes an upper bound of O~(rd/n) on the excess risk of the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA, whenever the target adaptation has rank at most r. A matching minimax lower bound of Omega(rd/n) is then proved via a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of R^{d x d}; the bound applies to any estimator whose output lies in the rank-r LoRA class. Combining the two yields a rank-selection dichotomy. For the constrained empirical risk minimizer, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r*, and over-ranking strictly hurts. For adaptive estimators of the nuclear-norm-then-truncate type, over-ranking is harmless and the rate saturates at Theta~(r* d / n) regardless of r. Taken together, the three results characterize the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning within the well-specified locally quadratic regime, and identify the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty as a property of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than of the LoRA class itself. Predictions of the theory are verified on a synthetic trace-regression benchmark and on real LoRA fine-tuning across three (model, task) configurations covering DistilBERT and RoBERTa on SST-2 and MRPC. All configurations exhibit the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with two showing statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p = 0.016).

</details>


### [293] [Event-Structured Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Differentiable Critical Clearing Boundaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27681)
*Baoli Hao,Chenxi Hu,Ming Zhong,Ren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) for transient-stability assessment in power systems, which aligns its representation with pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing dynamics, enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces, and uses a differentiable trajectory-induced stability margin to estimate the critical clearing time boundary. The method is validated on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems with a theoretical error bound connecting residual, trajectory, and CCT errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because fault-clearing dynamics require repeated expensive simulations across many fault severities and clearing times. Existing neural surrogates lack structure aligned with the event-based nature of power system dynamics (pre-fault, fault-on, post-clearing), leading to poor accuracy on stability boundaries. A physics-informed approach with explicit event chaining and a smooth, differentiability-friendly stability margin is needed.

Method: The method introduces an ES-PINN whose architecture explicitly segments the representation according to pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics. It enforces exact state chaining at event interfaces. A smooth trajectory-induced stability margin provides a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, enabling boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction via a distilled readout. A local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate is proven, where exact event chaining removes separate state-interface defect terms.

Result: Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses demonstrate effectiveness and computational efficiency.

Conclusion: ES-PINN provides an accurate and efficient framework for transient-stability assessment and CCT estimation by embedding event structure into a physics-informed neural network, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance on standard benchmark power systems.

Abstract: Transient-stability assessment determines whether a power system can recover after a disturbance and is therefore essential to preventing generator trips and cascading outages. A key metric is the critical clearing time (CCT), which specifies the maximum time available to clear a fault before synchronism is lost. Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because complicated fault-clearing dynamics require repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times. We propose an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) that aligns its representation with the pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics and enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces. A smooth trajectory-induced stability margin defines a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, enabling accurate boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction through a distilled readout. We further prove a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate, in which exact event chaining eliminates separate state-interface defect terms. Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show that ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed framework.

</details>


### [294] [NMINE: Normalized Mutual Information Neural Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27710)
*Petra Eerikinharju,Marko Tuononen,Ville Hautamäki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables, combining a MINE-based mutual information estimator with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators. Experiments on Gaussian data from 1-8 dimensions show improved accuracy over KSG-based baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mutual information is unbounded, making its values incomparable across datasets, dimensions, or applications. Normalized mutual information addresses this limitation, but existing estimators remain sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability. A more robust neural estimator is needed.

Method: The approach estimates mutual information via the Donsker-Varadhan representation (MINE-based) and estimates marginal entropies by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution. Combining these yields a neural normalized mutual information estimator.

Result: Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show the proposed estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline.

Conclusion: Neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.

Abstract: Mutual information is a general measure of statistical dependence that captures both linear and nonlinear relationships between random variables. For continuous and multidimensional variables For continuous multidimensional variables, mutual information must be estimated from samples. Because mutual information is unbounded, its values are not directly comparable across datasets, dimensions, or applications. Normalized mutual information addresses this limitation by converting mutual information into a normalized dependency score. Recent work has demonstrated the practical value of normalized mutual information in applications such as molecular dynamics {arXiv:2405.04980} and interpretable machine learning {arXiv:2409.16768}, but existing estimators remain sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability {arXiv:2410.07642}.
  In this paper, we propose a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables. The proposed approach combines a MINE-based neural mutual information estimator {arXiv:1801.04062} with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators {arXiv:1905.12957}. Mutual information is estimated using the Donsker--Varadhan representation, while marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution, from which entropy is recovered. The resulting estimator provides a neural alternative to k-nearest-neighbor-based normalized mutual information estimation {arXiv:2405.04980}.
  Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show that the proposed estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline. These results indicate that neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.

</details>


### [295] [VESTIGE: A Knowledge-Guided Masking Strategy for Corruption-Aware Fine-Tuning of Genomic Transformers, Validated on Ancient DNA Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27712)
*Angshuman Chakravertty,Rahul Maheshwari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VESTIGE is a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns masking probability with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile, instead of uniform masking. Applied to ancient DNA reconstruction with DNABERT-2, it outperforms standard MLM across all tested widths (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13%, and achieves near-perfect protein structure reconstructions even under 10-30x amplified damage. The approach is domain-agnostic and applicable to any position-specific corruption profile such as FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard MLM fine-tuning assumes reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic by using uniform masking probability. This fails when degradation is concentrated at predictable positions, causing underperformance at peak damage sites compared to random predictors. A position-aware masking strategy is needed for corrupted sequence inputs.

Method: VESTIGE replaces the uniform masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile (PMD array from mapDamage2 for aDNA). Masking rates are rescaled so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15%, identical to standard MLM, isolating spatial redistribution as the sole variable. Model, data, seed, and hyperparameters are held fixed across DNABERT-2 runs.

Result: Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE outperforms standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8). Validation cross-entropy drops 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757). ESMFold reconstructions achieve TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions even under 10-30x amplified damage. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier returns AUC = 0.935, clearing 98.2% of reconstructed windows.

Conclusion: The principle is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile (FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore) can substitute for the PMD array, making VESTIGE a knowledge-guided training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

Abstract: Standard masked-language-model fine-tuning applies a uniform masking probability across every token position, assuming reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic. When the degradation process is characterised and concentrated at predictable positions, this assumption fails: at peak damage sites the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor. We introduce VESTIGE, a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns the masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile. We apply it to ancient DNA (aDNA) reconstruction, where cytosine deamination produces a position-dependent C-to-T / G-to-A gradient quantified per-position by mapDamage2. Rescaling so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15% - identical to standard MLM - isolates spatial redistribution as the sole variable, with model, data, seed, and hyperparameters held fixed across both DNABERT-2 runs on a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes). Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE leads standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions (three genes) even under damage amplified 10-30x beyond authentic PMD rates. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier returns AUC = 0.935 and clears 98.2% of reconstructed windows, the 1.76% remainder attributable to reference-genome features, not reconstruction artefacts. The principle is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile - FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore - substitutes directly for the PMD array, making VESTIGE a knowledge-guided training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

</details>


### [296] [Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27731)
*Jiaxiang Li,Zhiqi Bu,Shiyun Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper derives a joint mathematical characterization of training loss as a function of both learning rate and batch size schedules, yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any given learning rate schedule, and demonstrates that dynamic batch size scaling laws outperform static batch size baselines in large language model training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern deep learning typically keeps batch size static throughout training, overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on training dynamics. The authors aim to study this interplay through the lens of convex optimization.

Method: The paper analyzes deep learning dynamics via convex optimization, deriving a joint characterization of loss in terms of both learning rate and batch size schedules applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. From this characterization, a closed-form optimal batch size schedule is derived for any prescribed learning rate schedule, and joint scaling laws are developed.

Result: The derived joint scaling laws with dynamic batch size schedules consistently outperform static batch size baselines, demonstrating the significance of dynamic batch size scheduling in large language model training.

Conclusion: Dynamic batch size scheduling, when jointly optimized with learning rate schedules, provides a significant improvement over the conventional static batch size approach in large-scale deep learning training.

Abstract: Modern deep learning typically keeps the batch size static throughout training, thus overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on the training dynamics. In this paper, we study the deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization and derive a joint characterization of loss in terms of both schedules, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This characterization yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule, and further leads to joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static batch size baselines, highlighting the significance of dynamic batch size schedule in large language model training.

</details>


### [297] [Improving the Robustness/Accuracy Tradeoff Against Adversarial Attacks Using Information Bottleneck Distillation Through Dual Teachers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27737)
*Vincent Ryusuke Takahashi,Yoshinari Takeishi,Jun'ichi Takeuchi,Kave Salamatian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper extends Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) by adding a second "clean teacher" model trained only on clean inputs alongside the existing robust teacher, transferring features from both via a cross-layer attention matrix to improve clean accuracy while maintaining adversarial robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adversarial robustness countermeasures like IBD improve robustness to adversarial inputs but degrade classification accuracy on clean inputs. The authors aim to mitigate this trade-off by leveraging knowledge from both a clean teacher (for clean accuracy) and a robust teacher (for adversarial robustness) in the distillation process.

Method: The method extends the IBD framework by introducing an additional clean teacher trained solely on clean inputs. Both the clean and robust teachers' features are transferred to the student model via a cross-layer attention matrix during distillation. The approach is evaluated on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The impact of different training settings on the attention module is also analyzed.

Result: On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, the proposed method improves clean-sample classification accuracy compared to the original IBD while maintaining similar adversarial accuracy. The method is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, including the dual-teacher distillation framework B-MTARD, particularly regarding the harmonic mean of clean and robust accuracy.

Conclusion: Dual-teacher distillation with both clean and robust teachers, combined with cross-layer attention-based feature transfer, effectively balances clean accuracy and adversarial robustness, outperforming single-teacher IBD and matching state-of-the-art dual-teacher methods.

Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in classical machine learning problems. However, they are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Countermeasures proposed in the literature, notably Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) introduced by Kuang et al., degrade the classification accuracy on clean inputs while improving the robustness to adversarial inputs. In this work, we extend the IBD framework by introducing an extra teacher model (clean teacher) trained with only clean inputs, into the distillation process from a robust teacher model trained by adversarial training. The features of both clean and robust teachers are transferred to the student through a cross-layer attention matrix. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets show that the proposed method improves classification accuracy on clean samples compared to the original IBD, while maintaining similar accuracy on adversarial samples. Furthermore, our methods are competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, including the recent dual-teacher distillation framework B-MTARD, particularly in terms of the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. We also analyze the impact of different training settings that have different influences on the attention module.

</details>


### [298] [ROCS: Request-Oriented Compute Sharing for Efficient Large-Scale Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27744)
*Yuxin Chen,Liang Luo,Buyun Zhang,Jian Jiao,Boda Li,Haoyu Wang,Tongyi Tang,Ao Cai,Zijian Shen,Zhengkai Zhang,Wenyi Xie,Ryan Dick,Han Liu,Neng Shi,Bin Yu,Jianbo Xiao,Shuyao Bi,Hongtao Yu,Yuanwei Fang,Zhuoran Zhao,Sijia Chen,Yang Chen,Shuqi Yang,Qianru Li,Zikun Liu,Wei Ling,Sihan Zeng,Longhao Jin,Jiaxin Lu,Yinbin Ma,Jiawei Li,Yichen Ruan,Yong Ler Lee,Birmingham Guan,Zijian Li,Jianbo Sun,Zhengyu Zhang,Zeliang Chen,Xiaohan Wei,Yuchen Hao,GP Musumeci,Venkatesh Ranganathan,Yantao Yao,Chunqiang Tang,Wenlin Chen,Santanu Kolay,Ellie Dingqiao Wen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ROCS (Request-Oriented Compute Sharing) is a modeling and inference paradigm for recommendation systems that exploits the fact that request-side features are shared across candidates. By deferring request-candidate interactions as late as possible and isolating candidate-dependent representations, ROCS evaluates large model portions once per request instead of once per candidate, achieving significant inference efficiency gains (up to 3x QPS improvement) while maintaining or improving prediction quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern recommendation models improve prediction quality by scaling feature-interaction and sequence modules, but production cost constraints limit how far systems can scale. The key insight is that existing approaches waste computation by redundantly evaluating request-side features for every candidate when they are shared across all candidates in a single user request.

Method: ROCS introduces three key technical components: (1) Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, (2) Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures, and (3) In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) for efficient GPU deployment that accelerates model execution.

Result: On public benchmarks, ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. On production-scale workloads, ROCS achieves up to 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation, and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. It has been deployed across large-scale recommendation systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, and more than two orders of magnitude in inference complexity.

Conclusion: ROCS represents a practical and deployable paradigm for recommendation inference that significantly reduces infrastructure cost while maintaining or improving prediction quality. The paradigm exploits the structure of recommendation inference (request shared across many candidates) to avoid redundant computation, delivering substantial online gains at reduced cost across diverse production systems.

Abstract: Modern recommendation models gain prediction quality by scaling feature-interaction and sequence modules, but production cost constraints cap how far systems can scale.
  In this work, we propose Request-Oriented Compute Sharing (ROCS), a modeling and inference paradigm that exploits a unique property of recommendation inference: each user request is evaluated against many candidates, while request-side features are shared across candidates. ROCS defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates substantial portions of the model once per request rather than once per candidate, significantly improving inference efficiency while maintaining or improving prediction quality. To realize this paradigm, we develop Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, and Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures. To support efficient GPU deployment, we co-design In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) that significantly accelerates ROCS model execution.
  Experiments on public benchmarks show that ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. On production-scale workloads, ROCS achieves up to a 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. ROCS has been deployed across large-scale recommendation systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, and more than two orders of magnitude in inference complexity, delivering significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.

</details>


### [299] [DAS-PMVC: A Framework for Partial Multi-View Clustering via Dual Alignment and Structure Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27761)
*Shubin Ma,Liang Zhao,Chuanye He,Zhenjiao Liu,Liang Zou,Lin Yuanbo Wu,Yu Shao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DAS-PMVC is a partial multi-view clustering framework that addresses the partial view alignment problem (PVAP) caused by misaligned data across views. It combines anchor graph structure alignment, structure-enhanced feature learning with multi-view GCNs, and a dual alignment strategy using contrastive learning and the Hungarian algorithm, achieving state-of-the-art clustering performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-view clustering suffers from view asymmetry and irrelevant samples caused by data collection device limitations, which lead to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP). This misalignment degrades clustering performance, and existing methods fail to adequately mitigate these issues.

Method: The DAS-PMVC framework consists of three components: (1) anchor graph structure alignment—deriving sample joint embedding representations with consistent latent space from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; (2) structure-enhanced feature learning—pretraining to learn view structure information combined with multi-view graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure, improving representation discriminability; (3) a dual alignment strategy—initial alignment via the anchor graph during pretraining, then contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm during training to further optimize latent feature alignment.

Result: Experimental results on multiple datasets show that DAS-PMVC outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, demonstrating its effectiveness and superiority.

Conclusion: The proposed DAS-PMVC framework effectively handles partial multi-view clustering by leveraging view structure consistency and semantic relevance through dual alignment and structure enhancement, achieving superior clustering results compared to existing approaches.

Abstract: In recent years, multi-view clustering has attracted widespread research interest. However, due to limitations in data collection devices, data across different views often suffer from misalignment, leading to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP). To mitigate the impact of view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, this paper proposes a framework for partial multi-view clustering via dual alignment and structure enhancement (DAS-PMVC), which leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance. Specifically, DAS-PMVC includes three parts: \textbf{anchor graph structure alignment}, where sample joint embedding representations with consistent latent space are derived from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; \textbf{structure-enhanced feature learning}, where the model learns view structure information through pretraining and combines multi-view graph convolutional networks to further extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure to improve the discriminative power of representations; and \textbf{a dual alignment strategy}, where initial alignment is performed through the anchor graph in the pretraining phase, and contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm are introduced in the training phase to further optimize the alignment of latent features. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the DAS-PMVC framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, showcasing its effectiveness and superiority.

</details>


### [300] [Train Small, Deploy Large: Zero-Shot GNN Transfer Through Geometric Renormalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27767)
*Robert Jankowski,Pedro Almagro-Blanco,Marián Boguñá,Melanie Weber,M. Ángeles Serrano*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a zero-shot transfer protocol where GNNs trained on geometrically renormalized (GR) smaller-scale graph replicas have their weights directly transferred to the full-resolution graph without retraining, demonstrating preserved predictive performance and alignment of learned representations across scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNNs face scalability challenges at millions of nodes. The authors ask whether a model trained on a smaller scaled-down replica can be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining, which would significantly reduce training costs for large graphs.

Method: The approach uses geometric renormalization (GR) to coarse-grain graphs into scaled-down replicas. A GNN is trained on these GR-reduced graphs, and the resulting weights are transferred directly (zero-shot) to the original full-resolution graph without any fine-tuning or retraining.

Result: Across synthetic and real-world networks, training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. Learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales.

Conclusion: Structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, which opens a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can operate on large graphs but become infrastructure-sensitive at the scale of millions of nodes and typically require scalable training techniques for even larger graphs. This raises a central question: when can a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica of a graph be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining? We introduce a zero-shot transfer protocol in which a GNN is trained on a graph coarse-grained by geometric renormalization (GR), and the resulting weights are transferred directly to the original network. Across synthetic and real-world networks, training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. We further find that learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales. These findings suggest that structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

</details>


### [301] [Beyond the Best Teacher: Expanding and Compressing the Reasoning Solution Manifold](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27770)
*Songshuo Lu,Zhi Chen,Yaohua Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RL-trained policies act as incomplete teachers that amplify only a subset of valid reasoning modes. The paper proposes an expand-then-compress framework (RGRPO + TU-OPD with Consensus-Residual Decomposition) that trains complementary teachers and distills them into a single student, outperforming the best individual teacher on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A single RL run produces policies that are strong reasoners but incomplete teachers, amplifying only a subset of valid solution modes. Viewing RL-trained policies as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold, the authors argue that relying on any single teacher is suboptimal and that complementary teacher aggregation could yield stronger students.

Method: The framework has two stages: (1) Expansion via Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO), which trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization and redirects each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. (2) Compression via reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD), where the student learns from its own response prefixes, with only reliable teachers contributing and their sampled-token OPD losses weighted by per-example quality. Consensus-Residual Decomposition preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over reliable peers to prevent specialist suppression during aggregation.

Result: Using a Qwen3-1.7B student, experiments across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show consistent outperformance over the strongest individual teacher, with relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9% respectively, while retaining single-model inference.

Conclusion: Stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union.

Abstract: A single reinforcement-learning run can produce a strong reasoner yet an incomplete teacher: it often amplifies only a subset of the valid solution modes. We argue that reinforcement learning (RL)-trained policies should therefore be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold, rather than as globally reliable supervisors. Based on this view, we propose an expand-then-compress framework that couples teacher construction with multi-teacher policy distillation. In the expansion stage, Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization and redirects each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. In the compression stage, reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes. For each example, only reliable teachers contribute, and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by their per-example quality. We further introduce Consensus-Residual Decomposition, which preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over its reliable peers, preventing specialist behavior from being suppressed during teacher aggregation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show that the resulting Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, yielding relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while retaining single-model inference. These results establish a simple but powerful principle: stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union.

</details>


### [302] [LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO): A Sampling-Time Low-Rank Scaffold for Recovering Reinforcement-Learning Gradient on Zero-Reward Cliff Prompts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27787)
*Ken Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LSPO is a sampling-time mechanism for RLVR that detects "cliff" prompts (where all sampled rollouts in a group fail), fits a small LoRA adapter via supervised learning on their solutions, re-rolls these prompts with the base+adapter model, splices successful completions back into the RL batch with importance sampling, and takes GRPO steps on the base model only. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, it beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells with gains up to +10.7 points, averaging +3.8 points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard GRPO-style RLVR assigns group-normalized advantages, which are identically zero on "cliff" prompts where every sampled rollout in a group fails. This means no gradient signal is produced on precisely the hardest prompts at the frontier of the model's capability, creating a structural blind spot that limits mathematical reasoning improvement.

Method: Each RL step: (1) detect cliff prompts where all rollouts fail; (2) fit a small LoRA adapter via a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions; (3) re-roll cliffs with the base-plus-adapter model; (4) splice successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction; (5) take a GRPO step on the base model alone. The adapter receives only supervised gradients and is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model.

Result: On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins, one exact tie), with gains up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1, averaging +3.8 points across the 16 cells.

Conclusion: LSPO successfully recovers the lost gradient on cliff prompts in RLVR for mathematical reasoning, consistently outperforming the DAPO baseline across all benchmark and pass@k combinations. The base-only model output at checkpoint, with the adapter discarded, ensures no inference-time overhead while capturing the benefits of supervised fine-tuning on frontier-level prompts.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning suffers from a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts-those on which every sampled rollout in a group fails-the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, so GRPO produces no gradient on precisely the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. We introduce LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO), a sampling-time mechanism that recovers this lost gradient. Each RL step, LSPO detects cliff prompts, fits a small low-rank (LoRA) adapter by a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions, re-rolls the cliffs with the base-plus-adapter model, splices the now-successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base alone; the adapter receives only the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins and one exact tie), with gains of up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; averaged over the 16 cells the improvement is +3.8 points.

</details>


### [303] [Revisiting Predictive Process Monitoring in the Age of Foundation Models: A Comparative Study of Sequence, Tabular, and LLM Approaches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27797)
*Lennart Fertig,Lukas Kirchdorfer,Tobias Sesterhenn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper systematically benchmarks three predictive process monitoring paradigms—classical sequence-based deep models (e.g., LSTM), large language models (LLMs), and tabular foundation models—across multiple datasets and tasks, finding that sequence models excel at next-activity prediction, tabular foundation models compete well on temporal tasks, and LLMs typically underperform despite higher cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PPM has shifted from training deep sequence models from scratch toward exploiting foundation models, especially LLMs. However, tabular foundation models with in-context learning have not been systematically benchmarked for PPM, leaving it unclear whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive in this evolving landscape.

Method: The authors compare the three modeling paradigms (sequence models, LLMs, and tabular foundation models) both conceptually and empirically, using a controlled benchmark spanning multiple datasets and prediction tasks in predictive process monitoring.

Result: Sequence models consistently achieve the best performance for next-activity prediction; tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal prediction tasks; LLMs generally lag behind despite incurring higher costs.

Conclusion: The findings suggest that classical sequence-based models still hold an edge for certain PPM tasks, while tabular foundation models are a viable alternative for temporal predictions; LLMs offer limited value relative to their cost for the tested PPM tasks.

Abstract: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) leverages event logs to forecast the future of running process instances, for instance, predicting the next activity, the remaining time until case completion, or the time to the next event. While PPM research in recent years has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, foundation-model approaches---particularly large language models (LLMs)---are increasingly explored for PPM. At the same time, tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities offer a promising alternative but have not yet been systematically benchmarked for PPM. Thus, it remains unclear whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive in this evolving landscape. This paper compares the three modeling paradigms both conceptually and empirically through a controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks. The results show that sequence models consistently perform best for next activity prediction, whereas tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, with LLMs usually lagging behind despite higher cost.

</details>


### [304] [Learning-Augmented and Randomized Algorithms for Line Aggregation with Delays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27807)
*Tianhang Lu,Runtian Ren,Shengcai Liu,Ke Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents deterministic and randomized learning-augmented algorithms for online aggregation with delays on a line metric, achieving improved robustness/consistency trade-offs and a randomized competitive ratio of e+1 (beating the deterministic lower bound of 4).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to improve both the classical adversarial competitiveness and the learning-augmented robustness-consistency trade-offs for online aggregation with delays on a line metric, closing gaps between known upper and lower bounds for randomized algorithms.

Method: The authors propose a deterministic learning-augmented Balance algorithm with (4/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (4+λ)-consistency, a randomized algorithm with (e+1)-competitive ratio against an oblivious adversary, and a hybrid randomized learning-augmented algorithm with (e/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (e+λ)-consistency. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate theoretical findings.

Result: The randomized algorithm achieves an (e+1)-competitive ratio, improving over the deterministic 5-competitive Balance benchmark and beating the deterministic lower bound of 4. A lower bound of e for randomized algorithms is established, improving the previous e/(e-1) bound. The learning-augmented variants achieve favorable robustness-consistency trade-offs.

Conclusion: Randomization provably helps for online aggregation with delays, yielding improved competitive ratios and learning-augmented trade-offs; numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical results.

Abstract: This paper studies learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric. We consider advice given as online suggested service lengths, and evaluate the algorithms in terms of robustness and consistency. For each $λ\in (0,1]$, we first propose a deterministic learning-augmented \textsc{Balance} algorithm that is $(4/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(4+λ)$-consistent. We also propose a randomized algorithm for the problem in the classical adversarial model, which is $(e+1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary, improving over the deterministic $5$-competitive \textsc{Balance} benchmark~\cite{bienkowski2013chain}. Notably, this competitive ratio is even lower than the lower bound of $4$ for deterministic online algorithms. Moreover, we establish a lower bound of $e$ on the competitive ratio of randomized online algorithms, improving the previous lower bound of $e/(e-1)$. Besides, we combine the two ideas and obtain a randomized learning-augmented algorithm that is $(e/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(e+λ)$-consistent. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to complement our theoretical analysis and evaluate the empirical performance of our algorithms.

</details>


### [305] [Contrastive Concept Importance: Explaining Pairwise Class Decisions Through Automatically Extracted Concept Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27904)
*Roel Visser,Isaac Roberts,Barbara Hammer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Contrastive Concept Importance (CCI), a method that attributes the logit margin between a target class and a foil/contrast class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis, producing signed scores that indicate whether a concept supports the target over the foil or vice versa, and that can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional concept-based feature attribution methods answer non-contrastive "why P?" questions by computing attributions for a single output class. However, in situations like misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question is "why P rather than Q?" — a contrastive question that existing methods cannot directly answer.

Method: CCI attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast (foil) class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. It produces signed attribution scores (positive = supports target over foil, negative = supports foil over target) and decomposes these into target-logit and foil-logit effects, enabling distinction between globally important concepts and class-pair-specific ones.

Result: Evaluated on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases, insertion/deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition, and semantic class hierarchy analysis. Results show CCI reveals class-pair-specific model behavior not captured by ordinary concept importance, and highly contrastive concepts can be assessed against semantic superclass structure to determine whether they affect fine-grained distinctions or broad category evidence.

Conclusion: Contrastive concept importance provides a more natural and informative explanation framework for contrastive "why P rather than Q?" questions, uncovering class-pair-specific decision behavior that standard non-contrastive attribution methods miss, and offers a way to evaluate fine-grained vs. broad-category concept effects via semantic hierarchy analysis.

Abstract: Concept-based explanations are a prevalent way to explain the decisions of complex black-box methods through semantically meaningful, human-interpretable concepts. To attribute the contribution of such concepts to a model's decisions, feature attribution methods are used to quantify how strongly each concept contributes to a model output. These attributions are typically computed for a single output class and therefore answer a non-contrastive "why P?" question. In many situations, however, such as cases of misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question to ask is "why P rather than Q?".
  We introduce contrastive concept importance (CCI), which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast, or foil, class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. The resulting scores are signed, indicating whether a concept supports the target over the foil or the foil over the target, and can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects. This makes it possible to distinguish globally important concepts from concepts that specifically influence a class-pair distinction, including whether their effect is shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.
  We evaluate the method on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases, insertion and deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy. The results show that contrastive concept importance reveals class-pair-specific model behavior that is not captured by ordinary concept importance alone, and that highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to assess whether they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.

</details>


### [306] [Class-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Counterfactual Explanation Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27905)
*Muhammad Adil Saleem,Syed Ali Raza,Mary-Anne Williams*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether including an instance's predicted class in the reinforcement learning (RL) state representation improves counterfactual explanation (CFE) generation. The proposed class-aware RL method outperforms a class-blind RL variant, demonstrating faster convergence, better reward optimization, shorter episodes, and significantly more valid CFEs across seven datasets, with class information ranking among the most influential features in action selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous RL-based CFE generation methods formulate RL states using only predictor-derived features from the supervised dataset, potentially missing critical decision-boundary information. The authors hypothesize that incorporating the instance's predicted class into the state representation could enhance exploration efficiency and improve policy optimality in generating counterfactual explanations.

Method: The authors propose a class-aware RL method for CFE generation, where the RL state includes both predictor-derived features and the instance's predicted class. They compare this against a class-blind RL baseline (identical but excluding class information). The comparison uses seven diverse datasets of varying sizes, with evaluation on training convergence, reward optimization, episode length, and CFE validity. SHAP and LIME analyses are employed to assess the influence of the class feature in action-selection.

Result: The class-aware RL method achieves faster convergence, better reward optimization, and reduced episode lengths during training. It generates significantly more valid CFEs than class-blind RL. SHAP and LIME analyses confirm the predicted class feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in RL action-selection across datasets.

Conclusion: Class-awareness in RL state representation substantially benefits CFE generation, leading to clearer explanations, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets. This underscores the importance of incorporating predicted class information into RL formulations for counterfactual explanations.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) enhance the interpretability of black-box models by generating alternative instances with adjusted feature values that achieve a contrastive outcome. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach for CFE generation, enabling efficient exploration of counterfactual instances while ensuring control over key metrics like validity, sparsity, and proximity. Previous studies have formulated RL states exclusively using features derived from the predictors in the supervised dataset. This study explores the impact of including an instance's predicted class, alongside features derived from the predictors, in the RL state representation for generating CFEs. The hypothesis is that class-awareness enhances exploration efficiency and improves policy optimality. We compare the proposed class-aware RL method with the class-blind RL method, which is similar but excludes the instance's class information from the state representation. The comparison was conducted using seven datasets from diverse domains, varying in size. The results show that during training, class-aware RL offers benefits in terms of convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction. Moreover, it generates significantly more valid CFEs compared to class-blind RL. Finally, the instance's class-based feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in RL's action-selection, as shown by the SHAP and LIME values, underscoring the significance of class-awareness in RL for CFE generation. The impact is heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets.

</details>


### [307] [S-CEReBrO: Breaking the Memory Barrier in Continuous EEG Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27913)
*Glenn Anta Bucagu,Thorir Mar Ingolfsson,Yawei Li,Luca Benini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: S-CEReBrO introduces a Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism that factorizes attention into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory for continuous EEG monitoring. It processes signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention, uses 55% less memory with 2.1X higher throughput than linear attention, and achieves SOTA on 7/11 downstream tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters, pre-trained on >25,000 hours of EEG data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer-based architectures for EEG analysis face a critical bottleneck: global attention mechanisms couple the attention memory state to signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. This limits the practicality of foundation models for real-time, long-duration EEG applications.

Method: The paper proposes Windowed Alternating Attention, which factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, ensuring constant KV cache memory by requiring resident attention maps only for the active window. This is applied to CEReBrO, creating S-CEReBrO, pre-trained on over 25,000 hours of recordings from more than 12,000 subjects.

Result: Empirical scaling analysis shows windowed alternating attention processes signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. On long contexts, it requires only 55% of the memory of linear attention while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters.

Conclusion: S-CEReBrO represents a significant step toward efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring, addressing the memory bottleneck of global attention while maintaining competitive downstream task performance.

Abstract: Foundation models offer a promising paradigm for Electroencephalography (EEG) analysis, leveraging generalizable representations from vast unlabeled datasets. Yet, Transformer-based architectures face a critical bottleneck: global attention mechanisms couple the attention memory state to the signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. To address this, we introduce S-CEReBrO (Streaming CEReBrO), an evolution of the CEReBrO architecture designed for continuous monitoring. Our novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory as only the active window requires resident attention maps. Empirical scaling analysis confirms that windowed alternating attention can process signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. Compared to low-rank linear attention on long contexts, windowed alternating attention requires 55% of the memory while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. Pre-trained on >25,000 hours of recordings from >12,000 subjects, S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks, with up to 60% fewer parameters. This work represents a significant step toward the realization of efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring. An accompanying code repository is available.

</details>


### [308] [Exact Action Values Are Not Enough: Rollout-Verified Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of a Reasoning Model for Multi-Zone VAV Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27914)
*Takumi Shioda,Kohei Terashima,Tatsuo Nagai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether frontier LLMs can achieve competitive multi-zone VAV control from text without building-specific training, and whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer control knowledge into a smaller open-weight model. In a four-zone physics-based emulator over three summer days, GPT-5 achieved the largest electricity reduction (6.2%) but reduced ventilation margin, while TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% with better comfort compliance.
