However, RFT into the open-weight model failed: a learned critic with near-perfect correlation (r=0.9998) still had unreliable within-state ranking (5/10), 200 RFT steps produced no improvement, and transition predictions remained worse than persistence—motivating transition-focused SFT before value-based RFT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-zone VAV control must balance thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and electricity across continuous actuators. MPC and RL are widely studied but typically require building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. The paper asks whether an LLM with inference-time computation can achieve competitive control from text without building-specific training, and whether TD3-guided RFT can distill that knowledge into a locally deployable open-weight model.

Method: Five controllers were evaluated in a physics-based four-zone emulator over three summer days: Guideline 36-based baseline, TD3 (RL), GPT-5 (frontier LLM without building-specific training), and an open-weight model trained with 200 steps of deterministic-rollout TD3-guided RFT. RFT restores a saved state, applies one candidate action, and follows TD3 to score each action; a learned critic was audited against these exact rollout scores. Metrics include HVAC electricity, temperature/CO2 compliance, ventilation margin, and five-minute transition prediction error versus persistence.

Result: TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% relative to baseline with improved temperature and CO2 compliance. GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but reduced the ventilation margin. The learned critic had near-perfect across-time correlation (r=0.9998) yet failed within-state ranking, selecting the rollout-best candidate in only 5 of 10 states. Even with the rollout verifier, 200 RFT steps yielded no sustained improvement in sampled-action return; the open-weight model used more electricity than baseline before and after training, and its five-minute predictions remained worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better. Exact rollout scores rank actions but reveal neither next-state effects nor an improvement direction.

Conclusion: Frontier LLMs can achieve competitive VAV control from text without building-specific training, but transferring this via value-based RFT to a small open-weight model fails. The critic's global fit masks poor within-state action ranking, and value-based RFT improves neither action selection nor transition modeling. The unchanged transition errors motivate a transition-focused supervised fine-tuning stage before value-based RFT, suggesting future work should prioritize next-state prediction before value learning.

Abstract: Multi-zone variable-air-volume control must balance thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and electricity use across several continuous actuators. Model predictive control and reinforcement learning are widely studied, but deployment typically requires building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. We first test whether a frontier reasoning model (an LLM trained to use additional inference-time computation) can achieve competitive VAV control from text without building-specific training. With that capability established, we then test whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer control knowledge into a locally deployable open-weight model. Five controllers are evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator. Relative to a Guideline 36-based baseline, TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% while improving temperature and CO$_2$ compliance. Without building-specific training, GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but reduced the ventilation margin. For RFT, deterministic rollouts restore a saved state, apply one candidate, and follow TD3 to score each action. Auditing a learned critic against these rollouts exposed a failure hidden by its near-perfect across-time correlation ($r=0.9998$): within-state ranking was unreliable; the critic selected the rollout-best candidate in only 5 of 10 states. Even with the rollout verifier, 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement in sampled-action return; the open-weight controller used more electricity than the baseline before and after training, and its five-minute predictions remained worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better. Exact rollout scores rank sampled actions but reveal neither next-state effects nor an improvement direction. The unchanged transition errors motivate transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.

</details>


### [309] [ODEWorld: A Continuous Predictive Architecture via Physical-Time Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27924)
*Dongxiu Liu,Haoyi Niu,Peng Cheng,Yuan Gao,Xirui Kang,Sangli Teng,Koushil Sreenath,Xianyuan Zhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PT-Flow learns a continuous latent velocity field parameterized by an ODE in a structured representation space, and ODEWorld (built on PT-Flow) is a continuous-time latent world model that supports arbitrary temporal resolution, backward prediction, long-horizon visual reconstruction, and downstream policy learning, outperforming discrete-time baselines in both video generation and robotic control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physical space and time are continuous, but existing world models operate in discrete time, which is inefficient at capturing physical dynamics. This mismatch motivates a continuous-time paradigm for modeling the physical world.

Method: PT-Flow learns a continuous latent velocity field whose dynamics are parameterized by an ODE in a structured representation space, enabling future prediction via temporal integration with an ODE solver. ODEWorld builds on this by extracting time-variant features and enforcing ODE properties on both the representation space and latent velocity field, addressing representation collapse and supporting continuous-time prediction.

Result: ODEWorld achieves high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction, supports arbitrary temporal resolution and backward prediction, provides planning-oriented information, and excels in both video generation and robotic control benchmarks.

Conclusion: Continuous-time latent world modeling via ODE-based dynamics reconciles planning-conducive abstraction with visual realism, offering a versatile and efficient alternative to discrete-time world models across perception and control tasks.

Abstract: In the physical world we inhabit, space and time are fundamentally continuous. However, existing machine learning paradigms for world modeling are largely confined to discrete-time prediction, thereby exhibiting significant inefficiency in capturing the dynamics of physical world. We introduce Physical-Time Flow (\textbf{PT-Flow}), a novel approach that learns a continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time. Crucially, the underlying dynamics of sequential data are parameterized by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) embedded in a well-structured representation space. Under this paradigm, the prediction of future can be recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space. Building upon PT-Flow, we construct \textbf{ODEWorld}, a continuous-time latent world model that is both efficient and versatile. By extracting time-variant features and enforcing ODE properties on both the dynamical representation space and the latent velocity field, ODEWorld effectively addresses the long-standing representation collapse issue in latent world model literature. This also enables high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction. Moreover, its continuous nature allows for arbitrary temporal resolution and even backward prediction, which is impossible for most discrete-time models. Lastly, ODEWorld can provide rich planning-oriented information to facilitate downstream policy learning. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control. \href{https://dstate.github.io/odeworld_website/}{Project Website}.

</details>


### [310] [Harnessing the Potential of Optimizing Data Mixtures via Bayesian Domain Reweighting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27928)
*Xiang Yuan,Kaiqing Lei,Zhenyu Jin,Jun Shu,Deyu Meng,Zongben Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Bayesian domain weighting method for LLM pre-training that infers optimal domain weights from a Dirichlet distribution using Gamma prior information. Unlike existing function-fitting approaches that rely on structural assumptions (e.g., rank invariance, scaling laws) and suffer from estimation bias, or direct optimization methods that are unstable and computationally expensive, the proposed approach achieves stable and efficient domain weight learning while consuming substantially less data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The distributional composition of multi-domain pre-training data critically impacts LLM performance. Existing methods either rely on proxy function fitting with strong structural assumptions that are often violated (causing estimation bias), or use direct optimization from data that suffers from unstable optimization trajectories and prohibitive computational overhead. There is a need for a method that combines accuracy, stability, and efficiency.

Method: The paper presents a Bayesian domain weighting method that models domain weights as samples from a Dirichlet distribution, incorporating Gamma prior information learned from observed data to perform posterior inference of optimal domain weights.

Result: Experimental results show the proposed method achieves stable and efficient domain weight learning, identifies optimal data mixtures while consuming substantially less data than search-based function-fitting approaches.

Conclusion: The Bayesian domain weighting approach revitalizes optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale LLM pre-training applications by overcoming the instability and computational bottlenecks of prior direct optimization methods while avoiding the structural assumption biases of proxy-based fitting methods.

Abstract: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) is fundamentally influenced by the distributional composition of multi-domain pre-training data. While manual heuristics were prevalent in early models, they increasingly fail to capture the intricate synergies between domains as data complexity grows. To overcome the issue, a dominant approach seeks to fit a proxy function mapping between domain weights and their corresponding validation losses, and then find the optimal domain weights to minimize validation losses. These methods rely on strong structural assumptions, such as rank invariance or scaling laws, which are often violated, resulting in non-negligible estimation bias. A promising approach is to directly optimize the weighting scheme from data. However, it suffers from unstable optimization trajectory and prohibitive computational overhead, limiting its potential to search better domain weights configurations. This paper presents a Bayesian domain weighting method to infer the weights from a Dirichlet distribution via introducing Gamma prior information learned from observations. Experimental results demonstrate that proposed method could achieve stable and efficient domain weights learning, and identifies optimal mixtures while consuming substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods, revitalizing optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale applications.

</details>


### [311] [TriShield: Zero-Utility-Loss Defense Against Privacy Backdoors in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning via Orthogonal Gradient Projection and Optimizer State Entanglement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27940)
*Cheng Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TriShield is a three-layer deterministic defense against NeuroImprint-style privacy backdoor attacks in federated LLM fine-tuning, achieving 0% reconstruction rate with zero model utility loss and no additional communication rounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated fine-tuning of LLMs is vulnerable to NeuroImprint, a malicious-parameter-server attack that uses memorization neurons in PEFT adapters to reconstruct 59%-79% of client training data. Existing defenses like LDP and gradient clipping either fail or impose unacceptable utility degradation.

Method: TriShield comprises three layers: (1) a Parameter Artifact Detector that identifies memory-neuron signatures before local training; (2) a Stateful Virtual Iteration mechanism that forces Adam/AdamW momentum to entangle gradients across virtual steps, invalidating closed-form inversion; and (3) a Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection operator using SVD to project gradients onto the main-task semantic subspace, eliminating private-memorization gradient components.

Result: Theory proves mutual information between uploaded gradients and individual samples is zero after Layers 2 and 3. Experiments on GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B show NeuroImprint reconstruction rate drops to 0% across all attack variants, while maintaining or improving training accuracy with less than 5% additional GPU compute overhead.

Conclusion: TriShield delivers a provably effective, deterministic defense against NeuroImprint-style reconstruction that preserves utility and communication efficiency, offering a practical solution for secure federated LLM fine-tuning.

Abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) enables collaborative training without exposing raw data. However, a recent attack, NeuroImprint [1] (arXiv:2606.20553), demonstrates that a malicious parameter server can corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor: by assigning a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and ensuring each neuron updates at most once, the server can analytically reconstruct 59\%--79\% of client training data with high semantic fidelity. Existing defenses---including local differential privacy (LDP) [8] and gradient clipping---either fail against this attack or impose unacceptable utility degradation. We present \textbf{TriShield}, a three-layer deterministic defense that completely prevents NeuroImprint-style reconstruction with \textbf{zero model utility loss} and \textbf{no additional communication rounds}. TriShield consists of: (1) a \textbf{Parameter Artifact Detector} that identifies memory-neuron signatures in distributed model parameters before local training begins; (2) a \textbf{Stateful Virtual Iteration} mechanism that forces Adam/AdamW's momentum state to irreversibly entangle gradients across virtual steps, invalidating NeuroImprint's closed-form inversion; and (3) a \textbf{Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection} operator that projects all local gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace computed via SVD, physically eliminating any gradient components that carry private memorization. We prove theoretically that after Layers 2 and 3, the mutual information between the uploaded gradient and any individual training sample is zero. Experiments on GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B verify that TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to \textbf{0\%} across all tested attack variants, while maintaining or improving training accuracy, with less than 5\% additional GPU computation overhead.

</details>


### [312] [AutoPref: Automatic Discovery of Task-Specific Preference Objectives for Neural Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27953)
*Shengda Gu,Kai Li,Xinyi Ke,Haobo Fu,Yifan Zhang,Jian Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AutoPref is the first LLM-guided framework that automatically discovers preference-based objective functions for neural combinatorial optimization (NCO), factorizing the objective into a pairwise loss program and a set-aware weighting program, and using a staged conditional search with behavioral gates to efficiently find improved objectives that outperform hand-designed baselines across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing preference-based NCO objectives combine two design choices—what learning signal to extract from solution pairs and how to weight pairs relative to the sampled set—in manually specified, one-size-fits-all formulations, limiting performance. The paper aims to automate the discovery of preference objectives rather than relying on hand-crafted designs.

Method: AutoPref decomposes the preference objective into (1) a pairwise loss program defining the learning signal and (2) a set-aware weighting program determining each pair's relative contribution. These compositions form a unified programmatic objective space that generalizes existing preference objectives. A staged conditional search with behavioral gates filters inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation to keep search tractable, with the LLM guiding program generation and refinement.

Result: AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed preference-objective baselines across multiple problem scales on four NP-hard combinatorial optimization benchmarks: TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, demonstrating both effectiveness and scalability of automated objective discovery.

Conclusion: Automated, LLM-guided objective discovery can replace manual preference-objective design in NCO, yielding better-performing objectives that scale across problem types and sizes, opening a new direction for programmatic objective search in learning-based combinatorial optimization.

Abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) underpin many real-world decisions, but their exponentially large search spaces make high-quality solutions costly to obtain. Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) learns fast construction policies, typically with reinforcement learning (RL), while preference-based NCO improves sample efficiency by learning from relative solution quality. However, existing preference objectives combine two distinct design choices in manually specified, one-size-fits-all formulations: what learning signal to extract from each solution pair and how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set. We present AutoPref, the first LLM-guided framework for automated preference-objective discovery in NCO. AutoPref factorizes the objective into a pairwise loss program, which defines the learning signal, and a set-aware weighting program, which determines each pair's relative contribution. Their composition forms a unified programmatic objective space containing existing preference objectives as special cases. To make its search tractable, we introduce a staged conditional search strategy with behavioral gates that filter inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation. Across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across problem scales, demonstrating the benefits and scalability of automated objective discovery for NCO.

</details>


### [313] [What Makes Graph Unified? Principles and Generative Sliding-Window Transformer for Graph Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27966)
*Dongxiao He,Siqi Liu,Jitao Zhao,Yawen Li,Yi Wang,Di Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SliGFM is a Graph Foundation Model that unifies heterogeneous node features across graph domains via topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction, guided by four desiderata: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph Foundation Models aim for general-purpose graph learning across diverse domains, but heterogeneous node features—varying in dimensionality and semantics across datasets—pose a fundamental input-level barrier. Existing methods merely project features to fixed dimensions, implicitly assuming dimensional uniformity equals effective feature unification, but this does not guarantee preserved semantics or transferable patterns for cross-domain knowledge transfer.

Method: The paper proposes SliGFM, which: (1) establishes four desiderata for cross-domain graph feature unification (formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility); (2) orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness; (3) scans reordered features with a shared sliding-window feature encoder to transform heterogeneous features into ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens; (4) employs a smoothness-aware transformer to capture transferable relational patterns among feature tokens within each node; and (5) uses a generative reconstruction objective to preserve original feature information.

Result: The paper introduces the SliGFM framework addressing the conceptual gap in graph feature unification, demonstrating that feature tokens ordered by topological smoothness and processed through a shared sliding-window encoder can effectively support cross-domain transfer in graph foundation models while maintaining information fidelity through generative reconstruction.

Conclusion: Dimensional uniformity alone is insufficient for effective cross-domain feature unification in Graph Foundation Models; topology-aware ordering and generative reconstruction provide a principled approach to unifying heterogeneous node features while preserving their informative semantics and enabling transferable knowledge.

Abstract: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose graph learning, aiming to learn reusable knowledge that generalizes across diverse graph domains and downstream tasks, reducing the need for specific model development. Achieving this goal requires reconciling the substantial heterogeneity in node features, graph structures, and semantic information across domains. Among them, heterogeneous node features constitute a fundamental input-level barrier, as their dimensionality and semantics vary substantially across datasets. Existing studies typically project or map heterogeneous node features into a fixed-dimensional space, often implicitly equating dimensional uniformity with effective feature unification. Yet dimensional consistency alone does not ensure that the unified features preserve informative semantics and capture transferable patterns that can support cross-domain knowledge transfer. To bridge this conceptual gap, we distill four desiderata for cross-domain graph feature unification: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility. Guided by these principles, we propose SliGFM, a graph foundation model built upon topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction. SliGFM orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness and scans the reordered features with a shared sliding-window feature encoder, transforming heterogeneous features into a common space of ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens. This formulation enables a smoothness-aware transformer to capture transferable relational patterns among feature tokens within each node, while the generative reconstruction objective encourages preservation of the original feature information.

</details>


### [314] [Beyond Binary Rewards: A Comparative Study of Reward Design for Reinforcement Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27968)
*Efstratios Zaradoukas,Davide Gabrielli,Bardh Prenkaj,Gjergji Kasneci*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies how reward design affects the efficiency of machine unlearning within a Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) framework. The authors propose a reward decomposition framework that separates verifiability from sparsity, introducing two new reward functions—an exponential reward based on forbidden-concept occurrence counts and a PageRank-inspired reward weighted by semantic importance. Experiments on the RWKU benchmark show both rewards outperform binary rewards, achieving up to 3× faster convergence while preserving general model utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine unlearning is increasingly necessary due to privacy regulations like GDPR and the EU AI Act, but existing RLVR-based unlearning methods use sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal, indicating only whether forbidden content was avoided while limiting convergence speed. The paper argues that reward design is a key but underexplored factor in unlearning efficiency.

Method: The paper introduces a principled reward decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity within the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework. It proposes two new reward functions: (1) an exponential reward providing graded penalties based on the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and (2) a PageRank-inspired reward that weights penalties by semantic importance. Experiments are conducted on the Real World Knowledge Unlearning (RWKU) benchmark.

Result: Both proposed reward functions consistently outperform the binary reward baseline on the RWKU benchmark, achieving similar forgetting performance up to 3× faster while preserving general model utility.

Conclusion: Reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency, and the proposed graded and semantically-aware reward functions offer a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning.

Abstract: Machine unlearning seeks to selectively remove specific knowledge from trained language models without full retraining, a growing necessity under privacy regulations such as GDPR and the EU AI Act. Recent work has reformulated unlearning as a Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) problem, where models are optimized against verifiable rewards computed directly from their outputs. However, existing methods rely on sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal, indicating only whether forbidden content was avoided, and limiting convergence speed. In this paper, we study how reward design affects unlearning efficiency within the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework. We introduce a principled reward decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity, and propose two new reward functions: an exponential reward that provides graded penalties based on the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and a PageRank inspired reward that weights penalties by semantic importance. We conduct experiments on the Real World Knowledge Unlearning (RWKU) benchmark, demonstrating that both rewards consistently outperform the binary setting, while reaching similar forgetting performance up to $3\times$ faster and preserving general model utility. Our results show that reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning.

</details>


### [315] [TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27973)
*Cong Li,Peixi Peng,Yisen Zhao,Xinyu Hu,Shudong Liu,Zhan Su,Zhuojian Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TAPO is a unified training framework for LLM agents that alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision, using action-conditioned next-observation prediction on a shared backbone to leverage dense environmental feedback alongside sparse task rewards. It is a lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement for existing agent RL algorithms, consistently improving task performance on WebShop and ALFWorld.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL methods for LLM agent post-training rely predominantly on sparse task rewards, failing to exploit dense supervisory signals naturally present during online interaction — namely, environmental feedback following action execution. Recent theoretical work shows that generalization in multi-step goal-oriented tasks depends on predictive knowledge of environmental consequences, motivating the need to incorporate transition-aware supervision into policy optimization.

Method: TAPO alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision. Beyond standard RL updates, rollout data is repurposed to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model, enhancing sensitivity to environmental transition dynamics while concurrently optimizing the policy. It requires no extra expert data, additional sampling costs, or inference-time overhead, making it a plug-and-play module for existing agent RL algorithms.

Result: Systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld, integrating foundation models of various scales with different policy optimization algorithms, show that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.

Conclusion: TAPO effectively leverages dense environmental feedback to enhance LLM agent RL training at negligible additional cost, and consistently outperforms standard policy optimization across tasks and model scales.

Abstract: Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial paradigm for the post-training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents. However, existing methods predominantly rely on sparse task rewards for policy optimization, failing to fully exploit another class of inherently dense supervisory signals naturally present during online interaction: environmental feedback following action execution. Recent theoretical studies suggest that generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks hinges on predictive knowledge of environmental consequences. Inspired by this, we propose TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents, a unified training framework that alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision. Beyond standard RL updates, TAPO repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model. This approach enhances the model's sensitivity to environmental transition dynamics and action consequences while concurrently optimizing the policy. It serves as a computationally lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement module for existing agent RL algorithms, requiring no additional expert data, extra sampling costs, or inference-time overhead. We conduct systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld, integrating foundation models of various scales with different policy optimization algorithms. Empirical results demonstrate that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.

</details>


### [316] [Generalization Bounds on Optimal Control for Transformer Training and Wasserstein Distributional Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27975)
*Kağan Akman,Naci Saldi,Serdar Yüksel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper derives finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions, using a quantized model based on a doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation to interpret training as a Markovian control problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide rigorous finite-sample generalization guarantees for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions, which is an important but underexplored area in understanding Transformer generalization.

Method: The approach builds on a doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, treating datasets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures and framing training as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. The authors quantize state, action, and measure-state spaces, derive bounds via concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces, and use a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function. Bounds are transferred to the base model with an explicit approximation error. The same machinery also yields a distributionally robust control formulation via Wasserstein DRO.

Result: Explicit finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions, including an explicit approximation error term when transferring results from the quantized model to the base model, and a connection to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

Conclusion: The presented framework yields provable generalization guarantees and simultaneously reveals a distributionally robust interpretation of Transformer training, linking generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

Abstract: We derive finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions. Building on the doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, we view data sets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures, allowing us to interpret the training problem as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. We then analyze a quantized model, derived by quantizing the state, action, and measure-state spaces, and derive explicit finite-sample generalization bounds using concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces together with a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function. These bounds are transferred to the base model at the cost of an explicit approximation error. Finally, we show that the same machinery yields a distributionally robust control formulation of the training problem, connecting Transformer generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

</details>


### [317] [It's All Just Vectorization: einx, a Universal Notation for Tensor Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27987)
*Florian Fervers,Sebastian Bullinger,Christoph Bodensteiner,Michael Arens*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces einx, a universal notation for tensor operations based on vectorization as a unifying concept, which reduces complex tensor APIs to a small set of elementary operations with consistent rules, providing a readable and maintainable alternative to Numpy-like tensor programming.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Numpy-like tensor notation is difficult to read/write and prone to shape errors due to inconsistent rules across a large collection of operations. Existing alternatives like einsum and einops are restricted to few operations and lack the generality for a universal model of tensor programming.

Method: The authors revisit vectorization as a foundational function for transforming tensor operations. Vectorization is used to both lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations and decompose higher-order operations back to lower-order ones. This leads to einx, a notation using declarative, pointful expressions analogous to loop notation that represent vectorized tensor operations.

Result: einx reduces the large APIs of existing tensor frameworks to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and enables clean, readable, and writable code representations. An implementation embedded in Python that integrates with existing tensor frameworks is provided.

Conclusion: Vectorization provides a universal foundation for tensor operation notation, and einx demonstrates a practical, consistent, and general alternative to existing Numpy-like tensor programming paradigms.

Abstract: Tensor operations represent a cornerstone of modern scientific computing. However, the Numpy-like notation adopted by predominant tensor frameworks is often difficult to read and write and prone to so-called shape errors, i.a., due to following inconsistent rules across a large, complex collection of operations. Alternatives like einsum and einops have gained popularity, but are inherently restricted to few operations and lack the generality required for a universal model of tensor programming.
  To derive a better paradigm, we revisit vectorization as a function for transforming tensor operations, and use it to both lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations, and conceptually decompose higher-order operations to lower-order operations and their vectorization.
  Building on the universal nature of vectorization, we introduce einx, a universal notation for tensor operations. It uses declarative, pointful expressions that are defined by analogy with loop notation and represent the vectorization of tensor operations. The notation reduces the large APIs of existing frameworks to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and enables a clean, readable and writable representation in code. We provide an implementation of einx that is embedded in Python and integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks: https://github.com/fferflo/einx

</details>


### [318] [Building a User Foundation Model for the Open Web](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28019)
*Solal Vernier,Ivan Can Arisoy,Merwan Barlier,Blaž Škrlj*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents a user foundation model for open-web real-time bidding (RTB), where user identity is fragmented and non-persistent. The model uses self-supervised learning (masked language modeling + contrastive objective) on user browsing histories with a Transformer encoder, fine-tuned for click prediction. An LLM-in-the-loop optimization pipeline searches over code-level edits (lifters) to improve pre-training. The method yields significant improvements across multiple production tasks, confirmed by both offline metrics and a 7-day live A/B test.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing user foundation models assume stable, persistent user identities, which does not hold in open-web RTB where user identity is fragmented, browsing history is non-persistent due to privacy choices, and a significant portion of traffic has no historical data. Historical signals are typically aggregated into counters and recency buckets, leaving sequential structure of user behavior unexploited.

Method: The authors pre-train a Transformer encoder using masked language modeling combined with a sequence-level contrastive objective on user browsing histories. The encoder is then fine-tuned on the click prediction task. Additionally, the pre-training pipeline is optimized via an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of reviewable, code-level edits (lifters), demonstrating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in industry.

Result: The same encoder representation yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker. A 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR and -1.13% eCPC, with 80% confidence intervals excluding zero on both metrics.

Conclusion: Self-supervised learning on user browsing histories is viable for open-web RTB environments despite fragmented and non-persistent user identity. The learned representations improve multiple downstream production tasks, and the LLM-in-the-loop optimization of the pre-training pipeline proves effective in an industrial setting.

Abstract: User foundation models have demonstrated strong results in e-commerce and social recommendation, but most industrial deployments assume environments where user identity is stable and persistent. Open-web real-time bidding (RTB) operates on a structurally different data distribution: user identity is fragmented and non-persistent across browsing sessions, and the availability of browsing history depends on user privacy choices. Consequently, a significant portion of traffic carries no historical data, and available records often consist of relatively short, disjointed sessions. As a result, historical signals in this domain are typically represented as aggregated counters and recency buckets, leaving the sequential structure unexploited. To address this limitation, we present a user foundation model that applies self-supervised learning on user browsing histories and show that the learned representation improves multiple downstream production tasks, demonstrating the viability of this approach on the open web. We pre-train a Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective, then fine-tune it on the click prediction task. We optimize the encoder's pre-training pipeline with an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of reviewable, code-level edits (lifters), instantiating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in an industrial setting. The same encoder representation yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker; a 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR, -1.13% eCPC (80% CI excluding zero on both metrics).

</details>


### [319] [Flux-OPD: On-Policy Distillation with Evolving Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28022)
*Yuran Wang,Zekun Wang,Bohan Zeng,Ruixu Zhang,Wenxuan Liu,Liu Yang,Yifan Dai,Yang Shi,Bozhou Li,Chengzhuo Tong,Daili Hua,Yuanxing Zhang,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Flux-OPD, an OPD (Offline Preference Distillation) paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to capture task preferences in open-ended domains where verifiable rewards are unavailable. It decomposes the reverse KL objective to reveal that the student distills toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and identifies a conflict term measuring disagreements among these teachers. Flux-OPD uses the differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual corrections injected into the context-free teacher anchor, with correction strength weighted by the conflict term. Experiments on open-ended tasks demonstrate superior performance over existing OPD paradigms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In open-ended domains, LLM training lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences hard to formalize as supervision. Contexts convey preferences but provide little additional supervision once distilled into the student, motivating the use of contexts that evolve with student performance. However, evolving contexts as in-training supervision cause unstable distillation targets and conflicting distributions, requiring stabilization mechanisms and conflict downweighting.

Method: The paper analyzes the reverse KL objective to decompose the effect of contexts, revealing that (1) the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and (2) the objective contains a conflict term measuring disagreements among these teachers. Based on this decomposition, Flux-OPD treats differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, and weights correction strength using the conflict term as an indicator.

Result: Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining teacher supervision with evolving contexts and highlighting the value of the proposed decomposition and conflict-aware weighting mechanism.

Conclusion: Flux-OPD successfully leverages evolving contexts as in-training supervision for open-ended preference distillation by decomposing the reverse KL objective, injecting contextual corrections into a context-free teacher anchor, and using the conflict term to weight correction strength, achieving state-of-the-art performance in open-ended domains.

Abstract: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize as effective supervision. Contexts can convey such preferences, yet provide little additional supervision once distilled into the student, motivating contexts that evolve with student performance. However, directly using evolving contexts as in-training supervision results in an unstable distillation target and conflicting distributions, requiring mechanisms to stabilize target and downweight conflicts. In this paper, we analyze the effect of contexts through a decomposition of the reverse KL objective, revealing two findings: the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and the objective contains a conflict term that measures conflicts among these teachers. Based on this decomposition, we propose Flux-OPD, an OPD paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to capture task preferences in open-ended domains. Flux-OPD treats the differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, and weights their correction strength using the conflict term as an indicator. Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, highlighting the potential to combine teacher supervision with evolving contexts.

</details>


### [320] [Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization via Privileged Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28026)
*Xingjian Wu,Junlin Liu,Xingchen Liu,Xuhang Zhu,Jianing Wang,Linsen Guo,Xiaoyu Li,Xuezhi Cao,Xunliang Cai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CRPO is a contrastive learning-based method that reformulates on-policy self-distillation for agentic LLM post-training by using predictive entropy to distinguish reliable (reflective) from biased (exposure) positions, outperforming existing RL and self-distillation baselines across 13 reasoning and deep-search benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OPSD provides dense logit-level supervision but suffers from exposure bias from the self-teacher's privileged information. In multi-turn agentic settings, this leads to reasoning route convergence and loss of clear optimization directions.

Method: CRPO reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective, using predictive entropy to distinguish positive positions (reflective exploration) from negative positions (exposure bias), and conducts group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals.

Result: Across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks, CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, with significantly improved training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

Conclusion: CRPO effectively mitigates exposure bias in agentic self-distillation by leveraging contrastive learning, providing a more stable and generalizable training paradigm for long-horizon LLM agentic reasoning.

Abstract: Recent advances in post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) or On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD). While OPSD provides dense, logit-level supervision, it inherently suffers from exposure bias due to the privileged information of the self-teacher. In multi-turn agentic settings, this leads to reasoning route convergence and the loss of clear optimization directions. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization (CRPO), which reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective. By leveraging predictive entropy to distinguish between positive positions (reflective exploration) and negative positions (exposure bias), CRPO conducts group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals. Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, significantly enhancing training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

</details>


### [321] [Enhancing Irregular Time Series Forecasting with Continuous-Time Modeling Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28035)
*Tianen Shen,Zhengyu Li,Yutong Li,Xiangfei Qiu,Xingjian Wu,Bin Yang,Jilin Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WrapFlow is a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular multivariate time series forecasting that uses Continuous-Time Tokenization to encode raw events and gap-aware tokens, processed by a standard Transformer backbone, with a simulation-free Residual Flow Matching training paradigm for efficient high-quality continuous forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Irregular multivariate time series present challenges from asynchronous observations and non-uniform sampling intervals. Existing methods either use discretization-based preprocessing (interpolation/imputation/aggregation) which disrupts continuous-time semantics, or ODE-based continuous-time modeling which requires specialized architectures and incurs heavy computational overhead from numerical solvers.

Method: WrapFlow has two key components: (1) Continuous-Time Tokenization on the input side, which directly encodes raw observation events and models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens, then processes them with a standard Transformer backbone; (2) a simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching on the output side, which learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions without numerical-solver simulation or backpropagation during training, requiring only a few fixed rollout steps at inference.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance for irregular time series forecasting.

Conclusion: The proposed WrapFlow framework effectively addresses the limitations of both discretization-based and ODE-based approaches by combining continuous-time tokenization with a standard Transformer and a simulation-free flow matching paradigm, enabling efficient and high-quality continuous forecasting.

Abstract: Irregular multivariate time series are widely encountered in applications such as healthcare monitoring, human activity recognition, and environmental sensing. Their core challenges stem from asynchronous observations, non-uniform sampling intervals, and the fact that temporal patterns themselves carry critical dynamic information. Existing approaches either rely on discretization-based preprocessing (e.g., interpolation, imputation, or aggregation), which disrupts the underlying continuous-time semantics, or adopt continuous-time modeling via ODE-based frameworks, which typically require specialized architectures and incur substantial computational overhead due to numerical solvers. To address these limitations, we propose WrapFlow, a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular time series forecasting. On the input side, WrapFlow introduces Continuous-Time Tokenization, which directly encodes raw observation events and explicitly models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens. The resulting continuous-time tokens are then processed by a standard Transformer backbone to capture long-range temporal dependencies. On the output side, we develop a simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching, which learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions while avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training. This design enables high-quality continuous forecasting using only a small number of fixed rollout steps at inference. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance.

</details>


### [322] [Learning features from Newton's algorithm: a way to accelerate nonlinear parametrized PDE solvers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28036)
*Rémy Vallot,Florian de Vuyst,Thibault Dairay,Mathilde Mougeot*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy that learns features from parameter-space sampling and precomputed solutions to accelerate Newton's method for nonlinear systems. It constructs two complementary reduced spaces (solution feature space and corrective search direction feature space) from discrete Newton trajectories, predicts a surrogate solution via regression, applies a residual-minimizing correction using GMRES, and uses the result as an initial guess for high-fidelity Newton convergence, reducing iterations and CPU time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Newton's method converges faster when the initial guess is closer to a root, and poor initial guesses can lead to slow convergence or failure. The authors aim to improve convergence by generating high-quality initial guesses using learned features from precomputed solution data.

Method: The method builds two complementary reduced spaces from discrete Newton trajectories: a solution feature space from converged states and a corrective search direction feature space from intermediate Newton increments. A regression model predicts a surrogate solution for unseen parameters, followed by a residual-minimizing correction computed via a GMRES-based approach (only requiring residual evaluations and a small least-squares problem). This corrected state serves as the initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method. The approach is weakly intrusive, requiring only residual fields and a script-based interface.

Result: Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems demonstrate quantifiable speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization in terms of reduced Newton iterations and overall CPU time, with significant speedups observed.

Conclusion: The proposed two-stage initialization strategy is a generic, weakly intrusive method applicable to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems, effectively reducing Newton iterations and computational cost.

Abstract: It is well known that Newton's method converges faster when the initial guess is closer to a root of a system of nonlinear equations. In this paper, a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed by learning features from a parameter-space sampling and a database of precomputed solutions. The method uses discrete Newton trajectories to construct two complementary reduced spaces: a solution feature space, built from converged states, and a corrective search direction feature space, built from intermediate Newton increments. For an unseen parameter, a regression model is used to predict a surrogate solution approximation. Then, in a second step, a residual-minimizing correction is computed using a dedicated GMRES-based approach. The resulting state is then used as an initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method, which completes convergence. The corrective step is computationally inexpensive since it only requires residual evaluations and the solution of a small least-squares problem. The methodology is weakly intrusive once the high-fidelity residual fields and a script-based programming interface are available. This strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and decreases the overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization. Significant speedups are observed. This generic approach can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

</details>


### [323] [ClawTrack: Towards Trace-Level Evaluation and Improvement of Real-World Autonomous Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28037)
*Xingjian Wu,Xuhang Zhu,Xingchen Liu,Junlin Liu,Jianing Wang,Linsen Guo,Xiaoyu Li,Xuezhi Cao,Xunliang Cai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ClawTrack is a dual-assessment benchmark for LLM-based agents that evaluates both what an agent achieves (Task Score) and how it achieves it (Process Score), comprising 320 tasks across 8 domains with deterministic mock services and 12,541 rubric items. Evaluating 21 models over 16,000+ trials, the framework attributes success/failure to specific reasoning dimensions, identifies result verification as the systematic bottleneck, shows robustness to evaluator choice, and demonstrates that process-based trajectory filtering improves post-training across model scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based agents only evaluate final outcomes, which cannot distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies—especially problematic for long-horizon, multi-step workflows where attribution is critical.

Method: ClawTrack provides a dual-assessment benchmark with a Task Score for outcomes and a Process Score for reasoning quality. A Process Grader evaluates each reasoning turn across four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, result verification) using 12,541 task-specific rubric items. The benchmark includes 320 tasks across 8 domains and 25+ deterministic mock services.

Result: Across 21 models and 16,000+ trials, ClawTrack found that (1) process scores attribute success/failure to specific reasoning dimensions and filter lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation; (2) the four dimensions are complementary with result verification being the systematic bottleneck; (3) the framework is robust across different judge LLMs; (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.

Conclusion: ClawTrack addresses the evaluation gap by providing a complementary process-level assessment that enables attribution of agent reasoning quality and yields actionable insights, including downstream training improvements through process-based trajectory filtering.

Abstract: As LLM-based agents are deployed in complex, multi-step workflows, a critical evaluation gap has emerged: most existing benchmarks judge only final outcomes, unable to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies, hindering attribution in long-horizon tasks.
  In this work, we present ClawTrack, a dual-assessment benchmark that simultaneously measures what an agent achieves (Task Score) and how it achieves it (Process Score). ClawTrack comprises 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader scores each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification), anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. Evaluating 21 models over 16,000+ trials, we find that: (1) process scores effectively attribute success and failure to specific reasoning dimensions, filtering lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation; (2) the four dimensions are complementary, with result verification as the systematic bottleneck; (3) the framework is robust to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs; and (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.

</details>


### [324] [GVR-Coder: A Visual-Feedback Framework for Structured SVG Generation in Complex Document and Meeting Scenarios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28073)
*Yiming Xu,Jihua Kang,Chunsai Du,Qifan Zhang,Wangqiu Zhou,Yiting Wu,Tianqi Li,Qi Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces DocMeetSVG-100K, a large-scale SVG dataset, and GVR-Coder, a framework for generating logical diagrams from lengthy professional texts. GVR-Coder uses curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning, layout constraint modeling, reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, and a generate-verify-repair agent loop to produce logically coherent and visually appealing SVG diagrams.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lengthy professional texts impose high cognitive load in document authoring and meeting review scenarios. Transforming verbose text into clear diagrams is essential, and SVG offers editability and resolution independence. However, Text-to-SVG generation faces three key challenges: scarcity of complex diagram datasets, absence of explicit layout priors leading to chaotic arrangements, and lack of fine-grained visual feedback for validating rendered outputs.

Method: The proposed GVR-Coder framework: (1) leverages the DocMeetSVG-100K dataset for training; (2) adopts curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning to progressively enhance complex structure modeling; (3) incorporates explicit layout constraint knowledge during training; (4) introduces reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, using implicit reward signals to jointly optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics; (5) designs a generate-verify-repair agent loop for explicit, fine-grained feedback and targeted refinement.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines, reliably producing logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams from lengthy professional texts.

Conclusion: The combination of a high-quality dataset (DocMeetSVG-100K), curriculum-based training, layout prior modeling, reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, and an iterative generate-verify-repair loop enables high-quality logical diagram generation, addressing the identified data, layout, and feedback challenges in Text-to-SVG generation.

Abstract: In demanding professional environments and meeting review scenarios, lengthy text often imposes a high cognitive load. To facilitate efficient information communication, transforming verbose text into logically clear diagrams is essential. Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) provide an effective representation for this purpose due to their editability and resolution independence. However, current research on Text-to-SVG generation remains hindered by three major challenges: (1) the scarcity of datasets for complex, logic-rich diagrams; (2) the absence of explicit layout priors, which leads to chaotic spatial arrangements; and (3) the lack of fine-grained visual feedback to validate rendered outputs and correct aesthetic defects. To address these challenges, at the data level, we introduce DocMeetSVG-100K, a large-scale SVG dataset tailored for document authoring and meeting review scenarios. At the model level, we propose GVR-Coder, a novel framework designed to generate high-quality logical diagrams from lengthy professional texts. Specifically, we adopt a curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning to progressively enhance the model's capability in modeling complex structures, while explicitly incorporating layout constraint knowledge during training. In addition, we introduce reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, a mechanism that provides implicit feedback through reward signals to jointly optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics. Furthermore, we design a generate-verify-repair agent loop, which improves generation quality through explicit, fine-grained feedback and targeted refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines and reliably produces logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams. Code and data are available at https://github.com/CurryaNa/GVR-Coder.

</details>


### [325] [Chem World: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Physics-Informed Framework for Trustworthy Chemical Property Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28079)
*Tianyou Bai,Huan Wang,Mingchen Gao,Fangyue Lin,Pinze Ren,Zhenlin Zhao,Siming Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Chem World is a comprehensive benchmark for chemical property prediction integrating 17 datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples across diverse properties, paired with Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network framework that incorporates chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning for improved prediction accuracy, robustness, and reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for chemical property prediction suffer from limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, making it difficult to systematically assess the reliability and generalization of AI models in computational chemistry.

Method: The paper introduces Chem World, a unified benchmark platform integrating 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples covering properties such as density, electrical conductivity, solubility, and other molecular characteristics. It also proposes Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network framework that incorporates chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning.

Result: Extensive experiments on Chem World demonstrate the effectiveness of Mixture-PINN compared with existing methods across multiple chemical property prediction tasks.

Conclusion: By combining large-scale standardized evaluation with physics-informed learning, Chem World provides a foundation for developing trustworthy AI systems for computational chemistry and advancing AI-driven scientific discovery.

Abstract: Chemical property prediction plays a critical role in accelerating scientific discovery in chemistry, materials science, and drug development. However, existing benchmarks often suffer from limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, making it challenging to systematically assess the reliability and generalization of AI models. In this work, we introduce Chem World, a comprehensive benchmark for chemical property prediction that integrates 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples, covering various properties including density, electrical conductivity, solubility, and other molecular characteristics. Chem World provides a unified platform for evaluating AI models across multiple property prediction tasks. Furthermore, we propose Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network based prediction framework that incorporates chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning, improving the accuracy, robustness, and reliability of chemical property prediction. Extensive experiments on Chem World demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared with existing methods. By combining large-scale standardized evaluation with physics-informed learning, Chem World establishes a foundation for developing trustworthy AI systems for computational chemistry and advancing AI-driven scientific discovery.

</details>


### [326] [From Expert Reduction to Behavioral Divergence: Tracing Numerical State through Sparse MoE Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28097)
*Tianyang Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that mathematically equivalent expert-reduction orders in sparse MoE models produce observably different executions. By isolating aggregation semantics in DeepSeek-V4-Flash with frozen local MoE state, it shows that different reduction schemes (A, B, C modes with varying operand representation and accumulator precision) yield different continuation basins, structural classes, token sequences, and trajectories. Controls identify post-mHC as an intra-token boundary and full persistent state as a cross-token boundary, showing identical tokens can still diverge autoregressively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish whether mathematically equivalent reduction orders can produce observably different sparse-MoE executions despite being algebraically identical, addressing a numerical compatibility concern for MoE runtimes and hardware backends.

Method: Freezing local MoE state in native DeepSeek-V4-Flash and varying only aggregation semantics across four schemes that separate operand representation from accumulator precision. Tests include 720 A-mode and B-mode orders at a layer-5 fork, controllable B-branch endpoint reconstruction, and 192-trajectory persistent state checks per scheme.

Result: A-mode orders yield 10 continuation basins, B-mode orders form 360 structural classes and 11 basins. Under a Chinese prompt, B classes split into 202 layoffs, 113 hiring, and 45 other continuations. P32, A, and B change every native-reference route trajectory while C preserves routes, tokens, and texts. C matches native MoE bitwise across 192 trajectories. FP64 reconstruction reproduces downstream states over seven steps.

Conclusion: Expert operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order form a numerical compatibility contract for sparse-MoE runtimes and hardware backends. Identical tokens need not imply identical autoregressive state—divergence can survive a token boundary and manifest later. Results establish controlled causal possibility, not deployment incidence, with C's order invariance limited to evaluated states and schedules.

Abstract: Mathematically equivalent expert-reduction orders can produce observably different sparse-MoE executions. We isolate this effect in native DeepSeek-V4-Flash by freezing local MoE state and varying only aggregation semantics. Four schemes separate operand representation from accumulator precision. At one layer-5 fork, 720 A-mode orders yield 10 continuation basins; 720 B-mode orders form 360 exact structural classes and 11 basins. Under one Chinese prompt, the B classes split into 202 layoffs, 113 hiring, and 45 other continuations. Maximum-L-infinity B-branch selection separates 12, 24, and 36 of 50 prompts by 8, 16, and 32 tokens. Across 192 persistent trajectories per scheme, P32, A, and B change every native-reference route trajectory, while C preserves routes, token sequences, and texts. A separate 192-trajectory C check matches native MoE, post-mHC, next-router, and LM states bitwise. For one controlled B branch, exact post-mHC endpoint reconstruction reproduces the measured downstream trajectory. At the next decode boundary, exact FP64 reconstruction of the branch's full persistent state yields agreement for 301 downstream post-mHC states, 301 persistent-state checkpoints, 301 routes, predictions, and text over seven steps, given the same naturally generated next input. These controls identify post-mHC as an intra-token boundary and full persistent state as a cross-token continuation boundary. Identical tokens need not imply identical autoregressive state: divergence can survive a token boundary and become visible later. These results make expert operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order part of a numerical compatibility contract for sparse-MoE runtimes and hardware backends. They establish controlled causal possibility, not deployment incidence; C's order invariance is limited to evaluated six-term states and schedules.

</details>


### [327] [Information Bottleneck Learning for Faithful Time Series Forecasting Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28124)
*Xu Zheng,Wei Cheng,Zhuomin Chen,Mo Sha,Jingchao Ni,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IB-Forecast is an inherently interpretable multivariate time-series forecasting framework that decomposes forecasting into a learned periodic component and a residual component with explainable masks over input tokens, using a budget-constrained information bottleneck to enable user-controlled explanation sparsity. It matches black-box forecasting accuracy while providing faithful explanations with no additional inference cost, outperforming gradient-, occlusion-, and optimization-based baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing interpretable-by-design forecasters reveal internal structures but do not guarantee these structures faithfully reflect the evidence driving predictions, while faithfulness-oriented methods are almost exclusively designed for post-hoc classification tasks. There is a gap for inherently interpretable forecasting with faithful explanations.

Method: IB-Forecast decomposes forecasting into a learned periodic component and a residual component computed with explainable masks over input tokens. A budget-constrained information bottleneck enables end-to-end optimization and direct user control over explanation sparsity, with a rigorous faithfulness evaluation protocol.

Result: IB-Forecast matches the forecasting error of leading black-box models while providing faithful explanations at no additional inference cost. Under matched sparsity budgets, native explanations consistently surpass gradient-, occlusion-, and optimization-based baselines across all datasets, requiring only 14-20% of observations for low-error predictions.

Conclusion: Whereas existing interpretable forecasters exhibit poor explanation faithfulness, IB-Forecast guarantees high explanation fidelity with strong predictive performance, effectively bridging the gap between inherent interpretability and faithful evidence attribution in multivariate time-series forecasting.

Abstract: As forecasts increasingly drive decisions in fields such as energy, transportation, and healthcare, understanding the historical data behind these predictions has become as crucial as the predictions themselves. Although existing interpretable-by-design forecasters reveal their internal structures, they offer no guarantee that these structures faithfully reflect the underlying evidence driving the predictions. In contrast, while faithfulness-oriented methods explicitly verify model behavior, they are almost exclusively designed for post-hoc classification tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose IB-Forecast, an inherently interpretable multivariate time-series forecasting framework. It decomposes forecasting into a learned periodic component and a residual component computed with explainable masks over input tokens. With a budget-constrained information bottleneck, end-to-end optimization enables users to directly control explanation sparsity. With a rigorous faithfulness evaluation protocol, extensive experiments demonstrate that IB-Forecast matches the forecasting error of leading black-box models while providing faithful explanations at no additional inference cost. Furthermore, under a matched sparsity budget, these native explanations consistently surpass gradient-based, occlusion-based, and optimization-based baselines across all evaluated datasets. Ultimately, whereas the native explanations of existing interpretable forecasters exhibit poor faithfulness, IB-Forecast guarantees high explanation fidelity, requiring only 14-20% of the observations to deliver low-error predictions.

</details>


### [328] [LM-GRASP: Instance-Specific Language Models for Combinatorial Construction via Online Imitation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28135)
*Mohand Mezmaz,Grégoire Danoy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LM-GRASP is a metaheuristic framework that reformulates GRASP's randomized constructive phase as an online imitation learning task, training a decoder-only Transformer from scratch on each problem instance via behavioral cloning on elite trajectories discovered during the search itself. It requires no offline pretraining or problem-specific feature engineering, outperforming GPU-GRASP on the Taillard PFSP benchmark by 28.4 makespan units.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural constructors for combinatorial optimization typically require expensive offline pretraining on large datasets for a fixed problem class and generalize poorly outside the training distribution. The authors propose an alternative that avoids these costs by learning instance-specific construction policies online from high-quality solutions discovered during the search itself.

Method: The approach reformulates GRASP's randomized constructive phase as online imitation learning: a local search procedure acts as an expert oracle providing demonstrations, while a decoder-only Transformer serves as the constructive policy. The framework follows a learn-infer-improve cycle, training the policy online via behavioral cloning on a dynamic archive of elite trajectories, interfacing with the domain only through the objective evaluator used by local search.

Result: On the Taillard PFSP benchmark (ta51-ta60), LM-GRASP outperforms GPU-GRASP by 28.4 makespan units on average—comparable to the performance gain from GPU acceleration over sequential execution (27.2 units), though standard deviations overlap.

Conclusion: Instance-specific, online-trained language models offer a promising, practical alternative to hand-engineered constructors, particularly for optimization landscapes resistant to classical greedy construction, with no external data or offline pretraining required.

Abstract: Machine learning for combinatorial optimization typically relies on neural constructors trained via reinforcement learning on large offline datasets for a fixed problem class-incurring high pretraining costs and generalizing poorly outside the training distribution. We propose an alternative: a metaheuristic framework that reformulates the randomized constructive phase of GRASP as an online imitation learning task, trained from scratch on each problem instance. A local search procedure acts as an expert oracle, while a decoder-only Transformer serves as the constructive policy. Unlike classical GRASP, which relies on static, myopic heuristic rules based on localized scalar costs, our approach is fully data-driven: the construction policy emerges from high-quality solutions discovered during the search itself, with no problem-specific feature engineering required.
  We instantiate this as LM-GRASP, a hybrid metaheuristic following an iterative learn-infer-improve cycle, training the policy online via behavioral cloning on a dynamic archive of elite trajectories-no external data or offline pretraining needed. The pipeline interfaces with the domain solely through the objective evaluator used by local search.
  Evaluated on the Taillard PFSP benchmark (ta51-ta60), the most discriminating block due to half its optima being unknown, LM-GRASP outperforms GPU-GRASP by 28.4 makespan units on average-comparable to the gain from GPU acceleration over sequential execution (27.2 units), though with overlapping standard deviations. This suggests instance-specific, online-trained language models are a promising, practical alternative to hand-engineered constructors, especially for landscapes resistant to classical greedy construction.

</details>


### [329] [Search Strategies for Optimal Classification and Regression Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28170)
*Jacobus G. M. van der Linden,Mim van den Bos,Emir Demirović*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a general algorithmic framework for optimal decision trees (ODTs) that unifies and compares 18 search strategies. The best strategy under this framework achieves significantly better anytime performance for classification and over an order of magnitude faster runtime for regression compared to state-of-the-art methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Optimal decision trees are compact and interpretable but lack scalability. While various search strategies have been proposed, the precise contribution of each strategy is unclear, motivating the need for a unified framework to understand and compare them.

Method: The authors propose a general algorithmic framework for ODTs that instantiates previously used search strategies and allows the definition of new ones. They empirically evaluate 18 search strategies within this unified framework.

Result: The best strategy identified in the evaluation achieves significantly better anytime performance for classification and improves runtime by more than an order of magnitude for regression compared to the state of the art.

Conclusion: A unified framework enables systematic analysis and comparison of ODT search strategies, revealing that certain strategies substantially outperform existing approaches in both classification quality and regression runtime.

Abstract: Optimal decision trees (ODTs) are compact, interpretable machine learning models that globally optimize a given objective, but their scalability remains challenging.
