While recent work has proposed a variety of search strategies to improve scalability, the precise contribution of each strategy remains unclear. To address this gap, we introduce a general algorithmic framework for ODTs that instantiates previously used search strategies and enables the definition of new ones. This provides a common lens through which to understand and compare different strategies, which we use to empirically investigate the effect of 18 search strategies. Compared to the state of the art, the best strategy in our evaluation achieves significantly better anytime performance for classification, and improves runtime by more than an order of magnitude for regression.

</details>


### [330] [Multi-channel Uplift Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28182)
*Changjian Liu,Tianyu Wang,Xiaoxuan Deng,WenTao Zhu,Yuwei Xu,Jungqi Jin,Yong Gao,Chuan Yu,Jian Xu,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReAlloc is a fast-slow causal framework for allocating fixed marketing budgets across e-commerce channels, formulated as a simplex-constrained uplift decision problem. It uses an Orthogonal Teacher to extract unbiased local gradients and an Explanation-Guided Student to distill them into a structured marginal field, enabling support-aware, conservative decisions that capture cross-channel substitutions. Validation on simulations and large-scale Taobao A/B tests shows simultaneous lifts in pay orders and income.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard predict-then-optimize (PTO) paradigms fail in the compositional budget allocation space for e-commerce due to observational confounding and severe extrapolation, making it necessary to formulate a new decision framework that accounts for these issues.

Method: The proposed ReAlloc framework formulates budget allocation as a simplex-constrained uplift decision problem. It comprises an Orthogonal Teacher (fast component) that extracts unbiased local gradients from short-term logs, and an Explanation-Guided Student (slow component) that distills these gradients into a structured marginal field over long-term horizons, enabling support-aware, conservative decisions capturing cross-channel substitutions.

Result: Extensive simulations and large-scale online A/B tests on the Taobao platform demonstrate that ReAlloc achieves simultaneous lifts in both pay order volume and income.

Conclusion: ReAlloc provides an effective causal solution for multi-channel marketing budget allocation in e-commerce, outperforming standard PTO approaches by handling confounding and extrapolation while enabling conservative, support-aware decisions.

Abstract: E-commerce platforms must allocate fixed marketing budgets across multiple channels to maximize business utility. However, standard predict-then-optimize (PTO) paradigms fail in this compositional space due to observational confounding and severe extrapolation. We formulate this challenge as a simplex-constrained uplift decision problem and propose ReAlloc, a fast-slow causal framework. Specifically, an agile Orthogonal Teacher extracts unbiased local gradients from short-term logs, while an Explanation-Guided Student distills them into a structured marginal field over long-term horizons. This design enables support-aware, conservative decisions that capture cross-channel substitutions. Extensive simulations and large-scale online A/B tests on Taobao platform demonstrate that ReAlloc achieves simultaneous lifts in both pay order and income.

</details>


### [331] [Persistent Gaussian Perturbations Prevent Oversmoothing in Recurrent Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28185)
*Mostafa Haghir Chehreghani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies a stochastic recurrent GNN where Gaussian noise is injected after each propagation step, proving via Markov chain analysis that the hidden representations converge to a unique invariant measure and maintain a positive lower bound on expected stationary Dirichlet energy proportional to noise variance and graph spectral gap—thereby rigorously preventing asymptotic oversmoothing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Oversmoothing fundamentally limits the depth of GNNs by causing node representations to collapse toward a low-dimensional subspace. Existing deterministic remedies (residual connections, normalization, rewiring) mitigate but do not rigorously guarantee diversity. The authors seek a fundamentally different mechanism—stochastic perturbation—that provably prevents asymptotic representation collapse.

Method: The paper models a recurrent GNN with independent Gaussian noise injected after every propagation step as a stochastic dynamical system. Under a global contraction assumption on the deterministic update, the authors prove the hidden representations form a geometrically ergodic Markov chain with a unique invariant probability measure, and derive an explicit lower bound on the expected stationary Dirichlet energy proportional to noise variance and the graph's spectral gap.

Result: The main theoretical result establishes a positive lower bound on expected stationary Dirichlet energy, proving stationary representations cannot collapse onto the constant manifold (non-vanishing Dirichlet energy). Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear recurrent GNNs closely match theoretical predictions, confirming the emergence of a stationary distribution and the predicted dependence of limiting Dirichlet energy on noise intensity.

Conclusion: Persistent stochastic perturbations constitute a fundamentally distinct and theoretically rigorous mechanism for combating oversmoothing, complementary to deterministic approaches. Injecting noise guarantees, in a probabilistic sense, that hidden representations retain energy and diversity even at infinite depth.

Abstract: Oversmoothing is a fundamental limitation of deep graph neural networks (GNNs), where repeated message passing causes node representations to become increasingly similar, eventually collapsing toward a low-dimensional subspace. This phenomenon limits the effective depth of message-passing architectures and motivates the search for mechanisms that preserve representation diversity. In this paper, we study a recurrent graph neural network in which independent Gaussian noise is injected after every propagation step and analyze the resulting architecture as a stochastic dynamical system. Under a standard global contraction assumption on the deterministic update, we prove that the hidden representations form a geometrically ergodic Markov chain admitting a unique invariant probability measure. Our main theoretical result establishes an explicit positive lower bound on the expected stationary Dirichlet energy, proportional to both the noise variance and the spectral gap of the underlying graph. Consequently, the stationary representations cannot collapse onto the constant manifold, providing a rigorous guarantee that asymptotic oversmoothing is prevented in the sense of non-vanishing Dirichlet energy. Our analysis reveals persistent stochastic perturbations as a fundamentally different mechanism for combating oversmoothing, complementing existing deterministic approaches based on residual connections, normalization, and graph rewiring. Finally, numerical experiments on both linear and nonlinear recurrent graph neural networks closely match the theoretical predictions, illustrating the emergence of a stationary distribution and the predicted dependence of the limiting Dirichlet energy on the noise intensity.

</details>


### [332] [TopoFormer: Topology Meets Attention for Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28259)
*Md Joshem Uddin,Astrit Tola,Cuneyt Gurcan Akcora,Baris Coskunuzer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Topoformer is a lightweight, scalable graph representation learning framework that encodes topology into attention-friendly sequences via Topo-Scan, a module that decomposes graphs into ordered topological tokens over filtrations, achieving SOTA performance on graph classification and molecular benchmarks while remaining parallelizable and efficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional persistent homology pipelines are computationally expensive and difficult to integrate with deep learning. There is a need for a framework that captures multi-scale topological structure in graphs while being efficient, parallelizable, and compatible with standard architectures like Transformers.

Method: Topoformer introduces Topo-Scan, a module that slices graphs over node or edge filtrations to produce short, ordered sequences of topological tokens capturing multi-scale structural patterns. These sequences are processed by a Transformer encoder to produce graph-level embeddings. The method provides theoretical stability guarantees and avoids costly persistence diagram computations.

Result: Topoformer matches or exceeds strong GNN and topology-based baselines on graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks, offering state-of-the-art performance with predictable and efficient compute.

Conclusion: This work opens a new path for parallelizable and unifying graph representation learning by integrating topological inductive biases into attention frameworks.

Abstract: We introduce Topoformer, a lightweight and scalable framework for graph representation learning that encodes topological structure into attention-friendly sequences. At the core of our method is Topo-Scan, a novel module that decomposes a graph into a short, ordered sequence of topological tokens by slicing over node or edge filtrations. These sequences capture multi-scale structural patterns, from local motifs to global organization, and are processed by a Transformer to produce expressive graph-level embeddings. Unlike traditional persistent homology pipelines, Topo-Scan is parallelizable, avoids costly diagram computations, and integrates seamlessly with standard deep learning architectures. We provide theoretical guarantees on the stability of our topological encodings and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks. Our results show that Topoformer matches or exceeds strong GNN and topology-based baselines while offering predictable and efficient compute. This work opens a new path for parallelizable and unifying approaches to graph representation learning that integrate topological inductive biases into attention frameworks.

</details>


### [333] [HARGO: Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization for RL Post-Training of LLMs on HPC Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28301)
*Tiangang Li,Xiangbo Tian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HARGO is a heterogeneity-aware reward-guided optimization method for RL post-training of LLMs on high-performance computing tasks. It uses confidence-modulated advantage (combining group-level reward contrast and reference model log-probability confidence) to compute per-response importance weights without task-type labels, outperforming uniform-weight methods like GRPO across four HPC tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) gives LLMs domain knowledge but not task-appropriate behavior—models can classify data races well yet produce verbose, imprecise answers. HPC tasks exhibit extreme heterogeneity (58x answer-length differences, three distinct reward distributions, varying SFT accuracy), making uniform-weight RL methods like GRPO suboptimal for post-training.

Method: HARGO introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage. It computes a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast and a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities, then modulates the advantage to derive per-response weights—all without requiring task-type labels.

Result: Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves the best performance on all primary metrics: WinRate 54.62%, Data Race F1 91.30%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablations confirm both the discrimination and confidence signals contribute complementary benefits.

Conclusion: HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks, demonstrating that heterogeneity-aware reward-weighted optimization outperforms uniform-weight RL post-training approaches.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can equip large language models (LLMs) with domain knowledge for high-performance computing (HPC) tasks such as data race detection and benchmark question answering. However, knowledge alone does not guarantee task-appropriate behavior: the same SFT model that correctly classifies 88.65\% of C/C++ data race samples produces verbose, imprecise answers to factual queries, with 65.9\% of MLPerf responses exceeding 40 characters. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training addresses this gap by optimizing for task-specific rewards rather than token-level imitation. Yet HPC tasks exhibit extreme heterogeneity, with binary classification, factual QA, and semantic generation differing by 58x in answer length, spanning three distinct reward distributions, and showing widely varying SFT accuracy. This makes uniform-weight RL methods such as GRPO suboptimal. We propose HARGO, Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization, which introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage: computing a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast and a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities, then modulating the advantage before computing per-response weights, without requiring task-type labels. Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves the best performance on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62\%, Data Race F1 91.30\%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation confirms complementary contributions from both signals. HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks.

</details>


### [334] [Semi-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graphs via Ensemble Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28304)
*Rasmus Tirsgaard,Laurits Fredsgaard,Marisa Wodrich,Mikkel Jordahn,Mikkel N. Schmidt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that semi-supervised learning methods based on ensemble consensus can improve predictive accuracy, robustness, and calibration across diverse molecular datasets, task types, and graph neural network architectures—without requiring label-preserving augmentations that are difficult to design for molecular data. Notably, an individual ensemble member trained this way outperforms a full traditionally-supervised ensemble in almost all cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Labeled molecular data is costly and time-consuming to acquire, while unlabeled molecular data is abundant. Standard semi-supervised learning relies on label-preserving augmentations, which are challenging in molecular domains because minor structural changes can drastically alter molecular properties, making it difficult to apply conventional semi-supervised approaches.

Method: The authors employ semi-supervised learning methods that rely on ensemble consensus rather than label-preserving augmentations. They train graph neural networks with an ensemble consensus objective on unlabeled molecular data, evaluating across diverse molecular datasets, task types, and GNN architectures.

Result: Training with an ensemble consensus objective increases model robustness and exhibits an effect similar to knowledge distillation. An individual ensemble member trained this way outperforms a full ensemble trained in a traditional supervised fashion in almost all cases. Additionally, this semi-supervised training approach reduces calibration error.

Conclusion: Ensemble-consensus-based semi-supervised learning is an effective and broadly applicable strategy for molecular machine learning, overcoming the augmentation-design challenge and yielding stronger individual models, improved robustness, and better-calibrated predictions.

Abstract: Machine learning is transforming molecular sciences by accelerating property prediction, simulation, and the discovery of new molecules and materials. Acquiring labeled data in these domains is often costly and time-consuming, whereas large collections of unlabeled molecular data are readily available. Standard semi-supervised learning methods often rely on label-preserving augmentations, which are challenging to design in the molecular domain, where minor changes can drastically alter properties. In this work, we show that semi-supervised methods that rely on an ensemble consensus can boost predictive accuracy across a diverse range of molecular datasets, task types, and graph neural network architectures. We find that training with an ensemble consensus objective increases robustness in models and exhibits an effect similar to knowledge distillation; an individual member of an ensemble trained this way outperforms a full ensemble trained in a traditional supervised fashion in almost all cases. In addition, this type of semi-supervised training reduces calibration error.

</details>


### [335] [Beyond Geometric Complementarity: Coherent Overlap in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28308)
*Huiyuan Tian,Bonan Xu,Shijian Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper disentangles three confounded quantities in sparse MoE language models—route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interaction—using an Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI), matched-route residuals, and a prefix-controlled 2x2 factorial design. Across six MoE architectures, expert subspaces overlap substantially, yet selected experts explain token representations better than unselected rivals in every experimental cell, though the actual prefix consistently narrows this advantage. This geometric narrowing does not translate to functional redundancy: adding later experts improves next-token prediction in most frozen-route comparisons, and a controlled training study favors Top-2 over Top-1 across all seeds. The authors term this joint pattern "coherent overlap," arguing geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To clarify the geometric account of why sparse MoE models benefit from routing tokens to multiple experts, by separating often-conflated factors: route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interaction—which existing evidence fails to distinguish.

Method: The authors introduce an Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI) to measure subspace overlap, matched-route residuals to compare route quality against alternatives, and a prefix-controlled 2x2 factorial design to isolate context interaction effects. They also use frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-k training study across six MoE architectures including OLMoE, Mixtral, and DeepSeek, spanning 39 factorial cells.

Result: (1) Expert subspaces overlap substantially across all six architectures, yet actual routes explain token representations better than matched alternatives. (2) In all 39 factorial cells, the selected candidate explains more residual representation than the strongest unselected rival, but the actual prefix narrows this advantage, with all interactions negative and every 95% CI below zero. (3) Geometric narrowing does not imply functional redundancy: later experts improve next-token prediction in 24/39 frozen-route comparisons (15 inconclusive), and controlled training favors Top-2 over Top-1 in all three seeds.

Conclusion: The joint pattern of "coherent overlap" shows that routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood while useful multi-expert computation persists without disjoint linear coverage. Consequently, geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value in MoE models.

Abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models route each token to multiple experts, suggesting a geometric account of their benefit: co-selected experts should contribute distinct representation directions. Existing evidence often conflates route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interaction. We distinguish these quantities using an Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI), matched-route residuals, and a prefix-controlled $2\times2$ factorial; frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-$k$ study assess functional value. Three paired contrasts organize the findings. First, across six MoE architectures, expert subspaces overlap substantially, yet actual routes explain token representations better than matched alternatives. Second, across the 39 factorial cells in OLMoE, Mixtral, and DeepSeek, the selected candidate explains more of the residual representation than the strongest unselected rival in every cell, yet the actual prefix narrows this advantage throughout: all interactions are negative, and every 95% confidence interval lies below zero. Third, this geometric narrowing does not imply functional redundancy: adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24 of 39 frozen-route comparisons, while the other 15 estimates are inconclusive; a controlled training study also favors Top-2 over Top-1 in all three seeds. We call this joint pattern coherent overlap: routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood, while useful multi-expert computation persists without disjoint linear coverage. Separating these quantities clarifies why geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value.

</details>


### [336] [Measuring Distortion in the Empty Regions of Dimensionality Reduction Scatterplots with the Gap Index](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28324)
*Jaume Ros,Alessio Arleo,Fernando Paulovich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Gap Index (GI), a new quality metric for 2D dimensionality reduction projections that measures visual distortion in empty areas of a layout by decomposing space into empty triangles and comparing their deformation against high-dimensional counterparts. Unlike popular metrics that focus on point-to-point relationships, GI captures distortions in empty regions that have high visual impact, while being fast to compute and interpretable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing quality metrics for dimensionality reduction projections primarily capture direct relationships between points (distances or neighborhoods) but neglect distortions in empty areas of the layout, even though these empty regions often compose visually relevant features of a 2D projection. This gap limits the ability to reliably assess how confident users can be in the structures they see.

Method: The Gap Index decomposes the projection space into empty triangles, compares each triangle to its high-dimensional counterpart to compute deformation, and aggregates this per-triangle deformation into either a single scalar value or an overlay on the projection to visualize regional distortion patterns.

Result: Contrary to popular quality metrics, the Gap Index is sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact. It is also fast to compute and interpretable.

Conclusion: The Gap Index fills a gap in quality assessment by capturing visual distortion in empty areas of projections, complementing existing point-based metrics, and providing both global scalar assessment and localized visualization of distortion patterns.

Abstract: Quality metrics play a crucial role in the proper use of dimensionality reduction projections for visual analysis of high-dimensional data. They quantify the degree of distortion of a projection compared to the high-dimensional data and provide a reliable indication of how confident users can be in the structures they see in the resulting layouts. However, most popular metrics focus on capturing direct relationships between points (e.g., distances or neighborhoods) while neglecting distortions in empty areas of the layout, even though these often compose visually relevant features of a 2D layout. In this paper, we introduce the Gap Index (GI), a quality metric for 2D projections that captures visual distortion by measuring spatial distortion in empty areas of a projection. It does so by decomposing the space into empty triangles, which are then compared to their high-dimensional counterparts to compute the deformation. This per-triangle deformation can be aggregated into a single scalar value or overlaid on a projection to visualize regional distortion patterns. Results show that, contrary to popular quality metrics, the GI is sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact. It is also fast to compute and interpretable.

</details>


### [337] [Encryption-Compatible Clustered Federated Learning via Distributed Expectation-Maximization over Metadata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28338)
*Michael Ben Ali,Imen Megdiche,André Péninou,Olivier Teste*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FLAMECHE reformulates metadata-based Clustered Federated Learning as a distributed Expectation-Maximization procedure using only additive server updates, making it compatible with practical secure FL schemes and improving the privacy-communication-efficiency trade-off in the CFL trilemma.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CFL methods face a trade-off between privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency (the CFL trilemma). Metadata-based clustering approaches are communication- and computation-efficient but are incompatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms.

Method: FLAMECHE reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure, restricting server updates to additive operations while preserving efficiency. This design enables compatibility with practical secure FL schemes for encryption-compatible clustering.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios show FLAMECHE improves the effectiveness of client models and enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, enhancing its positioning within the CFL trilemma.

Conclusion: FLAMECHE successfully addresses the CFL trilemma by making metadata-based clustering compatible with privacy-preserving secure FL mechanisms through a distributed EM formulation, achieving improved client model effectiveness without sacrificing privacy, communication, or computational efficiency.

Abstract: Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) addresses data heterogeneity in federated settings by grouping clients with similar data distributions to enable effective training. Existing methods face a trade-off between privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency. We formalize this as the CFL trilemma, according to which improving two of these dimensions comes at the expense of the third. A prominent paradigm relies on metadata (i.e., low-dimensional representations of client datasets shared with the server) to enable communication- and computation-efficient clustering. However, such approaches are not compatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms. To address this limitation, we propose FLAMECHE, which reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure, restricting server updates to additive operations while preserving efficiency. This design enables compatibility with practical secure FL schemes. We conducted extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios. Results show that FLAMECHE improves the effectiveness of client models. It enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, enhancing its positioning within the CFL trilemma.

</details>


### [338] [LEDGERMIND: Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28374)
*Enjun Du,Hange Zhou,Chenxu Du,Siyi Liu,Zirong Chen,Ziyu Zheng,Yongqi Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LedgerMind is a provenance-constrained framework for multimodal agent trajectories that uses a Structured Evidence Ledger as trajectory state, enforces grounding at entity and numeric levels, and applies typed state transitions for repair—improving both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness across multimodal reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of multimodal agents for VQA reduces to final-answer accuracy, which cannot distinguish whether correct answers were reached through grounded evidence, language priors, or accidental error cancellation. Four failure patterns go undetected: unsupported intermediate reasoning, citation-backed entity hallucination (Phantom Grounding), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification.

Method: LedgerMind treats multimodal agent trajectories as provenance-constrained state machines. Tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger serving as trajectory state; reasoning and decision claims may cite only active ledger entries; grounding is checked at entity and numeric levels; repair is realized as typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance. It is augmented with a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher for matching reasoning depth to question complexity, and an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee.

Result: Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs show that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness, targeting the four recurring failure patterns that final-answer accuracy tends to obscure.

Conclusion: Provenance-constrained trajectory modeling with a structured evidence ledger yields more faithful and accurate multimodal agentic reasoning, addressing evaluation gaps left by aggregate final-answer metrics.

Abstract: Multimodal agents for visual question answering increasingly operate as multi-step trajectories that interleave perception, retrieval, and reasoning, yet evaluation still largely reduces to final-answer accuracy. This aggregate signal cannot tell whether a correct answer was reached through grounded evidence, language priors, or accidental error cancellation. We propose to treat a multimodal agent trajectory as a provenance-constrained state machine: tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger that serves as the trajectory state, downstream reasoning and decision claims may cite only active ledger entries, grounding is checked at the entity and numeric level, and repair is realized as typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance. We instantiate this design as LedgerMind (Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger), augmented by a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher that matches reasoning depth to question complexity, and an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee. We use LedgerMind to target four recurring failure patterns that final-answer accuracy tends to obscure: unsupported intermediate reasoning, citation-backed entity hallucination (Phantom Grounding), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification. Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs show that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness.

</details>


### [339] [Hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo for Order-Optimal Neural Actor-Critic in Average-Reward CMDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28390)
*Ankur Naskar,Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper resolves the bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation for average-reward Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) by introducing a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic. This leads to the first primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm with order-optimal convergence guarantees (optimality gap and constraint violation of order O~(T^{-1/2})) for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, without requiring knowledge of the mixing time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While primal-dual actor-critic methods with linear critics are well understood for CMDPs, extending order-optimal convergence guarantees to neural critics in average-reward settings has remained an open problem. The fundamental challenge is a bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation: under NTK analysis, reducing critic bias substantially increases optimization cost, which prevents achieving order-optimal convergence in the primal-dual framework.

Method: The paper introduces a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that performs debiasing simultaneously across trajectory sampling and critic optimization. This estimator achieves the bias of a long critic optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. Building on this estimator, the authors develop a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization.

Result: The proposed algorithm achieves both an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order O~(T^{-1/2}), establishing the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics. The method eliminates the need to know the underlying mixing time. The results are novel even in the unconstrained setting.

Conclusion: The hierarchical MLMC neural critic effectively decouples bias reduction from optimization cost in neural critic estimation, enabling order-optimal convergence in primal-dual methods for average-reward CMDPs. This represents a significant theoretical advancement, filling a gap that existed for neural critics in safety-constrained reinforcement learning.

Abstract: Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) provide a natural framework for reinforcement learning in safety-critical applications, where agents maximize long-term reward while satisfying long-term constraints. Although primal-dual actor-critic methods with linear critics are well understood, extending order-optimal convergence guarantees to neural critics in average-reward CMDPs has remained open. The main challenge is a fundamental bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation: under Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) analysis, reducing critic bias substantially increases critic optimization cost, preventing order-optimal convergence in the primal-dual framework. We resolve this bottleneck by introducing a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that performs debiasing simultaneously across trajectory sampling and critic optimization. The resulting estimator attains the bias of a long critic optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. Building on this estimator, we develop a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm that achieves both an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$. This establishes the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, while eliminating the need to know the underlying mixing time. Our results are novel even in the unconstrained setting.

</details>


### [340] [Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late? Decode on the Decision-Time Critical Path, Tested with Pre-Compiled Policy Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28399)
*Zihan Dong,Rui Qian,Qishi Zhan,Dongshen Peng,Kaixin Li,Yu Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AAPT eliminates decision-time decoding delays in computer-use agents by using idle screen periods to construct a bounded conditional policy tree with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines, enabling immediate execution on transient GUI events.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Computer-use agents frequently fail on transient GUI events because they generate the correct action only after the relevant window has closed. The root cause is expensive autoregressive decoding sitting on the decision-time critical path.

Method: During idle screen periods, the frozen multimodal model builds a bounded conditional policy tree with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines, sized to cover the model's own decoding latency. A lightweight observer then matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and executes the corresponding action instantly without text generation.

Result: AAPT improves success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 (p=1.8e-3) in paired trials, with no incorrect actions. Open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines achieve zero success. The effect is reproduced on an independent general-purpose model over 126 paired trials (p=4.9e-13). Ablations identify fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing as key requirements, with branch routing shown via oracle probe to be the causal bottleneck. On an external benchmark, AAPT matches reactive baseline performance with complementary strengths.

Conclusion: AAPT performs best when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, whereas reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot. The anticipatory tree-based approach is an effective latency mitigation strategy for transient GUI events.

Abstract: Computer-use agents often fail on transient GUI events because they produce the correct action only after the relevant window has already closed. We identify the main cause as expensive autoregressive decoding on the decision-time critical path. We propose Adaptive Anticipatory Policy Trees (AAPT), which eliminates this delay without modifying the underlying model. During idle screen periods, the same frozen multimodal model constructs a bounded conditional policy tree with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines. The tree is sized to cover the model's own decoding latency. When an event occurs, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and immediately executes the corresponding action without generating new text. In paired trials with pre-registered endpoints and exact McNemar tests, AAPT improves the success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 within a contested decision window ($p=1.8\times10^{-3}$), while producing no incorrect actions. Both open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines achieve zero success because they still decode during execution. A preparation-time sweep shows that the gain emerges where the latency-based tree-sizing rule predicts, and ablations reveal three key requirements: fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing. A pre-registered oracle probe rejects our initial hypothesis and instead points to branch routing as the causal bottleneck. We further reproduce the effect on an independent general-purpose multimodal model over 126 paired trials ($p=4.9\times10^{-13}$). On an external benchmark, AAPT matches the overall performance of a reactive baseline, although the two methods exhibit complementary strengths. Together, these results suggest that AAPT performs best when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, whereas reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot.

</details>


### [341] [On-Policy and Off-Policy Learning for Large Action Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28408)
*Imad Aouali*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This thesis studies policy learning in contextual bandits with very large action spaces, covering both on-policy learning (regret minimization via sequential interaction) and off-policy learning (from logged data). It proposes structured Bayesian methods (meTS and dTS) for on-policy learning and structured direct methods, concave policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives, and differentiable pessimistic regularized importance-sampling estimators for off-policy learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large action spaces in interactive systems pose fundamental challenges for both on-policy and off-policy learning, including inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes. These challenges hinder the practical deployment of contextual bandit algorithms in real-world interactive systems.

Method: On-policy: introduces meTS (mixed-effect Thompson sampling) and dTS (diffusion-inspired prior Thompson sampling) to model dependencies between actions and share information. Off-policy: proposes sDM (structured direct method) based on latent variables, introduces concave policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives that are efficiently optimizable, and develops differentiable pessimistic methods based on exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds.

Result: The proposed methods yield regret guarantees that depend on an effective number of actions rather than the full action space size. The analysis shows that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces, motivating the concave objectives. The pessimistic regularized importance-sampling estimators control the bias-variance trade-off.

Conclusion: Structured methods that exploit dependencies between actions, combined with carefully designed optimization objectives and pessimistic regularization, provide principled and efficient solutions to policy learning in large action spaces for both on-policy and off-policy settings.

Abstract: This thesis studies policy learning in interactive systems where an agent observes a context, selects an action from a very large set, and receives partial feedback. The main framework is contextual bandits, with two paradigms: on-policy learning, where the agent interacts sequentially with the environment and minimizes regret, and off-policy learning, where it learns from logged data collected by a logging policy. In large action spaces, both settings face major challenges: inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes. The first part develops structured Bayesian methods for on-policy learning. We introduce meTS, a mixed-effect extension of Thompson sampling, and dTS, which leverages diffusion-inspired priors to model dependencies between actions. These methods share information across actions and yield regret guarantees depending on an effective number of actions. The second part addresses off-policy learning. We propose sDM, a structured direct method based on latent variables, show that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces, and introduce concave, efficiently optimizable policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives. Finally, we develop differentiable pessimistic methods based on exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds to control the bias-variance trade-off of regularized importance-sampling estimators.

</details>


### [342] [QAdapt: A Noise-Adaptive Neural Pre-Decoding Framework for Quantum Error Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28422)
*Ran Miao,Rui Luo,Xiaohan Shan,Xiaoming Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QAdapt is a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction that captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, adapts to evolving noise conditions while preventing catastrophic forgetting, and forwards residual syndromes to a conventional decoder—reducing logical error rates by up to 5.79% and backend decoding latency by 9.32% on Google's Willow benchmark without target-domain fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing performance is constrained not only by physical noise but also by the latency of classical decoders processing rapidly generated syndrome data. This is worsened by strong, heterogeneous, nonstationary hardware noise and the simulation-to-hardware distribution shift that degrades fixed neural decoders.

Method: QAdapt is a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework that (1) captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data via a neural network, (2) sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while employing techniques to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, and (3) forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder for final error correction.

Result: Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations for rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt consistently reduces logical error rate relative to the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data, without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves up to 5.79% reduction in logical error rate and 9.32% reduction in backend decoding latency on the residual syndrome.

Conclusion: QAdapt provides a practical and decoder-compatible approach to improving the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise conditions.

Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) relies on quantum error correction to suppress physical errors and preserve logical information at scale. In practice, however, performance is constrained not only by physical noise but also by the latency of classical decoders processing rapidly generated syndrome data. This challenge is exacerbated by hardware noise that is strong, heterogeneous, and nonstationary, as well as by the simulation-to-hardware distribution shift that can substantially degrade fixed neural decoders. We present QAdapt, a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction. QAdapt captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder. Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations for rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt consistently reduces the logical error rate relative to the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data, without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves reductions of up to 5.79 percent in logical error rate and 9.32 percent in backend decoding latency on the residual syndrome. These results demonstrate that QAdapt provides a practical and decoder-compatible approach to improving the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise.

</details>


### [343] [Kohn-Sham Spectral Embedding on Sparse Graphs at the Nishimori Temperature for Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28428)
*V. S. Usatyuk,D. A. Sapozhnikov,S. I. Egorov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KSSE is a physics-inspired energy-based model that replaces dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding solved via a Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian on low-density parity-check graphs. It achieves 88.93% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1000 with only ~21.24M parameters using frozen EfficientNet-B4 features, outperforming Swin-L (197M) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M) while reducing model footprint by 10-30x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense CNN classifiers are computationally and parametrically expensive. The authors aim to replace them with a more efficient, physics-inspired spectral embedding approach that leverages graph structure and statistical physics (Random-Bond Ising Model, Nishimori temperature) to achieve competitive accuracy with dramatically reduced model footprint.

Method: KSSE maps pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic LDPC graphs and constructs a regularized Laplacian acting as a Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian. It solves D independent channel spectral problems in O(N log N + k²_mode N) time using FFT on circulant blocks and low-order Rayleigh refinement. Graph topology is optimized via star-domain surgery that creates local convexity around codewords while bounding residual frustration. Six theoretical results are proven including a generalized Ihara-Bass identity and frustration-bounding surgery theorem.

Result: On ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features (D=1792), KSSE achieves 88.93% Top-1 accuracy using ~21.24M parameters, outperforming Swin-L (197M, 86.4-87.3%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0-89.5%), with 10x and 30x reductions in model footprint respectively.

Conclusion: KSSE demonstrates that physics-inspired spectral graph methods can replace dense classifiers with orders of magnitude fewer parameters while maintaining or exceeding SOTA accuracy, suggesting a viable alternative paradigm for efficient classification at scale.

Abstract: We introduce Kohn--Sham Spectral Embedding (KSSE), a physics-inspired energy-based model replacing dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding evaluated at the Nishimori temperature of an associated Random-Bond Ising Model. By mapping pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check graphs and constructing a regularized Laplacian acting as a Kohn--Sham Hamiltonian, we solve $D$ independent channel spectral problems in $\mathcal{O}(N\log N + k^2_{\text{mode}} N)$ time via FFT on circulant blocks (leveraging Pontryagin self-duality of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$) and low-order Rayleigh refinement. Graph topology is optimized using \emph{star-domain surgery}: rather than destroying information-carrying codewords by removing frustrated cycles, we construct edge shifts creating local convexity around codewords while bounding residual frustration to $ρ(B_γ)\leq 1+δ$. Multi-scale fractal analysis ($D_2$ spectrum) and fractal learning-rate landscape certifies a landscape transition from rough regimes ($D_2>3$) to star-domain basins ($D_2<1$), enabling Rayleigh refinement with $k_{\text{mode}}=5$ modes. We prove six theoretical results: a generalized Ihara--Bass identity linking belief propagation to the Laplacian; trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence; additive channel separability with an explicit exchange-correlation bound; a surgery theorem bounding frustration with attractor width $Ω(1/\sqrt{d_{\min}})$; a quasi-stationarity perturbation bound; and a fixed-point convergence theorem. In a transductive protocol on ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features ($D=1792$), KSSE achieves \textbf{88.93\%} Top-1 accuracy using $\approx 21.24$M parameters, outperforming Swin-L (197M, 86.4--87.3\%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0--89.5\%) under standard inductive setups, while reducing model footprint by $10\times$ and $30\times$, respectively.

</details>


### [344] [Oracle-Budgeted Molecular Optimization with Short-Term Graph Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28437)
*Jiannan Yang,Veronika Thost,Xiang Ling,Tengfei Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces short-term graph memory, a plug-in module that uses an online graph neural surrogate to pre-screen candidate molecules before querying a limited oracle budget. It improves molecular optimization scores across multiple generators at no extra oracle cost, with gains dependent on the generator's exploration/exploitation characteristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Molecular optimization is typically constrained by a limited oracle budget, making the choice of which molecules to evaluate as important as which ones to generate. Existing methods focus on improving generation but neglect the selection strategy for oracle queries under budget constraints.

Method: The module maintains an online graph neural surrogate that pre-screens each round's candidate pool, allowing the fixed oracle budget to be spent on molecules with higher predicted utility. It is a plug-in that preserves both the generator architecture and native update rule, learning from previously evaluated molecules to prioritize subsequent queries.

Result: Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard benchmark, it improves the mean top-10 score at no extra oracle cost and never falls behind the base on any oracle. The gain extends to all four generators tested at a tight budget of 1,000 calls. Analysis shows the benefit at larger budgets correlates with how broadly the backbone searches and how effectively its native search exploits oracle feedback.

Conclusion: Surrogate-guided selection provides a simple, architecture-agnostic way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively. The paper offers evidence about which generators benefit most and explains the gain through the interaction with exploration/exploitation behavior of different backbones.

Abstract: Molecular optimization is commonly performed under a limited oracle budget, which makes deciding what to evaluate as important as deciding what to generate. We introduce short-term graph memory, a plug-in module that preserves the generator architecture and native update rule while learning from previously evaluated molecules to prioritize subsequent oracle queries. The module maintains an online graph neural surrogate that pre-screens each round's candidate pool, so the fixed oracle budget is spent on molecules with higher predicted utility. Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard molecular optimization benchmark, it improves the mean top-10 score at no extra oracle cost and never falls behind the base on any oracle; the gain extends to all four generators we tested at a tight budget of one thousand calls. We then analyze how surrogate-guided selection interacts with the exploration and exploitation behavior of different generators. Its benefit at larger budgets is consistent with two properties of the backbone: how broadly it searches, and how effectively its native search already exploits oracle feedback. We provide a simple way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively, and evidence on which generators benefit from it.

</details>


### [345] [Cybersecurity Detection Classification with Reasoning-enabled Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28460)
*Amol Khanna,Manu Nandan,Cristian Viorel Popa,Joan Pujol-Roig,Diana Bolocan,Laura Vasilie,Alexandru Apostu,Chase Helwig,Mihaela Gaman,Michael Brautbar,Edward Raff,Chase Midler,Sven Krasser*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses alert fatigue in Security Operations Centers by training a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real human-labeled Windows endpoint detections. The system combines automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, plus a separately trained calibrator that reads the full reasoning trace to estimate verdict confidence. It achieves 82.6% test accuracy, improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier at the high-confidence operating point, and shows that a finetuned 30B model outperforms frontier general-purpose models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SOCs face alert fatigue because the volume of detections exceeds staff triage capacity. Prior work using LLMs emits triage labels directly but does not train the model to reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat, limiting accuracy and calibration.

Method: The authors train a CoT reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections using a combination of automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Because CoT reasoning degrades label-token probabilities relied on by automated triage, they separately train a calibrator that reads the full reasoning trace and estimates the probability that the verdict is correct.

Result: The system reaches 82.6% test accuracy. At the high-confidence operating point governing automated triage, it improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. The calibrator is necessary—an untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero. A finetuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models.

Conclusion: Targeted training of reasoning-enabled triage models with dedicated calibration is more effective than relying on scale or general-purpose frontier models, motivating specialized fine-tuning over simply scaling up model size for SOC triage tasks.

Abstract: A major issue in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) is alert fatigue, as the number of detections reported is more than staff can triage in a given day. Prior work prompts or fine-tunes large language models (LLMs) to emit a triage label directly, but does not train them to reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat. We train a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections by combining automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. We find that CoT reasoning also degrades the label-token probabilities that automated triage relies on, so we separately train a calibrator that reads the full reasoning trace and estimates the probability that the verdict is correct. Our system reaches 82.6% test accuracy and, at the high-confidence operating point that governs automated triage, improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. We further show that the trained calibrator is necessary - an untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero - and that a finetuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models, motivating targeted training over scale.

</details>


### [346] [Stage-Replay Divergence Follows the KV Cache: Fixed-Prefix Precision Controls and Bidirectional Cache Transplantation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28495)
*Alexander Boesgaard Lorup*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper audits the stage-replay assumption in a Qwen2.5-derived LLM system, testing whether reconstructing intermediate token prefixes and continuing from a fresh prefill reproduces the retained live cache's behavior. Across matched experiments comparing live cache vs. fresh prefill in BF16/FP32, the authors find replicas are not bit-exact (166 divergent suffixes in BF16) yet accuracy differences are minimal (1 point, CI [-3.5, +5.5]). K/V cache transplantation (48 layers) makes divergent continuations follow the cache donor (24/24 and 43/43), showing that boundary K/V cache causally carries divergent trajectories while numerical precision moderates their behavioral expression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to audit the foundational assumption underlying stage-replay diagnostics: that reconstructing an intermediate token prefix and performing fresh-prefill continuation is equivalent to continuing from the original decoder state at that prefix. This matters because replay-based debugging and reproducibility tools rely on this assumption.

Method: The authors run a matched 200-item experiment comparing retained live cache with one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens, using exact replicas on both sides. They use a fixed-prefix 2x2 design holding all 200 token states constant while crossing construction (live vs. prefill) and precision (BF16 vs. FP32). They additionally perform bidirectional transplantation of all 48 key/value layers to test causality, plus a prospective bridge for incremental token-by-token caches and a saved-ledger audit.

Result: In BF16, replicas remain exact while the constructions differ on 166 suffixes and 20 correctness labels, with an accuracy difference of only one point (paired 95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). BF16 disagreements recur in the 2x2, while FP32 produces no decoded disagreement (95% Wilson upper bound 1.88%). The prospective bridge makes incremental and retained live caches bit-exact on 12/12 rows. Bidirectional K/V layer transplantation makes all tested divergent continuations follow the cache donor (24/24 and 43/43).

Conclusion: Exact-token replay can be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity. On the tested states, the boundary K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of the divergent trajectory, while numerical precision moderates its behavioral expression. This implies stage-replay diagnostics are behaviorally valid despite non-bit-exact state reconstruction.

Abstract: Stage-replay diagnostics reconstruct intermediate token prefixes and treat fresh-prefill continuation as continuation from the decoder state that originally reached the prefix. We audit that assumption at a whole reasoning-stage boundary in a Qwen2.5-derived system. A matched 200-item experiment compares retained live cache with one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens and places an exact replica on both sides. In BF16, replicas remain exact while the constructions differ on 166 suffixes and 20 correctness labels; the accuracy difference is only one point (paired 95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). A fixed-prefix 2x2 holds all 200 token states constant while crossing construction and precision. The BF16 disagreements recur, whereas FP32 produces no decoded disagreement (95% Wilson upper bound 1.88%). A prospective bridge makes token-by-token incremental and retained live caches bit-exact on 12/12 rows; an all-200 saved-ledger audit reproduces every retained trajectory and comparison fingerprint. Bidirectional transplantation of all 48 key/value layers makes every tested divergent continuation follow its cache donor, both on a selected set at the primary checkpoint (24/24) and an outcome-blind replication at a later checkpoint (43/43). Exact-token replay can therefore be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity. On the tested states, boundary K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of the divergent trajectory, while numerical precision moderates its behavioral expression.

</details>


### [347] [The Role of Causality in Algorithmic Recourse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28497)
*Srikanth Avasarala,Varun Gupta,Shahin Jabbari,Saber Salehkaleybar,Juba Ziani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formalizes algorithmic recourse through a causal performative framework, showing that recourse policies ignoring causal structure induce misaligned behavioral responses and degrade model accuracy, while causal recourse achieves stable equilibria that reduce strategic gaming incentives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing algorithmic recourse approaches focus only on flipping model predictions without accounting for whether recommended changes genuinely improve individuals' qualifications or merely enable strategic gaming of the classifier. This can degrade predictive accuracy and render recourse ineffective after model retraining.

Method: The authors formalize recourse through a causal performative framework, modeling how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model that captures feature interactions and their effect on the true label. They characterize conditions for performatively stable solutions computable via simple iterative dynamics.

Result: Experiments on semi-synthetic and real credit datasets show the causal recourse approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization while reducing the need for repeated model retraining caused by distribution shifts from strategic agent behavior.

Conclusion: Causal recourse leads to stable equilibria that reduce gaming incentives, whereas non-causal recourse policies can induce large, misaligned behavioral responses. Despite inducing a non-convex optimization problem even under convex losses, stable solutions exist and can be efficiently computed.

Abstract: Algorithmic recourse aims to provide individuals with actionable changes to improve their predicted outcomes in high-stakes classification settings, such as loan and mortgage applications. However, most existing approaches focus only on flipping a model's prediction, without accounting for whether the recommended changes lead to genuine improvement in an individual's true qualifications or merely enable strategic gaming of the classifier. Consequently, deployed recourse policies can induce behavioral responses that degrade predictive accuracy and become ineffective after model retraining.
  In this work, we formalize this failure mode through a causal performative framework for recourse. We model how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model, capturing interactions among features as well as their effect on the true label. These causal responses induce a non-convex optimization problem, even under standard convex losses. We characterize conditions under which performatively stable solutions exist and can be efficiently computed via simple iterative dynamics. Our analysis reveals that recourse policies that ignore causal structure can induce large, misaligned behavioral responses, whereas causal recourse leads to stable equilibria that reduce incentives for gaming. Experiments on both semi-synthetic and real credit datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization while reducing the need for repeated model retraining to accommodate distribution shifts caused by strategic agent behavior.

</details>


### [348] [Same Graph Cross-Task Transfer in GNNs: Protocols and Predictors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28525)
*Neelam Akula,Surbhi Kumar,Murat Kantarcioglu,Baris Coskunuzer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formalizes same-graph NC-to-LP transfer with a leakage-free protocol and finds transfer is strongly directional: NC→LP is beneficial on homophilic graphs while LP→NC is fragile, becoming positive mainly in structure-dominant regimes. It introduces the CoTask Score (CTS) for joint utility and shows homophily can guide mechanism choice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world graphs often support both node classification and link prediction over the same structure, presenting an opportunity to reuse supervision across tasks. However, existing evaluations use incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and inconsistent negative sampling, making conclusions about same-graph cross-task transfer unreliable.

Method: The authors formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and propose a leakage-free protocol that fixes node and edge splits, uses a shared message-passing graph excluding evaluated edges, and employs fixed negatives for LP. They evaluate three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS) and introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility.

Result: NC→LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP→NC is fragile and can degrade accuracy under naive representation reuse. LP→NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated. Simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can guide mechanism choice and avoid negative transfer.

Conclusion: Cross-task transfer on shared graphs is strongly directional and predictable, with NC→LP serving as reliable structural pretraining on homophilic graphs, while LP→NC requires careful regime matching. The CoTask Score and homophily-based guidance provide practical tools for deciding when to share an encoder across both tasks.

Abstract: Many real-world graphs support multiple predictive tasks over the same underlying structure, creating an opportunity to reuse supervision across node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP). However, existing evaluations often rely on incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and negative sampling rules, making conclusions about same-graph cross-task transfer unreliable. We formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and propose a leakage-free protocol that fixes node and edge splits, uses a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and employs fixed negatives for LP. Across three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS), we find that transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC $\to$ LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP $\to$ NC is fragile and can even degrade accuracy under naive representation reuse. LP $\to$ NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated, suggesting that LP acts as structural pretraining. Finally, we introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility when a shared encoder must serve both tasks, and show that simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.

</details>


### [349] [APO: Unsupervised Atomic Policy Optimization for 3D Structure Prediction of Atomic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28553)
*Shentong Mo,Yatao Bian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: APO is a fully unsupervised alignment framework for 3D atomic structure prediction that uses group-relative policy optimization with a dual-reward mechanism (eigen-decomposition-based structural mode reinforcement and thermodynamic stability enforcement) to self-correct generated structures without ground-truth labels, outperforming supervised baselines on crystal and antibody benchmarks while improving inference efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing flow-matching models for 3D atomic structure prediction rely on supervised preference learning aligned with ground-truth coordinates, which is prohibitively expensive to obtain for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins. This creates a bottleneck for structural modeling in data-scarce regimes.

Method: APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments, eliminating the need for ground-truth references. It uses a dual-reward mechanism: (i) a latent structural mode reward that reinforces dominant modes via eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (ii) a thermodynamic stability reward. The model self-corrects by identifying physically plausible configurations within sampled groups.

Result: APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines on crystal and antibody structure prediction benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art match rates and structural fidelity. It also straightens probability paths, significantly improving inference efficiency.

Conclusion: Intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy, supervised coordinate matching, suggesting unsupervised self-correcting approaches are viable and effective for 3D atomic structure prediction.

Abstract: Predicting the 3D structures of atomic systems is fundamental to advancing material science and drug discovery. While flow-matching models (, FlowDPO) have recently shown promise in this domain, their performance relies heavily on alignment with ground-truth coordinates via supervised preference learning. However, obtaining experimental labels for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins is prohibitively expensive, creating a bottleneck for structural modeling in data-scarce regimes. In this work, we propose (Atomic Policy Optimization), a fully unsupervised alignment framework that eliminates the need for ground-truth reference structures. APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments, utilizing a novel dual-reward mechanism: (i) a that reinforces the policy's dominant latent structural modes through eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (ii) a that enforces thermodynamic stability. Our framework enables the model to ``self-correct'' by identifying physically plausible configurations within sampled groups. Extensive benchmarks on crystal and antibody structure prediction demonstrate that APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines, achieving a new state-of-the-art in match rates and structural fidelity. Furthermore, we show that APO effectively straightens probability paths, significantly improving inference efficiency. Our results suggest that intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy, supervised coordinate matching.

</details>


### [350] [$β$-OPSD: Deriving with Policy Optimization, Training with Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28582)
*Jiawei Xu,Minghui Liu,Juzheng Zhang,Tom Goldstein,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: β-OPSD generalizes on-policy self-distillation by introducing a controllable KL regularization parameter β, deriving the optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between a reference policy and a privileged teacher, and implementing it efficiently via logit mixing for distillation. It improves optimization stability and reasoning performance on math benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vanilla on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is promising for improving reasoning language models but is brittle and requires substantial engineering effort. The paper identifies a structural source of this difficulty: vanilla OPSD is exactly the β=1 case of a broader policy-optimization family, where β weights the KL penalty to a reference policy. This turns β into a controllable regularization parameter, enabling a trade-off between proximity to a reference policy and privileged teacher guidance.

Method: Introduces β-OPSD, a general formulation where the optimal policy is derived in closed form as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher. Rather than optimizing the RL objective directly (which is costly and high-variance), the paper converts the closed-form solution into a distillation target. Each β value selects a target along the reference-to-teacher path, implemented by mixing token-level logits. Return-to-go credit assignment is also incorporated to align token updates with the sequence-level objective while preserving OPSD simplicity.

Result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show β-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, improving both optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance.

Conclusion: β-OPSD provides a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back, without sacrificing the efficiency that makes OPSD practical in the first place.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising approach to improve reasoning language models, but it remains brittle in practice: making it work reliably often requires substantial engineering effort. We identify a structural source of this difficulty: vanilla OPSD is precisely the $β=1$ member of a broader policy-optimization family, where $β$ weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. This equivalence turns $β$ from an implicit value fixed at one into a controllable regularization parameter, yielding a more general formulation that trades off proximity to a reference policy against privileged teacher guidance. We introduce $β$-OPSD and derive its optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher. Directly optimizing this objective with reinforcement learning, however, would be costly and high-variance. Rather than optimize the RL objective directly, we turn its closed-form solution into a distillation target. Each value of $β$ selects a target along the reference-to-teacher path, which we implement efficiently by mixing their token-level logits. In this way, inexpensive distillation approximates the solution of expensive policy optimization. Return-to-go credit assignment further aligns token updates with the sequence-level objective while retaining the simplicity of OPSD. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that $β$-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, improving optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance. Our results provide a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back without sacrificing the efficiency that makes OPSD practical.

</details>


### [351] [KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28608)
*Sparsh Roy,Samuel Girmachew,Nishita Chavan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KAISEN is a five-phase audit pipeline for subgroup fairness in clinical risk models, stress-tested to failure on a synthetic benchmark. Key findings: significance tracking depends on minimum detectable effects; threshold optimization robustly reduces equalized-odds disparity while Platt scaling does not; mechanism diagnostics fail silently under proxy misspecification; and CUSUM drift thresholds do not transfer across cohorts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical risk models show strong aggregate performance but heterogeneous error rates across patient subgroups. Audit pipelines exist to detect this, yet their components are rarely stress-tested, leaving unclear which parts can be trusted and under what conditions.

Method: The authors evaluate a five-phase audit pipeline (subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring) on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections, testing each component to the point of failure.

Result: Four findings: (i) significance correlates with axis gap only after standardizing by minimum detectable effect (rho from 0.56 to 0.78); (ii) threshold optimization improves EOD in 48/48 runs while Platt scaling is a coin flip (19/48), suggesting audits should report variance not averages; (iii) mechanism diagnostics achieve perfect classification on controlled cases but fail all 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification with no failure signal; (iv) CUSUM false alarms and missed shifts track cohort seed rather than disease, so thresholds don't transfer across cohorts.

Conclusion: Audit pipeline components have heterogeneous reliability: some (threshold-based mitigation) are robust, while others (Platt scaling, mechanism diagnostics under misspecification, CUSUM thresholds) can fail silently. Audit reports should emphasize variance and stress-testing rather than point estimates, and all results are synthetic with no claimed clinical validity.

Abstract: Clinical risk models routinely achieve strong aggregate performance while producing materially different error rates across patient subgroups. Audit pipelines have been proposed to catch this, but their components are rarely stress-tested, so it is unclear which parts of an audit can be trusted and under what conditions. We present KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline covering subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring, evaluated to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Four findings follow. (i) Significance tracks each axis's gap against its own minimum detectable effect: rank correlation between significance count and raw equalized-odds difference (EOD) across the 15 axes is rho = 0.56, rising to rho = 0.78 once EOD is standardized by that floor. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48 of 48 held-out runs (paired delta = -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]), while group-wise Platt scaling -- the better calibrator -- behaves as a coin flip on EOD (19 of 48 runs improved, 95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with mean effect near zero, so what an audit should report is the variance, not the average.
