(iii) The mechanism diagnostic classifies 144 of 144 controlled cases correctly but recovers none of 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no signal that it failed. (iv) CUSUM failures and false alarms track cohort realization far more than disease: at the reference threshold, all 27 false alarms and 7 of 8 missed shifts come from different seeds (chi-squared p = 0.002), so a threshold tuned on one cohort fails to transfer. All results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity. Code, artifacts, and scripts reproducing every number are released.

</details>

### [352] [OwlPath: Lossless Knowledge Compression for LLM Bug Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27249)
*Bo Zhang,Ren Pan,Huan Chen,Xiang Song*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: OwlPath is an OWL2 reasoning layer atop CodeGraph that encodes source code into a lossless OWL2 ontology for structural code retrieval, using tree-sitter parsing and transitive-closure SPARQL queries to help LLM-based software engineering agents resolve multi-hop code dependencies (subclass chains, transitive callers, interface implementations) with minimal context. It achieves 68.4% strict-apply rate on SWE-bench Pro, cuts token usage by 28.8% and runtime by 39.5%, and improves retrieval recall 2.06x over the CodeGraph baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based software engineering agents are constrained by limited context windows (~100K tokens) and standard retrieval models treat code as plain text, forcing agents to resolve multi-hop structural dependencies (subclass chains, transitive callers, interface implementations) through slow trial-and-error. Existing approaches fail to efficiently capture these structural relations.

Method: OwlPath encodes source code into an OWL2 ontology using tree-sitter parsing, supporting multiple languages (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, etc.). It employs two complementary modules: (1) a transitive-closure engine that fetches all structurally linked symbols via single SPARQL property-path queries; and (2) OWL-SKM, a precomputed compact 3KB summary with module trees, core APIs, and issue-related symbols that directs agents to target modules in the first query. The system is offered as a unified CLI atop CodeGraph.

Result: On 18 SWE-bench Pro instances, OwlPath achieves 68.4% strict-apply rate vs 66.7% baseline, cutting token usage by 28.8% and runtime by 39.5%. In offline retrieval over 67 instances, it improves recall 2.06x (0.464 vs 0.226) and reaches 88.1% hit rate vs 59.7%. On a 37-question structural retrieval benchmark, recall rises from 4.4% to 28.8%, with 69-80% accuracy on transitive caller and interface tasks.

Conclusion: OwlPath demonstrates that a lossless OWL2 ontology-based knowledge compression approach for code can significantly improve structural code retrieval for LLM agents, cutting token usage and runtime while improving accuracy on multi-hop dependency resolution tasks compared to plain-text retrieval baselines.

Abstract: LLM-based software engineering agents are constrained by limited context windows: roughly 100K tokens must store structurally relevant code  subsets to resolve bugs. Standard retrieval models treat code as plain text, forcing agents to resolve multi-hop dependencies including subclass  chains, transitive callers and interface implementations through slow trial and error. We tackle this limitation with lossless knowledge  compression, encoding source code into an OWL2 ontology to answer structural queries using minimal relevant code fragments.
  We present OwlPath, an OWL2 reasoning layer atop CodeGraph, a widely used code intelligence platform with 500K+ GitHub stars, offering a unified  CLI for structural code retrieval. Powered by tree-sitter parsing, OwlPath supports multi-language repositories (Python, JavaScript,  TypeScript, Go, etc.) and encodes language-specific semantics into a unified OWL2 ontology. It adopts two complementary modules. First, a  transitive-closure engine fetches all structurally linked symbols via single SPARQL property-path queries, capturing multi-hop relations missed  by string matching. Second, the OWL Software Knowledge Map (OWL-SKM) precomputes a compact 3KB summary with module trees, core APIs and  issue-related symbols, directing agents to target modules in the first query.
  Evaluated on 18 SWE-bench Pro instances, OwlPath obtains a 68.4% strict-apply rate versus 66.7% for the CodeGraph baseline, cutting token usage  by 28.8% and runtime by 39.5%. In offline retrieval tests over 67 instances, OwlPath improves recall 2.06 times (0.464 vs 0.226) and reaches  88.1% hit rate compared to CodeGraph's 59.7%. On a 37-question structural retrieval benchmark, recall rises from 4.4% to 28.8%, with 69-80%  accuracy on transitive caller and interface tasks.

</details>


### [353] [Do Context Files Help Coding Agents? A Two-Agent Ablation Study on Real Repositories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27250)
*Prakhar Khatri*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A controlled ablation study across two frontier AI coding agents (Claude Code and Codex) on 288 evaluated runs over 17 real tasks shows that persistent context files (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) do not measurably improve correctness (bounded to ≤10-15pp via equivalence testing). Failure-mode triage reveals agents fail on implementation skill—not missing repository knowledge—and a probe confirms context files never convert a near-miss to a pass. Agent-specific borderline task difficulty (Spearman rho=0.75) explains prior contradictions in single-agent studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent context files are standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, yet existing evidence for their effectiveness is contradictory. The authors aim to resolve this contradiction through a controlled, rigorous evaluation.

Method: Controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), 17 real tasks from 3 repositories (15 shared + 2 Codex-only), and 288 evaluated runs with gold-test evaluation. Includes failure-mode triage, a manipulation probe testing whether AGENTS.md converts near-misses to passes, and correlation analysis of task difficulty across agents.

Result: Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent (bounded to ≤10-15pp via equivalence testing). Failure-mode triage shows agents fail on implementation skill (feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring) rather than missing repository knowledge. A manipulation probe confirms the real AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass on either agent. Borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman rho=0.75), explaining prior contradictory findings.

Conclusion: Persistent context files provide no measurable correctness benefit for frontier coding agents; the bottleneck is implementation skill, not repository knowledge. Prior contradictions in the literature stem from single-agent studies drawing tasks from different agents' informative difficulty bands. All code, data, and analysis are released for reproducibility.

Abstract: Persistent context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) are standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, yet evidence for their effectiveness is contradictory. We present a controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), 17 real tasks from 3 repositories (15 shared + 2 Codex-only), and 288 evaluated runs with gold-test evaluation. Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent (bounded to <=10-15pp via equivalence testing). A failure-mode triage reveals why: agents fail on implementation skill---feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring---not missing repository knowledge that a context file could supply; a manipulation probe confirms the real AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass on either agent. We further show that borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman rho=0.75), offering a candidate explanation for prior contradictions: single-agent studies draw tasks from different agents' informative bands. We release all code, data, and analysis.

</details>


### [354] [AgentS4D: Benchmarking Runtime Risks across the Execution Lifecycle of LLM-Based Workspace Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27294)
*Jiajun Zhou,Zhaoxuan Ke,Jihang Ye,Xuanze Chen,Shanqing Yu,Qi Xuan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AgentS4D is a sandboxed benchmark for lifecycle-wide runtime safety evaluation of LLM-based workspace agents. It introduces a four-dimensional runtime-safety framework with six risk-entry sources, six induction strategies, nine target harms, and seven lifecycle checkpoints. The benchmark contains 328 risk-injected cases evaluated across 20 harness-LLM combinations (6,560 runs), finding that 68.0% trigger unsafe signals, 66.22% of runs are unsafe yet complete, and safety varies significantly with both configuration and how risk is introduced—demonstrating that task completion cannot establish runtime safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based workspace agent safety have advanced executable safety testing and trajectory-aware verification but fail to provide a unified account of where risks enter, how they elicit unsafe behavior, which harms they target, and where supporting evidence appears during execution. A comprehensive lifecycle-wide safety evaluation framework is needed to address this gap.

Method: The authors construct AgentS4D, a sandboxed benchmark built on a four-dimensional runtime-safety framework: six risk-entry sources, six induction strategies, and nine target harms guide case construction, while seven lifecycle checkpoints organize post-run evidence. They create 328 risk-injected cases and evaluate all 20 combinations of four harnesses (Hermes, OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and five LLM backends (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3, Qwen3.7-Plus), yielding 6,560 runs.

Result: 4,461 runs (68.0%) trigger prespecified unsafe signals. Safety varies with both harness-LLM pairing and risk introduction method. The same induction strategy behaves differently through different risk carriers, and the same target harm elicits different responses through different carriers and strategies. Notably, 4,344 runs (66.22%) are unsafe yet complete, showing task completion does not guarantee runtime safety.

Conclusion: Agent safety is configuration-dependent and risk-condition-dependent; evaluations must examine complete agent configurations across diverse risk conditions and retain evidence throughout execution. Task completion is insufficient as a safety criterion, and testing only one form of a risk can conceal important safety weaknesses.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based workspace agents execute stateful, multi-step workflows across heterogeneous resources, external tools, and persistent state. Their safety must therefore be assessed from actions, side effects, and state changes throughout execution. Although recent benchmarks have advanced executable safety testing and trajectory-aware verification, they rarely provide a unified account of where risks enter, how they elicit unsafe behavior, which harms they target, and where supporting evidence appears during execution. We introduce AgentS4D, a sandboxed benchmark for lifecycle-wide runtime safety evaluation. Its four-dimensional runtime-safety framework uses six risk-entry sources, six induction strategies, and nine target harms to guide case construction, while seven lifecycle checkpoints organize post-run evidence. AgentS4D contains 328 risk-injected cases. We evaluate all 20 combinations of four harnesses (Hermes, OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex) and five LLM backends (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3, and Qwen3.7-Plus) on these cases, yielding 6,560 runs. Overall, 4,461 runs (68.0%) trigger prespecified unsafe signals. Across the 20 configurations, the observed safety of an agent system varies with both its harness-LLM pairing and how risk is introduced. Agent systems exhibit markedly different safety behavior when the same induction strategy reaches them through different risk carriers. They also respond differently to the same target harm when it is realized through different carriers and strategies. Moreover, 4,344 runs (66.22% overall) are unsafe yet complete. Thus, task completion cannot establish runtime safety, and testing only one form of a risk can conceal important weaknesses. Evaluations should examine complete agent configurations across diverse risk conditions and retain evidence throughout execution.

</details>


### [355] [A Taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork Requirements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27302)
*Anastasia Mavridou,Hazel M. Taylor,Sandy Lozito,Louise A. Dennis,Michael Fisher,Marie Farrell*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper presents a two-level hierarchical taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements, derived from 361 requirements across 14 sources and validated via expert evaluation and an independent corpus of 448 requirements from 19 additional sources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing requirements for Human-Robot teamwork are fragmented across disparate sources with no unified framework addressing the complexities of collaborative Human-Robot tasks in safety- and mission-critical domains.

Method: The authors extracted 361 requirements from 14 cross-domain sources (academic, industrial, standards, and regulatory guidance), performed iterative classification and refinement to develop a two-level hierarchical taxonomy comprising 6 high-level categories and 21 low-level subcategories, and validated it through expert evaluation with 5 domain specialists plus a utility demonstration on an independent corpus of 448 requirements from 19 sources spanning six HRT domains.

Result: The resulting taxonomy covers six high-level categories: information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, and foundational system capabilities.

Conclusion: The HRT requirements taxonomy provides a unified framework for organizing and understanding requirements in collaborative Human-Robot teamwork, validated through expert input and demonstrated utility on independent data.

Abstract: Autonomous systems are increasingly deployed in safety- and mission-critical domains where humans and robots must operate as a team to complete complex tasks. Existing requirements for Human-Robot teamwork remain fragmented across disparate sources, with no unified framework that addresses complexities of collaborative Human-Robot tasks. We address this gap by presenting a taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements derived from analysis of (academic and industrial) literature, standards and regulatory guidance. We extracted a construction corpus of 361 requirements from 14 cross-domain sources. Through iterative classification and refinement, we develop a two-level hierarchical taxonomy comprising 6 high-level categories and 21 low-level subcategories that distinguish information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, and foundational system capabilities. We validate the taxonomy through expert evaluation with 5 domain specialists and a utility demonstration on an independently assembled corpus of 448 requirements drawn from 19 sources spanning six HRT domains.

</details>


### [356] [SIGIL: Compiling Agent Skills into Typed Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27309)
*Jayanaka Dantanarayana,Savini Kashmira,Lingjia Tang,Jason Mars*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper introduces Skill Compilation, realized in a system called SIGIL, which compiles prose skill files into executable harnesses using a typed agentic intermediate representation (AG-IR). This separates model-owned cognition from code-owned mechanism, improving procedural adherence from 56% to 86% of mandated steps, completing full procedures 2.3x more often, using 0.58x the tokens, and providing model-independent guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents acquire capabilities from prose skill files loaded into context and run via tool-calling loops. However, since skills are only described to the runtime rather than encoded in it, models re-derive control flow on every run and may skip mandated verification. Across 30 skills and two model generations, prose agents perform only 56% of steps their own skills mandate. The known remedy—hand-writing harnesses—is tedious and discards the authoring surface that made skills successful, motivating a need for automatic compilation from prose to executable structure.

Method: The paper introduces Skill Compilation, realized in SIGIL, which compiles a prose skill into an executable harness. At its core is AG-IR (agentic intermediate representation), a typed representation that separates model-owned cognition from code-owned mechanism, allowing the deterministic parts of a procedure to be enforced by code while the model retains responsibility for reasoning-heavy parts.

Result: Compiled harnesses perform 86% of mandated steps (vs. 56% for prose), complete the full procedure 2.3x more often, and require 0.58x the tokens. The guarantee is model-independent: the harness holds at 86% across two model generations while prose performance swings from 56% to 68%.

Conclusion: Skill Compilation via SIGIL effectively bridges the gap between flexible prose-based skill authoring and reliable executable harnesses, achieving significantly better procedural compliance and efficiency while decoupling performance guarantees from the underlying model.

Abstract: AI-Integrated agents increasingly acquire capability from skills: prose procedure files loaded into a model's context and run by a tool-calling loop. A skill is described to the runtime but never encoded in it, so the model re-derives its control flow on every run and may skip mandated verification. Across 30 skills and two model generations, a prose agent performs only 56% of the steps its own skill mandates, while producing artifacts that pass output checks. The remedy is known: write a harness, in which the procedure is program structure. However, hand-writing harnesses is tedious and discards the authoring surface that made skills succeed. To address this limitation, we introduce Skill Compilation, realized in SIGIL, which compiles a prose skill into an executable harness. At its center is AG-IR, a typed agentic intermediate representation separating model-owned cognition from code-owned mechanism. Compiled harnesses perform 86% of mandated steps, complete the full procedure 2.3x as often, and require 0.58x the tokens. Notably, the guarantee is model-independent: the harness holds at 86% across two model generations while prose swings from 56% to 68%.

</details>


### [357] [TrustChain-Review: A Risk-Adaptive Blockchain and Game-Theoretic Framework for Trustworthy AI-Assisted Code Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27310)
*Mohammad Naserameri*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: TrustChain-Review is a framework combining blockchain-based verifiable evidence, game-theoretic incentives, and risk-sensitive governance to support trustworthy AI-assisted code review. Simulations show full-evidence governance maximizes reputation, trust, and detection but at high cost, while a risk-adaptive configuration offers a more practical cost-efficiency balance for routine changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-assisted software development accelerates coding and review but weakens accountability—developers may submit insufficiently verified code, reviewers may approve with limited inspection, and centralized reputation records are hard to audit.

Method: The framework integrates three components: (1) a blockchain-based evidence layer for verifiable records, (2) a three-player game-theoretic model involving developers, reviewers, and the platform, and (3) a risk-sensitive governance rule that activates stronger controls when expected benefit outweighs cost. Evaluation used a controlled simulation calibrated with the Diff Quality Estimation dataset, comparing six governance configurations over 30 runs on metrics including reputation accuracy, trust convergence, malicious/superficial review detection, net platform utility, governance cost, and cost-efficiency.

Result: The full-evidence configuration achieved the strongest reputation, trust, and detection results but incurred the highest governance cost. The risk-adaptive configuration reduced cost and improved cost-efficiency by selectively applying stronger controls, though at the cost of somewhat lower trust and detection outcomes.

Conclusion: Strong evidence-based governance is best suited for high-risk or audit-sensitive changes, while selective governance provides a more practical trade-off between trustworthiness and operational cost for routine or lower-risk contributions.

Abstract: Context: AI-assisted software development can speed up coding and review, but it also makes accountability harder to establish. Developers may submit insufficiently verified code, reviewers may approve changes with limited inspection, and centralized reputation records may be difficult to audit. Objectives: This study introduces TrustChain-Review, a framework that combines verifiable evidence, strategic incentives, and risk-sensitive governance to support more trustworthy code review. Methods: The framework includes a blockchain-based evidence layer, a three-player game-theoretic model for developers, reviewers, and the platform, and a rule that applies stronger governance when the expected benefit justifies its cost. The evaluation uses a controlled simulation calibrated with the Diff Quality Estimation dataset. Six governance configurations are compared over 30 independent runs using reputation accuracy, trust convergence, malicious-review detection, superficial-review detection, net platform utility, governance cost, and cost-efficiency. Results: The full-evidence configuration produces the strongest reputation, trust, and detection results, but it also has the highest governance cost. The risk-adaptive configuration lowers this cost and improves cost-efficiency by applying stronger controls selectively, although its trust and detection results are lower than those of the full-evidence setting. Conclusion: Strong evidence-based governance is most appropriate for high-risk or audit-sensitive changes. For routine or lower-risk contributions, selective governance offers a more practical balance between trustworthiness and operational cost.

</details>


### [358] [PROGRESS: Property-Guided Regression Search for Semantic Falsification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27359)
*Davis Tocheuk Mo,Noshin Ulfat,Matthew B. Dwyer,Soneya Binta Hossain*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: PROGRESS integrates intent-driven properties from a language-model pipeline into coverage-guided search-based test generation (EvoSuite's DynaMOSA) to reach deep program states and detect semantic faults that regression-test generation misses. Evaluated on 25 large-scale Java systems, it detects 58% of current-version bugs (vs. none for regression tests) and satisfies preconditions for 70/150 hard-to-reach properties (vs. 18 for standalone jqwik), while preserving structural coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Search-based regression-test generation achieves high structural coverage but derives oracles from the system under test, so existing faults are recorded as expected behavior rather than exposed. Property-based testing provides independent semantic oracles but relies on high-quality properties and offers little guidance for reaching deep states or satisfying selective preconditions. Neither approach alone sufficiently addresses the goal of detecting real faults in complex programs.

Method: PROGRESS combines three components: (1) an intent-bearing code-context extraction step feeding a language-model pipeline that generates executable jqwik properties while minimizing implementation leakage; (2) an extension of EvoSuite's DynaMOSA with a per-property search objective and property-aware fitness function that rewards progress through preconditions and prioritizes falsifying executions; and (3) binding of property parameters to jqwik-provided generators to connect quantified inputs with evolving test sequences, steering search toward both coverage and bug detection.

Result: On 25 large-scale Java systems, PROGRESS detects 328/562 (58%) current-version bugs versus none for regression-test generation, and satisfies preconditions for 70/150 hard-to-reach properties versus 18 for standalone jqwik. Ablation studies show that documentation and caller/callee context are critical for generating valid executable properties. PROGRESS preserves structural exploration while exposing faults missed by regression-derived assertions.

Conclusion: PROGRESS demonstrates that integrating language-model-generated, intent-driven properties into coverage-guided evolutionary search effectively bridges the gap between structural coverage and semantic bug detection. The approach enables reaching deep program states and exposing faults that regression-based oracle generation fundamentally misses, without sacrificing structural exploration. A comprehensive artifact package is released.

Abstract: Search-based regression-test generation effectively explores complex program structures, yielding high structural coverage, but its oracles are derived from the system under test: faults already present are recorded as expected behavior rather than exposed. Property-based testing offers independent semantic oracles, but depends on high-quality properties and gives little guidance for reaching deep states or satisfying selective preconditions.
  We present PROGRESS (PROperty-Guided REgression Search for Semantic Falsification), integrating intent-driven properties into coverage-guided, search-based evolutionary test generation to reach deep program states and detect violations of intended behavior. PROGRESS (1) extracts intent-bearing code context and uses a language-model pipeline to generate executable jqwik properties while limiting implementation leakage; (2) extends EvoSuite's DynaMOSA with a search objective and property-aware fitness function per property, rewarding progress through preconditions and prioritizing falsifying executions; and (3) binds property parameters and uses jqwik-provided generators to connect quantified inputs to evolving test sequences, steering generation toward coverage and bug-detection goals.
  We evaluate PROGRESS on 25 large-scale Java systems against regression-test generation, standalone property-based testing, and context ablations. PROGRESS detects 328/562 current-version bugs (58%) versus none for regression-test generation, and satisfies all preconditions for 70/150 hard-to-reach properties versus 18 for standalone jqwik. Ablations show documentation and caller/callee context are key to generating valid executable properties. PROGRESS preserves structural exploration while exposing faults missed by regression-derived assertions; we release a comprehensive artifact package.

</details>


### [359] [From Backlog Items to Security Guidance: Towards Continuous Security Compliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27374)
*Ignacio García Núñez,Florian Angermeir,Fabiola Moyón Constante*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper presents an NLP-based backlog enrichment system that detects security-relevant backlog items and links them to relevant security requirements using a security-relevance classifier combined with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. The system was developed and evaluated in a large regulated enterprise, achieving F2=0.774 in-distribution classification performance, releasing a 288-item labeled dataset (Fleiss' κ=0.787), and preliminary RAG results where 12 of 24 retrieved clauses were rated ≥4/5 for relevance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Engineers in regulated domains must ensure security throughout the development lifecycle, but security requirements are rarely explicit in backlog items. Engineers must infer security relevance from brief, free-form descriptions without timely guidance on applicable requirements, making proactive security compliance difficult in continuous software engineering.

Method: The approach combines a security-relevance classifier with a four-stage retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline grounded in security requirements documents. The classifier performs security relevance detection on backlog items, while the RAG pipeline retrieves and generates relevant security requirement clauses from company-internal security policies and CIS Benchmarks.

Result: A dataset of 288 backlog items labeled by nine practitioners (Fleiss' κ=0.787) was released. The recall-oriented classifier achieved F2=0.774 in-distribution and mean zero-shot G-measure ≈0.65 across five benchmarks, matching or outperforming published classical-ML and open-source GPT baselines. In the RAG evaluation, 12 of 24 retrieved clauses received relevance ratings of at least 4/5 from two practitioners.

Conclusion: NLP-based product backlog enrichment can support engineers in identifying security requirements early in the development process, facilitating continuous security compliance through proactive introduction of security requirements in continuous software engineering workflows.

Abstract: Continuous software engineering in regulated domains requires engineering teams to address security throughout the development lifecycle. Yet making security requirements explicit in backlog items is still problematic. Engineers must instead infer security relevance of backlog items from brief, free-form descriptions and often lack timely guidance on applicable requirements. We present an NLP-based backlog enrichment system that detects security-relevant backlog items and links them to relevant security requirements. The approach combines a security-relevance classifier with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline over security requirements documents. The approach was developed and evaluated in the context of a large enterprise in highly regulated domains. We present three contributions. First, we release a dataset of 288 backlog items labeled for security relevance by nine security practitioners, with substantial agreement (Fleiss' $κ=0.787$). Second, a recall-oriented classifier achieving $F2=0.774$ in-distribution and mean zero-shot G-measure $\approx 0.65$ across five established benchmarks, matching or outperforming most published classical-ML and open-source GPT baselines. Third, we preliminarily evaluated a four-stage security requirements document-grounded RAG pipeline with two practitioners on industrial backlogs using company-internal security policies and CIS Benchmarks. Of the retrieved 24 clauses, 12 were rated at least 4/5 for relevance. Our findings provide first indicators that NLP-based product backlog enrichment can support engineers in identifying security requirements early in the development process. With this work we aim to facilitate continuous security compliance through proactive introduction of security requirements in continuous software engineering.

</details>


### [360] [SWE-NFI: Studying and Benchmarking Coding Agents for Non-Functional Improvements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27409)
*Pengyu Xue,He Yang Yuan,Xin Wang,Junkai Chen,Haonan Zhang,Boyuan Chen,Zishuo Ding,Zhenhao Li,Weiyi Shang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents SWE-NFI, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on non-functional improvements (NFIs) beyond functional correctness, containing 188 tasks from real merged pull requests with 92 executable rules. Evaluations show that even the best coding agents achieve 70% functional correctness but fall short of human developers in NFI capability, especially in structural code improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing coding agent benchmarks primarily evaluate functional correctness and provide limited support for assessing non-functional improvements, while real-world software development requires continuous quality improvements without changing observable behavior. This gap motivates the need for a dedicated benchmark for NFI evaluation.

Method: The authors construct SWE-NFI, a benchmark with 188 tasks derived from real merged pull requests in open-source Python projects. They operationalize developer-oriented NFIs into 92 executable rules and build an evaluation suite that combines functional correctness testing with rule-based NFI evaluation.

Result: The best-performing agent achieves 70.0% functional correctness, but all evaluated agents generally underperform human developers in overall NFI capability. The gap is most pronounced in structural code improvements, where agents' NFI scores range from 0.0 to 1.3 compared to 1.5 for the human reference.

Conclusion: The benchmark and findings provide a reproducible foundation for evaluating and advancing coding agents beyond functional correctness, highlighting a significant gap in agents' ability to perform non-functional improvements compared to humans.

Abstract: Although coding agents have achieved impressive performance on correctness-oriented benchmarks, their ability to make behavior-preserving non-functional improvements (NFIs) remains underexplored. In real-world software development, developers continuously improve software quality without changing observable behavior, yet existing benchmarks primarily evaluate functional correctness and provide limited support for assessing these non-functional improvements.
  In this paper, we present SWE-NFI, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on NFIs beyond functional correctness. Our benchmark contains 188 tasks constructed from real merged pull requests in open-source Python projects. We operationalize developer-oriented NFIs into 92 executable rules and develop a comprehensive evaluation suite that combines functional correctness testing with rule-based NFI evaluation.
  We evaluate state-of-the-art commercial and open-source coding agents. Although the best-performing agent achieves a 70.0\% functional correctness rate, all evaluated agents generally fall short of human developers in overall NFI capability. The gap is particularly evident for structural code improvements, where agents' NFI scores range from 0.0 to 1.3, compared with 1.5 for the human reference. Our benchmark and findings provide a reproducible foundation for evaluating and advancing coding agents beyond functional correctness.

</details>


### [361] [LimICE: Integrating LLM into ICE Framework for Efficient Loop Invariant Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27606)
*Kai Fan,ShiWen Yu,GuangSheng Fan,HaoAng Chi,WanWei Liu,Ji Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes Incremental ICE, a novel learning framework for incremental loop invariant synthesis that integrates the incremental philosophy of IC3 into the ICE learning framework. It instantiates this framework into a tool called LimICE, which uses LLMs to generate an ordered sequence of lemmas (rather than a single monolithic invariant) and employs ICE-DT as a fallback mechanism. Experiments show LimICE solves 349/367 linear and 47/50 nonlinear benchmarks, outperforming LLM-based and non-LLM baselines in both solved instances and runtime.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Loop invariant synthesis is undecidable and challenging. Existing machine learning-based methods adopt a monolithic approach that cannot strictly constrain the learning process, making it difficult to simultaneously consider all necessary conditions and generate complete invariants for complex problems. The key insight is that a loop invariant is often an ordered sequence of lemmas rather than a single formula, motivating an incremental synthesis framework.

Method: The paper integrates the incremental philosophy of IC3 into the general invariant learning framework ICE. It introduces a lemma-specific learning objective and a counterexample filtering mechanism to achieve sound incremental learning. The framework instantiates a tool, LimICE, that leverages LLMs to generate the ordered sequence of lemmas and incorporates ICE-DT (decision tree-based invariant learning) as a fallback mechanism to complement the lemma sequence.

Result: Experiments on 367 linear and 50 nonlinear benchmarks show LimICE solves 349 linear problems (avg 15.2s) and 47 nonlinear problems (avg 8.8s). Compared to the state-of-the-art LLM-based baseline, it solves 12-24% more instances while running 36-63% faster. It also consistently outperforms strong non-LLM baselines, solving at least 86 and 27 additional instances on linear and nonlinear benchmarks respectively.

Conclusion: The incremental synthesis approach for loop invariants is both sound and effective. Treating invariants as ordered sequences of lemmas, rather than a single monolithic formula, enables better coverage of all necessary conditions. Combining LLMs with decision-tree-based fallback mechanisms yields significant improvements in both effectiveness and efficiency over existing state-of-the-art methods.

Abstract: Loop invariant synthesis is a fundamental problem in program verification, yet the inherent undecidability makes it highly challenging. Recent studies have increasingly employed various machine learning techniques to generate loop invariants. However, most of these methods adopt a monolithic approach. Due to the inability to strictly constrain the learning process, learning-based methods struggle to simultaneously consider all necessary conditions and generate complete invariants when tackling complex problems. In fact, a loop invariant is often an ordered sequence of lemmas, rather than a single invariant formula. This motivates us to propose Incremental ICE, a novel learning framework for incremental synthesis. Our framework integrates the incremental philosophy of IC3 into the general invariant learning framework ICE. By defining a lemma-specific learning objective and introducing a counterexample filtering mechanism, we can achieve sound incremental learning. Under this framework, we instantiate a loop invariant synthesis tool, LimICE, which leverages LLMs to generate the ordered sequence of lemmas and incorporates ICE-DT as a fallback mechanism to complement the lemma sequence. Experiments on 367 linear benchmarks and 50 nonlinear benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. LimICE solves 349 (out of 367) linear problems on an average of 15.2 seconds and 47 (out of 50) nonlinear problems on an average of 8.8 seconds. Compared to the state-of-the-art LLM-based baseline, our approach solves 12-24% more instances while running 36-63% faster across linear and nonlinear benchmarks. LimICE also consistently outperforms strong non-LLM baselines and solves at least 86 and 27 additional instances on the linear and nonlinear benchmarks, respectively.

</details>


### [362] [Not as Sweet by Another Name: An Empirical Study of Format Robustness in LLM Document Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27648)
*Xiaoyu Zhang,Xianyun Cheng,Tianlin Li,Yuwei Zheng,Yue Yang,Yang Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes a format-aware metamorphic testing framework to evaluate the robustness of end-to-end LLM document workflows against document format variations. Through a large-scale empirical study (48,000 executions across four workflows, tasks, and formats), it reveals that format changes can cause up to 53.63% accuracy drop and decision drifts in over 41% of instances. Lightweight user-side mitigation strategies recover up to 44.21% of format-induced decision drift without model retraining, demonstrating that document format is a critical factor affecting LLM system reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing testing work focuses on robustness and reliability of LLM systems with single-prompt-string inputs, leaving an unanswered critical question: whether document-centric LLM workflows remain robust when the same semantic content arrives in different document formats (e.g., CSV). This gap is significant as LLM-driven systems are rapidly evolving from plain-text conversations to document-centric end-to-end workflows.

Method: The paper proposes a format-aware metamorphic testing framework with three metamorphic relations to comprehensively evaluate the format robustness of end-to-end LLM document workflows. A large-scale empirical study is conducted spanning four representative LLM workflows, four real-world tasks, and four document formats, totaling 48,000 workflow executions. Lightweight user-perspective mitigation strategies are also designed to recover format-induced decision drift.

Result: Format variation poses a systematic and serious threat: merely switching formats causes accuracy to drop by up to 53.63% and triggers decision drifts in over 41% of instances. The proposed mitigation strategies recover up to 44.21% of format-induced decision drift without requiring model retraining.

Conclusion: Document format is not a neutral wrapper but a critical factor affecting the reliability of LLM software systems. The findings call for corresponding testing and safeguards when deploying such systems in real-world high-stakes scenarios.

Abstract: LLM-driven software systems are rapidly evolving from plain-text conversations to document-centric end-to-end workflows, where the same semantic content can be delivered in diverse document formats (e.g., CSV) through file upload interfaces. Yet existing testing work focuses on the robustness and reliability of models and systems whose input is a single prompt string, leaving a critical question unanswered: Can these document workflows maintain robust behaviors when the same content arrives in a different document format? To fill the gap, in this paper, we propose a format-aware metamorphic testing framework with three metamorphic relations to comprehensively evaluate the format robustness of end-to-end LLM document workflows. Based on this framework, we conduct a large-scale empirical study spanning four representative LLM workflows, four real-world tasks, and four document formats, comprising a total of 48,000 workflow executions. Our findings reveal that format variation poses a systematic and serious threat. Merely switching formats can cause accuracy to drop by up to 53.63% and trigger decision drifts in over 41% of instances. We further design lightweight mitigation strategies from the users' perspective that recover up to 44.21% of format-induced decision drift without model retraining. Our study demonstrates that document format is not a neutral wrapper but a critical factor affecting the reliability of LLM software systems, calling for corresponding testing and safeguards in the deployment in real-world high-stakes scenarios.

</details>


### [363] [Can Large Language Models Resolve Real Java Merge Conflicts? An Evaluation with a Calibrated LLM-as-Judge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27674)
*Bowen Shen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper studies LLM-based merge conflict resolution on real Java conflicts from ConflictBench. It builds an LLM solver as a generate-validate-retry agent using only inference-time signals, and evaluates it with a two-metric suite: a calibrated LLM-as-judge (G-Eval) for developer-match and a deterministic structural-validity check. The judge reaches 100% precision at 64.6% recall, and LLM solvers match developer resolutions on ~55% of true conflicts, beating AutoMerge (36.7%) by 18-22 points due almost entirely to coverage. Notably, the LLM judge accepted 4 of 5 structurally invalid resolutions, showing structural checks must not be delegated to LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Merge conflicts are a recurring cost in collaborative software development. Traditional structured/semi-structured merge tools frequently abstain, leaving conflicts unresolved when their heuristics fail. LLMs can propose candidate resolutions for almost any conflict, but evaluating whether these resolutions are truly good at scale is hard because human judgments do not scale. The paper studies both problems together: building an LLM solver and a scalable evaluation methodology.

Method: The authors build an LLM-based merge conflict solver as a generate-validate-retry agent that only uses inference-time signals (conflict markers, a Java parser, duplicate-declaration checks) and never sees the developer's answer. They evaluate with two metrics: (1) a developer-match LLM-as-judge implemented as a calibrated G-Eval metric (calibrated against ConflictBench's human labels), and (2) a deterministic structural-validity check that uses no LLM. They conduct a meta-evaluation on 292 human-labeled cases.

Result: The calibrated judge reaches 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall. Under this judge, LLM solvers match the developer's resolution on about 55% of true conflicts (a conservative floor). In a coverage-fair comparison, LLMs (55-59%) beat AutoMerge (36.7%) by 18-22 points. This advantage comes almost entirely from coverage: traditional tools abstain on 20-90% of conflicts while the LLM under forced resolution abstains on none. Additionally, the LLM judge accepted 4 of the 5 resolutions that failed the deterministic structural check.

Conclusion: LLM-based solvers substantially outperform traditional merge tools due to full coverage rather than raw accuracy. A properly calibrated LLM-as-judge can provide trustworthy, conservative evaluations at scale, but structural correctness must not be delegated to LLMs since the LLM judge accepted a majority of structurally invalid resolutions—deterministic checks remain essential.

Abstract: Merge conflicts are a recurring cost of collaborative software development, and the traditional structured and semi-structured merge tools that address them frequently abstain: when their heuristics do not apply, they leave the conflict unresolved. Large language models (LLMs) can instead produce a candidate resolution for almost any conflict, but measuring whether those resolutions are actually good at scale is hard, because obtaining human desirability judgments for every model output does not scale. We study both problems together on real Java merge conflicts from ConflictBench. We first build an LLM solver as a generate-validate-retry agent that uses only inference-time signals (conflict markers, a Java parser, and duplicate-declaration checks) and never sees the developer's answer. We then evaluate its resolutions with a two-metric suite: (1) a developer-match LLM-as-judge implemented as a G-Eval metric and, crucially, calibrated against ConflictBench's human labels before use, and (2) a deterministic structural-validity check that uses no LLM. On a meta-evaluation of 292 human-labeled cases, the judge reaches 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall, so every acceptance is trustworthy and every downstream rate is a conservative lower bound. Under this validated judge, LLM solvers match the developer's own resolution on about 55% of true conflicts (conservative floor), and under a coverage-fair comparison the LLMs (55-59%) beat the strongest traditional tool (AutoMerge, 36.7%) by roughly 18-22 points; the edge comes almost entirely from coverage, not raw accuracy, since the tools abstain on 20-90% of conflicts while the LLM under forced resolution abstains on none. Finally, the LLM judge accepted 4 of the 5 resolutions that fail the deterministic structural check, evidence that structural correctness must not be delegated to an LLM.

</details>


### [364] [A comparative analysis of automated techniques for security bug report identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27893)
*Muhammad Laiq*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a comparative analysis of automated techniques for identifying security-related bug reports, evaluating traditional ML methods (Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest) and modern approaches (GPT-5.2, BERT-base, RoBERTa, SetFit) on benchmark datasets. SetFit achieves the best overall performance (F1=0.80, winning on 3 of 4 datasets), with RoBERTa as a close competitor, while GPT-5.2 performs poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The literature on automatically identifying security-related bug reports is fragmented, with studies using different techniques, baselines, and experimental setups, making it difficult to compare results and draw reliable conclusions about which approaches are most effective for practitioners.

Method: The authors conducted a comparative empirical study evaluating Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, GPT-5.2, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and SetFit (a state-of-the-art few-shot learning framework) on benchmark datasets for identifying security-related bug reports, including cross-project transfer learning experiments.

Result: SetFit achieves the best overall performance with an F1-score of 0.80, outperforming other techniques on three of four datasets. RoBERTa performs competitively, approaching SetFit in some projects. Traditional ML, especially Logistic Regression, remains a strong baseline in certain contexts. GPT-5.2 performs poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. Cross-project experiments show transfer learning helps projects with limited data but can degrade performance for projects with strong project-specific characteristics.

Conclusion: There is no one-size-fits-all solution; SetFit is the most robust choice overall, RoBERTa is a viable alternative, and traditional ML methods remain competitive in specific contexts. Practitioners should consider transfer learning benefits and risks depending on their project's data availability and specificity.

Abstract: Timely identification of security-related bug reports is essential to minimize the window of vulnerabilities in software systems. Manually screening incoming bug reports to identify security-related issues is time-consuming, error-prone, and non-scalable for large-scale software systems. Thus, a variety of automatic techniques, including traditional machine learning (ML) techniques and large language models, have been proposed to facilitate this task. However, the literature remains fragmented. Most studies introduce or optimize a particular technique and evaluate it against a limited set of baselines, often under different experimental setups. As a result, it is difficult to compare their results and draw reliable conclusions about the effectiveness of existing approaches, leaving researchers and practitioners without clear guidance on which techniques are most suitable for the task.
  To address this gap, we conducted a comparative analysis of several promising automated techniques to identify security-related bug reports using benchmark datasets. We evaluated Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, OpenAI's GPT-5.2, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and SetFit (a state-of-the-art few-shot learning framework).
  Our results indicate that SetFit achieves the best overall performance, achieving an F1-score of 0.80 and outperforming other techniques on three of the four datasets. RoBERTa performs competitively and approaches SetFit in some projects, while traditional ML techniques, particularly Logistic Regression, remain a strong baseline in certain contexts. In contrast, GPT-5.2 performs poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. In addition, cross-project experiments demonstrate that transfer learning can improve performance for projects with limited data, but may degrade results for projects with strong project-specific characteristics.

</details>


### [365] [The Case for Vibe Modeling: A Missing Step in AI-Based Trustworthy Software Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27923)
*Shalini Chakraborty,Michael Mittermaier,Judith Michael*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes "vibe modeling" as a lightweight intermediate abstraction between natural language prompts and code generation in LLM-based software development. A student survey study examines perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust, and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling across AI-assisted development scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI-based software development practices over-emphasize direct code generation from natural language prompts, while insufficiently preserving human intent and supporting reasoning about system behavior. This raises challenges related to understanding, validation, traceability, and trust in generated artifacts.

Method: The authors argue for "vibe modeling" as an intermediate representation between natural language interaction and code generation, and conduct a student survey study to explore perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust, and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling across multiple AI-assisted development scenarios.

Result: The study provides survey-based empirical evidence on how students perceive understanding, validation effort, trust, and the usefulness of vibe modeling in AI-assisted software development scenarios.

Conclusion: The findings aim to inform future studies for trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering through the adoption of vibe modeling as an intermediate abstraction layer.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate software artifacts from natural language prompts. While this enables rapid prototyping and lowers the barrier to software creation, it also introduces challenges related to understanding, validation, traceability, and trust. In this paper, we argue that current AI-based development practices focus too heavily on the direct generation of code and insufficiently on intermediate representations that preserve human intent and support reasoning about system behavior. We argue for vibe modeling as a lightweight intermediate abstraction between natural language interaction and code generation. To explore its potential, we present a student survey study that examines perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling across several AI-assisted development scenarios. Our results are intended to inform future studies for trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering via vibe modeling.

</details>


### [366] [Specification-Guided Synthesis of Deadlock-Free Communication Protocol Refinements with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27964)
*Yang Li,Ping Hou,Nobuko Yoshida*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Syntropy is a framework that combines multiparty session types (MPST) with large language models (LLMs) to synthesize protocol refinements that preserve correctness guarantees, achieving 95.6%-99.5% validity with high syntactic correctness and diverse non-trivial refinements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Protocol refinement in distributed systems is essential for safely substituting protocols while preserving correctness and compatibility. While LLMs excel at code generation, they lack mechanisms for reliable behavioral correctness, and formal approaches like MPST offer strong guarantees but limited automatic refinement support. There is a gap between these two approaches.

Method: Syntropy integrates refinement constraints directly into the LLM-driven generation process, guided by MPST specifications. This ensures that generated protocol variants inherently satisfy correctness guarantees such as deadlock freedom during synthesis.

Result: Comprehensive evaluation shows Syntropy achieves 95.6%-99.5% validity while maintaining high syntactic correctness, and produces diverse, non-trivial refinements across multiple different LLMs.

Conclusion: Syntropy demonstrates that combining formal specification (MPST) with LLM capabilities can yield reliable protocol refinement synthesis that preserves behavioral correctness while benefiting from LLM generation diversity.

Abstract: Ensuring behavioural correctness in communication protocols is a central challenge in distributed software systems, as subtle inconsistencies can lead to deadlocks. In such settings, protocol refinement - the safe substitution of a protocol that preserves correctness and compatibility with other components - is essential. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and program synthesis, yet lack mechanisms to reliably produce outputs with correct behaviour. Formal specification approaches, such as multiparty session types (MPST), offer rigorous guarantees, including deadlock freedom, but provide limited support for automatically constructing protocol refinements. In this paper, we present Syntropy, a framework for synthesising protocol refinements guided by MPST specifications and LLMs. It incorporates refinement constraints directly into the generation process, ensuring the generated variants satisfy these guarantees. Our comprehensive evaluation indicates that Syntropy achieves 95.6%-99.5% validity while maintaining high syntactic correctness, and produces diverse, non-trivial refinements across multiple LLMs.

</details>


### [367] [Advancing Awkward Arrays for High-Performance CPU and GPU Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28145)
*Ianna Osborne,Manasvi Goyal*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents recent developments in the Awkward Array GPU backend, including CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CCCL, optimized memory management, and segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays, preserving the Python programming model while significantly improving GPU throughput on irregular workloads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-energy physics analyses at HL-LHC increasingly rely on accelerator hardware, but nested and variable-length data structures in Awkward Array are difficult to accelerate on GPUs due to indirect indexing, segmented operations, and irregular memory access patterns.

Method: The paper presents CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CUDA Core Compute Libraries (CCCL), optimized memory management strategies, and segmented reduction algorithms specifically designed for ragged arrays, while preserving the existing Python programming model.

Result: Benchmark results compare CPU, CuPy, and CUDA implementations, demonstrating substantially improved GPU throughput on irregular workloads.

Conclusion: The Awkward Array GPU backend achieves significant performance gains on irregular data workloads through CUDA-accelerated implementations, with an automated validation framework ensuring correctness while maintaining the familiar Python interface.

Abstract: Awkward Array is a Python library for representing and processing nested, variable-length data that is widely used in high-energy physics. As HL-LHC analyses increasingly rely on accelerator hardware, efficient execution of irregular workloads has become essential. While dense numerical arrays map naturally to GPUs, nested and variable-length data structures remain significantly more difficult to accelerate because they require indirect indexing, segmented operations, and irregular memory access patterns. We present recent developments in the Awkward Array GPU backend, including CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CUDA Core Compute Libraries (CCCL), optimized memory management, and segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays. These developments preserve the existing Python programming model while substantially improving GPU throughput on irregular workloads. We describe the backend architecture, automated validation framework, and benchmark results comparing CPU, CuPy, and CUDA implementations.

</details>


### [368] [Integrating AI into Requirements Quality Learning in Software Engineering Education: A TPACK-Guided Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28176)
*Hansika Ekanayake Mudiyanselage,Rohan Jai Dharmaraj,Malik Abdul Sami,Zheying Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study examines a TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level requirements engineering assignment on requirements quality analysis, using a mixed-methods design (N=100; 72 submissions analyzed). Results show students used the AI selectively as analytical support rather than automation, with improvements most evident for structurally concrete quality dimensions (value articulation, testability) and mixed effects on negotiability. Students reported conditional trust, active refinement, and increased awareness of quality criteria. The findings support TPACK-guided scaffolding for responsible AI integration in RE education.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid adoption of generative AI in software engineering practice creates a need for pedagogically grounded approaches to AI integration in SE education, especially in conceptually intensive subjects like requirements engineering.

Method: Mixed-methods study (N=100; 72 submissions analyzed) examining a TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level RE assignment on requirements quality analysis, assessing how structured assignment design shaped AI use, understanding of user story quality criteria, and perceptions of AI benefits/limitations.

Result: Students used the AI tool selectively, primarily as support for analysis and evaluation rather than automation. Alignment improvements were most evident for structurally concrete quality dimensions (value articulation, testability), while negotiability showed mixed effects. Students reported conditional trust, active refinement, and increased awareness of quality criteria, alongside moderate usability challenges.

Conclusion: TPACK-guided scaffolding can align AI affordances with pedagogical goals and RE content, offering design guidance for responsible AI integration in RE education.

Abstract: The rapid adoption of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in software engineering (SE) practice creates a need for pedagogically grounded approaches to AI integration in SE education, especially in conceptually intensive subjects such as requirements engineering (RE). This study examines a TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level RE assignment on requirements quality analysis. Using a mixed-methods design (N=100; 72 submissions analysed), we examine how structured assignment design shaped students' AI use, affected their understanding of user story quality criteria, and influenced their perceptions of AI's benefits and limitations. Results show that students used the AI tool selectively, mainly as support for analysis and evaluation rather than automation. Alignment improvements were most evident for structurally concrete requirements quality dimensions, such as value articulation and testability, while negotiability showed mixed effects. Students reported conditional trust, active refinement, and increased awareness of quality criteria, alongside moderate usability challenges. The findings show that TPACK-guided scaffolding can align AI affordances with pedagogical goals and RE content, offering design guidance for responsible AI integration in RE education.

</details>


### [369] [Agentic Metaverse Services: A New As-a-Service Paradigm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28242)
*Xiaofei Xu,Quan Z. Sheng,Zhongjie Wang,Boualem Benatallah,Xiao Wang,Ruipeng Han*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper overviews the evolution of agentic services empowered by Generative AI, introducing two new concepts: Agentic Metaverse Service (AMServ) and Meta-AaaS (Agent-as-a-Service in the metaverse). It presents their forms, characteristics, principles, typical applications, and future research directions in the context of the convergence of agentic AI and the metaverse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI has shifted digital agents from conversational chatbots to agentic AI, enabling new service paradigms. Combining agentic services with the metaverse creates novel business opportunities and service forms that need systematic definition, characterization, and exploration.

Method: The paper provides a conceptual and systematic overview: it traces the evolution of GenAI-empowered agents and services, defines the roles and principles of agentic services in the metaverse, formalizes the concepts of AMServ and Meta-AaaS, showcases typical application examples, and outlines emerging trends and research directions.

Result: The paper defines AMServ as a new form of metaverse service for business processing, and Meta-AaaS as the realization approach within the metaverse environment. It articulates their forms, characteristics, principles, application examples, and identifies future research directions and development tendencies.

Conclusion: AMServ and Meta-AaaS represent a significant new paradigm at the intersection of agentic AI and the metaverse, promising substantial opportunities for human society and services in the AI era, and contributing to the growth of emerging service industries.

Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reconstructing the digital virtual world, upgrading agents through enhancing their abilities in autonomous learning, multi-modal interaction, content generation, and collaborative decision-making. In particular, the shift from conversational chatbots to agentic AI, the most recent significant technical breakthrough of GenAI, has brought a new form of services, agentic services and Agent-as-a-Service (AaaS), in which the agent's abilities are encapsulated, such as perception, decision-making, execution, collaboration, and content generation, to provide the customized agent services to users. The metaverse is a virtual ecosystem for human life, work, creation, and entertainment, supported by the new generation of digital technologies. Through combining agentic services and the metaverse, an Agentic Metaverse Service, denoted as AMServ, is produced for metaverse business processing, as a new form of metaverse service. The AaaS in the metaverse environment, denoted as Meta-AaaS, as an approach to realize AMServ, has become a new paradigm of agentic services and service computing. This paper overviews the evolution and new features of agents and services empowered by GenAI, reveals the roles and principles of agentic services in the metaverse environment, presents the forms, characteristics, and principles of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS, discusses the typical application examples of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS, and finally points out the new tendencies and research directions of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS. The AMServ and the Meta-AaaS will bring great opportunities to human society and services in the AI era, and promote the rapid development of emerging service industries in the future.

</details>


### [370] [Agentic Method for Deterministic Validation of Legacy Code Migration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28271)
*Andras Ferenczi,Jordan Docherty,Mariya Bessonov,Matthew Findlay,Krishna Lingamneni*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes "Locksmith Loop," an agentic test-synthesis method for validating COBOL-to-Java migrations. It uses two instrumented runtime environments (COBOL source and Java target) with iterative witness search and parity-preserving mutations to penetrate program branches, identifying "locked paragraphs" when routing boundaries are reached. Across three case studies (430-4,114 LOC), it achieves nearly complete coverage on open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on a production-like COBOL program, with generated Java matching COBOL under deterministic parity checks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Migrating legacy COBOL programs to Java requires extensive testing, but this is complicated by a lack of test data and difficulty validating all corner cases. A novel, deterministic validation approach is needed.

Method: A two-step process: (1) prepare two runtime environments where COBOL source and generated Java are each instrumented with mocks and executed off-mainframe on commodity hardware; (2) run an iterative agentic loop performing Witness Search over input mocks to penetrate branches, followed by parity-preserving mutations. When routing boundaries are reached, an analyzer identifies a "Locked Paragraph"—a condition preventing deeper exploration.

Result: Across three COBOL-Java case studies (two open-source programs and one internal production-like program, ranging 430-4,114 LOC), Locksmith consistently improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus, reaching nearly complete coverage on the two open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on the internal production-like COBOL program. Generated Java matched COBOL under deterministic parity checks in all accepted test cases.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates a novel approach for validating agentic coding output using a deterministic oracle, showing that the Locksmith Loop effectively addresses coverage gaps and provides reliable parity validation in legacy COBOL-to-Java migration scenarios.

Abstract: Migration of legacy COBOL programs to Java requires extensive testing to ensure correct functionality. This effort is often complicated by the lack of test data and the difficulty of validating all corner cases. In this paper we propose a novel agentic test-synthesis method, the "Locksmith Loop," which is initiated by preparing two runtime environments: the COBOL source and the generated Java target are each instrumented with mocks and executed off-mainframe on commodity hardware, then an iterative agentic loop performs Witness Search over input mocks to penetrate program branches, followed by parity-preserving mutations. When routing boundaries are reached, an analyzer identifies a Locked Paragraph: a condition preventing deeper exploration. Across three COBOL-Java case studies, spanning two open-source programs and one internal production-like COBOL program and ranging from 430 to 4,114 source lines, Locksmith consistently improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus, reaching nearly complete coverage on the two open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on the internal production-like COBOL program. The generated Java matched the COBOL reference under deterministic parity checks in all accepted test cases. Through these findings we demonstrate, to the best of our knowledge, a novel approach for validating agentic coding output using a deterministic oracle.

</details>


### [371] [From Textual Requirements to Microservice Architectures - A Comprehensive Evaluation of LLM-Based Design Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28307)
*Danyllo Albuquerque,José Renan,Guillermo Rodríguez,Guillermo Rodríguez,Emanuel Dantas,Ademar França,Mirko Perkusich,Kyller Gorgônio,Angelo Perkusich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study empirically evaluates whether OpenAI o3 can synthesize complete microservice architectures (service definitions and inter-service interactions) purely from natural-language requirements, using zero-shot (ZS) and few-shot (FS) prompting across two systems. FS prompting achieves higher F1 scores for both service identification (0.97 vs 0.79) and communication recovery (0.82 vs 0.61), and expert evaluations confirm FS outputs are more modular, coherent, and plausible. However, results are model- and context-specific from only two small systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Microservice decomposition remains largely manual and code-centric, limiting its applicability in early design stages where only textual requirements exist. While LLMs have advanced, there is limited empirical evidence on their ability to generate complete microservice architectures directly from natural-language requirements, including both service definitions and inter-service interactions.

Method: A mixed-method study using OpenAI o3 under zero-shot (ZS) and few-shot (FS) prompting across two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic), with one execution per system/condition. Architectures are evaluated via (i) structural comparison against reference architectures using precision, recall, and F1-score for service identification and communication recovery, and (ii) blinded expert assessment of correctness, completeness, modularity, and plausibility, plus open feedback synthesis.

Result: OpenAI o3 identifies services with higher agreement under FS prompting (F1 = 0.97 vs 0.79 for ZS). Communication recovery is more challenging: ZS yields dense architectures with high recall but low precision (F1 = 0.61), while FS improves agreement to F1 = 0.82 and reduces unsupported dependencies. Expert evaluation corroborates these quantitative results, with FS architectures perceived as more modular, coherent, and plausible.

Conclusion: OpenAI o3 shows potential for requirements-driven microservice synthesis when guided by exemplar (few-shot) prompting. However, findings are model- and context-specific, derived from two small systems, and do not constitute model-independent proof of general capability.

Abstract: Microservice architectures have become dominant for modernizing monolithic systems, yet identifying appropriate services remains challenging and largely manual. Existing decomposition approaches are predominantly code-centric, limiting applicability in early design stages where only textual requirements are available. Despite advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), limited empirical evidence exists on their ability to synthesize complete microservice architectures from natural-language requirements, including service definitions and inter-service interactions. This study investigates whether an LLM can bridge requirements engineering and architectural design, generating architectures solely from textual requirements and evaluating structural agreement and perceived quality of results. We conduct a mixed-method study using OpenAI o3 under zero-shot (ZS) and few-shot (FS) prompting across two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic), one execution per system/condition. Architectures are evaluated through (i) comparison with reference architectures using precision, recall, and F1-score for service identification and communication recovery, and (ii) a blinded expert assessment of correctness, completeness, modularity, and plausibility, plus open feedback synthesis. OpenAI o3 identifies services with higher agreement under FS prompting (F1 = 0.79 for ZS versus = 0.97 for FS). Communication recovery is more challenging: ZS produces dense architectures with high recall but low precision (F1 = 0.61), while FS improves agreement, reaching F1 = 0.82 and reducing unsupported dependencies. Expert evaluation corroborates these results, with FS architectures perceived as more modular, coherent, and plausible than ZS outputs. OpenAI o3 shows potential for requirements-driven synthesis when guided by exemplar prompting. Results are model- and context-specific from two small systems, not model-independent proof.

</details>


### [372] [Structural Validation of LLM-Generated Microservice Decompositions Using Source-Code Dependencies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28331)
*Daniel Silva,Renan Alves,Emanuel Dantas Filho,Ademar Sousa Neto,Mirko Perkusich,Danyllo Wagner Albuquerque,Kyller Gorgônio,Angelo Perkusich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether LLM-generated microservice decompositions preserve structural dependencies in source code. Using OpenAI o3 on PetClinic and Bookstore systems, the authors propose an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis, comparing zero-shot and few-shot prompting with TPD and TVD metrics. After normalizing for class-to-service mapping coverage, both prompting strategies achieved equivalent structural adherence (TPD: 68.0% PetClinic, 83.3% Bookstore), demonstrating that mapping coverage must be controlled to avoid methodological bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs can produce semantically plausible microservice decompositions from textual requirements, it is unclear whether these proposals preserve the structural dependencies implemented in the original source code. This paper addresses the need to evaluate the structural adherence of such decompositions to the actual codebase dependencies.

Method: The authors propose an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis. They evaluate OpenAI o3-generated microservice decompositions for the PetClinic and Bookstore systems under zero-shot and few-shot prompting conditions, measuring dependency preservation (TPD) and dependency violation (TVD). A robustness analysis is conducted to control for differences in class-to-service mapping coverage between conditions.

Result: After normalization for mapping coverage, both prompting strategies produced statistically equivalent structural adherence, with TPD values of 68.0% for PetClinic and 83.3% for Bookstore. The apparent differences between prompting strategies were attributed to methodological bias from mapping coverage discrepancies rather than genuine differences in architectural quality.

Conclusion: Structural evaluations of LLM-generated microservice decompositions should explicitly control for mapping coverage. Without such normalization, apparent differences between prompting strategies may reflect methodological artifacts rather than genuine architectural quality differences.

Abstract: Decomposing monolithic systems into microservices is a key activity in software modernization. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate semantically plausible decompositions from textual requirements, it remains unclear whether these proposals preserve the structural dependencies implemented in the source code. This paper evaluates the structural adherence of microservice decompositions generated by OpenAI o3 for the PetClinic and Bookstore systems. We propose an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis and compare zero-shot and few-shot prompting using dependency preservation (TPD) and dependency violation (TVD) metrics. A robustness analysis was conducted to control for differences in class-to-service mapping coverage. After normalization, both prompting strategies produced equivalent structural adherence, achieving TPD values of 68.0% (PetClinic) and 83.3% (Bookstore). The findings demonstrate that structural evaluations of LLM-generated decompositions should explicitly control for mapping coverage, as apparent differences between prompting strategies may otherwise reflect methodological bias rather than genuine architectural quality.

</details>


### [373] [Demystifying Solana Bots: From GitHub Blueprints to On-Chain Fingerprints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28424)
*Xiaoye Zheng,Yujing Chen,Minghao Wu,David Lo,Difan Xie,Daoyuan Wu,Xiaohu Yang,Zhiyuan Wan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a large-scale empirical study of Solana bots from two complementary views: 586 GitHub bot repositories and 200 on-chain bot addresses with over 44 million transactions. It derives an implementation-grounded taxonomy of 15 bot categories across five domains, identifies a shared five-stage operational pipeline, and uncovers systematic variations in on-chain trading behaviors across platforms and assets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
