Motivation: Despite Solana's rapid growth and the significant daily trading volume of bot transactions on decentralized exchanges (exceeding $250M in January 2026), prior research lacks a systematic understanding of what Solana bots actually implement and how these implementations manifest as observable on-chain execution fingerprints.

Method: A large-scale empirical study combining two complementary data sources: (i) static analysis of 586 bot repositories collected from GitHub, and (ii) on-chain analysis of 200 bot addresses on Solana, covering over 44 million transactions. The study derives taxonomies from implementation code and correlates them with observable on-chain behavior.

Result: The study produces an implementation-grounded taxonomy of Solana bots with 15 categories grouped into five domains (e.g., Trading Operations, MEV, On-chain Analytics), identifies a largely shared five-stage operational pipeline across bot implementations, and uncovers systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors across diverse trading platforms and assets.

Conclusion: The findings highlight future research directions for Solana bot ecosystems and provide practical recommendations for building and operating bots on the Solana blockchain.

Abstract: Solana is an emerging blockchain platform designed for high throughput and low transaction fees, making it inexpensive to submit transactions at scale and, consequently, increasing exposure to bot spamming and related financial exploitation. Solana bots are typically off-chain software systems that operate in a competitive on-chain execution environment by constructing and submitting transactions, and the bot-related transactions on the decentralized exchanges exceed 250 million dollars in daily trading volume in January 2026. Prior studies on Solana have examined system performance, smart-contract security, and specific on-chain phenomena. However, we still lack a systematic understanding of what Solana bots implement in practice and how these implementations manifest as observable on-chain execution fingerprints. To address this gap, we performed a large-scale empirical study of Solana bots from two complementary views: (i) 586 bot repositories collected from GitHub, and (ii) 200 bot addresses on Solana, with over 44 million on-chain transactions. Our study derives an implementation-grounded taxonomy of Solana bots comprising 15 categories grouped into five domains (e.g., Trading Operations, MEV, and On-chain Analytics), identifies a largely shared five-stage operational pipeline manifested in bot implementations, and uncovers systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors of Solana bots across diverse trading platforms and assets. Based on our findings, we highlight future research directions, and provide recommendations for building and operating bots on the Solana blockchain.

</details>


### [374] [Emerging Challenges in Threat Modeling for GenAI-Augmented Systems: A View from the Trenches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28431)
*Nicolás E. Díaz Ferreyra,Manish Mahesh Kumar,Nohemí Villarreal,Pankaj Pantel,Immo Brueggemann,Riccardo Scandariato*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents an exploratory assessment of GenAI-aware threat modeling methods in an SME context, comparing three shortlisted techniques on an industrial GenAI-augmented system and finding gaps in coverage of supply chain and human-centered security risks, along with practitioner feedback on usability and integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional threat modeling methods like STRIDE are insufficient for assessing emerging GenAI-specific risks, yet there is limited understanding of how GenAI-aware alternatives perform in real-world settings, particularly in resource-constrained SME environments.

Method: The authors conducted a rapid literature review to select relevant GenAI-aware threat modeling techniques, shortlisted three methods, and systematically applied them to an industrial case study of a GenAI-augmented system within an SME. Practitioner perceptions on usability and integration were also gathered.

Result: The assessment revealed differences in threat identification across the three techniques and highlighted limited coverage of certain GenAI-specific risk categories, notably software supply chain risks and human-centered security issues. Practitioner feedback indicated usability concerns and adoption challenges in SME development workflows.

Conclusion: Current GenAI-aware threat modeling methods show promise but exhibit gaps in addressing key GenAI-specific risk categories, and their practical adoption in SMEs faces usability and integration barriers that need to be addressed.

Abstract: Threat modeling remains a central task in secure software engineering, as it enables the identification of security issues from system architectures. As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly pervasive across software systems, traditional threat modeling methods (e.g., STRIDE) are insufficient to assess emerging GenAI-specific risks. In this work, we present the first results from an exploratory assessment of GenAI-aware threat modeling methods in a Small and Medium Enterprise (SME) setting. For this, we conducted a rapid literature review to select relevant techniques and systematically applied three shortlisted methods to an industrial case study involving a GenAI-augmented system. The results highlight differences in the threats identified by each technique and reveal limited support for certain GenAI-specific risk categories, particularly those related to software supply chains and human-centered security issues. We further report practitioners' perceptions of the usability and integration of these methods in SME development workflows, including their perceived effort and adoption challenges.

</details>


### [375] [CoGate: Confidence-Gated Co-Decoding for Secure Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28529)
*Minghao Hu,Lannan Luo,Allen Roush,Phillip Howard*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CoGate is a confidence-gated co-decoding approach that controls the security expert model's influence during decoding-time code generation steering based on its confidence, improving secure code generation over existing co-decoding methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing co-decoding approaches for secure code generation do not account for the security expert model's confidence. When the expert encounters unseen patterns or out-of-distribution contexts, its guidance can be misleading, leading to insecure code outputs.

Method: CoGate gates the expert model's influence on the co-decoding process based on its confidence. Instead of naively combining the target and expert models at every decoding step, CoGate modulates the expert's contribution according to how confident the expert is in its guidance.

Result: CoGate outperforms existing co-decoding methods (CoSec+) across multiple benchmarks, achieving up to a 12.6% gain of Func-Sec@10 on CWEval. It was evaluated across multiple LLM backends including CodeGen, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen-Coder, and StarCoder on HumanEval, security suite, and CWEval benchmarks.

Conclusion: Confidence-gating the expert model's influence during co-decoding is an effective strategy for improving secure code generation, particularly when the expert may be uncertain due to out-of-distribution contexts or unseen patterns.

Abstract: Large language models are widely used for code generation, but they can also produce insecure programs due to patterns learned from their pretraining data. Decoding-time steering has become an important solution to this problem: a small expert model is combined with the target model at each step to generate more secure code, which is referred to as co-decoding. However, the acceptance rule for existing co-decoding approaches does not consider the expert model's confidence. When the security expert is unconfident due to unseen patterns or out-of-distribution (OOD) contexts, its guidance can therefore be misleading. To address the challenge, we propose CoGate, a confidence-gated co-decoding approach that controls the expert's influence on the co-decoding process based on its confidence. We implement our approach and evaluate it across multiple LLM backends (CodeGen, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen-Coder, StarCoder) on several code generation benchmarks (HumanEval, security suite, and CWEval). Our approach outperforms existing co-decoding methods (CoSec+) across multiple benchmarks, achieving up to a 12.6% gain of Func-Sec@10 on CWEval.

</details>


### [376] [PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28587)
*Manyi Wang,Junjielong Xu,Pinjia He*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper studies misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks, finding 13.6% of SWE-bench Verified instances are misaligned across five patterns and eleven scenarios. It proposes PAIChecker, a multi-agent system for detecting PR-Issue misalignment using a three-phase design (pattern identification, cross-agent label synthesis, and code-level validation), achieving up to 92.12% and 91.67% binary accuracy on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SWE-bench-like benchmarks are widely used but their PR-Issue pairings are often misaligned due to the complexity of large repositories, undermining benchmark validity. Reliable and scalable construction of such benchmarks requires automatic detection of these misalignments.

Method: The authors systematically analyze SWE-bench Verified instances and identify five misalignment patterns across eleven fine-grained scenarios. They propose PAIChecker, a multi-agent system with a three-phase design: specific pattern identification, cross-agent label synthesis, and code-level validation, enabling accurate, generalizable, and progressively verified detection.

Result: Experiments on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual show PAIChecker achieves the best performance across all four LLM backbones, with up to 92.12% and 91.67% binary accuracy respectively.

Conclusion: PAIChecker provides a reliable and scalable solution for detecting PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks, improving benchmark quality and enabling more trustworthy evaluation of LLM issue resolution capabilities.

Abstract: SWE-bench-like benchmarks are widely used for evaluating LLM's issue resolution capability. They typically follow a common construction pipeline: each PR (Pull Request) is paired with its linked issue by extracting issue references from the PR description; the issue description is used as the problem statement, and the PR patch serves as the test oracle. However, due to the inherent complexity of developing and maintaining large repositories, such PR-Issue pairings are often misaligned in practice. In this work, we systematically study SWE-bench Verified instances, finding that 13.6% exhibit misalignment across five patterns in eleven fine-grained scenarios. To enable reliable and scalable construction of those benchmarks in the future, we propose PAIChecker, a multi-agent system for checking PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks. Specifically, PAIChecker adopts a three-phase design that combines specific pattern identification, cross-agent label synthesis, and code-level validation, thereby enabling more accurate, generalizable, and progressively verified detection. Experiments on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual show that PAIchecker achieves the best performance across all four LLM backbones, reaching up to 92.12% and 91.67% binary accuracy, respectively.

</details>


### [377] [Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28591)
*Haomin Qi,Xingliang Wang,Xuanqi Gao,Baihui Sang,Xin Zhang,Minghua Ma,Pengfei Gao,Yu Kang,Qingwei Lin,Saravan Rajmohan,Dongmei Zhang,Qi Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Change2Task converts merged pull requests from repository history into verified coding agent tasks on modern, healthy repository revisions. It reconstructs task states via Patch Reversal, Code Mapping, or Agent Reconstruction, and validates the task lifecycle from base state to task state and back. Motivation: Scaling coding agents requires a continuous supply of executable training and evaluation data, where each task couples a realistic software state with specifications, development tools, and reliable verification. Existing sources are limited, so there is a need to expand the supply of such verified task data.

Method: Change2Task is a system grounded in repository history that converts merged pull requests into verified tasks on healthy modern revisions of the same repository. It aligns historical evidence with evolved code, reconstructs task states using three strategies (Patch Reversal, Code Mapping, or Agent Reconstruction), and validates the full lifecycle from a healthy base to a task state and back to a restored state.

Result: Across five task families (Bug Fix, Feature Addition, Test Generation, API Migration, Security Repair), starting from 1,130 eligible source changes, Change2Task achieves 79.6% verified task construction success. It recovers 29.2% more verified tasks than a pull-request-based baseline on matched candidates. Historical and reconstructed cases reach up to 98.0% matched outcome agreement under agent evaluation, and reuse of modern bases reduces measured pipeline expenditure by 10.8%.

Conclusion: Change2Task demonstrates a scalable, repository-history-driven approach for producing verified, executable coding agent tasks from merged pull requests. It reduces environment setup, storage, and task construction overhead while providing high-quality task data for coding agent training and evaluation across multiple task families.

Abstract: Scaling coding agents requires a continuing supply of executable data for training, benchmarking, and continuous evaluation. Each task must couple a realistic software state with a specification, development tools, and reliable verification. To expand this supply, we present Change2Task, a system grounded in repository history that converts merged pull requests into verified tasks on healthy modern revisions of the same repository. It aligns historical evidence with evolved code, reconstructs task states through Patch Reversal, Code Mapping, or Agent Reconstruction, and validates the lifecycle from a healthy base to a task state and a restored state. By deriving multiple tasks grounded in developer evidence from maintained environments, Change2Task provides executable data for coding agent training and evaluation while reducing repeated environment setup, storage, and task construction effort. We evaluate the system through five common and widely adopted coding agent task families: Bug Fix, Feature Addition, Test Generation, Application Programming Interface Migration, and Security Repair. Starting from 1,130 source changes eligible for construction, Change2Task achieves 79.6% verified task construction success across these task families. On a matched candidate set, it recovers 29.2% more verified tasks than a construction baseline based on pull requests. Historical and reconstructed cases achieve up to 98.0% matched outcome agreement under agent evaluation, while reuse of modern bases reduces measured expenditure across the complete pipeline by 10.8%.
